NAMES.name: vertical_ion_momentum_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short:
Effective vertical convection velocity that advects a chosen component of
ion momentum density for a specified ion species, represented as the
density-weighted mean over all charge states. The vertical label names the
velocity direction, not the transported momentum component.
NAMES.long:
The vertical ion momentum convection velocity is the vertical effective
velocity that advects a chosen component of ion momentum density for a
specified ion species. The vertical direction is the $Z$ projection in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius,
$\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; the vertical label
names the velocity direction, not the transported momentum component.
Because this is an intensive species-level quantity, it is the
density-weighted mean over all charge states of that species.

The vertical convective flux density of an ion-momentum component is
represented by:

$$
\Gamma^{\mathrm{conv}}_{p_{i,a},Z} = p_{i,a}\,V_{i,\mathrm{mom,conv},Z}
$$

where $p_{i,a}=n_i m_i u_{i,a}$ is the ion momentum density associated with
ion flow component $u_{i,a}$, $n_i$ is the ion density, $m_i$ is the ion
mass, $a$ labels the momentum component being transported,
$V_{i,\mathrm{mom,conv},Z}$ is the vertical ion momentum convection
velocity, and $\Gamma^{\mathrm{conv}}_{p_{i,a},Z}$ is the corresponding
vertical convective flux density of that momentum component.

This quantity is the convective coefficient multiplying local ion momentum
density; it excludes diffusive viscosity, residual stress, and explicit
momentum sources. It is not generally identical to the bulk [vertical ion
velocity](name:vertical_ion_velocity), because it characterizes transport of
momentum density rather than the mean particle flow. The unprojected
coefficient is [ion momentum convection
velocity](name:ion_momentum_convection_velocity); other projections specify
their own directions.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the effective convection carries the selected
ion momentum density toward increasing vertical height $Z$ in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Component along the height axis, one scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.
sources.parent_definition: Momentum effective convection, on various grid subsets

NAMES.name: vertical_total_current_density
NAMES.short:
Vertical total current density is the net conventional electric-charge flux
per unit area along the toroidal symmetry axis, summed algebraically over
all included contributions.
NAMES.long:
Vertical total current density is the signed projection of the total
electric-current-density vector along the toroidal symmetry axis. It
represents net local charge transport in the vertical direction.

The projection and algebraic aggregation are defined by:

$$
j_{\mathrm{tot},Z} = \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{tot}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}} = \sum_a \mathbf{j}_a\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}}
$$

where $j_{\mathrm{tot},Z}$ is the vertical total current density,
$\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total current-density vector,
$\mathbf{j}_a$ is an included current-density contribution, and $a$ labels
contributions in the decomposition of the total. The unit vector
$\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ points along increasing vertical height in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius,
$\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

In the edge plasma, all included contributions are summed algebraically, so
oppositely directed contributions can cancel. The quantity is not species-
or mechanism-resolved, and it is neither a vector magnitude, a surface
average, nor an area-integrated current.

This quantity specializes [total current
density](name:total_current_density) by fixing its common signed projection
basis to the vertical direction. It is a component of [current
density](name:current_density), distinct from [radial total current
density](name:radial_total_current_density), which describes charge
transport along increasing major radius, and [toroidal total current
density](name:toroidal_total_current_density), which describes transport
around the symmetry axis.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when net conventional electric charge flows in the
direction of increasing vertical height $Z$.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_neutral_temperature
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short:
Volume-averaged neutral temperature is the translational kinetic
temperature, expressed as energy per particle, of a neutral population
throughout the plasma volume inside the last closed magnetic flux surface
during plasma initiation.
NAMES.long:
Volume-averaged neutral temperature is the translational kinetic temperature
of a neutral population during plasma initiation, representing random
translational energy after removal of mean flow. It excludes energy stored
in internal excitation or other internal quantum states.

The volume average is defined by

$$
\overline{T}_{n} = \frac{1}{V_{\mathrm{LCFS}}}\int_{V_{\mathrm{LCFS}}} T_n(\mathbf{x})\,\mathrm{d}V
$$

where $\overline{T}_{n}$ is the volume-averaged neutral temperature,
$T_n(\mathbf{x})$ is the local translational kinetic temperature of the
neutral population at position $\mathbf{x}$, $V_{\mathrm{LCFS}}$ is the
plasma volume enclosed by the last closed magnetic flux surface, and
$\mathrm{d}V$ is the differential physical-volume element.

The quantity applies to the represented neutral population throughout the
volume enclosed by the last closed magnetic flux surface during plasma
initiation. Its aggregation convention is an arithmetic spatial volume
average of the local temperature, not a local value or a density-weighted
particle average. It does not select only the cold or energetic neutral
component and is not restricted to a particular internal quantum state.

This quantity is obtained by applying the volume-averaging transformation to
[neutral temperature](name:neutral_temperature), with the local population
and state aggregation inherited from that quantity. [Cold neutral
temperature](name:cold_neutral_temperature) and [hot neutral
temperature](name:hot_neutral_temperature_at_plasma_boundary) are
population-restricted alternatives, while [neutral internal state
temperature](name:neutral_internal_state_temperature) resolves a specified
internal state rather than the generic neutral population.

sources.leaf_definition: Volume averaged temperature of this neutral species (averaged over the plasma volume up to the LCFS)
sources.parent_definition: Quantities related to the different neutral species

NAMES.name: calibration_polarization_angle_of_optical_element
NAMES.short:
Calibration polarization angle of an optical element is the signed angle
from a reference transverse polarization direction to the element's selected
polarization axis, viewed along its line of sight toward the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Calibration polarization angle of an optical element is the orientation
angle of the polarization-selective axis of that element in the plane
perpendicular to its line of sight. It identifies the electric-field
component selected by the element relative to a defined transverse reference
direction.

The signed angle is defined by

$$
\alpha_\mathrm{cal} = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left[-\hat{\ell}\cdot\left(\hat{e}_\mathrm{ref}\times\hat{e}_\mathrm{sel}\right),\ \hat{e}_\mathrm{ref}\cdot\hat{e}_\mathrm{sel}\right]
$$

where $\hat{\ell}$ is the line-of-sight unit vector directed from the
optical element toward the plasma, $\hat{e}_\mathrm{ref}$ is the reference
polarization unit vector in the plane normal to $\hat{\ell}$, and
$\hat{e}_\mathrm{sel}$ is the selected polarization-axis unit vector in the
same transverse plane.

This quantity is an axis-alignment calibration parameter, not a measure of
polarization ellipticity, polarization purity, or the handedness of a full
polarization state.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the selected polarization axis is rotated
counter-clockwise from the reference transverse polarization direction as
seen looking from the optical element toward the plasma along the line of
sight.

sources.leaf_definition: Alignment angle of the polarizer in the (x1,x2) plane. Electric fields parallel to the polarizer angle will be reflected. The angle is defined with respect to the x1 unit vector, positive in the counter-clockwise direction when looking towards the plasma
sources.parent_definition: Set of polarizers placed in front of the diagnostic (if any). Polarizers are assumed to be orthogonal to the line of sight, so that the x3 unit vector is aligned with the line of sight

NAMES.name: electron_number_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Free-electron column abundance associated with an electromagnetic
propagation path, before a narrower line, chord, or complete-path qualifier
is fixed. It counts unbound electrons accumulated by a path integral, not a
local volume density or a path-averaged density.
NAMES.long:
Electron number density for electromagnetic-wave propagation is the
path-accumulated abundance of free electrons associated with a specified
propagation path. It represents unbound-electron population in a column
along that path, rather than a charge-weighted, mass-weighted, or
energy-weighted density.

For an electromagnetic propagation path $\mathcal{C}$, the parent column
quantity is defined by

$$
N_e[\mathcal{C}] = \int_{\mathcal{C}} n_e(\mathbf{r}(l))\,dl
$$

where $N_e[\mathcal{C}]$ is the electron number density as a path-column
quantity, $\mathcal{C}$ is the propagation path or path portion specified by
the more specific quantity, $n_e(\mathbf{r}(l))$ is the local [free-electron
number density](name:electron_density) at position $\mathbf{r}(l)$,
$\mathbf{r}(l)$ is position along the path, $l$ is path distance, and $dl$
is the differential path length.

The scope is free electrons accumulated along an electromagnetic propagation
path. The aggregation convention at this parent level is path-column
accumulation; the parent does not itself fix a complete-path, one-way,
return-path, chord-specific, or normalized convention. Bound electrons,
ions, neutral particles, local volume density, path-averaged density, volume
integrals, and charge-weighted densities are excluded.

The [line-integrated electron number
density](name:line_integrated_electron_number_density) specializes this
parent by fixing a line-integration path convention. The parent supplies the
free-electron population and column-accumulation semantics, while the child
supplies the additional path qualifier. The [line-averaged electron
density](name:line_averaged_electron_density) is the corresponding path
average and is obtained only after dividing the column quantity by the total
path length for the same chosen path.

NAMES.name: initial_spun_twist_phase_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor
NAMES.short:
Initial azimuthal phase specifying the starting orientation of the spun
fiber’s polarization axis along a fiber-optic current sensor.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the azimuthal orientation of the spun fiber’s polarization
axis at the starting end of a fiber-optic current sensor. It specifies the
initial state for polarization evolution along the sensing fiber.

$$
\theta_0 = \theta(s=0)
$$

where $\theta_0$ is the initial spun twist phase, $\theta(s)$ is the
polarization-axis azimuth at position $s$ along the fiber centerline, and
$s=0$ denotes the starting end.

This is an intrinsic fiber-frame orientation parameter, not the temporal
phase of an electromagnetic wave. The phase variation along the fiber is
characterized separately by the [twist period of the fiber-optic current
sensor](name:twist_period_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor); the zero and
positive angular sense follow the defined local polarization-frame
convention.

sources.parent_definition: Intrinsic properties of the fibre installed on the vacuum vessel

NAMES.name: launched_wave_duration
NAMES.short:
Duration of a single frequency sweep during which a probing electromagnetic
wave is launched.
NAMES.long:
Launched wave duration is the time interval of one complete swept-frequency
launch of a probing electromagnetic wave. It is defined by the start and end
times of the same launched-wave sweep, independent of how any received
signal is analyzed.

For a sweep beginning at $t_{\mathrm{start}}$ and ending at
$t_{\mathrm{end}}$, the launched wave duration is:

$$
\Delta t_{\mathrm{lw}} = t_{\mathrm{end}} - t_{\mathrm{start}}
$$

where $\Delta t_{\mathrm{lw}}$ is the launched wave duration, and
$t_{\mathrm{start}}$ and $t_{\mathrm{end}}$ are the sweep start and end
times, all measured in seconds.

The corresponding launched frequency during this interval is described by
launched_wave_frequency. This quantity specifies only the duration of the
complete sweep; it does not define the detailed frequency waveform, dwell
time at individual frequencies, received-wave interval, or signal-analysis
interval.

sources.leaf_definition: Duration of a sweep
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels, e.g. different reception antennas or frequency bandwidths of the reflectometer

NAMES.name: length_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor
NAMES.short:
Total physical arclength of the optical fiber centerline in a fiber-optic
current sensor, defining its optical propagation distance and distributed
magneto-optic interaction length.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the total arclength of the optical fiber centerline forming
the fiber-optic current sensor. It includes the complete winding path and is
not the straight-line distance between endpoints or the length of the sensor
outline.

For a centerline parameterized by an arbitrary parameter $u$, the fiber
length is defined by

$$
L = \int_{u_0}^{u_1} \left|\frac{d\mathbf{r}}{du}\right|\,du
$$

where $L$ is the total fiber arclength, $\mathbf{r}(u)$ is the centerline
position, and $u_0$ and $u_1$ delimit the fiber path. The length sets the
optical propagation distance; accumulated Faraday rotation additionally
depends on the magnetic-field projection along the winding and the [Verdet
constant](name:verdet_constant_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor).

NAMES.name: length_of_interferometer_beam
NAMES.short:
Length of an interferometer beam is the signed beam-level optical
path-length difference produced by plasma, relative to the corresponding
no-plasma reference for the same interferometer beam. It denotes the
family-level interferometric length signal, not the unperturbed geometric
beam length.
NAMES.long:
Length of an interferometer beam is the signed optical path-length
difference assigned to a complete interferometer beam by comparing
propagation through plasma with the corresponding no-plasma reference for
that same beam. It is a beam-level interferometric length quantity, not the
geometric length of the beam trajectory.

For a beam $b$, the quantity is defined as the difference between the plasma
and reference effective optical path lengths:

$$
\Delta L_b = L_{\mathrm{eff},b} - L_{\mathrm{ref},b}
$$

where $\Delta L_b$ is the length of the interferometer beam,
$L_{\mathrm{eff},b}$ is the effective optical path length for beam $b$ with
plasma present, and $L_{\mathrm{ref},b}$ is the corresponding no-plasma
reference effective optical path length for the same beam.

The scope is the complete interferometer beam path, with the plasma
contribution accumulated over that beam as a whole. This quantity excludes
local refractive-index perturbation, phase shift, line-integrated density,
absolute effective optical path length, and unperturbed geometric path
length.

The more specific [length variation of interferometer
beam](name:length_variation_of_interferometer_beam) uses variation
terminology for this same signed difference relative to the reference path;
this entry is the parent family quantity for interferometer-beam optical
path-length changes.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the effective optical path length with plasma
present is greater than the corresponding no-plasma reference effective
optical path length.

NAMES.name: length_variation_of_interferometer_beam
NAMES.short:
Signed plasma-induced change in the effective optical path accumulated along
an interferometer beam relative to its corresponding no-plasma reference
path.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed plasma-induced change in effective optical path
length accumulated along an electromagnetic propagation path represented by
an interferometer beam. It describes an optical delay or advance caused by
the plasma, rather than the unperturbed geometric path length.

The variation is defined as

$$
\Delta L = L_{\mathrm{plasma}} - L_{\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $\Delta L$ is the optical path-length variation, $L_{\mathrm{plasma}}$
is the effective optical path along the beam in the presence of plasma, and
$L_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the corresponding effective path without plasma.

This quantity applies to the net change accumulated along the interferometer
beam's complete line of sight. It is a path-integrated optical quantity, not
a local path-length density, an unperturbed geometric length, or a separate
phase-calibration coefficient. As the variation of [length of an
interferometer beam](name:length_of_interferometer_beam), it expresses the
plasma-induced departure from the reference path. The associated phase shift
provides the optical information used to derive [line-integrated electron
number density](name:line_integrated_electron_number_density).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the plasma-affected effective optical path
length exceeds the corresponding no-plasma reference path.

NAMES.name: line_integrated_electron_number_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Line-integrated electron number density is the free-electron column
abundance along the complete propagation path, including forward and return
segments when present.
NAMES.long:
Line-integrated electron number density counts free electrons accumulated
along the complete electromagnetic-wave propagation path. It is the
complete-path specialization of [electron number
density](name:electron_number_density).

The defining line integral is

$$\int_0^L f\,dl$$

where $N_e$ is the free-electron column abundance, $n_e$ is the local
free-electron number density, $l$ is distance along the propagation path,
and $L$ is the total path length.

For reflected paths, forward and return segments both contribute, without a
factor-of-two correction. Electrons bound in atoms, molecules, or ions are
excluded.

This quantity is neither a local volume density nor the [line-averaged
electron density](name:line_averaged_electron_density), which divides the
corresponding line integral by the length of its averaging path.

NAMES.name: normalized_fluctuating_electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Normalized fluctuating electron density is the electron-density fluctuation
level given by the fluctuation amplitude divided by a reference electron
density. It represents the relative amplitude dn_e/n_e, not a signed
instantaneous perturbation.
NAMES.long:
Normalized fluctuating electron density is the relative amplitude level of
fluctuations in [electron density](name:electron_density). It is formed from
the amplitude of the fluctuating component of electron density and the
reference electron density about which that fluctuation is defined.

The normalized fluctuation level is defined by

$$
\left(\frac{\delta n_e}{n_e}\right)_\mathrm{amp} = \frac{A[\tilde n_e]}{n_{e,\mathrm{ref}}}
$$

where $A[\tilde n_e]$ is the amplitude measure of the fluctuating component
of [electron density](name:electron_density), and $n_{e,\mathrm{ref}}$ is
the reference [electron density](name:electron_density) for the same plasma
region and fluctuation definition.

This is an amplitude-level quantity: $A[\tilde n_e]$ is non-negative and may
represent the explicitly defined rms, spectral, envelope, or other
fluctuation amplitude convention. It is distinct from the signed
instantaneous fractional perturbation $\tilde n_e/n_{e,\mathrm{ref}}$.

NAMES.name: polarization_ellipticity_of_polarimeter_beam
NAMES.short:
Signed ratio of the minor to major semiaxes of the polarization ellipse of a
polarimeter beam after propagation through magnetized plasma. It describes
the beam's post-propagation transverse polarization state, not the incident
state or the ellipse orientation.
NAMES.long:
Signed ratio of the minor to major semiaxes of the polarization ellipse of a
polarimeter beam after propagation through magnetized plasma is the
ellipticity of that beam. It characterizes the relative electric-field
semiamplitudes of the post-propagation transverse polarization ellipse.

The ellipticity is defined by

$$
\varepsilon = \frac{b}{a}
$$

where $\varepsilon$ is the polarization ellipticity, $a$ is the major-axis
semiamplitude of the electric-field polarization ellipse, and $b$ is the
signed minor-axis semiamplitude of that ellipse. The magnitude satisfies
$|\varepsilon| \leq 1$.

This quantity applies to the polarimeter beam after it has traversed the
magnetized plasma and is therefore distinct from the [initial polarization
ellipticity](name:initial_polarization_ellipticity_of_polarimeter_beam). It
is a polarization-shape parameter and excludes the orientation of the
ellipse; rotation of that orientation is represented by the [Faraday
angle](name:faraday_angle). The quantity refers to a single beam
polarization state, with no aggregation over distinct beam paths.

Magnetized-plasma birefringence can transform the [initial polarization
ellipticity](name:initial_polarization_ellipticity_of_polarimeter_beam) into
this post-propagation ellipticity by changing the polarization ellipse
during propagation; that change is distinct from Faraday rotation of the
ellipse orientation.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the electric-field vector rotates in a
right-handed sense about the beam-propagation direction.

sources.leaf_definition: Ellipticity
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (lines-of-sight)

NAMES.name: radiative_temperature_at_ece_channel
NAMES.short:
Equivalent blackbody temperature of electron cyclotron emission intensity
detected by a frequency-selective ECE channel, representing the radiation
brightness temperature.
NAMES.long:
Radiative temperature at an ECE channel is the equivalent blackbody
temperature associated with the detected electron cyclotron emission
intensity at that channel's selected frequency. It is a
brightness-temperature representation of the radiation, not the kinetic
temperature of the electron population.

For specific intensity represented by a blackbody spectrum, the radiation
temperature $T_{\mathrm{rad}}$ is defined by

$$
I_\nu = \frac{2h\nu^3}{c^2}\left[\exp\left(\frac{h\nu}{T_{\mathrm{rad}}}\right)-1\right]^{-1}
$$

where $I_\nu$ is the detected specific intensity at frequency $\nu$, $h$ is
Planck's constant, $c$ is the speed of light, and $T_{\mathrm{rad}}$ is the
energy-equivalent blackbody temperature.

The quantity applies to one ECE channel and its selected frequency; it is
not summed or averaged over channels. It excludes the separate kinetic
electron temperature and polarization-resolved radiation quantities. When
the emitting plasma is optically thick, $T_{\mathrm{rad}}$ approaches the
local electron temperature. The [radiative temperature at the magnetic
axis](name:radiative_temperature_at_magnetic_axis) uses the same
brightness-temperature definition at a different evaluation locus.

NAMES.name: reference_frequency_of_wave_beam
NAMES.short:
Reference temporal carrier frequency of a probing electromagnetic wave beam,
specified before frequency conversion or modulation and used as the
phase-measurement baseline.
NAMES.long:
The reference frequency of a probing electromagnetic wave beam is its main
temporal carrier frequency before frequency upshifting or modulation. It
establishes the baseline wave frequency for phase changes caused by plasma
refraction, including electron-density-dependent propagation.

The carrier frequency is related to the wave's angular frequency by:

$$
f = \frac{\omega}{2\pi}
$$

where $f$ is the carrier frequency and $\omega$ is the angular frequency
describing temporal phase evolution.

This quantity denotes the beam's main reference frequency, not a
subsequently upshifted or modulated frequency, a received frequency, or a
local-oscillator frequency. The associated phase quantity is the [wave phase
of a wave beam](name:wave_phase_of_wave_beam), while [launched wave
duration](name:launched_wave_duration) describes the temporal extent of a
sweep rather than its carrier frequency.

sources.leaf_definition: Main frequency used to probe the plasma (before upshifting and modulating)
sources.parent_definition: Set of frequency bandwidths

NAMES.name: refractive_index
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless ratio of an electromagnetic wave’s phase-gradient vector to
its vacuum wavenumber, retaining propagation direction and signed
components.
NAMES.long:
The refractive-index vector describes electromagnetic phase propagation
relative to propagation in vacuum. It preserves the direction of the wave
phase gradient while expressing its magnitude relative to the vacuum
reference.

The defining relation is

$$
\mathbf{n} = \frac{\mathbf{k}}{k_0}, \qquad k_0 = \frac{\omega}{c}
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ is the refractive-index vector, $\mathbf{k}$ is the wave
vector, $k_0$ is the vacuum wavenumber, $\omega$ is the wave angular
frequency, and $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum.

Directional representations include the projection parallel to the local
magnetic field, represented by
[parallel_refractive_index](name:parallel_refractive_index), and the
magnitude of the perpendicular projection, represented by
[perpendicular_refractive_index](name:perpendicular_refractive_index). The
same normalized phase-propagation concept applies to propagation through an
optical element.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_refractive_index
NAMES.short:
Magnitude of the electromagnetic wave vector perpendicular to the local
background magnetic field, normalized by the vacuum wave number at the same
frequency.
NAMES.long:
The perpendicular refractive index is the magnitude of the component of the
[refractive-index vector](name:refractive_index) perpendicular to the local
background magnetic field. It describes the field-transverse part of
electromagnetic phase propagation.

Its defining relation is

$$
n_\perp = \left|\mathbf{n} - (\mathbf{n}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}})\hat{\mathbf{b}}\right| = \frac{k_\perp}{k_0}
$$

where $n_\perp$ is the perpendicular refractive index, $\mathbf{n}$ is the
refractive-index vector, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the unit vector along the
local background magnetic field, $k_\perp$ is the [perpendicular wave-vector
magnitude](name:perpendicular_wave_vector_magnitude), and $k_0$ is the
vacuum wave number at the same wave frequency. Vertical bars denote the
Euclidean vector magnitude.

This quantity is evaluated locally along a beam or ray path, rather than
averaged or integrated along that path, and is not restricted to electron
cyclotron emission. It is nonnegative and retains no direction within the
perpendicular plane; it is therefore distinct from a signed projection onto
a specified transverse axis.

For a real phase-gradient vector, $|\mathbf{n}|^2 = n_\parallel^2 +
n_\perp^2$, where $n_\parallel$ is the signed [parallel refractive
index](name:parallel_refractive_index). The two quantities resolve the
parent vector's magnitude relative to the magnetic-field direction.

NAMES.name: right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part
NAMES.short:
Signed imaginary quadrature of the right-hand circular E-minus wave
electric-field phasor along a beam or ray path, relative to a specified
phase reference.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the imaginary quadrature of the right-hand circularly
polarized E-minus component of a wave [electric field](name:electric_field)
phasor along its propagation path. It retains signed phase information and
is not the field amplitude or the instantaneous physical electric field.

The defining relation is:

$$
E_{-,I} = \operatorname{Im}(E_-)
$$

where $E_{-,I}$ is the signed imaginary quadrature, $E_-$ is the [right-hand
circularly polarized wave electric-field
phasor](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field), and
$\operatorname{Im}$ selects its imaginary part.

The parent polarization component is transverse to the local static magnetic
field. This quadrature is evaluated locally along the beam or ray
propagation path, including electron cyclotron emission paths; it is not
integrated along that path. It inherits the circular-polarization basis and
phase reference of the parent phasor.

Together with the [right-hand circularly polarized real
part](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part),
it reconstructs the parent component through $E_- = E_{-,R} + iE_{-,I}$,
where $E_{-,R}$ is the real, in-phase quadrature and $i$ is the imaginary
unit. Changing the phase reference mixes the two quadratures without
changing the physical polarization.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the E-minus phasor lies in the upper half of
the complex plane defined by the specified phase reference.

sources.leaf_definition: Imaginary part
sources.parent_definition: Right hand polarised electric field component

sources.leaf_definition: Imaginary part
sources.parent_definition: Right hand polarised electric field component

NAMES.name: right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part
NAMES.short:
Signed in-phase quadrature of the right-hand circular E-minus wave
electric-field phasor, transverse to the local equilibrium magnetic field
and defined relative to a chosen phase reference.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed in-phase quadrature of the right-hand circularly
polarized wave electric-field phasor, transverse to the local equilibrium
magnetic field. It describes the E-minus contribution to local wave
polarization along a beam or ray path.

Its defining relation is

$$
E_{-,r} = \operatorname{Re}(\widetilde{E}_{-})
$$

where $E_{-,r}$ is the real quadrature defined here, $\widetilde{E}_{-}$ is
the [right-hand circularly polarized wave electric-field
phasor](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field), and
$\operatorname{Re}$ denotes the real-part operator relative to the chosen
phase reference.

The quantity applies locally along the propagation path, including
electron-cyclotron-emission beam or ray paths; it is not integrated or
averaged along that path. It is distinct from the phasor modulus and from
the instantaneous physical electric field.

Together with the [imaginary
quadrature](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part),
denoted $E_{-,i}$, it reconstructs the parent phasor through
$\widetilde{E}_{-}=E_{-,r}+iE_{-,i}$, where $i$ is the imaginary unit. Both
quadratures must use the same polarization basis and phase reference. The
[left-hand real
quadrature](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part)
instead resolves the E-plus polarization contribution.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the E-minus phase differs from the chosen
zero-phase reference by less than a quarter-cycle, modulo a full cycle.

sources.leaf_definition: Real part
sources.parent_definition: Right hand polarised electric field component

sources.leaf_definition: Real part
sources.parent_definition: Right hand polarised electric field component

NAMES.name: spectral_calibration_factor_at_line_of_sight
NAMES.short:
Wavelength-specific interferometric conversion coefficient that converts a
signed phase change along a line of sight into electron column density.
NAMES.long:
The spectral calibration factor is the wavelength-specific proportionality
that maps an interferometric phase change along one line of sight to the
electron column density on that optical path.

The conversion is defined by

$$
N_{e,\mathrm{line}} = K_{\mathrm{spec}}\,\Delta\varphi
$$

where $N_{e,\mathrm{line}}$ is the [line-integrated electron number
density](name:line_integrated_electron_number_density), $K_{\mathrm{spec}}$
is this spectral calibration factor, and $\Delta\varphi$ is the signed
interferometric phase change.

The factor applies to the complete electron-density integral along the
associated line of sight and to its corresponding probing wavelength. It
represents the electron contribution only and is not a local density, a
line-averaged density, or an optical phase itself.

Applying this factor produces the line-integrated electron number density;
dividing that result by the optical chord length gives [line-averaged
electron density](name:line_averaged_electron_density). The associated
wavelength is the spectral parameter of the probing electromagnetic wave,
related to [wavelength of wave beam](name:wavelength_of_wave_beam).

sources.leaf_definition: Conversion factor to be used to convert phase into line density for this wavelength
sources.parent_definition: Set of wavelengths used for interferometry

NAMES.name: toroidal_coordinate_at_beam_tracing_point
NAMES.short:
Azimuthal location of a beam-tracing point around the machine symmetry axis,
expressed by the toroidal angle in the right-handed (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal coordinate $\phi$ identifies the azimuthal location of a
beam-tracing point about the machine symmetry axis. It is the angular
coordinate of that geometric point, rather than a beam direction or a field
value sampled at the point.

The coordinate is defined from the point's horizontal Cartesian position by:

$$
\phi = \operatorname{atan2}(Y,X)
$$

where $X$ and $Y$ are the horizontal position coordinates in the
right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis, with
$\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $R$
is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height; the $\phi=0$ reference follows
the facility coordinate convention. This is the beam-tracing-point instance
of the general [toroidal coordinate](name:toroidal_coordinate).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the point lies in the direction of increasing
toroidal angle $\phi$, counter-clockwise when viewed from above along
$+\hat{Z}$.

sources.leaf_definition: Toroidal angle
sources.parent_definition: Position of the ray/beam along its path

NAMES.name: toroidal_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.short:
Signed toroidal projection of the local electromagnetic wave vector on a
beam-tracing beam, specifying spatial phase variation around the toroidal
symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal wave-vector component is the signed projection of an
electromagnetic wave’s local spatial phase gradient onto the toroidal
direction, evaluated on the beam-tracing beam.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the component is defined
by

$$
k_\phi = \mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\phi} = \frac{1}{R}\frac{\partial S}{\partial\phi}
$$

where $k_\phi$ is the toroidal wave-vector component, $\mathbf{k}$ is the
local [wave vector](name:wave_vector), $S$ is the spatial wave phase, and
$\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector toward increasing toroidal angle. Here $R$
is major radius measured from the symmetry axis, $\phi$ is the [toroidal
angle at the beam-tracing
point](name:toroidal_coordinate_at_beam_tracing_point), increasing
counter-clockwise when viewed from above, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies locally along the beam, including at its launch point
when specifying the launched wave; it is not averaged along the propagation
path. It retains the magnitude dependence of the wave vector, unlike the
[normalized toroidal
component](name:normalized_toroidal_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam), which
equals $k_\phi/|\mathbf{k}|$, where $|\mathbf{k}|$ is the wave-vector
magnitude.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the local wave vector has a projection toward
increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

sources.leaf_definition: Component along the toroidal direction
sources.parent_definition: Wavevector at launch point

sources.parent_definition: Wave vector of the ray/beam along its path

NAMES.name: total_electron_count
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Total inventory of free electrons within the plasma, including thermal and
fast populations and excluding electrons bound in atoms or molecules.
NAMES.long:
The total free-electron count is the number of unbound electrons contained
within the plasma volume, aggregated over all electron populations.

$$
N_e = \int_V n_e(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $N_e$ is the total free-electron count, $n_e(\mathbf{x})$ is the local
[total electron density](name:total_electron_density), $\mathbf{x}$ is
position, $dV$ is the differential volume element, and $V$ is the plasma
volume.

This quantity includes thermal, fast, and other free-electron populations
present within $V$ and sums them over the entire plasma volume. It excludes
electrons bound in neutral atoms or molecules and is distinct from local or
volume-averaged density, which describes electrons per physical volume
rather than the integrated inventory.

The count is obtained by integrating the complete local electron density; a
[line-averaged electron density](name:line_averaged_electron_density)
represents a chord average and cannot substitute for this volume integral.

sources.leaf_definition: Total number of electrons in the plasma, estimated from the line densities measured by the various channels
sources.parent_definition: Interferometer diagnostic

NAMES.name: twist_period_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor
NAMES.short:
Repeat arclength along the sensing-fiber centerline at which the effective
birefringent-axis orientation completes one spatial cycle.
NAMES.long:
The twist period is the repeat arclength along the sensing-fiber centerline
for the effective birefringent-axis orientation to return to the same state.

Let $s$ denote arclength along the fiber centerline and $Q(s)$ denote the
specified effective birefringent-axis state. The twist period $L_{\rm tw}$
is defined by

$$
Q(s + L_{\rm tw}) = Q(s)
$$

where $L_{\rm tw}$ is the smallest positive repeat arclength.

This is the twist-specific member of the fiber optic current sensor period.
It describes spatial repetition of the optical anisotropy, not the total
fiber arclength, the [initial twist
phase](name:initial_spun_twist_phase_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor), or the
polarization beat length.

sources.leaf_definition: Twist period
sources.parent_definition: Intrinsic properties of the fibre installed on the vacuum vessel

NAMES.name: verdet_constant_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor
NAMES.short:
Magneto-optic coefficient relating optical polarization rotation in a fiber
to the magnetic-field component along the optical propagation path.
NAMES.long:
The Verdet constant is the material- and wavelength-dependent coefficient
governing Faraday rotation in an optical fiber. It characterizes the fiber's
intrinsic magneto-optic response for a specified material state and optical
wavelength.

For a uniform fiber segment, the Faraday rotation is defined by

$$
\theta_F = V B_{\parallel} L
$$

where $\theta_F$ is the Faraday polarization-rotation angle, $V$ is the
Verdet constant, $B_{\parallel}$ is the magnetic-field component along the
local optical propagation direction, and $L$ is the optical path length
through the fiber segment.

This quantity is a local fiber property, not the path-integrated
polarization rotation of a complete sensor. It applies to the optical fiber
material and state specified by the physical system and does not represent
the total magnetic-field magnitude or a field component transverse to the
propagation direction.

For a nonuniform fiber or magnetic field, the accumulated rotation is
obtained from the path integral of the local product $V B_{\parallel}$ along
the optical path; the [length of the fiber-optic current
sensor](name:length_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor) supplies the
corresponding total propagation distance but is not itself part of the
Verdet constant.

sources.leaf_definition: Verdet constant
sources.parent_definition: Intrinsic properties of the fibre installed on the vacuum vessel

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_ece_channel
NAMES.short:
Signed vertical coordinate of an electron-cyclotron-emission channel’s
measurement position in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of an electron-cyclotron-emission (ECE) channel is
the signed projection of its measurement position onto the vertical
direction.

$$
Z_{\mathrm{ECE}} = \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{ECE}} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{ECE}}$ is the vertical coordinate,
$\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{ECE}}$ is the position vector of the channel’s
measurement location, and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity applies to the measurement position associated with one ECE
channel and is not averaged or summed over channels. It describes the
channel position rather than an ECE signal, frequency, or plasma-field
value.

It is distinct from the radial coordinate $R$ and toroidal angle $\phi$. The
[vertical coordinate of a measurement
position](name:vertical_coordinate_of_measurement_position) expresses the
same geometric quantity for a generic measurement location, whereas this
entry retains the ECE-channel locus.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the ECE channel measurement position lies in
the direction of increasing vertical coordinate $Z$.

sources.leaf_definition: Height
sources.parent_definition: Position of the measurements (taking into account the suprathermal shift)

NAMES.name: vertical_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.short:
Signed vertical component of the electromagnetic wave vector along a
beam-tracing beam, giving local spatial phase variation with vertical
height.
NAMES.long:
The vertical wave-vector component is the signed projection of the local
electromagnetic wave vector onto the vertical direction, evaluated locally
along a beam-tracing beam.

The component is defined by

$$
k_Z = \mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}} = \frac{\partial S}{\partial Z}.
$$

Here $k_Z$ is the vertical wave-vector component, $\mathbf{k}$ is the local
[wave vector](name:wave_vector), and $S$ is the wave phase whose spatial
gradient is $\mathbf{k}$. The unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ points along
the positive toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and
$Z$ is the [vertical coordinate of the beam
position](name:vertical_coordinate_of_beam_tracing_beam).

This quantity applies pointwise along the beam path and is not restricted to
the launch point; no path integration or averaging is implied. It retains
the spatial phase scale, unlike the [normalized vertical wave-vector
component](name:vertical_wave_vector_normalized_of_beam_tracing_beam), which
equals $k_Z/|\mathbf{k}|$ for a nonzero wave vector, where $|\mathbf{k}|$ is
the wave-vector magnitude.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the wave vector has a component toward
increasing vertical coordinate $Z$.

NAMES.name: wave_voltage
NAMES.short:
Wave voltage is the electrical potential-difference signal associated with a
detected electromagnetic probing wave returned after interaction with a
plasma cutoff layer. It is the generic wave-related voltage quantity; child
names specify scalar forms such as amplitude.
NAMES.long:
Wave voltage is the electrical potential-difference signal associated with a
detected electromagnetic probing wave returned after interaction with a
plasma cutoff layer. It denotes the wave-related voltage quantity
generically, without restricting it to a particular scalar form such as
amplitude.

As a voltage, the underlying signed signal is a potential difference:

$$
V_\mathrm{wave}(t) = \Phi_\mathrm{sig}(t) - \Phi_\mathrm{ref}(t)
$$

where $V_\mathrm{wave}$ is the wave-voltage signal, $\Phi_\mathrm{sig}$ is
the electric potential at the signal terminal of the receiving circuit,
$\Phi_\mathrm{ref}$ is the electric potential at its reference terminal, and
$t$ is time.

The scope is limited to voltage quantities representing the received probing
wave after plasma cutoff-layer interaction. It excludes source or launcher
drive voltage, voltages unrelated to the returned probing wave, and
non-voltage wave quantities such as electric field, phase, or frequency.

Child names specify the scalar form or reduction of this parent quantity.
The [wave-voltage amplitude](name:wave_voltage_amplitude) is the amplitude
of the same detected wave-voltage signal, not a separate kind of wave
signal; the parent itself does not impose an amplitude, envelope, or
root-mean-square convention unless a child qualifier states one.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the electric potential at the signal terminal
of the receiving circuit is greater than the electric potential at its
reference terminal.

NAMES.name: left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part
NAMES.short:
Signed in-phase quadrature of the E-plus, left-hand circular wave
electric-field phasor along a beam or ray path, relative to its chosen phase
reference.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the signed in-phase real quadrature of the complex
[left-hand circularly polarized wave electric
field](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field) phasor,
conventionally called E-plus. It describes the circular polarization
contribution transverse to the local equilibrium magnetic field along an
electron cyclotron emission beam or ray path.

Its defining relation is

$$
E_{+,\mathrm{real}} = \operatorname{Re}(\widetilde{E}_+)
$$

where $E_{+,\mathrm{real}}$ is the signed in-phase quadrature,
$\widetilde{E}_+$ is the complex E-plus electric-field phasor, and
$\operatorname{Re}$ denotes taking the real part.

This is a local polarization quadrature of the wave [electric
field](name:electric_field), not a path-integrated field, phasor magnitude,
intensity, or complete instantaneous electric field. Its value depends on
the chosen transverse polarization basis and phase reference; changing the
phase reference mixes the real and imaginary quadratures.

Together with the [E-plus imaginary
quadrature](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part),
it reconstructs the complex E-plus phasor. The [right-hand circular real
quadrature](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part)
instead resolves the opposite circular polarization, E-minus.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the E-plus phasor phase lies within
one-quarter cycle of the chosen in-phase reference, modulo a full cycle.

sources.leaf_definition: Real part
sources.parent_definition: Left hand polarised electric field component

NAMES.name: line_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Number density of free electrons averaged along a specified plasma chord
with equal path-length weighting, excluding electrons bound in atoms,
molecules, or ions.
NAMES.long:
Number density of electron

The line average is defined by

$$\bar{f} = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^L f\,dl$$

where $\bar{n}_e$ is the line-averaged electron density, $n_e$ is the local
free-electron number density evaluated along the chord, $L$ is the positive
length of the specified chord, and $l$ is distance along it. The integration
interval and length denominator refer to the same chord segment.

The electron population includes thermal and nonthermal free electrons over
the full velocity distribution; electrons bound in atoms, molecules, or ions
are excluded. The average uses equal path-length weighting, without
additional density or volume weighting.

Unlike [volume-averaged electron
density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density), this quantity averages
along a chord rather than over the plasma volume. It equals the local
density everywhere on the chord only when that density is uniform. The
[line-integrated electron number
density](name:line_integrated_electron_number_density) is instead a column
abundance; dividing that abundance by its corresponding path length yields
this mean when both quantities refer to the same path.

The [line-averaged xenon density](name:line_averaged_xenon_density) applies
the same chord-mean operation to xenon ions rather than electrons. The
[ratio of line-averaged electron density to Greenwald
density](name:ratio_of_line_averaged_electron_density_to_greenwald_density)
uses this electron chord mean as its numerator and is a separate normalized
quantity.

sources.leaf_definition: Line average density inferred from interferometer measurements. Corresponds to the density integrated along the full line-of-sight and then divided by the length of the line-of-sight
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (lines-of-sight)

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Electron density

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_ece_channel_emission_position
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless magnetic-surface label assigned to an electron-cyclotron
emission location, locating that emission on nested toroidal-flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The normalized toroidal-flux coordinate at an electron-cyclotron-emission
channel's emission position is the magnetic-surface label assigned to the
location from which the channel's emission originates.

The coordinate is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = \left(\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}\right)^{1/2}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the normalized toroidal-flux coordinate,
$\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux of the magnetic surface
passing through the emission position, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}$ is that
flux at the magnetic axis, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}}$ is that flux
at the equilibrium boundary.

This quantity is a point evaluation for one electron-cyclotron-emission
channel position, applying to the magnetic surface intersecting that
position. It has no sum, average, or integration over channels,
line-of-sight points, or emission locations, and it is not a cylindrical
radial distance.

It is the emission-position specialization of the [normalized toroidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate): within the normalized
interval, it is zero at the magnetic axis and reaches one at the equilibrium
boundary. Its locus differs from the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate at
measurement
position](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_measurement_position),
which is evaluated at a measurement position rather than an
electron-cyclotron emission position.

sources.leaf_definition: Normalized toroidal flux coordinate of the measurement
sources.parent_definition: Radiation temperature from the closest channel to the magnetic axis, together with its radial location

NAMES.name: wave_electric_field
NAMES.short:
Complex vector phasor of a coherent electromagnetic-wave electric field,
capturing its local amplitude, phase, and polarization as the oscillatory
contribution to the total electric field.
NAMES.long:
The wave electric field is the complex vector phasor representing the
oscillatory electromagnetic-wave contribution to the local [electric
field](name:electric_field). It retains the wave amplitude, phase, and
polarization before any spatial projection or spectral mode decomposition.

For a single angular frequency, the physical wave field is defined by

$$
\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{wave}}(\mathbf{r},t)=\operatorname{Re}\left\{\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}_{\mathrm{wave}}(\mathbf{r},\omega)e^{-i\omega t}\right\}
$$

where $\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}_{\mathrm{wave}}$ is the complex
wave-electric-field phasor, $\mathbf{r}$ is position, $t$ is time, and
$\omega$ is angular frequency. Its projections include the [parallel wave
electric field](name:parallel_wave_electric_field) and [vertical wave
electric field](name:vertical_wave_electric_field); its toroidal Fourier
components are represented by the per-toroidal-mode electric field. The
quantity excludes electrostatic and non-wave contributions unless they are
explicitly part of the identified electromagnetic wave.

NAMES.name: parallel_wave_electric_field
NAMES.short:
Complex phasor of the wave electric field projected along the local
equilibrium magnetic-field direction in a magnetized plasma.
NAMES.long:
The parallel wave electric field is the complex phasor obtained by
projecting the electromagnetic-wave electric-field phasor onto the local
equilibrium magnetic-field direction. It retains both amplitude and phase
and is a component of the [wave electric field](name:wave_electric_field).

The parallel component is defined by

$$
E_{\parallel}=\mathbf{E}_{w}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}},\qquad \hat{\mathbf{b}}=\frac{\mathbf{B}_{0}}{|\mathbf{B}_{0}|}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}_{w}$ is the complex wave-electric-field phasor,
$\mathbf{B}_{0}$ is the local equilibrium magnetic field, and
$\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is its unit direction. The phasor carries the phase of
the harmonic field under the selected time convention.

This quantity is the complex component rather than its magnitude. Its
modulus gives the parallel wave electric field amplitude, while its
quadratures include the [parallel wave electric field imaginary
part](name:parallel_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part) and the
corresponding real part.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the electric-field component is directed
along the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$.

NAMES.name: parallel_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part
NAMES.short:
Signed imaginary quadrature of a wave electric-field phasor projected along
the local equilibrium magnetic field, relative to a specified phase
reference.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed imaginary quadrature of the wave [electric
field](name:electric_field) phasor projected along the local equilibrium
magnetic field. It describes the field-aligned contribution to the complex
wave polarization at each point along a propagation path.

The defining projection and quadrature extraction are

$$
E_{\parallel,I}=\operatorname{Im}\!\left(\widetilde E_\parallel\right)=\operatorname{Im}\!\left(\widetilde{\mathbf E}\cdot\hat{\mathbf b}\right).
$$

Here $E_{\parallel,I}$ is the signed imaginary quadrature, $\widetilde
E_\parallel$ is the [parallel wave electric-field
phasor](name:parallel_wave_electric_field), $\widetilde{\mathbf E}$ is the
wave electric-field phasor, and $\operatorname{Im}$ extracts its imaginary
coefficient. The unit vector $\hat{\mathbf b}=\mathbf B_0/|\mathbf B_0|$
points along the local equilibrium magnetic field $\mathbf B_0$.

This is a local field contribution, not a path integral or average. Parallel
refers to the equilibrium magnetic-field direction, not necessarily the
propagation direction. Unlike the [left-hand circularly polarized imaginary
quadrature](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part),
it does not resolve transverse circular polarization.

Together with the [parallel wave electric-field real
part](name:parallel_wave_electric_field_real_part), this quadrature
determines the full parallel phasor. It is neither the phasor magnitude nor
the instantaneous physical field; its value depends on the chosen phase
reference and temporal Fourier convention.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the imaginary-quadrature projection points
along, rather than opposite to, the local equilibrium magnetic field, with
the phasor phase reference and temporal Fourier convention held fixed.

sources.leaf_definition: Imaginary part
sources.parent_definition: Parallel to magnetic field polarised electric field component

sources.leaf_definition: Imaginary part
sources.parent_definition: Parallel to magnetic field polarised electric field component

NAMES.name: parallel_wave_electric_field_real_part
NAMES.short:
Signed in-phase quadrature of the coherent wave electric-field phasor
projected along the local equilibrium magnetic field, relative to the chosen
wave phase reference.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed in-phase quadrature of the wave electric-field
phasor parallel to the local equilibrium magnetic field. It describes local
wave polarization along a beam or ray path relative to a chosen phase
reference.

The defining projection and real-part operation are

$$
E_{\parallel,\mathrm{R}} = \operatorname{Re}\widetilde E_\parallel = \operatorname{Re}\left(\widetilde{\mathbf E}\cdot\hat{\mathbf b}\right)
$$

where $E_{\parallel,\mathrm{R}}$ is this real quadrature, $\widetilde
E_\parallel$ is the [parallel wave electric-field
phasor](name:parallel_wave_electric_field), $\widetilde{\mathbf E}$ is the
full wave electric-field phasor, and $\hat{\mathbf b}$ is the unit vector
along the local equilibrium magnetic field.

Together with the [imaginary
quadrature](name:parallel_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part), denoted
$E_{\parallel,\mathrm{I}}$, it reconstructs the parent phasor through
$\widetilde E_\parallel=E_{\parallel,\mathrm{R}}+iE_{\parallel,\mathrm{I}}$,
where $i$ is the imaginary unit. Its value depends on the phase reference;
it is neither the phasor magnitude nor the instantaneous oscillating field.

The quantity is local along the propagation path, not a path integral or
average, and excludes the equilibrium electric field. Unlike the [left-hand
circularly polarized wave electric-field real
part](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part), it
resolves the field-aligned component rather than a transverse circular
polarization component.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the in-phase wave electric-field projection
points along the local equilibrium magnetic field at the chosen phase
reference.

sources.leaf_definition: Real part
sources.parent_definition: Parallel to magnetic field polarised electric field component

sources.leaf_definition: Real part
sources.parent_definition: Parallel to magnetic field polarised electric field component

NAMES.name: toroidal_wave_electric_field
NAMES.short:
Complex phasor component of an electromagnetic-wave electric field projected
onto the toroidal direction, preserving local amplitude, phase, and toroidal
polarization.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal wave electric field is the complex phasor obtained by
projecting the electromagnetic-wave electric-field phasor onto the toroidal
direction. It retains the local amplitude and phase of the toroidal
component of the [wave electric field](name:wave_electric_field).

For a single angular frequency, the toroidal component is defined by

$$
\widetilde{E}_{\phi}(\mathbf{r},\omega)=\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}_{\mathrm{wave}}(\mathbf{r},\omega)\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}
$$

where $\widetilde{E}_{\phi}$ is the toroidal component phasor,
$\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}_{\mathrm{wave}}$ is the complex wave-electric-field
phasor, $\mathbf{r}$ is position, $\omega$ is angular frequency, and
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is the toroidal unit vector in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

This quantity is the wave contribution only and is distinct from the total
[toroidal electric field](name:toroidal_electric_field). Its axis projection
is analogous to the [vertical wave electric
field](name:vertical_wave_electric_field), but it represents the component
along increasing toroidal angle rather than the vertical direction.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the projected electric-field vector points in
the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

sources.leaf_definition: Lower Hybrid electric field component in the toroidal direction
sources.parent_definition: Physics quantities measured from polarized light spectroscopy

NAMES.name: vertical_wave_electric_field
NAMES.short:
Complex phasor of an electromagnetic-wave electric field projected onto the
vertical Z direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame,
preserving local amplitude and phase.
NAMES.long:
The vertical wave electric field is the complex phasor obtained by
projecting the electromagnetic-wave electric-field phasor onto the vertical
basis direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. It is
the Z-directed component of the [wave electric
field](name:wave_electric_field), retaining its local amplitude and phase.

The projection is defined by

$$
\widetilde{E}_Z(\mathbf{r},\omega)=\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}_{\mathrm{wave}}(\mathbf{r},\omega)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{Z}}
$$

where $\widetilde{E}_Z$ is the vertical wave-electric-field phasor,
$\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}_{\mathrm{wave}}$ is the complex wave-electric-field
vector phasor, $\mathbf{r}$ is position, $\omega$ is angular frequency, and
$\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the vertical unit vector. This wave contribution is
distinct from the static [vertical electric
field](name:vertical_electric_field) and from the field-aligned [parallel
wave electric field](name:parallel_wave_electric_field).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the electric-field phasor projection is along
$+\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$, the direction of increasing vertical coordinate $Z$ in
the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Lower Hybrid electric field component in the vertical direction
sources.parent_definition: Physics quantities measured from polarized light spectroscopy

NAMES.name: alpha_angle_of_plasma_filament
NAMES.short:
Signed inclination of the first side of a plasma-filament oblique
cross-section, measured counterclockwise from the outward radial direction
in the poloidal plane.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed inclination of the first side of the oblique
parallelogram representing an individual plasma-filament cross section. It
specifies the orientation of that side in the poloidal plane relative to the
outward radial direction.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major
radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the angle is
defined by

$$
\alpha = \operatorname{atan2}\left(\mathbf{a}_1\cdot\hat{\mathbf{e}}_Z,\,\mathbf{a}_1\cdot\hat{\mathbf{e}}_R\right)
$$

where $\alpha$ is the first-side inclination, $\mathbf{a}_1$ is the directed
vector along the first parallelogram side, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_R$ is the
outward radial unit vector in the direction of increasing $R$,
$\hat{\mathbf{e}}_Z$ is the positive vertical unit vector, and
$\operatorname{atan2}$ returns the signed angle from the radial projection
toward the vertical projection.

The quantity applies separately to each discrete plasma-carrying filament
and is not an aggregate orientation averaged over the plasma. It describes
only the first side of the oblique cross section; it is not the inclination
of the second side or either side length.

The companion [tilt angle of a plasma
filament](name:tilt_angle_of_plasma_filament) specifies the inclination of
the other parallelogram side, while the [major length of a plasma
filament](name:major_length_of_plasma_filament) and [minor length of a
plasma filament](name:minor_length_of_plasma_filament) specify
cross-sectional dimensions. Together these geometric quantities define the
filament cross-section orientation and shape.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the directed first side is rotated
counterclockwise from the outward radial direction toward the positive
vertical direction in the poloidal plane.

sources.leaf_definition: Inclination of first angle measured counter-clockwise from horizontal outwardly directed radial vector (grad R).
sources.parent_definition: Parallelogram description of the element

NAMES.name: beta
NAMES.short:
Global beta compares volume-averaged total perpendicular plasma pressure
with combined magnetic pressure; for a common pressure, 1/beta =
1/beta_toroidal + 1/beta_poloidal because B^2 = B_toroidal^2 + B_poloidal^2.
NAMES.long:
Beta-family quantities are dimensionless equilibrium measures comparing
total perpendicular plasma pressure, aggregated over the plasma volume, with
a magnetic-pressure scale. The scale may be based on the toroidal field, the
poloidal field, or their combined magnitude; a normalized toroidal form
applies an additional scaling to the toroidal beta.

For a common volume-averaged pressure and orthogonal toroidal and poloidal
magnetic-field components, the component betas satisfy

$$
\frac{1}{\beta} = \frac{1}{\beta_{\mathrm{tor}}} + \frac{1}{\beta_{\mathrm{pol}}}
$$

where $\beta$ is the beta based on the combined magnetic field,
$\beta_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the [toroidal beta](name:toroidal_beta), and
$\beta_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the [poloidal beta](name:poloidal_beta). The
relation follows because the toroidal and poloidal fields add in quadrature
to give the squared total field strength.

This parent covers global equilibrium measures using total perpendicular
plasma pressure aggregated over the plasma volume and all populations
included in that total. It is not a local pressure ratio, a species-specific
pressure measure, or a magnetic-pressure quantity by itself.

The toroidal and poloidal children differ by the magnetic-field reference
used in the denominator. The [normalized toroidal
beta](name:normalized_toroidal_beta) is a separately scaled toroidal-beta
variant; it is not substituted for the unnormalized toroidal beta in the
reciprocal relation.

NAMES.name: current_density
NAMES.short:
Current density is the vector flux density of conventional electric charge,
equal to electric current per unit area normal to the flow. It points in the
direction of positive charge transport and includes all charged-particle
contributions unless a narrower current-density quantity is specified.
NAMES.long:
Current density $\mathbf{J}$ is the vector density of conventional electric
charge flux at a point. It represents the signed flow of electric charge
carried by charged particles, with direction defined by positive charge
transport.

A kinetic definition is the charge-weighted first velocity moment of the
particle distribution functions:

$$
\mathbf{J}(\mathbf{x},t) = \sum_s q_s \int \mathbf{v}\, f_s(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v},t)\, d^3v
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $t$ is time, $s$ indexes charged species,
$q_s$ is the species charge, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and $f_s$ is
the velocity-space distribution function. In quasistatic equilibrium it is
the source term in Ampere's law, $\nabla \times \mathbf{B} = \mu_0
\mathbf{J}$ when displacement current is neglected, and steady charge
conservation gives $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}=0$.

This quantity excludes displacement-current density and is distinct from a
scalar electric current, which is the flux of $\mathbf{J}$ through a
specified surface. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame,
where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical
height, the geometric components are the projections along $(\hat{R},
\hat{\phi}, \hat{Z})$: radial_current_density, toroidal_current_density, and
vertical_current_density. The full vector has direction rather than a single
scalar sign; scalar components and projections inherit the positive
direction of their defining basis vector or unit vector.

NAMES.name: current_of_passive_structure
NAMES.short:
Current in a passive structure is the signed rate of conventional charge
transport circulating toroidally through one axisymmetric member.
NAMES.long:
Current of passive structure

The current $I$ is defined by

$$
I = \int_S \mathbf{J}\cdot\hat{\phi}\,dS
$$

where $S$ is the member's full poloidal cross-section, $\mathbf{J}$ is the
[conventional electric current density](name:current_density), and $dS$ is a
surface-area element. The vector $\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal unit vector in
the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius,
$\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

This quantity integrates current density over one member's cross-section; it
is not a sum over all passive structures and excludes plasma and active-coil
currents. When the specified member is a passive loop, it equals the
[current of that loop](name:current_of_passive_loop).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when conventional electric current flows in the
direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: current_of_plasma_filament
NAMES.short:
Electric current carried by a plasma current-carrying filament element is
the signed toroidal current assigned to a single discrete element in an
axisymmetric filamentary representation of the distributed plasma current.
NAMES.long:
Electric current carried by a plasma current-carrying filament element is
the signed toroidal current assigned to one discrete element in an
axisymmetric filamentary representation of the distributed plasma current.
It represents that element's contribution to the plasma current rather than
a geometric property of the element.

For filament element $k$, the current is the cross-sectional integral of the
toroidal plasma current density over that element:

$$
I_k = \int_{A_k} j_\phi \, dA
$$

where $I_k$ is the electric current carried by plasma filament element $k$,
$A_k$ is the area of the plasma filament element in the poloidal
cross-section, $j_\phi$ is the toroidal component of the plasma current
density in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major
radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical height, and $dA$ is a
differential area element of the poloidal cross-section.

The scope is one plasma current-carrying filament element, with no
aggregation over multiple elements. It applies only to plasma-current
filaments in the axisymmetric representation and excludes currents in coils,
passive conductors, and other non-plasma structures. It is an integrated
current, not a current density and not a geometric descriptor; the element
geometry is described separately by [inner
radius](name:inner_radius_of_plasma_filament),
[height](name:height_of_plasma_filament), and area.

The represented [plasma current](name:plasma_current) of a collection of
plasma current-carrying filament elements is the algebraic sum of their
signed filament currents.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the current of the plasma filament element
flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius,
$\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; this is
counter-clockwise when viewed from the positive $Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Number density of electrons counts free electrons per physical volume,
excluding electrons bound in atoms, molecules, or ions.
NAMES.long:
Number density of electron

The underlying local density is defined by

$$
n_e = \int f_e(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $n_e$ is the electron number density, $f_e$ is the electron
phase-space number distribution at the location and time considered,
$\mathbf{v}$ is electron velocity, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume
element. The integral extends over all velocities represented by the
distribution.

The unqualified quantity imposes no thermal or nonthermal population
restriction and specifies no particular plasma region. Electrons bound in
atoms, molecules, or ions are excluded. No line, surface, or volume
averaging is implicit.

[Thermal electron density](name:thermal_electron_density) and [fast electron
density](name:fast_electron_density) restrict the electron population to
thermal and suprathermal electrons, respectively. [Total electron
density](name:total_electron_density) explicitly includes the complete
free-electron population, summing thermal and nonthermal contributions.

Spatially averaged forms retain this underlying number-density meaning:
[line-averaged electron density](name:line_averaged_electron_density) is the
local density integrated along a specified plasma chord and divided by its
length, while [volume-averaged electron
density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density) is the local density
integrated over the plasma volume inside the last closed flux surface and
divided by that volume.

NAMES.name: elongation_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Elongation of a flux surface is the ratio of its poloidal cross-section’s
vertical extent to its radial extent, independent of overall size.
NAMES.long:
Elongation of flux surface

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major
radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the defining
relation is:

$$
\kappa = (Z_{\max} - Z_{\min})/(R_{\max} - R_{\min})
$$

where $\kappa$ is the elongation, $Z_{\max}$ and $Z_{\min}$ are the maximum
and minimum vertical coordinates of the cross-section, and $R_{\max}$ and
$R_{\min}$ are its maximum and minimum major radii.

The quantity applies to an individual flux surface, not an average over
nested surfaces. For an elliptical cross-section, it equals the ratio of the
vertical to horizontal semi-axes; the extent-based definition does not
require an ellipse. It is not restricted to the plasma boundary: evaluating
it there gives the [elongation of the plasma
boundary](name:elongation_of_plasma_boundary).

The [derivative of elongation with respect to normalized minor
radius](name:derivative_of_elongation_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_normalized_minor_radius)
describes how this ratio changes between neighboring surfaces, rather than
the shape ratio itself.

A surface formed by points sharing the same magnetic-flux label in a
nested-flux-surface configuration. Where $\psi(R, Z) = \mathrm{const}$,
$\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux.

sources.parent_definition: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux

NAMES.name: elongation_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Elongation of the plasma boundary is the ratio of its poloidal
cross-section’s vertical extent to its radial extent, independent of overall
size.
NAMES.long:
Elongation of plasma boundary

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major
radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the defining
relation is:

$$
\kappa = (Z_{\max} - Z_{\min})/(R_{\max} - R_{\min})
$$

where $\kappa$ is the elongation, $Z_{\max}$ and $Z_{\min}$ are the maximum
and minimum vertical coordinates of the plasma-boundary cross-section, and
$R_{\max}$ and $R_{\min}$ are its maximum and minimum major radii.

The extrema apply to the full plasma-boundary cross-section, not an average
over nested surfaces. Equivalently, elongation is the vertical half-height
divided by the geometric minor radius, defined as half the major-radius
width. For an elliptical cross-section with vertically and radially aligned
axes, it equals the vertical-to-horizontal semi-axis ratio; the extent-based
definition does not require an ellipse.

This quantity is the [elongation of a flux
surface](name:elongation_of_flux_surface) evaluated specifically at the
plasma boundary. The [derivative of elongation with respect to normalized
minor
radius](name:derivative_of_elongation_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_normalized_minor_radius)
instead describes how this ratio changes between neighboring surfaces,
rather than the boundary shape ratio itself.

The last closed magnetic flux surface: the outermost flux surface on which
field lines close on themselves, bounding the confined plasma. Where $\psi =
\psi_{\mathrm{LCFS}}$, $\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux;
$\psi_{\mathrm{LCFS}}$ is its value on the last closed flux surface.
