NAMES.name: external_loop_voltage
NAMES.short:
Electromotive-force contribution to the plasma loop voltage caused by
changing externally generated poloidal magnetic flux, including flux linked
through active coils and passive conducting structures.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the inductive electromotive-force contribution to the
plasma loop voltage produced by time-varying poloidal magnetic flux
generated by active coil circuits and magnetically coupled passive
conducting structures. It excludes resistive voltage drops and other
non-inductive contributions.

The contribution is defined by Faraday's law:

$$
V_{\mathrm{ext}}(t) = -\frac{d\Phi_{\mathrm{ext}}(t)}{dt}
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is the externally generated poloidal magnetic
flux linked by the considered toroidal plasma circuit and $t$ is time. It
contributes to the total [loop voltage at the plasma
boundary](name:loop_voltage_at_plasma_boundary); currents in passive
conductors are represented by the linked-flux response of structures such as
those described by [current of passive
structure](name:current_of_passive_structure).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the induced electromotive force has a
positive line integral in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$
in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: External voltage, i.e. time derivative of psi_external_average (with a minus sign : - d_psi_external_average/d_time)
sources.parent_definition: 0D parameters of the equilibrium

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_major_radius
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface-averaged nonnegative perpendicular distance from the toroidal
symmetry axis to points on a nested magnetic flux surface, giving the mean
major-radius coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Major radius is the nonnegative perpendicular distance from the toroidal
symmetry axis to a geometric point or specified location. For this
flux-surface-averaged quantity, that distance is averaged over each nested
magnetic flux surface in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame,
where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical
height.

The flux-surface average of major radius is defined by

$$
\langle R\rangle_\psi = \frac{\oint_\psi R\,dl/B_p}{\oint_\psi dl/B_p}
$$

where $\langle R\rangle_\psi$ is the averaged major-radius coordinate,
$\psi$ is the magnetic-flux label identifying the surface, $l$ is poloidal
arc length along that surface, and $B_p$ is the magnitude of the poloidal
magnetic field. The contour integral extends around the complete poloidal
intersection of the nested magnetic flux surface.

This quantity applies to a complete magnetic flux surface and aggregates the
local [major radius](name:major_radius) using the flux-surface weighting
defined by the inverse poloidal-field magnitude. It is therefore distinct
from pointwise major radius and contains no point-specific or localized
evaluation.

The quantity is the flux-surface-averaged counterpart of [major
radius](name:major_radius). It must not be confused with
[flux-surface-averaged inverse of major
radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_major_radius), which averages
the reciprocal $1/R$ rather than averaging $R$ itself; consequently, it is
not generally the reciprocal of that neighboring average.

sources.leaf_definition: Flux surface averaged R
sources.parent_definition: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface average of the squared magnitude of the total equilibrium
magnetic field, providing a geometric coefficient for equilibrium and
neoclassical transport relations.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the surface-averaged squared strength of the total magnetic
field on a nested magnetic flux surface. It is a geometric metric
coefficient used in equilibrium descriptions and in bounce-averaged and
neoclassical transport relations.

The flux-surface average is defined by

$$
\left\langle B^2 \right\rangle_\psi = \frac{\displaystyle\oint_{S(\psi)} \frac{B^2}{\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert}\,dS}{\displaystyle\oint_{S(\psi)} \frac{1}{\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert}\,dS}
$$

where $B^2$ is the [square of the magnetic-field
magnitude](name:square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude), $\psi$ is the poloidal
magnetic-flux label of the surface, $S(\psi)$ is the closed magnetic flux
surface with that label, $\nabla\psi$ is the gradient of the flux label, and
$dS$ is the surface-area element.

The quantity applies to the total equilibrium magnetic field, including all
of its components, and is aggregated over each closed flux surface with the
inverse-$\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert$ weighting shown above. It is not the
pointwise value of $B^2$, the square of a flux-surface-averaged
magnetic-field magnitude, or a single magnetic-field component.

It is the flux-surface-averaged form of
[square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude](name:square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude).
It differs from
[flux_surface_averaged_magnetic_field_magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_magnetic_field_magnitude),
which averages the field magnitude before squaring, and from
[flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude),
which averages its reciprocal.

NAMES.name: gap_at_closest_wall_point
NAMES.short:
Gap at the closest-wall point measures the minimum Euclidean separation
between the plasma separatrix and limiter or wall material.
NAMES.long:
Gap at closest wall point

The gap is defined by

$$
g = \min_{\mathbf{x}\in\Gamma_{\mathrm{sep}},\,\mathbf{y}\in\Gamma_{\mathrm{pw}}}\left\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\right\|_2
$$

where $g$ is the gap, $\Gamma_{\mathrm{sep}}$ is the plasma separatrix,
$\Gamma_{\mathrm{pw}}$ is the combined eligible limiter-or-wall boundary,
$\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{y}$ are physical points on those respective
boundaries, and $\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\|_2$ denotes their Euclidean
separation.

The minimum is taken over all eligible boundary-point pairs, rather than
averaged over the wall or restricted to a major-radius separation. The gap
is nonnegative and vanishes when the boundaries touch.

For identical boundaries, its value equals the [gap at the plasma
boundary](name:gap_at_plasma_boundary). The [vertical coordinate of the
closest-wall point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point)
specifies the vertical position of the evaluation locus, not its clearance
from the plasma.

sources.leaf_definition: Distance to the plasma boundary
sources.parent_definition: Position and distance to the plasma boundary of the point of the first wall which is the closest to plasma boundary

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Distance between the separatrix and the nearest limiter or wall element

NAMES.name: gap_at_outboard_midplane
NAMES.short:
Gap at the outboard midplane is the major-radius separation between the
inner and outer separatrices in a double-null or near-double-null
equilibrium.
NAMES.long:
Gap at outboard midplane

The separation is defined by

$$
g = \left|R_{\mathrm{outer}}-R_{\mathrm{inner}}\right|
$$

where $g$ is the gap, and $R_{\mathrm{outer}}$ and $R_{\mathrm{inner}}$ are
the major-radius coordinates of the outer and inner separatrices. Both
coordinates are evaluated at the same vertical height, selected by the inner
separatrix's outboard-midplane point. In the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $R$ denotes major radius, $\phi$ toroidal angle, and $Z$
vertical height.

The quantity is a local separation, not a spatial average or a minimum
distance over the separatrix surfaces. It is nonnegative and vanishes when
the two separatrices coincide at the evaluation point.

Unlike [gap at closest wall point](name:gap_at_closest_wall_point), this
quantity compares two magnetic separatrices rather than a plasma boundary
and a material surface. It also differs from [radial separatrix distance at
outboard midplane](name:radial_separatrix_distance_at_outboard_midplane),
which compares a measurement position mapped along its flux surface with a
separatrix.

The low-field-side equatorial midplane: the point of maximum major radius on
the flux surface in question. For a value at the separatrix intersection use
outboard_midplane_separatrix. Where $R = \max_{S} R,\quad R >
R_{\mathrm{axis}}$, $S$ is the magnetic flux surface the point lies on;
$R_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is major radius of the magnetic axis.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Distance between the inner and outer separatrices, in the major radius direction, at the plasma outboard and at the height corresponding to the maximum R for the inner separatrix.

NAMES.name: height_of_plasma_filament
NAMES.short:
Full vertical extent of the rectangular cross-section of a discrete plasma
current-carrying filament element, measured along the machine’s vertical
axis.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the full vertical dimension of the rectangular
cross-section associated with one discrete plasma current-carrying filament.
It is a geometric extent, not the filament current or its current density.

The height $H$ is defined by the difference between the upper and lower
vertical coordinates:

$$
H = Z_{\mathrm{upper}} - Z_{\mathrm{lower}}
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{upper}}$ and $Z_{\mathrm{lower}}$ are the upper and lower
coordinates in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, with $Z$
denoting vertical height and $\hat{Z}$ the vertical basis direction.

This quantity applies only to the vertical dimension of the rectangular
filament cross-section. The horizontal full width is defined separately by
[plasma filament width](name:plasma_filament_width), while the in-plane
thickness is defined by thickness of plasma filament.

sources.leaf_definition: Vertical full height
sources.parent_definition: Rectangular description of the element

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_plasma_filament
NAMES.short:
Inner radius of a plasma filament is the geometric radius of the inner
circular boundary of the annular cross-section representing a
current-carrying plasma filament. It marks the boundary between the hollow
central region and the conducting annular region.
NAMES.long:
Inner radius of a plasma filament is the geometric radius of the inner
circular boundary of the annular cross-section representing a
current-carrying plasma filament. It marks the boundary between the hollow
central region and the conducting annular region.

For the inner circular boundary in the poloidal cross-section of the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the inner radius
$a_\mathrm{inner}$ is the distance from the filament cross-section center
$(R_c, Z_c)$ to any point $(R, Z)$ on that boundary:

$$
a_\mathrm{inner} = \sqrt{(R - R_c)^2 + (Z - Z_c)^2}
$$

where $R$ is major radius, $Z$ is vertical height, $(R_c, Z_c)$ is the
center of the annular cross-section, and $(R, Z)$ is a point on the inner
circular boundary.

This quantity applies to the hollow-disk annular representation of a
discrete plasma current-carrying filament and denotes the smaller of its two
concentric boundary radii. The current-carrying cross-section occupies the
region outside $a_\mathrm{inner}$ and inside $a_\mathrm{outer}$, where
$a_\mathrm{outer}$ is the [outer radius of the plasma
filament](name:outer_radius_of_plasma_filament), with $0 \le
a_\mathrm{inner} \le a_\mathrm{outer}$.

Together with the [outer radius of the plasma
filament](name:outer_radius_of_plasma_filament), this quantity determines
the width of the plasma filament as the radial thickness of the annulus and
the area of the plasma filament as the area of the current-carrying annular
region. It excludes the outer boundary radius itself, the annular width or
area, the [height of the plasma filament](name:height_of_plasma_filament),
the curvature radius of a noncircular contour segment, and the major radius
of a filament centerline about the toroidal symmetry axis.

sources.leaf_definition: Inner radius
sources.parent_definition: The element is an annulus of centre R, Z, with inner radius radius_inner and outer radius radius_outer

NAMES.name: inverse_of_major_radius
NAMES.short:
Reciprocal major-radius coordinate for a geometric point or specified
location, serving as a positive geometric factor in toroidal equilibrium
relations.
NAMES.long:
Reciprocal major radius is the inverse of the perpendicular distance from
the toroidal symmetry axis to a geometric point or specified location. It is
a geometric quantity used to represent the radial dependence of toroidal
equilibrium relations.

$$
R^{-1} = \frac{1}{R}
$$

where $R$ is the [major radius](name:major_radius), namely the radial
coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

At the parent level, the quantity is evaluated pointwise or at a specified
geometric location and has no averaging or integration implied. It is
positive wherever the major radius is positive, and it is distinct from the
major radius itself because it reverses the radial dependence rather than
specifying the distance from the symmetry axis.

A flux-surface-averaged instance applies the flux-surface averaging
operation to this reciprocal quantity;
[flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_major_radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_major_radius)
is the corresponding geometric coefficient obtained by averaging over a
magnetic flux surface.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_major_radius
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface average of reciprocal major radius, providing a geometric
equilibrium coefficient for toroidal geometry in flux-coordinate equations.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the geometric average of the reciprocal major radius over a
complete magnetic flux surface. It is an equilibrium metric coefficient
independent of plasma species, population, magnetic-field component, and
physical transport process.

For a magnetic flux surface identified by the label $\psi$, the defining
flux-surface average is:

$$
g_{1/R}(\psi) =
\left\langle \frac{1}{R} \right\rangle_\psi =
\frac{\displaystyle\oint_{\mathcal{S}(\psi)}
\frac{dS}{|\nabla\psi|}\,\frac{1}{R}}
{\displaystyle\oint_{\mathcal{S}(\psi)}
\frac{dS}{|\nabla\psi|}}
$$

Here $g_{1/R}$ denotes the metric coefficient, $R$ is the major-radius
coordinate, $\psi$ is the magnetic flux-surface label, $\mathcal{S}(\psi)$
is the corresponding closed magnetic flux surface, $dS$ is its surface-area
element, and $\nabla\psi$ is the spatial gradient of the flux-surface label.
The coordinate $R$ belongs to the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$
frame, where $\phi$ is the toroidal angle and $Z$ is the vertical
coordinate.

The aggregation is over the entire closed flux surface using the
flux-surface weighting shown in the defining relation; this is not the local
reciprocal radius at a point. The quantity is distinct from the flux-surface
average of reciprocal squared major radius, [flux-surface-averaged inverse
square of major
radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_major_radius).

It is the flux-surface-averaged specialization of [inverse major
radius](name:inverse_of_major_radius): the averaging operator is applied to
the local reciprocal-major-radius quantity without introducing a species,
field-component, or process restriction.

sources.leaf_definition: Flux surface averaged 1/R
sources.parent_definition: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux

NAMES.name: inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Reciprocal square of total magnetic-field strength, providing a positive
magnetic-geometry factor for equilibrium and flux-surface-averaged transport
relations.
NAMES.long:
The inverse square of total magnetic-field strength is a local
magnetic-geometry factor that increases as the total field weakens and
remains positive wherever the field magnitude is nonzero.

It is defined as the reciprocal of the [square of magnetic-field
magnitude](name:square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude):

$$
B^{-2} = \frac{1}{B^2} = \frac{1}{\lvert \mathbf{B} \rvert^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic-field vector and $B$ is its
magnitude.

The quantity applies to the full magnetic field in an equilibrium plasma,
including all vector components and without restriction to a particle
population. At the parent level it is a local quantity with no flux-surface
or volume aggregation; it is distinct from the squared field magnitude
itself and from the reciprocal square of any selected field component.

The [flux-surface-averaged inverse square of magnetic-field
magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude)
is obtained by applying a flux-surface average to this local factor. The
averaging is a separate aggregation operation and does not alter the
reciprocal-square transformation.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface average of the reciprocal square of total magnetic-field
strength, a geometric coefficient in neoclassical and flux-surface-averaged
transport relations.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the flux-surface average of the reciprocal square of the
total magnetic-field strength on a nested magnetic surface. It captures
field-strength geometry independently of the magnetic-field direction.

The defining relation is

$$
\left\langle \frac{1}{|\mathbf{B}|^2} \right\rangle_\psi
=
\frac{\displaystyle \int_{S(\psi)} |\mathbf{B}|^{-2}\,\frac{dS}{|\nabla\psi|}}
{\displaystyle \int_{S(\psi)} \frac{dS}{|\nabla\psi|}}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic-field vector, $|\mathbf{B}|$ is its
magnitude, $\psi$ is the flux-surface label, $S(\psi)$ is the magnetic
surface labeled by $\psi$, $dS$ is its surface-area element, and
$\nabla\psi$ is the spatial gradient of the flux-surface label.

The quantity applies to the complete magnetic flux surface and uses the
inverse-$|\nabla\psi|$ weighting shown in the defining relation. It is not a
pointwise inverse-square field value and has no selection by magnetic-field
direction, component, species, or source.

It is the flux-surface-averaged transformation of the parent [inverse square
of magnetic-field
magnitude](name:inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude), with the
reciprocal square formed locally before averaging. It is distinct from
[flux-surface-averaged magnetic-field
magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_magnetic_field_magnitude) and
[flux-surface-averaged square of magnetic-field
magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude),
because nonlinear inversion and squaring do not commute with surface
averaging.

sources.leaf_definition: Flux surface averaged 1/B^2
sources.parent_definition: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux

NAMES.name: magnetic_field
NAMES.short:
Local total magnetic-induction vector in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ,
Z) frame, where R is major radius, φ is toroidal angle, and Z is vertical
height; it does not select a source contribution, perturbation state,
component, magnitude reduction, or evaluation locus.
NAMES.long:
Local total magnetic-induction vector is the magnetic flux-density vector at
a point, carrying both the local field direction and field strength. It is
the unqualified parent quantity before selecting a source contribution,
perturbation state, component, scalar reduction, spatial aggregation, or
evaluation locus.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the vector resolves
into radial, toroidal, and vertical components as

$$
\mathbf{B} = B_R\hat{\mathbf{R}} + B_\phi\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} + B_Z\hat{\mathbf{Z}}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is this local total magnetic-induction vector; $B_R$ is
its radial projection, $B_\phi$ is its [toroidal magnetic-field
component](name:toroidal_magnetic_field), and $B_Z$ is its [vertical
magnetic-field component](name:vertical_magnetic_field); and
$\hat{\mathbf{R}}$, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$, and $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ are
the corresponding basis vectors. The frame is right-handed with
$\hat{\mathbf{R}} \times \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} = \hat{\mathbf{Z}}$; $R$ is
major radius measured from the symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle
increasing counterclockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$, and
$Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies wherever a local magnetic induction is defined,
including confined plasma and surrounding vacuum regions, and no particle
species or population is selected or aggregated. It is pointwise and
vector-valued: it is not the [magnetic field
magnitude](name:magnetic_field_magnitude), a flux-surface-average magnetic
field, or an extremum such as the [maximum magnetic
field](name:maximum_magnetic_field). No cylindrical component, source
contribution, perturbation state, or named locus is implied by the
unqualified name.

When a [magnetic vector potential](name:magnetic_vector_potential)
$\mathbf{A}$ is used, $\mathbf{B} = \nabla \times \mathbf{A}$; $\mathbf{A}$
is the magnetic vector potential and $\nabla \times$ is the curl operator,
and a gage change affects $\mathbf{A}$ without changing $\mathbf{B}$.
Source-qualified fields such as the [vacuum magnetic
field](name:vacuum_magnetic_field) and [plasma magnetic
field](name:plasma_magnetic_field) are vector contributions of the same kind
and add vectorially when they belong to the same electromagnetic state; the
[toroidal vacuum magnetic field](name:toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field) is the
toroidal projection of the vacuum contribution. The [reference magnetic
field](name:reference_magnetic_field) is a reference total
magnetic-induction vector of the same kind, not a source-specific
contribution; the [toroidal magnetic field at the magnetic
axis](name:toroidal_magnetic_field_at_magnetic_axis) is the toroidal
projection evaluated at the magnetic-axis locus.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the vacuum toroidal magnetic-field component
is directed along increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: magnetic_field_at_pedestal_top_high_field_side
NAMES.short:
Magnetic field at the high-field-side pedestal top is the local total
magnetic-induction vector evaluated at the high-field-side pressure-pedestal
top. It retains field strength and direction before any component selection
or magnitude reduction.
NAMES.long:
Magnetic field at the high-field-side pedestal top is the local total
magnetic-induction vector evaluated at the high-field-side pressure-pedestal
top. It includes all directional components of the local magnetic field at
that locus and preserves both field strength and direction.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ major radius,
$\phi$ toroidal angle, and $Z$ vertical height, the vector may be decomposed
as

$$
\mathbf{B} = B_R \hat{R} + B_\phi \hat{\phi} + B_Z \hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field at the high-field-side pedestal
top, $B_R$, $B_\phi$, and $B_Z$ are its radial, toroidal, and vertical
components at the same locus, and $\hat{R}$, $\hat{\phi}$, and $\hat{Z}$ are
the corresponding unit basis vectors.

The scope is restricted to the high-field-side branch of the
pressure-pedestal top, not to arbitrary plasma positions or to the
low-field-side pedestal top. The high-field side is the smaller-major-radius
side in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where the
toroidal magnetic-field magnitude is larger. The quantity is local at that
locus; it is not a spatial average or a flux-surface average.

This is a vector quantity, not the scalar [magnetic-field magnitude at the
high-field-side pedestal
top](name:magnetic_field_magnitude_at_pedestal_top_high_field_side), a
single component, a projection, an absolute value, or a vacuum-field
approximation. The scalar magnetic-field magnitude at the same locus is the
Euclidean norm $|\mathbf{B}|$ of this vector and therefore removes
directional information while retaining the shared high-field-side
pedestal-top evaluation locus.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when a signed component of $\mathbf{B}$ points
along the positive direction of the basis vector used for that component; in
the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame these directions are
$+\hat{R}$, increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, and $+\hat{Z}$.

NAMES.name: magnetic_flux
NAMES.short:
Magnetic flux is the signed scalar surface integral of the magnetic field
through an oriented surface. Its sign is set by the chosen surface
orientation, while specializations identify the particular surface, field
contribution, or averaging convention.
NAMES.long:
Magnetic flux is a signed scalar associated with an oriented surface. It
represents the net normal component of the magnetic field threading that
surface; the flux itself is not a vector and is not directed, although its
sign depends on the surface orientation.

The magnetic flux $\Phi$ through an oriented surface $S$ is defined by the
surface integral:

$$
\Phi(S) = \int_S \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{A}
$$

where $\Phi(S)$ is the magnetic flux through $S$, $S$ is the oriented
surface, $\mathbf{B}$ is the [magnetic-field vector](name:magnetic_field),
$d\mathbf{A}=\hat{\mathbf{n}}\,dA$ is the oriented area element,
$\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the chosen unit normal to $S$, and $dA$ is the scalar
surface-area element.

The unqualified quantity denotes the net integral over the specified
oriented surface with no source restriction and no averaging. More specific
flux quantities supply the surface family, source contribution, projection,
or weighting that narrows this definition.

Magnetic flux is distinct from the local magnetic field, from a
magnetic-field component or magnitude, from a flux-coordinate label
normalized from a flux, and from a time derivative such as loop voltage.
[Poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) and [toroidal magnetic
flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux) are specializations obtained by choosing
different surfaces and orientations for the same integral; source-restricted
or weighted quantities, such as [poloidal-current-weighted average external
magnetic
flux](name:poloidal_current_weighted_average_external_magnetic_flux), retain
the magnetic-flux meaning while restricting the included magnetic field or
applying the stated averaging convention.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the net magnetic-field projection through the
specified surface is along the chosen orientation of its area element.

NAMES.name: external_magnetic_flux
NAMES.short:
External magnetic flux is the signed surface integral of the magnetic field
generated by sources outside the plasma current distribution over an
oriented surface.
NAMES.long:
External magnetic flux is the signed surface integral of the magnetic field
generated by sources outside the plasma current distribution over an
oriented surface. It is the source-separated member of the [magnetic
flux](name:magnetic_flux) family.

The defining surface integral is:

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{ext}}(S) = \int_S \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{ext}} \cdot d\mathbf{A}
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{ext}}(S)$ is the external magnetic flux associated with
the oriented surface $S$, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is the magnetic-field
vector produced by sources outside the plasma current distribution, and
$d\mathbf{A}$ is the oriented surface-area element.

The scope is the external-source contribution integrated over the complete
surface specified by a concrete specialization. At this parent level, no
poloidal or toroidal projection, spatial locus, or averaging weight is
imposed; the quantity is a signed surface aggregate, not a local
magnetic-field value, a flux-surface average, or a contribution generated by
the plasma current itself.

The child [average external magnetic
flux](name:average_external_magnetic_flux) is a concrete poloidal
specialization with averaging over the plasma cross-section. The related
[current-weighted average external magnetic
flux](name:current_weighted_average_external_magnetic_flux) uses
plasma-current weighting for that aggregation; both remain source-separated
instances of external magnetic flux.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the net external magnetic field points along
the positive normal of the oriented integration surface in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: average_external_magnetic_flux
NAMES.short:
Poloidal magnetic flux generated by external circuits and averaged over the
plasma cross-section, with weighting defined by each concrete variant.
NAMES.long:
External magnetic flux averaged over the plasma poloidal cross-section
represents the externally generated contribution to the poloidal flux
function, excluding flux produced by the plasma current. It is an
averaging-level specialization of external magnetic flux; concrete variants
can differ in their weighting and normalization.

For a weighting function $w(\mathbf{x})$, the general weighted average is

$$
\langle \psi_{\rm ext} \rangle_w = \frac{\int_{\mathcal{P}} w(\mathbf{x})\,\psi_{\rm ext}(\mathbf{x})\,dS}{\int_{\mathcal{P}} w(\mathbf{x})\,dS}
$$

where $\psi_{\rm ext}(\mathbf{x})$ is the externally generated poloidal
magnetic flux, $\mathbf{x}$ is position in the plasma poloidal cross-section
$\mathcal{P}$, $w(\mathbf{x})$ is the prescribed averaging weight, and $dS$
is the cross-sectional area element. The representative [current-weighted
average external magnetic
flux](name:current_weighted_average_external_magnetic_flux) uses the
toroidal current density as $w$ and the plasma current as the normalization.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the underlying poloidal flux is positive for
a vertical magnetic field in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction of the right-handed
cylindrical $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$ basis on the defining horizontal
disk.

NAMES.name: current_weighted_average_external_magnetic_flux
NAMES.short:
Current-weighted average external magnetic flux is the component-wise mean
of magnetic flux produced by sources outside the plasma, weighted over the
plasma current-carrying region by the corresponding current density. It
excludes flux generated by the plasma current itself; concrete children
specify components such as the poloidal component.
NAMES.long:
Current-weighted average external magnetic flux is the component-wise mean
of externally generated magnetic flux over the plasma current-carrying
region. It represents the part of the magnetic flux linked by the plasma
current that is generated by sources outside the plasma, with the plasma
self-generated flux excluded.

For any component $a$, the current-weighted component average is

$$
\overline{\Phi}_{\mathrm{ext},a}^{J}
=
\frac{\int_{\Omega_a} \Phi_{\mathrm{ext},a}(\mathbf{x})\, j_a(\mathbf{x})\, dA}
     {\int_{\Omega_a} j_a(\mathbf{x})\, dA}
$$

where $a$ labels a magnetic-flux component,
$\overline{\Phi}_{\mathrm{ext},a}^{J}$ is the current-weighted average
external magnetic-flux component, $\Phi_{\mathrm{ext},a}(\mathbf{x})$ is the
externally generated magnetic-flux component at position $\mathbf{x}$,
$j_a(\mathbf{x})$ is the corresponding plasma current-density component used
as the weight, $\Omega_a$ is the current-carrying plasma cross-section for
that component, and $dA$ is its area element. The denominator is the
corresponding total plasma current component and must be nonzero.

This parent quantity does not specify a particular magnetic-flux component
or surface orientation. Concrete component names supply that specialization;
for example, [poloidal current-weighted average external magnetic
flux](name:poloidal_current_weighted_average_external_magnetic_flux) is the
poloidal component. External magnetic flux includes contributions from
active conductors and passive induced currents outside the plasma and
excludes flux produced by the plasma current.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the current-density-weighted integral of the
selected external magnetic-flux component has the same sign as the total
plasma current component used for its normalization, with both signs
evaluated in the positive orientation of that component.

NAMES.name: magnetic_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short:
Vector magnetic-flux contribution of the pressure-gradient-driven
diamagnetic response in a plasma equilibrium, defined relative to the
corresponding reference magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
The diamagnetic magnetic-flux contribution is the vector magnetic flux
associated with the pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic response in a
plasma equilibrium, measured relative to a corresponding reference field
without that response.

For an integration surface $S$, the contribution is defined by

$$
\boldsymbol{\Phi}_{\mathrm{dia}} = \int_S \Delta \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{dia}}\,dS
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Phi}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the diamagnetic magnetic-flux
vector, $\Delta \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the equilibrium magnetic-field
difference attributable to the pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic
response, and $dS$ is the scalar surface-area element on $S$.

This quantity applies to the plasma equilibrium as a whole at the surface
used to define the magnetic flux. It retains the vector component
information and the aggregation over the selected surface; it is not
restricted to a single axis projection, species, normalization, or spatial
region.

The reference-field subtraction excludes magnetic flux already present
without the diamagnetic response and distinguishes this contribution from
the total equilibrium magnetic flux. The [toroidal magnetic flux due to
diamagnetic drift](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) is
the toroidal component of this general vector quantity.

Components are resolved in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame,
where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical
height.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when a resolved magnetic-flux component points
along the corresponding positive basis direction of the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame; the toroidal component is positive toward
increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: magnetic_shear_at_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Magnetic shear at a flux surface is the logarithmic derivative of the safety
factor with respect to the outward normalized toroidal flux radius.
NAMES.long:
Magnetic shear at flux surface

The defining relation is

$$
\hat{s} = \frac{\rho}{q}\frac{dq}{d\rho}
$$

where $\hat{s}$ is the magnetic shear at the specified flux surface, $q$ is
the safety factor, and $\rho$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius
increasing outward from the magnetic axis. The derivative is taken with
respect to that coordinate.

This quantity is a single flux-surface evaluation, not an average over
neighboring flux surfaces or an integral across a plasma region. The
definition requires a nonzero safety factor and an existing derivative. It
is distinct from the unnormalized safety-factor derivative and from magnetic
shear defined using geometric minor radius; a nonlinear change of radial
label generally changes the shear.

The [magnetic shear at an internal transport
barrier](name:magnetic_shear_at_internal_transport_barrier) is a
locus-specific specialization of this quantity, using the same defining
relation at the barrier's flux-surface location.

A surface formed by points sharing the same magnetic-flux label in a
nested-flux-surface configuration. Where $\psi(R, Z) = \mathrm{const}$,
$\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux.

NAMES.name: magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short:
Magnetic shear evaluated at the magnetic axis, defined as the limiting
normalized logarithmic derivative of the safety factor with respect to
normalized toroidal flux radius.
NAMES.long:
Magnetic shear at the magnetic axis is the limiting value of [magnetic
shear](name:magnetic_shear_at_flux_surface) as the flux-surface label
approaches the magnetic axis.

Using the [normalized toroidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate)
$\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ as the radial label, with
$\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}=0$ at the magnetic axis, the defining relation is

$$
s_{\mathrm{axis}} = \lim_{\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}\to 0} \frac{\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}}{q}\frac{dq}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}}
$$

where $q$ is the safety factor and $s_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the magnetic-shear
limit. For a smooth equilibrium with finite [safety factor at the magnetic
axis](name:safety_factor_at_magnetic_axis), this limit is zero. It therefore
differs from evaluations on finite-radius surfaces such as [magnetic shear
at the plasma boundary](name:magnetic_shear_at_plasma_boundary).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $q^{-1}dq/d\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is
positive as the normalized toroidal flux radius increases outward from the
magnetic axis.

NAMES.name: major_length_of_plasma_filament
NAMES.short:
Length of the major oblique side of a plasma-filament cross-section,
inclined relative to the major-radius axis and distinct from the
height-oriented side.
NAMES.long:
Major length of a plasma filament is the Euclidean length of the oblique
parallelogram side associated with the major-radius direction.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the side lies in the
poloidal $R$-$Z$ cross-section and is defined by

$$
L_{\mathrm{major}} = \sqrt{(\Delta R)^2 + (\Delta Z)^2}
$$

where $L_{\mathrm{major}}$ is the major oblique-side length, $\Delta R$ is
the difference in major-radius coordinates between the side endpoints, and
$\Delta Z$ is the corresponding difference in vertical coordinates.

This quantity applies to one discrete plasma current-carrying filament
element and describes only its major oblique side. It is an individual
geometric length, not a sum, average, or aggregate over filament elements,
and it excludes the other oblique side represented by the [minor length of a
plasma filament](name:minor_length_of_plasma_filament).

It is the major-qualified component of length of a plasma filament,
selecting the side associated with the major-radius direction rather than
defining an additional length to be added to the parent quantity. Its
inclination is described separately by the [inclination angle of a plasma
filament](name:alpha_angle_of_plasma_filament).

sources.leaf_definition: Length of the parallelogram side inclined with angle alpha with respect to the major radius axis
sources.parent_definition: Parallelogram description of the element

NAMES.name: maximum_magnetic_field
NAMES.short:
Largest value attained by a selected magnetic-field quantity over its
specified evaluation domain, without fixing its source, projection,
magnitude, or locus.
NAMES.long:
The maximum magnetic-field quantity is the extremal value of a selected
magnetic-field quantity evaluated over a specified domain. It is a
domain-level reduction of the local [magnetic field](name:magnetic_field),
rather than the local magnetic-field vector itself.

The maximum operation can be represented abstractly as

$$
M = \max_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{D}} Q(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $M$ is the resulting maximum magnetic-field value, $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is
the selected local magnetic-field quantity, $\mathbf{x}$ is an evaluation
point, and $\mathcal{D}$ is the specified evaluation domain.

This parent fixes the maximum aggregation over the domain but imposes no
particular magnetic-field source, physical state, projection, magnitude
selection, population, or plasma or vacuum region. The result is one
extremal value for the selected domain, not a local value, average,
integral, or mode-resolved quantity.

It is distinct from the local [magnetic field](name:magnetic_field) and does
not by itself determine whether the selected quantity is a total field,
source contribution, signed component, or field magnitude. The child
[maximum magnetic-field magnitude](name:maximum_magnetic_field_magnitude)
specializes this parent by selecting the magnitude of the total local
magnetic-field vector before applying the maximum operation.

NAMES.name: minor_length_of_plasma_filament
NAMES.short:
Length of the minor oblique parallelogram side of a plasma-filament element,
inclined at angle beta to the vertical height axis.
NAMES.long:
The minor oblique parallelogram-side length of a plasma-filament element is
the Euclidean length of the side inclined at angle beta to the vertical
height direction. It characterizes one side of the element's oblique
cross-sectional geometry.

The side length is defined by the separation of its two endpoints:

$$
\ell_\beta = \left\lVert \mathbf{x}_{\beta,2} - \mathbf{x}_{\beta,1} \right\rVert
$$

where $\ell_\beta$ is the minor side length, $\mathbf{x}_{\beta,1}$ and
$\mathbf{x}_{\beta,2}$ are the position vectors of its endpoints, and
$\lVert\cdot\rVert$ denotes the Euclidean norm. The inclination angle
$\beta$ is measured relative to the vertical height direction in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius,
$\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies to one discrete plasma current-carrying filament
element and is neither summed nor averaged over elements. It excludes the
complementary major oblique side and therefore is distinct from [major
length of the plasma filament](name:major_length_of_plasma_filament).

This quantity specializes length of the plasma filament by selecting its
minor, beta-inclined side. The paired major-length quantity selects the
complementary oblique side of the same element.

sources.leaf_definition: Length of the parallelogram side inclined with angle beta with respect to the height axis
sources.parent_definition: Parallelogram description of the element

NAMES.name: non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field
NAMES.short:
Non-axisymmetric magnetic-field vector of the local vacuum induction
generated by external coils, with its toroidally averaged component removed.
NAMES.long:
The non-axisymmetric magnetic field $\mathbf{B}_{\rm NA}$ is the vector part
of the external-coil vacuum [magnetic induction](name:magnetic_field) that
varies with toroidal angle after its toroidally averaged component is
removed. It retains the full field direction rather than selecting a
cylindrical component or a magnitude.

The non-axisymmetric component is defined by

$$
\mathbf{B}_{\rm NA}(R,\phi,Z) = \mathbf{B}_{\rm vac}(R,\phi,Z) - \left\langle \mathbf{B}_{\rm vac} \right\rangle_\phi(R,Z)
$$

where $\mathbf{B}_{\rm NA}$ is the non-axisymmetric magnetic induction,
$\mathbf{B}_{\rm vac}$ is the magnetic induction generated by external coil
currents with plasma-current contributions omitted, and $\langle
\mathbf{B}_{\rm vac} \rangle_\phi$ is its average over the toroidal angle.
The variables $R$, $\phi$, and $Z$ are respectively major radius, toroidal
angle, and vertical height in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$
frame.

This quantity is a local vector field defined for the external-coil vacuum
contribution, without restriction to a particular plasma population or
spatial region. Its aggregation convention is the removal of the
toroidal-angle average, so only non-axisymmetric toroidal variation remains.

It excludes the toroidally symmetric vacuum field, magnetic induction
generated by plasma currents, and any scalar magnitude reduction. It
therefore does not represent the full local [magnetic
induction](name:magnetic_field) when those omitted source contributions are
present.

The vector is the common parent for its cylindrical projections: the [radial
non-axisymmetric magnetic
field](name:radial_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field), [toroidal
non-axisymmetric magnetic
field](name:toroidal_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field), and [vertical
non-axisymmetric magnetic
field](name:vertical_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field) each resolve this same
vector along one direction of the right-handed cylindrical frame.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when a resolved component points along its
corresponding positive basis direction in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: normal_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field
NAMES.short:
Signed normal projection of the external-coil vacuum magnetic field with its
toroidally averaged component removed, evaluated on a generic control
surface.
NAMES.long:
Normal non-axisymmetric magnetic field is the signed component of the
toroidally varying external-coil vacuum magnetic field normal to a generic
control surface. It is a scalar projection evaluated at points on that
surface, rather than the full magnetic-field vector.

The defining projection is

$$
B_n(R,\phi,Z)=\mathbf{B}_{\rm NA}(R,\phi,Z)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}(R,\phi,Z)
$$

where $B_n$ is the normal magnetic-field component, $\mathbf{B}_{\rm NA}$ is
the [non-axisymmetric magnetic field](name:non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field),
and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the oriented unit normal to the control surface.
The coordinates $R$, $\phi$, and $Z$ are major radius, toroidal angle, and
vertical height in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

This quantity applies to the external-coil vacuum contribution at each
selected point of a generic control surface, which is not assumed to be a
magnetic flux surface. Its aggregation convention is the inherited removal
of the toroidal-angle average from the vacuum field; no surface or area
average is implied.

It excludes the toroidally symmetric vacuum field and magnetic-field
contributions generated by plasma currents. It also excludes tangential
components and is distinct from cylindrical projections such as the
[vertical non-axisymmetric magnetic
field](name:vertical_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field); the normal direction
is defined by the control surface rather than by the cylindrical basis.

The scalar $B_n$ is the surface-normal component of the vector
[non-axisymmetric magnetic field](name:non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field).
Reversing the assigned orientation of the control-surface normal reverses
$B_n$, while the parent vector itself is unchanged.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the non-axisymmetric magnetic field points in
the direction of the chosen positive unit normal to the control surface.

NAMES.name: normalized_minor_radius_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless minor-radius label of a magnetic flux surface, obtained by
normalizing its major-radius half-width to a specified positive reference
length.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the dimensionless minor-radius label assigned to a magnetic
flux surface from its radial extent in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{minor}} = \frac{R_{\max}-R_{\min}}{2L_{\mathrm{ref}}}
$$

where $R_{\max}$ and $R_{\min}$ are the maximum and minimum major-radius
coordinates of the surface, each in m, and $L_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the
specified positive reference length in m.

The label is a geometric normalization of the surface half-width; it is not
a magnetic-flux normalization and therefore is distinct from the [normalized
toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate). Its
numerical value depends on the chosen reference length.

sources.parent_definition: Flux surface characteristics

NAMES.name: normalized_plasma_internal_inductance
NAMES.short:
Normalized internal inductance measures internal poloidal magnetic energy
relative to squared plasma current and the plasma's geometric-axis major
radius.
NAMES.long:
Normalized internal inductance measures the poloidal magnetic energy
contained within the entire plasma using the geometric-axis normalization
known as li(3). It characterizes poloidal-field peaking associated with the
plasma current distribution.

The normalized internal inductance $l_i$ is defined by

$$
l_i = \frac{2\int_V B_{\mathrm{p}}^2\,dV}{\mu_0^2 I_{\mathrm{p}}^2 R_{\mathrm{geo}}}
$$

where $B_{\mathrm{p}}$ is the poloidal magnetic-field magnitude, $V$ is the
plasma volume, $dV$ is a volume element, $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability,
$I_{\mathrm{p}}$ is the total toroidal plasma current, and
$R_{\mathrm{geo}}$ is the major radius of the plasma's geometric axis.

The integral covers the full plasma volume and excludes magnetic energy
outside the plasma and energy associated with the toroidal magnetic field.
The normalization requires nonzero plasma current and uses the geometric
axis rather than the magnetic axis.

The corresponding dimensional internal inductance $L_i$ satisfies $L_i =
\mu_0 R_{\mathrm{geo}}l_i/2$. This normalization distinguishes the quantity
from dimensional [plasma inductance](name:plasma_inductance).

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_beta
NAMES.short:
Normalized toroidal beta scales the whole-plasma toroidal pressure ratio by
minor radius and reference toroidal field relative to plasma current using
the Troyon convention.
NAMES.long:
Normalized toroidal beta compares whole-plasma pressure with toroidal
magnetic pressure and applies the Troyon size-and-current normalization. It
is a normalized member of the [beta family](name:beta), rather than an
unmodified pressure ratio.

With dimensional inputs represented by their numerical values in coherent
SI, the defining normalization is

$$\beta = \frac{2\mu_0 \langle p\rangle}{B^2}$$

where $\beta_{\mathrm{N}}$ is normalized toroidal beta, $\beta_{\mathrm{t}}$
is [toroidal beta](name:toroidal_beta), $a$ is the plasma minor radius,
$B_0$ is the reference toroidal magnetic-field magnitude, and $I_p$ is the
total plasma-current magnitude. The factor 100 implements the percentage
convention for beta, while the denominator factor $10^{-6}$ implements the
conventional Troyon current scaling.

The underlying pressure ratio is $\beta_{\mathrm{t}} = 2\mu_0\langle
p\rangle/B_0^2$, where $\mu_0$ is vacuum permeability and $\langle p\rangle$
is total perpendicular plasma pressure averaged over the plasma volume. The
reference field is the same field used in the Troyon normalization.

The pressure includes contributions from all plasma populations, including
thermal and nonthermal populations; thermal-pressure-only normalized beta is
a distinct quantity. This is a global volume-averaged pressure measure, not
a point-local or pedestal beta. It is defined only for nonzero reference
toroidal field and plasma-current magnitude.

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate
NAMES.short:
Normalized toroidal flux coordinate labels magnetic surfaces by the square
root of their axis-to-boundary toroidal-flux fraction, spanning zero at the
magnetic axis to one at the equilibrium boundary.
NAMES.long:
Normalized toroidal flux coordinate

The coordinate is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = \rho_{\mathrm{tor}}/\rho_{\mathrm{tor,b}}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the normalized toroidal flux coordinate,
$\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal flux coordinate of the selected
surface, and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,b}}$ is the [toroidal flux coordinate at the
plasma boundary](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_plasma_boundary). Both
unnormalized coordinates use the same magnetic-axis origin and flux
reference.

Equivalently, $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}^2 =
(\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}-\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}})/(\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,b}}-\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}})$,
where $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the
selected surface, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}$ and $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,b}}$
are its magnetic-axis and equilibrium-boundary values.

On nested closed magnetic surfaces, the nonnegative coordinate is constant
on each surface, zero at the magnetic axis, and one at the last closed flux
surface used as the boundary. It is a surface label, not a surface average,
volume integral, geometric distance, toroidal angle, or vector component.
The boundary normalization must be nonzero; the definition does not itself
specify a continuation outside the last closed flux surface. Signed
line-of-sight variants attach an additional geometric branch sign, while
their absolute value retains this normalization.

Locus-specific quantities, such as the [coordinate at a constraint
position](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_constraint_position),
evaluate this same label on the magnetic surface containing the specified
position. The [coordinate at the
separatrix](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_separatrix) equals
one when the separatrix defines the equilibrium boundary.

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_constraint_position
NAMES.short:
Normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the constraint position gives a
magnetic-surface label ranging from zero at the magnetic axis to one at the
equilibrium boundary.
NAMES.long:
Normalized toroidal flux coordinate

At the constraint position, the coordinate is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = \rho_{\mathrm{tor}}/\rho_{\mathrm{tor,b}}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the normalized toroidal flux coordinate
at the constraint position, $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the unnormalized
toroidal flux coordinate of the magnetic surface containing that position,
and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,b}}$ is its [value at the plasma
boundary](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_plasma_boundary).

The quantity applies pointwise at one specified constraint position,
independently of which physical quantity is constrained; it is not an
average over positions or a sum over constraints. It specifies a
magnetic-surface label, not the constrained physical quantity, an
unnormalized flux radius, or a geometric distance.

It is the locus-specific evaluation of the parent [normalized toroidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate). For nested closed
magnetic surfaces and a nonzero boundary coordinate, it spans zero at the
magnetic axis to one at the equilibrium boundary. When that boundary is a
separatrix, the outer endpoint is the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate
at the separatrix](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_separatrix).

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_minimum_absolute_safety_factor
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless magnetic-surface label giving the normalized toroidal flux at
the closed surface where the magnitude of the safety factor reaches its
minimum.
NAMES.long:
This quantity identifies the nested closed magnetic surface on which the
magnitude of the safety factor is minimized, using the normalized toroidal
magnetic-flux coordinate of that surface.

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the normalized toroidal-flux coordinate,
$\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the
evaluated surface, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}$ is its value at the magnetic
axis, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}}$ is its value at the equilibrium
boundary.

The value is a single equilibrium coordinate evaluated at the surface of
minimum safety-factor magnitude; it is not a flux-surface profile, an
average over surfaces, or the minimum safety-factor value itself. It is
distinct from a cylindrical radial distance and from a local vector
component. The parent [normalized toroidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate) supplies the
coordinate definition, while [normalized poloidal flux coordinate at minimum
absolute safety
factor](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_at_minimum_absolute_safety_factor)
gives the analogous poloidal-flux label at the same physical locus.

NAMES.name: outer_radius_of_plasma_filament
NAMES.short:
Outer radius of a plasma filament is the geometric radius of the outer
circular boundary of the annular cross-section representing a
current-carrying plasma filament. It marks the external boundary of the
conducting annular region.
NAMES.long:
Outer radius of a plasma filament is the geometric radius of the outer
circular boundary of the annular cross-section representing a
current-carrying plasma filament. It marks the external boundary of the
conducting annular region; material outside this boundary is not part of
that annular filament cross-section.

For the outer circular boundary in the poloidal cross-section of the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the outer radius
$r_\mathrm{outer}$ is the distance from the filament cross-section center
$(R_c, Z_c)$ to any point $(R, Z)$ on that boundary:

$$
r_\mathrm{outer} = \sqrt{(R - R_c)^2 + (Z - Z_c)^2}
$$

where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical height,
$(R_c, Z_c)$ is the center of the annular cross-section, and $(R, Z)$ lies
on the outer circular boundary.

The quantity applies only to the outer boundary of an annular
plasma-filament cross-section and is a single geometric radius for that
boundary, not an average over the conducting region. It is the outer member
of radius of a plasma filament, paired with the [inner
radius](name:inner_radius_of_plasma_filament) $r_\mathrm{inner}$; by
definition $0 \le r_\mathrm{inner} \le r_\mathrm{outer}$, and the
current-carrying cross-section occupies the annular region between the two
radii. For the same annular geometry, the area of a plasma filament $A$
satisfies $A = \pi(r_\mathrm{outer}^2 - r_\mathrm{inner}^2)$, where $A$ is
the area of the annular plasma-filament cross-section and $\pi$ is the
circle constant. This quantity excludes the major radius of the filament
center about the toroidal symmetry axis and rectangular cross-section
dimensions such as [plasma filament width](name:plasma_filament_width) and
[height of a plasma filament](name:height_of_plasma_filament).

NAMES.name: parallel_current_density_at_constraint_position
NAMES.short:
Parallel current density at a specified constraint position is the signed
scalar field-aligned component of conventional current density associated
with an equilibrium constraint locus. It sums charge transport from all
charged-particle populations unless a narrower component or population is
specified.
NAMES.long:
Parallel current density at a specified constraint position is the signed
scalar field-aligned component of conventional current density associated
with an equilibrium constraint position. The constraint position supplies
the spatial locus or selected magnetic surface to which the value applies,
while narrower quantities may add an averaging or population qualifier.

The field-aligned projection is defined by

$$
j_\parallel = \mathbf{j} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}
$$

where $j_\parallel$ is this parallel current density, $\mathbf{j}$ is the
[current density](name:current_density), $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the unit
vector along the local [magnetic field](name:magnetic_field), $\mathbf{B}$
is the local magnetic-field vector, and $|\mathbf{B}|$ is its magnitude.

The supported scope is the conventional charge-current sum over all
charged-particle populations at the specified constraint locus unless a
narrower population is explicitly specified. This excludes the unprojected
[current density](name:current_density), other vector components of current
density, and current-density quantities not associated with a constraint
position.

Narrower quantities specialize this parent by retaining the same
field-aligned projection and constraint-position scope while adding further
qualification. For example, the [flux-surface-averaged parallel current
density at constraint
position](name:flux_surface_averaged_parallel_current_density_at_constraint_position)
is the flux-surface average of $j_\parallel$ over the selected closed
magnetic surface; this parent itself does not impose that averaging
convention.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the conventional current density has a
component in the direction of the local magnetic field.

NAMES.name: plasma_current
NAMES.short:
Plasma current is the signed integral of a plasma current-density component
over a poloidal cross-section; its global equilibrium value is the net
toroidal current.
NAMES.long:
Plasma current represents conventional electric charge transport carried by
the plasma, integrated over a poloidal cross-section and resolved along a
specified direction. Its global equilibrium value is the total toroidal
current through the full plasma poloidal cross-section.

The component-resolved current is defined by

$$
I_a(S) = \int_S \mathbf{j}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{e}}_a\,dA
$$

where $I_a(S)$ is the integrated plasma current in direction $a$, $a$ labels
the selected component, $S$ is the selected poloidal cross-sectional region,
$\mathbf{j}$ is the total plasma [current density](name:current_density),
$\hat{\mathbf{e}}_a$ is the local unit vector along that component's
positive direction, and $dA$ is an unsigned area element.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $R$ is distance from the
symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The
global plasma current is $I_p=I_\phi(S_p)$, where $I_p$ denotes the total
toroidal plasma current, $S_p$ is the full plasma poloidal cross-section,
and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\phi$ points toward increasing toroidal angle.

The current density includes all charged-particle contributions with their
electric-charge signs. The integral is therefore a net conventional current,
not a particle flux or a sum of unsigned current magnitudes. Currents
carried by external coils and conducting structures are excluded.

The [cumulative plasma current inside a flux
surface](name:cumulative_inside_flux_surface_plasma_current) restricts the
integration region to the poloidal cross-section enclosed by that surface
while retaining the specified current component. For the toroidal component,
it equals the global plasma current when its integration region coincides
with the full plasma cross-section.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the integrated conventional-current
contribution is along the selected positive component direction; for the
global toroidal current, this is increasing $\phi$, counterclockwise when
viewed from above along the positive vertical axis.

NAMES.name: poloidal_angle_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Poloidal angle at a point on a flux surface, measured about the magnetic
axis from the outward horizontal ray. It increases clockwise in the poloidal
cross-section, with major radius to the right and vertical height upward.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal angle of flux surface

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major
radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the angle is
defined by:

$$
\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(Z_{\mathrm{axis}} - Z,\; R - R_{\mathrm{axis}})
$$

Here, $\theta$ is the poloidal angle at the point; $R$ and $Z$ are its major
radius and vertical height; and $R_{\mathrm{axis}}$ and $Z_{\mathrm{axis}}$
are the major radius and vertical height of the magnetic axis. The function
$\operatorname{atan2}$ is the quadrant-resolving two-argument inverse
tangent. The angle is undefined at the magnetic axis, where both arguments
vanish, and values differing by $2\pi$ represent the same direction.

The quantity applies pointwise to positions on a flux surface; it is not a
single angle for the entire surface and is not a surface average. It is a
geometric positional angle, distinct from a straight-field-line poloidal
angle. The [poloidal magnetic flux at a flux
surface](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_flux_surface) identifies the
surface, while this angle distinguishes positions around it. It uses the
same geometric convention as the [poloidal angle at a measurement
position](name:poloidal_angle_of_measurement_position), with the evaluation
locus here being a flux surface.

A surface formed by points sharing the same magnetic-flux label in a
nested-flux-surface configuration. Where $\psi(R, Z) = \mathrm{const}$,
$\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the angle increases clockwise from the
outward horizontal ray in the poloidal cross-section, with $R$ increasing to
the right and $Z$ increasing upward.

NAMES.name: poloidal_angle_of_gyrokinetic_eigenmode
NAMES.short:
The geometric poloidal angle coordinate associated with a gyrokinetic
eigenmode, measured about the flux-surface cross-section center from the
low-field-side midplane.
NAMES.long:
This geometric coordinate labels position around the poloidal cross-section
associated with a gyrokinetic eigenmode. It expresses poloidal variation of
equilibrium and eigenmode quantities and refines the general [poloidal
angle](name:poloidal_angle_of_flux_surface) concept for the eigenmode
coordinate.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the angle is defined
relative to the geometric center $(R_0,Z_0)$ of the flux-surface
cross-section:

$$
\theta = \operatorname{wrap}_{[-\pi,\pi]}\left[-\operatorname{atan2}(Z-Z_0,R-R_0)\right]
$$

where $R$ is major radius, $Z$ is vertical height, $R_0$ and $Z_0$ are the
center coordinates, and `wrap` selects the representative angle in the
stated interval. The coordinate is geometric rather than a coil-orientation
parameter or a straight-field-line angle.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when moving clockwise from the low-field-side
midplane in the poloidal cross-section.

NAMES.name: poloidal_angle_of_plasma_boundary_gap
NAMES.short:
Poloidal angle of a plasma-boundary gap specifies its measurement direction,
measured clockwise from the outward horizontal direction in the poloidal
cross-section.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal angle of plasma boundary gap

For a nonzero directed segment aligned with the measurement direction, the
defining relation is:

$$\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(Z_{\mathrm{axis}} - Z,\; R - R_{\mathrm{axis}})$$

where $\theta$ is the gap-measurement direction angle, $(R_0, Z_0)$ and
$(R_1, Z_1)$ are the segment's start and end coordinates, and
$\operatorname{atan2}$ is the two-argument inverse tangent. The right-handed
cylindrical frame is $(R, \phi, Z)$, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is
toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The angle applies separately to each plasma-boundary gap, not to an average
over the boundary. It describes a direction rather than the positional
poloidal angle of the gap's reference point about the magnetic axis. Zero
corresponds to the outward horizontal direction, and angles differing by a
full turn describe the same direction.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the measurement direction rotates clockwise
from increasing $R$ toward decreasing $Z$, viewed with $R$ to the right and
$Z$ upward.

NAMES.name: poloidal_beta
NAMES.short:
Poloidal beta compares volume-averaged total perpendicular plasma pressure
with a magnetic-pressure scale set by the net plasma current and reference
major radius.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal beta is the ratio of volume-averaged total perpendicular plasma
pressure to a reference poloidal magnetic-pressure scale. The reference
scale is defined by a whole-plasma, current-based normalization rather than
by the poloidal field at a particular point.

The defining pressure ratio and its current-based normalization are

$$\beta = \frac{2\mu_0 \langle p\rangle}{B^2}$$

Here $\beta_{\mathrm{p}}$ is poloidal beta, $p$ is total perpendicular
plasma pressure, $V$ is the entire plasma volume, $dV$ is a volume element,
and $\langle p\rangle$ is the pressure averaged over that volume. The
quantities $R_0$, $I_{\mathrm{p}}$, and $\mu_0$ are the reference major
radius, net toroidal plasma current, and vacuum permeability, respectively.
The effective reference poloidal field $B_{\mathrm{p,ref}}$ satisfies
$B_{\mathrm{p,ref}}^2=\mu_0^2 I_{\mathrm{p}}^2R_0/(2V)$; it is not a local
poloidal-field magnitude.

The pressure includes contributions from all plasma populations, rather than
electrons alone or only thermal particles. This global quantity differs from
a point-local or pedestal-top electron beta. The definition requires nonzero
net plasma current and a positive reference major radius.

Poloidal beta is the poloidal-field-normalized member of the
[beta](name:beta) family, whereas [toroidal beta](name:toroidal_beta) uses a
reference toroidal magnetic field. For the same pressure average and a
combined reference field formed by adding the squared poloidal and toroidal
reference fields, $1/\beta=1/\beta_{\mathrm{p}}+1/\beta_{\mathrm{t}}$, where
$\beta$ is combined-field beta and $\beta_{\mathrm{t}}$ is toroidal beta.

NAMES.name: poloidal_current_function
NAMES.short:
Major-radius-weighted toroidal magnetic-field function used in axisymmetric
equilibria and vacuum fields; in ideal-MHD plasma it is constant on each
magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal current function is the major-radius-weighted toroidal magnetic
field that defines the equilibrium $F$-function. It provides a common
description for the toroidal field in axisymmetric plasma equilibria and in
current-free vacuum magnetic fields.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the defining relation is

$$
F(R,Z) = R B_\phi(R,Z)
$$

where $F$ is the poloidal current function, $R$ is major radius measured
from the machine symmetry axis, $B_\phi$ is the toroidal component of the
magnetic field, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For an axisymmetric ideal-MHD plasma equilibrium, $F$ is a flux function: it
is constant on each nested magnetic flux surface and can therefore be
expressed as a function of the poloidal magnetic-flux coordinate. The
quantity describes the full toroidal magnetic field represented by the
equilibrium; it is not a surface or volume integral, an average, or a
restriction to a particular current source.

The [vacuum poloidal current
function](name:vacuum_poloidal_current_function) is the corresponding
external-coil contribution in a current-free vacuum region, whereas the
unqualified quantity denotes the general $F$-function. The [product of the
poloidal current function and its derivative with respect to the poloidal
magnetic flux
coordinate](name:product_of_poloidal_current_function_and_derivative_of_poloidal_current_function_with_respect_to_poloidal_magnetic_flux_coordinate)
is a distinct Grad–Shafranov source term formed from $F$ and its flux
derivative.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $B_\phi$ points in the direction of
increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Diamagnetic function (F=R B_Phi)

NAMES.name: poloidal_current_weighted_average_external_magnetic_flux
NAMES.short:
Poloidal magnetic flux from all external active coils and passive loops is
averaged over the plasma cross-section with toroidal-current-density
weighting, excluding plasma-generated flux.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux averaged with toroidal plasma current density
represents the externally generated flux linked by the distributed plasma
current. It is the poloidal specialization of [current-weighted average
external magnetic
flux](name:current_weighted_average_external_magnetic_flux), and an
averaged, source-separated form of [magnetic flux](name:magnetic_flux).

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major
radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counterclockwise when viewed
from above, and $Z$ is vertical height, the average is defined by

$$
\overline{\Phi}_{\mathrm{p,ext}} = \frac{1}{I_{\mathrm{p}}}\int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{p}}}\Phi_{\mathrm{p,ext}}(R,Z)\,j_\phi(R,Z)\,dA_{RZ}
$$

where $\overline{\Phi}_{\mathrm{p,ext}}$ is the current-weighted average
external poloidal magnetic flux, $\Omega_{\mathrm{p}}$ is the plasma
poloidal cross-section, $j_\phi$ is the toroidal plasma current density, and
$dA_{RZ}$ is the poloidal cross-sectional area element. The normalization is
the signed [plasma current](name:plasma_current),
$I_{\mathrm{p}}=\int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{p}}}j_\phi\,dA_{RZ}$. The local
external contribution $\Phi_{\mathrm{p,ext}}$ follows the [poloidal magnetic
flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) definition: flux through a horizontal
disk centered on the toroidal symmetry axis and bounded by the toroidal
circle through the evaluation point.

The external contribution includes all active coils and passive conducting
loops, including induced currents in conducting structures, but excludes
flux generated by the plasma current itself. The weighting uses signed
toroidal plasma current density, not its absolute value; consequently, this
quantity is distinct from an unweighted area average. The definition
requires nonzero total plasma current.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the external disk flux, averaged with the
signed weights $j_\phi/I_{\mathrm{p}}$, threads the horizontal disks in the
$+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: poloidal_length_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Poloidal arc length of a closed magnetic-flux-surface contour in an
equilibrium poloidal cross-section, measuring the perimeter of that selected
surface.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal length is the perimeter of the closed contour formed by one
selected magnetic flux surface in a poloidal cross-section. It is a
geometric property of the surface boundary, rather than its enclosed area,
volume, or toroidal circumference.

The contour length is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$
frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is
vertical height:

$$
L_{\mathrm{pol}} = \int_{\theta_a}^{\theta_b} \sqrt{\left(\frac{dR(\theta)}{d\theta}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{dZ(\theta)}{d\theta}\right)^2}\,d\theta
$$

Here $L_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the poloidal length, $\theta$ is any smooth
parameter along the contour, $R(\theta)$ and $Z(\theta)$ are its cylindrical
coordinate functions, and $\theta_a$ and $\theta_b$ are parameter values at
the same contour point after one complete circuit. The contour is taken at
fixed toroidal angle $\phi$.

The quantity applies to one magnetic flux surface and includes the complete
closed poloidal contour, with no averaging or summation over multiple
surfaces. It excludes local arc segments and geometric quantities associated
with the enclosed region. The selected surface may be labeled by the
[normalized poloidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate).

Unlike [elongation of a flux surface](name:elongation_of_flux_surface),
which describes a scale-independent cross-sectional shape ratio, the
poloidal length retains the absolute geometric scale of the contour.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_field
NAMES.short:
Poloidal magnetic field is the strength of local magnetic induction in the
plane containing the toroidal symmetry axis and the evaluation point,
excluding the toroidal contribution.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic field is the magnitude of the projection of the local
[magnetic induction](name:magnetic_field) onto the poloidal plane. It
retains the radial and vertical contributions while excluding the toroidal
contribution.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major
radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, it is defined
by:

$$
B_{\mathrm{p}} = \sqrt{B_R^2 + B_Z^2}
$$

where $B_{\mathrm{p}}$ is the poloidal magnetic-field strength, $B_R$ is the
cylindrical radial magnetic-field component, and $B_Z$ is the vertical
magnetic-field component.

This is a local quantity without a prescribed evaluation locus, spatial
averaging, or restriction to a particular field source. It is neither the
full magnetic-field magnitude nor the signed sensing-axis projection
associated with the [poloidal magnetic field of a magnetic-field
probe](name:poloidal_magnetic_field_of_magnetic_field_probe).

The [poloidal magnetic field at the pedestal
top](name:poloidal_magnetic_field_at_pedestal_top) specializes this quantity
by fixing its evaluation locus.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_field_at_pedestal_top_high_field_side
NAMES.short:
Poloidal magnetic field at the high-field-side pedestal top is the magnitude
of the equilibrium magnetic-field projection onto the poloidal plane.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic field at the high-field-side pedestal top is the local
strength of the poloidal-plane projection of the equilibrium [magnetic
field](name:magnetic_field).

The field strength is defined by

$$
B_{\mathrm{p}} = \sqrt{B_R^2 + B_Z^2}
$$

where $B_{\mathrm{p}}$ is the poloidal magnetic-field magnitude, and $B_R$
and $B_Z$ are the radial and vertical magnetic-field components, all
evaluated at the stated locus. These components refer to the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is
toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The toroidal contribution is excluded, distinguishing this quantity from the
magnitude of the [total magnetic field at the same
locus](name:magnetic_field_at_pedestal_top_high_field_side). This is a local
value, not the [flux-surface-averaged poloidal magnetic field at the
pedestal
top](name:flux_surface_averaged_poloidal_magnetic_field_at_pedestal_top).
The [low-field-side
counterpart](name:poloidal_magnetic_field_at_pedestal_top_low_field_side)
evaluates the same component magnitude at its separately specified locus.
