NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_field_of_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
Poloidal magnetic field of a magnetic-field probe is the signed local
poloidal magnetic-field value represented by a poloidal field probe after
its nonlinear response calibration, sensed in the R-Z plane of the
right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic field of a magnetic-field probe is the signed local
poloidal magnetic-field value represented by a poloidal field probe after
its nonlinear response calibration. The sensed component lies in the $R$-$Z$
plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is
major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The defining relation applies the probe's nonlinear calibration curve to the
linearly calibrated projection of the local field onto the probe's sensitive
direction:

$$
B_{\mathrm{probe}} = f_{\mathrm{nl}}\!\left(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{probe}} \cdot \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{probe}})\right)
$$

where $B_{\mathrm{probe}}$ is this quantity,
$\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{probe}})$ is the local [magnetic-field
vector](name:magnetic_field) at the probe sensing position
$\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{probe}}$, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{probe}}$ is the
unit vector along the probe's positive poloidal sensitive direction in the
$R$-$Z$ plane, and $f_{\mathrm{nl}}$ is the probe's nonlinear calibration
curve, which maps the linearly calibrated field value to the field value
corrected for nonlinear sensor response such as Hall-sensor saturation or
hysteresis. Where the sensor responds linearly, $f_{\mathrm{nl}}$ reduces to
the identity and the quantity equals the plain projection.

Scope is limited to an individual probe and to the point or small sensing
volume it represents; no averaging over multiple probes, flux surfaces, or
spatial regions is implied. The probe's position in the poloidal plane is
given by the [radial coordinate of the poloidal magnetic-field
probe](name:radial_coordinate_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe) and the
[vertical coordinate of the poloidal magnetic-field
probe](name:vertical_coordinate_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe). The
[toroidal angle of a poloidal magnetic-field
probe](name:toroidal_angle_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe) characterizes
the orientation of the probe's sensitive axis and is not a spatial
coordinate of this quantity's locus.

This quantity is a single signed poloidal component: it is not the toroidal
component, not the magnitude of the full magnetic-field vector, and not an
unsigned poloidal-field magnitude. It is the calibrated field value, not the
raw electrical signal, and is therefore distinct from the [voltage of a
poloidal magnetic-field
probe](name:voltage_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe); it is also distinct
from the linearly calibrated value before the nonlinear correction is
applied. Probe hardware descriptors such as the [turn count of a poloidal
magnetic-field probe](name:turn_count_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe)
characterize the sensor and are not components of the field.

This quantity is the probe-local, oriented-component counterpart of the
[poloidal magnetic field](name:poloidal_magnetic_field), evaluated at one
sensing position along one fixed sensitive direction rather than as a field
over the plasma domain.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the local magnetic-field vector at the probe
sensing position has a positive projection along the probe's positive
poloidal sensitive direction in the $R$-$Z$ plane of the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux
NAMES.short:
Poloidal magnetic flux is the signed magnetic flux through a horizontal disk
centered on the toroidal symmetry axis, labeling magnetic surfaces in
axisymmetric equilibrium.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux is the net magnetic flux through a horizontal disk
centered on the toroidal symmetry axis and bounded by the toroidal circle
through the evaluation point. It specializes [magnetic
flux](name:magnetic_flux) by specifying the integration surface and its
orientation. In axisymmetric equilibrium, its level sets define magnetic
surfaces.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius,
$\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counterclockwise when viewed from above,
and $Z$ is vertical height. The full poloidal magnetic flux is defined by

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{p}}(R,Z) \equiv \psi(R,Z) = 2\pi \int_0^R B_Z(R',Z)\,R'\,dR'
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{p}}$, also denoted $\psi$, is the poloidal magnetic
flux, $B_Z$ is the vertical magnetic-field component, and $R'$ is the radial
integration variable. The factor $2\pi$ accounts for integration around the
complete toroidal circle.

This quantity includes contributions from plasma currents and external
sources, unlike [external magnetic flux](name:external_magnetic_flux), which
excludes the plasma-generated contribution. It is the full flux, not flux
divided by $2\pi$, a normalized coordinate, or a cross-sectional average. It
differs from [toroidal magnetic flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux), which
integrates the toroidal magnetic field through a poloidal cross-section.

The [magnetic-axis value](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis) and
[plasma-boundary value](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary) are
evaluations of this same function and provide the endpoint references for
poloidal-flux normalization. For nested surfaces enclosing positive toroidal
plasma current flowing toward increasing $\phi$, the poloidal flux decreases
from the magnetic axis to the plasma boundary.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the magnetic field threading the horizontal
disk has a net component toward increasing $Z$, along the upward surface
normal.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_constraint_position
NAMES.short:
Poloidal magnetic flux at the constraint position is the signed flux through
a horizontal disk centered on the toroidal symmetry axis and bounded by the
toroidal circle through that position.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux at the constraint position is the signed [magnetic
flux](name:magnetic_flux) through a horizontal disk centered on the toroidal
symmetry axis and bounded by the toroidal circle through that position.

In an axisymmetric equilibrium, its defining relation in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame is

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{p}}(R,Z) = 2\pi \int_0^R B_Z(R',Z)\,R'\,dR'
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{p}}$ is the poloidal magnetic flux, $R$ is major
radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical height, $B_Z$ is the
vertical component of the total equilibrium magnetic field, and $R'$ is the
major-radius integration variable. The expression is evaluated at the
constraint position.

This is a point evaluation of [poloidal magnetic
flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux), not a spatial average, and includes both
externally generated and plasma-generated contributions. Within a region of
nested magnetic surfaces, it labels the surface passing through that
position and supplies a surface coordinate for transport coefficients and
plasma source terms. Unlike [toroidal magnetic
flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux), it is not flux through a poloidal
cross-section.

For plasma current flowing in the direction of increasing $\phi$, the flux
decreases from the [magnetic-axis
value](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis) to the [plasma-boundary
value](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the net magnetic field threading the
horizontal disk is oriented toward increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short:
Poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis is the signed equilibrium flux
through a horizontal disk bounded by the toroidal circle at that location.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis is the signed equilibrium flux
through a horizontal disk centered on the toroidal symmetry axis and bounded
by the toroidal circle at that location. It is the magnetic-axis value of
[poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux), a component-specific
specialization of [magnetic flux](name:magnetic_flux).

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major
radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the defining
flux is

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{axis}} = 2\pi \int_0^{R_{\mathrm{axis}}} B_Z(R', Z_{\mathrm{axis}})\,R'\,dR'
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{axis}}$ is the poloidal magnetic flux at the
magnetic axis, $R_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is its major radius, $Z_{\mathrm{axis}}$
is its [vertical coordinate](name:vertical_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis),
$B_Z$ is the vertical component of the total equilibrium magnetic field, and
$R'$ is the integration coordinate along major radius.

The value includes both plasma-generated and externally generated
equilibrium flux, rather than only [external magnetic
flux](name:external_magnetic_flux). It is neither an axis-to-boundary flux
difference nor a normalized flux label, and it need not vanish at the
magnetic axis.

Together with the [poloidal magnetic flux at the plasma
boundary](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary), denoted by
$\Phi_{\mathrm{p},b}$, it defines the normalized flux fraction $f =
(\Phi_{\mathrm{p}}-\Phi_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{axis}})/(\Phi_{\mathrm{p},b}-\Phi_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{axis}})$,
where $\Phi_{\mathrm{p}}$ is the equilibrium poloidal flux at the evaluation
location and the denominator must be nonzero. This fraction supplies the
reference for the [normalized poloidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate), with zero at the
magnetic axis and unity at the plasma boundary. These reference values
remain applicable when the region being described does not extend to either
endpoint.

The closed magnetic-field line about which nested toroidal magnetic flux
surfaces are arranged. Where $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{p}}(R_{\mathrm{axis}},
Z_{\mathrm{axis}}) = 0$, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{p}}$ is poloidal magnetic
field; $R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the O-point inside the
nested closed flux surfaces.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the net vertical magnetic flux through the
defining disk is directed toward increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Poloidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary is the signed flux through a
horizontal disk centered on the symmetry axis and bounded by a toroidal
circle through a boundary point.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary is the signed equilibrium flux
through a horizontal disk centered on the toroidal symmetry axis and bounded
by a toroidal circle through a boundary point. It is a locus-specific
poloidal specialization of [magnetic flux](name:magnetic_flux).

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major
radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the boundary
poloidal flux is defined by

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{p},b} = \int_0^{R_b} B_Z(R',Z_b)\,2\pi R'\,dR'
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{p},b}$ is the boundary poloidal magnetic flux, $R_b$
and $Z_b$ are the coordinates of a boundary point, $R'$ is the integration
major radius, and $B_Z$ is the vertical magnetic-field component. The disk
is oriented along the positive vertical unit vector $\hat{Z}$.

This definition applies to an axisymmetric equilibrium and includes
contributions from both external sources and plasma current, rather than
only [external magnetic flux](name:external_magnetic_flux). It differs from
[toroidal magnetic flux at the plasma
boundary](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary), which threads the
boundary-enclosed poloidal cross-section rather than a horizontal disk.

This is the boundary flux-function value, not the axis-to-boundary flux
difference. Together with the magnetic-axis flux, it supplies the outer
reference for poloidal-flux normalization; the [normalized poloidal flux
coordinate of the plasma
boundary](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary)
equals unity when those values define the normalization endpoints.

The last closed magnetic flux surface: the outermost flux surface on which
field lines close on themselves, bounding the confined plasma. Where $\psi =
\psi_{\mathrm{LCFS}}$, $\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux;
$\psi_{\mathrm{LCFS}}$ is its value on the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the net vertical magnetic flux through the
defining disk is directed along $+\hat{Z}$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_of_flux_loop
NAMES.short:
Poloidal magnetic flux of an individual flux loop is the measured, signed
vertical-field integral over a horizontal disk centered on the toroidal
symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux of an individual flux loop is the signed poloidal
flux represented by that loop's measured value.

For an axisymmetric magnetic field, its defining relation is

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{p}} = 2\pi \int_0^{R_\ell} B_Z(R', Z_\ell)\,R'\,dR'
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{p}}$ is the poloidal magnetic flux, $B_Z$ is the
vertical magnetic-field component, and $R'$ is the integration radius. In
the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$
is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; $R_\ell$ and $Z_\ell$ specify
the evaluation location at the flux loop. The integration disk has its
positive normal toward increasing $Z$.

This is the loop-specific value of [poloidal magnetic
flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux), not a sum or average over multiple
loops. It represents an integrated flux rather than a local magnetic-field
value and is distinct from [toroidal magnetic
flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the net magnetic flux through the integration
disk is directed toward increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Area enclosed by a magnetic flux-surface contour in a poloidal plane at
fixed toroidal angle, including the complete planar interior.
NAMES.long:
Area of flux surface

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the enclosed area is
defined by

$$
A_{\mathrm{p}} = \iint_{\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{p}}} dR\,dZ
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{p}}$ is the poloidal-plane cross-sectional area,
$\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{p}}$ is the planar region enclosed by the selected
contour, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical
height, and $dR\,dZ$ is the unsigned poloidal-plane area element.

This quantity applies to any selected closed flux-surface contour and
includes its entire interior, not merely the region between neighboring
contours. It is not a local area element, a flux-surface average, or the
[surface area of the flux surface](name:surface_area_of_flux_surface), which
covers its full poloidal and toroidal extent.

At the plasma boundary, it becomes the [poloidal-plane cross-sectional area
of the plasma
boundary](name:poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_plasma_boundary). Its
local variation between neighboring surfaces is described by the [derivative
with respect to poloidal magnetic flux
coordinate](name:derivative_of_poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_poloidal_magnetic_flux_coordinate)
or the [derivative with respect to toroidal flux
coordinate](name:derivative_of_poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_toroidal_flux_coordinate),
according to the coordinate used.

A surface formed by points sharing the same magnetic-flux label in a
nested-flux-surface configuration. Where $\psi(R, Z) = \mathrm{const}$,
$\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux.

NAMES.short:

metric for flux-surface averages.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the geometric derivative of the area enclosed by a nested,
closed magnetic flux surface in a poloidal cross-section. It describes how
neighboring flux surfaces differ in enclosed poloidal-plane area.

$$
\frac{dA}{d\psi}
$$

where $A(\psi)$ is the area enclosed by the flux surface labeled by signed
poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$. The area is measured in the poloidal plane of
the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major
radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies to the cumulative enclosed area of each nested closed
flux surface and is not a local area density, toroidal surface area, or
enclosed-volume derivative. The corresponding [derivative of volume of flux
surface with respect to poloidal magnetic flux
coordinate](name:derivative_of_volume_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_poloidal_magnetic_flux_coordinate)
differentiates enclosed volume rather than cross-sectional area, while the
derivative of area of flux surface with respect to toroidal flux coordinate
uses the toroidal magnetic flux coordinate instead of $\psi$.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the enclosed poloidal-plane area increases in
the direction of increasing signed poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$, with
positive flux oriented by the $+Z$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Radial derivative of the cross-sectional area of the flux surface with respect to psi
sources.parent_definition: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux

NAMES.name: derivative_of_poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_toroidal_flux_coordinate
NAMES.short:
Local geometric rate of change of a flux surface’s enclosed poloidal
cross-sectional area as its toroidal-flux coordinate varies.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the local geometric rate at which the poloidal
cross-sectional area enclosed by a nested magnetic flux surface changes
along the family of surfaces labeled by the toroidal-flux coordinate.

The derivative is defined by:

$$
\frac{dA}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}}
$$

where $A$ is the [poloidal-plane cross-sectional area of a flux
surface](name:poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_flux_surface), and
$\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal-flux coordinate labeling the nested
surfaces.

The area is enclosed by one closed magnetic-flux-surface contour in a
fixed-toroidal-angle poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and
$Z$ is vertical height. The quantity applies to one flux surface at a time;
it is not the area of the full three-dimensional flux surface, a derivative
of enclosed volume, or an average over multiple surfaces.

This is the derivative transformation of the cross-sectional-area quantity
linked above. It differs from [the radial derivative of poloidal magnetic
flux](name:radial_derivative_of_poloidal_magnetic_flux), which
differentiates signed poloidal magnetic flux rather than geometric
cross-sectional area.

sources.leaf_definition: Radial derivative of the cross-sectional area of the flux surface with respect to rho_tor
sources.parent_definition: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux

NAMES.name: poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Area enclosed by the last closed magnetic flux surface in a poloidal plane,
defining the equilibrium plasma cross-sectional size at the plasma boundary.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the geometric area enclosed by the last closed magnetic
flux surface (LCFS), which forms the plasma boundary, in a poloidal
cross-section.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the enclosed area is
defined by

$$
A_{\rm LCFS} = \iint_{\mathcal{S}_{\rm LCFS}} dR\,dZ
$$

where $A_{\rm LCFS}$ is the LCFS cross-sectional area, $\mathcal{S}_{\rm
LCFS}$ is the region enclosed by the LCFS contour at fixed toroidal angle
$\phi$, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical
height, and $dR\,dZ$ is the poloidal-plane area element.

This is a global equilibrium quantity for the complete plasma-boundary
contour. It is not a local surface element, a flux-surface average, or the
area of a toroidal surface formed by revolving the contour.

It is the plasma-boundary specialization of [poloidal plane cross-sectional
area of a flux
surface](name:poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_flux_surface), whose
corresponding area is defined for an arbitrary closed magnetic flux surface;
the LCFS is the outermost such surface enclosing the plasma.

sources.leaf_definition: Area of the LCFS poloidal cross section
sources.parent_definition: 0D parameters of the equilibrium

NAMES.name: product_of_poloidal_current_function_and_derivative_of_poloidal_current_function_with_respect_to_poloidal_magnetic_flux_coordinate
NAMES.short:
Grad–Shafranov equilibrium source term formed by multiplying the poloidal
current function by its derivative with respect to signed poloidal magnetic
flux.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the flux-surface-dependent product of the poloidal current
function and its derivative with respect to the signed poloidal
magnetic-flux coordinate. It represents the toroidal-field contribution to
the Grad–Shafranov equilibrium source term.

The defining relation is

$$
G(\psi)=F(\psi)\frac{dF(\psi)}{d\psi}
$$

where $G(\psi)$ denotes this quantity, $F(\psi)$ is the [poloidal current
function](name:poloidal_current_function), $\psi$ is the signed poloidal
magnetic-flux coordinate, and $dF/d\psi$ is the derivative of that current
function with respect to $\psi$. The function $F$ is defined by $F=R
B_\phi$, where $R$ is major radius in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame and $B_\phi$ is the toroidal magnetic-field component.

This quantity applies to an axisymmetric equilibrium description on nested
magnetic flux surfaces. It is a local flux-function value with no additional
spatial averaging, species summation, or volume integration. It is distinct
from the poloidal current function itself and from its derivative alone.

Within the Grad–Shafranov balance, this product combines the toroidal-field
contribution with the pressure-gradient contribution to determine the
equilibrium relation for toroidal current density and force balance.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $F$ and $dF/d\psi$ have the same sign for the
chosen orientation of the signed poloidal magnetic flux.

sources.leaf_definition: Derivative of F w.r.t. Psi, multiplied with F
sources.parent_definition: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_at_inboard_midplane
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of a magnetic flux surface at its inboard midplane
intersection, locating the high-field-side point relative to the toroidal
symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the major-radius coordinate of the point where a magnetic
flux surface intersects the inboard midplane, identifying the
high-field-side location of that surface relative to the toroidal symmetry
axis. It is a locus-specific form of the [radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate).

For a magnetic flux surface $\mathcal{S}$, the inboard-midplane radial
coordinate is defined by

$$
R_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S}) = R\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S})\right)
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S})$ is the quantity defined here,
$R(\mathbf{x})$ is the major-radius coordinate of spatial position
$\mathbf{x}$, $\mathcal{S}$ is the specified magnetic flux surface, and
$\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S})$ is its inboard midplane
intersection. The coordinates are expressed in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and
$Z$ is vertical height.

The scope is one coordinate value for each specified magnetic flux surface
at its inboard, high-field-side midplane intersection. It is not a
flux-surface average, a poloidal or toroidal average, or the corresponding
outboard-midplane coordinate; the latter is represented by [radial
coordinate at outboard
midplane](name:radial_coordinate_at_outboard_midplane). Unlike [radial
magnetic field](name:radial_magnetic_field), this quantity describes the
location of a surface and not a magnetic-field component.

This quantity specializes [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate) by
fixing the evaluation locus to the inboard midplane. Comparing it with the
outboard-midplane value characterizes the horizontal extent and radial
placement of the same magnetic flux surface.

sources.leaf_definition: Radial coordinate (major radius) on the inboard side of the magnetic axis
sources.parent_definition: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_at_outboard_midplane
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of a magnetic flux surface at the outboard midplane,
locating the surface's low-field-side point relative to the toroidal
symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
Major-radius coordinate at outboard midplane

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the major-radius
coordinate is related to the horizontal Cartesian coordinates by:

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $R$ is the [major-radius coordinate](name:radial_coordinate) measured
as perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is the
toroidal angle increasing counterclockwise when viewed from above
$+\hat{Z}$, $Z$ is vertical height, and $x$ and $y$ are the horizontal
Cartesian coordinates of the evaluated point in the right-handed Cartesian
$(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$ and origin on the
toroidal symmetry axis.

The quantity applies separately to each magnetic flux surface, identified by
its poloidal magnetic-flux label $\psi$, where $\psi$ denotes the flux
function labeling nested magnetic surfaces. It is a point value evaluated at
the outboard midplane of the specified surface; it is not a flux-surface
average and excludes the inboard intersection.

For an up-down-symmetric equilibrium, the outboard midplane of every flux
surface lies at the vertical height of the magnetic axis, so this quantity
coincides with the major radius of the surface's low-field-side intersection
with the horizontal plane through the magnetic axis. For a
non-up-down-symmetric equilibrium, the outboard midplane of a surface lies
at a different height, and the low-field-side intersection taken at the
magnetic-axis height does not coincide with this quantity.

It is a locus-specific specialization of the general [major-radius
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate), evaluated at the outboard midplane. The
corresponding [radial coordinate at the inboard
midplane](name:radial_coordinate_at_inboard_midplane) locates the distinct
high-field-side intersection of the same type of magnetic surface.

The low-field-side equatorial midplane: the point of maximum major radius on
the flux surface in question. For a value at the separatrix intersection use
outboard_midplane_separatrix. Where $R = \max_{S} R,\quad R >
R_{\mathrm{axis}}$, $S$ is the magnetic flux surface the point lies on;
$R_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is major radius of the magnetic axis.

sources.leaf_definition: Radial coordinate (major radius) on the outboard side of the magnetic axis
sources.parent_definition: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate R of the first-wall point nearest the plasma
boundary, measured from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the major-radius coordinate of the wall point selected as
closest to the plasma boundary. It identifies that point’s perpendicular
distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R, phi, Z)$ frame.

The defining geometric relation is

$$
R_{\mathrm{cw}} = \left\lVert \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{cw},\perp} \right\rVert
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{cw}}$ is the radial coordinate of the closest wall point
and $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{cw},\perp}$ is the perpendicular displacement
vector from the toroidal symmetry axis to that point.

The scope is the single wall point selected by its minimum proximity to the
plasma boundary. This is a pointwise geometric coordinate with no
plasma-population dependence and no averaging, summation, or integration. It
is not the wall-to-boundary separation distance, nor is “closest” a
statement that the point has the smallest major radius among all wall
points.

This quantity is a locus-specific instance of [radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate), restricted to the closest wall point
rather than an arbitrary geometric reference position.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: Position and distance to the plasma boundary of the point of the first wall which is the closest to plasma boundary

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_conductor_cross_section
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of a conductor cross-section's geometric center,
equal to its perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
Major-radius coordinate of conductor cross section

It is the [major-radius coordinate](name:radial_coordinate) specialized to
this locus:

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are the Cartesian coordinates of that center in the
right-handed $(x, y, z)$ frame, with $z$ the vertical coordinate and the
origin on the toroidal symmetry axis.

The quantity applies individually to conductor cross-sections represented as
rectangles, without averaging over conductors. It specifies the center
position, not a cross-sectional width or an outline-point coordinate.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_control_surface
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of each point on a control-surface outline, measured
as perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the
right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of a control-surface outline point is its major-radius
location, measured as perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry
axis. It identifies the point's position in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

The defining geometric relation is

$$
R = \sqrt{X^2 + Y^2}
$$

where $R$ is the major-radius coordinate, and $X$ and $Y$ are the Cartesian
coordinates perpendicular to the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed
Cartesian $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis. The cylindrical angle $\phi$ is
the toroidal angular coordinate and $Z$ is the vertical coordinate of the
same point.

This quantity applies to each point defining the control-surface outline.
The control surface is defined by an outline in a poloidal plane and extends
in the toroidal direction with axisymmetric geometry; this quantity is the
local coordinate of an outline point, not a surface average or an integrated
surface property. It is distinct from displacement along a flux-surface
normal, which describes a different geometric direction.

This entry specializes [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate) by
restricting its locus to a point on a control-surface outline while
retaining the same major-radius definition.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: Set of points defining the surface in a poloidal plane. The surface then extends in the toroidal direction in an axisymmetric way

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_current_center
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of the plasma-current centroid, obtained by
normalizing the toroidal-current first moment over the poloidal plasma
cross-section by total plasma current.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of the current center is the major-radius location of
the centroid of the toroidal plasma-current distribution. It identifies a
current-weighted position and is distinct from the geometric centroid or the
magnetic axis.

The coordinate is defined by the toroidal-current first moment:

$$
R_c = \frac{\displaystyle\int_{D_p} R\,j_\phi\,dS}{I_p}
$$

where $R_c$ is the major-radius coordinate of the current center, $R$ is the
major-radius coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$
frame, $j_\phi$ is the toroidal component of the plasma [current
density](name:current_density), $dS$ is an element of poloidal
cross-sectional area, $D_p$ is the plasma current-carrying poloidal
cross-section, and $I_p$ is the total toroidal plasma current, equal to the
corresponding integral of $j_\phi$ over $D_p$.

The quantity applies to the full plasma-current distribution and uses a
current-weighted first-moment aggregation over the poloidal cross-section.
It excludes weighting by particle density, pressure, magnetic-field
strength, or geometric area alone; the resulting position is therefore not a
generic geometric center.

This quantity is a locus-specific instance of the general [radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate), evaluated at the current center. Its
vertical counterpart, [vertical coordinate of the current
center](name:vertical_coordinate_of_current_center), supplies the
corresponding vertical position needed to locate the current centroid in the
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius of the current center, defined as integral over the poloidal cross section of (j_tor*r*dS) / Ip
sources.parent_definition: Position and vertical velocity of the current centre

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_dr_dz_zero_point
NAMES.short:
Radial coordinate of the dR/dZ zero point is the R coordinate, in the
right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, of a plasma-boundary or separatrix
point where R is locally stationary with respect to Z.
NAMES.long:
Radial coordinate of the dR/dZ zero point is the $R$ coordinate, in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, of a specified point on a
plasma-boundary or separatrix contour where $R$ is locally stationary with
respect to $Z$. In this frame, $R$ is major radius measured from the
toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical
height.

The coordinate is defined by the stationary-radius condition on the
specified contour:

$$
R_{\mathrm{dR/dZ=0}} = R(P_0), \qquad \left.\frac{dR}{dZ}\right|_{C,P_0} = 0
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{dR/dZ=0}}$ is the radial coordinate of the dR/dZ zero
point, $P_0$ is the specified dR/dZ zero point, $C$ is the plasma-boundary
or separatrix contour on which $P_0$ lies, $R(P_0)$ is the major-radius
coordinate of $P_0$, $Z$ is the vertical-height coordinate, and $dR/dZ$ is
the derivative of the contour coordinate $R$ with respect to $Z$ along $C$.

The scope is a single specified geometric point on the contour; the value is
not an average over the contour, over toroidal angle $\phi$, or over all
stationary points. If several points on the contour satisfy $dR/dZ=0$, the
definition does not by itself impose an inboard, outboard, upper, or lower
selection rule; each specified zero point has its own radial-coordinate
value.

This quantity is only the cylindrical $R$ coordinate of the point, not a
flux-surface-normal displacement or a flux-label coordinate. Together with
the vertical coordinate of the dR/dZ zero point, it locates the point in the
poloidal $(R, Z)$ cross-section at fixed $\phi$ of the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is distinct from the [radial coordinate
of an X-point](name:radial_coordinate_of_x_point), which locates a magnetic
null on a separatrix rather than a radial extremum of a boundary or
separatrix contour.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: Outboard point on the separatrix on which dr/dz = 0 (local maximum of the major radius of the separatrix). In case of multiple local maxima, the closest one from z=z_magnetic_axis is chosen.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_geometric_axis
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of the plasma boundary's geometric axis, equal to
its perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
Major-radius coordinate of geometric axis

The coordinate is defined by

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are the horizontal coordinates of the same reference
position in the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame, with $z$ the
vertical coordinate along the same axis as $Z$.

This nonnegative coordinate specifies one reference position associated with
the plasma boundary, rather than separate positions for interior flux
surfaces. It is not a minor radius or a magnetic flux label, and it need not
equal the magnetic-axis major radius.

The [radial outline of the plasma
boundary](name:radial_outline_of_plasma_boundary) instead specifies
major-radius coordinates along the boundary contour. Within the same
coordinate family, the [radial coordinate of a conductor
cross-section](name:radial_coordinate_of_conductor_cross_section) locates a
device reference position rather than this plasma reference position.

The axis defined solely by the geometry of the relevant object or plasma
cross-section. Where $R_{\mathrm{geo}} = (R_{\max} + R_{\min})/2,\quad
Z_{\mathrm{geo}} = (Z_{\max} + Z_{\min})/2$, $R_{\max}, R_{\min}$ is the
radial extrema of the cross-section; $Z_{\max}, Z_{\min}$ is its vertical
extrema.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: RZ position of the geometric axis (defined as (Rmin+Rmax) / 2 and (Zmin+Zmax) / 2 of the boundary)

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: RZ position of the geometric axis of the magnetic surfaces (defined as (Rmin+Rmax) / 2 and (Zmin+Zmax) / 2 of the surface)

sources.leaf_definition: Value

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_measurement_position
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of a measurement position, equal to its
perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
Major-radius coordinate of measurement position

The coordinate is defined by

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are the horizontal coordinates of the same position in the
right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame, whose origin lies on the toroidal
symmetry axis and whose vertical coordinate $z$ is aligned with $Z$.

This quantity evaluates the parent coordinate at the specified measurement
position; no summation, averaging, or weighting is implied. It is
nonnegative and vanishes on the toroidal symmetry axis. It is distinct from
a minor-radius distance measured from the magnetic axis and from a magnetic
flux label.

The [radial coordinate of a line of
sight](name:radial_coordinate_of_line_of_sight) specifically locates that
line's second reference point; this quantity does not impose that
reference-point convention.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_plasma_filament
NAMES.short:
Radial coordinate of a plasma filament is the major-radius coordinate, in
the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, of the oblique reference point
anchoring one current-carrying filament element's rectangular cross-section.
NAMES.long:
Radial coordinate of a plasma filament is the major-radius coordinate of the
oblique reference point that anchors one current-carrying plasma filament
element's rectangular cross-section. It is defined in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius from the machine
symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies to a single plasma filament element represented by
oblique rectangular cross-sectional geometry. It is the coordinate of the
reference point used by that representation, not the filament width, height,
centroid position, magnetic-axis position, or a flux-surface radial
coordinate; no averaging or summation over filament elements is implied.

Together with the vertical coordinate of the plasma filament, it locates the
oblique reference point in the poloidal plane. The [alpha angle of the
plasma filament](name:alpha_angle_of_plasma_filament) and beta angle of the
plasma filament are defined relative to this same reference point, and the
[plasma filament width](name:plasma_filament_width) is a rectangular
cross-section extent anchored by it.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius of the reference point (from which the alpha and beta angles are defined, marked by a + on the diagram)
sources.parent_definition: Parallelogram description of the element

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_poloidal_magnetic_flux
NAMES.short:
Rate of change of signed poloidal magnetic flux with the dimensionful
toroidal-flux radius labeling nested equilibrium flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The radial derivative of poloidal magnetic flux is the rate at which the
signed poloidal magnetic flux changes across nested equilibrium magnetic
flux surfaces. It is a metric coefficient relating the poloidal-flux and
toroidal-flux coordinate descriptions.

The defining relation is

$$
\frac{d\psi}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}}
$$

where $\psi$ is the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux),
and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the dimensionful toroidal-flux radius that
labels the nested surfaces.

This quantity is evaluated as a function of the toroidal-flux radius, with
one derivative value associated with each nested equilibrium surface. It is
not a surface integral or average, and it is distinct from a derivative with
respect to the cylindrical major radius, minor radius, or a normalized flux
coordinate.

Relative to [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux), this
quantity describes how the flux label changes in the outward
toroidal-flux-radial direction. It has the same independent coordinate as
the derivative with respect to toroidal flux coordinate of area of flux
surface, but differentiates poloidal magnetic flux rather than enclosed
surface area.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the poloidal magnetic flux increases as
$\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ increases outward from the magnetic axis toward the
plasma boundary.

sources.leaf_definition: Derivative of Psi with respect to Rho_Tor
sources.parent_definition: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux

NAMES.name: radial_outline_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of a point on a poloidal magnetic-flux level-set
contour, expressed in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Radial outline of a flux surface is the major-radius coordinate $R$ of a
point on a contour of constant poloidal magnetic flux. The contour is
described in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is
major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal
angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For a point whose Cartesian coordinates are $(x,y,z)$ in the right-handed
Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$, the
corresponding major-radius coordinate is

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are Cartesian coordinates in the plane perpendicular to
the toroidal symmetry axis.

This quantity is the radial coordinate component of the flux-surface
outline, paired with the vertical outline of a flux surface. It is a
specialization of [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate) to points on a
poloidal magnetic-flux level set and does not denote the flux label, a
flux-surface-normal displacement, or the radial component of a vector field.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius

NAMES.name: radial_outline_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short:
Non-negative major-radius coordinate of a point on an iron-core segment
cross-sectional outline in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame,
where R is measured away from the symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
Non-negative major-radius coordinate of a point on an iron-core segment
cross-sectional outline is the distance of that point from the toroidal
symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$
is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It
identifies the radial location of an outline point; increasing $R$ is
directed away from the symmetry axis along $+\hat{R}$.

For a point whose position perpendicular to the symmetry axis is described
in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis with
$\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$, the coordinate is

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are the Cartesian coordinates in the plane normal to the
symmetry axis.

The quantity applies only to the outline locus of the iron-core segment. It
is distinct from the [radial coordinate of an arc-of-circle
center](name:radial_coordinate_of_arc_of_circle_center), which locates a
geometry-defining center rather than the radial coordinate of each outline
point.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the element. Repeat the first point since this is a closed contour

NAMES.name: radial_outline_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of each point on the plasma-boundary contour in a
poloidal cross-section.
NAMES.long:
This quantity gives the major-radius coordinate associated with each point
of the plasma-boundary outline in a poloidal cross-section. It represents
the contour point locations measured from the toroidal symmetry axis rather
than a single representative boundary radius.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the major radius of a
point is defined by

$$
R = \sqrt{X^2 + Y^2}
$$

where $R$ is the major-radius coordinate, $X$ and $Y$ are horizontal
Cartesian coordinates measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is
the toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the vertical height. The quantity is
evaluated pointwise along the plasma-boundary contour, with no averaging or
summation over its points.

It is distinct from a flux-label quantity such as the [normalized poloidal
flux coordinate of the plasma
boundary](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary), and
it retains the full radial variation of the contour rather than reducing it
to one size parameter. The radial extrema of the outline provide the
horizontal extent used by the [minor radius of the plasma
boundary](name:minor_radius_of_plasma_boundary).

sources.parent_definition: RZ outline of the plasma boundary

NAMES.name: radial_outline_of_plasma_filament
NAMES.short:
Radial outline of a plasma filament is the major-radius coordinate of each
filament-outline point in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame,
where R is distance from the toroidal symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
Radial outline of a plasma filament is the major-radius coordinate $R$ of
each point on the plasma-filament outline in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is distance from the toroidal symmetry axis
and $Z$ is vertical height. It gives the radial location of the outline
locus and is the filament-outline specialization of the generic [radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate).

For an outline point with Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ in a right-handed
Cartesian frame with basis $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$, with the $z$ axis
coincident with the toroidal symmetry axis, the coordinate is defined by:

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are the Cartesian coordinates perpendicular to the
toroidal symmetry axis.

This quantity is a coordinate of each outline point, not a signed radial
vector projection, flux-surface-normal displacement, filament width, or
aggregate radius. It should not be confused with the [outer radius of a
plasma filament](name:outer_radius_of_plasma_filament), which denotes an
outer radial extent rather than the coordinate of an individual outline
point.

NAMES.name: reference_major_radius
NAMES.short:
Reference major radius is the perpendicular distance from the toroidal
symmetry axis to the designated location at which the vacuum toroidal
magnetic field is specified.
NAMES.long:
Reference major radius is the geometric [radius](name:radius) measured
perpendicularly from the toroidal symmetry axis to the designated location
where the vacuum toroidal magnetic field is specified. It is a selected
reference value of [major radius](name:major_radius).

For an axisymmetric vacuum toroidal field, the reference radius and its
associated field value determine the inverse-major-radius dependence:

$$
B_{\phi,\mathrm{vac}}(R)=B_0\frac{R_0}{R}
$$

where $R_0$ is the reference major radius, $B_0$ is the vacuum toroidal
magnetic-field component at that radius, $R$ is the major-radius coordinate,
and $B_{\phi,\mathrm{vac}}(R)$ is the vacuum toroidal magnetic-field
component at $R$. The right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame uses
toroidal angle $\phi$ and vertical coordinate $Z$.

The reference location is prescribed; it need not coincide with the magnetic
axis or the equatorial midplane. Unlike the [flux-surface-averaged major
radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_major_radius), this quantity is not an
average over a magnetic flux surface. The reference radius and associated
vacuum field provide the reference parameters used in toroidal-flux
coordinate definitions and current-density normalizations.

NAMES.name: square_of_major_radius
NAMES.short:
Geometric equilibrium coefficient with inverse-square major-radius scaling,
spanning direct reciprocal-square factors and flux-coordinate metric ratios
in toroidal plasma geometry.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is a geometric coefficient in toroidal plasma equilibrium
whose scale contains the reciprocal square of the [major
radius](name:major_radius). It includes both direct inverse-square radius
factors and geometric factors formed from a flux-coordinate gradient divided
by the squared major radius.

Its common form is

$$
G = \frac{g}{R^2}
$$

where $G$ is the geometric coefficient, $R$ is the major radius, and $g$ is
a dimensionless geometric factor. For
[inverse_of_square_of_major_radius](name:inverse_of_square_of_major_radius),
$g=1$; for
[ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_major_radius](name:ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_major_radius),
$g$ is the squared magnitude of the gradient of the toroidal flux
coordinate.

The quantity is a metric factor for flux-coordinate equilibrium and
transport formulations, not the major radius or its square itself. Its
specific numerator is determined by the concrete member of this
geometric-coefficient family.

NAMES.name: inverse_of_square_of_major_radius
NAMES.short:
Geometric inverse-square-major-radius coefficient for toroidal plasma
equilibrium, including flux-surface-averaged forms used in magnetic-geometry
relations.
NAMES.long:
This quantity represents the reciprocal-square major-radius dependence of a
geometric coefficient in toroidal plasma equilibrium. It characterizes the
metric scaling associated with the distance from the machine symmetry axis.

For the direct inverse-square form, the coefficient is defined by

$$
K_R = \frac{1}{R^2}
$$

where $K_R$ is the inverse-square-major-radius coefficient and $R$ is the
major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

The quantity applies to toroidal equilibrium geometry and is not the major
radius itself or its direct square. It denotes the inverse-square geometric
factor; any aggregation over a magnetic flux surface is an additional
operation rather than part of the unaggregated quantity.

The [flux-surface-averaged inverse-square-major-radius
coefficient](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_major_radius)
is the corresponding instance obtained by averaging this inverse-square
factor over a magnetic flux surface. The quantity is therefore the
reciprocal-square counterpart of
[square_of_major_radius](name:square_of_major_radius), with the inverse
relationship supplying the geometric scaling.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_major_radius
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface average of reciprocal squared major radius, providing a
geometric metric coefficient for parallel-gradient and neoclassical
transport calculations.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the flux-surface average of the reciprocal square of the
major radius on a nested equilibrium magnetic flux surface. It is a positive
geometric metric coefficient used in parallel-gradient operators and
neoclassical and gyrokinetic transport equations.

It is defined by

$$
g_{m1}(\psi)=\left\langle \frac{1}{R^2}\right\rangle_{\psi}
$$

where $g_{m1}$ denotes this metric coefficient, $R$ is the major radius
measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic
flux labeling the surface, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\psi}$ denotes the
flux-surface average on that surface.

The quantity applies to the entire magnetic flux surface and has no species,
field-component, or source-process restriction. Its aggregation convention
is a flux-surface average of the local reciprocal-square geometric factor;
it is not the reciprocal square of a flux-surface-averaged major radius.

It is the flux-surface-averaged form of the pointwise [inverse of square of
major radius](name:inverse_of_square_of_major_radius). It differs from the
related [flux-surface-averaged inverse of major
radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_major_radius), which averages
the first reciprocal power of $R$ rather than its reciprocal square.

NAMES.name: squareness_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Squareness of a flux surface is the Luce (2013) shape coefficient for each
nested closed magnetic flux surface, including the outer closed boundary
when present, quantifying signed corner-sector departure from a reference
ellipse in the poloidal cross-section. Positive values are box-like;
negative values are diamond-like.
NAMES.long:
Squareness of a flux surface is the Luce (2013) shape coefficient that
quantifies the signed departure of a nested closed magnetic-flux-surface
contour from a reference ellipse in the corner sectors of its poloidal
cross-section. Positive values describe box-like corner sectors relative to
the reference ellipse, and negative values describe diamond-like or
inward-pinched corner sectors.

The contour is considered in a poloidal cross-section of the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is
toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The quantity is defined
separately for each member of the one-parameter family of nested closed flux
surfaces, including the plasma boundary when it is the outer closed flux
surface; it excludes open-field-line regions and material limiter, wall, or
divertor surfaces.

It is a contour-shape coefficient, not a flux-surface label, not a
coordinate of the contour, not a boundary-only quantity, and not an average
over neighboring flux surfaces. It captures corner departure from the
reference ellipse; [elongation](name:elongation_of_flux_surface) captures
the vertical stretching of the contour, and
[triangularity](name:triangularity_of_flux_surface) captures the
major-radius displacement of the upper and lower extrema.

Sector-resolved squareness quantities use the same Luce reference-ellipse
convention on named corner sectors: [upper outer
squareness](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface) on the upper-$Z$,
larger-$R$ sector, [upper inner
squareness](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface) on the upper-$Z$,
smaller-$R$ sector, [lower outer
squareness](name:lower_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface) on the lower-$Z$,
larger-$R$ sector, and [lower inner
squareness](name:lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface) on the lower-$Z$,
smaller-$R$ sector. [Outer
squareness](name:outer_squareness_of_flux_surface) restricts the quantity to
larger-$R$ corner sectors, [inner
squareness](name:inner_squareness_of_flux_surface) restricts it to
smaller-$R$ corner sectors, and [squareness of the plasma
boundary](name:squareness_of_plasma_boundary) is the boundary specialization
of the flux-surface quantity.

NAMES.name: inner_squareness_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless Luce shape coefficient quantifying how much the
high-field-side (inner) corners of a nested magnetic flux surface deviate
from a reference ellipse; positive values indicate a boxier corner, negative
values a more diamond-like or indented corner.
NAMES.long:
The inner squareness of a flux surface is the dimensionless Luce (2013)
shape coefficient that characterizes how much the high-field-side (inboard,
smaller major radius) corners of a nested toroidal magnetic flux surface
depart from a reference ellipse sharing the same center, horizontal
half-width, and [elongation](name:elongation_of_flux_surface). It is the
inboard counterpart within the
[squareness_of_flux_surface](name:squareness_of_flux_surface) family,
complementing the outboard variants
[upper_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface)
and
[lower_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:lower_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface).
This parent quantity abstracts over the quadrant-resolved coefficients
[upper_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface)
and
[lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface),
which independently describe the upper and lower high-field-side corners.

The coefficient $\zeta$ enters the parametric flux-surface shape model as an
additional harmonic beyond elongation $\kappa$ and triangularity $\delta$,
evaluated at the high-field-side corners of the poloidal cross-section in
the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius
and $Z$ is vertical height. A value of zero recovers the reference ellipse
precisely; deviations capture corner shaping not expressible through
$\kappa$ and $\delta$ alone.

The inner squareness is inferred from equilibrium reconstruction by fitting
closed flux-surface contours to a multi-parameter shape model. Asymmetry
between upper and lower inner quadrants can arise in vertically asymmetric
or diverted configurations, motivating the quadrant-resolved child
quantities.

NAMES.name: lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless Luce (2013) squareness coefficient for the lower-inner,
high-field-side quadrant of a nested magnetic flux surface, measuring signed
departure from a reference ellipse.
NAMES.long:
The lower-inner squareness of a flux surface is the dimensionless Luce
(2013) shape coefficient that characterizes how the lower, high-field-side
quadrant of a nested toroidal magnetic flux surface departs from a reference
ellipse sharing the same center, horizontal half-width, and
[elongation](name:elongation_of_flux_surface). It is the lower-quadrant
component of [inner squareness of a flux
surface](name:inner_squareness_of_flux_surface), complementary to
[upper-inner squareness of a flux
surface](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface).

The reference ellipse is parameterized in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,
\phi, Z)$ frame by

$$
\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{ref}}(\theta)=\left(R_0+a\cos\theta,\;Z_0+\kappa a\sin\theta\right)
$$

where $R$ is major radius, $Z$ is vertical height, $\theta$ is a poloidal
parameter, $(R_0,Z_0)$ is the ellipse center, $a$ is its horizontal
half-width, and $\kappa$ is its elongation. Within the Luce model,
$\zeta_{\mathrm{li}}=0$ represents no additional lower-inner corner shaping;
positive values indicate an outward, boxier corner and negative values an
inward, more indented corner.

This coefficient describes only the lower high-field-side quadrant and is
not an average of the upper and lower inner coefficients.

sources.leaf_definition: Lower inner squareness (definition from T. Luce, Plasma Phys. Control. Fusion 55 (2013) 095009)
sources.parent_definition: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux

NAMES.name: outer_squareness_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless Luce shape coefficient for the outboard corners of nested
magnetic flux surfaces, measuring signed departure from a co-centered
reference ellipse across upper and lower quadrants.
NAMES.long:
The outer squareness of a flux surface is the dimensionless Luce (2013)
shape coefficient that characterizes how much the outboard (larger major
radius) corners of a nested toroidal magnetic flux surface depart from a
reference ellipse sharing the same center, horizontal half-width, and
[elongation](name:elongation_of_flux_surface). It is the outboard
counterpart within the
[squareness_of_flux_surface](name:squareness_of_flux_surface) family,
complementing the [inner squareness](name:inner_squareness_of_flux_surface),
and abstracts over the quadrant-resolved coefficients [upper outer
squareness](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface) and [lower outer
squareness](name:lower_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface).

At the modeled outboard corners, the reference condition is

$$
\zeta_{\rm out}=0 \Longleftrightarrow \mathcal{C}_{\rm out}=\mathcal{E}_{\rm out}
$$

where $\zeta_{\rm out}$ is the outer squareness coefficient,
$\mathcal{C}_{\rm out}$ is the modeled outboard corner of the flux-surface
cross-section, and $\mathcal{E}_{\rm out}$ is the corresponding reference
ellipse. The cross-section is described in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and
$Z$ is vertical height.

This quantity does not select either the upper or lower outboard quadrant;
those quadrant-specific coefficients may differ for an up-down asymmetric
flux surface. Positive values describe boxier outward corners, while
negative values describe corners indented relative to the reference ellipse.

NAMES.name: lower_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless Luce shape coefficient for the lower outboard quadrant of
nested magnetic flux surfaces, measuring signed departure from a reference
ellipse with the same center, horizontal half-width, and elongation.
NAMES.long:
The lower outer squareness $\zeta_{\rm lo}$ is the dimensionless Luce (2013)
shape coefficient for the lower outboard ($-Z$, larger-$R$) corner of each
nested magnetic flux surface, measuring its departure from a reference
ellipse sharing the same center, horizontal half-width, and elongation.

At the modeled lower outboard corner, the reference condition is

$$
\zeta_{\rm lo}=0 \Longleftrightarrow \mathcal{C}_{\rm lo}=\mathcal{E}_{\rm lo}
$$

where $\zeta_{\rm lo}$ is the lower outer squareness coefficient,
$\mathcal{C}_{\rm lo}$ is the modeled lower outboard corner, and
$\mathcal{E}_{\rm lo}$ is the corresponding reference ellipse. The
cross-section is described in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$
frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is
vertical height.

This coefficient selects the lower outboard quadrant and is the lower
component of [outer squareness](name:outer_squareness_of_flux_surface),
complementing [upper outer
squareness](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface). Up-down asymmetry
allows the two quadrant-specific coefficients to differ; positive values
describe boxier outward corners, while negative values describe corners
indented relative to the reference ellipse.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the modeled lower outboard corner extends
toward increasing $R$ beyond the corresponding reference ellipse in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Lower outer squareness (definition from T. Luce, Plasma Phys. Control. Fusion 55 (2013) 095009)
sources.parent_definition: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux

NAMES.name: squareness_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Squareness of the plasma boundary is a dimensionless Luce shape coefficient
quantifying the whole-boundary corner deviation of the last closed flux
surface from the reference ellipse set by the boundary minor radius,
elongation, and triangularity. Positive values make the corner regions
boxier, approaching the circumscribing rectangle; negative values make them
more diamond-like.
NAMES.long:
Squareness of the plasma boundary is a dimensionless Luce shape coefficient
quantifying the deviation of the corner regions of the last closed flux
surface from the reference ellipse whose semi-axes are set by the boundary
minor radius, elongation, and triangularity. It is the whole-boundary
summary of the quadrant-level squareness values, characterizing whether the
poloidal cross-section corners bulge outward toward the circumscribing
rectangle or are pinched inward relative to the elliptical reference
contour.

In a poloidal cross-section at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$ of the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, each quadrant of the boundary
is bounded by its radial extremum (innermost or outermost major-radius
point) and its vertical extremum (topmost or bottommost point), and a
reference ellipse is constructed through these two extrema; the semi-axes of
this ellipse are fixed by the boundary minor radius, elongation, and
triangularity. Along the diagonal from the ellipse center $O$ toward the
corner $F$ of the rectangle circumscribing the quadrant, the quadrant
squareness is

$$
\zeta = \frac{\overline{OD} - \overline{OE}}{\overline{OF} - \overline{OE}}
$$

where $D$ is the intersection of the diagonal with the plasma boundary, $E$
its intersection with the reference ellipse, and $\overline{OD}$,
$\overline{OE}$, $\overline{OF}$ are distances from the ellipse center. With
this construction $\zeta = 0$ when the boundary follows the elliptical arc,
$\zeta = 1$ when it passes through the rectangle corner, and $\zeta < 0$
when the corner is indented inside the ellipse (diamond- or bean-like).

This whole-boundary quantity summarizes the four quadrant-resolved members
[upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary),
[upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary),
[lower_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:lower_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary),
and
[lower_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:lower_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary),
and decomposes into
[inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary)
on the high-field side (smaller major radius $R$) and
[outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary)
on the low-field side (larger $R$). Use the quadrant- or side-resolved
members when the boundary corners are shaped asymmetrically; this quantity
carries no information about up-down or in-out asymmetry of the corner
shaping.

NAMES.name: inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Inner squareness of the plasma boundary is the Luce shape coefficient for
the high-field-side corner pair, referenced to an ellipse defined by
boundary size and shaping.
NAMES.long:
Inner squareness of the plasma boundary is a dimensionless Luce shape
coefficient characterizing how the high-field-side corners of the last
closed flux surface depart from a reference ellipse. It covers the inner
corner behavior represented separately by the [upper-inner
squareness](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary) and [lower-inner
squareness](name:lower_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary) quantities,
rather than selecting one vertical quadrant.

In a poloidal cross-section at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$ of the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the coefficient for an inner
quadrant is

$$
\zeta = \frac{\overline{OD} - \overline{OE}}{\overline{OF} - \overline{OE}}
$$

where $O$ is the reference-ellipse center, $D$ is the boundary intersection
along the corner diagonal, $E$ is the corresponding ellipse intersection,
and $F$ is the corner of the circumscribing rectangle; the overbars denote
distances. The reference ellipse is set by the boundary minor radius,
elongation, and triangularity. This component refines the whole-boundary
[squareness of the plasma boundary](name:squareness_of_plasma_boundary) to
its high-field-side corners.

NAMES.name: lower_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless Luce squareness parameter for the lower-inner (below-midplane,
high-field-side) plasma boundary in a poloidal cross-section at fixed
toroidal angle φ in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, measuring
its departure from the reference ellipse set by boundary minor radius,
elongation, and triangularity.
NAMES.long:
The lower-inner squareness of the plasma boundary is the dimensionless Luce
shape coefficient quantifying how much the lower-inboard quadrant of the
last-closed flux surface deviates from the reference ellipse determined by
the boundary minor radius, elongation, and triangularity. The lower-inboard
quadrant is the part of the boundary at smaller major radius and below the
reference-ellipse center in a poloidal cross-section.

In the Luce higher-order boundary parameterization, the lower-inner boundary
contour at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,
\phi, Z)$ frame is represented over the lower-inboard interval of the
poloidal angle $\theta$ by the coefficient $\zeta_{\mathrm{LI}}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
R(\theta) &= R_{\mathrm{geo}} + a\cos\!\left[\theta + \arcsin(\delta_{\mathrm{ref}})\sin\theta - \zeta_{\mathrm{LI}}\sin(2\theta)\right],\\
Z(\theta) &= Z_{\mathrm{geo}} + a\kappa_{\mathrm{ref}}\sin\!\left[\theta + \zeta_{\mathrm{LI}}\sin(2\theta)\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

where $R(\theta)$ and $Z(\theta)$ are the major-radius and vertical
coordinates of the boundary point, $R_{\mathrm{geo}}$ and $Z_{\mathrm{geo}}$
are the coordinates of the geometric center of the reference ellipse, $a$ is
the boundary minor radius, $\kappa_{\mathrm{ref}}$ and
$\delta_{\mathrm{ref}}$ are the elongation and triangularity entering the
same reference boundary description, and $\theta=0$ labels the outboard
midplane with increasing $\theta$ first moving toward $+Z$. The geometric
center of the reference ellipse is not the magnetic-axis position unless
those points coincide for the chosen boundary geometry.

This quantity is restricted to the lower-inboard quadrant and excludes the
upper-inboard quadrant represented by
[upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary).
It is a quadrant-resolved component of
[inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary),
distinct from the outer-side squareness components, and complements
[elongation_of_plasma_boundary](name:elongation_of_plasma_boundary) and
[triangularity_of_plasma_boundary](name:triangularity_of_plasma_boundary) in
describing boundary shape beyond the reference ellipse. With the sign shown
in the Luce representation, positive $\zeta_{\mathrm{LI}}$ moves the
lower-inboard corner toward smaller $R$ and lower $Z$ relative to the
reference ellipse, making that corner more rectangular; negative values make
it rounder.

sources.parent_definition: Description of the plasma boundary. The boundary can be either the real separatrix (provided by a free boundary equilibrium solver) or the 0.99x psi_norm flux surface provided by a fixed boundary equilibrium

NAMES.name: outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless Luce shape coefficient measuring how both outboard
(low-field-side) corners of the plasma boundary depart from the reference
ellipse defined by minor radius, elongation, and triangularity.
NAMES.long:
The outer squareness of the plasma boundary is the Luce (2013) dimensionless
shape coefficient characterizing how the low-field-side (large-$R$) corners
of the last-closed flux surface poloidal cross-section depart from the
reference ellipse defined by the boundary minor radius $a$, elongation
$\kappa$, and triangularity $\delta$. It is the parent quantity for
[upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary)
and
[lower_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:lower_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary),
which resolve the upper-outboard and lower-outboard corner contributions
separately.

A positive outer squareness indicates the outboard corners of the plasma
cross-section lie outside the reference ellipse (a more rectangular
boundary), while a negative value indicates inward concavity at the outboard
corners. The outer squareness is particularly sensitive to X-point geometry
and the configuration of low-field-side shaping coils, making it relevant to
heat-load distribution and edge stability.

Outer squareness is inferred from equilibrium reconstruction by fitting the
poloidal boundary contour $\{R(\xi), Z(\xi)\}$, where $\xi$ is a poloidal
parameter, to external magnetic measurements and internal constraints. The
global single-coefficient summary is provided by
[squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:squareness_of_plasma_boundary), while
the high-field-side corner contributions are captured by
[lower_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:lower_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary)
and upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary.

NAMES.name: lower_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless Luce shape coefficient measuring how the lower outboard
(low-field-side) corner of the plasma boundary departs from the reference
ellipse defined by boundary minor radius, lower elongation, and lower
triangularity.
NAMES.long:
The lower outer squareness $\zeta_{lo}$ is one of four corner-specific shape
parameters in the Luce (2013) plasma boundary parameterization, describing
how much the lower outer quadrant of the plasma cross-section boundary
deviates from the reference ellipse defined by the boundary minor radius
$a$, lower elongation $\kappa_l$, and lower triangularity $\delta_l$. The
lower outer quadrant is the low-field-side, large-$R$ corner below the
magnetic-axis height in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame,
where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

Within the Luce corner parameterization, the coefficient is related to the
lower-outer superellipse exponent $n_{lo}$ by

$$
\zeta_{lo} = 1 - \frac{2}{n_{lo}}
$$

where $n_{lo}$ controls the local corner curvature of the lower-outboard
boundary segment. The reference ellipse corresponds to $n_{lo}=2$.

Positive values indicate that the lower-outboard boundary corner lies
outside the reference ellipse at the corresponding corner location, giving a
more rectangular boundary; $\zeta_{lo}=0$ indicates the reference ellipse;
negative values indicate that the corner lies inside the reference ellipse,
giving inward concavity relative to that ellipse. This coefficient excludes
the upper-outboard and high-field-side corner contributions represented by
[upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary),
[lower_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:lower_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary),
and
[upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary);
[outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary)
combines the outboard corner behavior, and
[squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:squareness_of_plasma_boundary) is the
global single-coefficient summary.

NAMES.name: surface_area_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Surface area of a complete magnetic flux surface, including its full
poloidal and toroidal extent rather than the enclosed poloidal
cross-section.
NAMES.long:
Area of flux surface

The area is defined by

$$
A = \iint_{\mathcal S} dS
$$

where $A$ is the surface area, $\mathcal S$ is the specified flux surface,
and $dS$ is the nonnegative geometric surface-area element.

This quantity applies to one complete flux surface, not solely to the plasma
boundary. It is integrated over the entire surface and is neither a local
area element nor a flux-surface average.

Unlike the [poloidal-plane cross-sectional
area](name:poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_flux_surface), it measures
the surface itself rather than the planar region enclosed by its contour. It
also differs from the [enclosed volume](name:volume_of_flux_surface), which
measures the full interior bounded by the same surface.

A surface formed by points sharing the same magnetic-flux label in a
nested-flux-surface configuration. Where $\psi(R, Z) = \mathrm{const}$,
$\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux.

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_control_surface
NAMES.short:
Toroidal angle locating each point of a control surface about the machine
symmetry axis, measured in the right-handed cylindrical frame from the
facility-defined zero direction.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal angle identifies the azimuthal location of a point on the
control surface about the machine symmetry axis. It is the geometrical
coordinate defined for [toroidal angle](name:toroidal_angle), with the
control-surface locus providing the points to which it applies.

For a point with Cartesian coordinates $x$ and $y$ in the right-handed
$(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis, the angle in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame is defined by:

$$
\phi = \operatorname{atan2}(y,x) \pmod{2\pi}
$$

where $R$ is the major radius, $Z$ is vertical height, and the zero of
$\phi$ follows the facility-defined reference direction. The angle is
periodic, so values differing by an integer multiple of $2\pi$ represent the
same toroidal direction; it is distinct from the vertical coordinate of the
control surface.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when
viewed from above the $+\hat{Z}$ direction.
