NAMES.name: toroidal_diamagnetic_magnetic_flux_at_inside_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Toroidal diamagnetic magnetic flux at an inside flux surface is the
diamagnetic contribution to the toroidal magnetic flux through the poloidal
cross-section enclosed by a selected closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal diamagnetic magnetic flux at an inside flux surface is the
diamagnetic contribution to the [toroidal magnetic
flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux) through the poloidal cross-section
enclosed by a selected closed flux surface. It is a surface-dependent
cumulative flux inside the plasma boundary, not only a boundary value.

For an axisymmetric equilibrium in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi,
Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing
counter-clockwise viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height,
let $S_\chi$ be the constant-$\phi$ poloidal cross-section enclosed by the
flux surface labeled by $\chi$. With $d\mathbf{A}_\phi = \hat{\phi}\,dA$
oriented toward increasing $\phi$, the enclosed diamagnetic toroidal flux is
defined by:

$$
\Phi_{\phi,\mathrm{dia}}(\chi) = \int_{S_\chi} \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{dia}}(R,Z) \cdot d\mathbf{A}_\phi = \int_{S_\chi} B_{\phi,\mathrm{dia}}(R,Z)\,dA
$$

where $\chi$ identifies the selected flux surface,
$\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the diamagnetic contribution to the
equilibrium magnetic field, $B_{\phi,\mathrm{dia}} =
\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{dia}}\cdot\hat{\phi}$ is its toroidal component,
$\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector toward increasing toroidal angle, and $dA$
is the positive scalar area element on $S_\chi$.

This quantity includes only the diamagnetic magnetic-field contribution. It
is distinct from the total
[toroidal_magnetic_flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux), which includes all
magnetic-field contributions, from
[toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary),
which is evaluated at the plasma boundary, and from
[toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary_due_to_poloidal_current](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary_due_to_poloidal_current),
which isolates the poloidal-current contribution at that boundary.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the net diamagnetic magnetic-field
contribution through the enclosed poloidal cross-section points in the
direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, counter-clockwise viewed from above
$+\hat{Z}$.

sources.leaf_definition: Diamagnetic flux
sources.parent_definition: In case of equilibrium reconstruction under constraints, measurements used to constrain the equilibrium, reconstructed values and accuracy of the fit. The names of the child nodes correspond to the following definition: the solver aims at minimizing a cost function defined as : J=1/2*sum_i [ weight_i^2 (reconstructed_i - measured_i)^2 / sigma_i^2 ]. in which sigma_i is the standard deviation of the measurement error (to be found in the IDS of the measurement)

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_coordinate
NAMES.short:
Toroidal flux coordinate is a non-negative, radius-like magnetic-surface
label derived from enclosed toroidal magnetic flux using a positive
reference vacuum toroidal field.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal flux coordinate

The coordinate is defined by

$$\rho_{\mathrm{tor}} = \sqrt{\Phi/(\pi B_0)}$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal flux coordinate, $\Phi$ is the
non-negative toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the flux surface, and $B_0$
is the positive reference vacuum toroidal magnetic-field strength at the
specified reference major radius.

The definition applies to any nested magnetic flux surface, without
restriction to a boundary, transport barrier, or mode-center locus. Each
surface carries a single label; this coordinate is neither a flux-surface
average nor a region integral and need not equal the surface's geometric
minor radius.

The [magnetic-axis value](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis) is
zero because the enclosed toroidal flux vanishes there. With the same
reference field used throughout, dividing the coordinate by its
[plasma-boundary value](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_plasma_boundary)
gives the [normalized toroidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate), which is zero at the
magnetic axis and one at that boundary.

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient
NAMES.short:
Toroidal flux coordinate gradient is the spatial variation of a flux-surface
label based on enclosed toroidal magnetic flux. It denotes the gradient
family itself, without fixing a particular norm, projection, component, or
flux-surface average.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal flux coordinate gradient is the spatial gradient of a flux-surface
label $\chi$ constructed from toroidal magnetic flux. It represents the
underlying gradient concept from which scalar measures, components,
projections, and averages of the coordinate variation are defined.

The relation between the coordinate change and the gradient is:

$$
d\chi = \nabla \chi \cdot d\mathbf{x}
$$

where $\chi$ is the toroidal-flux-based flux coordinate, $\nabla \chi$ is
its spatial gradient, and $d\mathbf{x}$ is an infinitesimal displacement in
physical space.

This parent name does not by itself specify a norm, component, projection
direction, surface average, or normalization of $\chi$. The [toroidal flux
coordinate gradient
magnitude](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude) is a concrete
child that selects the norm of the same underlying gradient; other qualified
children would select other scalar forms.

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Measure of how rapidly a toroidal magnetic-flux coordinate changes in space,
obtained from the magnitude of its spatial gradient.
NAMES.long:
This quantity represents the local geometric rate at which a toroidal
magnetic-flux coordinate changes through physical space. It is the
magnitude-based measure derived from the spatial gradient, independent of
any particular direction or projection.

The defining relation is

$$
\left|\nabla \chi\right| = \sqrt{\nabla\chi \cdot \nabla\chi}
$$

where $\chi$ is the toroidal magnetic-flux coordinate, $\nabla$ is the
spatial-gradient operator, and the dot denotes the Euclidean inner product
of the gradient with itself.

The local form is evaluated pointwise and is not intrinsically flux-surface
averaged or squared. The [flux-surface-averaged toroidal flux coordinate
gradient
magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude)
applies a flux-surface average to this measure, while [square of toroidal
flux coordinate gradient
magnitude](name:square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude)
applies the algebraic square. Both are derived from the underlying [toroidal
flux coordinate gradient](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient), which
retains the full spatial-gradient quantity rather than its magnitude.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Geometric metric coefficient formed by averaging the local magnitude of the
toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient over each nested magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the flux-surface average of the local geometric rate at
which the toroidal flux coordinate changes through physical space. It is a
scalar metric coefficient associated with nested magnetic surfaces.

The defining relation is

$$
\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{S}) = \left\langle \left|\nabla \rho_{\mathrm{tor}}\right| \right\rangle_{\mathcal{S}}
$$

where $\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{S})$ is the averaged metric coefficient,
$\mathcal{S}$ is a magnetic flux surface, $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the
toroidal flux coordinate labeling nested magnetic surfaces, $\nabla$ is the
spatial gradient, and the angle brackets with subscript $\mathcal{S}$ denote
averaging over that surface.

The quantity applies to the complete nested magnetic flux surface and is
aggregated over the surface rather than evaluated at a point, along a line,
or over a volume. It represents the average of the gradient magnitude, not a
directional component and not the local unaveraged value.

It is obtained by applying flux-surface averaging to the local [toroidal
flux coordinate gradient
magnitude](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude). Unlike
[flux-surface-averaged square of toroidal flux coordinate gradient
magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude),
it averages the magnitude itself rather than its square.

NAMES.name: square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Squared spatial gradient of a toroidal magnetic-flux coordinate, providing a
geometric coefficient for equilibrium descriptions in physical space.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the squared magnitude of the spatial gradient of a toroidal
magnetic-flux coordinate. It characterizes how rapidly the chosen flux
coordinate changes through physical space and serves as the geometric basis
for local and flux-surface equilibrium coefficients.

The underlying geometric measure is defined by

$$
G_\chi = \left|\nabla \chi\right|^2
$$

where $G_\chi$ is the squared flux-coordinate gradient magnitude, $\chi$ is
the toroidal magnetic-flux coordinate, $\nabla$ is the spatial gradient
operator, and the magnitude is taken with the physical-space metric.

The quantity applies to equilibrium magnetic geometry wherever the toroidal
flux coordinate and its spatial gradient are defined. Its aggregation is not
fixed at the parent level: concrete instances may be evaluated locally,
averaged over a magnetic flux surface, or formed into a ratio with another
geometric quantity.

It is distinct from the unsquared [toroidal flux-coordinate gradient
magnitude](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude), and it does
not itself prescribe a denominator such as magnetic-field strength or major
radius. The [flux-surface-averaged
square](name:flux_surface_averaged_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude)
is the averaged instance, while related ratio quantities compare this
squared geometric factor with the squared magnetic-field magnitude or
squared major radius.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface average of the squared magnitude of the gradient of the
normalized toroidal-flux radius. It is the averaged contravariant radial
metric coefficient for the flux coordinate rho_tor.
NAMES.long:
Flux-surface average of the squared magnitude of the gradient of the
toroidal flux coordinate is the average, over one magnetic flux surface, of
the squared norm of $\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}$. It is the
flux-surface-averaged contravariant radial metric coefficient associated
with the radial coordinate in the flux-coordinate system
$(\rho_\mathrm{tor}, \theta, \phi)$, where $\theta$ is a poloidal angle
label and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle.

The quantity is defined by the flux-surface average of the local radial
metric component:

$$
G_{\rho\rho}(\rho_\mathrm{tor}) = \left\langle |\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}|^2 \right\rangle_{\rho_\mathrm{tor}} = \frac{\int_{S(\rho_\mathrm{tor})} |\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}|^2\, dA / |\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}|}{\int_{S(\rho_\mathrm{tor})} dA / |\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}|}
$$

where $G_{\rho\rho}$ denotes this flux-surface-averaged metric coefficient,
$\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ is the normalized toroidal-flux radius,
$S(\rho_\mathrm{tor})$ is the magnetic flux surface with that label,
$\nabla$ is the spatial gradient operator, $dA$ is the surface-area element,
and $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\rho_\mathrm{tor}}$ denotes averaging over that
flux surface.

The coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ is constituted by
$\rho_\mathrm{tor}=\sqrt{\Phi/\Phi_b}$, where $\Phi$ is the toroidal
magnetic flux enclosed by the flux surface and $\Phi_b$ is its value at the
plasma boundary. The scope is closed nested equilibrium flux surfaces; the
aggregation convention is an average over the entire surface at fixed
$\rho_\mathrm{tor}$.

This is not the pointwise quantity $|\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}|^2$, not the
flux-surface average of $|\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}|$, and not a volume or
time average. It belongs to the same flux-surface-averaged geometric-metric
family as the [flux-surface-averaged inverse major
radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_major_radius), but it
characterizes the radial metric of the normalized toroidal-flux radius
rather than a major-radius factor.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Ratio of the square of the toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient magnitude to
the square of the local magnetic-field magnitude. It is the unaveraged
magnetic-geometry ratio whose flux-surface average defines the corresponding
averaged geometry coefficient.
NAMES.long:
Ratio of the square of the toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient magnitude to
the square of the local magnetic-field magnitude is a local scalar
magnetic-geometry coefficient. It expresses how the spatial metric of the
toroidal flux coordinate is weighted by the magnetic-field strength at the
same position.

The coefficient $K_{\rho B}$ is defined pointwise by:

$$
K_{\rho B}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{|\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}(\mathbf{x})|^2}{|\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})|^2}
$$

where $K_{\rho B}$ is this ratio, $\mathbf{x}$ is spatial position,
$\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ is the toroidal flux coordinate, $\nabla
\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ is its spatial gradient, $\mathbf{B}$ is the
magnetic-field vector, and $|\mathbf{B}|$ is the [magnetic-field
magnitude](name:magnetic_field_magnitude).

This quantity is the unaveraged, pointwise ratio evaluated where the
toroidal flux coordinate is differentiable and the magnetic-field magnitude
is nonzero. It does not include a flux-surface, volume, or time average, and
it is distinct from an averaged geometry coefficient.

The numerator is the [square of the toroidal flux-coordinate gradient
magnitude](name:square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude), and
the denominator is the square of the local magnetic-field magnitude at the
same position. The [flux-surface-averaged
ratio](name:flux_surface_averaged_ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude)
is obtained by applying a flux-surface average to this local quotient
itself, not by separately averaging the numerator and denominator.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface average of the squared toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient
magnitude divided by the squared local magnetic-field magnitude, a metric
coefficient for equilibrium geometry.
NAMES.long:
This coefficient describes the flux-surface-averaged geometric weighting of
a toroidal-flux radial coordinate by the inverse square of the local
magnetic-field magnitude.

The defining relation is

$$
\mathcal{G}_B = \left\langle \frac{|\nabla \rho_{\mathrm{tor}}|^2}{|\mathbf{B}|^2} \right\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}}
$$

where $\mathcal{G}_B$ is the averaged metric coefficient,
$\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal-flux radial coordinate, $\nabla$ is
the spatial gradient, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, and
$\langle\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}}$ denotes the average over a magnetic flux
surface.

The quantity applies to nested equilibrium magnetic flux surfaces and uses
the average of the pointwise ratio, not the ratio of separately averaged
numerator and denominator. It is nonnegative because both the gradient
magnitude and magnetic-field magnitude are squared.

It is the flux-surface-averaged form of the local [ratio of squared
toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient magnitude to squared magnetic-field
magnitude](name:ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude).
It shares the gradient-squared geometric factor with the
[flux-surface-averaged squared toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient
magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude),
but additionally applies the pointwise inverse-square magnetic-field
weighting before averaging. It is distinct from the corresponding
major-radius denominator variant, [flux-surface-averaged ratio of squared
toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient magnitude to squared major
radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_major_radius).

NAMES.name: ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_major_radius
NAMES.short:
Geometric equilibrium coefficient representing a squared flux-coordinate
gradient scaled by the inverse square of major radius.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is a geometric metric coefficient for nested magnetic flux
surfaces in toroidal plasma equilibrium. It measures spatial variation of a
flux coordinate after scaling by the inverse square of the major radius,
rather than representing a material, particle, or transport quantity.

For the gradient-ratio form represented by this family, the coefficient is
defined by:

$$
\mathcal{G}(\xi,R) = \frac{|\nabla \xi|^2}{R^2}
$$

where $\mathcal{G}$ is the geometric coefficient, $\xi$ is the relevant
flux-coordinate label, $\nabla \xi$ is its spatial gradient, $|\nabla \xi|$
is the gradient magnitude, and $R$ is the major-radius coordinate in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The scope is equilibrium magnetic geometry associated with nested flux
surfaces; no plasma population is selected, and the quantity is not a
density, magnetic-field strength, or transport coefficient. It is the
metric-ratio component of
[square_of_major_radius](name:square_of_major_radius), distinguished from a
bare reciprocal-square-radius factor by the flux-coordinate gradient in its
numerator. The parent quantity is not intrinsically flux-surface averaged;
averaging is an explicit aggregation applied by a child.

The representative [flux-surface-averaged gradient-ratio
coefficient](name:flux_surface_averaged_ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_major_radius)
is the flux-surface average of this geometric ratio. This distinguishes it
from
[flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_major_radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_major_radius),
which contains the reciprocal-square major-radius factor without the
flux-coordinate gradient factor.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_major_radius
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface-averaged magnetic-geometry coefficient measuring the squared
toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient relative to the squared major radius.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is a magnetic-geometry metric coefficient that characterizes
how a toroidal-flux radial coordinate varies across nested magnetic
surfaces, with the variation weighted by inverse squared major radius.

It is defined by

$$
g_2 = \left\langle \frac{|\nabla \rho|^2}{R^2} \right\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}}
$$

where $g_2$ is the flux-surface-averaged metric coefficient, $\rho$ is the
toroidal-flux radial coordinate, $\nabla\rho$ is its spatial gradient,
$|\nabla\rho|$ is the gradient magnitude, $R$ is the major radius, and the
subscript $\mathrm{FS}$ denotes the prescribed average over a complete
magnetic flux surface.

The quantity applies to an equilibrium magnetic flux surface and represents
an aggregate over that surface rather than a pointwise local value. It has
no species, population, or transport-channel restriction.

It is the flux-surface average of the local ratio defined by [ratio of
square of toroidal flux coordinate gradient magnitude to square of major
radius](name:ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_major_radius).
Unlike [flux-surface-averaged square of toroidal flux coordinate gradient
magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude),
it retains the inverse-square-major-radius weighting; the numerator is
constructed from the [toroidal flux coordinate gradient
magnitude](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude).

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short:
Value of the radius-like toroidal-flux label on the magnetic surface passing
through the magnetic axis; it is zero because enclosed toroidal flux
vanishes there.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal flux coordinate at the magnetic axis is the value of the
radius-like flux-surface label on the magnetic-axis reference surface. It
identifies the origin of the toroidal-flux radial coordinate and is not a
geometric distance from the machine symmetry axis.

The coordinate is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor}} = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}}{\pi B_0}}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal flux coordinate,
$\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the magnetic
surface, and $B_0$ is the positive reference vacuum toroidal magnetic-field
strength. At the magnetic axis, the enclosed toroidal flux is zero, so this
value is zero.

The quantity applies to the single magnetic-axis locus and is neither a
flux-surface average nor an integral over a finite region. It is the axis
value of the parent [toroidal flux
coordinate](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate), not the coordinate of an
arbitrary flux surface or a geometric major- or minor-radius measurement.

The [toroidal magnetic flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux) supplies the
enclosed-flux quantity in the defining relation, while the corresponding
normalized toroidal-flux coordinate uses axis and boundary values to form a
dimensionless radial label.

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_field_at_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Toroidal magnetic field at a flux surface is the signed component of the
equilibrium magnetic-field vector along the φ direction of the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame at a specified point on a magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal magnetic field at a flux surface is the coefficient $B_\phi$
multiplying $\hat{\phi}$ in the cylindrical decomposition of the equilibrium
magnetic-field vector at a point on a selected magnetic flux surface. The
direction $\hat{\phi}$ belongs to the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi,
Z)$ basis, where $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above
$+\hat{Z}$.

The component is the signed scalar projection onto the toroidal basis
vector:

$$
B_\phi(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \hat{\phi}(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is the point on the selected magnetic flux surface and
$\mathbf{B}$ is the equilibrium magnetic-field vector.

This is the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ toroidal component, not the poloidal
magnetic field at a flux surface, radial magnetic field at a flux surface,
vertical magnetic field at a flux surface, or magnetic-field magnitude at a
flux surface. The surface locus is specified independently, for example by
the [poloidal magnetic flux at a flux
surface](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_flux_surface); this quantity is not
the flux label itself.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the magnetic-field vector component is in the
direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_flux
NAMES.short:
Toroidal magnetic flux is the signed integral of the toroidal magnetic field
through the poloidal cross-section enclosed by a specified magnetic flux
surface.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal magnetic flux is the net flux of the toroidal magnetic-field
component through the poloidal cross-section enclosed by a specified
magnetic flux surface. It specializes [magnetic flux](name:magnetic_flux) by
selecting a surface whose normal points in the toroidal direction.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major
radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, it is defined
by

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}} = \int_{\Omega} \mathbf{B}\cdot\hat{\phi}\,dA_{RZ} = \int_{\Omega} B_\phi\,dA_{RZ}
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is toroidal magnetic flux, $\Omega$ is the
poloidal cross-sectional region enclosed by the selected magnetic flux
surface, $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic field, $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit
vector toward increasing toroidal angle, $B_\phi$ is the toroidal
magnetic-field component, and $dA_{RZ}$ is the positive poloidal
cross-sectional area element.

The integral includes both externally imposed toroidal field and the field
associated with plasma poloidal current, rather than only a selected source
contribution. It is cumulative inside the selected flux surface, vanishes as
that surface contracts to the magnetic axis, and becomes [toroidal magnetic
flux at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary)
when the selected surface is the plasma boundary. It is neither the
geometric toroidal angle nor a flux-surface average.

Unlike [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux), which threads
a horizontal disk centered on the symmetry axis, toroidal magnetic flux
threads a poloidal cross-section. The [difference of poloidal and toroidal
magnetic flux] is $\psi^* = \psi - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$, where $\psi$ is
poloidal magnetic flux and $\psi^*$ is the combined flux coordinate. The
[post-sawtooth-crash
difference](name:difference_of_poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_post_sawtooth_crash_and_toroidal_magnetic_flux)
uses the post-crash poloidal flux without changing this definition of
toroidal flux.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the net toroidal magnetic field threading the
enclosed poloidal cross-section points toward increasing toroidal angle
$\phi$, counterclockwise viewed from above.

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Toroidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary is the net flux of toroidal
magnetic field through the poloidal cross-section enclosed by the plasma
boundary, including externally imposed and plasma-poloidal-current
contributions.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary is the net flux of the
toroidal magnetic-field component through the poloidal cross-section
enclosed by the plasma boundary. It is the boundary value of toroidal
magnetic flux used to define toroidal-flux radial labels.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major
radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed
from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height, the boundary toroidal
flux is defined by

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{tor},b} = \int_{\Omega_b} \mathbf{B}\cdot\hat{\phi}\, dA_{RZ} = \int_{\Omega_b} B_\phi(R,Z)\, dA_{RZ} = \int_{\Omega_b} \frac{F(\psi(R,Z))}{R}\, dA_{RZ}
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor},b}$ is this boundary toroidal flux, $\Omega_b$ is
the boundary-enclosed region in the poloidal plane of the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field,
$B_\phi$ is its toroidal component in tesla, $dA_{RZ}$ is the poloidal
cross-sectional area element in square meters, $F(\psi)=R B_\phi$ is the
poloidal-current function in tesla meters, and $\psi$ is the equilibrium
poloidal magnetic-flux label.

The geometric measure of $\Omega_b$ is the [poloidal cross-sectional area of
the plasma
boundary](name:poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_plasma_boundary).
$\Phi_{\mathrm{tor},b}$ includes both externally imposed toroidal-field flux
and the contribution associated with plasma poloidal current, and is
distinct from [toroidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary due to poloidal
current](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary_due_to_poloidal_current),
which contains only that plasma-current contribution. It also differs from
[poloidal magnetic flux at the plasma
boundary](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary), which is magnetic
flux through a horizontal disk rather than through the boundary-enclosed
poloidal cross-section.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the net toroidal magnetic field threading the
plasma-boundary poloidal cross-section points in the direction of increasing
toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary_due_to_poloidal_current
NAMES.short:
Signed toroidal magnetic flux through the poloidal cross-section enclosed by
the plasma boundary, attributable specifically to plasma poloidal current.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the contribution to the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by
the plasma boundary that is generated by the plasma poloidal current. It is
a component of the [toroidal magnetic flux at the plasma
boundary](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary), distinct from
contributions attributed to other physical processes.

The contribution is defined by

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{pol}} = \int_{A_b} B_{\phi}^{\mathrm{pol}}\,\mathrm{d}A_p
$$

where $A_b$ is the poloidal cross-sectional area enclosed by the plasma
boundary, $B_{\phi}^{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the toroidal magnetic-field component
generated by the poloidal plasma current, and $\mathrm{d}A_p$ is the
oriented area element of that cross-section. The toroidal direction is
$\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity excludes toroidal-flux contributions attributed to other
mechanisms, such as the [toroidal magnetic flux due to diamagnetic
drift](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), and is not
necessarily the total boundary flux.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $B_{\phi}^{\mathrm{pol}}$ points in the
direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ through the poloidal
cross-section oriented with normal $+\hat{\phi}$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short:
Toroidal magnetic flux change through a poloidal cross-section caused by the
pressure-gradient-driven plasma response relative to a reference field
without that response.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal magnetic flux due to diamagnetic drift is the signed,
surface-integrated magnetic response associated with
pressure-gradient-driven plasma diamagnetism. It is the toroidal
specialization of the [magnetic-flux contribution due to diamagnetic
drift](name:magnetic_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), defined relative to a
corresponding reference field without that response.

The contribution through an oriented poloidal cross-section is defined by

$$
\Phi_{\phi,\mathrm{dia}} = \int_S \left(\mathbf{B}-\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{ref}}\right)\cdot\hat{\phi}\,\mathrm{d}S
$$

where $\Phi_{\phi,\mathrm{dia}}$ is the toroidal diamagnetic flux, $S$ is
the poloidal integration surface, $\mathbf{B}$ is the equilibrium magnetic
field, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the corresponding reference magnetic
field with the same external excitation but without the diamagnetic
response, and $\mathrm{d}S$ is a positive surface-area element. In the
right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is
toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical height, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector
toward increasing toroidal angle; the surface normal is chosen along
$\hat{\phi}$.

This is a global flux contribution over the specified cross-section, not a
local magnetic-field value or a flux value at a particular magnetic surface.
It excludes the reference-field flux and is distinct from both total
toroidal magnetic flux and poloidal magnetic flux. The [toroidal current
density due to diamagnetic
drift](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) instead
describes a local electric-current contribution, not this integrated
magnetic response.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the diamagnetic magnetic-field change
produces net flux in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: triangularity_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Signed dimensionless shape parameter measuring the normalized horizontal
displacement of a nested magnetic flux surface’s upper or lower vertical
extremum.
NAMES.long:
Triangularity of a nested magnetic flux surface is the signed shape
parameter formed from the horizontal displacement of an upper or lower
vertical extremum, normalized by the surface’s horizontal half-width.

For a selected upper or lower vertical extremum, triangularity is defined in
the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame by

$$
\delta_s = \frac{R_c - R_s}{a}
$$

where $\delta_s$ is the triangularity, $s$ identifies the selected upper or
lower vertical extremum, $R_s$ is its radial coordinate, $R_c$ is the radial
midpoint of the flux surface’s horizontal extent, and $a$ is the
corresponding horizontal half-width.

This is a geometric parameter of an individual nested magnetic flux surface
in an equilibrium plasma. The unqualified quantity covers either vertical
extremum and carries no aggregation over multiple flux surfaces, plasma
volume, or the plasma boundary.

Triangularity characterizes the radial displacement of a vertical extremum;
it is distinct from [elongation of a flux
surface](name:elongation_of_flux_surface), which describes the ratio of
vertical to horizontal extent, and from [outer squareness of a flux
surface](name:outer_squareness_of_flux_surface), which describes corner
deformation.

The upper and lower branch-specific quantities are [upper triangularity of a
flux surface](name:upper_triangularity_of_flux_surface) and [lower
triangularity of a flux surface](name:lower_triangularity_of_flux_surface);
each is an instance of this parent quantity with $s$ fixed to the
corresponding vertical extremum.

NAMES.name: lower_triangularity_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless lower triangularity shape parameter for a nested magnetic flux
surface, given by the normalized inward radial displacement of its lower
vertical extremum.
NAMES.long:
Lower triangularity of a flux surface is the dimensionless triangularity
shape parameter defined at the lower vertical extremum of a nested magnetic
flux surface. It is the normalized inward displacement in major radius $R$
of that lower extremum relative to the magnetic-axis reference.

For the lower vertical extremum, the defining relation is:

$$
\delta_{\mathrm{lower}} = \frac{R_{\mathrm{axis}} - R_{\mathrm{lower}}}{a}
$$

where $\delta_{\mathrm{lower}}$ is lower triangularity, $R_{\mathrm{axis}}$
is the major-radius coordinate of the magnetic axis, $R_{\mathrm{lower}}$ is
the major-radius coordinate of the lower vertical extremum, and $a$ is the
minor radius of the same flux surface. These coordinates are defined in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius
measured from the machine symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$
is vertical height.

This quantity applies independently to each nested magnetic flux surface and
is a geometrical property of the surface rather than a plasma-population
quantity. It resolves the lower vertical extremum only; it is not averaged
over flux surfaces or combined with the upper extremum. It is distinct from
[lower triangularity of a flux surface
boundary](name:lower_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary), which describes the
outer plasma boundary rather than an arbitrary nested surface.

It is the lower-extremum branch of [triangularity of a flux
surface](name:triangularity_of_flux_surface), whose parent quantity permits
the relevant upper or lower vertical extremum. The corresponding [upper
triangularity of a flux surface](name:upper_triangularity_of_flux_surface)
uses the upper vertical extremum, while [elongation of a flux
surface](name:elongation_of_flux_surface) describes vertical-to-horizontal
shaping rather than triangular displacement.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the lower vertical extremum lies at smaller
major radius $R$ than the magnetic-axis reference, corresponding to an
inward displacement.

NAMES.name: triangularity_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless shape parameter for the plasma-boundary poloidal
cross-section, expressing the aggregate inward radial displacement of its
upper and lower extrema relative to the geometric center.
NAMES.long:
Plasma-boundary triangularity is a dimensionless shaping parameter
describing the asymmetry of the boundary’s poloidal cross-section through
the inward displacement of its upper and lower radial extrema relative to
the geometric center. It characterizes the complete boundary rather than
either half-plane extremum alone.

For the upper and lower boundary extrema, the aggregate triangularity is
defined as

$$
\delta = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{R_0-R_u}{a}+\frac{R_0-R_l}{a}\right)
$$

where $\delta$ is the plasma-boundary triangularity, $R_0$ is the
major-radius coordinate of the geometric center, $R_u$ and $R_l$ are the
major-radius coordinates of the upper and lower boundary extrema, and $a$ is
the boundary minor radius. The coordinates refer to the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity applies to the entire plasma boundary and aggregates the upper
and lower extremal displacements into one shape parameter. It excludes the
separately resolved [upper triangularity of the plasma
boundary](name:upper_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary) and [lower
triangularity of the plasma
boundary](name:lower_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary), which retain only
one extremum. It also differs from [triangularity of a flux
surface](name:triangularity_of_flux_surface), which describes an individual
nested magnetic flux surface rather than the outer plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: upper_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
The upper-inner squareness of a flux surface is the dimensionless Luce
(2013) shape coefficient that characterizes how the upper, high-field-side
quadrant of a nested toroidal magnetic flux surface departs from a reference
ellipse; positive values are boxier and negative values are more
diamond-like or indented.
NAMES.long:
The upper-inner squareness of a flux surface is the dimensionless Luce
(2013) shape coefficient that characterizes how the upper, high-field-side
quadrant of a nested toroidal magnetic flux surface departs from a reference
ellipse sharing the same center, horizontal half-width, and
[elongation](name:elongation_of_flux_surface). It is the upper
quadrant-resolved component of
[inner_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:inner_squareness_of_flux_surface),
complementing
[lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface).
The upper-inner quadrant is the segment from the top of the surface to the
inner midplane, on the high-field side at smaller major radius in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and
$Z$ is vertical height.

The coefficient $\zeta_\mathrm{ui}$ enters the Luce parametric flux-surface
shape model as an additional harmonic beyond elongation $\kappa$ and
[triangularity](name:triangularity_of_flux_surface):

$$
Z(\theta)-Z_c = a\kappa\sin\!\left[\theta + \zeta_\mathrm{ui}\sin(2\theta)\right], \qquad \pi/2 \le \theta \le \pi
$$

where $Z(\theta)$ is the vertical coordinate of the contour, $Z_c$ is the
vertical coordinate of the surface center, $a$ is the horizontal half-width,
$\theta$ is the geometric poloidal angle measured about the surface center
in the $(R,Z)$ cross-section with $\theta=0$ at the outboard midplane and
increasing toward $+Z$, and $\zeta_\mathrm{ui}$ is the upper-inner
squareness coefficient. Setting $\zeta_\mathrm{ui}=0$ recovers the
corresponding reference ellipse for this quadrant.

This quantity is a quadrant-local squareness coefficient, not an average
over the two inner quadrants and not an outboard squareness coefficient in
the broader [squareness_of_flux_surface](name:squareness_of_flux_surface)
family. It describes corner shaping not represented by elongation or
triangularity alone.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the upper high-field-side corner of the
flux-surface cross-section is boxier than the reference ellipse; negative
values indicate a more diamond-like or indented corner.

NAMES.name: upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Upper-inner squareness of the plasma boundary is the dimensionless Luce
shape coefficient measuring the upper high-field-side corner’s signed
departure from a reference ellipse.
NAMES.long:
The upper-inner squareness of the plasma boundary is the dimensionless Luce
shape coefficient quantifying the departure of the upper inboard corner of
the last closed flux surface from a reference ellipse. It is the
upper-quadrant component of the [inner squareness of the plasma
boundary](name:inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary), paired with the
[lower-inner squareness of the plasma
boundary](name:lower_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary).

In a poloidal cross-section at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$ of the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the coefficient is

$$
\zeta_{\mathrm{UI}} = \frac{\overline{OD} - \overline{OE}}{\overline{OF} - \overline{OE}}
$$

where $O$ is the reference-ellipse center, $D$ is the upper-inner boundary
intersection along the corner diagonal, $E$ is the corresponding ellipse
intersection, and $F$ is the corner of the circumscribing rectangle. The
reference ellipse is determined by the boundary size and shaping parameters.

NAMES.name: upper_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless Luce shape coefficient for the upper outboard quadrant of each
nested flux surface, measuring the departure of that corner from a reference
ellipse with the same center, horizontal half-width, and elongation.
NAMES.long:
The upper outer squareness $\zeta_{uo}$ is the dimensionless Luce (2013)
shape coefficient for the upper outboard ($+Z$, large-$R$) corner of each
nested magnetic flux surface, measuring how much that quadrant departs from
a reference ellipse sharing the same geometric center, horizontal
half-width, and elongation. It is one of four quadrant-resolved squareness
parameters — alongside the [lower outer
squareness](name:lower_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface), [upper inner
squareness](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface), and [lower inner
squareness](name:lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface) — extending the
standard elongation-triangularity shape description to higher order.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the flux-surface
boundary in the upper outer quadrant is described by the Luce
parameterization as:

$$
R = R_\mathrm{geo} + a\cos\!\bigl(\theta + \delta_{uo}\sin\theta + \zeta_{uo}\sin 2\theta\bigr)
$$

with $Z = Z_\mathrm{geo} + \kappa\, a\sin\theta$, where $R_\mathrm{geo}$ and
$Z_\mathrm{geo}$ are the coordinates of the flux-surface geometric center,
$a$ is the minor radius, $\kappa$ is the elongation, $\delta_{uo}$ is the
upper outer triangularity, and $\theta \in [0, \pi/2]$ is the geometric
poloidal angle spanning the upper outboard quadrant.

Values near zero indicate an approximately elliptic corner; positive values
are characteristic of D-shaped cross-sections with a squared-off outboard
corner, while negative values correspond to a more concave or helmet-shaped
upper outer region. The coefficient is extracted from equilibrium
reconstruction by fitting computed flux-surface contours to the Luce
parameterization in the upper outboard region. The symmetric combination of
upper and lower outer quadrant values constitutes the aggregate
[outer_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:outer_squareness_of_flux_surface),
and the value at the outermost flux surface corresponds to
[upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the upper outer corner of the flux surface
protrudes beyond the reference ellipse, giving the cross-section a more
rectangular (D-shaped) outboard corner.

sources.leaf_definition: Upper outer squareness (definition from T. Luce, Plasma Phys. Control. Fusion 55 (2013) 095009)

NAMES.name: upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless Luce shape coefficient measuring how the upper outboard
(low-field-side) corner of the plasma boundary departs from the reference
ellipse defined by boundary minor radius, upper elongation, and upper
triangularity.
NAMES.long:
The upper outer squareness $\zeta_{uo}$ is one of four corner-specific shape
parameters in the Luce (2013) plasma boundary parameterization, describing
how much the upper outer quadrant of the plasma cross-section boundary
deviates from the reference ellipse defined by the boundary minor radius
$a$, upper elongation $\kappa_u$, and upper triangularity $\delta_u$. In the
poloidal cross-section expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi,
Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height, this
quadrant is the large-$R$, larger-$Z$ corner relative to the boundary shape
center.

With poloidal parameter $\theta$ increasing from the outboard midplane point
to the top point, the upper-outboard Luce boundary segment is parameterized
by

$$
\begin{aligned}
R(\theta) &= R_0 + a\cos\left[\theta + \arcsin(\delta_u)\sin\theta - \zeta_{uo}\sin(2\theta)\right],\\
Z(\theta) &= Z_0 + \kappa_u a\sin\left[\theta + \zeta_{uo}\sin(2\theta)\right],\quad 0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

where $(R(\theta), Z(\theta))$ is the boundary point in the poloidal
cross-section, $R_0$ and $Z_0$ are the shape-center coordinates, $a$ is the
boundary minor radius, $\kappa_u$ is the upper elongation, and $\delta_u$ is
the upper triangularity.

The value $\zeta_{uo}=0$ is the reference-ellipse case for the
upper-outboard quadrant after $a$, $\kappa_u$, and $\delta_u$ have been
fixed; nonzero values describe residual corner shaping rather than minor
radius, elongation, or triangularity. Together with
[lower_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:lower_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary),
[upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary),
and
[lower_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:lower_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary),
it forms the four-corner boundary squareness decomposition;
[outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary)
combines the two outboard corner contributions, while
[squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:squareness_of_plasma_boundary) is the
single-coefficient boundary summary.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the upper outer boundary corner lies outside
the reference ellipse at the same poloidal parameter, i.e., toward larger
$R$ and larger $Z$ relative to the shape center in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is
vertical height.

NAMES.name: upper_triangularity_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless upper triangularity shape parameter for a nested magnetic flux
surface, given by the normalized inward radial displacement of its upper
vertical extremum.
NAMES.long:
Upper triangularity of a flux surface is the dimensionless triangularity
shape parameter defined at the upper vertical extremum of a nested magnetic
flux surface. It is the normalized inward radial displacement of that upper
extremum in a poloidal cross-section.

For the upper vertical extremum, the defining relation is:

$$
\delta_u = \frac{R_{\mathrm{axis}} - R_u}{a}
$$

where $\delta_u$ is upper triangularity, $R_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the
major-radius coordinate of the magnetic axis, $R_u$ is the major-radius
coordinate of the upper vertical extremum, and $a$ is the minor radius of
the flux surface. These coordinates are defined in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is
toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

This quantity applies separately to each nested magnetic flux surface
identified by its poloidal magnetic-flux label. It represents only the upper
extremum and is not an aggregate over the upper and lower extrema or over
multiple flux surfaces.

It is distinct from [lower triangularity of a flux
surface](name:lower_triangularity_of_flux_surface), which uses the lower
vertical extremum. It also differs from [upper triangularity of the plasma
boundary](name:upper_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary), which applies only
to the outer plasma boundary rather than to an arbitrary nested flux
surface.

Upper triangularity is the upper-extremum branch of [triangularity of a flux
surface](name:triangularity_of_flux_surface), whose definition permits the
relevant upper or lower vertical extremum. The upper and lower quantities
together describe the asymmetric triangular shaping of a flux-surface
cross-section.

NAMES.name: upper_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Upper triangularity of the plasma boundary is the inward major-radius
displacement of its upper vertical extremum from the geometric axis, divided
by the boundary minor radius.
NAMES.long:
Triangularity of plasma boundary

Triangularity without a qualifier is the mean of the upper and lower
triangularities; upper and lower triangularity each use one extremum of the
cross-section.

The upper and lower triangularities and their mean are defined by:

$$\delta_{\mathrm{u,l}} = (R_{\mathrm{geo}} - R_{\mathrm{u,l}})/a,\quad \delta = (\delta_{\mathrm{u}} + \delta_{\mathrm{l}})/2$$

where $\delta_{\mathrm{u}}$ is upper triangularity, $\delta_{\mathrm{l}}$ is
[lower triangularity of the plasma
boundary](name:lower_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary), and $\delta$ is
[mean triangularity of the plasma
boundary](name:triangularity_of_plasma_boundary). Here $R_{\mathrm{geo}}$ is
the [major-radius coordinate of the geometric
axis](name:radial_coordinate_of_geometric_axis), $R_{\mathrm{u,l}}$ denotes
the major-radius coordinate of the upper or lower vertical extremum,
respectively, and $a$ is the boundary minor radius, equal to its horizontal
half-width. These coordinates use the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$
frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is
vertical height.

This quantity describes only the upper extremum of the plasma-boundary
cross-section; it is not an average over both extrema or over nested flux
surfaces. Unlike [upper triangularity of a flux
surface](name:upper_triangularity_of_flux_surface), its locus is restricted
to the plasma boundary. The upper and lower triangularities contribute
equally to the mean boundary triangularity and need not coincide.

The last closed magnetic flux surface: the outermost flux surface on which
field lines close on themselves, bounding the confined plasma. Where $\psi =
\psi_{\mathrm{LCFS}}$, $\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux;
$\psi_{\mathrm{LCFS}}$ is its value on the last closed flux surface.

NAMES.name: vacuum_magnetic_field
NAMES.short:
Local magnetic-induction vector generated by currents external to the plasma
with plasma-current contributions omitted, retaining field strength and
direction before selecting a component in the right-handed cylindrical (R,
φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vacuum magnetic field $\mathbf{B}_{\rm vac}$ is the local [magnetic
induction](name:magnetic_field) generated by currents external to the plasma
when plasma-current contributions are omitted. It represents a vector field
at a point, retaining field strength and direction rather than selecting a
cylindrical component or scalar magnitude.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the vacuum field may be
resolved as

$$
\mathbf{B}_{\rm vac}=B_{R,{\rm vac}}\hat{R}+B_{\phi,{\rm vac}}\hat{\phi}+B_{Z,{\rm vac}}\hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}_{\rm vac}$ is the vacuum magnetic field, $B_{R,{\rm vac}}$
is its signed radial component, $B_{\phi,{\rm vac}}$ is the [toroidal vacuum
magnetic field](name:toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field), $B_{Z,{\rm vac}}$ is
its signed vertical component, and $\hat{R}$, $\hat{\phi}$, and $\hat{Z}$
are the basis vectors for increasing major radius, toroidal angle, and
vertical height.

This quantity is the externally sourced, plasma-current-omitted contribution
to the local field and may be evaluated inside the confined-plasma region as
well as in vacuum regions; it does not denote only the space outside the
plasma. It has no species population, and its aggregation convention is a
local point value, not a spatial average, flux-surface average, or
finite-volume reduction.

It is distinct from the [plasma magnetic field](name:plasma_magnetic_field),
which represents the magnetic-field contribution associated with the
confined plasma, and from the unrestricted local [magnetic
induction](name:magnetic_field), which does not by name isolate the vacuum
contribution. The [non-axisymmetric magnetic
field](name:non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field) is the toroidally varying part
of the external-coil vacuum field after its toroidally averaged component is
removed, while a [perturbed vacuum magnetic
field](name:perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field) denotes a perturbative vacuum
contribution rather than the full vacuum vector.

The [vacuum magnetic vector
potential](name:vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential) $\mathbf{A}_{\rm vac}$ is
a potential for this field, with $\mathbf{B}_{\rm
vac}=\nabla\times\mathbf{A}_{\rm vac}$, where $\mathbf{A}_{\rm vac}$ is the
vacuum magnetic vector potential and $\nabla$ is the spatial differential
operator. Different gage choices of $\mathbf{A}_{\rm vac}$ that have the
same curl represent the same vacuum magnetic field; in regions containing no
external current density, $\mathbf{B}_{\rm vac}$ is curl-free, and the field
is solenoidal.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when a resolved component of $\mathbf{B}_{\rm
vac}$ points along the corresponding positive basis vector of the
right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where the positive directions
are increasing major radius $R$, increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, and
increasing vertical height $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_constraint_position
NAMES.short:
Vertical coordinate of the constraint position gives its signed height
relative to the zero-height plane in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z)
frame.
NAMES.long:
Vertical coordinate of the constraint position is its signed height relative
to the zero-height plane in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.
Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical
height parallel to the toroidal symmetry axis.

The coordinate is defined by

$$
Z = \mathbf{x}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}}
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is the position vector of the constraint position
measured from the coordinate origin, $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is the unit vector
along the positive vertical direction, and the dot denotes the Euclidean
scalar product.

The quantity applies to an individual constraint position, not an average
over constraint positions or a vertical component of the constrained
physical quantity. It uses the same geometric projection as the [vertical
coordinate of a measurement
position](name:vertical_coordinate_of_measurement_position), with the locus
restricted to the constraint position.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the constraint position lies above the
zero-height plane along $+\hat{\mathbf{z}}$.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_current_center
NAMES.short:
Signed vertical position of the plasma-current centroid, obtained by
weighting the toroidal current distribution by height in the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of the plasma-current center is the
current-density-weighted centroid height of the plasma current distribution
in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

$$
Z_{\mathrm{c}} = \frac{\int_{\mathcal{A}} Z\,j_{\phi}(R,Z)\,dA}{\int_{\mathcal{A}} j_{\phi}(R,Z)\,dA}
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{c}}$ and $Z$ are vertical coordinates in m, $R$ is major
radius in m, $j_{\phi}$ is toroidal current density in A m$^{-2}$, $dA$ is
differential poloidal cross-sectional area in m$^{2}$, and $\mathcal{A}$ is
the region carrying plasma current. The current-weighted center is distinct
from the geometric axis; its radial counterpart is the [radial coordinate of
the current center](name:radial_coordinate_of_current_center).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the plasma-current centroid lies in the $+Z$
direction from the coordinate origin.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short:
Vertical coordinate of the magnetic axis specifies its signed height above
or below the zero-height plane in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z)
frame.
NAMES.long:
Vertical coordinate of the magnetic axis is its signed height relative to
the zero-height plane in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.
Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical
height.

The coordinate is defined by

$$
Z_{\mathrm{axis}} = \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{axis}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}}
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the magnetic-axis height,
$\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the position vector of a point on the
magnetic axis relative to the coordinate origin, and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is
the unit vector along the positive vertical direction, parallel to the
toroidal symmetry axis.

This quantity is a coordinate of the magnetic axis, not a height averaged
over the plasma or the [vertical coordinate of an
X-point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_x_point), which refers to a different
equilibrium location.

In an axisymmetric equilibrium, this coordinate and the major-radius
coordinate of the magnetic axis together specify its position in a poloidal
cross-section.

The closed magnetic-field line about which nested toroidal magnetic flux
surfaces are arranged. Where $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{p}}(R_{\mathrm{axis}},
Z_{\mathrm{axis}}) = 0$, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{p}}$ is poloidal magnetic
field; $R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the O-point inside the
nested closed flux surfaces.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the magnetic axis lies on the $+Z$ side of
the zero-height plane in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.short:
Vertical coordinate of the measurement position, specifying signed height

Vertical coordinate of the measurement position specifies its signed height
along the symmetry-axis direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi,

The coordinate is defined by

$$
Z = \mathbf{x}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}}
$$

where $Z$ is the vertical coordinate, $\mathbf{x}$ is the position vector
from the coordinate origin to the measurement position, and
$\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is the unit vector along the symmetry axis in the
positive vertical direction. The other frame coordinates are $R$, the major
radius, and $\phi$, the toroidal angle.

This quantity applies to the specified measurement position without an
implied spatial average. It is a geometric coordinate, not a measured field
value or a vertical extent. The [vertical coordinate of a line-of-sight
reference point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_line_of_sight) uses the same
projection for that distinct locus.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the displacement from the coordinate origin
to the measurement position has a positive projection along the positive
vertical direction.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary_gap_reference_point
NAMES.short:
Vertical coordinate of the plasma-boundary gap reference point, expressed as
signed height from the coordinate origin in the right-handed cylindrical (R,
φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Vertical coordinate of the plasma-boundary gap reference point specifies its
signed height relative to the coordinate origin in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

$$
Z = \mathbf{x}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}}
$$

where $Z$ is the reference point's vertical coordinate, $\mathbf{x}$ is its
position vector relative to the coordinate origin, and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is
the unit vector along the toroidal symmetry axis in the positive vertical
direction. The coordinates $R$ and $\phi$ denote major radius and toroidal
angle, respectively.

The quantity applies to one reference point, without averaging over the
plasma boundary. It is a point coordinate, not the gap distance or a
vertical clearance between the plasma and the wall. The [vertical coordinate
of the closest wall point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point)
uses the same vertical-axis convention but locates a separately defined
point.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the displacement from the coordinate origin
to the reference point has a positive projection onto $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$.

sources.leaf_definition: Height of the reference point
sources.parent_definition: Set of gaps, defined by a reference point and a direction.

sources.parent_definition: Set of gaps, defined by a reference point and a direction.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_primary_x_point
NAMES.short:
Signed vertical position of the primary magnetic X-point, the poloidal-field
null where separatrix branches meet, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ,
Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The primary X-point is the main poloidal magnetic-field null on the plasma
boundary, where separatrix branches meet. This quantity gives that point’s
vertical coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

$$
Z_{\mathrm{X,primary}} = \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{X,primary}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}}
$$

Here, $Z_{\mathrm{X,primary}}$ is the vertical coordinate of the primary
X-point, $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{X,primary}}$ is its position vector relative
to the coordinate origin, and $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the vertical unit vector
of the cylindrical frame.

The locus is specifically the primary, or main, boundary X-point rather than
an unspecified or secondary X-point. This is a pointwise geometric
coordinate with no spatial averaging, surface integration, population
aggregation, or species dependence; it excludes the radial coordinate of the
same point.

The generic [vertical coordinate of an
X-point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_x_point) represents the same signed Z
coordinate without restricting the locus to the primary X-point, while the
[radial coordinate of an X-point](name:radial_coordinate_of_x_point)
supplies the corresponding major-radius coordinate.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the primary X-point lies in the direction of
increasing vertical coordinate $Z$.

sources.leaf_definition: Height
sources.parent_definition: RZ position of the main X-point

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_strike_point
NAMES.short:
Vertical coordinate of a selected divertor strike point, giving its signed
height relative to the origin in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z)
frame.
NAMES.long:
Vertical coordinate of a selected divertor strike point specifies its signed
height relative to the coordinate origin in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle,
and $Z$ is vertical height along the toroidal symmetry axis.

$$
Z_{\mathrm{s}} = \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{s}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}}
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{s}}$ is the strike-point vertical coordinate,
$\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{s}}$ is the position vector of that point relative to
the coordinate origin, and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is the unit vector along the
positive vertical direction.

The value applies to one identified strike point. Inner and outer strike
points have separate values; no averaging or summation over them is implied.
The generic quantity does not select a particular strike-point branch.

This coordinate specifies a different geometric location from the [vertical
coordinate of an X-point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_x_point). It also
differs from the [vertical coordinate of the divertor-target
center](name:z_coordinate_of_divertor_target), which locates the target's
geometric center rather than the selected strike point.

The point where a divertor separatrix branch intersects a plasma-facing
target. Where $\psi(R_{\mathrm{s}}, Z_{\mathrm{s}}) = \psi_{\mathrm{X}}$,
$R_{\mathrm{s}}, Z_{\mathrm{s}}$ is the point on the target surface;
$\psi_{\mathrm{X}}$ is poloidal magnetic flux at the primary X-point.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the displacement from the coordinate origin
to the strike point has a positive projection onto the positive vertical
direction $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_x_point
NAMES.short:
Signed vertical (Z) coordinate of an X-point, the magnetic null where
separatrix branches meet, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of an X-point is its signed height along $Z$ in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \\phi, Z)$ frame. An X-point is a poloidal
magnetic null at which separatrix branches meet.

This quantity identifies the vertical location of the X-point and is
distinct from the [vertical coordinate of the magnetic
axis](name:vertical_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis) and the [vertical
coordinate of the strike point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_strike_point).

NAMES.name: vertical_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field
NAMES.short:
Vertical magnetic field on a control surface is the signed axial component
of the external-coil vacuum field remaining after its toroidal mean is
removed.
NAMES.long:
Vertical magnetic field of the non-axisymmetric vacuum contribution is the
signed component parallel to the toroidal symmetry axis, evaluated at
individual points on a control surface. It contains only the toroidally
varying external-coil contribution to the [magnetic
induction](name:magnetic_field).

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the component is defined
by

$$
B_{Z,\mathrm{NA}}(R,\phi,Z)=\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{NA}}(R,\phi,Z)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}}=B_{Z,\mathrm{vac}}(R,\phi,Z)-\left\langle B_{Z,\mathrm{vac}}\right\rangle_\phi(R,Z)
$$

where $B_{Z,\mathrm{NA}}$ is the vertical non-axisymmetric component,
$\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{NA}}$ is the [non-axisymmetric magnetic-field
vector](name:non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field), and $B_{Z,\mathrm{vac}}$ is
the vertical component of the external-coil vacuum field before
toroidal-mean removal. The brackets denote averaging over a complete
toroidal circuit at fixed major radius $R$ and vertical coordinate $Z$;
$\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is the unit vector
parallel to the symmetry axis toward increasing $Z$.

The axisymmetric vacuum contribution and fields generated by plasma currents
are excluded. Each value is a local component, not a surface average,
surface integral, or Fourier coefficient. Unlike the [normal
non-axisymmetric magnetic
field](name:normal_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field), this projection follows
the fixed vertical direction rather than the local control-surface normal.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the non-axisymmetric vacuum magnetic field
has a component toward increasing vertical coordinate $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_outline_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Signed vertical height of each point on the plasma-boundary outline in the
right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, defining its poloidal
cross-sectional shape.
NAMES.long:
The vertical outline coordinate is the signed height of each point on the
plasma-boundary contour in a poloidal cross-section. It describes the
boundary geometry rather than a field, flux, or scalar boundary summary.

The coordinate is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$
frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is
vertical height. Each outline point has its own $Z$ value; the quantity is
neither an average nor an extremum over the boundary.

This quantity applies specifically to the plasma-boundary outline and
excludes the outline of a plasma-facing component. Together with the
corresponding [radial outline of the plasma
boundary](name:radial_outline_of_plasma_boundary), it specifies the boundary
contour in the poloidal $(R,Z)$ plane. The analogous vertical coordinate for
a component boundary is [vertical outline of the plasma-facing
component](name:vertical_outline_of_plasma_facing_component).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the point lies in the direction of increasing
vertical coordinate $Z$.

sources.leaf_definition: Height
sources.parent_definition: RZ outline of the plasma boundary

NAMES.name: vertical_velocity_at_current_center
NAMES.short:
Vertical velocity of the plasma-current centroid, defined by the rate of
change of its vertical position.
NAMES.long:
The vertical velocity at the current center is the kinematic velocity of the
centroid of the plasma current distribution, describing motion along the
vertical direction rather than a local fluid velocity sampled at that point.

$$
v_{Z,c}(t)=\frac{dZ_c(t)}{dt}
$$

where $Z_c$ is the vertical coordinate of the current center in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $t$ is time, and $v_{Z,c}$ is
the corresponding signed velocity. The position $Z_c$ is defined by the
[vertical coordinate of the current
center](name:vertical_coordinate_of_current_center).

This quantity describes motion of the current-density-weighted
plasma-current centroid and is distinct from the local [vertical plasma
velocity](name:vertical_plasma_velocity) evaluated at that location.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the current center moves toward increasing
$Z$.

NAMES.name: volume_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Volume enclosed by a magnetic flux surface, including the entire plasma
interior from the magnetic axis rather than only a shell between neighboring
surfaces.
NAMES.long:
Volume of flux surface

The volume is defined by

$$
V = \int_{\Omega} d^3\mathbf{x}
$$

where $V$ is the enclosed volume, $\Omega$ is the spatial domain inside the
selected magnetic flux surface, $\mathbf{x}$ is spatial position, and
$d^3\mathbf{x}$ is the differential volume element.

The integration covers the entire interior from the magnetic axis to the
selected surface and excludes regions outside it. The result is the total
enclosed volume, not the volume of a shell between neighboring surfaces or
the volume of material structures.

The volume tends to zero as the selected surface contracts to the magnetic
axis. It equals the [volume enclosed by the plasma
boundary](name:volume_of_plasma_boundary) when the selected surface
coincides with that boundary.

Differentiating this cumulative volume with respect to the poloidal magnetic
flux coordinate gives the [poloidal-flux volume
derivative](name:derivative_of_volume_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_poloidal_magnetic_flux_coordinate);
differentiation with respect to the toroidal-flux coordinate gives the
[toroidal-flux volume
derivative](name:derivative_of_volume_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_toroidal_flux_coordinate).
Enclosed-volume increments provide the geometric integration measure that
converts flux-surface-averaged densities into enclosed totals.

A surface formed by points sharing the same magnetic-flux label in a
nested-flux-surface configuration. Where $\psi(R, Z) = \mathrm{const}$,
$\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux.
