NAMES.name: derivative_of_volume_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_poloidal_magnetic_flux_coordinate
NAMES.short:
Geometric rate of change of the cumulative volume enclosed by a nested
magnetic flux surface as its signed poloidal flux coordinate varies.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the geometric derivative of the cumulative volume enclosed
by a nested magnetic flux surface with respect to its signed poloidal
magnetic-flux coordinate.

It is defined by

$$
\frac{dV}{d\psi}=\frac{d}{d\psi}V(\psi)
$$

where $V(\psi)$ is the volume enclosed by the flux surface labeled by
$\psi$, $\psi$ is the signed poloidal magnetic-flux coordinate, and
$d/d\psi$ denotes differentiation with respect to that coordinate.

The quantity applies separately to each nested closed flux surface. The
underlying volume is cumulative from the magnetic axis to the selected
surface, so this derivative describes the change in enclosed volume along
the flux coordinate rather than a local volume density, a shell volume, or a
plasma-population-weighted quantity.

It is the derivative of [volume enclosed by a flux
surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface); integrating it between two
flux-coordinate values gives the difference between the corresponding
enclosed volumes. It is distinct from the derivative with respect to the
toroidal flux coordinate, which is represented by [derivative of volume with
respect to toroidal flux
coordinate](name:derivative_of_volume_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_toroidal_flux_coordinate).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the enclosed volume increases in the
direction of increasing signed poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$.

sources.leaf_definition: Radial derivative of the volume enclosed in the flux surface with respect to Psi
sources.parent_definition: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux

NAMES.name: derivative_of_volume_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_toroidal_flux_coordinate
NAMES.short:
Geometric rate at which the cumulative volume enclosed by a nested magnetic
flux surface changes with its dimensionful toroidal-flux coordinate.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the geometric derivative of the cumulative volume enclosed
by a nested magnetic flux surface with respect to the dimensionful
toroidal-flux coordinate. It describes how rapidly the enclosed region
expands as the flux-surface label changes.

The defining relation is

$$
\frac{dV}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}}
$$

where $V$ is the [volume enclosed by a flux
surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface) and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the
dimensionful toroidal-flux coordinate labeling the nested surfaces.

The quantity applies to the three-dimensional region inside each selected
nested magnetic flux surface. The volume is cumulative, beginning at the
magnetic axis and extending to the specified surface; this is not a local
plasma-population quantity and carries no species weighting. It is the
derivative with respect to the toroidal-flux coordinate, not the volume
itself or the derivative of the enclosed poloidal area.

As the derivative of [volume enclosed by a flux
surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface), it provides the volume increment
associated with a change in toroidal-flux coordinate and serves as a
geometric coefficient in flux-surface-averaged transport relations. The
derivative of area with respect to the toroidal-flux coordinate is the
analogous area derivative, while [the temporal derivative of this volume
derivative](name:time_derivative_of_derivative_of_volume_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_toroidal_flux_coordinate)
describes its change in time.

sources.leaf_definition: Radial derivative of the volume enclosed in the flux surface with respect to Rho_Tor
sources.parent_definition: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux

NAMES.name: volume_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Volume enclosed by the plasma boundary, representing the total
confined-plasma region inside the last closed magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the geometric volume of the confined plasma enclosed by the
plasma boundary, identified with the last closed magnetic flux surface. It
represents the full enclosed region rather than a local flux-surface shell
or material volume.

The volume is defined by

$$
V = \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{plasma}}} d^3\mathbf{x}
$$

where $V$ is the enclosed plasma volume, $\Omega_{\mathrm{plasma}}$ is the
spatial domain inside the plasma boundary, and $d^3\mathbf{x}$ is the
differential volume element at position $\mathbf{x}$.

The integration domain is the entire confined-plasma region bounded by the
last closed magnetic flux surface, and the result is the total volume
aggregated over that domain. It excludes regions outside the plasma boundary
and volumes belonging to material structures or other non-confined regions.

This quantity is the terminal enclosed value of [volume of a flux
surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface) when the flux surface coincides with
the plasma boundary. It provides the integration domain for volume-averaged
quantities such as [volume-averaged ion
temperature](name:volume_averaged_ion_temperature).

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Volume of the confined plasma

NAMES.name: weight_of_interferometer_beam
NAMES.short:
Weight of an interferometer beam is the scalar factor assigned to the
residual for one interferometer beam, controlling how strongly that beam's
line-integrated electron-density constraint contributes to a weighted
objective. It applies per beam, not to an entire interferometer system.
NAMES.long:
Weight of an interferometer beam is the scalar factor assigned to the
residual for one interferometer beam in a weighted objective. The residual
is associated with that beam's line-integrated electron-density constraint,
so the weight controls that beam's relative influence among simultaneously
weighted constraints.

For a quadratic weighted objective, the contribution from one beam is
represented by:

$$
\Phi_b = w_b r_b^2
$$

where $w_b$ is the weight of the interferometer beam, $r_b$ is the residual
between the modeled and reference line-integrated electron density for the
same beam, and $\Phi_b$ is that beam's contribution to the objective.

The scope is a single interferometer beam. No summation, averaging, or
normalization over multiple beams is implied; a set of beams has separate
weights and separate residual contributions. This quantity is not the
line-integrated electron density, not the residual itself, not an
uncertainty, and not a weight for a whole interferometer system or for other
constraint types.

The [equilibrium weight of an interferometer
beam](name:equilibrium_weight_of_interferometer_beam) is the
equilibrium-specific specialization of this parent quantity. Changing $w_b$
changes only the relative contribution of the corresponding beam term in the
objective; it does not change the definition of the beam residual.

NAMES.name: equilibrium_weight_of_interferometer_beam
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless factor controlling the relative contribution of an
interferometer beam’s line-integrated electron-density residual to an
equilibrium objective function.
NAMES.long:
The equilibrium weight assigned to an interferometer-beam constraint is a
nonnegative factor that sets the relative importance of its line-integrated
electron-density residual in an equilibrium objective function. It applies
to the constraint associated with one interferometer beam rather than to the
electron density itself.

A weighted least-squares objective containing this constraint is defined by

$$
J = \frac{1}{2} \sum_i w_i^2 \left(\frac{y_i^{\mathrm{rec}} - y_i^{\mathrm{meas}}}{\sigma_i}\right)^2
$$

where $J$ is the equilibrium objective function, $i$ indexes individual
constraints, $w_i$ is the equilibrium weight, $y_i^{\mathrm{rec}}$ is the
reconstructed line-integrated electron density for constraint $i$,
$y_i^{\mathrm{meas}}$ is its measured line-integrated electron density, and
$\sigma_i$ is the standard deviation assigned to its measurement error.

For this quantity, $i$ denotes an interferometer-beam line-integrated
electron-density constraint. The weight is specific to that individual
constraint; the objective function aggregates all constraint contributions
through the summation. It is not the line-integrated electron density,
either its measured or reconstructed value, and it is distinct from the
[calibration coefficient of an interferometer
beam](name:spectral_calibration_factor_at_line_of_sight), which
characterizes signal calibration rather than equilibrium-objective
weighting.

This quantity has the same objective-function role as the equilibrium weight
of a flux loop and the equilibrium weight of a poloidal magnetic-field
probe; those related weights differ by the physical measurement constraint
to which they apply.

sources.leaf_definition: Weight given to the measurement
sources.parent_definition: Set of line integrated density measurements

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface average of the local magnetic-field strength, retaining the
pointwise modulus before averaging over each magnetic surface.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the flux-surface average of the magnitude of the total
equilibrium magnetic-field vector. It represents the mean field strength on
a magnetic surface, rather than a component or a vector average.

The flux-surface average is defined by

$$
\left\langle \lvert\mathbf{B}\rvert \right\rangle_{\psi} = \frac{\oint_{\psi} \lvert\mathbf{B}\rvert\,\mathrm{d}S/\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert}{\oint_{\psi} \mathrm{d}S/\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the total equilibrium magnetic-field vector, $\psi$ is
the scalar label of the magnetic flux surface, $\mathrm{d}S$ is the
surface-area element, and $\nabla\psi$ is the spatial gradient of that
surface label. The aggregation is the normalized surface integral with
weighting $\mathrm{d}S/\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert$.

The quantity applies to all components of the equilibrium field on the
selected magnetic flux surface and is non-negative. It excludes any signed
field component, any species or source decomposition, and the magnitude of a
vector obtained by averaging $\mathbf{B}$ before taking its modulus.

It is the flux-surface-averaged transformation of [magnetic-field
magnitude](name:magnetic_field_magnitude). It differs from
[flux-surface-averaged square of magnetic-field
magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude),
which averages the squared field strength rather than the field strength
itself.

sources.leaf_definition: Flux surface averaged modulus of B (always positive, irrespective of the sign convention for the B-field direction).
sources.parent_definition: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_parallel_current_density
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface-averaged parallel current density is the surface average of
conventional current density dotted with the magnetic field, divided by a
single global reference toroidal field.
NAMES.long:
Flux-surface-averaged parallel current density is the signed field-aligned
contribution of the total plasma current density, averaged over a closed
magnetic flux surface with magnetic-field weighting.

The defining relation is

$$\langle f\rangle = \oint f\,dS/|\nabla\psi| \,/\, \oint dS/|\nabla\psi|$$

where $j_\parallel^{\mathrm{FS}}$ denotes this averaged parallel current
density, $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux labeling the surface,
$\mathbf{j}$ is the total conventional plasma [current
density](name:current_density), $\mathbf{B}$ is the local magnetic-field
vector, and $B_0$ is the nonzero signed global reference toroidal magnetic
field. The brackets denote the normalized flux-surface average, weighted by
the inverse magnitude of the poloidal magnetic-flux gradient. The same $B_0$
applies to every surface; it is not a surface-dependent magnetic-field
magnitude.

The quantity includes all plasma current-carrying populations and mechanisms
and aggregates over the complete selected closed surface. It is not
restricted to a particular current-drive mechanism and is not a pointwise
current density.

The pointwise [parallel current density](name:parallel_current_density) is
$j_\parallel=\mathbf{j}\cdot\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$, where $|\mathbf{B}|$
is the magnetic-field magnitude. Consequently, this quantity equals $\langle
j_\parallel|\mathbf{B}|\rangle_\psi/B_0$, not generally $\langle
j_\parallel\rangle_\psi$. The [constraint-position
member](name:flux_surface_averaged_parallel_current_density_at_constraint_position)
evaluates the same quantity on the magnetic surface selected by a specified
constraint position; no such locus is prescribed here.

The reference field is positive toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in
the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius
and $Z$ is vertical height.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when
$\langle\mathbf{j}\cdot\mathbf{B}\rangle_\psi$ is positive for a reference
toroidal field directed toward increasing $\phi$, or negative for a
reference field directed toward decreasing $\phi$.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_toroidal_current_density
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface-averaged toroidal current density is the net conventional
toroidal charge flux per area, averaged over a closed magnetic surface with
additional inverse-major-radius weighting.
NAMES.long:
Flux-surface-averaged toroidal current density is the signed geometric
toroidal component of the net plasma current density, averaged over a closed
magnetic flux surface with additional inverse-major-radius weighting.

The defining weighted average is

$$\langle f\rangle = \oint f\,dS/|\nabla\psi| \,/\, \oint dS/|\nabla\psi|$$

where $j_\phi^{\mathrm{FS}}$ is this averaged current density, $j_\phi$ is
the local [toroidal current density](name:toroidal_current_density), $R$ is
major radius, and $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux labeling the selected
surface. Angle brackets denote the flux-surface average, defined by $\langle
f\rangle = \oint f\,dS/|\nabla\psi| \,/\, \oint dS/|\nabla\psi|$, where $f$
is the averaged quantity, $S$ is the closed magnetic surface, $dS$ is its
area element, and $\nabla\psi$ is the poloidal-flux gradient.

The quantity includes the net contribution from all plasma current-carrying
populations and mechanisms over the complete selected surface, including
closed surfaces in the core plasma. It is neither a pointwise current
density nor the total current through the enclosed plasma cross-section. The
additional inverse-major-radius weighting distinguishes it from the ordinary
flux-surface average $\langle j_\phi\rangle$.

The underlying [current-density vector](name:current_density) is projected
onto the geometric toroidal direction in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $\phi$ is toroidal angle and $Z$ is vertical
height. Unlike [flux-surface-averaged parallel current
density](name:flux_surface_averaged_parallel_current_density), this quantity
uses the geometric toroidal projection rather than a magnetic-field-aligned
projection.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the weighted net conventional current flows
in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, counterclockwise when
viewed from above.

NAMES.name: minimum_over_flux_surface_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Smallest total magnetic-field strength attained along a specified nested
magnetic flux surface, using the field magnitude rather than a signed
component.
NAMES.long:
The minimum magnetic-field magnitude is the smallest total field strength
attained anywhere on a specified nested magnetic flux surface. It is
sign-invariant because it uses the modulus of the magnetic-field vector
rather than a signed component.

For a surface labeled by the magnetic-flux coordinate $\psi$, the quantity
is defined by

$$
B_{\min}(\psi) = \min_{\mathbf{x} \in S(\psi)} \left|\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})\right|
$$

where $B_{\min}(\psi)$ is the minimum magnetic-field magnitude, $\mathbf{x}$
is a position on the surface, $S(\psi)$ is the set of positions belonging to
the flux surface labeled by $\psi$, and $\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})$ is the
total magnetic-field vector at that position.

The minimum is taken over all positions on each nested magnetic flux surface
and includes the complete equilibrium field, including its poloidal and
toroidal contributions. It is not a signed component minimum, a flux-surface
average, or a minimum taken across multiple flux surfaces.

Unlike the [flux-surface-averaged inverse square of magnetic-field
magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude),
this quantity reduces the field magnitude itself by a pointwise minimum
rather than averaging its reciprocal square.

NAMES.name: minimum_safety_factor
NAMES.short:
Signed safety-factor value on the closed magnetic flux surface where the
magnitude of field-line winding is smallest, distinct from that surface’s
location.
NAMES.long:
The minimum safety factor is the signed field-line winding number evaluated
on the nested closed magnetic flux surface where the magnitude of the safety
factor is smallest. It represents the extremal value of the safety-factor
function within the confined closed-surface domain.

The minimizing value is defined by

$$
q_{\min} = q(\rho_\ast), \qquad \rho_\ast \in \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{0 \leq \rho \leq 1} |q(\rho)|
$$

where $q(\rho)$ is the signed [safety factor](name:safety_factor) on the
flux surface labeled by $\rho$, $\rho_\ast$ is the label of a surface at
which the magnitude $|q(\rho)|$ is minimized, and $q_{\min}$ is the signed
value evaluated there. The label $\rho$ is a monotonic flux-surface
coordinate whose endpoints denote the magnetic axis and the last closed flux
surface. In flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, $\theta$ is the poloidal
angle and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle of the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

The extremum is taken over all nested closed magnetic flux surfaces and is
neither a flux-surface average nor a sum. The location-defining quantity is
separate: poloidal magnetic flux at minimum safety factor identifies the
corresponding surface, while this quantity reports only the signed safety
factor. It is also distinct from a safety factor evaluated at a prescribed
locus, such as the magnetic axis.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the toroidal angle advance of a magnetic
field line is in the direction of increasing $\phi$ as the poloidal angle
$\theta$ increases.

NAMES.name: normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Radial flux-surface location of the selected plasma boundary, expressed by
the normalized poloidal flux coordinate. It is the linear normalized
poloidal flux value, increasing from zero at the magnetic axis to one at the
separatrix, of the closed flux surface taken as the plasma boundary;
fixed-boundary equilibrium calculations commonly set it slightly below one
to select a surface just inside the separatrix.
NAMES.long:
The normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the plasma boundary is the value
of the [normalized poloidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate) on the closed flux
surface selected as the plasma boundary. It is the linear normalized
poloidal flux, labeling the boundary's radial position between the magnetic
axis and the last closed flux surface.

Its value is the poloidal flux difference from the magnetic axis normalized
to the axis-to-separatrix flux difference:

$$
\psi_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{boundary}} = \frac{\psi_{\mathrm{boundary}} - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}}{\psi_{\mathrm{sep}} - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}}
$$

where $\psi_{\mathrm{boundary}}$ is the [poloidal magnetic
flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) on the selected plasma-boundary surface,
$\psi_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the [poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic
axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis), and
$\psi_{\mathrm{sep}}$ is the poloidal magnetic flux at the separatrix (last
closed flux surface).

The label equals zero at the magnetic axis and equals one when the selected
plasma boundary coincides with the separatrix; a value below one selects an
internal closed flux surface. Its defining role is to specify, for
fixed-boundary equilibrium representations, which closed flux surface is
taken as the plasma boundary, commonly a surface just inside the separatrix
so that the boundary remains strictly closed.

This is the linear normalized poloidal flux value itself, not its square
root, and it is a flux-surface label rather than a signed poloidal-flux
value or a geometric minor-radius measure. It is distinct from the
toroidal-flux-based boundary label normalized toroidal flux coordinate at
the plasma boundary, and it belongs to the same locus-valued family as the
normalized poloidal flux coordinate at minimum safety factor and the
[normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the
pedestal](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_pedestal).

sources.leaf_definition: Value of the normalized poloidal flux at which the boundary is taken, the flux being normalized to its value at the separatrix (so psi_norm = 1 if the boundary is the separatrix)
sources.parent_definition: Description of the plasma boundary. The boundary can be either the real separatrix (provided by a free boundary equilibrium solver) or the 0.99x psi_norm flux surface provided by a fixed boundary equilibrium

NAMES.name: safety_factor_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short:
Safety factor at the magnetic axis is the signed toroidal-to-poloidal
field-line winding ratio at the innermost closed flux surface, the value
approached as nested closed magnetic flux surfaces contract toward the axis.
It gives the toroidal turns made by a magnetic field line per complete
poloidal circuit in that limit.
NAMES.long:
Safety factor at magnetic axis

On each neighboring nested closed magnetic flux surface, the [safety
factor](name:safety_factor) is defined by

$$
q = \frac{1}{2\pi}\oint \frac{\mathbf{B}\cdot\nabla\phi}{\mathbf{B}\cdot\nabla\theta}\,d\theta
$$

where $q$ is the safety factor, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field, $\nabla$
is the spatial gradient operator, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $\theta$
is the poloidal angle; the integral follows a magnetic field line through
one complete poloidal circuit. The toroidal angle $\phi$ belongs to the
right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $Z$
is vertical height, and $\phi$ increases counterclockwise when viewed from
above.

This quantity is the value of $q$ at the innermost closed flux surface:
writing $q_{\mathrm{axis}}$ for it,
$q_{\mathrm{axis}}=\lim_{\mathcal{S}\to\mathrm{axis}} q(\mathcal{S})$, where
$\mathcal{S}$ ranges over the nested closed magnetic flux surfaces
contracting toward the magnetic axis and $q(\mathcal{S})$ is the safety
factor on $\mathcal{S}$. It is a single signed equilibrium winding value
with no species, population, or charge-state aggregation. It is a limit from
neighboring closed surfaces, not a direct evaluation of the winding
integrand on the axis, not a value on a finite-radius surface, not a volume
average, and not a local ratio of magnetic-field component magnitudes.
Proximity of this value to low-order rational numbers indicates
susceptibility to core-resonant magnetohydrodynamic modes such as sawteeth.

It is the magnetic-axis specialization of the [safety
factor](name:safety_factor), which describes field-line winding as a
function of flux-surface label. The [minimum safety
factor](name:minimum_safety_factor) instead selects the closed surface where
the safety-factor magnitude is smallest, and the [safety factor at the
plasma boundary](name:safety_factor_at_plasma_boundary) is the confined-side
outer-boundary value. The [rotational transform](name:rotational_transform)
is the reciprocal winding ratio, $\iota = 1/q$, where $\iota$ is the signed
number of poloidal turns per toroidal turn.

The closed magnetic-field line about which nested toroidal magnetic flux
surfaces are arranged. Where $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{p}}(R_{\mathrm{axis}},
Z_{\mathrm{axis}}) = 0$, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{p}}$ is poloidal magnetic
field; $R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the O-point inside the
nested closed flux surfaces.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the toroidal angle advance of a magnetic
field line is in the direction of increasing $\phi$ as the poloidal angle
$\theta$ increases.

NAMES.name: toroidal_total_current_density
NAMES.short:
Toroidal total current density is the net conventional charge flux per unit
area around the symmetry axis, formed by algebraically summing all included
current contributions.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal total current density is the signed local projection of the net
[current density](name:current_density) onto the toroidal direction. It
combines all included contributions before or after projection onto that
same direction.

The projection and aggregation are defined by:

$$
j_\phi = \hat{\phi}\cdot\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{tot}} = \sum_k \hat{\phi}\cdot\mathbf{j}_k
$$

where $j_\phi$ is the toroidal total current density,
$\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total current-density vector,
$\mathbf{j}_k$ is an included current-density contribution, and $k$ labels
those contributions. The unit vector $\hat{\phi}$ points toward increasing
toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where
$R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The total is an algebraic sum, not a sum of magnitudes, and does not select
a particular species, charge state, or current-generation mechanism. The
quantity is local, with no restriction to a particular plasma region; it is
neither a current-density magnitude nor a flux-surface average or spatially
integrated current.

This quantity specializes [total current
density](name:total_current_density) by fixing its common signed projection
to the toroidal direction. The adjacent [radial total current
density](name:radial_total_current_density) instead projects the same net
charge-flux density onto the outward major-radius direction.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the net conventional charge transport is in
the direction of increasing toroidal angle, counterclockwise when viewed
from above along the negative vertical direction.

NAMES.name: fast_particle_pressure
NAMES.short:
Fast-particle pressure is the isotropic scalar pressure contribution of the
total suprathermal (nonthermal) particle population, combining its
field-parallel and transverse stress contributions.
NAMES.long:
Fast-particle pressure is the scalar kinetic pressure of the total
suprathermal (nonthermal) particle population. It represents the isotropic
pressure associated with the field-parallel and transverse stresses; the
directional stresses themselves need not be equal.

For a gyrotropic pressure tensor, the scalar pressure is one-third of its
trace:

$$
p_{\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{p_{\parallel,\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x}) + 2p_{\perp,\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x})}{3}
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{fast}}$ is fast-particle pressure, $\mathbf{x}$ is spatial
position, $p_{\parallel,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the [parallel fast-particle
pressure](name:parallel_fast_particle_pressure), and
$p_{\perp,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the [perpendicular fast-particle
pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_particle_pressure), defined per transverse
direction. Both components refer to the same population at the same
position; the factor of two accounts for the two transverse directions.

The quantity applies locally to the full suprathermal population, across all
velocities, pitch angles, and orbit classes. Contributions are summed over
fast-particle species and all charge states, not averaged. A flux-surface
average is a separate spatial aggregation of these local values; the
unqualified quantity does not require that average.

Fast-particle pressure excludes [thermal plasma
pressure](name:thermal_plasma_pressure). It is distinct from a
species-specific or charge-state-specific pressure, either directional
component, and pressure restricted to an individual orbit class.

Restricting the same pressure contribution to orbit classes gives the
[co-passing fast-particle pressure](name:co_passing_fast_particle_pressure),
[counter-passing fast-particle
pressure](name:counter_passing_fast_particle_pressure), and [trapped
fast-particle pressure](name:trapped_fast_particle_pressure). Their
contributions sum to the full fast-particle pressure when the classes form
an exhaustive, nonoverlapping partition of the population.

NAMES.name: total_counter_passing_particle_pressure
NAMES.short:
Total pressure of counter-passing particles is the flux-surface average of
one-third of their kinetic-stress trace, including thermal, nonthermal, and
directed-motion contributions.
NAMES.long:
Total pressure of counter-passing particles is the flux-surface-averaged
isotropic part of the kinetic stress carried by the thermal and nonthermal
populations of a specified species. Counter-passing particles occupy
untrapped guiding-center orbits whose orbit-averaged toroidal motion opposes
the plasma current.

The nonrelativistic kinetic definition is

$$
p_{s,\mathrm{cp}} = \left\langle \frac{m_s}{3}\int_{\mathrm{cp}} |\mathbf{v}|^2 f_s(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v \right\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}}
$$

where $p_{s,\mathrm{cp}}$ is the total counter-passing pressure of species
$s$, $m_s$ is its particle mass, $\mathbf{x}$ is spatial position,
$\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, $f_s$ is the [particle
distribution](name:particle_distribution) including its thermal and
nonthermal parts, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element. The
integration domain $\mathrm{cp}$ selects counter-passing orbits, and
$\langle\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}}$ denotes a magnetic-flux-surface average
weighted by the differential volume between neighboring surfaces. Velocity
is not centered on the counter-passing population's mean flow, so
directed-motion stress is retained.

“Total” denotes the additive thermal and nonthermal contributions within the
specified species, not a sum over all plasma species. Contributions from
multiple distributions representing that species are superposed. Trapped and
co-passing particles are excluded. This quantity is a flux-surface average
rather than a local pressure at a point on the surface; it combines all
three velocity degrees of freedom without assuming isotropy and is not a
single field-parallel or field-perpendicular stress component.

The [counter-passing fast-particle
pressure](name:counter_passing_fast_particle_pressure) restricts the kinetic
moment to suprathermal particles, whereas this quantity also includes the
thermal contribution. The [total co-passing particle
pressure](name:total_co_passing_particle_pressure) applies the
thermal-plus-nonthermal scope to the opposite passing-orbit class.

NAMES.name: voltage_of_valve
NAMES.short:
Voltage applied to a gas-injection valve to drive its opening, serving as
the electrical input to the valve's gas-flow response.
NAMES.long:
Voltage of valve

The applied voltage is defined by

$$
U = \varphi_{\mathrm{drive}} - \varphi_{\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $U$ is the valve drive voltage, $\varphi_{\mathrm{drive}}$ is the
electric potential of the driven terminal, and $\varphi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is
the electric potential of its circuit reference terminal.

The valve response relates this applied signal to the derived [gas flow of
the valve](name:gas_flow_of_valve). The voltage is the electrical input to
that relationship, not the resulting gas throughput or particle injection
rate.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the driven terminal is at higher electric
potential than its reference terminal.

NAMES.name: accumulated_deuterated_methane_prefill_count
NAMES.subject: deuterated_methane
NAMES.short:
Cumulative pre-breakdown inventory of deuterated methane (CD4), weighted by
ten equivalent electrons per molecule rather than reported as a molecular
count.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the cumulative amount of deuterated methane introduced
during the plasma prefill phase, expressed as an equivalent-electron
inventory. It represents neutral CD4 molecules before plasma breakdown, not
the post-breakdown gas-injection inventory.

The equivalent-electron count is defined by

$$
N_{e,\rm eq}^{\rm prefill} = \int_{t_0}^{t_b} \dot{N}_{e,\rm eq}^{\rm CD_4}(t)\,dt = 10N_{\rm CD_4}^{\rm prefill}
$$

where $N_{e,\rm eq}^{\rm prefill}$ is the accumulated equivalent-electron
inventory, $\dot{N}_{e,\rm eq}^{\rm CD_4}$ is the [deuterated methane source
rate](name:deuterated_methane_source_rate), $t_0$ and $t_b$ delimit prefill
before breakdown, and $N_{\rm CD_4}^{\rm prefill}$ is the accumulated number
of CD4 molecules. The factor ten is the total electron count of one fully
ionizable CD4 molecule. The species-resolved quantity contributes to the
[accumulated total prefill gas
count](name:accumulated_total_prefill_gas_count), which sums
equivalent-electron inventories across gas species.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Deuterated methane (CD4)

NAMES.name: accumulated_total_prefill_gas_count
NAMES.short:
Cumulative equivalent-electron inventory of all gas species introduced by
injection during the plasma prefill phase, summed over species.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the total gas inventory accumulated during the plasma
prefill phase, expressed as an equivalent-electron count and summed over all
injected species. It represents the integrated amount introduced before
plasma breakdown, rather than an instantaneous injection rate.

The accumulated equivalent-electron count is defined by

$$
N_{\mathrm{eq}}(t) = \sum_s \int_{t_0}^{\min(t,t_1)} \dot{N}_{s,\mathrm{eq}}(t')\,dt'
$$

where $s$ indexes injected gas species, $\dot{N}_{s,\mathrm{eq}}$ is the
equivalent-electron injection rate of species $s$, $t_0$ and $t_1$ delimit
the prefill phase, and $t$ is the evaluation time. The sum includes all
species; a species-specific quantity such as [accumulated hydrogen prefill
count](name:accumulated_hydrogen_prefill_count) is a component of this
total. The quantity is distinct from the instantaneous injection rate and
from inventories restricted to one species, while [accumulated prefill gas
count](name:accumulated_prefill_gas_count) denotes the near-equivalent total
inventory.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Total accumulated injected gas (sum over species)

NAMES.name: argon_density_at_separatrix
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short:
Charge-state-summed number density of argon ions, excluding neutral argon,
evaluated locally on the magnetic separatrix.
NAMES.long:
Argon ion density at the separatrix is the local number of charged argon
ions per physical volume on the last closed magnetic flux surface. It is the
argon-specific component of density at separatrix.

The charge-state-summed density is defined by

$$
n_{\mathrm{Ar}} = \sum_{q=1}^{18} n_{\mathrm{Ar}^{q+}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Ar}}$ is the argon ion number density, $q$ is the argon
ion charge-state index, and $n_{\mathrm{Ar}^{q+}}$ is the number density of
argon ions in charge state $q$. Neutral argon is excluded. Unlike
flux-surface-averaged argon density at the plasma boundary, this quantity
denotes the local value at the separatrix.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Argon (Ar)

NAMES.name: deuterated_methane_source_rate
NAMES.subject: deuterated_methane
NAMES.short:
Instantaneous injection rate of deuterated methane (CD4), counted as
equivalent electrons rather than molecules.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the instantaneous rate at which deuterated methane (CD4) is
supplied as an injected gas, with the rate counted in equivalent electrons.

The equivalent-electron source rate is defined by

$$
S_{e,\mathrm{CD4}}(t) = N_{e,\mathrm{CD4}}\,\dot{N}_{\mathrm{CD4}}(t) = 10\,\dot{N}_{\mathrm{CD4}}(t)
$$

where $S_{e,\mathrm{CD4}}$ is the equivalent-electron source rate,
$N_{e,\mathrm{CD4}}=10$ is the number of electrons in one neutral CD4
molecule, and $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{CD4}}$ is the molecular injection rate. It
counts carbon and deuterium electrons and is not a particle or mass source
rate.

The time integral of this rate gives the accumulated equivalent-electron
count, such as [accumulated deuterated methane count due to gas
injection](name:accumulated_deuterated_methane_count_due_to_gas_injection).

sources.parent_definition: Deuterated methane (CD4)

NAMES.name: electron_decay_time_at_magnetic_axis_due_to_disruption
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Exponential e-folding time for the electron-temperature decrease at the
magnetic axis during a disruption.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the characteristic e-folding time of the electron
temperature at the magnetic axis during a disruption. It describes
exponential temperature loss and is distinct from the [linear electron decay
time at the magnetic
axis](name:linear_electron_decay_time_at_magnetic_axis_due_to_disruption),
which uses a 20–80% definition.

For an exponential decay beginning at reference time $t_0$, the temperature
is represented by:

$$
T_e(t)=T_{e,0}\exp\left[-\frac{t-t_0}{\tau}\right]
$$

where $T_e(t)$ is the electron temperature at time $t$, $T_{e,0}$ is its
value at the reference time $t_0$, and $\tau$ is the decay time constant.
The quantity applies specifically to the magnetic-axis temperature and the
disruption-related decay; it is not a volume-averaged or runaway-electron
decay time.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Exponential decay time (tau) used when the process is described by an exponential function (exp(-(t-t0)/tau))). Here "t" is time and "t0" is the time where the decay process starts

NAMES.name: energy_confinement_enhancement_factor
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless ratio comparing the plasma energy confinement time with the
IPB98(y,2) reference scaling prediction.
NAMES.long:
The energy confinement enhancement factor is the multiplicative departure of
a plasma’s global energy confinement time from the IPB98(y,2) reference
scaling prediction. It indicates whether energy is retained longer or
shorter than the reference predicts for the corresponding scaling inputs.

The factor is defined by:

$$
h_{98} = \frac{\tau_E}{\tau_{E,\mathrm{IPB98(y,2)}}}
$$

where $h_{98}$ is the energy confinement enhancement factor, $\tau_E$ is the
plasma energy confinement time, and $\tau_{E,\mathrm{IPB98(y,2)}}$ is the
energy confinement time predicted by the IPB98(y,2) reference scaling.

This is a global plasma quantity: the numerator represents the confinement
of the total stored plasma energy relative to the corresponding net
energy-loss power, aggregated over the plasma rather than assigned to a
local region or individual transport channel. It is not itself an energy
confinement time, stored energy, power, or local transport coefficient.

A value of one denotes agreement with the reference scaling; a value greater
than one denotes longer confinement, and a value less than one denotes
shorter confinement than the reference prediction.

sources.parent_definition: Energy confinement time enhancement factor over the IPB98(y,2) scaling

NAMES.name: ipb98y2_confinement_time
NAMES.short:
IPB98(y,2) empirical-scaling reference for global energy confinement time,
providing the denominator for the H98 confinement enhancement factor.
NAMES.long:
The IPB98(y,2) energy confinement time is the global energy-confinement
timescale predicted by the IPB98(y,2) empirical scaling law. It is an
energy-channel performance benchmark rather than a species-resolved or local
transport time.

The underlying global energy confinement time is defined by

$$
\tau_E = \frac{W}{P_{\mathrm{loss}}}
$$

where $\tau_E$ is the global energy confinement time, $W$ is the total
thermal energy stored in the plasma, and $P_{\mathrm{loss}}$ is the net
power leaving the plasma. The quantity documented here is the IPB98(y,2)
scaling prediction of this timescale, not the directly evaluated confinement
time for a particular plasma state.

The value applies to the complete plasma energy content and its global loss
balance; it is not a local profile quantity, a particle confinement time, or
a confinement time assigned to an individual species. It is a single
empirical reference value for the energy channel.

The [energy confinement enhancement
factor](name:energy_confinement_enhancement_factor) compares the actual
global energy confinement time with this reference through $H_{98} = \tau_E
/ \tau_{E,98}$, where $H_{98}$ is the dimensionless confinement enhancement
factor and $\tau_{E,98}$ is this IPB98(y,2) scaling prediction.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Energy confinement time estimated from the IPB98(y,2) scaling

NAMES.name: neon_density
NAMES.subject: neon
NAMES.short:
Number density of neon impurity ions, summed over the included ionization
states; line-averaged and volume-averaged forms express the same elemental
content.
NAMES.long:
Neon density is the number of neon impurity ions per unit volume, summed
over all included charged ionization states. It represents elemental neon
content rather than the density of one selected charge state; neutral neon
atoms are excluded.

$$
n_{\mathrm{Ne}} = \sum_{z \in \mathcal{Z}_{\mathrm{Ne}}} n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{z+}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Ne}}$ is the charge-state-summed neon ion density,
$n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{z+}}$ is the density of neon ions in charge state $z+$, and
$\mathcal{Z}_{\mathrm{Ne}}$ is the set of included charged ionization
states.

This species-specific quantity is a member of density. The same
charge-state-summed field may be spatially averaged;
[volume_averaged_neon_density](name:volume_averaged_neon_density) represents
its volume average, while a charge-state-resolved quantity such as
[ion_charge_state_density](name:ion_charge_state_density) selects one
ionization state and is not equivalent.

NAMES.name: toroidal_helium_4_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: helium_4
NAMES.short:
Toroidal helium-4 velocity at the magnetic axis is the signed bulk-flow
velocity of helium-4 ions projected onto the toroidal φ direction of the
right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame at the magnetic axis.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal helium-4 velocity at the magnetic axis is the signed bulk-flow
velocity of helium-4 ions projected onto the toroidal basis vector of the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame at the magnetic axis. As a
species-level velocity, it is the density-weighted mean over all charge
states of helium-4 present at that locus.

The scalar projection is defined by:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{He}^4,\mathrm{axis}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{He}^4,\mathrm{axis}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{He}^4,\mathrm{axis}}$ is the density-weighted
mean helium-4 bulk-flow velocity vector at the magnetic axis and
$\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal basis vector in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is localized to the magnetic axis and is distinct from the
corresponding [toroidal helium-4 velocity at the plasma
boundary](name:toroidal_helium_4_velocity_at_plasma_boundary). It is
species-specific to helium-4 and is distinct from [toroidal helium-3
velocity at the magnetic
axis](name:toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_magnetic_axis).

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Helium isotope with 4 nucleons (4He)

NAMES.name: tritium_velocity
NAMES.subject: tritium
NAMES.short:
Tritium velocity is the directed motion of the tritium plasma population at
a physical location, represented by a velocity vector. As a species-level
intensive quantity, it denotes the density-weighted mean velocity over all
tritium charge states.
NAMES.long:
Tritium velocity is the fluid velocity vector of the tritium plasma
population at a specified physical location. It is the first velocity moment
of the tritium phase-space distribution and represents motion of the tritium
species as a vector, not a selected coordinate component.

For charge-state-resolved tritium populations, the species-level velocity is
the density-weighted mean over charge states:

$$
\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{T}} = \frac{\sum_q n_{\mathrm{T},q}\,\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{T},q}}{\sum_q n_{\mathrm{T},q}}
$$

where $q$ labels tritium charge state, $n_{\mathrm{T},q}$ is the number
density of tritium in charge state $q$, and $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{T},q}$ is
the velocity vector of tritium in charge state $q$.

It does not by itself select any scalar component or projection; a component
name supplies the associated axis or signed direction. The toroidal tritium
velocity is the projection of this vector onto the toroidal $\hat{\phi}$
direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is
major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

NAMES.name: argon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short:
Particle number density of argon ions evaluated on the flux surface assigned
to an internal transport barrier, summed over all argon ion charge states
and excluding neutral argon.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of argon ions evaluated on the flux surface assigned
to an internal transport barrier is the local density of the argon-ion
population at that flux-surface location.

The number density is defined by

$$
n = \lim_{\Delta V\to 0}\frac{\Delta N}{\Delta V}
$$

where $n$ is number density, $N$ is the number of counted particles, and $V$
is volume. For argon, the count is summed over all ionic charge states and
excludes neutral argon. This species-specific quantity is a member of
[density at the internal transport
barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier), alongside [boron
density at the internal transport
barrier](name:boron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier). The internal
transport barrier is the designated flux-surface location where reduced
cross-field turbulent transport permits steep density gradients.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Argon (Ar)

NAMES.name: krypton_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short:
Number density of krypton ions at the plasma boundary, evaluated as the
local, intensive particle count per physical volume on the last closed
magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Number density of krypton ions at the plasma boundary is the local,
intensive particle count per physical volume for the krypton-ion population
evaluated on the last closed magnetic flux surface. The plasma boundary is
the limiting closed magnetic flux surface separating confined plasma from
the open-field-line scrape-off-layer region.

The local krypton ion number density is the sum of the zeroth velocity
moments over all krypton ionization states at a boundary point:

$$
n_{\mathrm{Kr}}(\mathbf{x}_b,t) = \sum_{q \in \mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{Kr}}} \int f_{\mathrm{Kr}^{q+}}(\mathbf{x}_b,\mathbf{v},t)\,d^3v
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Kr}}$ is the krypton ion number density, $\mathbf{x}_b$ is
a point on the last closed magnetic flux surface, $t$ is time, $q$ is the
krypton ionization-state index, $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{Kr}}$ is the set of
all positively charged krypton ionization states, $f_{\mathrm{Kr}^{q+}}$ is
the phase-space distribution function for state $q$, $\mathbf{v}$ is
particle velocity, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element.

This quantity applies specifically to krypton ions and is summed over all
included ionization states. It excludes neutral krypton and all other ion
species, and it is a local boundary value with no averaging over the
boundary surface or over a volume.

It is the krypton-specific instance of [density at the plasma
boundary](name:density_at_plasma_boundary). The related [krypton
density](name:krypton_density) represents the same charge-state-summed ion
population at a general plasma location, whereas flux-surface-averaged
krypton density at the plasma boundary averages the krypton density over the
complete last closed magnetic flux surface rather than evaluating it
locally.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Krypton (Kr)

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_krypton_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short:
Charge-state-summed krypton ion number density averaged over the complete
separatrix, distinguishing a flux-surface value from the local boundary
value.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the charge-state-summed number density of krypton ions,
averaged over the complete plasma-boundary separatrix. It represents krypton
particle content associated with the last closed magnetic flux surface,
rather than a pointwise value; the corresponding local quantity is the
[krypton ion number density at the plasma
boundary](name:krypton_density_at_plasma_boundary).

The flux-surface average is defined by

$$
\left\langle n_{\mathrm{Kr}} \right\rangle_{\mathrm{FS},b} =
\frac{\displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{S}_b} n_{\mathrm{Kr}}\,\frac{dS}{\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert}}
{\displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{S}_b} \frac{dS}{\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Kr}}$ is the local krypton ion number density,
$\mathcal{S}_b$ is the plasma-boundary separatrix, $dS$ is the surface-area
element, and $\psi$ is the magnetic-flux surface label. All krypton ion
charge states are included in $n_{\mathrm{Kr}}$; neutral krypton and any
single-charge-state density are excluded.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Krypton (Kr)

NAMES.name: magnetic_field_at_pedestal_top_low_field_side
NAMES.short:
Magnetic field at the pedestal top low-field side is the local magnetic
induction vector evaluated at the low-field-side pressure-pedestal top. It
retains radial, toroidal, and vertical field components in the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame before component selection or magnitude
reduction.
NAMES.long:
Magnetic field at the pedestal top low-field side is the local magnetic
induction vector evaluated at the low-field-side top of the pressure
pedestal. It gives the total field direction and strength at that locus in
the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, whose basis is
$(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$ with $R$ the major-radius coordinate, $\phi$
the toroidal angle, and $Z$ the vertical coordinate.

The vector is decomposed as

$$
\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{ped,LFS} = B_R\hat{R} + B_\phi\hat{\phi} + B_Z\hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{ped,LFS}$ is the magnetic-field vector at the
low-field-side pressure-pedestal top, $B_R$ is its radial component,
$B_\phi$ is its toroidal component, $B_Z$ is its vertical component, and
$(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$ is the right-handed cylindrical basis.

The scope is locus-specific: it applies only at the low-field-side
pressure-pedestal top, not throughout the pedestal, not at the pedestal foot
or magnetic axis, and not as a spatial average over a flux surface or
volume. The quantity has no species, charge-state, or particle-population
aggregation; it is the electromagnetic field itself at the specified
location.

Relative to the unrestricted [magnetic field](name:magnetic_field), this
quantity adds the pedestal-top low-field-side evaluation locus while
retaining the same vector identity. Its child [magnetic-field magnitude at
the pedestal top low-field
side](name:magnetic_field_magnitude_at_pedestal_top_low_field_side) is the
Euclidean norm $|\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{ped,LFS}| = \sqrt{B_R^2+B_\phi^2+B_Z^2}$
and therefore removes direction and component signs; individual component or
projection names denote only the corresponding part of this vector.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when a component of $\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{ped,LFS}$
is directed along $+\hat{R}$, $+\hat{\phi}$, or $+\hat{Z}$, respectively, in
the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless magnetic-surface coordinate locating the internal transport
barrier between the magnetic axis and the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the internal transport barrier is
the dimensionless magnetic-surface label assigned to the flux surface
containing the barrier. It locates that surface within the nested
closed-flux region rather than giving a cylindrical distance or vector
component.

The coordinate is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(\mathrm{ITB}) = \left[\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathrm{ITB}) - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,LCFS}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}\right]^{1/2}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(\mathrm{ITB})$ is the normalized toroidal
flux coordinate at the internal transport barrier,
$\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathrm{ITB})$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed
by the flux surface containing the barrier, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}$ is
its value at the magnetic axis, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,LCFS}}$ is its value
at the last closed flux surface. The nonnegative square-root branch is used.

The value applies specifically to the flux surface assigned to the internal
transport barrier and is bounded from zero at the magnetic axis to unity at
the last closed flux surface for nested surfaces with monotonic toroidal
flux. It has no species, charge-state, or spatial averaging; it is a scalar
surface label.

This quantity is the internal-transport-barrier specialization of the
[normalized toroidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate). Unlike the [toroidal
flux coordinate at the internal transport
barrier](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_internal_transport_barrier), it
uses axis-to-last-closed-flux-surface normalization and is therefore
dimensionless.

sources.leaf_definition: Normalized toroidal flux coordinate. The normalizing value for rho_tor_norm, is the toroidal flux coordinate at the equilibrium boundary (LCFS or 99.x % of the LCFS in case of a fixed boundary equilibium calculation, see time_slice/boundary/b_flux_pol_norm in the equilibrium IDS)
sources.parent_definition: Radial position at which physics quantities are evaluated

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_pedestal_top
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless toroidal-flux label locating the top of the H-mode edge
pedestal on a nested magnetic surface relative to the magnetic axis and last
closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The normalized toroidal flux coordinate evaluated at the pedestal top is the
dimensionless magnetic-surface label assigned to the top of the H-mode edge
pedestal. It locates that position within the nested closed-flux-surface
family, rather than representing a cylindrical distance or a local vector
component.

For a nested equilibrium, the coordinate is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(\mathrm{ped}) = \left[\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathrm{ped}) - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathrm{axis})}{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathrm{LCFS}) - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathrm{axis})}\right]^{1/2}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(\mathrm{ped})$ is the normalized toroidal
flux coordinate at the pedestal top, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal
magnetic flux enclosed by a magnetic surface, $\mathrm{ped}$ denotes the
pedestal-top position, $\mathrm{axis}$ denotes the magnetic axis, and
$\mathrm{LCFS}$ denotes the last closed flux surface.

The value applies specifically at the top of the H-mode edge pedestal, the
inner shoulder of the edge transport barrier. Its position is defined by the
[normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the
pedestal](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_pedestal). This is a
single coordinate evaluation: no species, charge-state, or population
aggregation applies, and no surface averaging is implied. It is distinct
from a cylindrical radial distance and from the unnormalized [toroidal flux
coordinate at the pedestal
top](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_pedestal_top).

This entry is the pedestal-top specialization of the [normalized toroidal
flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate), with the same
axis-to-boundary normalization. It should not be interpreted as the
corresponding [normalized poloidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate), which labels surfaces
using poloidal rather than toroidal magnetic flux.

sources.leaf_definition: Normalized toroidal flux coordinate. The normalizing value for rho_tor_norm, is the toroidal flux coordinate at the equilibrium boundary (LCFS or 99.x % of the LCFS in case of a fixed boundary equilibium calculation, see time_slice/boundary/b_flux_pol_norm in the equilibrium IDS)
sources.parent_definition: Radial position at which physics quantities are evaluated

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_separatrix
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless toroidal-flux surface label at the magnetic separatrix,
identifying the outermost closed magnetic surface and its outer
normalization value.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the normalized toroidal-flux surface label evaluated at the
magnetic separatrix, which is the outermost closed magnetic surface. It
identifies the flux-coordinate location of separatrix quantities rather than
a cylindrical distance or a local vector component.

The normalized toroidal-flux coordinate at the separatrix is defined by

$$
\left.\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}\right|_{\mathrm{sep}} = \left(\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,sep}}-\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,LCFS}}-\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}\right)^{1/2}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the normalized toroidal-flux coordinate,
$\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,sep}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux at the separatrix,
$\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux at the magnetic
axis, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,LCFS}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux at the
last closed flux surface. The separatrix is the last closed flux surface for
this evaluation, so the value is the outer normalization value, equal to one
when the separatrix and last-closed-surface loci are identified.

This is a point evaluation of a scalar magnetic-surface label for the
separatrix locus; it is not a spatial average, volume integral, flux
integral, cylindrical radius, or vector component. The [normalized toroidal
flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate) represents the
same coordinate on general nested magnetic surfaces, while this quantity
fixes its evaluation at the separatrix.

The normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the plasma boundary uses the
plasma-boundary locus instead. Those loci may coincide when the plasma
boundary is defined as the last closed flux surface, but the two quantities
retain distinct locus semantics.

sources.leaf_definition: Normalized toroidal flux coordinate. The normalizing value for rho_tor_norm, is the toroidal flux coordinate at the equilibrium boundary (LCFS or 99.x % of the LCFS in case of a fixed boundary equilibium calculation, see time_slice/boundary/b_flux_pol_norm in the equilibrium IDS)
sources.parent_definition: Radial position at which physics quantities are evaluated

NAMES.name: oxygen_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: oxygen
NAMES.short:
Number density of oxygen ions at the plasma boundary, evaluated as the
local, intensive particle count per physical volume on the last closed
magnetic flux surface and summed over all charged oxygen ionization states.
NAMES.long:
Number density of oxygen ions at the plasma boundary is the local, intensive
particle count per physical volume for the oxygen-ion population evaluated
on the last closed magnetic flux surface. The plasma boundary is the
limiting closed magnetic flux surface separating confined plasma from the
open-field-line scrape-off-layer region.

The local charge-state-summed oxygen ion density at a boundary point is the
zeroth velocity moment of the oxygen-ion distribution functions:

$$
n_{\mathrm{O}}(\mathbf{x}_b,t)=\sum_{z=1}^{8}\int f_{\mathrm{O}^{z+}}(\mathbf{x}_b,\mathbf{v},t)\,d^3v
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{O}}$ is the oxygen-ion number density, $\mathbf{x}_b$ is a
point on the last closed magnetic flux surface, $t$ is time, $z$ is the
positive oxygen ionization state, $f_{\mathrm{O}^{z+}}$ is the phase-space
distribution function for that state, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and
$d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element.

This quantity applies specifically to oxygen ions and sums the populations
from singly ionized through fully stripped oxygen. It excludes neutral
oxygen and other ion species, and it is a local boundary value with no
averaging over the boundary surface or over a volume.

It is the oxygen-specific instance of [density at the plasma
boundary](name:density_at_plasma_boundary). The flux-surface-averaged oxygen
density at the plasma boundary represents the same charge-state-summed
oxygen-ion content averaged over the last closed magnetic flux surface
rather than evaluated locally.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Oxygen (O)

NAMES.name: tungsten_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: tungsten
NAMES.short:
Particle number density of tungsten ions evaluated on the flux surface
assigned to an internal transport barrier, summed over all tungsten ion
charge states and excluding neutral tungsten.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of tungsten ions evaluated on the flux surface
assigned to an internal transport barrier is the local density of the
tungsten-ion population at that flux-surface location.

The number density is defined by

$$
n_{\mathrm{W}} = \lim_{\Delta V\to 0}\frac{\Delta N_{\mathrm{W}}}{\Delta V}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{W}}$ is the tungsten-ion number density, $N_{\mathrm{W}}$
is the number of counted tungsten ions, and $V$ is volume.

This quantity is the tungsten-specific member of [density at the internal
transport barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier). The count is
summed over all tungsten ionic charge states and excludes neutral tungsten.
It is evaluated at the internal transport barrier rather than at a divertor
target, as distinguished by [tungsten density at the divertor
target](name:tungsten_density_at_divertor_target).

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Tungsten (W)

NAMES.name: logarithm_of_density
NAMES.short:
Logarithm of a selected plasma density, representing the natural-log
transform of that density relative to a specified reference for the same
density quantity. It is the base logarithmic density quantity from which
coordinate derivatives may be formed.
NAMES.long:
Logarithm of density is the natural logarithm of a selected plasma density
after normalization by a reference value for the same density quantity. It
represents the logarithmic density variable itself, not a spatial derivative
or gradient.

The defining logarithmic transform is

$$
L_n = \ln\!\left(\frac{n}{n_\mathrm{ref}}\right)
$$

where $L_n$ is the logarithm of density, $n$ is the selected plasma density,
and $n_\mathrm{ref}$ is the reference value used for the same selected
density.

The scope covers the logarithmic transform for any explicitly selected
density population or component; a more specific standard name supplies the
particular population, coordinate dependence, or reference convention. It
excludes the density $n$ itself, a density ratio before applying the
logarithm, and any coordinate derivative or gradient of $L_n$.

A derivative specialization such as [logarithmic-density derivative with
respect to normalized minor
radius](name:derivative_of_logarithm_of_density_with_respect_to_normalized_minor_radius)
denotes a derivative of $L_n$, not $L_n$ itself. For any coordinate $x$, the
corresponding logarithmic derivative is $dL_n/dx = (1/n)\,dn/dx$ when
$n_\mathrm{ref}$ is independent of $x$, where $x$ is the coordinate of
differentiation.

NAMES.name: derivative_of_logarithm_of_density_with_respect_to_normalized_minor_radius
NAMES.short:
Signed logarithmic derivative of a selected particle-species density with
respect to normalized minor radius, expressing the relative change of that
density as the normalized minor-radius coordinate increases. For
charge-state-aggregated ion species, the density is summed over all charge
states.
NAMES.long:
Signed logarithmic derivative of a selected particle-species density with
respect to normalized minor radius is the local derivative of that species
density's natural logarithm along the normalized minor-radius coordinate. It
represents the relative change of the selected species density with respect
to that coordinate.

The derivative is defined by

$$
G_{n_s} = \frac{\partial \ln n_s}{\partial \rho} = \frac{1}{n_s}\frac{\partial n_s}{\partial \rho}
$$

where $G_{n_s}$ is this logarithmic derivative, $n_s$ is the density of the
selected particle species $s$, and $\rho$ is the normalized minor radius,
the radial coordinate in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$
increasing from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

The scope is one selected particle species at the position where the
derivative is evaluated. When the selected species represents a
charge-state-aggregated ion population, $n_s$ is the charge-state-summed
density over all charge states; it is not a density-weighted charge-state
mean and not a total over unrelated species.

This quantity is the derivative of the logarithmic density with respect to
$\rho$, not the density itself, not the logarithm alone, and not a
coordinate-specialized value of a logarithm-of-density quantity.
Logarithmic-gradient conventions that add an extra minus sign or
differentiate with respect to an unnormalized minor-radius coordinate denote
different quantities.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $\ln n_s$ increases with increasing
normalized minor-radius coordinate $\rho$.

sources.leaf_definition: normalized logarithmic gradient (with respect to r_minor_norm) of the density
sources.parent_definition: Set of species (including electrons) used in the calculation and related quantities

NAMES.name: normalized_perturbed_parallel_gyrocenter_heat_flux_bessel_1
NAMES.subject: gyrocenter
NAMES.short:
Normalized first-Bessel-weighted parallel heat-flux moment of a perturbed
gyrocenter distribution in a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode.
NAMES.long:
This quantity represents the energy-weighted parallel motion carried by the
perturbed gyrocenter population. It is evaluated in the field-aligned
parallel direction and includes first-order Bessel weighting.

The normalized moment is defined by

$$
\widehat{q}_{\parallel,J_1}=\frac{1}{\mathcal{N}_q}\int \frac{1}{2}m v_{\parallel}v^2 J_1\,\delta f_g^{(1)}(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $\widehat{q}_{\parallel,J_1}$ is the normalized parallel heat-flux
moment, $\mathcal{N}_q$ is the normalization factor for the corresponding
heat-flux moment, $m$ is the gyrocenter particle mass, $v_{\parallel}$ is
the velocity component parallel to the magnetic field, $v$ is the
particle-speed magnitude, $J_1$ is the first-order Bessel weighting factor
at the prescribed gyrokinetic argument, $\delta f_g^{(1)}(\mathbf{v})$ is
the perturbed gyrocenter distribution function, $\mathbf{v}$ is the
velocity-space coordinate, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element.

The integral applies to the perturbed gyrocenter distribution associated
with a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode and aggregates the represented
distribution over velocity space. It excludes the equilibrium or unperturbed
distribution and is not an unweighted heat-flux moment.

The parallel projection distinguishes this quantity from the perpendicular
heat-flux moment perpendicular gyrocenter heat perturbed flux normalized of
gyrokinetic eigenmode. It belongs to the same first-Bessel-weighted
perturbed gyrocenter moment family as [normalized perturbed parallel
gyrocenter current density bessel
1](name:normalized_perturbed_parallel_gyrocenter_current_density_bessel_1),
but uses the energy-weighted heat-flux kernel rather than the
current-density kernel.

sources.leaf_definition: Normalized parallel heat flux (integral of 0.5 * m * v_par * v^2)
sources.parent_definition: Moments (normalized) of the perturbed distribution function of gyrocenters times 1st order Bessel function of the first kind

NAMES.name: normalized_perturbed_parallel_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Normalized perturbed parallel magnetic-field magnitude is the nonnegative
amplitude of a magnetic-field perturbation projected along the local
equilibrium magnetic-field direction and divided by a reference
magnetic-field magnitude. More specific names may add averaging conventions.
NAMES.long:
Normalized perturbed parallel magnetic-field magnitude is the normalized
amplitude of the component of a magnetic-field perturbation that is parallel
to the local equilibrium magnetic field. It is a nonnegative scalar
intensity formed from the absolute value of the parallel projection, not
from the full perturbation vector magnitude.

A representative definition is

$$
\widetilde{B}_{\parallel,N} = \frac{\left|\delta\mathbf{B}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}}_0\right|}{B_\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $\widetilde{B}_{\parallel,N}$ is the normalized perturbed parallel
magnetic-field magnitude, $\delta\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field
perturbation, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}_0$ is the unit vector along the local
equilibrium magnetic field, and $B_\mathrm{ref}$ is the reference
magnetic-field magnitude used for the normalization.

This parent quantity fixes the parallel projection and normalization by a
reference magnetic-field magnitude. It does not by itself fix temporal,
spatial, spectral, or flux-surface averaging; those aggregation conventions
are supplied only by more specific names.

This quantity excludes the normalized total perturbation magnitude,
perpendicular-to-field perturbation amplitudes, signed parallel
perturbations, and unnormalized perturbation amplitudes. The absolute value
in the definition makes the parent a magnitude, so reversal of the
perturbation sign along the equilibrium field does not change its value.

A concrete child such as [time-averaged normalized perturbed parallel
magnetic-field
magnitude](name:time_averaged_normalized_perturbed_parallel_magnetic_field_magnitude)
adds a time-average aggregation to the same parallel-projected normalized
magnitude; it is not a change from parallel projection to total-field
normalization.

NAMES.name: parallel_gyrocenter_momentum_flux_normalized_of_gyrokinetic_eigenmode_due_to_e_cross_b_drift
NAMES.subject: gyrocenter
NAMES.short:
Normalized parallel gyrocenter toroidal angular-momentum flux of a
gyrokinetic eigenmode due to E×B drift is the rotating-frame spectral
contribution from the perturbed electrostatic potential’s E×B drift to the
mode’s parallel gyrocenter momentum transport.
NAMES.long:
Normalized parallel gyrocenter toroidal angular-momentum flux of a
gyrokinetic eigenmode due to $E\times B$ drift is the normalized spectral
contribution, evaluated in the rotating frame, of the perturbed
electrostatic potential's $E\times B$ drift to the parallel gyrocenter part
of toroidal angular-momentum flux. The toroidal component is the
$\hat{\phi}$ component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame,
where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical
height.

The normalization is defined relative to the reference momentum-flux
normalization for the same eigenmode:

$$
\widehat{\Pi}_{\parallel,\phi}^{E\times B} = \frac{\Pi_{\parallel,\phi}^{E\times B}}{\Pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}
$$

where $\widehat{\Pi}_{\parallel,\phi}^{E\times B}$ is this normalized
contribution, $\Pi_{\parallel,\phi}^{E\times B}$ is the corresponding
unnormalized parallel gyrocenter toroidal angular-momentum-flux contribution
from the perturbed electrostatic-potential $E\times B$ drift in the rotating
frame, $\Pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the reference momentum-flux normalization,
$E$ is the perturbed electric field associated with the electrostatic
potential, $B$ is the magnetic field, the subscript $\parallel$ denotes the
part associated with gyrocenter motion parallel to $B$, and the subscript
$\phi$ denotes toroidal angular momentum about the symmetry axis.

The quantity applies to one specified linear gyrokinetic eigenmode and to
the rotating-frame representation of that mode; it is not summed over
eigenmodes, wave-number spectrum, or transport channels. Its aggregation
convention is a single-channel normalized eigenmode contribution, not a
total turbulent momentum flux.

It is the electrostatic-potential $E\times B$ channel in the additive
decomposition of the normalized parallel gyrocenter toroidal
angular-momentum flux. The perturbed parallel vector-potential channel and
the [perturbed parallel magnetic-field
channel](name:parallel_gyrocenter_momentum_flux_normalized_of_gyrokinetic_eigenmode_due_to_perturbed_parallel_magnetic_field)
are separate contributions and are excluded from this quantity.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the $E\times B$-drift contribution transports
positive parallel gyrocenter toroidal angular momentum across a magnetic
flux surface toward increasing flux label, with positive toroidal angular
momentum corresponding to the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Contribution of the perturbed electrostatic potential to the parallel component of the normalized toroidal momentum flux

NAMES.name: time_averaged_normalized_perturbed_parallel_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Time-averaged normalized perturbed parallel magnetic-field magnitude is the
time-averaged amplitude of a magnetic-field perturbation projected along the
local equilibrium magnetic field and normalized by a reference
magnetic-field magnitude. It does not include flux-surface averaging unless
a more specific name states that aggregation.
NAMES.long:
Time-averaged normalized perturbed parallel magnetic-field magnitude is the
time-averaged scalar amplitude of the component of a magnetic-field
perturbation parallel to the local equilibrium magnetic field, normalized by
a reference magnetic-field magnitude. It characterizes the parallel
perturbation amplitude after the sign of the parallel projection has been
removed.

The quantity is defined by averaging the normalized magnitude of the
parallel perturbation over the time interval defining the quantity:

$$
\overline{b}_{\parallel,\mathrm{pert}} = \left\langle \frac{\left|\delta \mathbf{B}\cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}_0\right|}{B_\mathrm{ref}} \right\rangle_t
$$

where $\overline{b}_{\parallel,\mathrm{pert}}$ is the time-averaged
normalized perturbed parallel magnetic-field magnitude, $\delta \mathbf{B}$
is the magnetic-field perturbation, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}_0$ is the unit vector
in the direction of the local equilibrium magnetic field, $B_\mathrm{ref}$
is the reference magnetic-field magnitude used for normalization, and
$\langle\cdot\rangle_t$ denotes averaging over the time interval defining
the quantity.

The scope is the time-averaged scalar amplitude before any spatial
aggregation is added by a more specific qualifier. It applies wherever the
magnetic-field perturbation, local equilibrium-field direction, and
normalization reference are defined; this parent by itself does not
prescribe a flux-surface, volume, line, or ensemble average.

This is not the instantaneous normalized perturbation, the signed normalized
parallel component, the perpendicular perturbation, or the total
magnetic-perturbation magnitude. The absolute value distinguishes it from
signed parallel-field perturbations by discarding the sign of the parallel
projection.

The [flux-surface-averaged time-averaged normalized perturbed parallel
magnetic-field
magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_time_averaged_normalized_perturbed_parallel_magnetic_field_magnitude)
is obtained by applying an additional magnetic-flux-surface average to this
already time-averaged quantity; the additional qualifier changes the spatial
aggregation, not the presence of time averaging.

NAMES.name: normalized_effective_particle_energy
NAMES.short:
Normalized effective particle energy is the ratio of a species effective
particle-energy coordinate to the positive species reference thermal-energy
scale.
NAMES.long:
Normalized effective particle energy is the ratio of a species effective
particle-energy coordinate to the positive species reference thermal-energy
scale. It is a dimensionless velocity-space coordinate for the effective
single-particle energy relative to that species reference, not an
independent temperature, mass, or charge ratio.

The normalization is

$$
\bar{\mathcal{E}}_s = \frac{\mathcal{E}^{*}_{\mathrm{eff},s}}{E_{\mathrm{th,ref},s}}
$$

where $\bar{\mathcal{E}}_s$ is the normalized effective particle energy, $s$
labels the particle species, $\mathcal{E}^{*}_{\mathrm{eff},s}$ is the
effective particle-energy coordinate for that species expressed on a scale
compatible with the denominator, and $E_{\mathrm{th,ref},s} > 0$ is the
species reference thermal-energy scale. If the reference is specified by a
species reference temperature $T_{\mathrm{ref},s}$, the corresponding
denominator is $E_{\mathrm{th,ref},s}=k_B T_{\mathrm{ref},s}$; the same
reference temperature appears in
[ratio_of_particle_temperature_to_reference_particle_temperature](name:ratio_of_particle_temperature_to_particle_reference_temperature).

It is distinguished from
[effective_particle_energy](name:effective_particle_energy), which denotes
the effective-energy coordinate without requiring this particular species
thermal normalization. If the effective particle energy contains an additive
effective-potential term $U_{\mathrm{eff},s}$, its normalized contribution
is $U_{\mathrm{eff},s}/E_{\mathrm{th,ref},s}$; with the same denominator
this is normalized_particle_effective_potential. The detailed split of the
effective energy into kinetic and potential terms and the choice of
potential-energy zero are not fixed by this name.
