NAMES.name: perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential
NAMES.short:
Gage-dependent perturbation of the vacuum magnetic vector potential
generated by external current sources; its curl gives the corresponding
induction perturbation excluding plasma-current contributions.
NAMES.long:
The perturbed vacuum magnetic vector potential is a gage-dependent vector
field representing the perturbation of the external-source contribution to
the [magnetic vector potential](name:magnetic_vector_potential) relative to
a specified reference state. It is the complete vector perturbation, not a
single directional component.

The corresponding perturbed vacuum magnetic induction is defined by:

$$
\delta \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}} = \nabla \times \delta \mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{vac}}
$$

where $\delta \mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the perturbed vacuum magnetic
vector potential, $\delta \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the
magnetic-induction perturbation produced by external sources, and $\nabla
\times$ is the curl operator. The perturbation remains gage-dependent:
replacing $\delta \mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ by $\delta
\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{vac}} + \nabla \chi$, where $\chi$ is a scalar gage
function, leaves $\delta \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ unchanged.

This quantity includes the aggregate perturbation of the external-source
contribution and excludes magnetic-vector-potential contributions generated
by plasma currents. It is distinct from the unperturbed [vacuum magnetic
vector potential](name:vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential) and from the full
magnetic vector potential that includes plasma-current contributions. Its
radial projection is represented by the [radial perturbed vacuum magnetic
vector potential](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential),
while the corresponding unperturbed radial component is the [radial vacuum
magnetic vector potential](name:radial_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential).
Components are resolved in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$
frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is
vertical height.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when a resolved component of the vector points
along its corresponding positive basis direction in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential
NAMES.short:
Radial component of a first-order perturbed magnetic vector-potential
eigenfunction in the vacuum region for a toroidal linear-MHD mode,
represented by its real or imaginary coefficient.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the radial projection of a first-order, complex perturbed
magnetic vector-potential eigenfunction in the vacuum region. It is the
common radial coefficient represented by separate real and imaginary
quadratures.

$$
\widetilde{A}_{1R} = \widetilde{\mathbf{A}}_1 \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}}
$$

where $\widetilde{A}_{1R}$ is the complex radial vector-potential
coefficient, $\widetilde{\mathbf{A}}_1$ is the complex first-order perturbed
magnetic vector-potential eigenfunction, and $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the unit
vector toward increasing major-radius coordinate $R$ in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The subscript $1$ denotes the first-order
perturbation.

The quantity applies to the vacuum-region radial component associated with a
toroidal linear-MHD mode. It represents one mode without summing over
toroidal modes and includes both quadratures; it is not restricted to either
the real or imaginary coefficient alone. It excludes the complete vector
potential and its poloidal and toroidal components.

The full vector quantity is [perturbed vacuum magnetic vector
potential](name:perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential), of which this
quantity is the radial projection. Its two quadrature-specific
representations are the [real
part](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential_real_part) and
[imaginary
part](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential_imaginary_part)
of the same complex radial coefficient.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the radial vector-potential coefficient
points toward increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential_imaginary_part
NAMES.short:
Imaginary coefficient of the radial component of a complex perturbed
magnetic vector-potential eigenfunction for one toroidal linear-MHD mode in
the vacuum region.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the imaginary coefficient of the radial component of the
complex perturbed magnetic vector-potential eigenfunction for a single
toroidal linear-MHD mode in the vacuum region.

The radial imaginary coefficient is defined by

$$
A_{R,\mathrm{imag}} = \operatorname{Im}\left(\widetilde{\mathbf{A}}_{\mathrm{vac}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}}\right)
$$

where $A_{R,\mathrm{imag}}$ is this quantity, $\operatorname{Im}$ extracts
the imaginary part, $\widetilde{\mathbf{A}}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the complex
perturbed magnetic vector-potential eigenfunction in the vacuum region, and
$\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the radial unit vector. The radial direction is
defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is
major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The scope is the vacuum region outside the plasma and one specified toroidal
Fourier mode; coefficients from different toroidal modes are not summed.
This quantity contains only the out-of-phase imaginary coefficient and
excludes the corresponding real part. The [parent radial perturbed vacuum
magnetic vector
potential](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential) is the
full complex radial component before imaginary-part extraction. It is
distinct from the [imaginary radial perturbed vacuum magnetic
field](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part), because
the magnetic-field perturbation is obtained from the curl of the vector
potential rather than being the vector-potential component itself.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the imaginary part of the vector-potential
coefficient points in the increasing-$R$ radial direction; its phase sign
follows the chosen phase reference of the complex eigenfunction.

sources.leaf_definition: Imaginary part
sources.parent_definition: First coordinate (radial)

NAMES.name: radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential_real_part
NAMES.short:
Real part of the first-order radial magnetic-vector-potential eigenfunction
for a single toroidal mode in the vacuum region.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the real radial projection of the first-order perturbed
magnetic vector-potential eigenfunction in the vacuum region for one
toroidal Fourier mode. The real part is defined relative to the phase
reference of that complex eigenfunction.

$$
A_{R,\mathrm{vac}}^{\mathrm{Re}} = \operatorname{Re}\!\left(\widetilde{\mathbf{A}}_{\mathrm{vac}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}}\right)
$$

Here $A_{R,\mathrm{vac}}^{\mathrm{Re}}$ is the requested real radial
component, $\widetilde{\mathbf{A}}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the complex
first-order perturbed magnetic vector-potential eigenfunction in the vacuum
region, $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the radial unit vector, and
$\operatorname{Re}$ denotes the real-part operation. The radial direction is
defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is
major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies outside the plasma and to one toroidal Fourier mode; it
is not summed over modes. It excludes the plasma-region perturbation, the
imaginary component, and the unreduced complex radial component. The [radial
perturbed vacuum magnetic vector
potential](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential) is the
full complex parent quantity, of which this entry is the real-part
component. It is distinct from the [radial perturbed vacuum magnetic
field](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field), which is a
magnetic-field perturbation rather than a vector potential.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the real radial projection points toward
increasing major radius $R$.

NAMES.name: area_of_flux_loop
NAMES.short:
The effective area of a flux loop is the non-negative field-to-flux
sensitivity area of the sensor, including the aperture enclosed by each
turn, the number of turns, and calibration factors. It converts a spatially
averaged magnetic-field component normal to the loop aperture into total
linked magnetic flux.
NAMES.long:
The effective area of a flux loop is the non-negative field-to-flux
sensitivity factor of the sensor. It represents the aperture area enclosed
by each turn, the number of turns, and calibration corrections that make the
total linked magnetic flux equivalent to a spatially averaged magnetic-field
component normal to the loop aperture.

The effective area $A_\mathrm{eff}$ is defined by the relation between
linked flux and averaged normal field:

$$
A_\mathrm{eff} = \frac{\Phi}{\bar{B}_n}
$$

where $\Phi$ is the signed magnetic flux threading the loop and $\bar{B}_n$
is the spatial average of the magnetic-field component along the chosen loop
normal.

For a specified loop normal and terminal polarity, Faraday's law gives $V =
-d\Phi/dt = -A_\mathrm{eff}\,d\bar{B}_n/dt$ when $A_\mathrm{eff}$ is
constant. Reversing the winding direction or terminal polarity reverses the
signed quantities $\Phi$ and $V$, not the non-negative effective area.

This quantity is the flux-loop analog of
[area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe)
for magnetic-field probes. It differs from
[area_of_rogowski_coil](name:area_of_rogowski_coil), which describes
coupling to enclosed current rather than linked magnetic flux; the
corresponding signed circuit response is
[voltage_of_flux_loop](name:voltage_of_flux_loop).

sources.leaf_definition: Effective area (ratio between flux and average magnetic field over the loop). Leave empty if ../type/index = 6 (differential loop)
sources.parent_definition: Flux loops; partial flux loops can be described. In case of differential loops, the geometry of differential flux loops is stored in the flux_loop indices of the primitive loops. Signals may be stored on the primitive loop indices but this is optional if the index of the primitive loop is referenced by a differential loop index

NAMES.name: area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
Geometric cross-sectional area enclosed by one winding turn of a poloidal
magnetic-field probe coil, defining its per-turn magnetic-flux coupling.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the geometric cross-sectional area enclosed by one winding
turn of a poloidal magnetic-field probe coil. It represents the
magnetic-flux coupling area of an individual pickup-coil turn and is
nonnegative.

For a winding composed of identical turns, the ideal effective flux-sensing
area is

$$
A_{\mathrm{eff}} = N A_{\mathrm{turn}}
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the signed effective geometric flux-sensing area
of the complete winding, $N$ is the signed number of winding turns, and
$A_{\mathrm{turn}}$ is the area of one turn.

This quantity is defined per turn and applies only to the probe-coil
geometry; it does not include the number of turns, winding orientation, or
calibration factors. Consequently, it is distinct from the complete
effective area of a flux-loop sensor, such as [area of a flux
loop](name:area_of_flux_loop). The corresponding [turn count of a poloidal
magnetic-field probe](name:turn_count_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe)
combines with this area to determine the winding's ideal effective
flux-sensing area.

sources.leaf_definition: Area of each turn of the sensor; becomes effective area when multiplied by the turns
sources.parent_definition: Poloidal field probes

NAMES.name: area_of_rogowski_coil
NAMES.short:
Area of a Rogowski coil is the effective cross-sectional area linked by one
sensing turn of the closed winding. It is a geometric area factor; with
winding turn density it determines the ideal current-sensing sensitivity.
NAMES.long:
Area of a Rogowski coil is the effective cross-sectional area linked by one
sensing turn of a closed Rogowski winding. It is a scalar geometry factor of
the winding, not the signed current threaded by the coil or the measured
coil voltage.

In the ideal uniformly wound limit, the area appears as the non-negative
sensitivity factor in the linear constitutive relation between coil voltage
and enclosed-current time derivative:

$$
V_R(t) = \sigma \mu_0 n A \frac{d I_\mathrm{enc}}{dt}
$$

where $A$ is the Rogowski-coil area, $n$ is the winding turn density along
the closed winding path, $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability,
$I_\mathrm{enc}$ is the signed [Rogowski-coil
current](name:current_of_rogowski_coil) threaded by the coil, $V_R$ is the
Rogowski-coil voltage, and $\sigma$ is the sign set by winding orientation
and terminal polarity.

The effective area may represent a calibrated equivalent for a real winding
with finite pitch or nonuniform cross-section, but it remains a per-turn
area factor. It is in the same geometric-coil-area family as [area of a
poloidal magnetic field probe](name:area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe)
and [area of a toroidal magnetic field
probe](name:area_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe); multiplying by turn
density, turn number, or path length gives related sensitivity factors, not
this quantity.

sources.leaf_definition: Effective area of the loop wrapped around the guiding centre. In case of multiple layers, sum of the areas of each layer
sources.parent_definition: Set of Rogowski coils. If some of the coils form a compound Rogowski sensor, they must be entered in contiguous order

NAMES.name: area_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
Geometric area enclosed by one complete winding turn of a toroidal
magnetic-field probe coil, setting its single-turn magnetic-flux
sensitivity.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the geometric area enclosed by one complete winding turn of
a toroidal magnetic-field probe coil. It characterizes the coil’s
single-turn coupling to magnetic flux and is independent of the number of
winding turns.

For a coil with multiple turns, the effective flux-coupling area is related
to the single-turn area by

$$
A_{\mathrm{eff}} = N A_{\mathrm{turn}}
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the effective flux-coupling area of the complete
winding, $N$ is the signed [turn count of the toroidal magnetic-field
probe](name:turn_count_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), and
$A_{\mathrm{turn}}$ is the area enclosed by one turn represented by this
quantity.

The scope is limited to the physical area of one turn of the toroidal
magnetic-field probe coil; no summation over turns, orientation sign, or
additional calibration factor is included. It is distinct from the
corresponding [area of a poloidal magnetic-field
probe](name:area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe) and from the probe’s
induced [voltage](name:voltage_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), which
results from time-varying linked magnetic flux. Together with the winding
count, this area determines the probe’s magnetic-flux sensitivity.

sources.leaf_definition: Area of each turn of the sensor; becomes effective area when multiplied by the turns
sources.parent_definition: Toroidal field probes

NAMES.name: calibration_reference_magnetic_field_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
Signed poloidal magnetic-field values forming the linear calibration axis
used to characterize a poloidal magnetic-field probe’s nonlinear response.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed poloidal magnetic field assigned to the
linear-response reference axis of a poloidal magnetic-field probe. It
represents the field value corresponding to the probe signal under an
assumed linear field-to-signal relation, rather than the corrected field on
a nonlinear response curve.

The linear calibration relation is represented by

$$
S_{\mathrm{lin}} = G B_{\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $S_{\mathrm{lin}}$ is the probe signal predicted by the
linear-response model, $G$ is the linear field-to-signal coefficient, and
$B_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the signed calibration-reference magnetic field
represented by this quantity.

The quantity applies to the local poloidal magnetic field at the sensing
location of the specified poloidal magnetic-field probe. It retains the
signed poloidal field rather than a field magnitude, and no summation over
probe locations or magnetic-field components is implied. It is an
independent calibration-axis quantity, not a plasma-wide or
equilibrium-field aggregate.

It is distinct from the local operational field represented by [poloidal
magnetic field of a magnetic-field
probe](name:poloidal_magnetic_field_of_magnetic_field_probe), which is the
probe field value itself, and from the equilibrium reference vector
[reference magnetic field](name:reference_magnetic_field). The reference
values are paired with the nonlinear-response characterization and do not
constitute a single fixed gain or an uncertainty/error quantity. The
poloidal component is resolved in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi,
Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is
vertical height.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the signed poloidal field points along the
probe's defined positive sensing direction.

sources.leaf_definition: Array of magnetic field values (corresponding to the assumption of a linear relation between magnetic field and probe coil current), for each of which the probe non-linear response is given in ../b_field_non_linear
sources.parent_definition: Non-linear response of the probe (typically in case of a Hall probe)

NAMES.name: current_of_rogowski_coil
NAMES.short:
Signed conventional current threading a Rogowski-coil winding contour, with
orientation set by the coil's assigned normal.
NAMES.long:
Signed conventional current threading a Rogowski-coil winding contour is the
net conventional electric current crossing an oriented surface bounded by
that contour. The surface orientation is specified by the coil's assigned
normal and the associated right-hand rule for the contour.

The enclosed current is defined by the surface integral of conventional
current density:

$$
I_{\mathrm{enc}} = \int_S \mathbf{J} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\, dS
$$

where $S$ is any surface whose boundary is the Rogowski-coil contour,
$\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the assigned unit normal to that surface, and
$\mathbf{J}$ is the conventional electric current density.

This is an enclosed-current quantity, not the electrical current carried by
the Rogowski-coil sensor winding. In the Rogowski-coil principle, the
induced winding voltage is proportional to $dI_{\mathrm{enc}}/dt$;
$I_{\mathrm{enc}}$ is the current whose time variation drives that signal.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the net conventional current crosses the
oriented surface in the direction of the assigned normal.

sources.leaf_definition: Measured current inside the Rogowski coil contour. The normal direction to the Rogowski coil is defined by the order of points in the list of guiding centre positions. The current is positive when oriented in the same direction as the normal.
sources.parent_definition: Set of Rogowski coils. If some of the coils form a compound Rogowski sensor, they must be entered in contiguous order

NAMES.name: length_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
Physical extent of a poloidal magnetic-field probe coil measured along its
assigned local normal sensing axis, contributing to the coil’s magnetic-flux
response.
NAMES.long:
The length of a poloidal magnetic-field probe is the physical extent of its
sensing coil along the coil’s assigned local normal sensing axis. It
describes the coil geometry rather than the length of a signal lead or the
distance between mounting points.

This quantity applies to one poloidal magnetic-field probe coil as a whole.
It is distinct from the [area of the poloidal magnetic-field
probe](name:area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe), which describes the area
enclosed by one winding turn, and from the [turn count of the poloidal
magnetic-field probe](name:turn_count_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe),
which describes the number and orientation of complete turns.

The coil length, its enclosed per-turn area, and its winding-turn count
jointly characterize the probe’s magnetic-flux coupling and effective
sensing geometry. The length does not itself specify the coil area, winding
count, or magnetic-field orientation.

sources.leaf_definition: Length of the sensor along it's normal vector (n)
sources.parent_definition: Poloidal field probes

NAMES.name: length_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
Physical length of a toroidal magnetic-field probe is the non-negative axial
extent of the probe coil along its local normal sensing axis. It
characterizes sensor geometry and effective sensing volume; magnetic-flux
sensitivity is associated with enclosed coil area and winding turn count
rather than this length alone.
NAMES.long:
Physical length of a toroidal magnetic-field probe is the non-negative axial
extent of the probe coil along its local normal sensing axis. The probe coil
is oriented so that its normal senses the toroidal magnetic-field component
$B_\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is
major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; the
length refers to sensor geometry, not to an extent of the magnetic field.

Using projection onto the local sensing axis, the length is the span of the
active winding region along that axis:

$$
L_\phi = \max_{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{C}} (\mathbf{r}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}) - \min_{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{C}} (\mathbf{r}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}})
$$

where $L_\phi$ is the physical length of the toroidal magnetic-field probe,
$\mathcal{C}$ is the active winding region of the probe coil, $\mathbf{r}$
is the position vector of a point in that region, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is
the normalized local normal sensing-axis direction.

This quantity applies to one physical toroidal magnetic-field probe coil; it
is not summed, averaged, or otherwise aggregated over a set of probes. As a
scalar span, it is non-negative and is not a signed displacement along
$\hat{\mathbf{n}}$. It excludes the probe's [enclosed
area](name:area_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), winding turn count, body
diameter, lead length, installation position, and any path length around the
device.

The product of this length with the [enclosed
area](name:area_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe) characterizes the probe's
effective sensing volume. Magnetic-flux sensitivity of the pickup coil is
associated with enclosed area and winding turn count, while the [probe
voltage](name:voltage_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe) is the response
quantity produced by changing magnetic flux; the corresponding
[poloidal-probe length](name:length_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe) uses
the same projected-span convention for its probe orientation.

sources.leaf_definition: Length of the sensor along it's normal vector (n)
sources.parent_definition: Toroidal field probes

NAMES.name: poloidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
Signed poloidal tilt angle of a toroidal magnetic-field probe’s
sensitive-axis normal in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame,
measured clockwise from +R.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the signed orientation angle of the normal defining a
toroidal magnetic-field probe’s sensitive axis. It specifies the probe’s
tilt in the poloidal cross-section, rather than the spatial angle of the
probe center.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major
radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, let $n_R$ and
$n_Z$ denote the components of the probe’s oriented sensitive-axis normal
along the increasing-$R$ and increasing-$Z$ directions. The poloidal angle
$\theta_{\rm pol}$ is defined by:

$$
\theta_{\rm pol} = \operatorname{atan2}(-n_Z,n_R)
$$

where $\operatorname{atan2}$ is the two-argument arctangent that preserves
the quadrant of the projected normal.

The scope is one toroidal magnetic-field probe and its oriented
sensitive-axis normal. This is a geometric sensor-orientation quantity, not
the poloidal coordinate of the probe center, the direction of the measured
magnetic field, or a plasma flux-surface coordinate; it has no
plasma-population or region aggregation and is not summed over probes or
coil windings.

It is a probe-specific application of the parent [poloidal
angle](name:poloidal_angle_of_flux_surface): the parent defines the
geometric angular measure, while this quantity applies it to the probe’s
oriented normal. The complementary
[toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe)
describes the toroidal orientation of the same probe normal, whereas
[poloidal_angle_of_measurement_position](name:poloidal_angle_of_measurement_position)
describes the angular location of a measurement point.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the sensitive-axis normal points from the
outward radial direction toward decreasing $Z$ in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, following the clockwise direction in the
poloidal plane.

sources.leaf_definition: Angle of the sensor normal vector (vector parallel to the the axis of the coil, n on the diagram) with respect to horizontal plane (clockwise theta-like angle). Zero if sensor normal vector fully in the horizontal plane and oriented towards increasing major radius. Values in [0 , 2Pi]
sources.parent_definition: Toroidal field probes

NAMES.name: radial_outline_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of each contour point defining a fiber-optic current
sensor boundary in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial outline coordinate gives the major radius of each point on the
geometric boundary of a fiber-optic current sensor in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, phi, Z)$ frame.

The major radius is the perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry
axis. In a right-handed Cartesian basis $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ with
$\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$, it is defined by:

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}
$$

where $R$ is the major-radius coordinate, and $x$ and $y$ are Cartesian
coordinates perpendicular to the vertical axis.

The quantity is evaluated independently at each outline point and is
distinct from the signed vertical coordinate, represented by the
corresponding [vertical outline
coordinate](name:vertical_outline_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor). As a
radial distance, it is non-negative.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: FOCS outline

NAMES.name: resistance_of_shunt
NAMES.short:
Lumped ohmic resistance of the selected shunt resistor, relating its
terminal voltage to the current flowing through that shunt.
NAMES.long:
The shunt resistance is the lumped electrical opposition between the
terminals of the selected shunt resistor. It characterizes one shunt member
used to relate its terminal voltage to the current flowing through it.

For nonzero shunt current, the resistance is defined by

$$
R_{\mathrm{sh}} = \frac{V_{\mathrm{sh}}}{I_{\mathrm{sh}}}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{sh}}$ is the selected shunt resistance, $V_{\mathrm{sh}}$
is the terminal voltage represented by [voltage of
shunt](name:voltage_of_shunt), and $I_{\mathrm{sh}}$ is the current through
the selected shunt.

The quantity applies to the individual selected shunt and is a lumped
circuit property; it is not a material resistivity, the resistance of the
entire divertor or vessel structure, or the shunt terminal voltage itself.
The associated current can be inferred from the terminal voltage as
$I_{\mathrm{sh}} = V_{\mathrm{sh}} / R_{\mathrm{sh}}$, so the resistance and
[voltage of shunt](name:voltage_of_shunt) jointly define this
current-inference relationship.

sources.leaf_definition: Shunt resistance
sources.parent_definition: Set of shunt resistances through which currents in the divertor structure are measured. Shunts are modelled as piecewise straight line segments in the poloidal plane.

NAMES.name: stray_breakdown_magnetic_field
NAMES.short:
Residual magnetic-field strength at the plasma position during initiation,
produced by imperfect cancelation of external coil fields and capable of
inhibiting electron-avalanche breakdown.
NAMES.long:
This quantity denotes the residual magnetic-field contribution present at
the plasma position during plasma initiation. It arises when external coil
fields are not completely canceled and is relevant because residual field
can inhibit the electron avalanche required for breakdown.

It is the stray contribution to the [breakdown magnetic
field](name:breakdown_magnetic_field), rather than the complete field
describing the initiation state. The associated [stray breakdown
magnetic-field magnitude](name:stray_breakdown_magnetic_field_magnitude)
provides the Euclidean magnitude when a direction-independent measure is
required; this parent quantity does not by itself specify a field direction.

NAMES.name: stray_breakdown_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Magnitude of the residual magnetic field at the plasma position during
initiation, whose incomplete cancelation can inhibit electron-avalanche
breakdown.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the total strength of the residual magnetic-field
contribution present at the plasma position during plasma initiation. It is
derived from the vector quantity [stray breakdown magnetic
field](name:stray_breakdown_magnetic_field) by removing directional
information.

$$
B_{\mathrm{stray}} = \left|\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{stray}}\right| = \sqrt{B_R^2 + B_\phi^2 + B_Z^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{stray}}$ is the residual magnetic-field vector,
and $B_R$, $B_\phi$, and $B_Z$ are its components in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The magnitude includes all spatial components caused by imperfect
cancelation of external coil fields. It is distinct from any individual
directional component and does not encode field orientation or sign.

sources.leaf_definition: Data
sources.parent_definition: Stray magnetic field at plasma position

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
Signed azimuthal orientation angle of a poloidal magnetic-field probe’s
sensitive-axis normal in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed toroidal orientation of the sensitive-axis
normal of a poloidal magnetic-field probe coil. It measures the normal’s
departure from the poloidal plane through the orientation of its horizontal
projection.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the angle is defined by

$$
\alpha_{\mathrm{tor}} = \operatorname{atan2}(n_\phi,n_R), \qquad n_R=\mathbf{n}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{R}}, \quad n_\phi=\mathbf{n}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}
$$

where $\alpha_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal orientation angle,
$\mathbf{n}$ is the probe’s sensitive-axis unit normal, $n_R$ and $n_\phi$
are its cylindrical radial and toroidal components, and $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$
and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ are the radial and toroidal unit vectors. Here
$R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height;
$\operatorname{atan2}$ returns the signed angle from the positive radial
direction to the horizontal projection of $\mathbf{n}$.

The quantity applies to the geometric orientation of each poloidal
magnetic-field probe coil. It is not the local plasma magnetic field, a
field component, or an angle averaged over probes, turns, or field samples.
The angle determines how the probe’s sensitive direction is related to the
local magnetic-field vector and therefore how the measured component is
projected. The corresponding toroidal orientation for a toroidal probe is
defined by
[toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe),
while its independent poloidal tilt is represented by
[poloidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:poloidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when rotation from the positive radial direction
toward the horizontal projection of the sensitive-axis normal is toward
increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Angle of the projection of the sensor normal vector (n) in the horizontal plane with the increasing R direction (i.e. grad(R)) (angle is counter-clockwise from above). Values should be taken modulo pi with values within (-pi/2,pi/2]. Zero if projected sensor normal is parallel to grad(R), pi/2 if it is parallel to grad(phi).
sources.parent_definition: Poloidal field probes

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
The toroidal angle of a toroidal magnetic-field probe is the signed
azimuthal orientation of the probe sensitive-axis normal projected onto the
horizontal plane, measured from +R toward increasing φ in the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. Opposite projected normals are folded into the
same principal orientation.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal angle of a toroidal magnetic-field probe is the signed
azimuthal orientation of the probe sensitive-axis normal after projection
onto the horizontal plane spanned by $\hat R$ and $\hat\phi$ in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius,
$\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. Its zero direction is
the outward radial direction, and the projected normal is treated as an
orientation axis rather than a directed vector.

The angle is defined by the two-argument arctangent of the horizontal normal
components, folded modulo $\pi$ into the principal interval $(-\pi/2,
\pi/2]$:

$$
\alpha_\phi = \mathcal{F}_{(-\pi/2,\pi/2]}\!\left(\operatorname{atan2}(n_\phi,n_R)\right)
$$

where $\alpha_\phi$ is this toroidal angle, $n_R$ and $n_\phi$ are the
radial and toroidal scalar components of the normalized probe sensitive-axis
normal vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and
$\mathcal{F}_{(-\pi/2,\pi/2]}(\beta)$ denotes the representative of an angle
$\beta$ after adding an integer multiple of $\pi$ that lies in $(-\pi/2,
\pi/2]$.

This quantity applies only to toroidal magnetic-field probes and is defined
separately for each probe. It describes sensor orientation, not the
[toroidal angle](name:toroidal_angle) that locates a point and not the probe
position; no aggregation over multiple probes is implied.

With the modulo-$\pi$ folding, projections parallel or antiparallel to
$+\hat R$ have $\alpha_\phi=0$, and projections parallel or antiparallel to
$+\hat\phi$ have the principal value $\alpha_\phi=\pi/2$. Together with the
[poloidal angle of a toroidal magnetic-field
probe](name:poloidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), it specifies
the orientation of the same sensitive-axis normal; it is the
toroidal-field-probe-specific counterpart of the [toroidal angle of a
magnetic-field probe](name:toroidal_angle_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the horizontal orientation is tilted from the
radial basis line toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Angle of the projection of the sensor normal vector (n) in the horizontal plane with the increasing R direction (i.e. grad(R)) (angle is counter-clockwise from above). Values should be taken modulo pi with values within (-pi/2,pi/2]. Zero if projected sensor normal is parallel to grad(R), pi/2 if it is parallel to grad(phi).
sources.parent_definition: Toroidal field probes

NAMES.name: turn_count_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
Signed count of complete winding turns in a poloidal magnetic-field probe
coil, fixing the orientation and magnitude of its magnetic-flux linkage.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the signed number of complete winding turns in a poloidal
magnetic-field probe coil. Its magnitude counts the turns, while its sign
records the winding orientation used to define magnetic-flux linkage.

For turns with a common flux orientation, the total flux linkage is

$$
\Lambda = N\Phi_1
$$

where $\Lambda$ is the total magnetic flux linkage of the coil, $N$ is the
signed winding-turn count, and $\Phi_1$ is the magnetic flux through one
turn using the probe's reference orientation.

This quantity applies to one physical poloidal magnetic-field probe coil and
aggregates all of its complete winding turns, assigning one signed
contribution to each turn. It is a literal coil-turn count, not the local
poloidal magnetic-field value and not the geometric area enclosed by a turn.

For this probe, the literal winding count provides the physical
specialization of the equivalent coupling count represented by
[effective_turn_count_of_passive_loop](name:effective_turn_count_of_passive_loop);
unlike that broader quantity, it is not a homogenized or equivalent
passive-loop count that may be fractional. Together with the
[area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe),
it determines the probe's per-turn magnetic-flux coupling. The corresponding
toroidal-coil quantity is
[turn_count_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:turn_count_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe).

sources.leaf_definition: Turns in the coil, including sign
sources.parent_definition: Poloidal field probes

NAMES.name: turn_count_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
Signed number of complete winding turns in a toroidal magnetic-field probe
coil, with orientation referenced to the positive toroidal direction.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed number of complete winding turns in a toroidal
magnetic-field probe coil. It represents the coil's oriented electromagnetic
coupling to the toroidal magnetic-field component, rather than a
magnetic-field value.

The scope is one toroidal magnetic-field probe coil. The count refers to its
physical complete windings, includes their common orientation, and does not
aggregate turns over multiple probes or channels. It excludes the coil's
enclosed area, length, induced voltage, and any calibration factor.

Reversing the winding orientation reverses the sign. Together with the [area
of the toroidal magnetic-field
probe](name:area_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), this count sets the
ideal flux-linkage sensitivity to the toroidal magnetic field. It is the
literal winding-count specialization related to the [effective turn count of
a passive loop](name:effective_turn_count_of_passive_loop), which can
represent equivalent or homogenized windings and may therefore differ from a
complete-turn count. The corresponding poloidal-orientation quantity is the
[turn count of a poloidal magnetic-field
probe](name:turn_count_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe).

The orientation is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$
frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is
vertical height.

sources.leaf_definition: Turns in the coil, including sign
sources.parent_definition: Toroidal field probes

NAMES.name: turns_per_metre_of_rogowski_coil
NAMES.short:
Linear winding density of a Rogowski coil, specifying the number of turns in
a single winding layer per unit coil length.
NAMES.long:
The turns-per-length quantity specifies the linear winding density of a
Rogowski coil. For a multilayer winding, it refers to one winding layer
rather than the combined count of all layers.

The winding density is defined by

$$
n_t = \frac{N_\ell}{\ell}
$$

where $n_t$ is the Rogowski-coil turns density, $N_\ell$ is the number of
complete winding turns in one layer over the selected winding length, and
$\ell$ is that winding length.

This quantity applies to the physical winding of the Rogowski coil and is a
linear density, not a discrete total turn count. It excludes the effective
cross-sectional area, which is a separate geometric quantity described by
the [area of the Rogowski coil](name:area_of_rogowski_coil), and it does not
represent the signed winding current described by the [current of the
Rogowski coil](name:current_of_rogowski_coil). The winding density and
effective cross-sectional area together determine the coil's electromagnetic
coupling and therefore its current-sensing sensitivity.

sources.leaf_definition: Number of turns per unit length. In case of multiple layers, turns are counted for a single layer
sources.parent_definition: Set of Rogowski coils. If some of the coils form a compound Rogowski sensor, they must be entered in contiguous order

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_flux_loop
NAMES.short:
Vertical Z coordinate of a position point associated with one flux loop in
the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the vertical coordinate $Z$ of a position point associated
with one flux loop. It locates that point along the vertical direction in
the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Here $Z$ denotes vertical height, $R$ denotes major radius from the symmetry
axis, and $\phi$ denotes toroidal angle. The value applies to an individual
position point of a single flux loop; it is not a loop-area quantity,
magnetic flux, voltage, or an aggregate over turns, points, or multiple
loops. No population or plasma-region restriction is implied.

Together with the corresponding radial and toroidal position coordinates,
this coordinate locates the flux-loop point in space. It is the
flux-loop-specific counterpart of the [vertical coordinate of a measurement
position](name:vertical_coordinate_of_measurement_position), which applies
the same geometric concept to a generic measurement location.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the flux-loop position lies in the +Z
direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Height
sources.parent_definition: List of (R,Z,phi) points defining the position of the loop (see data structure documentation FLUXLOOPposition.pdf). Leave empty if ../type/index = 6 (differential loop)

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
Vertical position of the geometric center of a poloidal magnetic-field
probe, expressed as its signed Z coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical
(R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical position of the geometric center of a poloidal magnetic-field
probe is the signed height coordinate of the probe center in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. It locates the probe center
along the vertical direction and does not define the orientation of the
probe's sensitive axis or the magnetic-field component measured by the
probe.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major
radius from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ the toroidal angle, and $Z$
the vertical coordinate, the probe-center coordinate is defined by

$$
Z_{\mathrm{probe}} = \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{probe}} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{probe}}$ is the vertical coordinate of the poloidal
magnetic-field probe center, $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{probe}}$ is the position
vector of that geometric center relative to the coordinate origin, and
$\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector.

This quantity applies to the geometric center of a poloidal magnetic-field
probe as a physical object. For a probe with finite extent, it refers to the
center position rather than to the probe size, winding distribution, support
structure, or any spatial average of the measured magnetic field.

Together with the [radial coordinate of a poloidal magnetic-field
probe](name:radial_coordinate_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe), it
specifies the probe-center position in the $(R,Z)$ poloidal cross-section at
a given toroidal angle. The same signed-coordinate concept is used for other
magnetic diagnostic objects, such as the [vertical coordinate of a toroidal
magnetic-field
probe](name:vertical_coordinate_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), the
[vertical coordinate of a flux loop](name:vertical_coordinate_of_flux_loop),
and the [vertical coordinate of a Rogowski
coil](name:vertical_coordinate_of_rogowski_coil), but those names apply to
different objects.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the probe-center position lies above the
machine midplane in the $+Z$ direction.

sources.leaf_definition: Height
sources.parent_definition: R, Z, Phi position of the coil centre

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_rogowski_coil
NAMES.short:
Vertical Z coordinate of the Rogowski coil position in the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, measured along the machine symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
The vertical Z coordinate locates the Rogowski coil along the machine
symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where
$Z$ measures height above the $Z = 0$ reference plane. Together with the
major radius given by
[radial_coordinate_of_rogowski_coil](name:radial_coordinate_of_rogowski_coil),
it fully specifies the coil's position in a poloidal cross-section, which is
required to associate the enclosed-current measurement with the correct
plasma geometry and to provide geometric inputs for magnetic equilibrium
reconstruction.

This coordinate is a fixed geometric parameter established from engineering
metrology of the installed coil. The same vertical-coordinate convention is
applied to
[vertical_coordinate_of_flux_loop](name:vertical_coordinate_of_flux_loop)
and vertical_coordinate_of_coil_conductor across the magnetic diagnostics
family.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the coil is located above the $Z = 0$
reference plane, in the upward direction along the machine symmetry axis.

sources.leaf_definition: Height
sources.parent_definition: List of (R,Z,phi) points defining the position of the coil guiding centre. Values defining a single segment must be entered in contiguous order

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
Vertical position of the geometric center of a toroidal magnetic-field probe
coil, expressed as the signed Z coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical
(R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate identifies the geometric center of an individual
toroidal magnetic-field probe coil in the right-handed cylindrical basis
$(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$, with coordinates $(R,\phi,Z)$. It locates
the coil and does not represent the magnetic field sensed by the probe.

The coordinate is the projection of the center position onto the vertical
basis direction:

$$
Z_{\mathrm{probe}} = \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{center}} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{probe}}$ is the probe-center vertical coordinate,
$\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{center}}$ is the position vector from the
cylindrical-frame origin to the geometric center of the coil, and $\hat{Z}$
is the vertical unit vector. Here $R$ denotes major radius, $\phi$ denotes
toroidal angle, and $Z$ denotes vertical coordinate.

The quantity applies to one toroidal magnetic-field probe coil center. It is
not summed, averaged, or weighted over windings, probes, or a spatial
region. It excludes the probe's sensitive-axis orientation and the local
magnetic-field value, and is distinct from the corresponding position
coordinate for a [poloidal magnetic-field
probe](name:vertical_coordinate_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe).

As the $Z$ component of the coil-center position, this coordinate
complements the radial and toroidal position coordinates in locating the
probe within the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the probe-coil center lies in the $+Z$
direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Height
sources.parent_definition: R, Z, Phi position of the coil centre

NAMES.name: vertical_outline_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor
NAMES.short:
Signed vertical Z coordinate of a contour point defining the geometric
boundary of a fiber-optic current sensor in the right-handed cylindrical (R,
φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical outline coordinate is the signed height of a point on the
geometric boundary of a fiber-optic current sensor, represented in a
poloidal cross-section. It describes the sensor boundary geometry, not the
sensed current or the optical path.

$$
Z = \mathbf{r} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{r}$ is the point position relative to the coordinate origin
and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector of the right-handed cylindrical
$(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The quantity is geometrically analogous to the contour
coordinate used for [vertical outline of wall
material](name:vertical_outline_of_plasma_facing_component), but applies to
the fiber-optic current sensor boundary.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the outline point lies in the direction of
increasing vertical coordinate $Z$.

sources.leaf_definition: Height
sources.parent_definition: FOCS outline

NAMES.name: voltage_of_flux_loop
NAMES.short:
Terminal voltage of a flux loop is the signed, unintegrated electrical
potential difference at the loop terminals. It is induced by the time
variation of the oriented magnetic flux linked by the loop and is related to
that flux by Faraday's law.
NAMES.long:
Terminal voltage of a flux loop is the signed, unintegrated electrical
potential difference between the designated terminals of a flux loop. It
represents the electromotive response of the loop to variation of the
oriented magnetic flux linked by its conducting contour.

The defining relation to the loop flux is Faraday's law for the oriented
loop contour:

$$
V_\mathrm{loop}(t) = -\frac{d\Phi_\mathrm{loop}(t)}{dt}
$$

where $V_\mathrm{loop}$ is the terminal voltage of the flux loop, $t$ is
time, and $\Phi_\mathrm{loop}$ is the [poloidal magnetic flux of the flux
loop](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_of_flux_loop) associated with the oriented
surface bounded by the loop; the contour orientation and surface normal are
related by the right-hand rule.

The quantity applies to an individual flux loop and to the terminal pair
with its specified polarity; it is not aggregated over multiple flux loops.
It is the raw terminal voltage, not the time-integrated flux, not the loop's
[area](name:area_of_flux_loop), and not an equilibrium-reconstructed
magnetic flux.

Time integration gives the linked flux up to an integration constant:
$\Phi_\mathrm{loop}(t)-\Phi_\mathrm{loop}(t_0) = -\int_{t_0}^{t}
V_\mathrm{loop}(t')\,dt'$, where $t_0$ is a reference time and $t'$ is the
integration time variable. The [area of the flux
loop](name:area_of_flux_loop) defines the geometric aperture entering the
flux linkage but is not itself part of the terminal-voltage quantity.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the oriented magnetic flux linked by the loop
decreases with time for the specified terminal polarity and loop
orientation.

sources.leaf_definition: Measured voltage between the loop terminals
sources.parent_definition: Flux loops; partial flux loops can be described. In case of differential loops, the geometry of differential flux loops is stored in the flux_loop indices of the primitive loops. Signals may be stored on the primitive loop indices but this is optional if the index of the primitive loop is referenced by a differential loop index

NAMES.name: voltage_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
Terminal voltage at a poloidal magnetic-field probe is the inductive voltage
at the coil terminals caused by time variation of the local poloidal
magnetic-field component in the R-Z plane of the right-handed cylindrical
(R, φ, Z) frame threading the probe windings.
NAMES.long:
Terminal voltage at a poloidal magnetic-field probe is the signed
coil-terminal electromotive force associated with the probe winding that
senses the local poloidal magnetic field. The sensed field component lies in
the $R$-$Z$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame and
is projected along the probe sensitive-axis normal.

For a probe with algebraic turn count $N$ and geometric per-turn area $A$,
Faraday's law relates the terminal voltage to the local poloidal field
component $B_p$ as:

$$
V = -N A \frac{dB_p}{dt}
$$

where $V$ is the terminal voltage at the coil terminals, $B_p$ is the local
poloidal magnetic-field component along the positive sensitive-axis normal,
$N$ is the algebraic turn count including winding direction, $A$ is the
[area of poloidal magnetic-field
probe](name:area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe), and $t$ is time.

The quantity applies to one poloidal-field probe coil and is not aggregated
over multiple probes. Its locus is specified by the major radius of poloidal
magnetic-field probe, [toroidal angle of poloidal magnetic-field
probe](name:toroidal_angle_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe), and poloidal
angle of poloidal magnetic-field probe; these position quantities identify
where the local field component is sampled and are not themselves voltages.

This quantity is distinct from the derived local poloidal magnetic field. It
is the poloidal-field-probe counterpart of [voltage of toroidal
magnetic-field probe](name:voltage_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), for a
coil oriented to sense the toroidal field, and is distinct from [voltage of
flux loop](name:voltage_of_flux_loop), which corresponds to a loop enclosing
magnetic flux rather than a local magnetic-field probe winding.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the poloidal magnetic flux threading the coil
in the direction of the probe's positive sensitive-axis normal is decreasing
with time.

sources.leaf_definition: Voltage on the coil terminals
sources.parent_definition: Poloidal field probes

NAMES.name: voltage_of_shunt
NAMES.short:
Signed terminal-potential difference across a resistive shunt, providing the
voltage used with its resistance to determine current in an associated
structure segment.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed electrical potential difference between the two
terminals of a shunt resistor. It applies to the shunt element associated
with a divertor or vessel structure segment, rather than to an individual
terminal potential or a voltage across another circuit element.

The defining terminal difference is

$$
V_{\mathrm{shunt}} = V_{\mathrm{first}} - V_{\mathrm{second}}
$$

where $V_{\mathrm{shunt}}$ is the shunt terminal voltage,
$V_{\mathrm{first}}$ is the electric potential of the first terminal, and
$V_{\mathrm{second}}$ is the electric potential of the second terminal.

The quantity is a direct terminal difference, with no spatial averaging or
charge-state aggregation. For an ohmic shunt, the associated
structure-segment current $I_{\mathrm{shunt}}$ is related to this voltage
and the [resistance of the shunt](name:resistance_of_shunt),
$R_{\mathrm{shunt}}$, by $I_{\mathrm{shunt}} =
V_{\mathrm{shunt}}/R_{\mathrm{shunt}}$. It does not itself represent the
current or the shunt resistance.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the electric potential of the first shunt
terminal exceeds that of the second shunt terminal.

sources.leaf_definition: Voltage on the shunt terminals (Vfirst_point-Vsecond_point)
sources.parent_definition: Set of shunt resistances through which currents in the divertor structure are measured. Shunts are modelled as piecewise straight line segments in the poloidal plane.

NAMES.name: voltage_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
Terminal voltage induced at the terminals of a toroidal magnetic-field probe
coil by time variation of the local toroidal magnetic-field component in the
right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame threading the coil windings.
NAMES.long:
Terminal voltage induced at the terminals of a toroidal magnetic-field probe
coil is the signed electric potential difference produced by Faraday
induction in a coil sensitive to the toroidal magnetic-field component. The
toroidal component is $B_\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi,
Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is
vertical height.

For fixed probe geometry, the defining Faraday-law relation is

$$
V_\phi(t) = -\frac{d\Lambda_\phi(t)}{dt}
$$

where $V_\phi$ is the terminal voltage, $\Lambda_\phi$ is the signed
magnetic-flux linkage of the toroidal magnetic-field probe, and $t$ is time.

This quantity applies to one toroidal magnetic-field probe coil and to the
local region whose magnetic flux threads that coil. It is not an aggregate
over multiple probes, and it excludes the integrated or calibrated local
toroidal magnetic-field component derived from the raw terminal voltage.

For a uniform local-field approximation, $\Lambda_\phi = N_\phi A_\phi
B_\phi$, where $N_\phi$ is the signed [turn count of the toroidal
magnetic-field probe](name:turn_count_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe) and
$A_\phi$ is the effective sensitive area set by the probe geometry,
including the [length of the toroidal magnetic-field
probe](name:length_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe). Relative to a
reference time $t_0$, the corresponding calibrated field change satisfies
$B_\phi(t)-B_\phi(t_0) = -(N_\phi A_\phi)^{-1}\int_{t_0}^{t}
V_\phi(t')\,dt'$ when the same fixed sensitivity applies. The corresponding
terminal-voltage quantity for a probe sensitive to the poloidal
magnetic-field component is [voltage of poloidal magnetic-field
probe](name:voltage_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the signed magnetic-flux linkage of the
toroidal magnetic-field probe is decreasing in time.

sources.leaf_definition: Voltage on the coil terminals
sources.parent_definition: Toroidal field probes

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_flux_loop
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of each geometric point defining a flux-loop
position, measured as perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis
in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the non-negative major-radius coordinate $R$ of each
geometric point defining a flux-loop position. In the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $R$ is the distance from the toroidal
symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For horizontal Cartesian coordinates $X$ and $Y$ in a right-handed Cartesian
$(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis whose vertical direction coincides with
cylindrical $\hat{Z}$, the coordinate is defined by:

$$
R = \sqrt{X^2 + Y^2}
$$

where $X$ and $Y$ are the point's Cartesian coordinates along $\hat{x}$ and
$\hat{y}$, and $R$ is its major-radius coordinate.

The quantity applies separately to every geometric point defining one
flux-loop position, including a partial loop; it is not a loop-wide average,
centroid, or other aggregation of those points. It is a geometric coordinate
only and does not represent the loop's other position coordinates, linked
magnetic flux, induced voltage, or [effective flux-loop
area](name:area_of_flux_loop).

This quantity is the flux-loop-specific specialization of the general
[radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate): it retains the same
major-radius definition while identifying the point as part of flux-loop
geometry. The complete point position requires its corresponding toroidal
and vertical coordinates.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: List of (R,Z,phi) points defining the position of the loop (see data structure documentation FLUXLOOPposition.pdf). Leave empty if ../type/index = 6 (differential loop)

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate locating the center of a poloidal magnetic-field
probe in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of a poloidal magnetic-field probe is the major-radius
location of the probe center relative to the toroidal symmetry axis,
expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, c6, Z)$ frame.

The coordinate is defined by the magnitude of the displacement perpendicular
to the toroidal symmetry axis:

$$
R = \left|\mathbf{r}_{\perp}\right|
$$

where $R$ is the major-radius coordinate and $\mathbf{r}_{\perp}$ is the
displacement from the toroidal symmetry axis within the plane perpendicular
to that axis.

This quantity applies specifically to the geometric center of one poloidal
magnetic-field probe and is not an aggregate over multiple probes or a
coordinate of the measured magnetic field. It identifies the radial location
only; the corresponding vertical location is given by the [vertical
coordinate of the poloidal magnetic-field
probe](name:vertical_coordinate_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe).

It is the probe-specific specialization of the general [radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate), obtained by evaluating that coordinate
at the probe center.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: R, Z, Phi position of the coil centre

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_rogowski_coil
NAMES.short:
Radial coordinate of a Rogowski coil position, equal to the major-radius
coordinate of the coil's designated geometric point in the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of a Rogowski coil position is the major-radius
coordinate of the designated geometric point representing the coil position.
It is the non-negative perpendicular distance of that point from the
toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame,
where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical
height.

Using any point on the toroidal symmetry axis as reference, the coordinate
is defined by the transverse projection of the coil-position vector relative
to that axis:

$$
R_{\mathrm{coil}} = \left\| (\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{coil}} - \mathbf{o}_{\mathcal{A}}) - \left[(\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{coil}} - \mathbf{o}_{\mathcal{A}}) \cdot \hat{Z}\right]\hat{Z} \right\|
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{coil}}$ is the radial coordinate of the Rogowski coil
position, $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{coil}}$ is the position vector of the
designated geometric point, $\mathbf{o}_{\mathcal{A}}$ is any position
vector on the toroidal symmetry axis $\mathcal{A}$, $\hat{Z}$ is the
vertical unit vector along that axis, and $\|\cdot\|$ denotes the Euclidean
norm.

This quantity applies to the single designated geometric point used to
locate the Rogowski coil. It is not an average, integral, or other
aggregation over the winding path, aperture, conductor cross-section, or
physical extent of the coil.

This coordinate is the radial member of the Rogowski-coil position
coordinates and is distinct from the [vertical coordinate of the Rogowski
coil](name:vertical_coordinate_of_rogowski_coil) and any toroidal angular
coordinate of the same point. It is also distinct from the [area of the
Rogowski coil](name:area_of_rogowski_coil), the [current of the Rogowski
coil](name:current_of_rogowski_coil), coil orientation, and winding
geometry; those quantities do not change the definition of
$R_{\mathrm{coil}}$. As a named instance of [radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate), it is invariant under changes of
toroidal angle at fixed major radius.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: List of (R,Z,phi) points defining the position of the coil guiding centre. Values defining a single segment must be entered in contiguous order

NAMES.name: alpha_angle_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short:
Signed inclination of the first axis of an oblique parallelogram
cross-section of an axisymmetric ferritic element, measured
counter-clockwise from the outward radial direction.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the alpha orientation of the first axis of an oblique,
parallelogram-shaped cross-section belonging to a single axisymmetric
ferritic element. It specifies the primary orientation of that element in
the poloidal plane.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the signed inclination
is defined by

$$
\alpha = \operatorname{atan2}(\mathbf{a}_1 \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}},\, \mathbf{a}_1 \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}})
$$

where $\alpha$ is the alpha inclination angle, $\mathbf{a}_1$ is the
oriented unit vector along the first axis of the parallelogram
cross-section, $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the outward radial unit vector,
$\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the vertical unit vector, and $\operatorname{atan2}$
is the signed two-argument arctangent.

The quantity applies to one ferritic element and is not an aggregate over
multiple elements. It describes the first axis only; it is distinct from the
[tilt angle of the ferritic element](name:tilt_angle_of_ferritic_element),
which describes the inclination of the second side. Together, the alpha and
tilt angles specify the orientations of the two oblique sides of the
parallelogram cross-section.

The same alpha-orientation concept is used for other oblique component
cross-sections, including an [alpha angle of an iron core
segment](name:alpha_angle_of_iron_core_segment).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the first axis tilts from the outward radial
direction toward increasing $Z$, counter-clockwise in the poloidal $(R,Z)$
plane.

sources.leaf_definition: Inclination of first angle measured counter-clockwise from horizontal outwardly directed radial vector (grad R).
sources.parent_definition: Parallelogram description of the element

NAMES.name: alpha_angle_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short:
Signed inclination of the alpha-side edge of an iron core segment
cross-section, measured from the outward major-radius direction toward
increasing vertical height.
NAMES.long:
The alpha angle is the signed orientation of the designated alpha-side edge
of an iron core segment in the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It identifies the alpha-side orientation
and is independent of the edge length.

For an oriented alpha-side vector with signed radial and vertical components
$\Delta R$ and $\Delta Z$, the angle is defined by

$$
\alpha = \operatorname{atan2}(\Delta Z,\Delta R)
$$

where $\alpha$ is the alpha angle, $\Delta R$ is the component along the
outward major-radius direction, and $\Delta Z$ is the component along the
vertical direction. This quantity is the alpha-side specialization of the
general iron core segment orientation angle, not a length or cross-sectional
dimension.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the oriented alpha-side vector is inclined
from the outward $+R$ direction toward increasing $Z$.

sources.leaf_definition: Inclination of first angle measured counter-clockwise from horizontal outwardly directed radial vector (grad R).
sources.parent_definition: Parallelogram description of the element

NAMES.name: alpha_angle_of_passive_loop_element
NAMES.short:
Signed inclination of the first axis of an oblique passive conductor
loop-element cross-section, measured counterclockwise from the outward
radial direction in the poloidal plane.
NAMES.long:
The alpha angle is the signed inclination of the first axis of an oblique,
trapezoidal or parallelogram-shaped cross-section of one passive conductor
loop element. It specifies the orientation of that element’s cross-sectional
geometry in the poloidal plane.

The angle is defined from the directed first-axis vector:

$$
\alpha = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left(\mathbf{a}_1 \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}},\,\mathbf{a}_1 \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}}\right)
$$

where $\alpha$ is the alpha inclination angle, $\mathbf{a}_1$ is the
directed first axis of the cross-section, $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the outward
radial unit vector, $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the upward vertical unit vector,
and $\operatorname{atan2}$ returns the signed angle from the radial
component to the vertical component. These directions are defined in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius,
$\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies independently to each passive loop element and to its
own oblique cross-section; it is not an aggregate angle for a complete
passive loop or a collection of elements. It describes the first
cross-sectional axis only, not the transverse dimensions of the element and
not the overall loop reference-axis inclination represented by the [tilt
angle of the passive loop](name:tilt_angle_of_passive_loop). The alpha angle
supplies orientation information for interpreting the element’s other
cross-sectional geometry, but does not determine those dimensions.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the first axis rotates counterclockwise from
the outward radial direction toward the positive vertical direction in the
poloidal plane.

sources.leaf_definition: Inclination of first angle measured counter-clockwise from horizontal outwardly directed radial vector (grad R).
sources.parent_definition: Parallelogram description of the element

NAMES.name: area_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short:
Non-negative full geometric area of the conducting material in one
correction-coil cross-section, taken perpendicular to the local conductor
path and treated as constant along the coil length.
NAMES.long:
Non-negative full geometric area of the conducting material in one
correction-coil cross-section is the cross-sectional measure of the
electrical conductor on a plane normal to the local conductor path. It is a
property of one correction-coil conductor element, not a sum over separate
turns or parallel conductor elements.

The area includes the conducting material in that cross-section and excludes
voids, insulation, coolant channels, nonconducting supports, and any
winding-pack or coil-footprint area outside the conductor material. For
hollow or compound conductors, only regions that are part of the electrical
conductor are included.

It is distinct from radius_of_correction_coil,
[inner_radius_of_correction_coil](name:inner_radius_of_correction_coil), and
[width_of_correction_coil](name:width_of_correction_coil), which specify
particular dimensions of a cross-section; different cross-sectional shapes
can have the same area.

sources.leaf_definition: Area of the conductor cross-section, derived from the above geometric data
sources.parent_definition: The cross-section perpendicular to the conductor contour is described by a series of contour points, given by their relative position with respect to the start point of each element. If the size of this array of structure is equal to 1, then the cross-section is given only for the first element and translated along the conductor elements. Otherwise, it's given explictly for each element, allowing to describe changes of the cross section shape

NAMES.name: area_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short:
Area of a passive loop is the non-negative cross-sectional area of
conducting material in a passive loop element, taken on a section normal to
the local current path. It excludes the aperture enclosed by the loop.
NAMES.long:
Area of a passive loop is the non-negative cross-sectional area of the solid
conducting material of a passive conducting loop element, evaluated on a
surface normal to the local current path. It is a material cross-section of
the conductor, not the aperture enclosed by the loop or the area swept out
by the loop centerline.

The general geometric definition is the area of the conducting region
$\mathcal{S}$ in that normal cross-section:

$$
A = \int_{\mathcal{S}} dS
$$

where $A$ is the passive-loop conductor area, $\mathcal{S}$ is the subset of
the section occupied by conducting material, and $dS$ is the scalar
surface-area element.

For an annular cross-section, this definition gives $A = \pi(r_o^2-r_i^2)$,
where $r_i$ and $r_o$ are the [inner](name:inner_radius_of_passive_loop) and
[outer](name:outer_radius_of_passive_loop) radii measured from the annulus
center to the conducting boundaries. For a non-annular cross-section,
$\mathcal{S}$ is the bounded conducting region defined by the conductor
geometry; parameters such as thickness, width, or height describe that
boundary but are not themselves the area.

sources.leaf_definition: Cross-sectional areas of the element
sources.parent_definition: Each loop is comprised of a number of cross-section elements described  individually

NAMES.name: area_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short:
Non-negative full geometric area of the conducting cross section of one
poloidal-field-coil element in a poloidal plane at fixed toroidal angle φ of
the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z
is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
Non-negative full geometric area of the conducting cross section of one
poloidal-field-coil element is the surface measure of the conductor region
enclosed by that element boundary. It is defined in a poloidal plane at
fixed toroidal angle $\phi$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$
frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is
vertical height.

For an arbitrary conductor cross-section, the area is the integral of the
differential surface measure over the conductor region $\mathcal{S}$:

$$
A = \int_{\mathcal{S}} dS
$$

where $A$ is the area of the poloidal-field-coil element, $\mathcal{S}$ is
the conductor region in the poloidal plane, and $dS$ is the differential
surface measure on that plane.

The quantity is per coil element, not a sum over multiple elements or over a
complete coil. For a rectangular cross-section aligned with the $R$ and $Z$
directions of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $A = W H$,
where $W$ is
[width_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:width_of_poloidal_field_coil) and $H$ is
[height_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil);
[thickness_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:thickness_of_poloidal_field_coil) is
a separate geometric extent and is not the radial width in this
relationship. For an annular cross-section, $A =
\pi(r_\mathrm{out}^2-r_\mathrm{in}^2)$, where $r_\mathrm{out}$ is
[outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil)
and $r_\mathrm{in}$ is
[inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil).
An insulation envelope, winding-pack envelope, or effective conducting area
is a distinct quantity unless it is defined by the same boundary as
$\mathcal{S}$.

sources.leaf_definition: Cross-sectional areas of the element
sources.parent_definition: Each PF coil is comprised of a number of cross-section elements described  individually and connected serially

NAMES.name: area_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short:
Non-negative geometric area of the conducting material within a
toroidal-field-coil conductor’s cross-sectional boundary, measured normal to
its local centerline.
NAMES.long:
The area of a toroidal-field-coil conductor is the geometric area occupied
by conducting material in a cross-section normal to the conductor’s local
centerline. It excludes any void, bore, insulation, or surrounding aperture.

The area is defined by

$$
A_{\mathrm{cond}} = \iint_{S_{\mathrm{cond}}} dS
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{cond}}$ is the conductor cross-sectional area,
$S_{\mathrm{cond}}$ is the region enclosed by the conductor boundary, and
$dS$ is its differential area element.

This quantity complements the conductor dimensions represented by the [width
of the toroidal field coil](name:width_of_toroidal_field_coil) and [height
of the toroidal field coil](name:height_of_toroidal_field_coil); it is not
the area enclosed by a winding or loop.

sources.leaf_definition: Area of the conductor cross-section, derived from the above geometric data
sources.parent_definition: The cross-section perpendicular to the conductor contour is described by a series of contour points, given by their relative position with respect to the start point of each element. If the size of this array of structure is equal to 1, then the cross-section is given only for the first element and translated along the conductor elements. Otherwise, it's given explictly for each element, allowing to describe changes of the cross section shape

NAMES.name: binormal_coordinate_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short:
Signed displacement of a correction-coil conductor outline vertex along the
local Frenet–Serret binormal, measured from the conductor centerline.
NAMES.long:
The binormal coordinate specifies the signed position of a correction-coil
conductor cross-section outline vertex along the local Frenet–Serret
binormal direction. Together with the [normal coordinate of the correction
coil](name:normal_coordinate_of_correction_coil), it defines the vertex
position in the cross-sectional plane.

For vertex position $\mathbf{r}_v$ and corresponding centerline position
$\mathbf{r}_c$, the coordinate is

$$
b_v = (\mathbf{r}_v - \mathbf{r}_c) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}
$$

where $b_v$ is the binormal coordinate in m, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the local
unit binormal, and $\mathbf{r}_v$ and $\mathbf{r}_c$ are positions in m. The
local Frenet–Serret triad is oriented so that $\hat{\mathbf{b}} =
\hat{\mathbf{t}} \times \hat{\mathbf{n}}$, with $\hat{\mathbf{t}}$ the
tangent and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ the normal unit vector. This coordinate is a
signed vertex displacement, not the full conductor cross-section height
represented by the [height of the correction
coil](name:height_of_correction_coil).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the vertex displacement from the conductor
centerline points in the direction of the local unit binormal
$\hat{\mathbf{b}}$.

sources.leaf_definition: Coordinates along the binormal axis
sources.parent_definition: Polygonal outline of the cross section in the (normal, binormal) coordinate system. Do NOT repeat the first point.

NAMES.name: binormal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short:
Signed displacement of each toroidal-field-coil conductor cross-section
outline vertex along the local Frenet–Serret binormal from the conductor
centerline.
NAMES.long:
The binormal coordinate specifies the signed local displacement of a
toroidal-field-coil conductor cross-section outline vertex from the
conductor centerline in the direction perpendicular to both the local
tangent and normal.

$$
b_v = (\mathbf{r}_v-\mathbf{r}_c)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}}
$$

where $b_v$ is the binormal coordinate, $\mathbf{r}_v$ is the vertex
position in m, $\mathbf{r}_c$ is the corresponding centerline position in m,
and $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the unit binormal of the local Frenet–Serret
frame. Together with the [normal coordinate of the toroidal field
coil](name:normal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil), it defines the
conductor cross-section outline in the local normal–binormal plane; it is
not a global vertical coordinate.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the vertex displacement has a component in
the direction of the local Frenet–Serret binormal.

sources.leaf_definition: Coordinates along the binormal axis
sources.parent_definition: Polygonal outline of the cross section in the (normal, binormal) coordinate system. Do NOT repeat the first point.

NAMES.name: count_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short:
Count of discrete toroidal-field-coil modules forming the device’s toroidal
magnetic-field system; conductor turns within a module are not counted
separately.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal-field-coil module count is the number of distinct coil modules
forming the device’s toroidal magnetic-field system. Each module is counted
once, regardless of how many conductor turns or conductor elements it
contains.

This count is an inventory of coil modules, not a winding-turn count and not
a measure of electrical excitation or conductor geometry. Those properties
are described separately by the [current of a toroidal field
coil](name:current_of_toroidal_field_coil) and the [area of a toroidal field
coil](name:area_of_toroidal_field_coil).

sources.leaf_definition: Number of coils around the torus, in case is_periodic = 1
sources.parent_definition: Toroidal field coils

NAMES.name: current_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short:
Signed conventional electric current circulating in one axisymmetric passive
conducting loop, induced by changing linked magnetic flux and
electromagnetic coupling.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the conventional electric current circulating in a single
passive conducting loop. It represents the electromagnetically induced
response of the passive conductor to changing linked magnetic flux,
including transients caused by changing plasma currents, active-coil
currents, disruptions, and coupling to other conductors.
