For a passive loop with no separately applied circuit voltage, the linear
circuit response is represented by

$$
\mathcal{R} I(t) + L\frac{dI(t)}{dt} = -\frac{d\Phi_{\rm ext}(t)}{dt}
$$

where $I(t)$ is the loop current, $\mathcal{R}$ is the loop resistance, $L$
is its self-inductance, $t$ is time, and $\Phi_{\rm ext}(t)$ is the
externally linked magnetic flux, including mutual coupling and excluding
flux generated by the loop's own current. The negative sign expresses Lenz's
law.

The quantity applies to one passive conducting loop and denotes its net
circuit current, with all induced contributions aggregated into that loop
current. It excludes current imposed by an external power supply and is
distinct from the current carried by the plasma or by an actively driven
coil. The loop-resolved current contributes to the net [current of a passive
structure](name:current_of_passive_structure) when multiple passive
conducting elements form one structure.

The magnetic coupling and orientation of the loop are interpreted
consistently with its [effective turn
count](name:effective_turn_count_of_passive_loop), whose sign represents the
element orientation relative to positive loop current.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when conventional current circulates in the
direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is
toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

sources.leaf_definition: Passive loop current
sources.parent_definition: Passive axisymmetric conductor description in the form of non-connected loops; any connected loops are expressed as active coil circuits with no power supply attached.

NAMES.name: current_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short:
Current of a toroidal-field coil is the signed conventional electric current
carried by one toroidal-field-coil winding. Its sign is defined by the
toroidal magnetic-field component produced by that coil.
NAMES.long:
Current of a toroidal-field coil is the signed conventional electric current
carried by one toroidal-field-coil winding. It represents the coil current
that sources that coil's contribution to the toroidal magnetic field.

The signed current is the current-density flux through an oriented
cross-section of the winding conductor:

$$
I = \int_S \mathbf{J} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\, dA
$$

where $I$ is the coil current, $\mathbf{J}$ is the conventional current
density, $S$ is the oriented cross-section, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is its unit
normal, and $dA$ is the surface area element.

This quantity is an individual coil or coil-circuit current. It excludes
multiplication by the number of turns, summation over a toroidal-field-coil
set, and currents induced in passive conducting structures such as [current
of passive structure](name:current_of_passive_structure). It is distinct
from terminal [voltage of a toroidal-field
coil](name:voltage_of_toroidal_field_coil) and from [resistance of a
toroidal-field coil](name:resistance_of_toroidal_field_coil).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the toroidal component of the magnetic-field
contribution from the coil is positive, $B_\phi > 0$, in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Current in one turn of the coil (to be multiplied by the number of turns to calculate the magnetic field generated). Sign convention : a positive current flows in the direction in which conductor elements are ordered (from start to end for a positive polarity coil)
sources.parent_definition: Set of coils around the tokamak

NAMES.name: curvature_of_arc_of_circle_center
NAMES.short:
Geometric length scale of a curved boundary or line, with larger values
indicating gentler bending and smaller values indicating sharper bending.
NAMES.long:
The radius of curvature is the local geometric length associated with the
bending of a curve or boundary. It is the radius of the circle that most
closely represents the curve at the location of interest.

For curvature represented by its non-negative magnitude, the radius of
curvature is defined by

$$
\rho = \frac{1}{\kappa}
$$

where $\rho$ is the radius of curvature and $\kappa$ is the local curvature
magnitude.

This quantity applies to a geometric curve or boundary and is not the
position of the curve's center, its total length, or the full extent of the
object containing it. The [radius of curvature of an arc-of-circle
center](name:curvature_inverse_of_arc_of_circle_center) is a specialized
instance for an iron-core segment boundary; for an exact circular arc,
$\rho$ equals the circle radius and is constant along that arc.

NAMES.name: effective_turn_count_of_coil_conductor_element
NAMES.short:
Signed effective winding count used to weight the magnetic-field
contribution of an individual poloidal-field coil conductor element.
NAMES.long:
The effective turn count is the signed winding multiplicity assigned to one
poloidal-field coil conductor element for calculating its contribution to
the plasma magnetic field. Its magnitude represents the effective number of
turns attributed to that element, while its sign represents winding
orientation.

This quantity applies to an individual conductor element and is not the
total turn count of a complete coil or coil system. It is an effective
electromagnetic contribution rather than a purely geometric count of visible
conductor revolutions, and it excludes the separate winding counts of
magnetic-field probe coils.

For a fixed element current and geometry, the element’s magnetic-field
contribution scales with its effective turn count; reversing the count
reverses the corresponding field contribution. The same signed-winding
concept is used for a [poloidal magnetic-field probe turn
count](name:turn_count_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe) and a [toroidal
magnetic-field probe turn
count](name:turn_count_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), although this
quantity applies specifically to a poloidal-field coil conductor element.

sources.leaf_definition: Number of effective turns in the element for calculating the magnetic field from the coil/loop. Should be positive, unless the coil has elements going in opposite directions.
sources.parent_definition: Each PF coil is comprised of a number of cross-section elements described  individually and connected serially

NAMES.name: effective_turn_count_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short:
Effective turn count of a passive loop is the signed number of equivalent
windings assigned to a passive conducting loop for electromagnetic coupling.
It weights the passive-loop current contribution and may be fractional for
equivalent or homogenized loop elements.
NAMES.long:
Effective turn count of a passive loop is the signed number of equivalent
windings assigned to a passive conducting loop for electromagnetic coupling.
It may be fractional when the represented conductor is an equivalent or
homogenized passive-loop element rather than a literal winding.

The signed current-turn source strength represented by the passive loop is
defined by:

$$
\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{loop}} = N_{\mathrm{eff}} I_{\mathrm{loop}}
$$

where $\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is the signed current-turn source
strength of the passive loop, $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the effective turn count
of the passive loop, and $I_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is the [current of the passive
loop](name:current_of_passive_loop).

This quantity applies to the represented passive loop or passive-loop
element as one electromagnetic circuit contribution. It has no implicit
aggregation over multiple passive loops; if several represented windings or
conductor pieces are collapsed into one loop element, their net orientation
and coupling are represented by the single algebraic value of
$N_{\mathrm{eff}}$.

It is distinct from the [current of the passive
loop](name:current_of_passive_loop), which is multiplied by
$N_{\mathrm{eff}}$, and from the [area of the passive
loop](name:area_of_passive_loop), which describes conductor cross section.
It is not a turn count for magnetic probes, coil conductor elements,
toroidal-field coils, or magnetic field-line winding.

sources.leaf_definition: Number of effective turns in the element for calculating the magnetic field from the coil/loop. Should be positive, unless the coil has elements going in opposite directions.
sources.parent_definition: Each loop is comprised of a number of cross-section elements described  individually

NAMES.name: fast_neutron_flux_of_correction_coil
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short:
Incident crossing rate of fast neutrons per unit area on the inboard-facing
surface of a non-axisymmetric correction coil.
NAMES.long:
Fast neutron number flux is the incident crossing rate of the fast-neutron
population per unit area on the inboard-facing surface of a non-axisymmetric
correction coil. It is the fast-neutron component of neutron flux of
correction coil.

The differential number flux is defined by

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{fast}} = \frac{dN_{\mathrm{fast}}}{dA\,dt}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{fast}}$ is the number of fast neutrons incident on surface
area $A$ and $t$ is time; $A$ is measured in m$^2$ and $t$ in s.

The inboard-facing surface is the side directed toward decreasing major
radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. This
quantity includes only incident fast-neutron crossings and excludes outgoing
crossings and the energy-integrated neutron flux.

sources.leaf_definition: Fast neutron flux arriving on the inboard side of this coil
sources.parent_definition: Set of coils

NAMES.name: fast_neutron_flux_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short:
Incident crossing rate of fast neutrons per unit area on the inboard-facing
surface of a toroidal field coil.
NAMES.long:
Incident crossing rate of fast neutrons per unit area on the inboard-facing
surface of a toroidal field coil is the surface density of neutrons whose
kinetic energy is at or above the fast-neutron threshold and whose
trajectories cross that surface into the coil. The inboard-facing surface is
the side of the toroidal field coil facing the toroidal symmetry axis.

At a point on that surface, the defining angular-flux integral is:

$$
\Phi_\mathrm{fast}^{\mathrm{TF,in}}(\mathbf{x}) = \int_{E_\mathrm{fast}}^\infty \int_{4\pi} \varphi_n(\mathbf{x}, E, \hat{\Omega})\, \max\!\left(0, -\hat{\Omega}\!\cdot\!\hat{\mathbf{n}}_\mathrm{TF,in}(\mathbf{x})\right)\, d\Omega\, dE
$$

where $\Phi_\mathrm{fast}^{\mathrm{TF,in}}$ is the fast neutron flux of the
toroidal field coil at surface point $\mathbf{x}$, $\mathbf{x}$ is a point
on the inboard-facing surface, $E$ is neutron kinetic energy,
$E_\mathrm{fast}$ is the fast-neutron threshold, $\hat{\Omega}$ is neutron
flight direction, $\varphi_n$ is the angular neutron flux,
$\hat{\mathbf{n}}_\mathrm{TF,in}$ is the unit normal directed outward from
the coil material at the inboard-facing surface, and $d\Omega$ is the
solid-angle element.

The scope is limited to toroidal field coils and to their inboard-facing
surfaces; it does not include correction coils, poloidal field coils, the
outboard-facing surface, or a whole-coil combination of surfaces. The
quantity is normalized by the receiving surface area and is not the
area-integrated neutron rate, cumulative neutron fluence, total neutron
production rate, or material response caused by the neutron field.

The fast-neutron threshold is an essential part of the convention: neutrons
below $E_\mathrm{fast}$ are excluded, and a different threshold defines a
different fast-neutron flux. The analogous quantity for a correction coil is
[fast neutron flux of correction
coil](name:fast_neutron_flux_of_correction_coil); it uses the same incident
fast-neutron crossing concept but a different coil population.

sources.leaf_definition: Fast neutron flux arriving on the inboard side of this coil
sources.parent_definition: Set of coils around the tokamak

NAMES.name: force_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short:
Force of a poloidal-field coil is the signed electromagnetic load obtained
as a force-combination-matrix linear combination of the coil's radial and
vertical Lorentz-force components in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z)
frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
Force of a poloidal-field coil is a signed scalar electromagnetic load on an
individual poloidal-field coil. It is the Lorentz-force resultant selected
by a force-combination matrix from the coil's radial and vertical force
components in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$
is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The force-combination definition is

$$
F_{c\ell} = C_{\ell R} F_{R,c} + C_{\ell Z} F_{Z,c}
$$

where $F_{c\ell}$ is this force for coil $c$ and force-combination row
$\ell$, $C_{\ell R}$ and $C_{\ell Z}$ are the radial and vertical
coefficients of the force-combination matrix, $F_{R,c}$ is the [radial force
of a poloidal-field coil](name:radial_force_of_poloidal_field_coil), and
$F_{Z,c}$ is the [vertical force of a poloidal-field
coil](name:vertical_force_of_poloidal_field_coil).

The scope is one poloidal-field coil and one force-combination row; no
summation over multiple coils is implied. This quantity is distinct from the
radial and vertical component forces themselves, and it is not a magnetic
field, current, torque, or structural stress.

The [minimum force of a poloidal-field
coil](name:minimum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [maximum force of a
poloidal-field coil](name:maximum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil) are lower
and upper bounds on this same force-combination scalar.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $C_{\ell R}F_{R,c}+C_{\ell Z}F_{Z,c}>0$ after
taking $F_{R,c}$ positive outward toward increasing $R$ and $F_{Z,c}$
positive upward toward increasing $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,
\phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Force (positive when upwards for a vertical force, positive when outwards for a radial force)
sources.parent_definition: Description of force limits on the axisymmetric PF coil system

NAMES.name: height_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short:
Full non-negative extent of a rectangular correction-coil conductor
cross-section measured along the local Frenet–Serret binormal.
NAMES.long:
The correction-coil height is the full external-envelope dimension of its
rectangular conductor cross-section along the binormal direction of the
local Frenet–Serret frame $(\hat{\mathbf t}, \hat{\mathbf n}, \hat{\mathbf
b})$. It is distinct from the transverse dimension measured along the local
normal direction, defined by the [width of a correction
coil](name:width_of_correction_coil).

$$
h = b_{\max} - b_{\min}
$$

where $h$ is the conductor height and $b_{\max}$ and $b_{\min}$ are the
signed binormal coordinates of the opposing outer faces, consistent with the
[binormal coordinate of a correction
coil](name:binormal_coordinate_of_correction_coil). The quantity is the full
extent, not a half-height, centerline offset, or cross-sectional area.

sources.leaf_definition: Full height of the rectangle in the binormal direction, used only if geometry_type/index = 3
sources.parent_definition: The cross-section perpendicular to the conductor contour is described by a series of contour points, given by their relative position with respect to the start point of each element. If the size of this array of structure is equal to 1, then the cross-section is given only for the first element and translated along the conductor elements. Otherwise, it's given explictly for each element, allowing to describe changes of the cross section shape

NAMES.name: height_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short:
Height of an iron-core segment is the full, nonnegative vertical extent of
its rectangular cross-section.
NAMES.long:
Height of iron core segment

The defining relation is

$$
h = Z_{\max} - Z_{\min}
$$

where $h$ is the height, and $Z_{\max}$ and $Z_{\min}$ are the vertical
coordinates of the upper and lower edges of the rectangular cross-section.

This quantity is a full dimension, not a half-height or a vertical position.
It applies to one segment rather than the complete core. The [width of the
iron-core segment](name:width_of_iron_core_segment) is the complementary
full extent along the major-radius direction.

sources.leaf_definition: Vertical full height
sources.parent_definition: Rectangular description of the element

sources.leaf_definition: Vertical full height
sources.parent_definition: Rectangular description of the element

NAMES.name: height_of_passive_structure
NAMES.short:
Full vertical extent of a rectangular cross-section of a passive conducting
structure element, measured parallel to Z in the right-handed cylindrical
(R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The height is the full vertical extent of a rectangular cross-section of a
passive conducting structure element, measured along the vertical direction
in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

It is defined by the difference between the upper and lower vertical
coordinates:

$$
H = Z_{\max} - Z_{\min}
$$

where $H$ is the full height, and $Z_{\max}$ and $Z_{\min}$ are the vertical
coordinates of the upper and lower cross-section boundaries, respectively.

This quantity is the full height, not a half-height, local thickness, or
horizontal width. Its corresponding horizontal dimension is the [full
horizontal width of a passive conducting structure
element](name:width_of_passive_structure).

sources.leaf_definition: Vertical full height
sources.parent_definition: Rectangular description of the element

NAMES.name: height_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short:
Height of a poloidal field coil is the nonnegative full vertical extent of
the rectangular conductor cross-section of an individual active coil
element.
NAMES.long:
Height of poloidal field coil

The height is the difference between the upper and lower vertical boundary
coordinates:

$$
h = Z_{\mathrm{upper}} - Z_{\mathrm{lower}}
$$

where $h$ is the full height, and $Z_{\mathrm{upper}}$ and
$Z_{\mathrm{lower}}$ are the vertical coordinates of the upper and lower
boundaries in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. Here, $R$ is
major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when
viewed from above, and $Z$ is vertical height.

This quantity applies to an individual active coil element's rectangular
conductor cross-section; it is not an aggregate over elements or coils. It
is the full dimension, not a half-height or the vertical position of the
cross-section center, and is distinct from the radial cross-sectional extent
represented by the [width of a poloidal field
coil](name:width_of_poloidal_field_coil).

For a rectangular cross-section, the height and width determine the [area of
a poloidal field coil](name:area_of_poloidal_field_coil) as $A = wh$, where
$A$ is the cross-sectional area, $w$ is the width, and $h$ is the height.

sources.leaf_definition: Vertical full height
sources.parent_definition: Rectangular description of the element

sources.leaf_definition: Vertical full height
sources.parent_definition: Rectangular description of the element

NAMES.name: height_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short:
Full binormal extent of a rectangular toroidal-field-coil conductor
cross-section, measured across its external envelope in the local
Frenet–Serret frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the full dimension of a rectangular toroidal-field-coil
conductor cross-section along the binormal direction of its local
right-handed Frenet–Serret frame. The frame consists of tangent, normal, and
binormal unit vectors, with the binormal perpendicular to the conductor
centerline and the other two directions.

For opposing cross-section boundaries, the full binormal height is defined
by

$$
h_b = b_{\max} - b_{\min}
$$

where $b_{\max}$ and $b_{\min}$ are the extreme signed binormal coordinates
of the external cross-section envelope. The coordinate convention is
consistent with the [binormal coordinate of the toroidal field
coil](name:binormal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil), which describes
individual outline vertices.

This is a gross geometric envelope dimension; it is not the net
current-carrying material thickness, insulation thickness, or a local signed
coordinate.

sources.leaf_definition: Full height of the rectangle in the binormal direction, used only if geometry_type/index = 3
sources.parent_definition: The cross-section perpendicular to the conductor contour is described by a series of contour points, given by their relative position with respect to the start point of each element. If the size of this array of structure is equal to 1, then the cross-section is given only for the first element and translated along the conductor elements. Otherwise, it's given explictly for each element, allowing to describe changes of the cross section shape

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short:
Inner radius of a correction coil is the non-negative distance from the
center of an annular non-axisymmetric correction-coil conductor
cross-section to its inner circular boundary.
NAMES.long:
Inner radius of a correction coil is the non-negative distance from the
center of an annular non-axisymmetric correction-coil conductor or
winding-pack cross-section to its inner circular boundary. It defines the
bore size of the annular material region.

This quantity applies only to correction-coil cross-sections whose geometry
is annular. It is a local cross-sectional geometric distance for the
conductor or winding pack, not an aggregation over multiple coils or turns.

It is distinct from the correction-coil centerline position, from any
major-radius coordinate of the coil in space, from the outer cross-sectional
radius, and from the material cross-sectional area. It describes the inner
hole boundary, not the amount of conductor material.

For an annular correction-coil cross-section, this inner radius complements
the corresponding correction-coil radius in specifying the radial bounds of
the annulus. The [area of a correction coil](name:area_of_correction_coil)
is a related cross-sectional quantity, but its definition is
geometry-dependent and is not generally determined by this inner radius
alone.

sources.leaf_definition: Inner radius of the annulus, used only if geometry_type/index = 5
sources.parent_definition: The cross-section perpendicular to the conductor contour is described by a series of contour points, given by their relative position with respect to the start point of each element. If the size of this array of structure is equal to 1, then the cross-section is given only for the first element and translated along the conductor elements. Otherwise, it's given explictly for each element, allowing to describe changes of the cross section shape

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short:
Inner radial boundary of the annular cross-section of a ferritic element in
the axisymmetric equivalent geometry, defining the bore of the annulus
centered at a reference point in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z)
frame.
NAMES.long:
The inner radius specifies the internal boundary of the annular
cross-section used to represent a ferritic element in the axisymmetric
thick-line equivalent geometry. Ferritic elements are ferromagnetic inserts,
and each element is represented by an axisymmetric body whose cross-section
is an annulus centered at a reference point $(R_0, Z_0)$ in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius from the
toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical height,
$R_0$ is the major-radius coordinate of the annulus center, and $Z_0$ is its
vertical coordinate.

For an annular cross-section with inner radius $r_\mathrm{in}$ and outer
radius $r_\mathrm{out}$, the enclosed area is

$$
A = \pi\bigl(r_\mathrm{out}^2 - r_\mathrm{in}^2\bigr)
$$

where $A$ is the cross-sectional area, $r_\mathrm{in}$ is the inner radius,
and $r_\mathrm{out}$ is the [outer radius of the ferritic
element](name:outer_radius_of_ferritic_element); both radii are radial
distances from the annulus center in the cross-section. The constraint is $0
\leq r_\mathrm{in} < r_\mathrm{out}$.

This quantity applies to a single ferritic element in the axisymmetric
equivalent geometry and is not averaged or summed over multiple elements.
Together with the [outer radius of the ferritic
element](name:outer_radius_of_ferritic_element), it defines the annular
cross-section; the [radial coordinate of the ferritic
element](name:radial_coordinate_of_ferritic_element) specifies the
major-radius placement of the element rather than its inner boundary.

sources.leaf_definition: Inner radius
sources.parent_definition: The element is an annulus of centre R, Z, with inner radius radius_inner and outer radius radius_outer

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short:
Non-negative radial distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to the inner
boundary of an annular iron-core segment. Together with the outer radius, it
fixes the radial extent of the hollow cross section.
NAMES.long:
The inner radius of an iron-core segment is the non-negative major-radius
distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to the inner boundary of an annular
iron region. It is expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$
frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

For an annular cross-section, the inner radius $R_{\rm in}$ is the radial
location of the inner boundary, and it is smaller than the corresponding
outer radius $R_{\rm out}$:

$$
0 \le R_{\rm in} < R_{\rm out}
$$

The quantity specifies the hollow-bore boundary and radial extent, not the
position along the toroidal direction, vertical height, boundary thickness,
or local curvature of an arc. Unlike the curvature radius represented by
radius of an iron-core segment, it is a radial boundary dimension. Together
with the [outer radius of an iron-core
segment](name:outer_radius_of_iron_core_segment), it defines the annular
radial interval.

sources.leaf_definition: Inner radius
sources.parent_definition: The element is an annulus of centre R, Z, with inner radius radius_inner and outer radius radius_outer

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short:
Bore-side radius of one poloidal-field-coil element's annular conductor
cross-section, measured from the common center of its circular boundaries.
NAMES.long:
The inner radius is the smaller of the two radii bounding the annular
conductor cross-section of one poloidal-field-coil element. It extends from
the common annulus center to the inner conducting boundary in a poloidal
plane.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major
radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the inner
radius $R_{\mathrm{in}}$ is defined by

$$
R_{\mathrm{in}} = \sqrt{(R_b-R_c)^2 + (Z_b-Z_c)^2}
$$

where $R_b$ and $Z_b$ are the coordinates of any point on the inner circular
boundary, and $R_c$ and $Z_c$ are the coordinates of the annulus center, all
evaluated at the same toroidal angle.

Together with the [outer radius](name:outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil)
and their common center, this radius specifies the annular cross-section of
the individual element, not the combined geometry of all coil elements. The
radii satisfy $0 \le R_{\mathrm{in}} < R_{\mathrm{out}}$, where
$R_{\mathrm{out}}$ is the outer boundary radius. The inner radius is
distinct from the major-radius coordinate of the annulus center. It equals
the [circular-arc contour radius](name:radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) for an
arc lying on this inner circular boundary.

sources.leaf_definition: Inner radius
sources.parent_definition: The element is an annulus of centre R, Z, with inner radius radius_inner and outer radius radius_outer

sources.leaf_definition: Inner radius
sources.parent_definition: The element is an annulus of centre R, Z, with inner radius radius_inner and outer radius radius_outer

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short:
Inner radius of a toroidal field coil is the bore-side radius of an annular
conductor or winding-pack cross-section, measured from the geometric center
of that cross-section to its inner boundary.
NAMES.long:
Inner radius of a toroidal field coil is the non-negative radial distance in
the local cross-sectional plane normal to the local conductor or
winding-pack centerline, from the geometric center of an annular
toroidal-field-coil cross-section to its bore-side inner boundary. It
defines the bore size of the annular cross-section, not the spatial location
of the coil.

For an annular cross-section with circular inner and outer boundaries, the
conducting or winding-pack cross-sectional area satisfies:

$$
A = \pi\left(r_\mathrm{outer}^2 - r_\mathrm{inner}^2\right)
$$

where $A$ is the annular cross-sectional area in square meters,
$r_\mathrm{inner}$ is this inner radius in meters, and $r_\mathrm{outer}$ is
the corresponding outer radius in meters.

The quantity is defined for hollow annular conductor or winding-pack
cross-sections and obeys $0 \le r_\mathrm{inner} < r_\mathrm{outer}$; the
limiting value $r_\mathrm{inner}=0$ represents a solid circular
cross-section treated as an annulus with no bore. It is the inner-boundary
member of the toroidal-field-coil cross-section radius family:
outer_radius_of_toroidal_field_coil gives the outer boundary, while
radius_of_toroidal_field_coil denotes a generic non-negative cross-section
radius not tied specifically to the bore-side boundary.

sources.leaf_definition: Inner radius of the annulus, used only if geometry_type/index = 5
sources.parent_definition: The cross-section perpendicular to the conductor contour is described by a series of contour points, given by their relative position with respect to the start point of each element. If the size of this array of structure is equal to 1, then the cross-section is given only for the first element and translated along the conductor elements. Otherwise, it's given explictly for each element, allowing to describe changes of the cross section shape

NAMES.name: length_of_passive_loop_element
NAMES.short:
Geometric length of either inclined side of the oblique cross-section of a
passive loop element, including its major and minor sides.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the geometric side length of an oblique or parallelogram
cross-section belonging to a passive loop element. It describes the side
itself rather than an electrical or material property.

For side endpoints with position vectors $\mathbf{r}_1$ and $\mathbf{r}_2$
in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis, the
length $\ell$ is defined by

$$
\ell = \|\mathbf{r}_2 - \mathbf{r}_1\|
$$

where $\ell$ is the side length, and $\mathbf{r}_1$ and $\mathbf{r}_2$ are
the endpoint position vectors.

The scope includes both side orientations of the passive loop element's
oblique cross-section: the major-side instance [major length of a passive
loop element](name:major_length_of_passive_loop_element) and the minor-side
instance [minor length of a passive loop
element](name:minor_length_of_passive_loop_element). It excludes the
cross-section thickness measured perpendicular to the element's central
segment, represented separately by [thickness of a passive loop
element](name:thickness_of_passive_loop_element). The length is nonnegative
and is independent of which side orientation is selected.

NAMES.name: major_length_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short:
Euclidean length of the alpha-side of a ferritic element’s oblique
parallelogram cross-section, measured in the poloidal plane of the
right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the non-negative Euclidean length of the alpha-side, the
designated inclined edge of a ferritic element’s oblique parallelogram
cross-section. It is the alpha-side-specific component of length of a
ferritic element, rather than the length of an unspecified cross-sectional
edge.

For endpoints $(R_1,Z_1)$ and $(R_2,Z_2)$ of the alpha-side in the poloidal
plane,

$$
L_\alpha = \sqrt{(R_2-R_1)^2+(Z_2-Z_1)^2}
$$

where $R_i$ are major-radius coordinates and $Z_i$ are vertical coordinates,
both in meters, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. The
toroidal coordinate is fixed for this poloidal cross-sectional length. The
quantity is a magnitude and is therefore non-negative.

sources.leaf_definition: Length of the parallelogram side inclined with angle alpha with respect to the major radius axis
sources.parent_definition: Parallelogram description of the element

NAMES.name: major_length_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short:
Euclidean length of the alpha-side of an iron-core segment’s oblique
parallelogram cross-section in a constant-toroidal-angle poloidal plane of
the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. The side is inclined relative
to the major-radius direction and the value is a non-negative distance.
NAMES.long:
Euclidean length of the alpha-side of an iron-core segment’s oblique
parallelogram cross-section is the non-negative distance between the two
endpoints of that designated side. The edge lies in a constant-$\phi$
poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where
$R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height;
its inclination is specified by
[alpha_angle_of_iron_core_segment](name:alpha_angle_of_iron_core_segment).

For endpoints 1 and 2 of the designated alpha-side, the length is

$$
L_\alpha = \sqrt{(R_2 - R_1)^2 + (Z_2 - Z_1)^2}
$$

where $L_\alpha$ is this alpha-side length, and $R_i$ and $Z_i$ are the
major-radius and vertical coordinates of endpoint $i$.

The quantity is the alpha-side specialization of
[length_of_iron_core_segment](name:minor_length_of_iron_core_segment). It
excludes the other parallelogram side, the full cross-sectional extent, and
[height_of_iron_core_segment](name:height_of_iron_core_segment), which
denotes a different iron-core segment dimension. Because it is a Euclidean
length, it is not a signed orientation, coordinate displacement, or vector
projection.

sources.leaf_definition: Length of the parallelogram side inclined with angle alpha with respect to the major radius axis
sources.parent_definition: Parallelogram description of the element

NAMES.name: major_length_of_passive_loop_element
NAMES.short:
Geometric length of the alpha-inclined major side of a parallelogram-shaped
cross-section belonging to a passive conductor element.
NAMES.long:
The alpha-inclined side length is the geometric length of a
parallelogram-shaped cross-section of a passive conductor element.

For the two endpoints of the alpha side, the length is defined by

$$
\ell_{\alpha} = \left\|\mathbf{r}_{\alpha,2} - \mathbf{r}_{\alpha,1}\right\|
$$

where $\ell_{\alpha}$ is the alpha-side length, $\mathbf{r}_{\alpha,1}$ and
$\mathbf{r}_{\alpha,2}$ are the position vectors of its endpoints, and
$\|\cdot\|$ is the Euclidean norm. The side is inclined at angle $\alpha$ to
the outward major-radius direction $\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and
$Z$ is vertical height.

This quantity applies to one passive conductor element and selects its
alpha-inclined, major side; it is not an electrical or material property and
is not aggregated over sides or elements. The parent [length of passive loop
element](name:length_of_passive_loop_element) denotes the corresponding
inclined-side length without selecting one side, while [minor length of
passive loop element](name:minor_length_of_passive_loop_element) describes
the complementary beta-inclined side.

sources.leaf_definition: Length of the parallelogram side inclined with angle alpha with respect to the major radius axis
sources.parent_definition: Parallelogram description of the element

NAMES.name: maximum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short:
Upper allowable value of a signed electromagnetic force resultant for a
poloidal-field coil, with magnitude and sign defined by one
force-combination-matrix row.
NAMES.long:
Maximum force of a poloidal-field coil is the upper allowable value of a
signed electromagnetic force resultant acting on the coil. It bounds the
resultant derived from radial and vertical Lorentz-force components and is
distinct from the actual [force of a poloidal-field
coil](name:force_of_poloidal_field_coil).

For matrix row $m$, the associated force resultant is defined by

$$
F_m = a_m F_R + b_m F_Z
$$

where $F_R$ is the [radial force of a poloidal-field
coil](name:radial_force_of_poloidal_field_coil), $F_Z$ is the [vertical
force of a poloidal-field coil](name:vertical_force_of_poloidal_field_coil),
and $a_m$ and $b_m$ are the row-specific force-combination weights. The
maximum-force quantity is the upper allowable value assigned to the selected
resultant; it is not a separate Lorentz-force component.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the weighted combination of outward radial
force and upward vertical force, resolved in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, is positive.

sources.leaf_definition: Maximum force limit, for each limit (line of the combination matrix). EMPTY_FLT value means unbounded
sources.parent_definition: Description of force limits on the axisymmetric PF coil system

NAMES.name: minimum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short:
Lower allowable value of a signed electromagnetic force resultant for
poloidal-field coils, with its magnitude and sign defined by one row of the
force-combination matrix.
NAMES.long:
Minimum force of a poloidal-field coil is the lower allowable value of a
signed electromagnetic force resultant acting on the poloidal-field coil
system. Each row of the force-combination matrix defines one resultant by
weighting the radial and vertical components of the [force of a
poloidal-field coil](name:force_of_poloidal_field_coil).

For combination row $k$, the resultant is defined by

$$
F_{\mathrm{comb},k}=w_{kR}F_R+w_{kZ}F_Z
$$

where $F_R$ and $F_Z$ are the radial and vertical electromagnetic-force
components, $w_{kR}$ and $w_{kZ}$ are the row weights, and $k$ identifies
the combination row. The minimum value satisfies $F_{\min,k}\leq
F_{\mathrm{comb},k}$ for the applicable row. Unlike the [maximum force of a
poloidal-field coil](name:maximum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil), this
quantity specifies the lower structural bound rather than the upper bound.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the vertical force component is directed
upward along $+Z$ and the radial force component is directed outward along
increasing major radius $R$.

sources.leaf_definition: Minimum force limit, for each limit (line of the combination matrix). EMPTY_FLT value means unbounded
sources.parent_definition: Description of force limits on the axisymmetric PF coil system

NAMES.name: minor_length_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short:
Minor length of an iron-core segment is the non-negative Euclidean length of
the beta-side of the segment's oblique poloidal cross-section in the
right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. The beta-side is inclined with
respect to the height axis Z and defines the segment's extent along that
side.
NAMES.long:
Minor length of an iron-core segment is the non-negative Euclidean length of
the $\beta$-side of the segment's oblique poloidal cross-section in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius,
$\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The $\beta$-side is
the side whose direction in that poloidal cross-section is inclined by the
angle $\beta$ with respect to the height axis $Z$.

This quantity applies to the geometric cross-section of one iron-core
segment. Its aggregation convention is none: it is a single side length for
the specified segment. It is not the toroidal extent, material volume, or
any magnetic property of the iron core.

It is the $\beta$-side counterpart of the [major length of an iron-core
segment](name:major_length_of_iron_core_segment), which refers to the other
oblique side length. Together with the corresponding inclination angles,
these side lengths define the size of the segment's oblique poloidal
cross-section.

sources.leaf_definition: Length of the parallelogram side inclined with angle beta with respect to the height axis
sources.parent_definition: Parallelogram description of the element

NAMES.name: minor_length_of_passive_loop_element
NAMES.short:
Length of the minor, beta-inclined side of a parallelogram-shaped
cross-section in a passive conductor element.
NAMES.long:
The beta-inclined side length is the geometric length of a
parallelogram-shaped cross-section of a passive conductor element.

For the endpoints of the beta side, the length is defined by

$$
\ell_{\beta} = \left\|\mathbf{r}_{\beta,2} - \mathbf{r}_{\beta,1}\right\|
$$

where $\ell_{\beta}$ is the beta-side length, $\mathbf{r}_{\beta,1}$ and
$\mathbf{r}_{\beta,2}$ are the position vectors of its two endpoints, and
the norm is the Euclidean distance between those endpoints.

This quantity applies to one passive-loop conductor element and to its
minor, beta-inclined side only; it is not an aggregate over multiple
elements, the alpha-inclined major side, or the cross-sectional thickness.
The beta-side convention identifies this dimension as the minor counterpart
of the alpha-side dimension.

It is the minor-side component of the broader [length of a passive loop
element](name:length_of_passive_loop_element), which covers either inclined
side. The corresponding major-side quantity is the [major length of a
passive loop element](name:major_length_of_passive_loop_element); the two
side lengths describe distinct directions of the same oblique cross-section.

sources.leaf_definition: Length of the parallelogram side inclined with angle beta with respect to the height axis
sources.parent_definition: Parallelogram description of the element

NAMES.name: normal_coordinate_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short:
Signed coordinate of a correction-coil conductor cross-section outline
vertex along the normal axis of the local Frenet-Serret frame, measured from
the conductor centerline.
NAMES.long:
Signed coordinate of a correction-coil conductor cross-section outline
vertex along the normal axis of the local Frenet-Serret frame, measured from
the conductor centerline, is the scalar projection of the displacement from
the centerline point to that vertex onto the local normal direction. The
local frame is the right-handed Frenet-Serret frame $(\hat{\mathbf{t}},
\hat{\mathbf{n}}, \hat{\mathbf{b}})$ attached to the correction-coil
conductor centerline, with $\hat{\mathbf{b}} = \hat{\mathbf{t}} \times
\hat{\mathbf{n}}$.

The coordinate is defined by

$$
q_n = \left(\mathbf{x}_v - \mathbf{x}_c(s)\right) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}(s)
$$

where $q_n$ is the signed normal coordinate of the outline vertex,
$\mathbf{x}_v$ is the position vector of the outline vertex,
$\mathbf{x}_c(s)$ is the position vector of the conductor centerline at
centerline parameter $s$, $s$ identifies the corresponding location along
the conductor centerline, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}(s)$ is the normal basis
vector of the local Frenet-Serret frame.

The scope is the local cross-sectional boundary of a correction-coil
conductor; each value refers to one outline vertex at one centerline
location and describes only its normal-axis displacement in the local
$(\hat{\mathbf{n}}, \hat{\mathbf{b}})$ cross-section plane. It excludes the
binormal coordinate, any coordinate of the conductor centerline itself, and
any projection along a magnetic-flux-surface normal.

The paired [binormal coordinate of a correction
coil](name:binormal_coordinate_of_correction_coil) gives the complementary
component of the same outline vertex in the local $(\hat{\mathbf{n}},
\hat{\mathbf{b}})$ cross-section plane. Together, the paired outline
coordinates define the boundary whose enclosed [cross-sectional area of the
correction coil](name:area_of_correction_coil) is a related geometric
property. The [normal coordinate of a toroidal-field
coil](name:normal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil) has the same
local-coordinate meaning for a different coil class.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the displacement from the correction-coil
conductor centerline to the outline vertex has a component in the
$+\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ direction of the local Frenet-Serret frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Coordinate along the normal axis
sources.parent_definition: Polygonal outline of the cross section in the (normal, binormal) coordinate system. Do NOT repeat the first point.

NAMES.name: normal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short:
Signed coordinate of each toroidal-field-coil conductor cross-section
outline vertex along the local Frenet–Serret normal, perpendicular to the
conductor centerline and binormal directions.
NAMES.long:
The normal coordinate is the signed location of a toroidal-field-coil
conductor cross-section outline vertex along the local Frenet–Serret normal.
The cross-section lies in the plane perpendicular to the conductor
centerline, so this coordinate resolves displacement along one local
transverse direction.

For a vertex at centerline position $s$, the defining relation is:

$$
x_n(s) = \left[\mathbf{r}_v - \mathbf{r}_c(s)\right] \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}(s)
$$

where $x_n$ is the normal coordinate in m, $s$ is centerline arc length in
m, $\mathbf{r}_v$ and $\mathbf{r}_c(s)$ are the vertex and centerline
position vectors in m, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}(s)$ is the local Frenet–Serret
normal unit vector.

Together with the [binormal coordinate of the toroidal field
coil](name:binormal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil), this coordinate
specifies the conductor outline in the local cross-sectional plane. It is
distinct from a radial coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi,
Z)$ frame and has the same geometric role as the [normal coordinate of the
correction coil](name:normal_coordinate_of_correction_coil).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the vertex displacement has a positive
projection onto the local Frenet–Serret normal unit vector
$\hat{\mathbf{n}}(s)$.

sources.leaf_definition: Coordinate along the normal axis
sources.parent_definition: Polygonal outline of the cross section in the (normal, binormal) coordinate system. Do NOT repeat the first point.

NAMES.name: outer_radius_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short:
Outer radial boundary of the annular cross-section of a ferritic element in
the axisymmetric equivalent geometry, defining the external extent of the
annulus centered at a reference point in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ,
Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The outer radius specifies the external boundary of the annular
cross-section used to represent a ferritic element in the axisymmetric
thick-line equivalent geometry. Ferritic elements are ferromagnetic inserts,
and each element is represented by an axisymmetric body whose cross-section
is an annulus centered at a reference point $(R_0, Z_0)$ in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius from the
toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is vertical height.

For an annular cross-section with inner radius $r_\mathrm{in}$ and outer
radius $r_\mathrm{out}$, the enclosed area is

$$
A = \pi\bigl(r_\mathrm{out}^2 - r_\mathrm{in}^2\bigr)
$$

where $A$ is the cross-sectional area and $r_\mathrm{in}$ and
$r_\mathrm{out}$ are radial distances from the annulus center. The
constraint is $0 \leq r_\mathrm{in} < r_\mathrm{out}$. Together with [inner
radius of the ferritic element](name:inner_radius_of_ferritic_element), this
quantity defines the annular cross-section; [radius of the ferritic
element](name:radial_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid) specifies its
radial placement rather than its outer boundary.

sources.leaf_definition: Outer radius
sources.parent_definition: The element is an annulus of centre R, Z, with inner radius radius_inner and outer radius radius_outer

NAMES.name: outer_radius_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short:
Radius of an iron-core segment is the non-negative geometry radius used to
define its outer boundary in the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame about the toroidal symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
Radius of an iron-core segment is the non-negative geometry radius that
defines the outer boundary of an annular iron-core region. This member
specializes radius of an iron-core segment to the outermost boundary
measured from the toroidal symmetry axis. The relevant cross-section is the
plane spanned by $R$ and $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$
frame, where $R$ is major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis
and $Z$ is vertical height.

The outer radius is the maximum major-radius coordinate on the
cross-sectional boundary:

$$
r_{\rm out} = \max_{(R,Z)\in\partial A} R
$$

where $r_{\rm out}$ is the outer radius, $A$ is the iron-core
cross-sectional region, and $\partial A$ is its boundary; $R$, $Z$, and
$r_{\rm out}$ are expressed in meters.

For annular geometry, the outer radius together with the [inner radius of an
iron-core segment](name:inner_radius_of_iron_core_segment) determines the
radial thickness through $r_{\rm out}-r_{\rm in}$. It is an axis-referenced
outer extent, not the radius of a local circular arc about an explicit
off-axis center or the full rectangular extent described by the [width of an
iron-core segment](name:width_of_iron_core_segment).

sources.leaf_definition: Outer radius
sources.parent_definition: The element is an annulus of centre R, Z, with inner radius radius_inner and outer radius radius_outer

NAMES.name: outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short:
Nonnegative distance from the annulus center to the outer conducting
boundary of a poloidal field coil's annular conductor cross-section.
NAMES.long:
The outer [radius](name:radius) is the larger of the two radii bounding the
annular conductor cross-section of one poloidal field coil. It extends from
the common annulus center to the outer conducting boundary.

The outer radius is defined by

$$
R_{\mathrm{out}} = \left\|\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{b}}-\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{c}}\right\|
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{out}}$ is the outer radius, $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{b}}$ is
the position of any point on the outer conducting boundary,
$\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{c}}$ is the annulus-center position, and $\|\cdot\|$
denotes Euclidean distance within the cross-sectional plane.

The [inner radius](name:inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) bounds the
central aperture. Together, the inner radius, outer radius, and center
position specify the annulus geometry. For a nondegenerate conducting
annulus, $0 \leq R_{\mathrm{in}} < R_{\mathrm{out}}$, where
$R_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the inner radius.

This quantity describes one annular cross-section, not the coil's distance
from the machine symmetry axis. It is distinct from the [circular-segment
curvature radius](name:radius_of_poloidal_field_coil), which describes an
arc of the coil cross-sectional contour.

sources.leaf_definition: Outer radius
sources.parent_definition: The element is an annulus of centre R, Z, with inner radius radius_inner and outer radius radius_outer

sources.leaf_definition: Outer radius
sources.parent_definition: The element is an annulus of centre R, Z, with inner radius radius_inner and outer radius radius_outer

NAMES.name: plasma_filament_width
NAMES.short:
Full horizontal extent of the rectangular cross-section of a discrete plasma
current-carrying filament element, measured along the major-radius direction
in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Full horizontal extent of the rectangular cross-section of a discrete plasma
current-carrying filament element, measured along the major-radius direction
in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is the side length
of the idealized rectangular filament cross-section parallel to the $R$
coordinate, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

For a rectangular cross-section bounded by minimum and maximum major-radius
coordinates, the width $w$ is defined by:

$$
w = R_{\max} - R_{\min}
$$

where $R_{\min}$ and $R_{\max}$ are the lower and upper major-radius
coordinates of the rectangle boundary.

This quantity is a non-negative geometric extent: $w \ge 0$ and $R_{\max}
\ge R_{\min}$ are part of the definition. It is not a signed displacement, a
coordinate position, or the [current](name:current_of_plasma_filament)
assigned to the filament; it is distinct from the
[height](name:height_of_plasma_filament), the vertical extent along $Z$, and
from the thickness, a separate filament cross-section extent.

sources.leaf_definition: Horizontal full width
sources.parent_definition: Rectangular description of the element

NAMES.name: radial_force_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short:
Signed radial component of the net electromagnetic Lorentz force on an
individual poloidal-field coil, resolved along increasing major radius.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the net electromagnetic force on an individual
poloidal-field coil projected onto the radial direction. It describes the
resultant coil load, not the local electromagnetic body-force density.

The radial force is defined by

$$
F_R = \int_{V_\mathrm{coil}} (\mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}}\,dV
$$

where $V_\mathrm{coil}$ is the conductor volume, $\mathbf{J}$ is the
current-density vector, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector,
$\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the radial unit vector, and $dV$ is the volume
element. The radial and vertical components together determine the
[electromagnetic force of a poloidal-field
coil](name:force_of_poloidal_field_coil); the corresponding vertical
component is given by the [vertical force of a poloidal-field
coil](name:vertical_force_of_poloidal_field_coil). It is distinct from
[radial volumetric force](name:radial_volumetric_force), which is a local
force density rather than a net force.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the force points toward increasing major
radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Radial force applied on this coil (positive when outwards)
sources.parent_definition: Active PF coils

NAMES.name: radial_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid
NAMES.short:
Radial magnetic-field component at the geometric centroid of a ferritic
element, projected onto the outward major-radius direction in the
right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the magnetic-field component evaluated at a ferritic
element’s geometric centroid and projected along the cylindrical
major-radius direction. It describes the applied magnetic field, not the
ferritic element’s magnetization.

The radial component is defined by

$$
B_R = \mathbf{B} \cdot \hat{R}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector and $\hat{R}$ is the outward
major-radius unit vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$
frame. The evaluation point is the ferritic-element centroid; its radial
location is given by the [radial coordinate of the ferritic element
centroid](name:radial_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid). Together
with the [vertical magnetic field at the ferritic element
centroid](name:vertical_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid) and
[toroidal magnetic field at the ferritic element
centroid](name:toroidal_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid), it
specifies the local field vector.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $B_R$ points toward increasing major radius
$R$.

sources.leaf_definition: R component of the magnetic field at each centroid
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities, per time slice

NAMES.name: radial_magnetization_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short:
Signed radial component of the effective magnetization vector assigned to a
ferritic element in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Radial magnetization of a ferritic element is the projection of its
effective magnetization vector onto the cylindrical major-radius direction.
It describes the element's magnetization, not the radial component of the
surrounding magnetic field.

$$
M_R = \mathbf{M} \cdot \hat{R}
$$

where $M_R$ is the radial magnetization, $\mathbf{M}$ is the effective
magnetization vector assigned to the ferritic element, and $\hat{R}$ is the
outward radial unit vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$
frame. The [vertical magnetization of the ferritic
element](name:vertical_magnetization_of_ferritic_element) and [toroidal
magnetization of the ferritic
element](name:toroidal_magnetization_of_ferritic_element) are the
corresponding projections onto the other cylindrical directions. This
quantity is distinct from the [radial magnetic field at the ferritic element
centroid](name:radial_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid), which
describes magnetic flux density rather than magnetization.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the effective magnetization points toward
increasing major radius $R$.

sources.leaf_definition: R component of the magnetic moment of each element
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities, per time slice

NAMES.name: radial_outline_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short:
Non-negative major-radius coordinate of a point on a ferritic element
outline in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Non-negative major-radius coordinate $R$ of a point on a ferritic element
outline in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame is the distance
of that point from the toroidal symmetry axis. It specializes the [radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate) to ferritic-element outline points and
is paired with the vertical outline coordinate for the same outline point.

The major radius is equivalently the norm of the horizontal Cartesian
position vector:

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are horizontal Cartesian coordinate components in the
right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis, with $\hat{z}$
parallel to the vertical direction $\hat{Z}$.

This coordinate denotes an outline-point location and is not a signed radial
displacement, aggregate radial size, centroid position, or maximum radial
boundary coordinate. The aggregate radial size is represented by [width of
ferritic element](name:width_of_ferritic_element), the centroid position by
[radial coordinate of ferritic element
centroid](name:radial_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid), and the
maximum radial boundary coordinate by [outer radius of ferritic
element](name:outer_radius_of_ferritic_element).

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the element. Repeat the first point since this is a closed contour

NAMES.name: radial_outline_of_passive_loop_element
NAMES.short:
Radial outline of a passive-loop element is the major-radius coordinate of
each point on the irregular cross-sectional outline of a passive-loop
conductor element in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R
is measured from the machine symmetry axis and Z is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
Radial outline of a passive-loop element is the major-radius coordinate $R$
of a point on the irregular cross-sectional boundary contour of a
passive-loop conductor element. It is expressed in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major-radius coordinate
measured from the machine symmetry axis, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle
increasing counterclockwise when viewed from above, and $Z$ is the vertical
coordinate.

The scope is the boundary contour of the passive-loop conductor element,
evaluated pointwise over the outline rather than as an aggregate over the
element. Because $R$ is a distance from the symmetry axis, it is
non-negative. This quantity is not a radial thickness, a contour length, or
the radial coordinate of a passive-loop element, which denotes a
representative radial location of the element rather than an outline point.

Together with the vertical outline of a passive-loop element, it defines the
$(R,Z)$ position of the same passive-loop boundary contour in a poloidal
cross-section: this quantity supplies $R$, while the vertical outline
supplies $Z$ for the corresponding outline point.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the element. Repeat the first point since this is a closed contour

NAMES.name: radius_of_coil_conductor_element
NAMES.short:
Curvature radius of a circular arc defining an active poloidal-field coil's
cross-sectional contour, evaluated at the coil conductor element.
NAMES.long:
This radius specifies the bending of an individual circular arc defining the
cross-sectional contour of an active poloidal-field coil, evaluated at the
coil conductor element.

The defining relation is

$$
R = \frac{1}{\kappa}
$$

where $R$ is the arc's curvature radius and $\kappa$ is the magnitude of its
planar curvature.

The radius is constant along each circular arc and applies separately to
that arc, rather than representing an average over the contour. It describes
cross-sectional boundary curvature, not the curvature of the conductor path
around the device.

Each arc begins at a contour point and ends at the starting point of the
next arc. The [radial outline of the poloidal-field
coil](name:radial_outline_of_poloidal_field_coil) gives the major-radius
coordinates of these contour points; those coordinates locate the boundary
relative to the toroidal symmetry axis and are distinct from the arc
curvature radius.

sources.leaf_definition: Curvature radius of each arc of circle
sources.parent_definition: Description of the element contour by a set of arcs of circle. For each of these, the position of the start point is given together with the curvature radius. The end point is given by the start point of the next arc of circle.

sources.leaf_definition: Curvature radius of each arc of circle
sources.parent_definition: Description of the element contour by a set of arcs of circle. For each of these, the position of the start point is given together with the curvature radius. The end point is given by the start point of the next arc of circle.

NAMES.name: radius_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short:
Radius of the annular cross-section of a passive conducting loop element is
the Euclidean distance from the cross-section center to a specified
conducting boundary. It is nonnegative and does not denote the loop center's
major-radius position.
NAMES.long:
Radius of the annular cross-section of a passive conducting loop element is
the Euclidean distance, in the $(R,Z)$ plane at fixed toroidal angle $phi$
of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, phi, Z)$ frame, from the center of the
annular conductor cross-section to a specified conducting boundary of that
annulus. Here $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

The boundary radius is defined by the poloidal-plane distance from the
cross-section center to the selected boundary point:

$$
r = \sqrt{(R_b - R_c)^2 + (Z_b - Z_c)^2}
$$

where $(R_c,Z_c)$ is the center position of the annular cross-section and
$(R_b,Z_b)$ is the selected boundary position in the same fixed-$phi$
plane; all coordinate components in the equation are expressed in meters.

This parent quantity abstracts over
[inner_radius_of_passive_loop](name:inner_radius_of_passive_loop) and
[outer_radius_of_passive_loop](name:outer_radius_of_passive_loop). It
satisfies $r \ge 0$ and is a size of the conductor cross-section, not a
signed component along $\hat{R}$, $\hat{\phi}$, or $\hat{Z}$ and not the
major-radius coordinate of the loop center. For a circular annulus,
[area_of_passive_loop](name:area_of_passive_loop) is related by
$A=\pi(r_\mathrm{outer}^2-r_\mathrm{inner}^2)$, and
thickness_of_passive_loop is $r_\mathrm{outer}-r_\mathrm{inner}$.

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short:
Inner radius of the annular cross-section of a passive conducting loop
element is the Euclidean distance from the cross-section center to its inner
conducting boundary. It is nonnegative.
NAMES.long:
Inner radius of the annular cross-section of a passive conducting loop
element is the Euclidean distance, in the $(R,Z)$ plane at fixed toroidal
angle $phi$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,phi,Z)$ frame, from the
center of the annular conductor cross-section to its inner conducting
boundary. Here $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

The inner boundary radius is defined by the poloidal-plane distance from the
cross-section center to the selected inner-boundary point:

$$
r_\mathrm{inner} = \sqrt{(R_i - R_c)^2 + (Z_i - Z_c)^2}
$$

where $(R_c,Z_c)$ is the annular cross-section center and $(R_i,Z_i)$ is the
inner-boundary position in the same fixed-$\phi$ plane; all coordinate
components in the equation are expressed in meters.

This quantity specializes
[radius_of_passive_loop](name:radius_of_passive_loop) to the inner
conducting boundary and complements
[outer_radius_of_passive_loop](name:outer_radius_of_passive_loop). For a
circular annulus, the conductor thickness is the outer radius minus this
inner radius, and [area_of_passive_loop](name:area_of_passive_loop) is
determined by the difference of the squared outer and inner radii. It is a
cross-sectional size, not the loop center's major-radius coordinate or a
signed cylindrical component.

sources.leaf_definition: Inner radius
sources.parent_definition: The element is an annulus of centre R, Z, with inner radius radius_inner and outer radius radius_outer

NAMES.name: outer_radius_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short:
Outer radius of the annular cross-section of a passive conducting loop
element is the Euclidean distance from the cross-section center to its outer
conducting boundary.
NAMES.long:
Outer radius of the annular cross-section of a passive conducting loop
element is the Euclidean distance, in the $(R,Z)$ plane at fixed toroidal
angle $phi$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, phi, Z)$ frame, from the
center of the annular conductor cross-section to its outer conducting
boundary. Here $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

The outer boundary radius is defined by the poloidal-plane distance from the
cross-section center to the selected outer-boundary point:

$$
r_\mathrm{outer} = \sqrt{(R_\mathrm{outer} - R_c)^2 + (Z_\mathrm{outer} - Z_c)^2}
$$

where $(R_c,Z_c)$ is the annulus-center position and
$(R_\mathrm{outer},Z_\mathrm{outer})$ is the outer-boundary position in the
same fixed-$\phi$ plane; all coordinate components in the equation are
measured in meters.

This quantity is the outer member of the [radius of a passive
loop](name:radius_of_passive_loop) family. Together with the [inner radius
of a passive loop](name:inner_radius_of_passive_loop), it defines the
conducting annulus; for a circular annulus, the cross-sectional area is
$A=\pi(r_\mathrm{outer}^2-r_\mathrm{inner}^2)$ and the radial thickness is
$r_\mathrm{outer}-r_\mathrm{inner}$. It is nonnegative and is not the loop
center's major-radius coordinate or a signed cylindrical component.

sources.leaf_definition: Outer radius
sources.parent_definition: The element is an annulus of centre R, Z, with inner radius radius_inner and outer radius radius_outer

NAMES.name: resistance_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short:
Ohmic resistance of one passive conducting loop, relating its induced
current to the resistive voltage drop and determining dissipation during
electromagnetic transients.
NAMES.long:
The electrical resistance of a passive conducting loop is the
proportionality between its current and the voltage drop caused by ohmic
dissipation. It represents irreversible conversion of electrical energy into
heat in the conducting path.

$$
V_R = R_{\rm loop} I_{\rm loop}
$$

where $V_R$ is the resistive voltage drop in volts, $I_{\rm loop}$ is the
loop current in amperes, and $R_{\rm loop}$ is the resistance in ohms. For a
uniform conductor, the resistance is governed by $R_{\rm loop}=\rho\ell/A$,
where $\rho$ is electrical resistivity, $\ell$ is conductor length, and $A$
is cross-sectional area. The current is the [current of a passive
loop](name:current_of_passive_loop). This quantity excludes inductive
voltage and describes only the ohmic contribution; together with the loop
self-inductance, it determines the resistive electromagnetic decay
timescale. It is the loop-level counterpart of the [resistance of a vacuum
vessel](name:resistance_of_vacuum_vessel) and depends on the conductor
material described by its [resistivity](name:resistivity_of_wall_material).

sources.leaf_definition: Passive loop resistance
sources.parent_definition: Passive axisymmetric conductor description in the form of non-connected loops; any connected loops are expressed as active coil circuits with no power supply attached.

NAMES.name: resistance_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short:
Ohmic resistance of an individual poloidal-field coil winding, relating its
resistive voltage drop to current and determining Joule dissipation.
NAMES.long:
The ohmic resistance characterizes the opposition to electrical current in
an individual poloidal-field coil winding and the associated conversion of
electrical energy into heat.

For coil current $I$ and resistive voltage drop $V_R$, the resistance is
defined by

$$
V_R = R I
$$

where $R$ is the ohmic resistance, $I$ is the signed winding current in
amperes, and $V_R$ is the resistive voltage drop in volts.

This quantity excludes inductive back-EMF and other transient voltage
contributions represented by the [voltage of the poloidal field
coil](name:voltage_of_poloidal_field_coil). Its value may depend on the
conductor state, including the [temperature of the poloidal field
coil](name:temperature_of_coil_conductor), and is conceptually analogous to
the [resistance of the toroidal field
coil](name:resistance_of_toroidal_field_coil).

sources.leaf_definition: Coil resistance
sources.parent_definition: Active PF coils

NAMES.name: external_resistance_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short:
Additional externally introduced resistance in a poloidal-field coil
circuit, varying with time and added to the winding resistance to form the
effective coil resistance.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the additional lumped ohmic resistance introduced
externally in the circuit of an individual poloidal-field coil. It
represents resistance from added circuit elements such as dynamically
switchable resistors, rather than the coil winding itself.

At a given time, the effective coil resistance is defined by

$$
R_{\mathrm{eff}} = R_{\mathrm{winding}} + R_{\mathrm{ext}}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the total effective resistance of the coil
circuit, $R_{\mathrm{winding}}$ is the static winding resistance represented
by [resistance of a poloidal-field
coil](name:resistance_of_poloidal_field_coil), and $R_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is
this additional external resistance.

The quantity applies to one poloidal-field coil and is a scalar lumped
circuit property that may vary as the externally added resistance changes.
It excludes the static winding resistance itself and does not denote an
unrelated power-supply or Thevenin resistance. Its additive relationship to
[resistance of a poloidal-field
coil](name:resistance_of_poloidal_field_coil) distinguishes it from the
baseline winding resistance; together they determine the coil circuit's
effective ohmic opposition and resistive voltage drop.

sources.leaf_definition: Additional resistance due to e.g. dynamically switchable resistors. The coil effective resistance is obtained by adding this dynamic quantity to the static resistance of the coil.
sources.parent_definition: Active PF coils

NAMES.name: temperature_of_coil_conductor
NAMES.short:
Thermodynamic temperature of the conductor in an active poloidal-field or
central-solenoid coil, used to establish its allowable current limit.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the thermodynamic temperature of the conducting material in
an individual active poloidal-field coil, including central-solenoid and
shaping-coil conductors.

It applies to the conductor of one active coil and represents the coil's
thermal state, not the temperature of a coolant, surrounding structure, or
plasma. It is not an aggregate temperature over multiple coils and is
distinct from electrical properties such as the [resistance of a
poloidal-field coil](name:resistance_of_poloidal_field_coil).

The temperature serves as the independent variable for the coil's
temperature-dependent maximum allowable current. It therefore identifies the
operating-limit condition associated with the conductor temperature, but is
not itself a current, resistance, or operating-limit value.

sources.leaf_definition: List of values of the conductor temperature (coordinate for current_limit_max)
sources.parent_definition: Active PF coils

NAMES.name: thickness_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short:
Full non-negative toroidal extent of a rectangular iron-core segment between
its pair of opposite faces, measured along the toroidal direction φ in the
right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. It is perpendicular to the
segment's radial width along R and vertical height along Z.
NAMES.long:
Full non-negative toroidal extent of a rectangular iron-core segment between
its pair of opposite faces, measured along the toroidal direction $\phi$ in
the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major
radius from the machine symmetry axis, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise
when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is the vertical height.

The thickness is the face-to-face separation of paired points on the two
opposite toroidal-facing faces along the local toroidal unit vector:

$$
t = \left| (\mathbf{x}_+ - \mathbf{x}_-) \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} \right|
$$

where $t$ is the segment thickness in m, $\mathbf{x}_-$ and $\mathbf{x}_+$
are position vectors in m of paired points on the two opposite faces lying
on the same line parallel to $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$, and
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is the local toroidal unit vector of the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Together with the [width of the iron-core
segment](name:width_of_iron_core_segment), the radial extent along $R$, and
the [height of the iron-core segment](name:height_of_iron_core_segment), the
vertical extent along $Z$, the thickness completes the mutually orthogonal
triplet of extents describing the segment as a rectangular block whose cross
section lies in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane and is extruded along $\phi$. It
excludes any diagonal, chordwise, or arc-length measure across the segment.

sources.leaf_definition: Thickness
sources.parent_definition: The element is approximated by a rectangle defined by a central segment and a thickness in the direction perpendicular to the segment

NAMES.name: thickness_of_passive_loop_element
NAMES.short:
Transverse dimension of the rectangular cross-section used to represent each
passive conductor loop element, measured perpendicular to its central
segment.
NAMES.long:
The thickness is the transverse extent of an individual passive conductor
loop element's rectangular cross-section, measured in the direction
perpendicular to its central segment.

The thickness $t$ is defined by the separation of the two opposing
cross-section boundaries:

$$
t = \left|\mathbf{x}_{\perp,2} - \mathbf{x}_{\perp,1}\right|
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_{\perp,1}$ and $\mathbf{x}_{\perp,2}$ are the positions of
the opposing boundaries along the direction perpendicular to the central
segment, and $t$ is their separation.

This quantity applies to one passive loop element and describes a
cross-sectional dimension; it is not an aggregate over the loop or over
multiple elements. It excludes the longitudinal extent of the element and is
distinct from the [minor length of the passive loop
element](name:minor_length_of_passive_loop_element), which describes an
in-plane side length rather than the transverse thickness.

sources.leaf_definition: Thickness
sources.parent_definition: The element is approximated by a rectangle defined by a central segment and a thickness in the direction perpendicular to the segment

NAMES.name: tilt_angle_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short:
Signed inclination of the second side of a parallelogram-shaped oblique
cross-section of a ferritic element, measured counterclockwise from
vertically upward +Z toward decreasing R in the right-handed cylindrical (R,
φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Signed inclination of the second side of a parallelogram-shaped oblique
cross-section of a ferritic element is the $\beta$ orientation angle of that
side in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$
frame. It is measured from the vertically upward $+Z$ direction.

Let $\mathbf{t}_\beta$ be the directed vector along the second side, with
radial component $\Delta R_\beta$ along $\hat{R}$ and vertical component
$\Delta Z_\beta$ along $\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi,
Z)$ frame. The angle is defined by:

$$
\beta = \operatorname{atan2}(-\Delta R_\beta, \Delta Z_\beta)
$$

where $\operatorname{atan2}$ selects the signed quadrant of the directed
side vector.

This quantity specifies orientation only. The first-side $\alpha$
inclination is the inclination angle of a ferritic element, the length of
the $\alpha$ side is the [major length of a ferritic
element](name:major_length_of_ferritic_element), and the length of the
$\beta$ side is the minor length of a ferritic element. When the first-side
and second-side inclinations are both zero, the parallelogram-shaped oblique
cross-section reduces to the rectangular limiting geometry.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the directed second-side vector is rotated
counterclockwise from the $+Z$ direction toward decreasing $R$ in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Inclination of second angle measured counter-clockwise from vertically upwards directed vector (grad Z). If both alpha and beta are zero (rectangle) then the simpler rectangular elements description should be used.
sources.parent_definition: Parallelogram description of the element

NAMES.name: tilt_angle_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short:
Signed inclination of a passive conducting loop element’s overall geometric
reference axis in the poloidal plane, distinct from oblique cross-section
shape angles.
NAMES.long:
The tilt angle specifies the orientation of a passive conducting loop
element’s directed geometric reference axis in the poloidal plane. It
describes the overall orientation of the element, not an inclination
parameter defining the shape of an oblique cross-section, and is analogous
to the orientation defined for a [tilt angle of a plasma
filament](name:tilt_angle_of_plasma_filament).

Let the reference-axis direction have components $t_R$ and $t_Z$ along the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and
$Z$ is vertical height. The tilt angle is defined by

$$
\theta_{\mathrm{tilt}} = \operatorname{atan2}(t_Z,t_R)
$$

where $\operatorname{atan2}$ returns the directed angle from the outward
$+R$ direction toward the upward $+Z$ direction.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the reference axis rotates from $+R$ toward
$+Z$.

sources.leaf_definition: Inclination of second angle measured counter-clockwise from vertically upwards directed vector (grad Z). If both alpha and beta are zero (rectangle) then the simpler rectangular elements description should be used.
sources.parent_definition: Parallelogram description of the element

NAMES.name: tilt_angle_of_plasma_filament
NAMES.short:
Signed beta inclination of the beta-angle side of a plasma-filament
parallelogram cross-section in the poloidal plane of the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, measured counterclockwise from +Z toward
decreasing R.
NAMES.long:
The tilt angle of a plasma filament is the signed inclination $\beta$ of the
beta-angle side of a plasma-filament parallelogram cross-section. The angle
lies in the poloidal $(R,Z)$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical
