$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height,
and is referenced to the upward $+Z$ direction.

For the ordered parallelogram, let $\mathbf{u}_\beta =
u_R\hat{R}+u_Z\hat{Z}$ be the unit vector along the beta-angle side,
directed from the reference vertex shared with the base side toward the
adjacent beta-side vertex. The signed angle is defined by:

$$
\beta = \operatorname{atan2}(-u_R, u_Z)
$$

where $u_R$ and $u_Z$ are the components of $\mathbf{u}_\beta$ along
$\hat{R}$ and $\hat{Z}$, and $\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)$ returns the
principal branch $-\pi < \beta \le \pi$.

The beta-angle side terminology follows the same angle-labeled parallelogram
convention as [length of iron-core
segment](name:minor_length_of_iron_core_segment), identifying a side by its
inclination angle rather than by an ordinal label. The directed-edge and
branch conventions make $\beta$ unique: translating to the opposite parallel
edge leaves the value unchanged, while reversing the side direction is
excluded. This angle complements cross-section size quantities such as
[plasma-filament width](name:plasma_filament_width) and thickness of plasma
filament; it is not a filament-current direction or a magnetic-field pitch
angle.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the directed beta-angle side is rotated
counterclockwise from the upward $+Z$ direction in the poloidal $(R,Z)$
plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, drawn with $R$
increasing to the right.

sources.leaf_definition: Inclination of second angle measured counter-clockwise from vertically upwards directed vector (grad Z). If both alpha and beta are zero (rectangle) then the simpler rectangular elements description should be used.
sources.parent_definition: Parallelogram description of the element

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid
NAMES.short:
Signed projection of the magnetic-field vector onto the toroidal direction
at a ferritic element’s geometric centroid.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal magnetic-field component at a ferritic element’s geometric
centroid is the projection of the local magnetic-field vector onto the
toroidal direction. The projection is defined in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is
toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

$$
B_\phi(\mathbf r_c) = \mathbf B(\mathbf r_c) \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf B$ is the magnetic-field vector, $\mathbf r_c$ is the
ferritic-element centroid position, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in
the direction of increasing toroidal angle.

This quantity is the toroidal counterpart of the [radial magnetic field at a
ferritic element
centroid](name:radial_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid) and
[vertical magnetic field at a ferritic element
centroid](name:vertical_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid). It
describes magnetic field, not the material magnetization represented by
[toroidal magnetization of a ferritic
element](name:toroidal_magnetization_of_ferritic_element).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $B_\phi$ points in the direction of
increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

sources.leaf_definition: Toroidal component of the magnetic field at each centroid
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities, per time slice

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetization_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short:
Toroidal component of the ferritic-element magnetization vector: the signed
projection of the effective magnetization assigned to a discrete ferritic
element onto the positive toroidal direction in the right-handed cylindrical
(R, φ, Z) frame. This is the element-level convention, not a pointwise
bulk-material magnetization field.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal component of the ferritic-element magnetization vector is the
signed projection of the effective magnetization assigned to a discrete
ferritic element onto the toroidal basis direction of the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is
toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The projection is defined by:

$$
M_\phi^{\mathrm{fe}} = \mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{fe}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{fe}}$ is the ferritic-element magnetization
vector assigned to the element, $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the
direction of increasing toroidal angle, and $M_\phi^{\mathrm{fe}}$ is this
toroidal component.

In this family, ferritic-element magnetization denotes the effective
magnetization attributed to the individual ferritic element for its magnetic
source strength. It is not the pointwise bulk magnetization field inside the
material, and it is distinct from material properties such as magnetic
permeability. Together with the [radial
component](name:radial_magnetization_of_ferritic_element) and [vertical
component](name:vertical_magnetization_of_ferritic_element), it forms the
three cylindrical components of the same effective ferritic-element
magnetization vector.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $M_\phi^{\mathrm{fe}}$ points in the
direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise viewed from
above $+\hat{Z}$).

sources.leaf_definition: Toroidal component of the magnetic moment of each element
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities, per time slice

NAMES.name: turn_count_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short:
Total winding-turn count assigned to one non-axisymmetric correction coil,
including fractional values when the circuit represents partial coil
connections.
NAMES.long:
The correction-coil turn count is the total number of winding turns assigned
to one non-axisymmetric coil used for magnetic-field correction. It
represents the coil's winding count rather than a field, current, or
electromagnetic load.

The quantity applies to the selected correction coil and aggregates all
turns assigned to that coil. Fractional values are permitted when the
circuit description represents partial coil connections; they do not
indicate a fractional physical turn in an individual winding.

This un-oriented total winding count is distinct from the signed
equivalent-winding quantity for a passive conducting loop, [effective turn
count of a passive loop](name:effective_turn_count_of_passive_loop), which
weights electromagnetic coupling. Its treatment of fractional connections is
analogous to [turn count of a toroidal field
coil](name:turn_count_of_toroidal_field_coil), while retaining the
correction-coil ownership and non-axisymmetric scope.

sources.leaf_definition: Number of total turns in the coil. May be a fraction when describing the coil connections.
sources.parent_definition: Set of coils

NAMES.name: turn_count_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short:
Total winding count assigned to one toroidal-field coil, with fractional
values allowed for partial connections that do not make complete turns.
NAMES.long:
The turn count is the total number of conductor windings assigned to a
single toroidal-field coil. It represents the winding multiplicity used in
generating the coil's toroidal magnetic field, including fractional
contributions when the represented connection contains partial turns.

The quantity is non-negative and aggregates all winding turns belonging to
that one coil. It is not an average, a count of discrete coil modules, or a
signed orientation parameter; fractional values describe partial connections
rather than a separate type of turn.

At fixed coil geometry and winding current, the magnetic-field contribution
scales with the turn count. The signed direction is supplied by the [current
of a toroidal-field coil](name:current_of_toroidal_field_coil), whereas this
quantity supplies the winding multiplicity. It is distinct from the [count
of toroidal-field coils](name:count_of_toroidal_field_coil), which counts
discrete coil modules, and from the [effective turn count of a passive
loop](name:effective_turn_count_of_passive_loop), which represents signed
equivalent windings for passive-loop electromagnetic coupling. The analogous
[turn count of a correction coil](name:turn_count_of_correction_coil)
applies to a different coil class.

sources.leaf_definition: Number of total turns in the coil. May be a fraction when describing the coil connections.
sources.parent_definition: Set of coils around the tokamak

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_annulus_center
NAMES.short:
Vertical coordinate of the annulus center specifies its signed height from
the zero-height plane, parallel to the symmetry axis in the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Vertical coordinate of the annulus center is its signed height in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius,
$\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The coordinate is defined by

$$
Z = \mathbf{x}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}}
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is the position vector of the annulus center measured
from the coordinate origin, and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is the unit vector
parallel to the symmetry axis toward increasing $Z$.

The quantity applies to one annular cross-section, not to points along its
boundary or to an average over multiple elements. It specifies position
rather than the inner radius, outer radius, or vertical extent of the
annulus, and applies to both conducting and magnetizable components.

It uses the same vertical projection as the [vertical coordinate of an
arc-of-circle center](name:vertical_coordinate_of_arc_of_circle_center),
with a different geometric locus.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the annulus center lies above the zero-height
plane in the direction of increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_conductor_cross_section
NAMES.short:
Vertical coordinate of the geometric center of a rectangular conductor
cross-section in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Vertical coordinate of the geometric center of a rectangular conductor
cross-section in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where
$R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical position.

The coordinate is defined by

$$
Z = \mathbf{x}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}}
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is the position vector of the geometric center relative
to an origin on the toroidal symmetry axis in the chosen zero-height plane,
and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is the unit vector along that axis toward increasing
vertical position.

This is the [vertical coordinate of the rectangle
center](name:vertical_coordinate_of_rectangle_center) applied to a conductor
cross-section. It locates one cross-section center, not an average over
conductor elements, the rectangle's vertical extent, or an outline vertex.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the geometric center lies above the
zero-height plane in the direction of increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_passive_loop_element
NAMES.short:
Vertical coordinate of a passive-loop element's geometry-defining point: the
geometric center in oblique geometry or a specified endpoint in thick-line
geometry, expressed as signed height in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ,
Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Vertical coordinate of a point associated with a passive-loop element is its
signed position along the symmetry axis. It gives the geometric-center
height for oblique geometry and the height of the specified endpoint for
thick-line geometry.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius,
$\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the vertical coordinate. The [vertical
direction] is parallel to the toroidal symmetry axis, and the coordinate is
defined by its projection:

$$
Z = \mathbf{x}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}}
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is the point's position vector relative to the coordinate
origin and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is the unit vector along the symmetry axis
toward increasing $Z$.

The coordinate applies to the geometry-defining point for an individual
passive-loop element; it is not an aggregate across elements. For thick-line
geometry it refers to the specified endpoint, not the cross-sectional
geometric center or an average over the cross-section. It specifies a
location, not a transverse size such as the [thickness of the passive-loop
element](name:thickness_of_passive_loop_element).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the point lies in the $+Z$ direction from the
plane $Z=0$.

NAMES.name: vertical_force_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short:
Signed vertical component of the net electromagnetic Lorentz force on one
poloidal-field coil, resolved along increasing Z in the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the net electromagnetic Lorentz force on an individual
poloidal-field-coil conductor projected onto the vertical axis of the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The force component is defined by

$$
F_Z = \int_{V_{\mathrm{coil}}} (\mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}}\,\mathrm{d}V
$$

where $F_Z$ is the vertical force component, $V_{\mathrm{coil}}$ is the
conductor volume, $\mathbf{J}$ is the current-density vector, $\mathbf{B}$
is the magnetic-field vector acting on the conductor, $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is
the vertical unit vector, and $\mathrm{d}V$ is a differential volume
element.

This is a signed component rather than the force magnitude or resultant. The
radial component is represented separately by [radial force of a
poloidal-field coil](name:radial_force_of_poloidal_field_coil), while [force
of a poloidal-field coil](name:force_of_poloidal_field_coil) represents the
coil’s electromagnetic force resultant.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net force points toward increasing $Z$.

sources.leaf_definition: Vertical force applied on this coil (positive when upwards)
sources.parent_definition: Active PF coils

NAMES.name: vertical_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid
NAMES.short:
Signed vertical component of the magnetic-field vector at a ferritic
element’s centroid in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical magnetic field at a ferritic element’s geometric centroid is
the projection of the local magnetic-field vector onto the vertical
direction. The centroid location is identified by the [vertical coordinate
of the ferritic element
centroid](name:z_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid), while this
quantity describes the field component there, not the element’s
magnetization.

$$
B_Z(\mathbf r_c)=\mathbf B(\mathbf r_c)\cdot\hat{\mathbf Z}
$$

where $\mathbf r_c$ is the centroid position, $\mathbf B$ is the local
magnetic-field vector, and $\hat{\mathbf Z}$ is the vertical unit vector in
the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The radial, vertical, and
toroidal components together describe the local field; the corresponding
radial and toroidal quantities are [radial magnetic field at ferritic
element centroid](name:radial_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid)
and [toroidal magnetic field at ferritic element
centroid](name:toroidal_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $B_Z$ points in the direction of increasing
vertical coordinate $Z$.

sources.leaf_definition: Z component of the magnetic field at each centroid
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities, per time slice

NAMES.name: vertical_magnetization_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short:
Signed vertical component of the effective magnetization vector assigned to
a ferritic element in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Vertical magnetization of a ferritic element is the signed projection of its
assigned effective magnetization vector onto the vertical direction in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The defining projection is:

$$
M_Z^{\mathrm{eff}} = \mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{eff}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}}
$$

where $M_Z^{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the vertical magnetization component,
$\mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the effective magnetization vector assigned
to the ferritic element, and $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the unit vector toward
increasing vertical height. The corresponding radial projection is [radial
magnetization of a ferritic
element](name:radial_magnetization_of_ferritic_element); neither quantity is
the magnetic field at the element centroid, such as the [vertical magnetic
field at a ferritic element
centroid](name:vertical_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the effective magnetization vector has a
component toward increasing vertical height $Z$.

sources.leaf_definition: Z component of the magnetic moment of each element
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities, per time slice

NAMES.name: voltage_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short:
Signed terminal voltage across a poloidal-field-coil winding, equal to its
resistive voltage drop plus the voltage induced by changing magnetic flux
linkage.
NAMES.long:
The terminal voltage is the total voltage drop across a poloidal-field-coil
winding. It combines the ohmic voltage drop in the conductor with the
inductive voltage associated with changing magnetic flux linkage.

Using a consistent winding orientation, the voltage is defined by

$$
V_{\mathrm{term}} = R_{\mathrm{w}} I + \frac{d\Phi_{\mathrm{link}}}{dt}
$$

where $V_{\mathrm{term}}$ is the terminal voltage, $R_{\mathrm{w}}$ is the
winding resistance represented by the [poloidal-field-coil
resistance](name:resistance_of_poloidal_field_coil), $I$ is the conventional
current in the winding, $\Phi_{\mathrm{link}}$ is its signed total magnetic
flux linkage, and $t$ is time.

This quantity applies to the complete active winding and includes both
self-field and externally produced flux linkage. It is distinct from the
induced terminal voltage of a separate [poloidal magnetic-field
probe](name:voltage_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe) and is analogous to
the [toroidal-field-coil terminal
voltage](name:voltage_of_toroidal_field_coil).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the terminal potential drop is measured in
the direction of the winding's defined positive conventional-current
direction.

sources.leaf_definition: Voltage on the coil terminals (Vside1-Vside2) - including additional resistors if any
sources.parent_definition: Active PF coils

NAMES.name: volume_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short:
Geometric volume enclosed by the boundaries of a ferritic in-vessel element,
representing its complete material extent rather than a cross-sectional
dimension.
NAMES.long:
The volume of a ferritic in-vessel element is the non-negative geometric
measure of the material region bounded by the element’s physical boundary.
It represents the element as a whole, rather than a single cross-sectional
dimension such as its [ferritic-element
width](name:width_of_ferritic_element).

The volume is defined by

$$
V = \int_{\Omega} d^3x
$$

where $V$ is the element volume, $\Omega$ is the region occupied by the
ferritic element, and $d^3x$ is the differential volume element. The
quantity excludes surrounding plasma, vacuum, and unrelated neighboring
structures.

NAMES.name: width_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short:
Full non-negative extent of a non-axisymmetric correction-coil conductor
cross-section measured along its local normal axis; for circular sections it
is the diameter, and for annular sections it is the outer diameter.
NAMES.long:
Full non-negative extent of a non-axisymmetric correction-coil conductor
cross-section measured along its local normal axis is the characteristic
transverse size of that cross-section. It is a geometric property of the
conductor cross-section, not a signed displacement or orientation.

The defining geometric identification is:

$$
w = \begin{cases}
a_n, & \text{rectangular or square cross-section},\\
D, & \text{circular cross-section},\\
D_{\mathrm{out}}, & \text{annular cross-section}.
\end{cases}
$$

where $w$ is this width, $a_n$ is the full cross-section extent along the
local normal axis, $D$ is the circular cross-section diameter, and
$D_{\mathrm{out}}$ is the annular cross-section outer diameter.

The scope is one conductor cross-section of one non-axisymmetric correction
coil; the quantity is assigned to the whole cross-section. It is not a sum
or average over multiple coils, separate conductor segments, or turns, and
it is not the conductor path length or the spatial location of the coil.

The companion linear size for a rectangular or square section is the [height
of a correction-coil conductor
cross-section](name:height_of_correction_coil); the [area of a
correction-coil conductor cross-section](name:area_of_correction_coil) is
the corresponding area, not another linear dimension. For an annular
section, the [inner radius of a correction-coil conductor
cross-section](name:inner_radius_of_correction_coil) describes the central
opening, whereas this width describes the outer diameter. The [width of a
toroidal-field-coil conductor
cross-section](name:width_of_toroidal_field_coil) is the analogous geometric
quantity for a toroidal-field coil rather than a non-axisymmetric correction
coil.

sources.leaf_definition: Full width of the rectangle or square in the normal direction, when geometry_type/index = 3 or 4. Diameter of the circle when geometry_type/index = 2. Outer diameter of the annulus in case geometry_type/index = 5
sources.parent_definition: The cross-section perpendicular to the conductor contour is described by a series of contour points, given by their relative position with respect to the start point of each element. If the size of this array of structure is equal to 1, then the cross-section is given only for the first element and translated along the conductor elements. Otherwise, it's given explictly for each element, allowing to describe changes of the cross section shape

NAMES.name: width_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short:
Full non-negative radial extent of a ferritic element’s rectangular
cross-section, measured along major radius in the right-handed cylindrical
(R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the full non-negative radial extent of a ferritic element’s
rectangular cross-section, measured along the major-radius direction in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It spans the inner and outer
radial boundaries of the cross-section.

$$
w_R = R_{\mathrm{out}} - R_{\mathrm{in}}
$$

where $w_R$ is the radial extent, and $R_{\mathrm{out}}$ and
$R_{\mathrm{in}}$ are the outer and inner major-radius coordinates,
respectively, measured in meters.

This is a geometric width, not the radial coordinate of the [ferritic
element centroid](name:radial_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid), the
outer boundary radius of an annular representation, or the extent in the
vertical direction. It is analogous to the [width of an iron core
segment](name:width_of_iron_core_segment).

sources.leaf_definition: Horizontal full width
sources.parent_definition: Rectangular description of the element

NAMES.name: width_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short:
Full non-negative radial extent of an iron core segment’s rectangular
cross-section, measured along major radius in the right-handed cylindrical
(R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The iron core segment width is the complete radial span between the inner
and outer faces of its rectangular cross-section. It is a geometric extent,
not the radial position of the segment or the curvature radius of an arc
boundary.

The width is defined by

$$
w_{\rm iron} = R_{\rm outer} - R_{\rm inner}
$$

where $R_{\rm outer}$ and $R_{\rm inner}$ are the major-radius coordinates
in meters of the outer and inner radial faces, respectively, and $w_{\rm
iron}$ is the resulting full extent. The width complements the [height of
the iron core segment](name:height_of_iron_core_segment), while the [outer
radius of the iron core segment](name:outer_radius_of_iron_core_segment)
identifies a boundary position rather than a cross-sectional span.

sources.leaf_definition: Horizontal full width
sources.parent_definition: Rectangular description of the element

NAMES.name: width_of_passive_structure
NAMES.short:
Full radial extent of a rectangular passive conducting structure element in
the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial width is the full major-radius extent of a rectangular passive
conducting structure element, measured between its inner and outer radial
boundaries.

$$
W = R_{\mathrm{outer}} - R_{\mathrm{inner}}
$$

where $W$ is the radial width, and $R_{\mathrm{outer}}$ and
$R_{\mathrm{inner}}$ are the major-radius coordinates in meters of the outer
and inner boundaries in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The quantity is non-negative and describes radial extent only; it is
distinct from the full vertical extent given by [height of passive
structure](name:height_of_passive_structure) and from the element length
given by length of passive structure.

NAMES.name: width_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short:
Full geometric width of a toroidal-field-coil conductor cross-section,
measured as the boundary-to-boundary transverse extent along the normal
direction of the local Frenet-Serret frame. It is an unsigned extent, not a
centerline location or coil radius.
NAMES.long:
Full geometric width of a toroidal-field-coil conductor cross-section,
measured along the normal axis of the local right-handed Frenet-Serret frame
$(\hat{t}, \hat{n}, \hat{b})$. The tangent $\hat{t}$ follows the conductor
centerline, the normal $\hat{n}$ lies in the cross-section plane, and the
binormal $\hat{b} = \hat{t} \times \hat{n}$; the corresponding extent along
$\hat{b}$ is
[height_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:height_of_toroidal_field_coil).

The width is the boundary-to-boundary span of the outer conductor boundary
$\partial S$ projected onto $\hat{n}$:

$$
w = \max_{\mathbf{r} \in \partial S} (\mathbf{r} \cdot \hat{n}) - \min_{\mathbf{r} \in \partial S} (\mathbf{r} \cdot \hat{n})
$$

where $\mathbf{r}$ is the position of a boundary point in the cross-section
plane and $\hat{n}$ is the unit normal. Reversing the sense of $\hat{n}$
leaves $w$ unchanged, so it is an unsigned extent.

For a rectangular or square section this is the full side length along
$\hat{n}$; for a circular section it is the diameter; for an annular section
it is the outer diameter, not the bore diameter or wall thickness. It is a
geometric extent of the outer cross-section and is distinct from a
centerline location or from a coil radius such as
radius_of_toroidal_field_coil or
[inner_radius_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:inner_radius_of_toroidal_field_coil).

sources.leaf_definition: Full width of the rectangle or square in the normal direction, when geometry_type/index = 3 or 4. Diameter of the circle when geometry_type/index = 2. Outer diameter of the annulus in case geometry_type/index = 5
sources.parent_definition: The cross-section perpendicular to the conductor contour is described by a series of contour points, given by their relative position with respect to the start point of each element. If the size of this array of structure is equal to 1, then the cross-section is given only for the first element and translated along the conductor elements. Otherwise, it's given explictly for each element, allowing to describe changes of the cross section shape

NAMES.name: x_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid
NAMES.short:
Signed Cartesian x coordinate of a ferritic element’s geometric centroid in
the right-handed (x, y, z) frame, with z aligned with the vertical Z
direction.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the signed Cartesian x position of the geometric centroid of
a ferritic element. It gives the element’s absolute position in the
right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis, with $\hat{z}$
aligned with the vertical direction; it is not a radial coordinate or a
local displacement.

For an element occupying volume $V$, the centroid coordinate is defined by

$$
x_c = \frac{1}{V}\int_V x\,\mathrm{d}V
$$

where $x_c$ and $x$ are Cartesian x coordinates in meters, $V$ is the
element volume, and $\mathrm{d}V$ is a volume element. Together with the [y
coordinate of the ferritic element
centroid](name:y_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid) and [z coordinate
of the ferritic element
centroid](name:z_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid), it locates the
same geometric centroid; it is distinct from the [radial coordinate of the
ferritic element
centroid](name:radial_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the centroid lies in the $+x$ direction from
the Cartesian origin.

sources.leaf_definition: List of X coordinates
sources.parent_definition: List of positions of the centroids, in Cartesian coordinates

NAMES.name: z_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid
NAMES.short:
Vertical Z coordinate of the geometric centroid of a ferritic element in the
right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where Z increases upward from the
machine midplane.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $Z_\mathrm{cent}$ specifies the height of the
geometric centroid of a ferritic element along the $Z$-axis of the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius
from the symmetry axis, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle increasing
counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is the vertical
height measured from the machine midplane.

Ferritic elements are passive ferromagnetic components installed in some
tokamak configurations to reduce toroidal magnetic field ripple generated by
discrete toroidal field coils. The centroid position serves as the
representative reference point for each element in electromagnetic field
models that compute the perturbed equilibrium field arising from the
ferromagnetic material. Together with
[radial_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid](name:radial_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid),
this coordinate fully determines the axisymmetric centroid location in the
poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane.

For configurations requiring the full three-dimensional centroid location,
the Cartesian counterparts
[x_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid](name:x_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid)
and
[y_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid](name:y_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid)
provide the transverse displacement when the element's toroidal position is
also needed. Centroid coordinates are derived from the engineering design
geometry of the device and used as inputs to equilibrium reconstruction and
ripple-compensation analyzes.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the centroid lies above the machine midplane
in the $+Z$ direction.

sources.leaf_definition: List of Z coordinates
sources.parent_definition: List of positions of the centroids, in Cartesian coordinates

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_arc_of_circle_center
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of an iron-core segment’s annular cross-section
center in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the major-radius coordinate $R$ of the center of the
annular cross-section representing one iron-core segment. It identifies the
radial placement of that annular center in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and
$Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity is defined separately for each segment’s annulus center; it is
neither averaged nor summed over segments. It denotes the center coordinate
rather than the major-radius coordinate of an arc start point, arc endpoint,
or arbitrary outline point.

The [radial outline of the iron-core
segment](name:radial_outline_of_iron_core_segment) gives major-radius
coordinates for points on the cross-sectional boundary, whereas this
quantity gives the major-radius coordinate used to locate the annular
center.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_coil_conductor_element
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of a coil-conductor element reference point, equal
to its perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
Major-radius coordinate of coil conductor element

The coordinate is defined by

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are the reference point's transverse coordinates in a
right-handed Cartesian $(x,y,z)$ frame whose $z$ axis coincides with the
toroidal symmetry axis; $z$ denotes vertical height.

This quantity locates the selected reference point of an individual
coil-conductor element, without averaging over the conductor or coil. It is
not an arc radius or a displacement measured from the conductor centerline.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of a specified point of a ferritic element, equal to
its perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
Major-radius coordinate of ferritic element

The coordinate is defined by

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $R$ is major radius, $x$ and $y$ are horizontal position coordinates,
and $z$ is vertical position in the right-handed Cartesian $(x,y,z)$ frame
with its origin on the toroidal symmetry axis.

For thick-line geometry, the specified point is the first or second
endpoint, with each coordinate referring to one endpoint separately. For
oblique geometry, it is the designated geometric point. The coordinate is
not an average over the element and does not imply its centroid.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid
NAMES.short:
Nonnegative major-radius location of the geometric centroid of one ferritic
element in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the radial coordinate of the geometric centroid of one
ferritic element, locating that centroid by its distance from the toroidal
symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Here $R$
is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The centroid radial coordinate is defined by

$$
R_c = \sqrt{x_c^2+y_c^2}
$$

where $R_c$ is the radial coordinate of the ferritic-element centroid, and
$x_c$ and $y_c$ are its Cartesian coordinates in the right-handed Cartesian
$(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis, with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$.

This quantity applies independently to each ferritic element and is not
summed or averaged over elements. It is distinct from the [radial outline
coordinate of a ferritic element](name:radial_outline_of_ferritic_element),
which locates contour points, and from the [vertical coordinate of a
ferritic-element centroid](name:z_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid),
which provides the centroid's $Z$ coordinate. It is the
ferritic-element-centroid specialization of the general [radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate).

sources.leaf_definition: Curvature radius of each arc of circle
sources.parent_definition: Description of the element contour by a set of arcs of circle. For each of these, the position of the start point is given together with the curvature radius. The end point is given by the start point of the next arc of circle.

NAMES.name: vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential
NAMES.short:
Gage-dependent vacuum magnetic vector potential generated by external
current sources; its curl gives the magnetic induction when plasma-current
contributions are excluded.
NAMES.long:
The vacuum magnetic vector potential is a gage-dependent vector field
representing the external-source contribution to the [magnetic vector
potential](name:magnetic_vector_potential). It excludes the contribution
generated by plasma currents while retaining the gage dependence of the full
potential.

The defining relation between this potential and the corresponding vacuum
magnetic induction is:

$$
\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}} = \nabla \times \mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{vac}}
$$

where $\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the vacuum magnetic vector potential,
$\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the magnetic induction produced by the
external sources alone, and $\nabla \times$ is the curl operator. Replacing
$\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ by $\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{vac}} + \nabla \chi$,
where $\chi$ is an arbitrary scalar gage function, leaves
$\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ unchanged.

The vector may be resolved into components in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Its radial and vertical projections are represented by
the [radial vacuum magnetic vector
potential](name:radial_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential) and [vertical
vacuum magnetic vector
potential](name:vertical_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential), respectively.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when a component of the vector points along its
corresponding positive basis direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,
\phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential
NAMES.short:
Radial (R) component of the vacuum magnetic vector potential produced solely
by toroidal-field coil currents in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z)
frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial component $A_R$ of the vacuum magnetic vector potential is the
projection of $\mathbf{A}_\mathrm{vac}$ onto the radial direction $\hat{R}$
in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It represents the
$R$-directed component of the gage-dependent vector potential produced
solely by toroidal-field coil currents.

The component projection is defined by:

$$
A_R = \mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{vac}} \cdot \hat{R}
$$

where $\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the [vacuum magnetic vector
potential](name:vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential), $\hat{R}$ is the unit
vector in the direction of increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, $Z$ is
vertical height, and $\cdot$ denotes the scalar product.

The source population is the toroidal-field coil current system only.
Contributions from plasma currents and from other external-current systems
are excluded; the quantity is a pointwise scalar component, not a spatial
average, flux-surface average, integral, magnetic-induction component, or
the full [magnetic vector potential](name:magnetic_vector_potential).

The corresponding vacuum magnetic induction $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is
related to the parent vector by $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}} = \nabla \times
\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{vac}}$, with $\nabla \times$ denoting the curl operator.
Replacing $\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ by $\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{vac}} + \nabla
\chi$, where $\chi$ is an arbitrary scalar gage function, changes $A_R$ by
the radial projection of $\nabla \chi$ while leaving
$\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ unchanged; the [vertical vacuum magnetic vector
potential](name:vertical_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential) is the analogous
projection along $\hat{Z}$, the vertical basis direction of the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ has a projection
along $+\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: One scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.

NAMES.name: toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential
NAMES.short:
Toroidal (φ) component of the gage-dependent vacuum magnetic vector
potential produced solely by toroidal-field coil currents in the
right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal component $A_\u03c6$ of the vacuum magnetic vector potential is
the projection of $\mathbf{A}_\mathrm{vac}$ onto the toroidal direction
$\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It
represents the toroidally directed external-source contribution produced
solely by toroidal-field coil currents, excluding the contribution generated
by plasma currents.

The component is defined by

$$
A_\phi = \mathbf{A}_\mathrm{vac} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $A_\phi$ is the toroidal component, $\mathbf{A}_\mathrm{vac}$ is the
vacuum magnetic vector potential, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the
direction of increasing toroidal angle. Here, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is
toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

This scalar is the signed toroidal projection of the gage-dependent [vacuum
magnetic vector potential](name:vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential), not its
magnitude or full vector. Together with the [radial vacuum magnetic vector
potential](name:radial_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential) and [vertical
vacuum magnetic vector
potential](name:vertical_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential), it provides the
component decomposition of the vacuum vector potential; plasma-current
contributions remain excluded.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $A_\phi$ points in the direction of
increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

sources.leaf_definition: One scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.
sources.parent_definition: Toroidal component of the vacuum vector potential, given on various grid subsets

NAMES.name: vertical_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential
NAMES.short:
Vertical (Z) component of the vacuum magnetic vector potential produced
solely by toroidal-field coil currents in the right-handed cylindrical (R,
φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical component $A_Z$ of the vacuum magnetic vector potential is the
projection of $\mathbf{A}_\mathrm{vac}$ onto the vertical direction
$\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It
represents the $Z$-directed contribution of the vector field generated
exclusively by toroidal-field coil currents in the absence of plasma and
eddy-current contributions, forming part of the complete [vacuum magnetic
vector potential](name:vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential) vector $(A_R,
A_\phi, A_Z)$.

The vacuum magnetic field is related to the vector potential by

$$
\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac} = \nabla \times \mathbf{A}_\mathrm{vac}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac}$ is the vacuum magnetic field,
$\mathbf{A}_\mathrm{vac}$ is the vacuum magnetic vector potential, and
$\nabla \times$ is the curl operator. The curl is gage-invariant, whereas
$A_Z$ depends on the selected gage and is not itself a magnetic-field
component. The complementary radial component is
[radial_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential](name:radial_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential);
unlike
[vertical_magnetic_vector_potential](name:vertical_magnetic_vector_potential),
this quantity excludes plasma and eddy-current contributions.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $A_Z$ points in the direction of increasing
vertical height $Z$.

NAMES.name: vacuum_poloidal_current_function
NAMES.short:
Vacuum poloidal current function is the signed product of major radius and
the combined external-coil toroidal magnetic field, excluding plasma-induced
modifications.
NAMES.long:
Vacuum poloidal current function is the major-radius-weighted toroidal
magnetic field produced by the combined external coils, excluding
plasma-induced modifications. It is the vacuum specialization of the
[poloidal current function](name:poloidal_current_function).

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, it is defined by

$$
F = R B_{\phi}
$$

where $F$ is the vacuum poloidal current function, $R$ is major radius
measured from the symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical
height, and $B_{\phi}$ is the vacuum toroidal magnetic-field component in
the direction of increasing $\phi$.

In an axisymmetric, current-free vacuum region, $F$ is spatially constant
and the toroidal field varies inversely with major radius. Equivalently, $F
= R_0 B_0$, where $R_0$ is a reference major radius and $B_0$ is the vacuum
toroidal magnetic field evaluated there.

This quantity is the field product itself, not its [change relative to an
initial
value](name:difference_of_vacuum_poloidal_current_function_and_initial_vacuum_poloidal_current_function).
That change is $F-F_{\mathrm{initial}}$, where $F_{\mathrm{initial}}$ is the
initial vacuum poloidal current function.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the vacuum toroidal magnetic field points in
the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, counterclockwise when
viewed from above.

NAMES.name: difference_of_vacuum_poloidal_current_function_and_initial_vacuum_poloidal_current_function
NAMES.short:
Signed change in the combined external-coil vacuum poloidal current function
relative to its initial reference value, representing variation of the
toroidal field multiplied by major radius.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the signed difference between the present and initial values
of the vacuum poloidal current function produced by external coil currents.
It represents the change in the major-radius-weighted toroidal magnetic
field in the axisymmetric current-free vacuum region.

Let $F_{\rm vac}$ denote the [vacuum poloidal current
function](name:vacuum_poloidal_current_function). Its change relative to the
initial reference state is

$$
\Delta F_{\rm vac}=F_{\rm vac}-F_{\rm vac,initial}=R B_{\phi,\rm vac}-R B_{\phi,\rm vac,initial}
$$

where $\Delta F_{\rm vac}$ is the signed change, $F_{\rm vac}$ is the
present external-coil vacuum poloidal current function, $F_{\rm
vac,initial}$ is its value in the initial reference state, $R$ is major
radius, and $B_{\phi,\rm vac}$ is the vacuum toroidal magnetic-field
component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. Here $\phi$ is
toroidal angle and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity uses the combined vacuum contribution from external coil
currents and excludes plasma currents and induced currents in conducting
structures. It is a difference from one initial reference value, not the
absolute [vacuum poloidal current
function](name:vacuum_poloidal_current_function); within an axisymmetric
current-free region, it inherits the parent function's spatial constancy.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the present value of $R B_{\phi,\rm vac}$
exceeds its initial reference value, with $B_{\phi,\rm vac}$ positive in the
direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: alfven_frequency
NAMES.short:
Alfvén frequency at a given radial position for a single toroidal mode
number is the complex local shear-Alfvén continuum angular frequency; its
real part gives oscillation and its imaginary part gives growth or damping
for the stated time dependence.
NAMES.long:
Alfvén frequency at a given radial position for a single toroidal mode
number is the complex local shear-Alfvén continuum angular frequency for
perturbations propagating along the magnetic field on the flux surface at
that radial position. Its [real part](name:alfven_frequency_real_part) is
the oscillatory component, and its [imaginary
part](name:alfven_frequency_imaginary_part) is the temporal growth or
damping component.

The ideal shear-Alfvén continuum relation defining the underlying continuum
frequency is

$$
\omega_A = |k_\parallel| v_A
$$

where $\omega_A$ is the real continuum angular frequency, $k_\parallel$ is
the component of the wave vector parallel to the magnetic field, and $v_A$
is the Alfvén speed, $B/\sqrt{\mu_0\rho_m}$ with $B$ the magnetic-field
magnitude, $\mu_0$ the vacuum permeability, and $\rho_m$ the plasma mass
density.

This quantity denotes the full complex frequency
$\Omega_A=\operatorname{Re}(\Omega_A)+i\operatorname{Im}(\Omega_A)$, not
either component alone, and it is an angular frequency rather than a cyclic
frequency. The radial position is a flux-surface label in explicitly named
flux coordinates such as $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ or $(\psi,\theta,\phi)$, not a
cylindrical vector component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$
frame. At fixed toroidal mode number, $k_\parallel$ is determined by
field-line pitch, magnetic geometry, and poloidal harmonic content, with the
[safety factor](name:safety_factor) entering common single-harmonic
specializations.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $\operatorname{Im}(\Omega_A)$ makes
perturbations proportional to $\exp(-i\Omega_A t)$ grow exponentially in
time.

NAMES.name: alfven_frequency_imaginary_part
NAMES.short:
Damping rate when negative or growth rate when positive, the imaginary part
of the complex shear Alfvén continuum frequency, for a single toroidal mode
number at a given radial position.
NAMES.long:
The imaginary part of the complex shear Alfvén continuum frequency, $\gamma
= \operatorname{Im}(\omega_A)$, sets how fast a shear Alfvén perturbation
grows or decays at a given radial position for a chosen toroidal mode number
$n$. Together with the oscillation frequency
[alfven_frequency_real_part](name:alfven_frequency_real_part) it fixes the
full time dependence, which under the $e^{-i\omega_A t}$ convention evolves
as

$$
\delta f(t) \propto e^{\gamma t}\, e^{-i\omega_r t}
$$

so a positive $\gamma$ marks an unstable, growing response and a negative
$\gamma$ a linearly damped one. A linear MHD calculation resolves $\gamma$
as a function of minor radius and toroidal mode number. The continuum is
purely real in ideal MHD, and a finite $\gamma$ arises from resistive,
kinetic, or energetic-particle effects, the same drives that excite the
discrete Alfvén eigenmodes occupying the continuum gaps. The full complex
value is the [alfven_frequency](name:alfven_frequency).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the mode amplitude grows exponentially in
time under the $e^{-i\omega_A t}$ convention.

sources.leaf_definition: Imaginary part of the frequency, for a given radial position and every root found at this position
sources.parent_definition: Local shear Alfven spectrum as a function of radius (only in case grid/dim1 is a radial coordinate)

NAMES.name: alfven_frequency_real_part
NAMES.short:
Oscillation angular frequency, the real part of the complex angular
frequency of the local shear Alfvén continuum at a specified position across
magnetic flux surfaces for a single toroidal mode number.
NAMES.long:
Oscillation angular frequency is the real part of the complex angular
frequency of a local shear-Alfvén continuum root. It gives the signed
oscillatory component of that continuum branch at a specified position
across magnetic flux surfaces for one toroidal mode number.

The real part is defined from the complex continuum angular frequency by:

$$
\omega_{\mathrm{A,r}} = \operatorname{Re}\!\left(\Omega_{\mathrm{A}}\right)
$$

where $\omega_{\mathrm{A,r}}$ is this oscillation angular frequency,
$\Omega_{\mathrm{A}}$ is the [complex Alfvén
frequency](name:alfven_frequency), and $\operatorname{Re}$ denotes the
real-part operator.

The scope is one local shear-Alfvén continuum root at one position across
the magnetic flux surfaces and one toroidal mode number; it is not an
average, envelope, or sum over roots, positions, or mode numbers. The
toroidal mode number $n$ is the integer Fourier index of variation in
toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame,
where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed
from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height. This quantity excludes
global eigenmode frequencies and continua not belonging to the shear-Alfvén
branch.

The [complex Alfvén frequency](name:alfven_frequency) decomposes into this
quantity and its imaginary companion as $\Omega_{\mathrm{A}} =
\omega_{\mathrm{A,r}} + i\gamma_{\mathrm{A}}$, where $i$ is the imaginary
unit and $\gamma_{\mathrm{A}}$ is the [Alfvén-frequency imaginary
part](name:alfven_frequency_imaginary_part), representing growth or damping
under the same complex-frequency convention. The signed value
$\omega_{\mathrm{A,r}}$ identifies the selected real branch; the
non-negative magnitude $|\omega_{\mathrm{A,r}}|$ is an unsigned oscillation
rate and is not this quantity. The branch sign follows the phase convention
that the oscillatory perturbation is proportional to
$\exp[i(n\phi-\Omega_{\mathrm{A}}t)]$, where $t$ is time.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the temporal phase of the oscillatory factor
$\exp[-i\Omega_{\mathrm{A}} t]$ decreases with increasing time, so for
positive toroidal mode number $n$ the corresponding constant-phase surface
moves toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame with the position on the flux surface
otherwise held fixed.

sources.leaf_definition: Real part of the frequency, for a given radial position and every root found at this position
sources.parent_definition: Local shear Alfven spectrum as a function of radius (only in case grid/dim1 is a radial coordinate)

NAMES.name: alfven_time
NAMES.short:
Characteristic shear-Alfvén transit time across the magnetic-axis
major-radius scale, set by local ion inertia and the reference
magnetic-field strength.
NAMES.long:
The Alfvén time is the characteristic shear-Alfvén propagation time across a
reference major-radius scale in the confined plasma. It is a physical MHD
timescale, not an event timestamp or a growth rate.

Its defining relation is

$$
\tau_A(\rho) = \frac{R_0\sqrt{m_i n_i(\rho)}}{B_0}
$$

where $\tau_A(\rho)$ is the local Alfvén time, $R_0$ is the magnetic-axis
major-radius scale, $m_i$ is the mass of the reference ion population,
$n_i(\rho)$ is its number density at radial coordinate $\rho$, and $B_0$ is
the reference magnetic-field strength.

The quantity applies locally at each radial coordinate in the confined
plasma; it is not a radial average or radial integral, and it does not
represent a charge-state-resolved time unless the reference ion population
is so specified. As a timescale, it is distinct from the frequency
represented by [alfven_frequency](name:alfven_frequency) and from the
general temporal quantity time. It provides the characteristic time used to
normalize MHD growth rates and other dynamical rates.

NAMES.name: effective_charge
NAMES.short:
Effective charge of a plasma mixture is its second ionic charge-number
moment normalized by free-electron density, expressing the composition
factor for electron–ion Coulomb scattering.
NAMES.long:
Effective charge characterizes the charge-state composition of a plasma ion
mixture through its contribution to electron–ion Coulomb scattering. It
encompasses local values and explicitly specified spatial averages of those
values.

The underlying local effective charge is defined by:

$$
Z_{\mathrm{eff}} = \frac{\sum_s n_s Z_s^2}{n_e}
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the effective charge, $s$ labels each ion
species and charge-state population, $n_s$ is that population's number
density, $Z_s$ is its ionic charge number relative to the positive
elementary charge, and $n_e$ is the free-electron number density at the same
location.

The summation includes all ion species and charge states present, rather
than a selected species or charge state. Effective charge is neither a
single ion's charge number nor the net electric charge of the plasma.
Locus-specific quantities, such as [effective charge at the plasma
boundary](name:effective_charge_at_plasma_boundary), evaluate this
definition at their stated location.

For a quasineutral mixture of electrons and positive ions, $n_e = \sum_s n_s
Z_s$, making effective charge a charge-density-weighted mean ionic charge
number. It equals one when all ions are singly charged.

[Volume-averaged effective charge](name:volume_averaged_effective_charge)
averages the local effective charge over the confined plasma volume; a
global value inferred from ohmic resistive flux consumption during an ohmic
phase represents this volume-averaged instance. [Line-averaged effective
charge](name:line_averaged_effective_charge) instead averages it uniformly
along a specified line of sight. Neither averaging convention is implicit in
the unqualified quantity.

NAMES.name: electron_critical_temperature_at_pedestal_top
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Temperature of electrons at the pedestal top at which the pedestal reaches
marginal stability against coupled peeling–ballooning modes.
NAMES.long:
Temperature of electron at pedestal top

At the transition to instability, the threshold satisfies

$$
\gamma_{\mathrm{PB}}\!\left(T_{e,\mathrm{ped}}^{\mathrm{crit}}\right)=0
$$

where $T_{e,\mathrm{ped}}^{\mathrm{crit}}$ is the critical pedestal-top
electron temperature and $\gamma_{\mathrm{PB}}$ is the growth rate of the
peeling–ballooning mode becoming unstable, with the associated equilibrium
quantities evaluated self-consistently.

The threshold applies to the local electron population at the pedestal top,
not to an average over the pedestal region or over plasma species. Its value
depends on the pedestal pressure and current distributions, including the
self-consistent bootstrap-current contribution; it is not a universal
electron-temperature limit.

The [electron temperature at the pedestal
top](name:electron_temperature_at_pedestal_top) denotes the corresponding
local state quantity and equals this critical value only when the pedestal
lies on the stated stability boundary.

sources.parent_definition: Critical electron temperature at pedestal top determined with self-consistent runs with an MHD stability code. Details of the method for scanning parameters in the series of runs must be described in the 'source' node

NAMES.name: electron_temperature
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Temperature of electrons expressed as two-thirds of the mean random kinetic
energy per bulk electron, excluding directed-flow energy.
NAMES.long:
Temperature of electrons characterizes the random translational motion of
the bulk electron population relative to its mean flow. It is a kinetic
temperature, distinct from the equivalent blackbody temperature assigned to
emitted radiation.

The defining energy-equivalent relation is

$$
T_e = \frac{2}{3}\left\langle E_{e,\mathrm{rand}}\right\rangle_e
$$

where $T_e$ is the electron temperature, $E_{e,\mathrm{rand}}$ is an
electron's kinetic energy relative to the local mean electron flow, and
$\langle\cdot\rangle_e$ denotes a particle-number-normalized average over
the bulk electron velocity distribution. For a Maxwellian population, this
equals the thermodynamic temperature expressed as an energy.

This quantity applies to electrons in the core, edge, and scrape-off layer
without imposing a particular evaluation locus or spatial averaging
convention. It excludes directed-flow kinetic energy and does not include
ion thermal energy. As a single temperature, it does not resolve separate
directional kinetic temperatures.

The [line-averaged electron
temperature](name:line_averaged_electron_temperature) is a spatial average
of this quantity along a plasma chord, while the [volume-averaged electron
temperature](name:volume_averaged_electron_temperature) is its volume
average inside the last closed magnetic flux surface. These spatial averages
are distinct from the velocity-distribution average in the defining
relation.

NAMES.name: electrostatic_potential
NAMES.short:
Electrostatic interaction energy per positive test charge in a plasma or at
a material boundary, relative to a chosen electrical reference.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the electrostatic potential in a plasma or at a material
boundary, relative to a chosen electrical reference. It specifies
electrostatic interaction energy per positive test charge.

The defining energy relation is

$$
\Phi = \frac{\Delta U}{q}
$$

where $\Phi$ is the reference-relative electrostatic potential, $\Delta U$
is the change in electrostatic potential energy of a test charge moved from
the reference to the evaluation location, and $q$ is the positive test
charge.

The quantity applies across core plasma, edge plasma, the scrape-off layer,
and material boundaries. It may denote a local value or an explicitly
specified spatial average; no particular averaging operation or evaluation
locus is intrinsic to the general quantity. A flux-surface-averaged value is
the mean over a specified magnetic flux surface, not an assertion that the
local potential is constant on that surface.

For the local potential, the electrostatic electric field is
$\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{es}}=-\nabla\Phi$, where $\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{es}}$
denotes the electrostatic contribution to the electric field and $\nabla$ is
the spatial gradient. This relation excludes any inductive electric-field
contribution. Potential gradients therefore contribute to plasma rotation
through electric-field-cross-magnetic-field drift. Changing the electrical
reference adds a spatially constant offset without changing this electric
field.

The [potential at a Langmuir-probe
position](name:electrostatic_potential_at_langmuir_probe_position) is a
local plasma value, whereas the [floating electrostatic
potential](name:floating_electrostatic_potential) is the collector value
constrained by zero net current. A sheath can sustain a difference between
them. The [real part](name:electrostatic_potential_real_part) and [imaginary
part](name:electrostatic_potential_imaginary_part) are quadratures of a
complex representation; a fluctuation amplitude instead characterizes
magnitude, with any normalization specified separately.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when a positive test charge has greater
electrostatic potential energy at the evaluation location than at the chosen
reference.

NAMES.name: electrostatic_potential_imaginary_part
NAMES.short:
Electrostatic potential imaginary part is the signed quadrature component
that multiplies the imaginary unit in a complex representation of an
electrostatic potential. It denotes only that imaginary component, not the
full complex potential or its real part.
NAMES.long:
Electrostatic potential imaginary part is the signed quadrature component of
an electrostatic potential represented as a complex scalar. It is the part
multiplying the imaginary unit and is defined only after a complex phase
reference has been chosen.

For a complex electrostatic potential $\Phi$, the imaginary part $\Phi_I$ is
defined by the decomposition:

$$
\Phi = \Phi_R + i\Phi_I
$$

where $\Phi_R$ is the electrostatic-potential real part, $\Phi_I$ is the
electrostatic-potential imaginary part, and $i$ is the imaginary unit.

This quantity excludes the full complex electrostatic potential and excludes
the real quadrature component. A concrete specialization is the [perturbed
electrostatic-potential imaginary
part](name:perturbed_electrostatic_potential_imaginary_part) used for a
complex perturbation representation.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the coefficient of $+i$ in the chosen complex
representation of the electrostatic potential is positive.

NAMES.name: electrostatic_potential_real_part
NAMES.short:
Electrostatic potential real part is the real-valued quadrature of a complex
electrostatic-potential representation. It identifies the in-phase
scalar-potential component, not the full complex potential or its magnitude.
NAMES.long:
Electrostatic potential real part is the real-valued quadrature of a complex
electrostatic-potential field or eigenfunction. It represents the
scalar-potential component associated with the chosen real phase of the
complex representation, not the complete complex quantity.

The real part is defined by the complex decomposition of the electrostatic
potential:

$$
\phi_R = \operatorname{Re}\{\phi\}, \qquad \phi = \phi_R + i\phi_I
$$

where $\phi$ is the complex electrostatic potential, $\phi_R$ is this real
part, and $\phi_I$ is the corresponding imaginary part.

This quantity excludes the imaginary quadrature, the complex modulus, the
phase angle, and any reconstructed physical perturbation obtained after
applying additional mode or time phase factors. The [perturbed
electrostatic-potential real
part](name:perturbed_electrostatic_potential_real_part) is the first-order
perturbation-specific instance of this real-part quantity.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the real quadrature of the electrostatic
potential is above the chosen scalar-potential reference for the specified
complex phase.

NAMES.name: halo_current
NAMES.subject: halo
NAMES.short:
Halo current in the halo plasma region during a disruption is the electric
current vector carried by the halo plasma on open magnetic field lines
between the last closed flux surface and the first wall. Its poloidal and
toroidal components are obtained by integrating the halo current density
over oriented cross sections of the halo region.
NAMES.long:
Halo current in the halo plasma region during a disruption is the electric
current vector carried by the halo plasma flowing on open magnetic field
lines between the last closed flux surface and the first wall. It resolves
into a poloidal component and a toroidal component, each obtained by
integrating the halo current density over an oriented cross section of the
halo region.

The component currents are surface integrals of the halo current density,
and the current vector is their sum along the corresponding unit directions:

$$
\mathbf{I}_\mathrm{h} = I_{\mathrm{h},\theta}\,\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta + I_{\mathrm{h},\phi}\,\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}, \qquad I_{\mathrm{h},a} = \int_{S_a} \mathbf{J}_\mathrm{h}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{e}}_a\,dS,\quad a\in\{\theta,\phi\}
$$

where $\mathbf{J}_\mathrm{h}$ is the halo current density, $S_a$ is an
oriented cross section of the halo region with positive normal
$\hat{\mathbf{e}}_a$, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$ is tangent to increasing
poloidal angle $\theta$, and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is tangent to
increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi,
Z)$ frame. The poloidal angle $\theta$ is the angular coordinate in the
meridional plane of that $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame about the chosen magnetic-axis
reference and is distinct from the toroidal angle $\phi$.

The scalar coefficient $I_{\mathrm{h},\theta}$ is
[poloidal_halo_current](name:poloidal_halo_current) and
$I_{\mathrm{h},\phi}$ is
[toroidal_halo_current](name:toroidal_halo_current). This integrated current
vector is distinct from halo_current_density, the local field
$\mathbf{J}_\mathrm{h}$ prior to integration over $S_a$, and it counts only
current carried by the halo plasma itself, excluding current confined to
passive conducting structures after path closure outside the halo region.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the poloidal component is directed along
increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ and the toroidal component is directed
along increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,
\phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: ion_average_temperature_at_post_sawtooth_crash
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short:
Density-weighted mean random kinetic energy of all ion species and charge
states, expressed as an energy-equivalent temperature after a sawtooth
crash.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the energy-equivalent temperature of the ion population
after a sawtooth crash, averaged over every included ion species and charge
state. It characterizes the mean thermal energy of the post-crash ions and
is distinct from a temperature assigned to one species or charge state.

$$
T_i = \frac{\sum_s n_s T_s}{\sum_s n_s}
$$

where $T_i$ is the averaged ion temperature, $T_s$ is the temperature of ion
species and charge state $s$, and $n_s$ is its number density. The summation
includes all ion species and charge states in the defined population. The
corresponding general quantity is [ion average
temperature](name:ion_average_temperature), while [ion average temperature
at an internal transport
barrier](name:ion_average_temperature_at_internal_transport_barrier) applies
the same averaging concept at a different plasma locus.

NAMES.name: normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate
NAMES.short:
Normalized poloidal flux coordinate labels magnetic surfaces by their
poloidal-flux fraction or its square root, from zero at the magnetic axis to
one at the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Normalized poloidal flux coordinate

The linear normalized poloidal-flux fraction is defined by

$$
\psi_{\mathrm{N}} = \frac{\psi - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}}{\psi_{\mathrm{b}} - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}}
$$

where $\psi_{\mathrm{N}}$ is the linear normalized flux fraction, $\psi$ is
the [poloidal magnetic flux of the
surface](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_flux_surface),
$\psi_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is its [magnetic-axis
value](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis), and
$\psi_{\mathrm{b}}$ is its [boundary
value](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary) at the last closed
flux surface used as the normalization reference. The denominator must be
nonzero.

The square-root parameterization is $\rho_{\mathrm{pol,norm}} =
\sqrt{\psi_{\mathrm{N}}}$, where $\rho_{\mathrm{pol,norm}}$ is the
radius-like normalized poloidal flux coordinate. Both parameterizations
increase from zero at the magnetic axis to one at the last closed flux
surface, but their intermediate values differ. Neither is a geometric
radius, spatial average, or volume integral. Outside the last closed flux
surface, an extension labels flux levels rather than nested closed surfaces;
the square-root form requires a nonnegative flux fraction.

Locus-specific members evaluate the chosen parameterization without changing
its normalization references. The [coordinate at the reflectometer cutoff
position](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_at_reflectometer_cutoff_position)
uses the square-root form. The [coordinate of the selected plasma
boundary](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary) uses
the linear fraction and can be below one when that selected boundary lies
inside the last closed flux surface.

$$\psi_{\mathrm{N}} = (\psi - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}})/(\psi_{\mathrm{b}} - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}})$$

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_growth_rate
NAMES.short:
Per-toroidal-mode growth rate is the exponential growth or damping rate of a
single linear magnetohydrodynamic eigenmode with a specified toroidal mode
number. It is the imaginary part of the complex eigenfrequency under the
time dependence that makes positive values correspond to increasing
amplitude.
NAMES.long:
Per-toroidal-mode growth rate is the exponential rate associated with one
linear magnetohydrodynamic eigenmode at a specified toroidal mode number. It
characterizes the temporal change of that eigenmode's amplitude, separating
unstable growth from damping for the same toroidal harmonic.

For a linear perturbation represented by a toroidal Fourier eigenmode, the
defining convention is

$$
\delta q_n(R,Z,\phi,t) = \tilde{q}_n(R,Z)\exp[i n\phi - i\omega_n t], \qquad \gamma_n = \operatorname{Im}(\omega_n)
$$

where $\delta q_n$ is a perturbation of an MHD field quantity, $\tilde{q}_n$
is its eigenfunction, $n$ is the integer toroidal mode number, $R$ is major
radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $t$ is time, $i$ is the
imaginary unit, $\omega_n$ is the complex mode frequency of the eigenmode,
and $\gamma_n$ is the per-toroidal-mode growth rate.

The scope is a single eigenmode within a single toroidal harmonic; there is
no summation, averaging, maximization, or aggregation over toroidal mode
numbers or over distinct eigenbranches. This quantity applies to the linear
perturbation amplitude and excludes nonlinear saturation, mode-coupling
effects, and spectrum-wide instability measures.

This quantity is distinct from mode frequency as an oscillation-rate
quantity and from per-toroidal-mode perturbed energy as an energy-like
quadratic measure of the same toroidal harmonic. For fixed eigenfunction
normalization in the linear regime, a modal amplitude scales as
$\exp(\gamma_n t)$ and a quadratic perturbation measure scales as
$\exp(2\gamma_n t)$.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the mode amplitude increases exponentially in
time.

sources.leaf_definition: Linear growthrate of the mode
sources.parent_definition: Vector of toroidal modes. Each mode is described as exp(i(n_tor.phi - m_pol.theta - 2.pi.frequency.t - phase))

NAMES.name: perturbed_electrostatic_potential_imaginary_part
NAMES.short:
Imaginary part of the complex first-order electrostatic potential
perturbation eigenfunction for a specified toroidal Fourier mode in linear
MHD stability analysis.
NAMES.long:
The imaginary part of the perturbed electrostatic potential eigenfunction is
one of two real-valued components that together fully specify the complex
scalar perturbation $\delta\phi$ throughout the confined plasma for a single
linear magnetohydrodynamic eigenmode. The irrotational component of the
perturbed electric field is $\delta\mathbf{E}_\mathrm{es} =
-\nabla\delta\phi$, separate from the inductive contribution arising from
the perturbed magnetic vector potential.

The complex eigenfunction decomposes as:

$$
\delta\phi = \operatorname{Re}(\delta\phi) + i\,\operatorname{Im}(\delta\phi)
$$

where $\operatorname{Re}(\delta\phi)$ is the [real
part](name:perturbed_electrostatic_potential_real_part) and
$\operatorname{Im}(\delta\phi)$ — this quantity — encodes the spatial phase
distribution of the electrostatic perturbation for toroidal mode number $n$.

Linear MHD or extended-MHD stability solvers compute $\delta\phi$ as part of
the eigenmode solution for a specified $n$; the overall complex
normalization is fixed by the solver's phase convention, so the imaginary
part carries physical meaning only in conjunction with the real part. The
same complex decomposition pattern applies to
[perturbed_plasma_pressure_imaginary_part](name:perturbed_plasma_pressure_imaginary_part)
and
[perturbed_plasma_mass_density_imaginary_part](name:perturbed_plasma_mass_density_imaginary_part)
within the complete set of MHD perturbation eigenfunctions for the same
eigenmode.

sources.leaf_definition: Imaginary part
sources.parent_definition: Perturbed electrostatic potential for given toroidal mode number

NAMES.name: perturbed_electrostatic_potential_real_part
NAMES.short:
Real part of the complex first-order electrostatic potential perturbation
eigenfunction for a specified toroidal Fourier mode in linear MHD stability
analysis.
NAMES.long:
The perturbed electrostatic potential $\delta\hat{\phi}$ is a complex
spatial eigenfunction in linear MHD stability analysis, representing the
scalar potential part of the first-order electric field perturbation
$\delta\mathbf{E} = -\nabla\delta\phi - \partial_t\delta\mathbf{A}$ for a
single toroidal Fourier mode number $n$. This quantity is the real part
$\mathrm{Re}(\delta\hat{\phi})$, encoding the in-phase component of the
eigenfunction in the poloidal plane defined by the $(R, Z)$ coordinates of
the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The complex eigenfunction is fully specified by combining this quantity with
[perturbed_electrostatic_potential_imaginary_part](name:perturbed_electrostatic_potential_imaginary_part):

$$
\delta\hat{\phi}(R,Z) = \mathrm{Re}(\delta\hat{\phi}) + i\,\mathrm{Im}(\delta\hat{\phi})
$$

where the physical perturbation field at toroidal angle $\phi$ is recovered
as $\mathrm{Re}[\delta\hat{\phi}(R,Z)\,e^{in\phi}]$, and $n$ is the toroidal
mode number.

The absolute amplitude and phase of the eigenfunction depend on the
normalization convention adopted by the linear stability solver; only
relative amplitudes among simultaneously computed perturbation quantities
carry physical meaning. The analogous real-part components in the same
eigenfunction family include
[perturbed_plasma_pressure_real_part](name:perturbed_plasma_pressure_real_part)
and
[perturbed_plasma_mass_density_real_part](name:perturbed_plasma_mass_density_real_part),
all resolved on the same poloidal plane for a given toroidal mode.

sources.leaf_definition: Real part
sources.parent_definition: Perturbed electrostatic potential for given toroidal mode number

NAMES.name: plasma_mass_density
NAMES.short:
Local plasma mass per unit volume, forming the inertial term in the MHD
momentum equation and appearing in contexts from equilibrium transport
profiles to linear MHD stability perturbations.
NAMES.long:
The plasma mass density is the local plasma mass per unit volume, forming
the inertial term in the MHD momentum balance and the compressibility term
in the plasma continuity equation. This parent concept subsumes both
equilibrium-profile and linear-perturbation contexts: the equilibrium total
value summed over all charged species, and the complex first-order
perturbation amplitude used in linear MHD eigenvalue problems.

In the equilibrium formulation, the mass density is defined by:

$$
\rho = \sum_s m_s n_s
$$

where $m_s$ is the particle mass and $n_s$ the number density of charged
species $s$, summed over electrons, main-ion isotopes, and impurity charge
states; neutral atoms are excluded. Ion contributions dominate because $m_i
\gg m_e$.

In deuterium-dominated fusion plasmas at core electron densities of order
$10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, the mass density is approximately $3 \times 10^{-7}$ kg
m$^{-3}$, scaling directly with ion density and average ion mass. The mass
density sets the local Alfvén speed $v_A = B / \sqrt{\mu_0 \rho}$, where $B$
is the local magnetic-field magnitude and $\mu_0$ is the permeability of
free space, governing the [alfven_time](name:alfven_time) and ideal-MHD wave
dynamics. It enters inertial_current_density through the plasma-fluid
acceleration term and is inferred from electron_number_density measurements
combined with plasma composition analysis. This quantity is closely related
to [mass_density](name:total_plasma_mass_density), which covers the same
physical concept without explicit species qualification.

sources.leaf_definition: Mass density
sources.parent_definition: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux

NAMES.name: plasma_mass_density_imaginary_part
NAMES.short:
Plasma mass density imaginary part is the imaginary quadrature of a complex
plasma mass-density quantity. It is the component multiplying the positive
imaginary basis, not the complete complex density.
NAMES.long:
Plasma mass density imaginary part is the imaginary quadrature of a complex
plasma mass-density quantity. It represents the coefficient of the imaginary
basis in a complex representation of plasma mass density, not the complete
complex density itself.

The complex plasma mass density may be decomposed into real and imaginary
quadratures as

$$
\rho = \rho_{\mathrm{re}} + i\,\rho_{\mathrm{im}}
$$

where $\rho$ is the complex plasma mass density, $\rho_{\mathrm{re}}$ is its
real quadrature, $\rho_{\mathrm{im}}$ is the plasma mass density imaginary
part, and $i^2=-1$.

This parent quantity covers imaginary-part plasma mass-density fields
independent of the particular origin of the complex representation. The
[perturbed plasma mass density imaginary
part](name:perturbed_plasma_mass_density_imaginary_part) is a first-order
perturbation case. It excludes the real quadrature, the complex modulus, the
phase, and the complete complex plasma mass density.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the quadrature coefficient is along the $+i$
direction in the complex representation of plasma mass density.

NAMES.name: perturbed_plasma_mass_density_imaginary_part
NAMES.short:
Imaginary part of the complex first-order plasma mass density perturbation
eigenfunction for a specified toroidal Fourier mode in linear MHD stability
analysis.
NAMES.long:
The imaginary part of the complex perturbed plasma mass density
eigenfunction $\tilde{\rho}_m$ arises when the first-order mass density
perturbation is separated into in-phase and quadrature components relative
to a chosen eigenmode phase and normalization. In the standard perturbation
decomposition $\delta\rho(\mathbf{r}, t) =
\mathrm{Re}[\tilde{\rho}_m(\mathbf{r})\, e^{i(n\phi - \omega t)}]$, where
$n$ is the toroidal mode number, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $\omega$
is the complex eigenfrequency, the eigenfunction splits as:

$$
\tilde{\rho}_m = \tilde{\rho}_\mathrm{re} + i\,\tilde{\rho}_\mathrm{im}
$$

where $\tilde{\rho}_\mathrm{re}$ is the [real
part](name:perturbed_plasma_mass_density_real_part) and
$\tilde{\rho}_\mathrm{im}$ is this quantity. Together they encode the local
amplitude $|\tilde{\rho}_m|$ and spatial phase of the mass density
perturbation over the poloidal cross-section.

The equilibrium mass density about which the perturbation is defined is
$\rho_{m0} = \sum_s m_s n_s$, where $m_s$ and $n_s$ are the mass and number
density of species $s$; ion contributions dominate in fusion plasmas because
electron mass is negligible. These eigenfunctions are produced by linear MHD
eigenvalue solvers that Fourier-decompose perturbations in the toroidal
direction; the imaginary part is meaningful only relative to the phase
convention and normalization of the specific eigenmode calculation. The
companion quantities
