[perturbed_plasma_pressure_imaginary_part](name:perturbed_plasma_pressure_imaginary_part)
and
[perturbed_plasma_temperature_imaginary_part](name:perturbed_plasma_temperature_imaginary_part)
form a self-consistent set of perturbed thermodynamic eigenfunctions for the
same MHD mode.

sources.leaf_definition: Imaginary part
sources.parent_definition: Perturbed mass density for given toroidal mode number

NAMES.name: plasma_mass_density_real_part
NAMES.short:
Real part of a complex plasma mass-density quantity, representing the
in-phase quadrature relative to the chosen complex phase. It is the real
component only, not the full complex density or its imaginary quadrature.
NAMES.long:
Plasma mass density real part is the real-valued quadrature of a complex
plasma mass-density quantity. It represents the component aligned with the
chosen real phase of the complex representation and is not the full complex
quantity.

The decomposition into real and imaginary quadratures is

$$
\tilde{\rho} = \rho_R + i\rho_I,\qquad \rho_R = \operatorname{Re}\{\tilde{\rho}\}
$$

where $\tilde{\rho}$ is the complex plasma mass-density quantity, $\rho_R$
is its real part, and $\rho_I$ is its imaginary part.

This abstraction covers concrete real-part quantities such as the [perturbed
plasma mass density real
part](name:perturbed_plasma_mass_density_real_part). It excludes the
imaginary quadrature, the complex modulus, the phase, and the full complex
field; for linear-mode quantities, multiplication of the complex field by a
constant phase changes the numerical split between $\rho_R$ and $\rho_I$ but
not the represented physical mode.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the real quadrature represents an in-phase
increase of the local plasma mass density for the chosen complex phase.

NAMES.name: perturbed_plasma_mass_density_real_part
NAMES.short:
In-phase component of the complex first-order plasma mass-density
eigenfunction for one toroidal Fourier harmonic in linear MHD stability
theory.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the real, in-phase component of the complex first-order
plasma mass-density perturbation eigenfunction associated with one toroidal
Fourier harmonic in linear MHD stability theory. The complete complex
quantity is perturbed plasma mass density.

The real component is defined by

$$
\widetilde{\rho}_{n,\mathrm{real}}(\mathbf{x}) = \operatorname{Re}\!\left[\widetilde{\rho}_n(\mathbf{x})\right]
$$

where $\widetilde{\rho}_n$ is the complex first-order mass-density
eigenfunction, $n$ is the toroidal Fourier mode number, and $\mathbf{x}$
denotes position. The decomposition is relative to the phase convention of
the complex eigenfunction.

This quantity excludes the imaginary quadrature component and must not be
interpreted as the magnitude of the complex perturbation. Its meaning
parallels the real component of the corresponding temperature eigenfunction,
[perturbed plasma temperature real
part](name:perturbed_plasma_temperature_real_part).

sources.leaf_definition: Real part
sources.parent_definition: Perturbed mass density for given toroidal mode number

NAMES.name: plasma_temperature
NAMES.short:
Effective temperature of the plasma in a fluid or MHD description,
representing the average thermal kinetic energy per degree of freedom of the
combined charged particle population.
NAMES.long:
The plasma temperature is a fundamental thermodynamic state variable in
fluid and single-fluid MHD models, quantifying the mean random kinetic
energy of the charged particle population. In a single-fluid description it
is linked to thermal pressure via the equation of state

$$
p = n k_B T
$$

where $p$ is the scalar pressure, $n$ is the total particle number density,
and $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant.

In multi-species plasmas an effective plasma temperature may be obtained as
a density-weighted combination of electron and ion contributions;
applications requiring species resolution use explicitly qualified forms
such as particle_temperature or
[neutral_temperature](name:neutral_internal_state_temperature). This
quantity also appears as the equilibrium background in linear MHD stability
analysis, where its first-order perturbation is represented by the complex
eigenfunction perturbed_plasma_temperature, encoding the amplitude and phase
of the temperature fluctuation for a specified toroidal Fourier harmonic.
The total isotropic pressure of the plasma, including contributions summed
over all species, is captured by plasma_pressure.

NAMES.name: plasma_temperature_imaginary_part
NAMES.short:
Imaginary part of plasma temperature is the quadrature component of a
complex-valued plasma-temperature quantity. It is the coefficient of the
imaginary basis element and is distinct from both the real part and the full
complex temperature.
NAMES.long:
Imaginary part of plasma temperature is the scalar component multiplying the
imaginary basis element in a complex representation of a plasma-temperature
quantity. It represents the quadrature component relative to the chosen
complex phase reference, such as the phase used for a harmonic perturbation
or eigenfunction.

For a complex plasma-temperature quantity $T_c$, the decomposition is

$$
T_c = T_R + i T_I
$$

where $T_c$ is the complex plasma temperature, $T_R$ is the real part of
that quantity, $T_I$ is the imaginary part of plasma temperature, and $i$ is
the imaginary unit.

This quantity is not the full complex plasma temperature and does not
include the real component. The specialization [perturbed plasma temperature
imaginary part](name:perturbed_plasma_temperature_imaginary_part) applies
this same imaginary-part concept to a first-order plasma-temperature
perturbation.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the coefficient of $+i$ in the chosen complex
representation of the plasma temperature is positive.

NAMES.name: perturbed_plasma_temperature_imaginary_part
NAMES.short:
Quadrature (out-of-phase) component of the complex first-order
plasma-temperature eigenfunction for one toroidal Fourier harmonic in linear
MHD stability analysis.
NAMES.long:
The imaginary component of the complex first-order plasma-temperature
eigenfunction for a single toroidal Fourier harmonic in linear MHD. It is
the quadrature component relative to the real component under the selected
Fourier phase convention.

The defining decomposition is:

$$
\delta T = \delta T_R + i\,\delta T_I
$$

where $\delta T$ is the complex temperature amplitude, $\delta T_R$ is its
real component, $\delta T_I$ is the imaginary component represented by this
quantity, and $i$ is the imaginary unit.

Together with the [real component of the perturbed plasma
temperature](name:perturbed_plasma_temperature_real_part), this quantity
reconstructs the complex perturbed plasma temperature. In the perturbation
$T=T_0+\delta T e^{i(n\phi-\omega t)}$, $T_0$ is the equilibrium
temperature, $n$ is the toroidal mode number, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle
in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $\omega$ is the complex
eigenfrequency, and $t$ is time. Its value depends on the selected Fourier
phase origin and does not by itself represent the complete physical
temperature perturbation.

sources.leaf_definition: Imaginary part
sources.parent_definition: Perturbed temperature for given toroidal mode number

NAMES.name: plasma_temperature_real_part
NAMES.short:
Real quadrature of a first-order plasma-temperature perturbation
eigenfunction, giving the component in phase with the chosen complex
reference. It denotes the real part only, not the full complex
eigenfunction.
NAMES.long:
Real quadrature of a first-order plasma-temperature perturbation
eigenfunction is the in-phase scalar temperature perturbation component
associated with a linear magnetohydrodynamic mode. It denotes only the real
part of the plasma-temperature eigenfunction relative to the chosen complex
phase reference.

The complex temperature perturbation eigenfunction is decomposed into real
and imaginary quadratures as

$$
\widetilde{T} = T_R + i T_I
$$

where $\widetilde{T}$ is the complex first-order plasma-temperature
perturbation eigenfunction, $T_R$ is this real quadrature, $T_I$ is the
corresponding imaginary quadrature, and $i$ is the imaginary unit.

This parent quantity abstracts over concrete real-part plasma-temperature
perturbation names, such as [perturbed plasma temperature real
part](name:perturbed_plasma_temperature_real_part). It excludes the
imaginary quadrature, the modulus or phase of $\widetilde{T}$, and the
equilibrium plasma temperature about which the perturbation is linearized.
Changing the complex phase reference changes the numerical split between
$T_R$ and $T_I$.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $T_R$ represents an increase of the plasma
temperature relative to the equilibrium temperature at the chosen complex
phase reference.

NAMES.name: perturbed_plasma_temperature_real_part
NAMES.short:
In-phase component of the complex first-order plasma-temperature
eigenfunction for a specified toroidal Fourier harmonic in linear MHD
stability analysis.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the real, in-phase component of the first-order
plasma-temperature perturbation associated with one toroidal Fourier
harmonic. It is a component of the complex eigenfunction represented by
perturbed plasma temperature.

The in-phase component is defined from the complex perturbation amplitude by

$$
\delta T_{\mathrm{R}} = \operatorname{Re}\!\left(\delta T\right)
$$

where $\delta T_{\mathrm{R}}$ is the real temperature-perturbation component
and $\delta T$ is the full complex first-order temperature eigenfunction.
The result depends on the phase reference chosen for the harmonic and
excludes the quadrature component represented by the imaginary part. It is
not the equilibrium temperature or the complete complex perturbation.

sources.leaf_definition: Real part
sources.parent_definition: Perturbed temperature for given toroidal mode number

NAMES.name: plasma_velocity
NAMES.short:
Mass-weighted bulk center-of-mass velocity vector of the plasma fluid, whose
projections onto the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) coordinate
directions provide the radial, toroidal, vertical, and parallel flow
components.
NAMES.long:
The plasma velocity is the local center-of-mass (barycentric) flow velocity
of the bulk plasma, representing the momentum per unit mass carried
collectively by all plasma species. It is the primary kinematic quantity in
single-fluid and multi-fluid magnetohydrodynamic descriptions of plasma
transport, rotation, and momentum confinement.

The center-of-mass velocity vector is defined as:

$$
\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{cm} = \frac{\sum_s m_s n_s \mathbf{v}_s}{\sum_s m_s n_s}
$$

where the sum runs over all contributing plasma species $s$, $m_s$ is the
species mass, $n_s$ is the number density, and $\mathbf{v}_s$ is the mean
fluid velocity of species $s$.

The full velocity vector decomposes into projections along the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame: the [radial
component](name:radial_plasma_velocity) along $\hat{R}$, the [toroidal
component](name:toroidal_center_of_mass_velocity) along $\hat{\phi}$, the
[vertical component](name:vertical_plasma_velocity) along $\hat{Z}$, and the
[parallel component](name:parallel_plasma_velocity) along the local
magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{b}$. Individual projections are inferred
from Doppler spectroscopy, charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, and
motional-Stark-effect diagnostics; Mach probes provide parallel-flow access
in the scrape-off layer.

NAMES.name: parallel_plasma_velocity
NAMES.short:
Parallel component of the bulk plasma center-of-mass velocity along the
local magnetic-field direction, representing field-aligned mass transport of
all contributing species.
NAMES.long:
The parallel plasma velocity is the projection of the bulk [plasma
velocity](name:plasma_velocity) onto the local magnetic-field direction. It
represents the mass-weighted flow of all contributing plasma species along
magnetic field lines.

The parallel component is defined by:

$$
v_\parallel = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{cm} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}, \qquad \hat{\mathbf{b}} = \frac{\mathbf{B}}{|\mathbf{B}|}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{cm}$ is the center-of-mass plasma velocity,
$\mathbf{B}$ is the local magnetic-field vector, $|\mathbf{B}|$ is its
magnitude, and $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the corresponding unit vector. Unlike
the [radial plasma velocity](name:radial_plasma_velocity), this quantity
follows the local magnetic-field direction rather than the outward
major-radius direction.

The quantity is a bulk-plasma projection, not a species-resolved flow or a
diamagnetic-drift velocity.

sources.leaf_definition: One scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.
sources.parent_definition: Parallel (to magnetic field) component of the plasma velocity, given on various grid subsets

NAMES.name: perturbed_plasma_velocity
NAMES.short:
Complex vector eigenfunction of the first-order bulk plasma velocity
perturbation in linear MHD stability analysis, encoding the spatial
amplitude and phase of oscillatory plasma flow for a specified toroidal
Fourier mode.
NAMES.long:
In linear MHD stability theory, the perturbed plasma velocity is the complex
vector eigenfunction $\delta\hat{\mathbf{v}}(\mathbf{r})$ representing the
spatial structure of the first-order oscillatory perturbation of the bulk
plasma flow about a magnetohydrostatic equilibrium — the linearized
counterpart to the equilibrium [plasma_velocity](name:plasma_velocity). The
eigenfunction encodes both the spatial amplitude and the relative phase of
the velocity oscillation as a function of position in the plasma.

The full space-time perturbation field is assembled as:

$$
\delta\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{r},t) = \delta\hat{\mathbf{v}}(\mathbf{r})\,e^{i(n\phi - \omega t)}
$$

where $n$ is the toroidal mode number, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, and $\omega$ is the complex
mode frequency whose real part gives the oscillation frequency and imaginary
part gives the growth or damping rate. In ideal MHD the eigenfunction
satisfies $\delta\hat{\mathbf{v}} = -i\omega\boldsymbol{\xi}$, where
$\boldsymbol{\xi}$ is the plasma displacement vector.

The eigenfunction decomposes into three spatial projections:
[radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity),
[toroidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity),
and
[poloidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity),
all complex-valued. The overall amplitude and phase are
normalization-dependent unless anchored to a physical constraint such as
kinetic energy. The growth rate of the associated mode is characterized by
[per_toroidal_mode_growth_rate](name:per_toroidal_mode_growth_rate) and the
spatial phase reference by mode_phase; companion scalar perturbed
eigenfunctions include
[perturbed_plasma_temperature_real_part](name:perturbed_plasma_temperature_real_part)
and
[perturbed_plasma_pressure_imaginary_part](name:perturbed_plasma_pressure_imaginary_part).

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_halo_boundary
NAMES.short:
Poloidal magnetic flux evaluated on the outermost flux surface of the
halo-current region during a disruption. This is the wall-side halo boundary
of the halo-current domain, not the inner confined-plasma interface.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux at the halo boundary is the value of the [poloidal
magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) function on the outermost
magnetic flux surface of the halo-current region during a disruption. The
halo boundary is the wall-side flux-surface limit of the halo-current
domain, not the inner interface between that domain and any confined-plasma
core.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major
radius, $\phi$ the toroidal angle, and $Z$ the vertical height, the value on
a halo-boundary point $(R_h, Z_h)$ is defined by the flux of the vertical
magnetic field through the horizontal disk centered on the toroidal symmetry
axis:

$$
\psi_h = \psi(R_h, Z_h) = \int_0^{R_h} B_Z(R', Z_h)\,2\pi R'\,dR'
$$

where $\psi_h$ is the poloidal magnetic flux at the halo boundary,
$\psi(R_h, Z_h)$ is the poloidal magnetic flux function evaluated on that
boundary, and $B_Z$ is the vertical component of the magnetic field.

This quantity is the poloidal-flux counterpart of the [toroidal magnetic
flux at the halo boundary](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_halo_boundary). It
is a flux-surface value and does not denote the total magnetic flux through
the halo-current volume or the halo current itself.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $B_Z$ on the integration disk points in the
$+Z$ direction.

sources.leaf_definition: Poloidal flux at halo region boundary
sources.parent_definition: Global quantities

NAMES.name: poloidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity
NAMES.short:
Poloidal component of the complex first-order plasma velocity perturbation
eigenfunction in linear MHD stability analysis, projected onto the poloidal
direction in the flux-coordinate frame (ρ, θ, φ) for a single toroidal
Fourier mode.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal perturbed plasma velocity is the $\theta$-directed component of
the linearized plasma velocity perturbation eigenfunction
$\delta\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{r})$, obtained by projecting the full complex
perturbation vector onto the poloidal basis direction in the flux-coordinate
frame $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$, where $\rho$ is a radial flux surface label
and $\theta$ is the poloidal angle. It characterizes the oscillatory
poloidal plasma flow about a magnetohydrostatic equilibrium for a specified
toroidal Fourier mode number $n$, encoding both the spatial amplitude and
phase variation of that flow component along and across flux surfaces.

The physical perturbation follows the eigenfunction ansatz:

$$
\delta v_\theta(\rho, \theta, \phi, t) = \mathrm{Re}\!\left[\delta\hat{v}_\theta(\rho, \theta)\, e^{i(n\phi - \omega t)}\right]
$$

where $\delta\hat{v}_\theta(\rho, \theta)$ is the complex poloidal amplitude
profile, $n$ is the toroidal mode number, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle
increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $\omega$
is the complex MHD eigenfrequency whose imaginary part gives the mode growth
or damping rate.

The complex amplitude decomposes into its [real
part](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part) and [imaginary
part](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_imaginary_part), which
together specify the amplitude and spatial phase of the poloidal velocity
oscillation at each point on a flux surface. Alongside the [radial
component](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part) and the
[toroidal component](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part), the
poloidal projection completes the velocity eigenfunction and supports
incompressibility assessment and MHD energy partition calculations in linear
stability solvers.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the poloidal velocity is directed in the
direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate frame
$(\rho, \theta, \phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_imaginary_part
NAMES.short:
Quadrature poloidal velocity component of a complex first-order
plasma-velocity perturbation eigenfunction for a specified toroidal Fourier
harmonic. It is the imaginary part of the projection onto the positive
poloidal direction, paired with the in-phase real part.
NAMES.long:
Quadrature poloidal velocity component of a complex first-order
plasma-velocity perturbation eigenfunction is the imaginary part of the
poloidal projection of that eigenfunction for a specified toroidal Fourier
harmonic. The poloidal direction is the unit vector $\hat{\mathbf e}_\theta$
toward increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in a flux-coordinate basis
$(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, with $\phi$ the toroidal angle of the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is
vertical height.

The projected component and its imaginary part are defined by

$$
v_{\theta,\mathrm{im}} = \operatorname{Im}\!\left(\tilde v_\theta\right), \qquad \tilde v_\theta = \tilde{\mathbf v}\cdot\hat{\mathbf e}_\theta
$$

where $\tilde{\mathbf v}$ is the complex first-order plasma-velocity
perturbation eigenfunction, $\tilde v_\theta$ is its poloidal component, and
$v_{\theta,\mathrm{im}}$ is the coefficient of the imaginary term when
$\tilde v_\theta = v_{\theta,\mathrm{re}} + i v_{\theta,\mathrm{im}}$.

This quantity is the quadrature component paired with the [poloidal
perturbed plasma velocity real
part](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part); together they
specify the complex [poloidal perturbed plasma
velocity](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity) for the chosen harmonic
and phase convention. It is distinct from the corresponding [toroidal
perturbed plasma velocity imaginary
part](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_imaginary_part), which
projects the same complex velocity perturbation onto the toroidal direction.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the quadrature component of $\tilde{\mathbf
v}\cdot\hat{\mathbf e}_\theta$ is aligned with $+\hat{\mathbf e}_\theta$,
toward increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate basis
$(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

sources.leaf_definition: Imaginary part
sources.parent_definition: Second coordinate (poloidal)

NAMES.name: poloidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part
NAMES.short:
Real part of the poloidal perturbed plasma velocity is the in-phase
component of the complex first-order plasma-velocity amplitude for toroidal
mode number n, resolved tangent to increasing poloidal angle in the
flux-coordinate basis (ρ, θ, φ). The toroidal angle φ is that of the
right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame; equilibrium flow and the
quadrature component are excluded.
NAMES.long:
Real part of the poloidal perturbed plasma velocity is the in-phase
component of the complex first-order plasma-velocity perturbation amplitude
for one toroidal Fourier harmonic with mode number $n$. The poloidal
component is resolved along the local basis direction tangent to increasing
poloidal angle $\theta$ in a specified flux-coordinate basis
$(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, with $\phi$ the toroidal angle of the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius, $Z$ is vertical
height, and $\phi$ increases counterclockwise when viewed from above
$+\hat{Z}$. It is distinct from equilibrium plasma flow.

For a complex poloidal amplitude in that flux-coordinate basis, the real
part is defined by:

$$
v_{\theta,1}^{\mathrm{Re}}(\rho,\theta;n) = \operatorname{Re}\!\left[\tilde{v}_{\theta,1}(\rho,\theta;n)\right]
$$

where $v_{\theta,1}^{\mathrm{Re}}$ is this real poloidal perturbation
amplitude, $\tilde{v}_{\theta,1}$ is the [poloidal perturbed plasma
velocity](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity), $\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_1$
is the complex first-order plasma-velocity perturbation eigenfunction for
harmonic $n$, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$ is the local normalized direction
tangent to increasing $\theta$ with
$\tilde{v}_{\theta,1}=\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_1\cdot\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$,
$\rho$ is the radial flux label, and $n$ is the toroidal Fourier mode
number.

Together with [poloidal perturbed plasma velocity imaginary
part](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_imaginary_part), this quantity
specifies the complex poloidal velocity amplitude for the selected harmonic.
It is not the full real-space poloidal velocity at a particular toroidal
angle; the dependence on $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$
frame is supplied by the chosen Fourier harmonic convention. Multiplication
of the complex eigenfunction by a constant phase factor changes the split
between real and imaginary parts without changing the underlying linear
mode, so a fixed phase reference is required for this real component.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the real first-order velocity perturbation
component projects along $+\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$, the local direction of
increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate basis
$(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, after the complex eigenmode phase reference is fixed.

sources.leaf_definition: Real part
sources.parent_definition: Second coordinate (poloidal)

NAMES.name: radial_mode_number
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless non-negative integer labeling the radial branch of a linear
MHD eigenmode by its number of radial nodes between the magnetic axis and
plasma boundary.
NAMES.long:
Radial mode number is a dimensionless integer branch index that specifies
the radial branch of a linear MHD perturbation. It identifies radial
structure rather than periodicity in either angular direction.

The radial branch index is defined by

$$
n_r = N_{\mathrm{nodes}}[\xi(\rho)]
$$

where $n_r$ is the radial mode number, $\xi(\rho)$ is the radial
eigenfunction, $N_{\mathrm{nodes}}$ counts its interior zeros, and $\rho$ is
the radial coordinate within the flux-coordinate set $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$;
the count is taken between the magnetic axis and the plasma boundary.

The radial mode number is one component of the mode number, distinct from
the angular harmonics represented by the [poloidal mode
number](name:poloidal_mode_number) and [toroidal MHD mode
number](name:toroidal_mhd_mode_number).

sources.leaf_definition: Radial mode number
sources.parent_definition: Vector of toroidal modes. Each mode is described as exp(i(n_tor.phi - m_pol.theta - 2.pi.frequency.t - phase))

NAMES.name: radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity
NAMES.short:
Radial component of the complex first-order plasma velocity perturbation
eigenfunction for a specified toroidal Fourier mode in linear MHD stability
analysis, abstracting over its real and imaginary scalar parts.
NAMES.long:
The radial perturbed plasma velocity is the radial projection of the full
complex eigenfunction of
[perturbed_plasma_velocity](name:perturbed_plasma_velocity), characterizing
the component of first-order oscillatory plasma flow directed along the
major-radius coordinate $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$
frame. This component is central to stability analyzes of interchange,
ballooning, and peeling modes, where cross-field plasma displacement drives
the instability.

The physical time-domain radial perturbation is recovered as:

$$
\delta v_r(\mathbf{r}, t) = \mathrm{Re}\!\left[\delta\hat{v}_r(\mathbf{r})\, e^{-i\omega t}\right]
$$

where $\omega$ is the complex mode eigenfrequency and
$\delta\hat{v}_r(\mathbf{r})$ is the complex scalar radial eigenfunction
amplitude. As a complex phasor, it decomposes into the [real
part](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part)
$\mathrm{Re}(\delta\hat{v}_r)$, the in-phase fluid-velocity amplitude, and
the [imaginary part](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity_imaginary_part)
$\mathrm{Im}(\delta\hat{v}_r)$, the quadrature component relative to the
chosen eigenmode phase normalization. The radial plasma displacement
eigenfunction is related by $\xi_r = \delta\hat{v}_r / (-i\omega)$, linking
fluid velocity to flux-surface deformation.

This eigenfunction component is evaluated by linear MHD eigenvalue solvers
as part of the full toroidal Fourier harmonic decomposition of the perturbed
velocity field. It contributes to the per_toroidal_mode_perturbed_energy
alongside poloidal and toroidal velocity components, and couples to
eigenfunction components such as
[perturbed_plasma_pressure_real_part](name:perturbed_plasma_pressure_real_part)
through the linearized momentum equation.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the radial fluid motion is directed in the
direction of increasing major radius $R$.

NAMES.name: radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity_imaginary_part
NAMES.short:
Imaginary part of the complex amplitude of the radial plasma-velocity
perturbation for toroidal harmonic index n in linear MHD stability analysis.
Radial denotes the component along the R direction in the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Imaginary part of the complex amplitude of the radial plasma-velocity
perturbation is the quadrature component of the cylindrical $R$ projection
of the first-order plasma velocity eigenfunction for a specified toroidal
harmonic index $n$. The radial projection is along $\hat{R}$ in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame with basis
$(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is
toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The complex radial perturbation amplitude and its contribution to the
single-mode physical perturbation are represented by

$$
\delta v_R^{\mathrm{phys},(n)}(\mathbf{x},t)
=
\operatorname{Re}\!\left[
\left(\delta v_{R,\mathrm{re}}^{(n)}(\mathbf{x})
+i\,\delta v_{R,\mathrm{im}}^{(n)}(\mathbf{x})\right)
e^{i(n\phi-\omega t)}
\right]
$$

where $\delta v_{R,\mathrm{im}}^{(n)}$ is this quantity, $\delta
v_{R,\mathrm{re}}^{(n)}$ is
[radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part),
$\delta v_R^{\mathrm{phys},(n)}$ is the corresponding real physical
perturbation component, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\phi$ is the toroidal
angle of that position, $t$ is time, $\omega$ is the complex mode angular
frequency under the chosen temporal phase convention, $n$ is the integer
toroidal harmonic index, and $i$ is the imaginary unit.

The real and imaginary parts together reconstruct the complex radial
amplitude
[radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity). A
change of the arbitrary global eigenmode phase rotates these two parts, so
this imaginary part is meaningful only with the same phase reference and
eigenfunction normalization as the other perturbation components. It is the
cylindrical $R$ component, not a flux-surface-normal component and not a
component perpendicular to the magnetic field.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $\delta v_{R,\mathrm{im}}^{(n)}$ points in
the $+\hat{R}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Imaginary part
sources.parent_definition: First coordinate (radial)

NAMES.name: radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part
NAMES.short:
In-phase radial fluid-velocity component obtained from the real part of a
complex linear-MHD perturbation eigenfunction for a specified toroidal
Fourier mode.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed, in-phase radial component of the complex
first-order plasma-velocity eigenfunction. It is the real-part component of
[radial perturbed plasma velocity](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity),
not the velocity magnitude or its imaginary quadrature component.

$$
v_{r,\mathrm{Re}}(R,Z;n)=\operatorname{Re}\!\left[\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_1(R,Z;n)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{R}}\right]
$$

Here $\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_1$ is the complex perturbed plasma-velocity
eigenfunction, $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the radial unit vector, $R$ is major
radius, $Z$ is vertical height, and $n$ is the toroidal Fourier mode number,
all expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. The real
part depends on the selected eigenmode phase and normalization.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the radial perturbation velocity points
toward increasing major radius $R$.

sources.leaf_definition: Real part
sources.parent_definition: First coordinate (radial)

NAMES.name: radial_width_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode
NAMES.short:
Radial width of a neoclassical tearing mode is the full magnetic-island span
along the major-radius direction at a specified time.
NAMES.long:
Width of neoclassical tearing mode

The full width is defined by

$$
w(t) = R_+(t) - R_-(t)
$$

where $w$ is the full island width, $t$ is time, and $R_+$ and $R_-$ are the
larger and smaller major-radius coordinates of the opposite
island-separatrix intersections along a major-radius line through the island
center. Major radius $R$ measures distance from the toroidal symmetry axis
in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $\phi$ is
toroidal angle and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity describes an individual mode at each time, not a sum over modes
or a temporal average. It is the full width, not the half-width. Its value
at onset is the seed-island width; the same quantity describes the island
size during subsequent evolution.

This width is the island-size variable in the generalized Rutherford
equation. Its [radial-width time
derivative](name:radial_width_time_derivative_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode)
is $dw/dt$, which describes instantaneous island growth or shrinkage.

sources.leaf_definition: Full width of the mode
sources.parent_definition: Detailed NTM evolution on a finer timebase than the time_slice array of structure

sources.leaf_definition: Seed island full width at onset time
sources.parent_definition: NTM onset characteristics

sources.leaf_definition: Full width of the mode
sources.parent_definition: List of the various NTM modes appearing during the simulation. If a mode appears several times, use several indices in this array of structure with the same m,n values.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_plasma_upper_bound_current_to_plasma_initial_current_due_to_disruption
NAMES.short:
Fraction of the pre-disruptive plasma current represented by the upper
threshold used to define a custom linear current-quench decay interval.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the user-defined upper current threshold, expressed as a
fraction of the pre-disruptive plasma current during a disruption current
quench.

$$
X_2 = \frac{I_{\mathrm{upper}}}{I_{\mathrm{initial}}}
$$

where $X_2$ is the upper threshold fraction, $I_{\mathrm{upper}}$ is the
plasma current at that threshold, and $I_{\mathrm{initial}}$ is the
pre-disruptive plasma current.

The threshold is paired with a lower fraction $X_1$ to define a custom
linear decay interval, whose effective decay time is
$(t(X_2)-t(X_1))/(X_1-X_2)$; $t(X_j)$ is the time at which the plasma
current reaches fraction $X_j$ of its pre-disruptive value. This quantity is
a threshold fraction, not a decay time, unlike the [thermal energy decay
time due to disruption](name:thermal_energy_decay_time_due_to_disruption).

sources.leaf_definition: User-defined value, see description of linear_custom
sources.parent_definition: Decay time defined as (t(X2)-t(X1))/(X1-X2), where t(Xj) corresponds to the time where this quantity reaches Xj*100% of its pre-disruptive value

NAMES.name: reference_phase
NAMES.short:
Reference phase is the signed angular offset that fixes the phase origin of
a complex oscillatory perturbation relative to a chosen zero-phase
reference.
NAMES.long:
Reference phase is the signed angular offset that sets the phase origin for
a complex oscillatory perturbation relative to a chosen zero-phase
reference. It parameterizes a phase gage: changing it rotates the complex
amplitude without changing invariant perturbation properties such as
magnitude, growth rate, or eigenfunction shape.

A perturbation quantity $\tilde{q}$ whose zero-phase representation is
$\tilde{q}_0$ is shifted by the reference phase $\alpha$ as:

$$
\tilde{q} = \tilde{q}_0 \exp(i\alpha)
$$

where $\alpha$ is the reference phase and $\tilde{q}_0$ is the complex
perturbation at the chosen zero-phase reference.

This parent quantity covers reference phases that choose the complex phase
origin of perturbations, including the [mode reference
phase](name:mode_reference_phase). It is not a physical propagation phase, a
geometric position angle, or a phase difference between two independent
signals unless that phase difference specifically defines the chosen
reference offset.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the applied phase factor advances the
perturbation by increasing its complex argument relative to the zero-phase
reference.

NAMES.name: mode_reference_phase
NAMES.short:
Mode reference phase is the signed angular offset that sets the complex
phase origin of an oscillatory mode relative to its zero-phase reference. It
shifts the represented mode in phase without changing its amplitude,
frequency, or mode identifiers.
NAMES.long:
Mode reference phase is the scalar phase offset applied to the complex
representation of an oscillatory mode to define its phase origin. It is a
representation parameter for the mode as a whole, not a local value of the
oscillating physical field.

A modal perturbation can be represented with the reference phase added to
the modal phase argument:

$$
\delta f(\xi) = \Re\left\{\hat{f}(\xi)\exp\left[i\left(\Theta(\xi,t)+\varphi_\mathrm{ref}\right)\right]\right\}
$$

where $\delta f$ is the physical perturbation, $\hat{f}$ is its complex mode
amplitude, $\Theta$ is the modal phase argument excluding the reference
offset, and $\varphi_\mathrm{ref}$ is the mode reference phase.

This quantity fixes the arbitrary complex phase gage of a mode
representation; it does not define the mode frequency, mode number,
amplitude, or spatial eigenfunction. The [MHD mode reference
phase](name:mhd_mode_reference_phase) is the magnetohydrodynamic
specialization of this generic mode-level quantity.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the offset increases the modal phase argument
in the complex exponential representation.

NAMES.name: mhd_mode_reference_phase
NAMES.short:
Signed angular offset that fixes the complex phase of a mode relative to its
zero-phase reference.
NAMES.long:
A mode reference phase is the angular offset applied to a complex
perturbation or eigenfunction to establish its phase relative to a
zero-phase reference. It specifies phase orientation without defining the
mode number, amplitude, or geometric position angle.

For a complex mode amplitude, the reference phase is represented by

$$
\tilde{X} = |\tilde{X}| e^{i\phi_{\rm ref}}
$$

where $\tilde{X}$ is the complex perturbation amplitude, $|\tilde{X}|$ is
its magnitude, and $\phi_{\rm ref}$ is the reference phase. The quantity
generalizes the phase used by
[linear_mhd_mode_reference_phase](name:linear_mhd_mode_reference_phase) and
is the phase component of [mode_reference_phase](name:mode_reference_phase).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the complex mode phase is advanced in the
defined angular direction from its zero-phase reference.

NAMES.name: linear_mhd_mode_reference_phase
NAMES.short:
Signed angular offset that fixes the phase origin of a linear MHD eigenmode
relative to its zero-phase complex representation.
NAMES.long:
A reference phase is a signed angular offset that establishes the phase
origin of a complex linear magnetohydrodynamic perturbation or eigenmode.
For a vector of phase components, each component applies to the
corresponding angular dependence of the mode.

For one phase component, the offset rotates the zero-phase eigenfunction
according to

$$
\delta\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{x}) = \Re\left\{\hat{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{x})e^{i\phi_{\rm ref}}\right\}
$$

where $\delta\mathbf{X}$ is the real perturbation, $\hat{\mathbf{X}}$ is its
zero-phase complex eigenfunction, $\phi_{\rm ref}$ is the reference phase,
$\mathbf{x}$ is position, $i$ is the imaginary unit, and $\Re$ denotes the
real part. The quantity is the phase offset itself, not the mode amplitude,
mode number, or oscillation frequency. Poloidal and toroidal components
share this definition; the [toroidal linear MHD mode reference
phase](name:toroidal_linear_mhd_mode_reference_phase) is a concrete toroidal
instance, while [MHD mode reference phase](name:mhd_mode_reference_phase)
denotes the broader angular reference.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the complex phase is advanced in the positive
angular direction of the selected mode representation relative to its
zero-phase reference; for a toroidal component, this is increasing toroidal
angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$
is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

NAMES.name: rotation_frequency_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode
NAMES.short:
Instantaneous angular rate of phase evolution of an individual neoclassical
tearing mode, with its sign distinguishing phase advance from phase
regression.
NAMES.long:
The angular rotation frequency of a neoclassical tearing mode is the
instantaneous signed rate at which its phase changes. It applies to an
individual mode, without averaging over modes or over a time interval.

The defining relation is:

$$
\omega_{\mathrm{NTM}}(t) = \frac{d\Phi_{\mathrm{NTM}}(t)}{dt}
$$

where $\omega_{\mathrm{NTM}}$ is the mode's angular rotation frequency,
$\Phi_{\mathrm{NTM}}$ is its [phase](name:neoclassical_tearing_mode_phase),
followed continuously across complete turns, and $t$ is time.

This quantity describes mode-pattern phase motion, not the material angular
velocity of the plasma. It is distinct from the [cyclic rotation
frequency](name:frequency_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode): when both refer to
the same rotation phase, the angular rate equals $2\pi$ times the cyclic
rate. Its time derivative is the [angular acceleration of the
mode](name:rotation_frequency_time_derivative_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode),
not the rotation frequency itself.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the continuously followed mode phase
increases with time.

sources.leaf_definition: Time derivative of the phase of the mode
sources.parent_definition: Detailed NTM evolution on a finer timebase than the time_slice array of structure

sources.leaf_definition: Time derivative of the phase of the mode
sources.parent_definition: List of the various NTM modes appearing during the simulation. If a mode appears several times, use several indices in this array of structure with the same m,n values.

NAMES.name: sawtooth_period
NAMES.short:
Time interval between successive sawtooth crash events, representing the
duration of one complete sawtooth oscillation cycle in a tokamak plasma.
NAMES.long:
The sawtooth period is the elapsed time from one sawtooth crash to the next
consecutive crash, including the intervening growth and relaxation phases.

For successive crash times $t_k$ and $t_{k+1}$, the period is defined by

$$
T_{\mathrm{st}} = t_{k+1} - t_k
$$

where $T_{\mathrm{st}}$ is the sawtooth period and $t_k$ is the time of the
$k$th crash. The quantity refers to the temporal spacing of consecutive
crash events, not the duration of the crash itself or the duration of the
preceding growth phase alone.

sources.leaf_definition: Previous sawtooth period
sources.parent_definition: Detailed information about the sawtooth characteristics

NAMES.name: toroidal_halo_current
NAMES.subject: halo
NAMES.short:
Toroidal component of the electric current carried by halo plasma on open
magnetic field lines between the last closed flux surface and first wall
during a disruption.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal halo current is the toroidal component of the electric-current
vector carried by halo plasma on open magnetic field lines between the last
closed flux surface and the first wall during a disruption. It is the
toroidal member of the vector quantity [halo current](name:halo_current).

The component is defined by

$$
I_{\phi} = \mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{halo}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{halo}}$ is the integrated halo-current vector and
$\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal unit vector in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Unlike [poloidal halo
current](name:poloidal_halo_current), this component measures current along
the direction of increasing toroidal angle and excludes the poloidal
component.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the halo current flows in the direction of
increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

sources.leaf_definition: Toroidal halo current
sources.parent_definition: Global quantities

NAMES.name: toroidal_impurity_ion_velocity_at_measurement_position
NAMES.subject: impurity_ion
NAMES.short:
Toroidal component of the bulk-flow velocity of an impurity-ion population,
evaluated at a specified measurement position.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the impurity-ion bulk-flow velocity projected onto the
toroidal direction at the specified measurement position. It is a signed
velocity component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

$$
v_\phi(\mathbf{x}_m)=\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{imp}}(\mathbf{x}_m)\cdot\hat{\phi}
$$

where $v_\phi$ is the toroidal velocity component, $\mathbf{x}_m$ is the
measurement position, $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{imp}}$ is the bulk velocity of
the impurity-ion population, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the
direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

For an impurity population combined over charge states, the bulk velocity is
the density-weighted mean over the included charge states. The species and
charge-state aggregation must be interpreted from the defined population;
the related [toroidal ion velocity](name:toroidal_ion_velocity) provides the
corresponding generic ion quantity.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the impurity-ion flow points in the direction
of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

sources.leaf_definition: One scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.
sources.parent_definition: Toroidal component of the plasma velocity, given on various grid subsets

NAMES.name: toroidal_linear_mhd_mode_reference_phase
NAMES.short:
Signed angular offset that fixes the complex phase of a linear MHD
perturbation’s toroidal Fourier mode relative to its zero-phase reference.
NAMES.long:
The reference phase is the angular offset assigned to the complex
eigenfunction of a linear MHD perturbation with a specified toroidal
harmonic. It fixes the mode’s phase origin and is not a spatial displacement
or amplitude.

Using the complex-amplitude convention, the toroidal dependence of a
perturbation quantity is written as:

$$
\widetilde{Q}(R,Z,\phi)=\widehat{Q}(R,Z)\exp\!\left[i\left(n\phi+\phi_{\mathrm{ref}}\right)\right]
$$

where $\widetilde{Q}$ is the complex perturbation, $\widehat{Q}$ is its
complex amplitude, $n$ is the dimensionless integer toroidal mode number,
$\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $\phi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the reference phase.
$R$ and $Z$ are the major-radius and vertical coordinates in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. The toroidal harmonic is
identified by mode number, while its phase is carried by quantities such as
the [toroidal perturbed plasma magnetic
field](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field).

The reference phase does not specify perturbation amplitude, growth rate,
oscillation frequency, or temporal phase.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the complex mode phase advances in the
direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Additional phase offset of mode
sources.parent_definition: Vector of toroidal modes. Each mode is described as exp(i(n_tor.phi - m_pol.theta - 2.pi.frequency.t - phase))

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_halo_boundary
NAMES.short:
Signed toroidal magnetic flux through the poloidal cross-section bounded by
the outermost flux surface of the halo-current region during a disruption.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal magnetic flux function evaluated on the outermost flux surface
bounding the halo-current region during a disruption is the net toroidal
magnetic-field flux through the enclosed poloidal cross-section. It is
distinct from the [toroidal halo current](name:toroidal_halo_current), which
describes current rather than magnetic flux.

The flux is defined by

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathcal{A}_h)=\int_{\mathcal{A}_h}\mathbf{B}\cdot\hat{\phi}\,dA=\int_{\mathcal{A}_h}B_{\phi}\,dA
$$

where $\mathcal{A}_h$ is the poloidal area enclosed by the halo boundary,
$\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in tesla, $\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal
unit vector, $B_{\phi}$ is its toroidal component, and $dA$ is the poloidal
area element. The boundary value is the halo-region counterpart of [toroidal
magnetic flux at the plasma
boundary](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the toroidal magnetic field points in the
direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Toroidal flux at halo region boundary
sources.parent_definition: Global quantities

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_halo_boundary_due_to_poloidal_current
NAMES.short:
Toroidal magnetic flux at the halo boundary due to poloidal current is the
signed flux through the poloidal cross-section bounded by the outermost
halo-region flux surface, retaining only the toroidal magnetic-field
contribution generated by poloidal halo current. It excludes contributions
from all other current systems.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal magnetic flux at the halo boundary due to poloidal current is the
signed toroidal magnetic flux through the poloidal cross-section bounded by
the outermost halo-region flux surface. It contains only the magnetic-field
contribution generated by the
[poloidal_halo_current](name:poloidal_halo_current), the poloidal component
of halo current.

Let $S_h$ be the area enclosed by the halo-boundary contour in a plane of
constant toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi,
Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise
when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height. With the
oriented surface element $d\mathbf{S}=+\hat{\phi}\,dA$, the flux is

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{tor},h}^{(\mathrm{pol})} = \int_{S_h} \mathbf{B}_h^{(\mathrm{pol})}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \int_{S_h} B_{\phi,h}^{(\mathrm{pol})}\,dA
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor},h}^{(\mathrm{pol})}$ denotes this quantity,
$\mathbf{B}_h^{(\mathrm{pol})}$ is the magnetic-field contribution from
poloidal halo current, $B_{\phi,h}^{(\mathrm{pol})}$ is its component along
$+\hat{\phi}$ in tesla, $d\mathbf{S}$ is the oriented surface element in
square meters, and $dA$ is the corresponding scalar area element in square
meters.

This quantity is the poloidal-current source component of
[toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_halo_boundary](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_halo_boundary),
which includes all magnetic-field sources. It excludes toroidal flux
contributions generated by any current other than poloidal halo current and
is distinct from
[poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_halo_boundary](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_halo_boundary),
which concerns poloidal magnetic flux at the same halo boundary.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the magnetic-field contribution generated by
the poloidal halo current crosses $S_h$ in the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction of
the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Toroidal flux at halo region boundary generated by the plasma poloidal current
sources.parent_definition: Global quantities

NAMES.name: toroidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity
NAMES.short:
Toroidal component of the complex first-order plasma velocity perturbation
eigenfunction in linear MHD stability analysis, encoding the amplitude and
phase of toroidal bulk plasma oscillation for a specified Fourier mode.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal perturbed plasma velocity $\delta\hat{v}_\phi$ is the
projection of the complex vector eigenfunction
$\delta\hat{\mathbf{v}}(\mathbf{r})$ representing first-order oscillatory
perturbations of bulk plasma flow in linear MHD onto the $\hat{\phi}$
direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is
major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. For each toroidal Fourier harmonic
$n$, this component captures how the bulk plasma oscillates along the
toroidal direction about the magnetostatic equilibrium.

As a complex scalar, it decomposes into real and imaginary parts:

$$
\delta\hat{v}_\phi(\mathbf{r}) = \mathrm{Re}[\delta\hat{v}_\phi] + i\,\mathrm{Im}[\delta\hat{v}_\phi]
$$

where $\mathrm{Re}[\delta\hat{v}_\phi]$ is given by
[toroidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part)
and $\mathrm{Im}[\delta\hat{v}_\phi]$ by
[toroidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_imaginary_part](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_imaginary_part);
together they encode the spatial amplitude and phase of the toroidal flow
perturbation for the eigenmode.

This is the toroidal projection of the full vector eigenfunction described
by [perturbed_plasma_velocity](name:perturbed_plasma_velocity); analogous
complex structures exist for radial and poloidal projections, such as
[radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part)
and
[poloidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part).
The relative magnitudes of toroidal, poloidal, and radial components
characterize the mode polarization; the eigenfunction is evaluated by linear
MHD eigenvalue solvers applied to a reconstructed magnetostatic equilibrium.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $\delta\hat{v}_\phi$ points in the direction
of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_imaginary_part
NAMES.short:
Imaginary part of the complex amplitude of the mode-n toroidal
plasma-velocity perturbation in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z)
frame. It is the φ component of a single toroidal Fourier harmonic and is
not the equilibrium toroidal flow.
NAMES.long:
The imaginary part of the complex amplitude of the mode-$n$ toroidal
plasma-velocity perturbation is the coefficient of $i$ in the toroidal
component of the first-order plasma velocity perturbation for a single
toroidal Fourier harmonic. The toroidal component is the projection onto
$\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$
is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is
a perturbation eigenfunction component, not the equilibrium toroidal flow.

For a harmonic with phase dependence proportional to $e^{i(n\phi-\omega
t)}$, the full complex toroidal component combines this quantity with the
matched real part
[toroidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part):

$$
\delta \hat{v}_{\phi,n}(R,Z) = \delta \hat{\mathbf{v}}_n(R,Z)\cdot\hat{\phi} = \operatorname{Re}\!\left[\delta \hat{v}_{\phi,n}(R,Z)\right] + i\,\operatorname{Im}\!\left[\delta \hat{v}_{\phi,n}(R,Z)\right]
$$

where $\delta \hat{\mathbf{v}}_n$ is the complex first-order velocity
amplitude for toroidal mode number $n$, $\delta \hat{v}_{\phi,n}$ is its
toroidal projection, $\omega$ is the mode angular frequency in the phase
factor, and $i$ is the imaginary unit.

This quantity is defined for one specified toroidal mode number $n$;
contributions from other toroidal harmonics are excluded. A global phase
rotation of the eigenfunction changes the split between real and imaginary
parts, so this component must be interpreted with the matched real part and
the chosen eigenfunction phase reference.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the imaginary coefficient of the toroidal
velocity perturbation is directed along $\hat{\phi}$, the direction of
increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi,
Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Imaginary part
sources.parent_definition: Third coordinate (toroidal)

NAMES.name: toroidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part
NAMES.short:
Toroidal perturbed plasma velocity real part is the real part of the complex
amplitude of the toroidal component of the first-order plasma velocity
perturbation for a single toroidal Fourier harmonic with mode number n in
the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. It is the in-phase
eigenfunction component relative to the chosen complex phase, not the
equilibrium toroidal flow.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal perturbed plasma velocity real part is the real part of the complex
amplitude of the toroidal component of the first-order plasma velocity
perturbation for a single toroidal Fourier harmonic with mode number $n$.
The toroidal component is the projection along $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$,
the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is
vertical height. It represents the in-phase part of the linear
magnetohydrodynamic perturbation eigenfunction relative to the chosen
complex phase, not the equilibrium toroidal flow.

The component is defined by projecting the complex velocity eigenfunction
for the selected harmonic onto the toroidal basis direction and taking the
real part:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{Re},n}(R,Z) = \operatorname{Re}\!\left[\widetilde{\mathbf v}_n(R,Z)\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}\right]
$$

where $v_{\phi,\mathrm{Re},n}$ is this quantity, $\widetilde{\mathbf v}_n$
is the complex first-order plasma velocity eigenfunction for toroidal mode
number $n$, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is the toroidal unit vector, and
$\operatorname{Re}$ denotes the real part. With toroidal dependence
proportional to $\exp(i n\phi)$, $i$ is the imaginary unit.

Together with [toroidal perturbed plasma velocity imaginary
part](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_imaginary_part), this quantity
forms the complex toroidal perturbed velocity amplitude. Because a linear
eigenfunction may be multiplied by an arbitrary complex constant, the
division into real and imaginary parts depends on the selected normalization
and phase; the quadrature component is the linked imaginary part, not a
separate physical velocity direction.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the real toroidal velocity component points
in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Real part
sources.parent_definition: Third coordinate (toroidal)

NAMES.name: vertical_plasma_velocity
NAMES.short:
Vertical component of the bulk plasma center-of-mass velocity along the Z
direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, representing
vertical mass transport of all contributing plasma species.
NAMES.long:
The vertical plasma velocity is the projection of the bulk [plasma
velocity](name:plasma_velocity) onto the vertical basis direction $\hat{Z}$
of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, whose basis is
$(\hat{R}, \hat{\phi}, \hat{Z})$. It represents the mass-weighted
center-of-mass flow of all contributing plasma species in the vertical
direction.

The projected component is defined by:

$$
v_Z = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{plasma} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $v_Z$ is the vertical plasma velocity, $\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{plasma}$ is
the bulk [plasma velocity](name:plasma_velocity), and $\hat{Z}$ is the
vertical basis vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity applies to the bulk plasma mixture wherever a local fluid
center-of-mass velocity is defined. It uses the same aggregation convention
as the parent plasma velocity: species velocities are weighted by mass
density and combined over all contributing plasma species. It is a scalar
cylindrical projection, not the full velocity vector, not a vertical
position or displacement, and not a species-resolved velocity.

Together with the [radial plasma velocity](name:radial_plasma_velocity) and
the [toroidal center-of-mass
velocity](name:toroidal_center_of_mass_velocity), it forms the cylindrical
component decomposition of the bulk [plasma velocity](name:plasma_velocity).
The [parallel plasma velocity](name:parallel_plasma_velocity) is a separate
projection onto the local magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{b}$ and is not
generally identical to the vertical component.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the plasma center-of-mass velocity has a
component in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction, toward increasing vertical coordinate
$Z$.

sources.leaf_definition: One scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.
sources.parent_definition: Z component of the plasma velocity, given on various grid subsets

NAMES.name: vorticity
NAMES.short:
Vorticity is the curl of the plasma bulk velocity field, measuring the
signed local angular rotation of fluid elements. It is the parent quantity
for radial, toroidal, vertical, and field-aligned projections of that curl.
NAMES.long:
Vorticity is the curl of the plasma bulk velocity field and represents the
local rotational content of the single-fluid plasma flow. For solid-body
rotation it is twice the angular-velocity vector of a fluid element.

The vorticity field $\boldsymbol{\omega}$ is defined by the curl of the
plasma bulk velocity field:

$$
\boldsymbol{\omega} = \nabla \times \mathbf{v}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\omega}$ is the vorticity field, $\mathbf{v}$ is the
plasma bulk velocity, and $\nabla \times$ is the curl operator with
right-handed orientation.

The scope is the local magnetohydrodynamic plasma bulk-flow field at a point
in the plasma. The bare name carries no surface, volume, time, species, or
charge-state aggregation. It is not vorticity magnitude, flow shear, strain
rate, divergence, or magnetic-field-line twist.

The unqualified quantity is the parent for scalar directional projections of
the same curl. [Radial vorticity](name:radial_vorticity), [toroidal
vorticity](name:toroidal_vorticity), and [vertical
vorticity](name:vertical_vorticity) are projections onto $\hat{R}$,
$\hat{\phi}$, and $\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$
frame, respectively; [parallel vorticity](name:parallel_vorticity) is the
projection along the local magnetic-field direction. The bare name does not
designate a poloidal projection.

Related quantities: [poloidal_vorticity](name:poloidal_vorticity).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $\boldsymbol{\omega}$ has a positive
projection on the stated scalar direction: $+\hat{R}$, $+\hat{\phi}$, or
$+\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, or the
local magnetic-field direction for a field-aligned projection.

sources.leaf_definition: One scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.
sources.parent_definition: Vorticity, given on various grid subsets

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_sawtooth_mixing_radius
NAMES.short:
Normalized toroidal-flux surface label evaluated at the sawtooth mixing
radius, marking the outer boundary of the plasma region homogenized during a
sawtooth crash.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the normalized toroidal magnetic-flux label of the magnetic
surface passing through the sawtooth mixing radius. It identifies the outer
boundary of the plasma region homogenized during a sawtooth crash.

The coordinate is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(r_{\mathrm{mix}}) = \left(\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(r_{\mathrm{mix}}) - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}\right)^{1/2}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(r_{\mathrm{mix}})$ is the normalized
toroidal flux coordinate at the mixing radius, $r_{\mathrm{mix}}$ is the
sawtooth mixing radius, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(r_{\mathrm{mix}})$ is the
toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the mixing surface,
$\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux at the magnetic
axis, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux at
the equilibrium boundary.

The scope is the single magnetic surface at the sawtooth mixing radius
within the plasma region affected by the crash. This is a locus-specific
evaluation of the broader [normalized toroidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate), not a coordinate
assigned to every magnetic surface, a volume average, or a flux-surface
average. It is distinct from the corresponding coordinate at the [sawtooth
inversion
radius](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_sawtooth_inversion_radius),
because the mixing radius and inversion radius represent different sawtooth
characteristics.

sources.leaf_definition: Normalized toroidal flux coordinate at mixing radius
sources.parent_definition: Detailed information about the sawtooth characteristics

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode_center
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless magnetic-surface label locating the resonant flux surface at
the center of a neoclassical tearing-mode magnetic island.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the normalized toroidal-flux label of the magnetic surface
passing through the center of a neoclassical tearing-mode magnetic island.
It identifies the island’s resonant surface rather than describing the
island’s helical phase or radial extent.

At the island center, the normalized toroidal-flux coordinate is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = \left(\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}\right)^{1/2}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the normalized toroidal-flux coordinate,
$\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the enclosed toroidal magnetic flux at the island
center, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}$ is its value at the magnetic axis, and
$\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}}$ is its value at the equilibrium boundary.

The quantity applies to the center, or resonant-surface location, of one
specified neoclassical tearing-mode island and is a pointwise
magnetic-surface label, not an average over the island or a sum over modes.
It is not a cylindrical radial distance, a local vector component, or the
unnormalized toroidal-flux radius represented by [toroidal flux coordinate
at the neoclassical tearing-mode
center](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode_center).

It is the locus-specific evaluation of the parent [normalized toroidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate) at the neoclassical
tearing-mode center. The island’s helical orientation is described
separately by its [neoclassical tearing-mode
phase](name:neoclassical_tearing_mode_phase).

sources.leaf_definition: Normalized flux coordinate on which the mode is centred
sources.parent_definition: List of the various NTM modes appearing during the simulation. If a mode appears several times, use several indices in this array of structure with the same m,n values.

NAMES.name: perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field
NAMES.short:
The perturbed vacuum magnetic field is the complex first-order vector
eigenfunction of the magnetic-field perturbation for a single toroidal
harmonic in the current-free vacuum region surrounding the plasma. It is
defined relative to the background vacuum magnetic field and excludes the
equilibrium field while retaining all spatial components.
NAMES.long:
The perturbed vacuum magnetic field $\tilde{\delta\mathbf{B}}_\mathrm{vac}$
is the complex first-order vector eigenfunction of the magnetic-field
perturbation for a single toroidal harmonic in the current-free exterior
domain surrounding the plasma. It is defined relative to the background
[vacuum magnetic field](name:vacuum_magnetic_field), retains all spatial
components, and excludes the equilibrium field itself.

For this single-toroidal-mode quantity, the real time-dependent perturbation
is reconstructed from the complex amplitude by

$$
\delta\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac}(R,\phi,Z,t) = \operatorname{Re}\!\left[\tilde{\delta\mathbf{B}}_\mathrm{vac}(R,Z)\exp\!\left(i n\phi - i\omega t\right)\right]
$$

where $\delta\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac}$ is the real magnetic-field
perturbation, $\tilde{\delta\mathbf{B}}_\mathrm{vac}$ is the complex
eigenfunction defined here, $(R,\phi,Z)$ is the right-handed cylindrical
frame with $R$ major radius, $\phi$ the toroidal angle increasing
counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ vertical
height, $t$ is time, $\operatorname{Re}$ takes the real part, $i$ is the
imaginary unit, $n$ is the [toroidal MHD mode
number](name:toroidal_mhd_mode_number), and $\omega$ is the angular
eigenfrequency. The chosen temporal factor fixes the phase convention; using
the opposite temporal factor complex-conjugates the eigenfunction, and the
overall complex scale and phase are set only by an explicit normalization.

In the current-free vacuum domain, absence of free current and magnetic
monopoles requires
$\nabla\times\tilde{\delta\mathbf{B}}_\mathrm{vac}=\mathbf{0}$ and
$\nabla\cdot\tilde{\delta\mathbf{B}}_\mathrm{vac}=0$, where $\nabla$ is the
spatial derivative operator and $\mathbf{0}$ is the zero vector.
Equivalently, $\tilde{\delta\mathbf{B}}_\mathrm{vac}=-\nabla\delta\Phi$ with
$\nabla^2\delta\Phi=0$, where $\delta\Phi$ is the scalar magnetic potential
of the perturbation; this potential is defined up to an additive constant.
At the plasma-vacuum interface, the normal component of this vacuum
perturbation is the exterior counterpart of the plasma-side perturbed
magnetic field used for interface matching.

The scope is the current-free vacuum region outside the plasma and inside
the relevant conducting or far-field boundary; it does not include
current-carrying plasma regions or free-current regions in material
structures. The quantity is one complex vector for one toroidal mode number,
with no averaging over phase, space, or mode number and no summation over
multiple toroidal harmonics. It is distinct from scalar field strength, from
the unperturbed [vacuum magnetic field](name:vacuum_magnetic_field), and
from any real physical perturbation before the normal-mode reconstruction is
applied.

The vector decomposes in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame as
projections on $\hat{R}$, $\hat{\phi}$, and $\hat{Z}$; the
[radial](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field) and
[toroidal](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field) quantities are
component projections of the same complex eigenfunction. The [poloidal
projection](name:poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field) is defined
relative to the explicitly chosen flux-coordinate system $(s,\theta,\phi)$
for that component and is not the cylindrical $Z$ projection. The
decomposition
$\tilde{\delta\mathbf{B}}_\mathrm{vac}=\tilde{\delta\mathbf{B}}_{\mathrm{vac},\mathrm{Re}}+i\tilde{\delta\mathbf{B}}_{\mathrm{vac},\mathrm{Im}}$
separates real and imaginary phase quadratures; component quantities such as
the [radial real
part](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part), [radial
imaginary part](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part),
and [poloidal real
part](name:poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part) are
projections or quadratures of this parent vector.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when a real component projection of the
reconstructed perturbation points along its positive basis direction, with
$+\hat{R}$ increasing major radius, $+\hat{\phi}$ increasing toroidal angle
$\phi$, and $+\hat{Z}$ increasing vertical height in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field
NAMES.short:
Complex poloidal component of the first-order magnetic-field perturbation
eigenfunction in the current-free vacuum region outside the plasma boundary,
for a single toroidal Fourier mode in linear MHD stability analysis.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal component of the perturbed vacuum magnetic field is the
projection of the first-order magnetic-field eigenfunction onto the poloidal
direction in the current-free exterior region, where $\nabla \times
\delta\mathbf{B} = 0$ and $\nabla \cdot \delta\mathbf{B} = 0$. In this
vacuum region the perturbation derives from a Laplace-scalar magnetic
potential, and the poloidal projection is one of the three components
characterizing the full spatial structure of the eigenfunction. The complex
representation — its [real
part](name:poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part) and
[imaginary
part](name:poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part) together
— encodes amplitude and phase of the mode, arising from the toroidal Fourier
expansion for a single mode number $n$.

The poloidal projection is defined as:

$$
\delta B_\theta = \delta\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta
$$

where $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$ is the poloidal unit vector and
$\delta\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the full complex first-order vacuum
magnetic-field perturbation described by the parent
[perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field](name:perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field).

This component enters the plasma-vacuum interface matching conditions in
linear stability analysis, coupling the vacuum eigenfunction to the
plasma-region solution to determine free-boundary MHD stability. It
complements the toroidal counterpart documented in
[toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part)
and
[toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part)
in characterizing the angular structure of the eigenmode outside the plasma.
The eigenfunction amplitude is normalization-dependent; only its value
relative to the plasma-region solution carries physical meaning for
stability assessments.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $\delta B_\theta$ points in the direction of
increasing poloidal angle $\theta$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part
NAMES.short:
Imaginary component of the complex poloidal projection, along the
increasing-θ tangent in flux coordinates (ρ, θ, φ), of the first-order
magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction in the current-free vacuum region
outside the plasma boundary for a specified toroidal Fourier mode.
NAMES.long:
Imaginary component of the complex poloidal projection, along the
increasing-$\theta$ tangent in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, of the
first-order magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction in the current-free
vacuum region outside the plasma boundary for a specified toroidal Fourier
mode. It is a signed scalar magnetic-field amplitude of the complex vacuum
perturbation.

The complex poloidal vacuum perturbation amplitude is decomposed into real
and imaginary parts by:

$$
\delta B_{\theta}^{(V)}(\rho,\theta;n) = \operatorname{Re}\{\delta B_{\theta}^{(V)}(\rho,\theta;n)\} + i\,\operatorname{Im}\{\delta B_{\theta}^{(V)}(\rho,\theta;n)\}
$$

where $\delta B_{\theta}^{(V)}$ is the component of $\delta\mathbf{B}^{(V)}$
along the unit poloidal tangent
$\hat{e}_{\theta}=(\partial\mathbf{x}/\partial\theta)_{\rho,\phi}/|(\partial\mathbf{x}/\partial\theta)_{\rho,\phi}|$
in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\rho$
is the selected magnetic-flux-surface label, $\theta$ is the poloidal angle,
$\phi$ is the toroidal angle, $n$ is the integer toroidal Fourier mode
number, $i$ is the imaginary unit, and $\operatorname{Re}$ and
$\operatorname{Im}$ denote the real-part and imaginary-part operators. The
quantity named here is $\operatorname{Im}\{\delta B_{\theta}^{(V)}\}$, and
all magnetic-field amplitudes in the equation have units of tesla.

The superscript $V$ denotes the vacuum-region perturbation and excludes
perturbations in the plasma region. In that region the first-order
perturbation is current-free and solenoidal, satisfying
$\nabla\times\delta\mathbf{B}^{(V)}=0$ and
$\nabla\cdot\delta\mathbf{B}^{(V)}=0$. This quantity is paired with
[poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part](name:poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part);
a common complex rescaling of a linear eigenfunction changes absolute
amplitude and phase but not the component identity defined here.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the imaginary part of the poloidal projection
is directed along the unit tangent for increasing $\theta$ in flux
coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

sources.leaf_definition: Imaginary part
sources.parent_definition: Second coordinate (poloidal)

NAMES.name: poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part
NAMES.short:
Real part of the single-toroidal-mode poloidal perturbed vacuum magnetic
field, equal to the in-phase projection of the complex first-order vacuum
magnetic-field perturbation onto the poloidal unit tangent outside the
plasma.
NAMES.long:
Real part of the single-toroidal-mode poloidal perturbed vacuum magnetic
field is the in-phase scalar component of the complex first-order vacuum
magnetic-field perturbation projected onto the poloidal unit tangent outside
the plasma. The poloidal unit tangent is defined in a specified
flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ as the direction of increasing
poloidal angle $\theta$ at fixed $\rho$ and $\phi$, where $\phi$ is the
toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame with basis
$(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$. This poloidal direction is a local
flux-coordinate tangent, not a cylindrical-basis direction.

The real poloidal vacuum perturbation amplitude is defined by projecting the
complex vacuum perturbation onto the poloidal unit tangent and taking the
real part:

$$
\delta B_{\theta,\mathrm{real}}^{\mathrm{vac}}(\rho,\theta;n) = \operatorname{Re}\!\left[\delta\mathbf{B}^{\mathrm{vac}}(\rho,\theta;n) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}\right]
$$

where $\delta B_{\theta,\mathrm{real}}^{\mathrm{vac}}$ is this real poloidal
vacuum perturbation amplitude, $\delta\mathbf{B}^{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the
complex first-order [perturbed vacuum magnetic
field](name:perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field) amplitude, $n$ is the integer
toroidal mode number, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}$ is the poloidal unit
tangent defined above.

The vacuum qualifier restricts the quantity to the current-free region
exterior to the plasma, where the first-order perturbation satisfies
$\nabla\times\delta\mathbf{B}^{\mathrm{vac}}=0$ and
$\nabla\cdot\delta\mathbf{B}^{\mathrm{vac}}=0$. For a single toroidal mode,
the complex poloidal amplitude is reconstructed as $\delta
B_{\theta}^{\mathrm{vac}}=\delta
B_{\theta,\mathrm{real}}^{\mathrm{vac}}+i\,\delta
B_{\theta,\mathrm{imag}}^{\mathrm{vac}}$ and enters the toroidal dependence
through the factor $\exp(i n\phi)$; this quantity is the real part of that
mode amplitude, not a poloidal Fourier coefficient. It is distinct from the
[imaginary-part
counterpart](name:poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part),
the [radial](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part) and
[toroidal](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part) vacuum
projections, and the corresponding [plasma-region
component](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the in-phase magnetic-field perturbation
component points along $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}$, the unit tangent toward
increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ at fixed $\rho$ and $\phi$ in the
specified flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

sources.leaf_definition: Real part
sources.parent_definition: Second coordinate (poloidal)

NAMES.name: radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field
NAMES.short:
Complex first-order radial component of the magnetic-field perturbation
eigenfunction in the current-free vacuum outside the plasma, forming part of
a single-toroidal-mode linear MHD perturbation.
NAMES.long:
The radial component of the perturbed vacuum magnetic field is the
projection of the complex first-order magnetic-field eigenfunction onto the
cylindrical radial direction in the current-free exterior region. It is one
component of the full [perturbed vacuum magnetic
field](name:perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field), which satisfies source-free
Maxwell conditions in the vacuum.

The component is defined by

$$
\delta B_R = \delta\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac} \cdot \hat{R}
$$

where $\delta\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac}$ is the perturbed vacuum magnetic-field
vector, $\hat{R}$ is the radial unit vector, and $\delta B_R$ is its radial
projection in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. The radial
direction means increasing major radius $R$, not the normal to a magnetic
flux surface.

The complex value retains the eigenfunction amplitude and phase; its
in-phase and quadrature coefficients are represented by the [real radial
component](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part) and
[imaginary radial
component](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part). In
the current-free vacuum, the perturbation obeys
$\nabla\times\delta\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac}=0$ and
$\nabla\cdot\delta\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac}=0$.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the radial component is directed along
increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$
frame.

NAMES.name: radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part
NAMES.short:
Imaginary part of the complex radial component of the linearized
magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction in the current-free vacuum region
outside the plasma, for a specified toroidal Fourier mode in linear MHD
stability analysis.
