sources.parent_definition: List of the various NTM modes appearing during the simulation. If a mode appears several times, use several indices in this array of structure with the same m,n values.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_runaway_electron_kinetic_energy_density
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short:
Mean relativistic kinetic energy per unit volume of the runaway electron
population, obtained by averaging the local kinetic energy density over the
confined plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged runaway electron kinetic energy density is a global
scalar characterizing the mean suprathermal energy stored per unit volume in
the runaway electron (RE) population. It is obtained by integrating the
local relativistic kinetic energy density over the total confined plasma
volume $V$ and dividing by $V$.

The underlying local quantity is the relativistic kinetic energy moment of
the RE distribution function:

$$
u_\mathrm{RE}(\mathbf{r}) = \int f_\mathrm{RE}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{p})\,(\gamma - 1)\,m_e c^2 \, d^3p
$$

where $f_\mathrm{RE}$ is the runaway electron phase-space distribution
function, $\gamma = (1 + p^2 / m_e^2 c^2)^{1/2}$ is the Lorentz factor,
$m_e$ is the electron rest mass, $c$ is the speed of light, and $\mathbf{p}$
is the relativistic momentum. The volume average is then $\langle
u_\mathrm{RE} \rangle = V^{-1} \int_V u_\mathrm{RE}\,dV$.

This quantity is evaluated from kinetic or reduced-fluid runaway electron
models, particularly in disruption current-quench simulations where RE
populations can reach energies of several to tens of MeV per particle.
Multiplying by the plasma volume $V$ recovers the total stored relativistic
energy given by
[runaway_electron_kinetic_energy](name:runaway_electron_kinetic_energy). The
local non-averaged counterpart is runaway_electron_kinetic_energy_density,
and the corresponding global particle number density is
[volume_averaged_runaway_electron_density](name:volume_averaged_runaway_electron_density).

sources.leaf_definition: Runaways kinetic mean energy density
sources.parent_definition: Volume average runaways parameters

NAMES.name: coolant_absorbed_power_of_calorimetry_component
NAMES.short:
Thermal power removed from a calorimetry component by its coolant,
determined from the coolant enthalpy increase between inlet and outlet.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the instantaneous thermal power transferred from one
calorimetry component into its coolant. It is specific to the named
component and represents coolant-mediated heat extraction rather than a
group-wide or plant-wide power total.

The enthalpy-balance definition is

$$
P_{\mathrm{cool,abs}} = \dot{m}_{c}\left(h_{\mathrm{out}} - h_{\mathrm{in}}\right)
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{cool,abs}}$ is the coolant-absorbed thermal power,
$\dot{m}_{c}$ is the coolant mass flow rate, and $h_{\mathrm{in}}$ and
$h_{\mathrm{out}}$ are the coolant specific enthalpies at the component
inlet and outlet states. The enthalpy difference is evaluated from the
corresponding coolant thermodynamic states, including the inlet and outlet
temperatures.

The quantity excludes heat transferred by channels other than the coolant
and does not denote accumulated energy. Its time integral from pulse start
is the [accumulated coolant-absorbed energy of the calorimetry
component](name:accumulated_coolant_absorbed_energy_of_calorimetry_component),
while this quantity remains the instantaneous component-level extraction
rate. The coolant inlet state is related to the [coolant temperature at
inlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_inlet).

sources.leaf_definition: Power extracted from the component
sources.parent_definition: Set of components on which calorimetry measurements are carried out

NAMES.name: coolant_transit_time_of_plant_component_port
NAMES.short:
Elapsed time for coolant to traverse the associated plant component from
inlet to outlet, defining the thermal delay between the two coolant states.
NAMES.long:
Coolant transit time is the elapsed travel time for the coolant stream to
pass through the plant component associated with the specified port, from
its inlet to its outlet. It represents the transport delay between the inlet
and outlet thermal states.

The transit time is defined as

$$
\tau_{\mathrm{c}} = t_{\mathrm{out}} - t_{\mathrm{in}}
$$

where $\tau_{\mathrm{c}}$ is the coolant transit time, $t_{\mathrm{in}}$ is
the instant when the coolant crosses the component inlet, and
$t_{\mathrm{out}}$ is the instant when the same coolant stream crosses the
component outlet.

The quantity applies to the coolant path through one associated plant
component and uses the inlet-to-outlet interval as its aggregation
convention. It is not a plant-wide sum over components or ports, and it
excludes transport outside the component, instrumentation or network
latency, and a thermal time constant of the component material.

The transit time establishes the temporal correspondence between inlet
conditions and the delayed outlet state represented by the [coolant
temperature at outlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_outlet). It is distinct
from the [coolant mass flow rate](name:coolant_mass_flow_rate), which
describes transported mass per time rather than travel duration, and it
provides the thermal-delay correction relevant to [total thermal coolant
absorbed power at wall](name:total_thermal_coolant_absorbed_power_at_wall).

sources.leaf_definition: Transit time for the coolant to go from the input to the output of the component
sources.parent_definition: Set of components on which calorimetry measurements are carried out

NAMES.name: displacement_of_passive_structure
NAMES.short:
Displacement of a passive structure is the signed linear displacement of a
selected point or defined surface target on a passive component relative to
a reference configuration, projected along a defined positive direction.
NAMES.long:
Displacement of a passive structure is the signed scalar component of the
motion of a selected material point, attachment point, or defined reference
point on a passive structural component relative to a reference
configuration. It is the passive-structure instance of mechanical
displacement, not an absolute position, velocity, acceleration, or strain.

The signed projected displacement is defined by

$$
u(t) = \left[\mathbf{r}(t) - \mathbf{r}_\mathrm{ref}\right] \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_u
$$

where $u(t)$ is the scalar displacement, $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is the current
position vector of the selected point, $\mathbf{r}_\mathrm{ref}$ is the
position vector of the same point in the reference configuration, and
$\hat{\mathbf{e}}_u$ is the unit vector defining the positive direction of
the displacement component. All vectors and the unit direction are expressed
in the same right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame, with
$\hat{z}$ vertical.

The selected point, reference configuration, and positive direction are part
of the semantic definition of any instance. An undeformed, surveyed,
calibrated, initial, or previous-time configuration may serve as
$\mathbf{r}_\mathrm{ref}$ only if that choice is fixed; changing it changes
the displacement, and using a previous-time reference defines an incremental
displacement over the interval. A single value describes one projected local
displacement; deformation or strain requires spatial variation of
displacement or a separate deformation measure.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the selected point is displaced from
$\mathbf{r}_\mathrm{ref}$ in the direction of $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_u$.

sources.leaf_definition: Length measured by a displacement sensor
sources.parent_definition: Set of sensors

NAMES.name: neutral_gas_pressure_of_gauge
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short:
Neutral gas pressure of a gage is the pressure indicated by a barometry gage
for residual neutral gas in the vacuum vessel or surrounding vacuum system.
It represents local vacuum conditions rather than a kinetic neutral-particle
pressure moment.
NAMES.long:
Neutral gas pressure of a gage is the local residual-neutral-gas pressure
indicated by a barometry gage. The word gage identifies the instrument
producing the indication and does not mean a pressure difference relative to
atmosphere.

The quantity applies to neutral gas contributing to the gage response in the
vacuum vessel or surrounding vacuum system. It aggregates the gage response
without resolving thermal, fast, species, or internal-state components.

This instrument-indicated quantity is distinct from kinetic neutral-particle
pressures such as [total neutral pressure](name:total_neutral_pressure),
[thermal neutral pressure](name:thermal_neutral_pressure), [neutral
internal-state pressure](name:neutral_internal_state_pressure), and [total
neutral internal-state
pressure](name:total_neutral_internal_state_pressure). Those quantities
denote pressure moments or state-resolved sums of neutral particle
populations, whereas neutral gas pressure of a gage denotes the pressure
represented by the barometry gage response and need not equal any one
kinetic component.

sources.leaf_definition: Pressure
sources.parent_definition: Set of gauges

NAMES.name: temperature_of_sensor
NAMES.short:
Thermodynamic temperature associated with a selected thermocouple sensor
attached to a tokamak structural component.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the absolute thermodynamic temperature associated with one
selected sensor member, represented by the thermal state at its thermocouple
junction. It characterizes the local thermal condition of the attached
structural component at the sensor location.

For a system in thermodynamic equilibrium, temperature is defined by

$$
T = \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial S}\right)_{V,N}
$$

where $T$ is thermodynamic temperature, $U$ is internal energy, $S$ is
entropy, $V$ is volume, and $N$ is the amount of material or particle number
held fixed in the derivative.

The quantity applies to the selected sensor member individually and is not a
sum, average, or other aggregation over the sensor set. It denotes the
sensor or junction thermal state associated with a structural component, not
the temperature of a flowing coolant or of an entire plant connection.

It is distinct from [coolant temperature at
inlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_inlet), which describes fluid entering a
cooling system. Object-specific quantities such as [temperature of a coil
conductor](name:temperature_of_coil_conductor) and [temperature of a neutron
detector](name:temperature_of_neutron_detector) apply the same thermodynamic
concept to explicitly named hardware rather than to the generic sensor
locus.

sources.leaf_definition: Temperature measured by a thermocouple
sources.parent_definition: Set of sensors

NAMES.name: toroidal_coordinate_of_reciprocating_probe
NAMES.short:
Toroidal angular coordinate of the reciprocating probe’s average measurement
position during a plunge, referenced to the facility’s toroidal-angle
origin.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal coordinate $\bar{\phi}_{\rm probe}$ identifies the azimuthal
location of the reciprocating probe’s average position formed from its
measurement locations. It is an angular coordinate in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \\phi, Z)$ frame.

For an averaged position represented in the right-handed Cartesian $(x,y,z)$
basis, with $z$ aligned with $Z$, the coordinate is defined by

$$
\\bar{\\phi}_{\\rm probe} = \\operatorname{atan2}(\\bar{y}_{\\rm probe}, \\bar{x}_{\\rm probe})
$$

where $\\bar{x}_{\\rm probe}$ and $\\bar{y}_{\\rm probe}$ are the Cartesian
coordinates of the averaged position. This identifies the probe location
analogously to the toroidal coordinate at a [beam tracing
point](name:toroidal_coordinate_at_beam_tracing_point), but the locus here
is the reciprocating probe’s average position.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $\\bar{\\phi}_{\\rm probe}$ increases in the
direction of increasing toroidal angle $\\phi$.

sources.leaf_definition: Toroidal angle
sources.parent_definition: Average position of the measurements derived from multiple collectors

NAMES.name: x_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point
NAMES.short:
Signed Cartesian x coordinate locating the point where a sensor is
mechanically attached to a device component.
NAMES.long:
This quantity gives the x-coordinate of a sensor's mechanical attachment
point relative to the origin of the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$
frame.

The coordinate is defined by

$$
x_{\rm att} = \mathbf{r}_{\rm att} \cdot \hat{x}
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_{\rm att}$ is the position vector of the attachment point
relative to the Cartesian origin and $\hat{x}$ is the unit vector along the
positive x-axis. Together with the [y coordinate of the sensor attachment
point](name:y_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point) and [z coordinate of
the sensor attachment point](name:z_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point),
it specifies the attachment location. A displacement sensor may have two
mechanical attachment points; other sensor types have one.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the attachment point lies in the positive x
direction from the Cartesian origin.

sources.leaf_definition: Component along X axis
sources.parent_definition: Attachement point(s) of the sensor. Two for displacement sensors, one for the other types of sensors

NAMES.name: x_first_measurement_direction_unit_vector_of_strain_gauge
NAMES.short:
Signed direction cosine of a sensor’s unit measurement-direction vector
along the x axis of the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the x-directed component of a sensor’s oriented
measurement-direction vector. It describes orientation rather than the
sensor’s spatial attachment location, which is specified separately by the
[x coordinate of the sensor attachment
point](name:x_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point).

The direction cosine is defined by

$$
d_x = \hat{\mathbf d} \cdot \hat{\mathbf x}
$$

where $\hat{\mathbf d}$ is the sensor’s unit measurement-direction vector
and $\hat{\mathbf x}$ is the unit vector along the x axis of the
right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame. For a normalized
direction vector, $-1 \leq d_x \leq 1$; the corresponding y- and z-axis
components are represented by the [y direction unit vector of the
sensor](name:y_first_measurement_direction_unit_vector_of_strain_gauge) and
[z direction unit vector of the
sensor](name:z_first_measurement_direction_unit_vector_of_strain_gauge).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the sensor’s measurement direction has a
component toward increasing x.

sources.leaf_definition: Component along X axis
sources.parent_definition: Direction of the measurement (unit vector)

NAMES.name: x_second_measurement_direction_unit_vector_of_strain_gauge
NAMES.short:
Signed direction cosine of a strain gage’s second measurement direction
along the x axis of the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the x projection of the unit vector defining a strain gage’s
second measurement direction. It describes orientation, not the gage’s
spatial location or its first measurement direction.

The direction cosine is defined by:

$$
d_{2x} = \hat{\mathbf d}_2 \cdot \hat{\mathbf x}
$$

where $\hat{\mathbf d}_2$ is the unit vector along the second measurement
direction and $\hat{\mathbf x}$ is the x-axis unit vector in the
right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame. Together with
the y direction cosine of the second measurement direction and z direction
cosine of the second measurement direction, it specifies that direction. It
is distinct from the [x coordinate of the sensor attachment
point](name:x_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point), which locates the gage
rather than defining its orientation.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the second measurement direction has a
component along increasing x in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x},
\hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Component along X axis
sources.parent_definition: Second direction of measurement, in case of a rosette straing gauge

NAMES.name: y_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point
NAMES.short:
Signed Cartesian y coordinate of the point where a sensor is mechanically
attached to a device component, in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z)
machine frame with z vertical.
NAMES.long:
Signed Cartesian $y$ coordinate of the point where a sensor is mechanically
attached to a device component is the $\hat{y}$ component of the
attachment-point position. The coordinate is defined in the right-handed
Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis, with $\hat{z}$ vertical and
$(\hat{x}, \hat{y})$ spanning the horizontal plane.

The coordinate is the projection of the attachment-point position vector
onto the $\hat{y}$ basis direction:

$$
y_\mathrm{attach} = \mathbf{r}_\mathrm{attach} \cdot \hat{y}
$$

where $y_\mathrm{attach}$ is this signed coordinate,
$\mathbf{r}_\mathrm{attach}$ is the position vector of the sensor attachment
point relative to the Cartesian frame origin, and $\hat{y}$ is the positive
$y$-direction unit basis vector.

This quantity applies to the mechanical point where the sensor is attached
to a device component. It is not the sensor sensing point, line-of-sight
point, active volume position, sensor centroid, or a separate component
reference point; no averaging or aggregation over multiple attachment points
is implied.

Together with
[x_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point](name:x_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point)
and
[z_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point](name:z_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point),
it specifies the Cartesian position of the same attachment point. This
quantity is only the $y$ component and does not include the $x$ or $z$
components.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the attachment point is displaced in the
$+\hat{y}$ direction of the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y},
\hat{z})$ basis from the frame origin.

sources.leaf_definition: Component along Y axis
sources.parent_definition: Attachement point(s) of the sensor. Two for displacement sensors, one for the other types of sensors

NAMES.name: y_first_measurement_direction_unit_vector_of_strain_gauge
NAMES.short:
Y-axis component of the unit vector along the first measurement axis of a
structural strain-rosette gage, resolved in the right-handed Cartesian (x,
y, z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Y-axis component of the unit vector along the first measurement axis of a
structural strain-rosette gage is the scalar projection of that oriented
measurement-axis unit vector onto the $\hat{y}$ basis direction of the
right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{x}, \hat{y},
\hat{z})$. It is a direction cosine describing gage orientation, not a
strain value.

The component is defined by the dot product:

$$
u_{1y} = \mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \hat{y}
$$

where $u_{1y}$ is this y-axis component, $\mathbf{u}_1$ is the unit vector
along the first measurement axis of the structural strain-rosette gage, and
$\hat{y}$ is the y basis vector of the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$
frame.

Together with the corresponding x-axis component and z-axis component, it
specifies the full orientation of the first measurement axis and satisfies
the unit-vector normalization $u_{1x}^2 + u_{1y}^2 + u_{1z}^2 = 1$. It is
distinct from the y-axis component of the unit vector along the second
measurement axis.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the unit vector along the first measurement
axis of the structural strain-rosette gage has a component in the $+\hat{y}$
direction of the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Component along Y axis
sources.parent_definition: Direction of the measurement (unit vector)

NAMES.name: y_second_measurement_direction_unit_vector_of_strain_gauge
NAMES.short:
Signed y-axis direction cosine of the unit vector along a strain gage’s
second measurement direction in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the y-axis direction cosine of the unit vector defining a
strain gage’s second measurement direction. For a strain rosette, it
describes the orientation of that local sensing axis, not the gage’s spatial
location.

The component is defined by

$$
d_y = \hat{\mathbf{d}}_2 \cdot \hat{\mathbf{y}}
$$

where $\hat{\mathbf{d}}_2$ is the unit vector along the second measurement
direction and $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is the positive y-axis unit vector of the
right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame. Its value is one component of the
orientation represented by the corresponding x-axis second measurement
direction and z-axis second measurement direction. It is distinct from the
[y coordinate of the sensor attachment
point](name:y_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point), which locates the gage
rather than specifying its orientation.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the second measurement direction has a
component toward increasing y.

sources.leaf_definition: Component along Y axis
sources.parent_definition: Second direction of measurement, in case of a rosette straing gauge

NAMES.name: z_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point
NAMES.short:
Z coordinate of the point where a sensor is mechanically attached to a
device component, expressed in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame
with z vertical.
NAMES.long:
Z coordinate of the point where a sensor is mechanically attached to a
device component is the signed vertical Cartesian coordinate of the fixed
mechanical attachment point in the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame.
The $hat{z}$ direction is vertical and is aligned with $hat{Z}$ of the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius,
$\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

Let $\mathbf{r}_a$ be the position vector of the attachment point and
$\mathbf{r}_0$ the origin of the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame.
The coordinate is the projection on the vertical basis vector of that frame:

$$
z_a = (\mathbf{r}_a - \mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \hat{z}
$$

where $z_a$ is the sensor-attachment-point z coordinate and $\hat{z}$ is the
vertical unit vector of the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame.

Together with
[x_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point](name:x_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point)
and
[y_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point](name:y_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point),
this quantity locates the same mechanical attachment reference point. It is
not the sensor sensitive point, line-of-sight reference point, or
orientation vector. The zero level is the plane $z=0$ through the origin of
the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame; for a midplane-centered frame
this plane is the machine midplane.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the attachment point lies in the $+\hat{z}$
direction from the plane $z=0$ of the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$
frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Component along Z axis
sources.parent_definition: Attachement point(s) of the sensor. Two for displacement sensors, one for the other types of sensors

NAMES.name: z_first_measurement_direction_unit_vector_of_strain_gauge
NAMES.short:
Signed z-axis component of the unit vector along a strain gage's first
measurement direction in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame, with z
vertical.
NAMES.long:
Signed z-axis component of the unit vector along a strain gage's first
measurement direction is the scalar direction cosine of that
strain-sensitive direction with the vertical basis direction of the
right-handed Cartesian frame with basis $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$. It
represents the vertical part of the orientation of the gage's first defined
measurement direction.

The component is defined by the scalar projection of the first
measurement-direction unit vector:

$$
u_z^{(1)} = \mathbf{u}^{(1)} \cdot \hat{z}
$$

where $\mathbf{u}^{(1)}$ is the unit vector along the strain gage's first
measurement direction, $\hat{z}$ is the vertical basis vector of the
right-handed Cartesian frame with basis $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$, and
$u_z^{(1)}$ is the signed z-axis component of that unit vector.

The scope is one strain gage and its first defined measurement direction; no
averaging, summation, or aggregation over gages or measurement directions is
implied. This quantity is a direction component, not a position coordinate,
displacement, or strain value, and it is distinct from the corresponding
component of the second measurement direction.

Together with the x-axis component $u_x^{(1)}$ and y-axis component
$u_y^{(1)}$, it specifies the orientation of the first measurement
direction; because $\mathbf{u}^{(1)}$ is a unit vector, $(u_x^{(1)})^2 +
(u_y^{(1)})^2 + (u_z^{(1)})^2 = 1$.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the first measurement-direction unit vector
has a component in the $+\hat{z}$ direction of the right-handed Cartesian
frame with basis $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$.

sources.leaf_definition: Component along Z axis
sources.parent_definition: Direction of the measurement (unit vector)

NAMES.name: z_second_measurement_direction_unit_vector_of_strain_gauge
NAMES.short:
Signed z-axis direction cosine of a strain gage’s second
measurement-direction unit vector in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z)
frame.
NAMES.long:
The second measurement-direction unit vector of a strain gage specifies the
orientation of its second sensing axis. Its z-axis direction cosine is the
signed projection of that orientation onto the Cartesian z axis.

$$
d_{2z} = \hat{\mathbf{d}}_2 \cdot \hat{\mathbf{z}}
$$

where $d_{2z}$ is the z-axis direction cosine, $\hat{\mathbf{d}}_2$ is the
unit vector along the second measurement direction, and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$
is the unit vector of the z axis in the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$
frame. For a unit direction vector, $-1 \leq d_{2z} \leq 1$. The
second-direction component complements the z-axis direction cosine of the
first measurement direction and is distinct from the [z coordinate of the
sensor attachment point](name:z_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point),
which specifies location rather than orientation.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the second measurement direction has a
component toward increasing $z$.

sources.leaf_definition: Component along Z axis
sources.parent_definition: Second direction of measurement, in case of a rosette straing gauge

NAMES.name: back_surface_neutron_flux
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short:
Back-surface neutron flux is the scalar energy flux carried by fusion
neutrons escaping through the back surface of an applicable component or
module. It is aggregated over neutron energies, fusion reaction channels,
and reacting populations; it is not a maximum over the surface.
NAMES.long:
Back-surface neutron flux is the scalar surface density of power carried by
fusion neutrons crossing outward through the back surface of the applicable
component or module. It characterizes the local neutron energy load at that
rear surface, not a vector flux and not a surface aggregate.

The local scalar flux $q_n$ at a point $\boldsymbol{r}$ on the back surface
is defined by

$$
q_n(\boldsymbol{r}) = \frac{dP_{n,\mathrm{out}}}{dA}(\boldsymbol{r})
$$

where $q_n$ is the back-surface neutron flux, $\boldsymbol{r}$ is a point on
the back surface, $P_{n,\mathrm{out}}$ is the power carried by fusion
neutrons crossing outward through that surface, and $A$ is area on the back
surface.

The scope is the back surface only: the surface opposite the front or
plasma-facing side of the object under consideration. The quantity is
aggregated over neutron energies, fusion reaction channels, and reacting
populations unless a more specific standard name states a narrower
selection.

This quantity excludes neutron source strength in a volume, total neutron
power integrated over an area, flux at other surfaces, and any extremum
selected over the back surface. A surface aggregate such as [maximum
back-surface neutron flux](name:maximum_of_back_surface_neutron_flux) is
obtained by taking the maximum value of this quantity over the applicable
back surface; the maximum operation is not part of
`back_surface_neutron_flux` itself.

The area integral of $q_n$ over a chosen part of the back surface gives the
neutron power crossing outward through that part, while the local value
remains the surface-density quantity defined at each point.

NAMES.name: first_local_tangential_width_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short:
Full transverse extent of the rectangular collimating aperture associated
with a neutron detector, measured between its edges along the aperture’s
first local tangential direction.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the full transverse width of the neutron detector’s
collimating aperture along its first local tangential direction. It
describes the aperture opening rather than the external detector body,
housing, or shielding.

The width is defined by

$$
w_1 = x_{1,\max} - x_{1,\min}
$$

where $w_1$ is the first local tangential aperture width, and $x_{1,\max}$
and $x_{1,\min}$ are the positions of the two aperture edges along the first
local tangential axis.

This quantity applies only to a rectangular aperture and represents the
complete edge-to-edge opening dimension, not a radius or half-width. The
other transverse dimension is represented by the second local tangential
width of the neutron detector, whereas a circular opening is characterized
by the [radius of the neutron detector](name:radius_of_neutron_detector)
rather than by rectangular widths.

sources.leaf_definition: Full width of the aperture in the X1 direction, used only if geometry_type = 3
sources.parent_definition: Description of a set of collimating apertures

NAMES.name: maximum_of_back_surface_neutron_flux
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short:
Maximum neutron energy flux escaping through the rear surface of a breeding
blanket module toward vessel structures.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the greatest local neutron energy flux crossing outward
through the rear surface of one breeding blanket module. It measures the
escaping neutron load relevant to attenuation toward vessel structures.

The maximum is defined from the local back-surface neutron energy flux as

$$
q_{n,\max} = \max_{\mathbf{x}\in S_{\mathrm{back}}} q_n(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $q_n(\mathbf{x})$ is the local neutron energy flux at surface position
$\mathbf{x}$, and $S_{\mathrm{back}}$ is the rear surface of the module.

The quantity applies to fusion neutrons from all included neutron energies,
fusion reaction channels, and reacting populations, aggregated into a single
local energy-flux value before taking the maximum over the rear surface of
one module. It represents neutrons escaping outward from the module and
excludes a surface-integrated module power and neutron flux incident on the
module's front surface.

It is the maximum-over-surface transformation of [back-surface neutron
flux](name:back_surface_neutron_flux), which describes the local value
without selecting its maximum. It is distinct from [incident neutron power
of a breeder blanket
module](name:incident_neutron_power_of_breeder_blanket_module), which is the
total neutron power arriving at the module, and from [nuclear heating power
of a breeder blanket
module](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_module), which
describes energy deposited by neutron interactions within the module.

sources.leaf_definition: Maximum neutron flux escaping from the back of the blanket module
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities at various time slices

NAMES.name: neutron_response_function_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short:
Green-function coefficient giving expected neutron-detector counts from one
neutron emitted in a specified plasma voxel and energy bin.
NAMES.long:
The neutron-detector response function is the expected registered count
contribution from a neutron emitted in a specified plasma voxel and
neutron-energy bin. It characterizes the detector-specific mapping from
neutron emission to detected events.

The response enters the forward relation

$$
N_d = \sum_v \sum_k G_d(v,E_k)\,S(v,E_k)
$$

where $N_d$ is the total expected count for detector $d$, $G_d(v,E_k)$ is
this response function, $v$ labels a plasma voxel, $E_k$ labels the $k$th
neutron-energy bin, and $S(v,E_k)$ is the neutron yield from voxel $v$ in
that bin.

The quantity applies to one neutron detector and to the contribution of a
specified source voxel and energy bin; its count response is aggregated over
the detector events attributable to that source contribution. It is not the
neutron emissivity, the geometric acceptance alone, or an energy-dependent
efficiency alone. The geometric distinction is given by [solid angle of a
neutron detector](name:solid_angle_of_neutron_detector), while [spectral
efficiency of a hard X-ray
detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_hard_xray_detector) illustrates an
efficiency quantity that does not represent this neutron-specific
source-to-count response.

sources.leaf_definition: Number of events occurring in the detector from one neutron energy bin emitted by the current plasma voxel towards the detector
sources.parent_definition: Green function coefficients used to represent the detector response based on its field of view

NAMES.name: total_neutron_rate
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short:
Total neutron emission rate produced by deuterium–tritium,
deuterium–deuterium, and tritium–tritium fusion reactions in the plasma.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the aggregate number of neutrons emitted per unit time by
fusion reactions in the plasma.

The total rate is the sum of the neutron-emission rates from the included
fusion channels:

$$
S_n = R_{n,\mathrm{DT}} + R_{n,\mathrm{DD}} + R_{n,\mathrm{TT}}
$$

where $S_n$ is the total neutron emission rate, and $R_{n,\mathrm{DT}}$,
$R_{n,\mathrm{DD}}$, and $R_{n,\mathrm{TT}}$ are the neutron-emission rates
from deuterium–tritium, deuterium–deuterium, and tritium–tritium fusion
reactions, respectively.

The quantity includes all three stated fusion reaction channels and their
combined neutron production; it is not restricted to a single reaction
channel, neutron energy group, or local spatial region. It represents an
aggregate emission rate rather than a neutron flux per unit area.

The [deuterium–tritium neutron flux](name:deuterium_tritium_flux) describes
the deuterium–tritium channel contribution, which is included in this total
together with the deuterium–deuterium and tritium–tritium contributions.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Total neutron rate from all reactions

NAMES.name: neutron_flux_at_first_wall
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short:
Neutron-carried energy flux arriving at the plasma-facing first-wall
surface, providing the carrier-specific local contribution to energy
delivered from the plasma to first-wall material.
NAMES.long:
Neutron energy flux at the plasma-facing first-wall surface is the local
rate of neutron-carried energy delivered per unit surface area. It is the
neutron-specific contribution to the energy flux associated with plasma
loading of the first wall.

$$
q_n(\mathbf{x}) = \int_0^\infty E\,\Phi_n(E,\mathbf{x})\,dE
$$

where $q_n(\mathbf{x})$ is the local neutron energy flux, $\mathbf{x}$ is a
position on the first-wall surface, $E$ is neutron energy, and
$\Phi_n(E,\mathbf{x})$ is the differential neutron number flux at that
position and energy.

This quantity is local on the first-wall surface, integrates over neutron
energy, and includes only the neutron carrier. It is not integrated over the
surface and does not include photon, charged-particle, or other plasma-wall
energy carriers. It describes energy arriving at the surface rather than
nuclear energy deposited throughout the wall volume, which is represented by
[nuclear power density of breeder blanket
layer](name:nuclear_power_density_of_breeder_blanket_layer).

The quantity contributes to the total local energy flux represented by
[flux_at_first_wall](name:flux_at_first_wall). The representative
[neutron_flux_maximum_at_first_wall](name:neutron_flux_maximum_at_first_wall)
is obtained by taking the maximum of $q_n(\mathbf{x})$ over the relevant
first-wall surface, while this parent quantity remains the local
carrier-specific flux.

NAMES.name: neutron_flux_maximum_at_first_wall
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short:
Maximum neutron flux at the first wall of a breeding-blanket module is the
largest local neutron energy flux on that module first-wall surface,
identifying the highest local neutron loading relevant to material damage
and blanket lifetime.
NAMES.long:
Maximum neutron flux at the first wall of a breeding-blanket module is the
largest local neutron energy flux on the module first-wall surface. It
represents the peak neutron loading of that surface.

The quantity is defined by the surface maximum of the local neutron
energy-flux field:

$$
q_{n,\mathrm{FW}}^{\max} = \max_{\mathbf{x}\in S_{\mathrm{FW}}^{\mathrm{module}}} q_n(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $q_{n,\mathrm{FW}}^{\max}$ is the maximum neutron flux at the first
wall of a breeding-blanket module, $q_n(\mathbf{x})$ is the local neutron
energy flux at surface position $\mathbf{x}$, and
$S_{\mathrm{FW}}^{\mathrm{module}}$ is the first-wall surface of that
breeding-blanket module.

The scope is a single breeding-blanket module and only its first-wall
surface. The aggregation convention is a spatial maximum over that surface;
it is not an area average, a surface integral, or a module total. It
excludes neutron flux on the module back surface and on other module
surfaces, and it excludes contributions from non-neutron energy carriers.

The same local neutron energy-flux field can be evaluated on other surfaces;
[maximum of back-surface neutron
flux](name:maximum_of_back_surface_neutron_flux) is the corresponding
surface maximum on the module back surface. The related [energy-flux maximum
at the first wall](name:energy_flux_maximum_at_first_wall) is the maximum of
the total local energy-flux field; this neutron maximum is not generally the
neutron contribution evaluated at the location of the total maximum, because
the positions of the neutron-field maximum and total-field maximum can
differ.

sources.leaf_definition: Maximum neutron flux at the first wall
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities at various time slices

NAMES.name: beryllium_density
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short:
Local number density of beryllium impurity ions per unit plasma volume,
summed over all ionization states from singly ionized to fully stripped
(Be1+ through Be4+), excluding neutral beryllium atoms.
NAMES.long:
Beryllium (atomic number $Z = 4$) enters the plasma primarily through
sputtering or evaporation from beryllium first-wall surfaces. The local
beryllium ion number density $n_\mathrm{Be}$ aggregates contributions from
all four charged ionization stages:

$$
n_\mathrm{Be} = \sum_{z=1}^{4} n_{\mathrm{Be}^{z+}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Be}^{z+}}$ is the number density of beryllium ions in
charge state $z+$, with $z$ running from 1 (singly ionized) to 4 (fully
stripped). Neutral beryllium atoms are excluded from this sum.

Beryllium impurity content is inferred from passive spectroscopy of
beryllium emission lines or from active charge-exchange recombination
spectroscopy, with spatially resolved profiles reconstructed by tomographic
inversion of chord-integrated measurements. Spatially averaged
representations include
[line_averaged_beryllium_density](name:line_averaged_beryllium_density)
along a diagnostic chord and
[volume_averaged_beryllium_density](name:volume_averaged_beryllium_density)
integrated over the confined plasma volume. The relative impurity abundance
with respect to the electron population is characterized by the
ratio_of_beryllium_density_to_electron_density.

NAMES.name: diameter_of_diagnostic_aperture
NAMES.short:
Full transverse diameter of a circular diagnostic aperture, measured across
its center between opposite points on the circumferential boundary.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the full transverse extent of the clear circular opening at
the diagnostic entrance pupil, measured between opposite points on its
circumferential boundary.

The diameter is defined by

$$
D = 2r
$$

where $D$ is the aperture diameter and $r$ is the geometric radius given by
the [radius of the diagnostic aperture](name:radius_of_diagnostic_aperture).

The quantity describes the opening geometry only; it excludes aperture
thickness, housing dimensions, and the width of a noncircular aperture. The
diameter determines the geometric area and contributes to the solid-angle
acceptance together with the aperture-to-source distance.

sources.leaf_definition: Diameter of the base of the optical cone at the entrance pupil
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (lines-of-sight). The line-of-sight is defined by the centre of the collimating aperture and the position of the measurements.

NAMES.name: difference_of_fast_neutral_beam_motional_stark_wavelength_and_fast_neutral_beam_reference_wavelength_of_spectral_line
NAMES.short:
Signed wavelength displacement of a selected fast-neutral-beam spectral-line
component from its reference wavelength, caused by the motional Stark
electric field.
NAMES.long:
The motional-Stark wavelength displacement is the signed separation between
a selected spectral-line component from fast neutral beam particles and its
unshifted reference wavelength. It represents the Lorentz shift produced by
the electric field arising from particle motion across the magnetic field.

$$
\Delta\lambda_{\mathrm{MS}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{component}} - \lambda_{\mathrm{reference}}
$$

where $\Delta\lambda_{\mathrm{MS}}$ is the motional-Stark wavelength
displacement, $\lambda_{\mathrm{component}}$ is the wavelength of the
selected component, and $\lambda_{\mathrm{reference}}$ is the corresponding
unshifted wavelength. The motional electric field is
$\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{motional}} = \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}$, where
$\mathbf{v}$ is the fast-neutral velocity and $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic
field.

This quantity is distinct from the Doppler wavelength difference caused by
line-of-sight motion, represented by [difference of neutral-beam Doppler
wavelength and neutral-beam reference
wavelength](name:difference_of_neutral_beam_doppler_wavelength_and_reference_wavelength_of_spectral_line).
Positive displacement denotes a component at a longer wavelength than the
reference.

sources.leaf_definition: Lorentz shift due to the Lorentz electric field (vxB) in the frame of the diagnostic neutral beam particles moving with a velocity v across the magnetic field B
sources.parent_definition: Derived Beam Emission Spectroscopy (BES) parameters

NAMES.name: difference_of_neutral_beam_doppler_wavelength_and_reference_wavelength_of_spectral_line
NAMES.short:
Signed displacement of a neutral-beam spectral-line wavelength from its
reference value, produced by bulk neutral-beam motion along the viewing line
of sight.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed difference between the Doppler-displaced
wavelength of a neutral-beam spectral line and its unshifted reference
wavelength of the spectral line. It represents the bulk neutral-beam
velocity projected along the viewing line of sight.

The displacement is defined by

$$
\Delta\lambda_{\mathrm{D}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{D}} - \lambda_{\mathrm{ref}} \simeq \lambda_{\mathrm{ref}}\frac{v_{\mathrm{los}}}{c}
$$

where $\lambda_{\mathrm{D}}$ is the Doppler-displaced wavelength,
$\lambda_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the reference wavelength, $v_{\mathrm{los}}$ is
the signed bulk velocity component along the line of sight, and $c$ is the
speed of light. The approximation applies when the projected velocity is
small compared with $c$.

The quantity excludes the distinct wavelength displacement produced by the
Lorentz shift from the motional Stark electric field; that effect is
represented by [difference of fast neutral beam motional Stark wavelength
and fast neutral beam reference wavelength of spectral
line](name:difference_of_fast_neutral_beam_motional_stark_wavelength_and_fast_neutral_beam_reference_wavelength_of_spectral_line).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the Doppler-displaced wavelength exceeds the
reference wavelength, corresponding to a redshift.

sources.leaf_definition: Doppler shift due to the diagnostic neutral beam particle velocity
sources.parent_definition: Derived Beam Emission Spectroscopy (BES) parameters

NAMES.name: effective_area_of_langmuir_probe
NAMES.short:
Effective collection area of a Langmuir probe, obtained by projecting its
plasma-facing collector surface onto the plane normal to the local magnetic
field.
NAMES.long:
The effective area of a Langmuir probe is the plasma-facing collector
surface area projected onto the plane perpendicular to the local
magnetic-field direction. It represents the area governing particle
collection when the sheath is magnetized.

$$
A_{\mathrm{eff}} = \int_{S_{\mathrm{w}}} \left|\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}\right|\,dA
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the effective collection area, $S_{\mathrm{w}}$
is the plasma-exposed collector surface, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the local
outward unit normal, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the local magnetic-field unit
vector, and $dA$ is an element of collector surface area. The absolute dot
product gives the geometrical projection factor.

Unlike the total area of a Langmuir probe, this quantity accounts for
magnetic-field orientation; unlike the [wetted area of a Langmuir
probe](name:wetted_area_of_langmuir_probe), it is not the unprojected
plasma-exposed surface area.

sources.leaf_definition: Effective collection area of the probe surface, varying with time due to e.g. changes in the magnetic field line incidence angle
sources.parent_definition: Set of embedded (in a plasma facing component) probes

NAMES.name: first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short:
Signed coordinate of a neutron-detector outline vertex along the first local
tangential axis of the right-handed local basis (e1, e2, e3), paired with
the second coordinate to define the detector cross section.
NAMES.long:
Signed coordinate of a neutron-detector outline vertex along the first local
tangential axis is the scalar displacement of that vertex from the detector
cross-section local origin projected onto $\hat{e}_1$. The right-handed
local detector basis $(\hat{e}_1,\hat{e}_2,\hat{e}_3)$ has $\hat{e}_3$ as
the plasma-facing normal to the detector cross section, $\hat{e}_1$ as the
tangential axis whose positive sense is toward increasing toroidal angle
$\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, and $\hat{e}_2 =
\hat{e}_3 \times \hat{e}_1$.

The coordinate is defined by the local tangent-plane projection:

$$
\ell_1 = (\mathbf{r}_v - \mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \hat{e}_1
$$

where $\ell_1$ is this first local tangential coordinate, $\mathbf{r}_v$ is
the position vector of the outline vertex, $\mathbf{r}_0$ is the position
vector of the detector cross-section local origin, and $\hat{e}_1$ is the
first local tangential unit vector.

Together with the [second local tangential coordinate of the neutron
detector](name:second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_neutron_detector), this
coordinate specifies the in-plane position of an outline vertex of the
detector cross section. It is not a cylindrical $R$, $\phi$, or $Z$ position
in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame and does not denote
displacement normal to the detector cross section.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the outline vertex is displaced from the
local origin in the $+\hat{e}_1$ direction.

sources.leaf_definition: Positions along x1 axis
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the detector/aperture in the (X1, X2) coordinate system. Repeat the first point since this is a closed contour

NAMES.name: height_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short:
Full physical extent of a rectangular neutron-detector aperture along its
second local tangential direction, the X2 axis of the detector-local
Cartesian frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the full end-to-end extent of a rectangular neutron-detector
aperture along its second local tangential direction. This direction is the
$X_2$ axis of the detector-local Cartesian basis $(\hat{X}_1, \hat{X}_2)$.

The extent is defined by the separation of the two boundary coordinates
along $X_2$:

$$
H_2 = X_{2,\max} - X_{2,\min}
$$

where $X_{2,\max}$ and $X_{2,\min}$ are the maximum and minimum
aperture-boundary coordinates along $X_2$, and $H_2$ is the resulting
length.

This quantity describes the second local tangential dimension and is
distinct from the [width of the neutron
detector](name:first_local_tangential_width_of_diagnostic_aperture), which
measures the corresponding first local tangential dimension. For a circular
aperture, the radial size is instead characterized by the [radius of the
neutron detector](name:radius_of_neutron_detector).

sources.leaf_definition: Full width of the aperture in the X2 direction, used only if geometry_type = 3
sources.parent_definition: Detector geometry

NAMES.name: helium_3_density
NAMES.subject: helium_3
NAMES.short:
Local number density of charged helium-3 ions, obtained by summing their
populations over all included ionization states at a plasma location.
NAMES.long:
Helium-3 ion number density is the local count of charged helium-3 ions per
unit plasma volume at a specified plasma location. It is summed over the
singly ionized and fully stripped charge states and excludes neutral
helium-3 atoms.

$$
n_{{}^{3}\mathrm{He}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{Z=1}^{2} n_{{}^{3}\mathrm{He},Z}(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is the plasma location, $Z$ is the ionic charge state,
and $n_{{}^{3}\mathrm{He},Z}$ is the number density of helium-3 ions in
charge state $Z$, expressed in m$^{-3}$. The [volume-averaged helium-3
density](name:volume_averaged_helium_3_density) and [line-averaged helium-3
density](name:line_averaged_helium_3_density) are spatial averages of this
local quantity over their respective domains.

NAMES.name: helium_4_density
NAMES.subject: helium_4
NAMES.short:
Local number density of helium-4 ions per unit plasma volume, the principal
measure of fusion ash concentration in deuterium-tritium burning plasmas.
NAMES.long:
The helium-4 ion number density $n_{{}^4\text{He}}$ quantifies the local
concentration of ${}^4\text{He}$ nuclei at a given point in the plasma. At
fusion-relevant temperatures (several keV), helium-4 is fully stripped to
He$^{2+}$, and in deuterium-tritium burning plasmas it accumulates as the
primary fusion ash product of the reaction ${}^2\text{H} + {}^3\text{H}
\rightarrow {}^4\text{He} + n$; its buildup dilutes the fuel and reduces the
fusion reaction rate if not exhausted by the divertor system.

The time evolution of $n_{{}^4\text{He}}$ is governed by the particle
continuity equation

$$
\frac{\partial n_{{}^4\text{He}}}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{{}^4\text{He}} = S_{{}^4\text{He}}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{{}^4\text{He}}$ is the helium-4 particle flux
and $S_{{}^4\text{He}}$ is the volumetric source rate from fusion reactions
and ionization of recycled helium neutrals at the plasma edge.

The helium-4 density is measured primarily via charge exchange recombination
spectroscopy, where injected neutral beam atoms undergo charge exchange with
He$^{2+}$ ions to produce line emission from excited helium atoms; passive
spectroscopy of edge recycling emission provides a complementary approach.
Chord-averaged and volume-averaged forms are provided by
[line_averaged_helium_4_density](name:line_averaged_helium_4_density) and
[volume_averaged_helium_4_density](name:volume_averaged_helium_4_density)
respectively, while
[helium_4_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:helium_4_density_at_plasma_boundary)
gives the boundary value.

In D-T burning plasmas, central He-4 densities are in the range
$10^{18}$-$10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$, with the helium-to-electron density ratio —
captured by
[fraction](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_helium_4_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density)
— kept below approximately 5-10% in steady state to avoid excessive fuel
dilution.

NAMES.name: krypton_density
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short:
Number density of krypton ions at a point in the plasma, summed over all
ionized charge states from Kr1+ through fully stripped Kr36+ and excluding
neutral krypton atoms.
NAMES.long:
Number density of krypton ions at a point in the plasma, summed over all
ionized charge states from Kr$^{1+}$ through fully stripped Kr$^{36+}$;
neutral krypton atoms are excluded.

With krypton atomic number $Z_\mathrm{Kr}=36$, the ion density is the
charge-state sum:

$$
n_\mathrm{Kr} = \sum_{q=1}^{36} n_\mathrm{Kr}^{(q)}
$$

where $n_\mathrm{Kr}^{(q)}$ is the number density of krypton ions in charge
state $q$ and the neutral state $q=0$ is omitted from the sum.

This is an extensive, charge-state-summed species density, not a
density-weighted mean over charge states and not the charge-state-resolved
[ion charge-state density](name:ion_charge_state_density), which retains the
individual $n_\mathrm{Kr}^{(q)}$ terms. It is an absolute density, distinct
from the relative [krypton
fraction](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_krypton_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density)
normalized to the electron density. The locus-specific values
[krypton_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:krypton_density_at_magnetic_axis),
krypton_density_at_pedestal, and
[krypton_density_at_divertor_target](name:krypton_density_at_divertor_target)
share this ions-only charge-state scope. In contrast,
[volume_averaged_krypton_density](name:volume_averaged_krypton_density)
includes all krypton charge states from neutral through fully stripped, so
its charge-state scope differs from this ions-only local quantity; the
[line_averaged_krypton_density](name:line_averaged_krypton_density) likewise
carries its own averaging definition.

NAMES.name: launched_pulse_energy_of_thomson_scattering_laser
NAMES.short:
Optical energy carried by one Thomson-scattering laser pulse immediately
before it enters the vacuum vessel, before interaction with the plasma.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the optical energy carried by one Thomson-scattering
probing laser pulse at the vessel entrance, before the pulse interacts with
the plasma.

The pulse energy is defined by integrating the instantaneous laser power
over the pulse duration:

$$
E_{\rm pulse} = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} P_{\rm laser}(t)\,dt
$$

where $E_{\rm pulse}$ is the pulse energy, $P_{\rm laser}(t)$ is the
instantaneous optical power at the vessel entrance, and $t_0$ and $t_1$ are
the pulse start and end times.

The quantity applies to a single probing-laser pulse immediately before
vessel entry. It is an energy aggregation over that pulse only, not a sum
over multiple pulses or a time-integrated laser train.

It excludes energy lost after vessel entry, energy remaining after plasma
crossing, scattered optical energy, and laser-system energy not carried by
the incident pulse.

The incident pulse energy provides the normalization for absolute
interpretation of Thomson-scattered signal intensity. It is distinct from
the wavelength-dependent response described by the [spectral efficiency of
the Thomson-scattering
detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_thomson_scattering_detector).

sources.leaf_definition: Energy of the laser pulse measured just before entering the vacuum vessel
sources.parent_definition: Set of probing lasers

NAMES.name: line_averaged_beryllium_density
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short:
Chord-average of the beryllium ion number density along a diagnostic line of
sight, equal to the path integral of the local beryllium density divided by
the chord length.
NAMES.long:
The line-averaged beryllium ion number density quantifies the mean beryllium
ion content along a plasma diagnostic chord, normalized by chord length. It
is the chord-integrated analog of the local
[beryllium_density](name:beryllium_density) and is the most directly
accessible measure of beryllium impurity concentration from line-of-sight
diagnostics.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\bar{n}_{Be} = \frac{1}{L} \int_0^L n_{Be}(l) \, dl
$$

where $n_{Be}(l)$ is the local beryllium ion number density at path
coordinate $l$ along the chord and $L$ is the total chord length.

Inferred from passive spectroscopy of beryllium emission lines by inverting
chord-integrated emission intensities using atomic emissivity coefficients;
the result aggregates contributions from all beryllium ionization states
present along the chord. The
[volume_averaged_beryllium_density](name:volume_averaged_beryllium_density)
provides a complementary global volume average, while
[beryllium_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:beryllium_density_at_magnetic_axis)
gives the local on-axis value.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when beryllium ions populate the measurement
chord.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Beryllium (Be)

NAMES.name: line_averaged_helium_3_density
NAMES.subject: helium_3
NAMES.short:
Line-averaged helium-3 density is the chord-length average of local ionized
helium-3 density along a specified viewing path, excluding neutral atoms.
NAMES.long:
Line-averaged helium-3 density is the chord-length average of the local
helium-3 ion number density along a specified path. It includes singly
ionized $^3\mathrm{He}^{+}$ and fully stripped $^3\mathrm{He}^{2+}$ ions,
while excluding neutral helium-3 atoms.

The line average is defined by

$$
\overline{n}_{^3\mathrm{He}} = \frac{1}{L}\int_{0}^{L} n_{^3\mathrm{He}}(s)\,\mathrm{d}s
$$

where $\overline{n}_{^3\mathrm{He}}$ is the line-averaged density,
$n_{^3\mathrm{He}}(s)$ is the local charge-state-summed density at path
coordinate $s$, and $L$ is the chord length. Unlike the volume average in
[volume-averaged helium-3 density](name:volume_averaged_helium_3_density),
this quantity weights each position uniformly by distance along the path. It
is a path-integrated representation of [helium-3
density](name:helium_3_density), not a separate charge-state population.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Helium isotope with 3 nucleons (3He)

NAMES.name: line_averaged_helium_4_density
NAMES.subject: helium_4
NAMES.short:
Chord-averaged helium-4 ion number density along a specified line of sight
through the plasma, representing the path mean of local fusion-ash
concentration.
NAMES.long:
The line-averaged helium-4 ion number density is the path average of the
local helium-4 ion density along a specified chord through the plasma. It
represents an effective density for that chord, not the local value at a
point or a volume-wide mean.

The line average is defined by

$$
\overline{n}_{{}^4\mathrm{He}} = \frac{1}{L}\int_{0}^{L} n_{{}^4\mathrm{He}}(l)\,dl
$$

where $n_{{}^4\mathrm{He}}(l)$ is the local helium-4 ion number density from
[helium_4_density](name:helium_4_density), $l$ is distance along the chord,
and $L$ is the chord length; $l$ and $L$ are measured in m.

The average includes the local helium-4 ion density along the specified path
and uses uniform path-length weighting. Unlike
[volume_averaged_helium_4_density](name:volume_averaged_helium_4_density),
it is not averaged over the confined plasma volume.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Helium isotope with 4 nucleons (4He)

NAMES.name: line_averaged_krypton_density
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short:
Line-averaged krypton density is the chord-length average of the total local
krypton number density, summed over all charge states from neutral krypton
through fully stripped krypton.
NAMES.long:
Line-averaged krypton density is the chord-length average of the total local
krypton number density. It includes every krypton charge state, so it
measures elemental krypton abundance along a specified line of sight rather
than the density of one particular ionization state.

For a chord parameterized by path length, the line average is defined by:

$$
\langle n_\mathrm{Kr} \rangle_\mathrm{line} = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^L \sum_{q=0}^{36} n_\mathrm{Kr}^{(q)}(\ell)\,d\ell = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^L n_\mathrm{Kr}(\ell)\,d\ell
$$

where $\langle n_\mathrm{Kr} \rangle_\mathrm{line}$ has units of
$\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $L$ is the chord length in meters, $\ell$ is distance
along the chord in meters, $q$ is the integer charge-state index with $q=0$
for neutral krypton and $q=36$ for fully stripped krypton,
$n_\mathrm{Kr}^{(q)}$ is the local density of charge state $q$ in
$\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and $n_\mathrm{Kr}=\sum_{q=0}^{36} n_\mathrm{Kr}^{(q)}$
is the charge-state-summed local [krypton_density](name:krypton_density).

This quantity is a normalized path mean, not an unnormalized line integral.
It differs from
[volume_averaged_krypton_density](name:volume_averaged_krypton_density),
which averages the same charge-state-summed local density over a plasma
volume rather than along a chord.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Krypton (Kr)

NAMES.name: line_averaged_lithium_density
NAMES.subject: lithium
NAMES.short:
Path-length-averaged total number density of lithium ions along a specified
plasma chord, summed over Li+ through fully stripped Li3+ and excluding
neutral lithium.
NAMES.long:
This is the path-length average of lithium ion number density, summed over
all ionization stages from Li$^+$ through fully stripped Li$^{3+}$, along a
specified chord through the plasma.

The chord average is defined by

$$
\langle n_{Li} \rangle_L = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^L n_{Li}(s)\,ds
$$

where $n_{Li}(s)$ is the local lithium ion number density in m$^{-3}$, $s$
is path length in meters along the chord, and $L$ is the total chord length
in meters.

This quantity weights each path-length element equally and excludes neutral
lithium. It differs from the flux-surface-averaged lithium density at the
plasma boundary, which averages over a separatrix, and from [volume-averaged
lithium density](name:volume_averaged_lithium_density), which averages over
confined plasma volume.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Lithium (Li)

NAMES.name: line_averaged_total_ion_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short:
Total ion number density averaged along a specified plasma chord, summing
all ion species and charge states, including thermal and non-thermal ions.
NAMES.long:
The line-averaged total ion density is the chord average of the local [total
ion density](name:total_ion_number_density), including all ion species,
resolved charge states, and thermal and non-thermal ion populations. It
excludes electron density.

$$
n_{\mathrm{i,line}} = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^L n_{\mathrm{i,total}}(l)\,dl
$$

where $l$ is distance along the chord, $L$ is chord length,
$n_{\mathrm{i,total}}(l)$ is local total ion density, and
$n_{\mathrm{i,line}}$ is the resulting line average. Unlike the
[volume-averaged total ion density](name:volume_averaged_total_ion_density),
it averages along a chord rather than throughout a volume.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Total ion density (sum over species)

NAMES.name: neutral_pressure_of_mass_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short:
Neutral pressure of a mass-spectrometer channel is the calibrated
neutral-gas pressure equivalent assigned to a selected mass-to-charge
channel. It denotes a channel-resolved neutral contribution and does not
require correspondence to a unique neutral species.
NAMES.long:
Neutral pressure of a mass-spectrometer channel is the calibrated
neutral-gas pressure equivalent assigned to one mass-discriminated channel
of a mass spectrometer. The channel denotes a response in mass-to-charge
space after ionization, so the quantity is a pressure equivalent for
neutrals that can contribute to that channel, not a pressure of the detected
ions.

This quantity is neutral in scope: it excludes charged-particle plasma
pressure, electron pressure, and any pressure contribution not represented
as neutral gas before ionization. It is the neutral-specific counterpart of
pressure of a mass-spectrometer channel.

A channel value need not be the thermodynamic partial pressure of a single
species, because fragmentation, isotopologues, charge states of produced
ions, and isobaric species can overlap in the same mass-to-charge channel.
Summing channel values represents [total neutral
pressure](name:total_neutral_pressure) only when the calibrated channels are
non-overlapping, span the neutral mixture being represented, and treat
cross-sensitivities consistently.

sources.leaf_definition: Partial pressure (calibrated data)
sources.parent_definition: Set of mass channels, each corresponding to a given atomic mass measured continuously by the spectrometer

NAMES.name: neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short:
Fusion-neutron number flux incident on the neutron detector’s active
surface, giving the rate at which neutrons cross each unit of that surface.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the incident fusion-neutron number flux on the
neutron-sensitive active surface of the detector. It is the surface-crossing
flux, not the neutron production rate or the registered detection-event rate
described by rate of neutron detector. The parent quantity flux of neutron
detector expresses the same surface-transport concept.

The defining relation is

$$
\Phi_n = \frac{dN_n}{dA\,dt}
$$

where $\Phi_n$ is the incident neutron number flux, $N_n$ is the number of
neutrons crossing the active surface, $A$ is active surface area, and $t$ is
time. The surface is the neutron-sensitive area characterized by area of
neutron detector; passive housing, shielding, supports, and electronics are
excluded. Registered event rates additionally depend on detector response
and efficiency.

sources.leaf_definition: Neutron flux impinging on the detector, deduced from the measured count-rate (relevant only when mode/identifier/index = 1)
sources.parent_definition: Set of Measuring Modes simultaneously used by the detector

NAMES.name: neutron_maximum_energy_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short:
High-energy endpoint of the neutron kinetic-energy interval assigned to a
neutron detector energy band.
NAMES.long:
The maximum neutron energy of a detector band is the upper kinetic-energy
boundary used to classify energy-resolved neutron counts. It is an
instrumental band limit, not the maximum energy present in the neutron
population.

The selected energy interval is bounded by

$$
E_{\min} \leq E_n \leq E_{\max}
$$

where $E_n$ is neutron kinetic energy, $E_{\min}$ is the lower band
boundary, and $E_{\max}$ is this quantity. The lower boundary is represented
by lower-bound neutron-detector energy; neutron-detector energy denotes a
band boundary without specifying which edge.

sources.leaf_definition: Upper bound of the energy band
sources.parent_definition: Set of energy bands in which neutrons are counted by the detector

NAMES.name: nitrogen_density
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short:
Number density of nitrogen nuclei is the local count of nitrogen atomic
nuclei per plasma volume, summed over all charge states from neutral through
fully stripped nitrogen.
NAMES.long:
Number density of nitrogen nuclei is the local count of nitrogen atomic
nuclei per plasma volume. It is a species-level elemental density, so
neutral nitrogen and every ionized nitrogen charge state are included.

The charge-state aggregation is defined by

$$
n_N = \sum_{z=0}^{7} n_{N,z}
$$

where $n_N$ is the nitrogen density, $n_{N,z}$ is the number density of
nitrogen nuclei in charge state $z$, $z=0$ denotes neutral nitrogen, and
$z=7$ denotes fully stripped nitrogen because nitrogen has atomic number
$7$.

This quantity is local and is distinct from [line-averaged nitrogen
density](name:line_averaged_nitrogen_density) and [volume-averaged nitrogen
density](name:volume_averaged_nitrogen_density), which are spatial averages
of the same charge-state-summed species density. In the absence of a
population qualifier, the density includes thermal, fast, and other
nonthermal nitrogen nuclei.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_nitrogen_density
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short:
Line-averaged number density of all nitrogen nuclei along a specified plasma
chord, summed over every ionization state from neutral through fully
stripped nitrogen.
NAMES.long:
Line-averaged nitrogen density is the chord-length average of the local
number density of all nitrogen nuclei, including every nitrogen ionization
state from neutral nitrogen through fully stripped nitrogen.

The line average is defined by

$$
\overline{n}_N = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^L n_N(\ell)\,d\ell
$$

where $n_N(\ell)$ is the local charge-state-summed nitrogen density defined
by [nitrogen density](name:nitrogen_density), $\ell$ is distance along the
specified chord, and $L$ is the total chord length.

This quantity is the chord-integrated nitrogen inventory divided by chord
length, so it preserves the density dimension while removing variation along
the chord. It is distinct from the spatially averaged [volume-averaged
nitrogen density](name:volume_averaged_nitrogen_density), which averages
over the plasma volume rather than a chord.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Nitrogen (N)

NAMES.name: nuclear_target_atomic_fraction_of_neutron_detector_converter
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless fraction of all converter atoms that are nuclei of the target
species for the primary neutron-induced detection reaction.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the normalized composition factor for target nuclei in the
converter material of a neutron detector. It identifies the share of
converter atoms belonging to the nuclear species that produces the intended
neutron-induced detection reaction.

The target atomic fraction is defined by

$$
f_{\mathrm{target}} = \frac{N_{\mathrm{target}}}{N_{\mathrm{all}}}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{target}}$ is the number of target-species nuclei and
$N_{\mathrm{all}}$ is the total number of atoms in the converter material.
It is the nuclear-target realization of target atomic fraction of a neutron
detector converter, rather than a fraction based on converter volume, mass,
or detector efficiency. The fraction is bounded between zero and one.

sources.leaf_definition: Number of target nuclei in the dectector
sources.parent_definition: Set of neutron detection systems

NAMES.name: oxygen_density
NAMES.subject: oxygen
NAMES.short:
Total number density of oxygen atoms and ions across all charge states, from
neutral to fully stripped, giving the local oxygen impurity concentration at
a point in the plasma.
NAMES.long:
The local oxygen number density $n_\mathrm{O}$ quantifies the total
concentration of oxygen impurity per unit plasma volume, encompassing
neutral atomic oxygen and all ionic charge states up to fully stripped
O$^{8+}$. Oxygen is a ubiquitous low-Z impurity in fusion devices, entering
through wall outgassing and vessel conditioning; it contributes to radiative
power losses and dilutes the hydrogenic fuel inventory.

The total oxygen density is defined as the sum over all ionization states:

$$
n_\mathrm{O} = \sum_{Z=0}^{8} n_{\mathrm{O}^{Z+}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{O}^{Z+}}$ is the number density of oxygen in charge state
$Z^+$, with $Z$ ranging from 0 (neutral) to 8 (fully stripped).

The local density is inferred from passive extreme-ultraviolet spectroscopy,
charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, and soft X-ray emission
tomography. Spatially averaged forms include
[line_averaged_oxygen_density](name:line_averaged_oxygen_density) (chord
integral divided by chord length) and
[volume_averaged_oxygen_density](name:volume_averaged_oxygen_density)
(integral over the plasma volume). The dimensionless oxygen_fraction relates
this local density to the electron density as an impurity concentration
measure.

In well-conditioned fusion plasmas the core oxygen density is a small
fraction of the electron density; edge concentrations of $10^{15}$–$10^{17}$
m$^{-3}$ are representative of limiter and divertor configurations.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_oxygen_density
NAMES.subject: oxygen
NAMES.short:
Line-averaged oxygen density is the line-of-sight mean of the local oxygen
number density, summed over all charge states from neutral O0 through fully
stripped O8+, along a specified chord through the plasma.
NAMES.long:
The line-averaged oxygen density is the line-of-sight mean of the local
oxygen number density—summed over all charge states from neutral O$^0$
through fully stripped O$^{8+}$—along a specified chord through the plasma.
It represents the oxygen impurity concentration averaged by arclength rather
than the value at a single point.

For a chord of length $L$, the line-averaged oxygen density is defined by:

$$
\bar{n}_\mathrm{O} = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^L n_\mathrm{O}(\ell)\,d\ell
$$

where $\bar{n}_\mathrm{O}$ is the line-averaged oxygen density, $L$ is the
physical length of the chord segment included in the average, $\ell$ is
arclength along that chord, and $n_\mathrm{O}(\ell)$ is the [local oxygen
density](name:oxygen_density) at the point labeled by $\ell$.

The scope is the species-level oxygen impurity population intersected by the
specified chord: the density is charge-state-summed over neutral oxygen and
all oxygen ions, and the spatial aggregation is an arclength average along
the chord. It excludes charge-state-resolved oxygen densities, the local
point value [oxygen density](name:oxygen_density), and the spatial mean over
the confined plasma volume.

The essential relationship to [oxygen density](name:oxygen_density) is that
the local charge-state-summed density is the integrand of the chord average.
[Volume-averaged oxygen density](name:volume_averaged_oxygen_density) is the
analogous mean formed over a plasma volume, whereas this quantity is formed
only along the specified line of sight and is normalized by the chord
length.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Oxygen (O)

NAMES.name: requested_voltage_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short:
Voltage of a neutron detector specified as the high-voltage supply setpoint
that establishes the target detector bias, rather than the actual output
voltage.
NAMES.long:
Voltage of neutron detector

The requested bias is defined by:

$$
U = \varphi_{\mathrm{bias}}^{\mathrm{req}} - \varphi_{\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $U$ is the requested bias voltage,
$\varphi_{\mathrm{bias}}^{\mathrm{req}}$ is the commanded potential of the
biased detector terminal, and $\varphi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the supply
reference-terminal potential.

This setpoint is distinct from the actual supply output voltage and from the
low-voltage supply setting for detector electronics. The [requested voltage
of a spectrometer channel](name:requested_voltage_of_spectrometer_channel)
has the corresponding high-voltage bias-setpoint role for that channel.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the commanded detector-bias potential exceeds
the supply reference-terminal potential.

sources.parent_definition: Description of high voltage power supply

sources.leaf_definition: Voltage set
sources.parent_definition: Description of low voltage power supply

NAMES.name: second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short:
Second local tangential coordinate of a neutron detector is the signed
coordinate of an outline vertex along the detector’s second local tangential
axis; with the first local tangential coordinate it defines the detector
cross-section vertex in the right-handed detector-local basis (first
tangential, second tangential, plasma-facing normal), where first tangential
points toward increasing φ in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Second local tangential coordinate of a neutron detector is the signed
in-plane coordinate of a neutron-detector outline vertex along the
detector's second local tangential direction. It is a geometric coordinate
of the detector cross section expressed in the detector-local right-handed
orthonormal basis
$(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1,\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2,\hat{\mathbf{e}}_3)$, whose first
two directions are tangent to the cross-section plane and whose third
direction is the plasma-facing detector normal.

The coordinate is defined by the scalar projection of the vertex
displacement onto the second local tangential direction:

$$
x_2 = (\mathbf{r}_v - \mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_2
$$

where $x_2$ is the second local tangential coordinate of the neutron
detector, $\mathbf{r}_v$ is the position vector of the outline vertex,
$\mathbf{r}_0$ is the neutron-detector local origin, and
$\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$ is the second local tangential unit vector.

The local triad is defined by
$\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2=\hat{\mathbf{e}}_3\times\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$, with
$\hat{\mathbf{e}}_3$ the plasma-facing detector normal and
$\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$ the first local tangential direction chosen toward
increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame with basis unit vectors
$(\hat{\mathbf{R}},\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}},\hat{\mathbf{Z}})$, where $R$ is
major radius, $\phi$ increases counterclockwise when viewed from above
$+\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$, and $Z$ is vertical height. This quantity applies to
individual outline vertices of the neutron-detector cross section; it is not
summed, averaged, or interpreted as an extent over multiple vertices.

Together with the [first local tangential coordinate of a neutron
detector](name:first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_neutron_detector), it
specifies a vertex in the detector cross-section plane; both coordinates are
purely geometric outline coordinates. It is distinct from the detector's
normal extent, such as the [height of a neutron
detector](name:height_of_neutron_detector), from any cylindrical $R$,
$\phi$, or $Z$ position in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame,
and from quantities describing detector response or neutron populations.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the displacement from the neutron-detector
local origin to the outline vertex is in the direction of
$\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$, equivalently
$\hat{\mathbf{e}}_3\times\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$.

sources.leaf_definition: Positions along x2 axis
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the detector/aperture in the (X1, X2) coordinate system. Repeat the first point since this is a closed contour

NAMES.name: solid_angle_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short:
Geometric acceptance of a neutron detector aperture as viewed from a neutron
emission point, independent of detector efficiency and material response.
NAMES.long:
The solid angle is the geometric measure of the aperture’s apparent extent
from a neutron emission point. It is nonnegative and depends only on the
aperture geometry, its orientation, and the source-point location; detector
efficiency and converter response are excluded.

For a point source, the solid angle is defined by

$$
\Omega = \int_A \frac{\cos\theta}{r^2}\,dA
$$

where $A$ is the aperture surface, $r$ is the distance from the source point
to an aperture element, and $\theta$ is the angle between the aperture
normal and the line from the source point to that element. For a finite
source region, the quantity denotes the specified volume average of this
point-source solid angle; it does not imply weighting by the neutron
emission profile. The geometric aperture dimensions described by area of
neutron detector and [radius of neutron
detector](name:radius_of_neutron_detector) can determine the acceptance but
do not include detector efficiency, which is a separate quantity described
by [efficiency of neutron
detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_neutron_detector).

sources.leaf_definition: Average solid angle that the detector covers within the voxel
sources.parent_definition: Field of view associated to this detector. The field of view is described by a voxelized plasma volume. Each voxel, with indexes i_R, i_Z, and i_phi, has an associated solid angle scalar and a detector direction vector.

NAMES.name: spectral_efficiency_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short:
Energy-dependent probability that an incident neutron within a specified
