sources.leaf_definition: Power deposited on the wall due to electric currents (positive means power is deposited on the target)
sources.parent_definition: Simple 0D description of plasma-wall interaction

NAMES.name: radial_outline_of_limiter_tile
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate R locating each point on the boundary outline of a
plasma-facing limiter tile in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial outline coordinate is the major-radius value $R$ of each point on
the geometric boundary outline of a plasma-facing limiter tile. It describes
tile geometry rather than a plasma field or a flux-surface coordinate.

In a right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the major-radius
coordinate is defined from Cartesian coordinates by

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}
$$

where $R$ is the perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, and
$x$ and $y$ are Cartesian coordinate values along the $\hat{x}$ and
$\hat{y}$ axes of the right-handed $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis.

The quantity is evaluated pointwise for every contour point of the
limiter-tile outline. It is not an average, maximum, area, or integrated
boundary measure; for a closed contour, the first point is not repeated at
the end.

Together with the [vertical outline of the limiter
tile](name:vertical_outline_of_limiter_tile), it supplies the complementary
radial and vertical coordinates that locate the outline in a poloidal
cross-section. The related [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate)
expresses the same geometric coordinate concept without specifying the
limiter-tile outline locus.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the limiting surface. Repeat the first point in case of a closed contour

NAMES.name: radial_outline_of_wall
NAMES.long:
The radial outline coordinate is the major-radius position of each point on
the boundary contour designated as the wall. It locates the contour relative
to the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$
frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is
vertical coordinate.

For a contour point identified by parameter $s$, the coordinate is defined
by

$$
R(s)=\mathbf{r}(s)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{R}}(s)
$$

where $\mathbf{r}(s)$ is the position vector of the contour point measured
from the machine symmetry axis, $\hat{\mathbf{R}}(s)$ is the local outward
radial unit vector, and $s$ identifies the point along the outline.

The quantity applies point-by-point to the specified wall contour and
carries no contour averaging, integration, maximum, or other spatial
aggregation. The generic wall locus does not by itself distinguish a first
wall, vacuum-vessel wall, or limiter surface; that physical boundary
identity is determined by the applicable wall definition. It is a radial
coordinate, not a vertical coordinate, toroidal coordinate, surface-normal
coordinate, or wall-normal distance.

Its meaning is analogous to [radial outline of a limiter
tile](name:radial_outline_of_limiter_tile), but the evaluated boundary
differs; [radial outline of a coil conductor
element](name:radial_outline_of_coil_conductor_element) likewise applies the
same radial-coordinate concept to a conductor contour rather than a wall
contour.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the mobile unit, for a set of time slices. Repeat the first point in case of a closed contour

NAMES.name: radial_total_current_density_at_wall
NAMES.short:
Radial (R-direction) component of the total electric current-density vector
at a plasma-facing wall in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame,
where R is major radius and Z is vertical height. It is signed positive
toward increasing R.
NAMES.long:
Radial (R-direction) component of the total electric current-density vector
at a plasma-facing wall is the projection of the local total electric
current-density vector onto the $\hat{R}$ basis direction of the
right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. Here $R$ is major radius
measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$
is vertical height.

The defining projection at a wall point $\mathbf{x}_w$ is:

$$
j_{R,\mathrm{tot}}^{\mathrm{wall}}(\mathbf{x}_w) = \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{tot}}(\mathbf{x}_w) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}}(\mathbf{x}_w)
$$

where $j_{R,\mathrm{tot}}^{\mathrm{wall}}$ denotes this scalar quantity,
$\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total
[current_density](name:current_density), $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the local
unit vector toward increasing $R$, and $\mathbf{x}_w$ lies on the
plasma-facing material wall.

Total means all current-carrying contributions included in the physical
current-density vector, such as inductive, neoclassical, wave-driven,
kinetic, conductive, charged-particle, and sheath-mediated currents. This
quantity is the wall-evaluated radial projection of the total vector, not a
process-resolved contribution such as
[radial_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction](name:radial_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction).
A tile current such as
[current_of_divertor_tile](name:current_of_divertor_tile) is a surface
integral of the current-density component normal to that tile; it equals an
area integral of this radial component only where the tile normal is
parallel to $\hat{R}$.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{tot}}$ at the wall
points in the direction of increasing major radius $R$.

sources.leaf_definition: Component along the major radius axis, one scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.
sources.parent_definition: Total current density, given on various grid subsets

NAMES.name: surface_emissivity
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless ratio of thermal radiation emitted by a surface to blackbody
radiation at the same surface temperature, with the stated spectral and
angular averaging.
NAMES.long:
Surface emissivity is the effectiveness of a material surface in emitting
thermal electromagnetic radiation relative to an ideal blackbody at the same
temperature. It is a material property of the emitting surface and is
distinct from the emitted energy flux described by [energy flux due to
surface emission](name:energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_surface_emission).

The effective emissivity is defined by

$$
\varepsilon = \frac{M_{\mathrm{emit}}(T_s)}{M_{\mathrm{bb}}(T_s)}
$$

where $M_{\mathrm{emit}}$ is the surface thermal radiative exitance,
$M_{\mathrm{bb}}$ is the blackbody exitance, and $T_s$ is the surface
temperature. The ratio applies to the specified spectral band and angular
averaging; it is not a wavelength- and direction-resolved emissivity.
Incident radiation and geometric surface area, such as optical-element area,
are excluded.

sources.leaf_definition: Emissivity of the region of interest
sources.parent_definition: Set of regions of interest for the real-time monitoring of machine protection. Regions of interest are defined by a combination of polygons for each image

NAMES.name: surface_temperature
NAMES.short:
Surface temperature is the thermodynamic temperature of the exposed material
boundary of a plasma-facing component at a specified surface point. It
refers to the surface material state, not to an area aggregate or regional
extremum.
NAMES.long:
Surface temperature is the thermodynamic temperature of the material at the
exposed boundary of a plasma-facing component. It is a local scalar assigned
to a specified material surface point and time, representing the state of
the surface material rather than the temperature of the adjacent plasma,
sheath, neutral gas, or radiation field.

For an extended exposed surface, the unqualified quantity denotes the local
point value at each surface point, not an area average, integral,
percentile, or extremum. Region-level aggregates require distinct standard
names; the maximum over a specified exposed surface region is
[maximum_surface_temperature](name:maximum_surface_temperature).
[temperature_at_wall](name:temperature_at_wall) is the corresponding
boundary-locus temperature when the wall is the defining locus.

sources.leaf_definition: Processed image in apparent temperature. First dimension : row index (horizontal orientation). Second dimension: column index (vertical orientation). The size of this matrix is assumed to be constant over time
sources.parent_definition: Set of frames

NAMES.name: maximum_surface_temperature
NAMES.short:
Peak apparent temperature of the exposed plasma-facing surface over all
valid points within a defined infrared-camera region of interest.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the largest apparent temperature assigned to the exposed
material surface of a plasma-facing component within a specified
infrared-camera region of interest. It is an extremum of the local [surface
temperature](name:surface_temperature), not a local value, area average, or
heat-flux measure.

$$
T_{\mathrm{max,ROI}} = \max_{\mathbf{x} \in V_{\mathrm{ROI}}} T_s(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $T_s(\mathbf{x})$ is the surface temperature at surface position
$\mathbf{x}$, and $V_{\mathrm{ROI}}$ is the set of valid surface positions
in the defined region of interest. Points excluded from the valid set do not
contribute to the maximum.

sources.leaf_definition: Maximum apparent temperature measured in the region of interest
sources.parent_definition: Set of regions of interest for the real-time monitoring of machine protection. Regions of interest are defined by a combination of polygons for each image

NAMES.name: thermal_radiative_power_of_divertor
NAMES.short:
Thermal radiation emitted by all divertor target surfaces, with each surface
contribution weighted by its emissivity and summed over the divertor.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the total thermal radiative power emitted by the surfaces
of all divertor targets. It represents surface emission governed by the
local surface temperature and emissivity.

$$
P_{\mathrm{bb}} = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{D}} \int_{A_i} \epsilon_i\,\sigma_{\mathrm{SB}}\,T_i^4\,\mathrm{d}A
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{bb}}$ is the emitted thermal radiative power,
$\mathcal{D}$ is the set of divertor target surfaces, $A_i$ is the surface
area of target $i$, $\epsilon_i$ is its local thermal emissivity,
$\sigma_{\mathrm{SB}}$ is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant, $T_i$ is its local
absolute surface temperature, and $\mathrm{d}A$ is a surface-area element.

The quantity is aggregated over every divertor target surface and includes
emissivity effects. It describes radiation emitted by the targets, not
plasma power incident on them or radiation retained after reflection.

It is distinct from [absorbed radiated power of the
divertor](name:absorbed_radiated_power_of_divertor), which is the net
radiative power deposited on the targets after accounting for incident and
reflected radiation, and from [total incident power of the
divertor](name:total_incident_power_of_divertor), which describes incoming
plasma power rather than surface emission.

sources.leaf_definition: Black body radiated power emitted from the divertor targets (emissivity is included) (sum over all targets)
sources.parent_definition: Set of divertors

NAMES.name: total_incident_power_at_wall
NAMES.short:
Total plasma power arriving at all plasma-facing wall surfaces, summed over
conducted, convected, radiative, and other incident energy channels.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the total energy delivered from the plasma to plasma-facing
wall and divertor surfaces by all incident channels. It represents the
area-integrated power arriving at those surfaces before reflection or
re-emission.

The total incident power is defined by integrating the incident energy-flux
density over the complete plasma-facing area:

$$
P_{\mathrm{inc}} = \int_{A_{\mathrm{wall}}} q_{\mathrm{inc}}(\mathbf r)\,\mathrm{d}A
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{inc}}$ is the total incident power, $A_{\mathrm{wall}}$ is
the union of the relevant plasma-facing surfaces, $q_{\mathrm{inc}}(\mathbf
r)$ is the incident power per unit area at surface position $\mathbf r$, and
$\mathrm{d}A$ is a differential surface area. The integrand is the
area-density counterpart energy flux at wall. The total includes all
incident energy channels and excludes power emitted from the wall toward the
plasma or vacuum.

sources.leaf_definition: Total power incident on the wall. This power is split in the various physical categories listed below
sources.parent_definition: Simple 0D description of plasma-wall interaction

NAMES.name: total_ion_density_at_limiter
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short:
Charge-state-summed number density of all ion species in the boundary plasma
immediately on the plasma-facing side of a limiter surface.
NAMES.long:
Total ion density at a limiter is the local number density of all charged
ion species and ionization states at the plasma-side evaluation point
adjacent to the limiter. It is the charge-state-summed component of
ion_density_at_limiter.

The defining aggregation is

$$
n_{i,\mathrm{tot}} = \sum_s \sum_{Z\geq 1} n_{s,Z}
$$

where $n_{s,Z}$ is the number density of ion species $s$ in charge state
$Z$, and the sums include every ion species and positive charge state
present at the evaluation point.

Neutral atoms and molecules are excluded, as is electron density. The
limiter-local aggregation is distinct from the corresponding total quantity
at the plasma boundary,
[total_ion_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:total_ion_density_at_plasma_boundary),
because the evaluation locus is specifically the plasma-facing side of a
limiter surface.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Total ion density (sum over species)

NAMES.name: total_neutral_particle_rate_at_wall_due_to_surface_emission
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short:
Wall-integrated neutral-particle number rate emitted into the plasma by
surface-emission processes, with cold, thermal, and fast energy categories
represented separately.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the total number rate of neutral particles emitted from
plasma-facing wall surfaces into the adjacent plasma-facing region by
surface-emission processes. It represents the contribution from the selected
neutral population and energy category rather than a local surface flux.

The surface-integrated rate is defined by

$$
\dot{N}_{\mathrm{n,SE}}^{(c)} = \int_{A_{\mathrm{wall}}} \Gamma_{\mathrm{n,SE}}^{(c)}(\mathbf{x})\,\mathrm{d}A
$$

where $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{n,SE}}^{(c)}$ is the emitted neutral-particle number
rate, $\Gamma_{\mathrm{n,SE}}^{(c)}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local
neutral-particle flux density due to surface emission at wall position
$\mathbf{x}$, $A_{\mathrm{wall}}$ is the emitting wall surface,
$\mathrm{d}A$ is its differential area element, and $c$ identifies the cold,
thermal, or fast neutral energy category.

The aggregation is over the contributing wall surface; “total” does not
imply summation over the cold, thermal, and fast categories, which remain
distinct contributions. The quantity describes particles leaving the wall
and excludes neutral particles incident on the wall, net
incoming-minus-outgoing flux, and volumetric plasma sources.

It is the area integral of [neutral particle flux density due to surface
emission](name:neutral_particle_flux_at_wall_due_to_surface_emission),
whereas [incident neutral particle flux at the
wall](name:incident_neutral_particle_flux_at_wall) describes particles
arriving at the wall and is not included in this outgoing rate. It is also
distinct from the per-area recombination contribution represented by
[neutral particle flux at the wall due to
recombination](name:neutral_particle_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination).

sources.leaf_definition: Particle flux from the wall corresponding to the conversion into various neutral types (first dimension: 1: cold; 2: thermal; 3: fast)
sources.parent_definition: Quantities related to the various neutral species

NAMES.name: total_particle_source_rate_of_divertor_due_to_recycling
NAMES.short:
Total equivalent-electron rate of neutral and ion particles re-emitted from
all divertor surfaces into the plasma by recycling.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the aggregate particle source produced when neutral and ion
particles are re-emitted from divertor surfaces into the plasma by
recycling.

The defining rate is

$$
\Gamma_{\mathrm{rec}} = \frac{dN_{\mathrm{eq}}}{dt}
$$

where $\Gamma_{\mathrm{rec}}$ is the total recycled particle source rate,
$N_{\mathrm{eq}}$ is the cumulative equivalent-electron count of re-emitted
particles, and $t$ is time.

The quantity covers all divertor surfaces and combines the neutral and ion
contributions using equivalent-electron counting. It is a total source rate
rather than a local surface flux density, and it excludes particle sources
produced by processes other than recycling or originating outside the
divertor.

This is a gross re-emission rate and does not by itself represent the net
particle balance after incident-particle losses. Unlike [power of the
divertor due to recombination](name:power_of_divertor_due_to_recombination),
it counts recycled particles without weighting them by deposited energy.

sources.leaf_definition: Total recycled particle flux from  the divertor (in equivalent electrons)
sources.parent_definition: Set of divertors

NAMES.name: total_thermal_power_density_due_to_conductive_losses
NAMES.short:
Volumetric rate of thermal plasma energy removal by conductive transport
toward plasma-facing surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the local volumetric rate at which total thermal plasma
energy is removed by conductive transport toward plasma-facing surfaces. It
represents an aggregate thermal-population loss rather than a
species-resolved contribution, and is distinct from the corresponding
surface energy flux.

$$
P_{\mathrm{cond,loss}} = \nabla \cdot \mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{cond}}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{cond,loss}}$ is the conductive-loss power density and
$\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{cond}}$ is the total thermal conductive energy-flux
vector. The divergence is taken in physical space; conductive transport is
predominantly parallel to magnetic field lines.

Positive values denote net conductive energy leaving the local plasma
volume. Integrating this density over a volume gives the conductive power
removed from that volume and, when bounded by plasma-facing surfaces,
relates to [power due to conduction](name:power_due_to_conduction).
Radiative, convective, and particle-loss channels are excluded.

sources.leaf_definition: Power density of conductive losses to the wall (positive sign for losses)
sources.parent_definition: Radial profiles for a set of time slices

NAMES.name: total_xenon_fraction
NAMES.subject: xenon
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless abundance ratio of xenon ion number density, summed over
ionization states, to electron number density in the same plasma domain.
NAMES.long:
The xenon fraction measures the abundance of charged xenon relative to the
electron population in a plasma domain. It is a dimensionless
part-to-reference ratio, not a xenon density or an effective charge.

The fraction is defined by:

$$
f_{\mathrm{Xe}} = \frac{n_{\mathrm{Xe}}}{n_e}
$$

where $f_{\mathrm{Xe}}$ is the xenon fraction, $n_{\mathrm{Xe}}$ is the
total xenon ion number density summed over all positive ionization states,
and $n_e$ is the electron number density.

The numerator and denominator refer to the same plasma domain and use the
same spatial aggregation convention. Neutral xenon atoms are excluded, and
the quantity is not restricted to an individual xenon ionization state. The
specific volume-averaged realization applies the averaging operation to both
densities before forming the ratio, as defined by
[volume_averaged_total_xenon_fraction](name:volume_averaged_total_xenon_fraction).

The underlying xenon density is the charge-state-summed quantity represented
by [xenon_density](name:xenon_density); the fraction differs from it by
normalization to the electron density. The corresponding volume-averaged
xenon density is
[volume_averaged_xenon_density](name:volume_averaged_xenon_density), which
supplies the numerator for the volume-averaged realization.

NAMES.name: tritium_density_at_limiter
NAMES.subject: tritium
NAMES.short:
Local particle number density of tritium ions evaluated in the boundary
plasma immediately adjacent to a plasma-facing limiter surface, on the
plasma side of the magnetic presheath or sheath entrance.
NAMES.long:
Tritium density at a limiter is the local number density of tritium ions in
the boundary plasma immediately adjacent to a plasma-facing limiter surface.
The evaluation point is on the plasma side of the magnetic presheath or
sheath entrance, not inside limiter material or in neutral gas at the
surface. The quantity excludes neutral tritium atoms.

Because tritium is hydrogenic, its charge-state-summed ion density is the
density of singly charged tritium ions:

$$
n_{\mathrm{T}} = n_{\mathrm{T}^{+}} = \int f_{\mathrm{T}^{+}}(\mathbf{v})\,d^{3}v
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{T}}$ is the tritium ion number density,
$f_{\mathrm{T}^{+}}(\mathbf{v})$ is the velocity distribution function of
singly charged tritium ions, and $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity.

This isotope contribution is included in
[density_at_limiter](name:density_at_limiter). It is evaluated at a limiter
rather than at the separatrix, unlike
[tritium_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:tritium_density_at_plasma_boundary),
and is the tritium counterpart of
[deuterium_density_at_limiter](name:deuterium_density_at_limiter).

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Tritium (T)

NAMES.name: tungsten_density_at_limiter
NAMES.subject: tungsten
NAMES.short:
Local particle number density of tungsten ions evaluated in the boundary
plasma immediately adjacent to the plasma-facing limiter surface, summed
over ionization states and excluding neutral tungsten.
NAMES.long:
Number density of tungsten ions evaluated at the plasma-limiter interface on
the plasma side of the magnetic presheath or sheath entrance. The limiter
terminates open magnetic field lines in the scrape-off layer, so this
quantity describes the tungsten impurity population participating in
limiter-adjacent plasma–surface interactions.

The charge-state sum is defined by

$$
n_{\mathrm W} = \sum_{Z\ge 1} n_{\mathrm{W}^{Z+}} = \sum_{Z\ge 1}\int f_{\mathrm{W}^{Z+}}(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $n_{\mathrm W}$ is the total tungsten-ion number density, $Z$ is the
positive tungsten charge number, $n_{\mathrm{W}^{Z+}}$ is the density of
charge state $Z$, and $f_{\mathrm{W}^{Z+}}(\mathbf{v})$ is its velocity
distribution function. The sum includes all tungsten ionization states and
excludes neutral tungsten.

This quantity specializes [density_at_limiter](name:density_at_limiter) to
tungsten and contributes to ion_density_at_limiter. It is evaluated at the
limiter rather than the divertor-target location used by
[tungsten_density_at_divertor_target](name:tungsten_density_at_divertor_target).

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Tungsten (W)

NAMES.name: x_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture
NAMES.short:
Signed x coordinate of the geometric center of a diagnostic aperture,
measured from the origin of its right-handed camera Cartesian (x, y, z)
frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity locates the geometric center of a diagnostic aperture along
the x axis of its right-handed camera Cartesian basis
$(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$. It is a signed geometric position, not an
aperture dimension or orientation.

The coordinate is defined by

$$
x_A = (\mathbf{r}_A - \mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \hat{x}
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_A$ is the position of the aperture center, $\mathbf{r}_0$
is the frame origin, $\hat{x}$ is the unit vector along the x axis, and
$x_A$ is measured in m. The corresponding [y coordinate of the diagnostic
aperture](name:y_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture) uses the same origin and
camera basis; this quantity is distinct from cylindrical radial and vertical
aperture coordinates.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the aperture center lies in the direction of
increasing x from the frame origin.

sources.leaf_definition: Component along X axis
sources.parent_definition: Pinhole position in the (X,Y,Z) coordinate system

NAMES.name: x_coordinate_of_divertor_target
NAMES.short:
Signed Cartesian x-coordinate locating the geometric center of a divertor
target surface in the right-handed (x, y, z) frame, with +x at toroidal
angle φ = 0.
NAMES.long:
The x coordinate of a divertor target is the signed Cartesian position of
the geometric center of its target surface. It locates that center in the
right-handed Cartesian basis $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$, where $\hat{z}$
is vertical and the positive x direction is horizontal at toroidal angle
$\phi=0$.

The coordinate is defined by projection of the center position onto the
Cartesian x unit vector:

$$
x_c = \mathbf{r}_c \cdot \hat{\mathbf{x}}
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_c$ is the position vector of the target-surface geometric
center, $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ is the Cartesian x unit vector, and $x_c$ is the
resulting signed coordinate. The corresponding center location is completed
by the [y coordinate of the divertor
target](name:y_coordinate_of_divertor_target) and [z coordinate of the
divertor target](name:z_coordinate_of_divertor_target); this quantity does
not specify the target surface extent.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the target center lies in the direction of
increasing Cartesian x from the coordinate origin.

sources.leaf_definition: Component along X axis
sources.parent_definition: Position of the center of the targeted surface

NAMES.name: x_direction_unit_vector_of_camera
NAMES.short:
X-axis component of a camera's unit viewing-direction vector in the
right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the signed projection of a camera’s line-of-sight direction
unit vector onto the Cartesian x axis. It specifies one component of the
camera viewing orientation.

If $\hat{\mathbf d}_{\rm cam}$ is the camera’s line-of-sight direction unit
vector and $\hat{\mathbf x}$ is the x-axis unit vector, the component is
defined by:

$$
d_x = \hat{\mathbf d}_{\rm cam} \cdot \hat{\mathbf x}
$$

Here $d_x$ is this quantity, $\hat{\mathbf d}_{\rm cam}$ is the camera
direction vector, and $\hat{\mathbf x}$ is the unit vector along increasing
x in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ frame. The
corresponding y- and z-axis components are given by [y-direction unit vector
of camera](name:y_direction_unit_vector_of_camera) and [z-direction unit
vector of camera](name:z_direction_unit_vector_of_camera); these components
together specify the viewing direction and satisfy unit-vector
normalization.

sources.leaf_definition: Component along X axis
sources.parent_definition: Line of sight direction unit vector

NAMES.name: xenon_density_at_limiter
NAMES.subject: xenon
NAMES.short:
Xenon ion number density in the boundary plasma immediately adjacent to a
plasma-facing limiter surface, summed over all positive charge states and
excluding neutral xenon atoms.
NAMES.long:
Xenon density at the limiter is the local number density of xenon ions in
the boundary plasma immediately adjacent to a plasma-facing limiter surface.
The evaluation point is the plasma side of the magnetic presheath or sheath
entrance at the plasma-limiter contact, consistent with the parent quantity
[density_at_limiter](name:density_at_limiter).

When charge states are not individually resolved, this quantity represents
the sum over all positive xenon charge states $\text{Xe}^{q+}$, $q = 1,
\ldots, 54$:

$$
n_{\text{Xe}} = \sum_{q=1}^{54} n_{\text{Xe}^{q+}}
$$

where $n_{\text{Xe}^{q+}}$ is the number density of xenon in charge state
$q$. Neutral xenon atoms are excluded from this sum.

Xenon is used as a high-$Z$ impurity seed for radiative power exhaust
management in the scrape-off layer. Its concentration at the limiter is set
by the balance of ionization, recombination, and cross-field impurity
transport, and it determines the local particle flux, radiative power load,
and potential sputtering damage to the plasma-facing surface. This quantity
can be inferred from edge emission spectroscopy combined with
collisional-radiative modeling. For xenon impurity density inside the
confined plasma, see [xenon_density](name:xenon_density); for the analogous
quantity at a divertor surface, see
[xenon_density_at_divertor_target](name:xenon_density_at_divertor_target);
and for xenon at the last closed flux surface, see
[xenon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:xenon_density_at_plasma_boundary).

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Xenon (Xe)

NAMES.name: y_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture
NAMES.short:
Signed y coordinate of the geometric center of a diagnostic aperture in the
right-handed camera Cartesian (x, y, z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the signed Cartesian y coordinate of a diagnostic aperture's
geometric center, measured from the origin of the right-handed camera basis
$(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$. It locates the aperture along the
camera-frame y axis.

The coordinate is defined by projection of the center position vector:

$$
y_{\rm ap} = \mathbf{r}_{\rm ap} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{y}}
$$

where $y_{\rm ap}$ is the coordinate value, $\mathbf{r}_{\rm ap}$ is the
aperture-center position relative to the camera-frame origin, and
$\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is the positive y-axis unit vector; the length quantities
are expressed in m.

This camera-frame coordinate is distinct from the radial and vertical
coordinates in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Together
with the [x coordinate of the diagnostic
aperture](name:x_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture), it locates the aperture
center in the camera frame.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the aperture center lies in the positive y
direction from the camera-frame origin.

sources.leaf_definition: Component along Y axis
sources.parent_definition: Pinhole position in the (X,Y,Z) coordinate system

NAMES.name: y_coordinate_of_divertor_target
NAMES.short:
Signed Cartesian y-coordinate locating the geometric center of the divertor
target surface in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame; positive
values lie along the +y axis.
NAMES.long:
Signed Cartesian $y$-coordinate locating the geometric center of the
divertor target surface is the component of that center-point position
vector along $\hat{y}$ in the right-handed Cartesian $(x,y,z)$ frame with
basis $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$. Here $x$, $y$, and $z$ are Cartesian
position coordinates, $\hat{z}$ is vertical, and $\hat{x}$ is the horizontal
direction corresponding to zero toroidal angle.

The coordinate is related to the same point's position in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame by

$$
y = R\sin\phi
$$

where $y$ is the signed Cartesian coordinate defined here, $R$ is the major
radius of the target-surface center measured from the toroidal symmetry
axis, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle of that same point, and $Z$ is vertical
height in the cylindrical frame.

The scope is the geometric center point of the divertor target surface. It
is a point coordinate of that surface center, not a coordinate field over
the full target surface, a local surface-tangent coordinate, a cylindrical
coordinate, or an area average over target-surface elements.

Together with
[x_coordinate_of_divertor_target](name:x_coordinate_of_divertor_target) and
[z_coordinate_of_divertor_target](name:z_coordinate_of_divertor_target),
this quantity forms the Cartesian position vector of the same center point.
The cylindrical relation implies that the possible value is set by that
point's own $R$ through $|y|\le R$, rather than by a generic device major
radius.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the divertor target surface center is
displaced in the $+\hat{y}$ direction of the right-handed Cartesian
$(x,y,z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$.

sources.leaf_definition: Component along Y axis
sources.parent_definition: Position of the center of the targeted surface

NAMES.name: y_direction_unit_vector_of_camera
NAMES.short:
Signed direction cosine giving a camera’s pointing direction along the y
axis of the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The camera direction-vector component along the y axis is the signed
direction cosine of its pointing direction in the right-handed Cartesian
$(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis. It specifies the projection of the camera
viewing direction onto the Cartesian y axis.

The component is defined by

$$
d_y = \hat{\mathbf{d}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{y}}
$$

where $\hat{\mathbf{d}}$ is the camera pointing-direction unit vector and
$\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is the positive y-axis unit vector. Its value forms part
of the normalized direction vector together with the [x-axis camera
direction component](name:x_direction_unit_vector_of_camera) and [z-axis
camera direction component](name:z_direction_unit_vector_of_camera),
satisfying $d_x^2+d_y^2+d_z^2=1$.

This quantity describes camera pointing direction, not image-up orientation;
that distinct orientation is represented by the [camera y image-up
unit-vector component](name:y_image_up_unit_vector_of_camera).

sources.leaf_definition: Component along Y axis
sources.parent_definition: Line of sight direction unit vector

NAMES.name: y_image_up_unit_vector_of_camera
NAMES.short:
Y-axis component of a camera’s image-up orientation unit vector, expressed
in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The camera image-up unit vector specifies the orientation of increasing
image-up direction, distinct from the camera line-of-sight direction. This
quantity is its projection onto the Cartesian y-axis.

$$
u_{\mathrm{up},y} = \mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{up}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{y}}
$$

where $\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{up}}$ is the image-up orientation unit vector and
$\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is the y-axis unit vector of the right-handed Cartesian
$(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame. The complete image-up vector has unit
magnitude, so its components satisfy $u_{\mathrm{up},x}^2 +
u_{\mathrm{up},y}^2 + u_{\mathrm{up},z}^2 = 1$. This component is distinct
from the camera line-of-sight components represented by [x-direction unit
vector of camera](name:x_direction_unit_vector_of_camera) and [z-direction
unit vector of camera](name:z_direction_unit_vector_of_camera).

sources.leaf_definition: Component along Y axis
sources.parent_definition: Detector orientation unit vector

NAMES.name: z_coordinate_of_divertor_target
NAMES.short:
Vertical Cartesian coordinate of the geometric center of a divertor target
surface, identifying its location along the facility's vertical axis.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the vertical coordinate of the geometric center of a
divertor target surface. It identifies the center point rather than the
target's vertical extent or surface outline.

In the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame, the
coordinate is defined by

$$
z_{\mathrm{target}} = \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{target}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{z}}
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{target}}$ is the position vector of the target
surface center relative to the frame origin and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is the
vertical unit vector. The $z$ direction corresponds to $Z$ in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Together with the [x coordinate of the divertor
target](name:x_coordinate_of_divertor_target) and [y coordinate of the
divertor target](name:y_coordinate_of_divertor_target), this quantity
locates the target surface center. It is distinct from the [vertical length
of the divertor target](name:vertical_length_of_divertor_target) and the
[vertical outline of the divertor
tile](name:vertical_outline_of_divertor_tile), which describe extent and
boundary geometry rather than the center position.

sources.leaf_definition: Component along Z axis
sources.parent_definition: Position of the center of the targeted surface

NAMES.name: z_direction_unit_vector_of_camera
NAMES.short:
Signed Z-direction cosine of a camera’s viewing-direction unit vector in the
right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The camera direction component along the Cartesian Z axis is the signed
directional cosine of the camera’s viewing-direction unit vector. It
specifies how strongly the viewing direction points along the positive or
negative Z direction.

The component is defined by

$$
d_z = \mathbf{d} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{z}}
$$

where $d_z$ is the Z component, $\mathbf{d}$ is the camera’s direction unit
vector, and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is the positive-Z basis vector of the
right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame.

This quantity applies to the viewing direction of an individual camera, with
no spatial, population, or charge-state aggregation. It is a directional
component rather than the camera position, the image-up orientation, or the
magnitude of the direction vector.

Together with the corresponding [x direction unit vector of the
camera](name:x_direction_unit_vector_of_camera) and [y direction unit vector
of the camera](name:y_direction_unit_vector_of_camera), it specifies the
complete viewing-direction vector; the three components satisfy $d_x^2 +
d_y^2 + d_z^2 = 1$, where $d_x$ and $d_y$ are the X and Y components of that
same unit vector.

sources.leaf_definition: Component along Z axis
sources.parent_definition: Line of sight direction unit vector

NAMES.name: power_at_wall_due_to_conduction
NAMES.short:
Thermal power deposited on all plasma-facing wall and divertor surfaces by
parallel electron and ion heat conduction along open scrape-off-layer
magnetic field lines, excluding convective, radiative, and neutral-particle
channels.
NAMES.long:
The power at the wall due to conduction is the thermal energy deposited on
all plasma-facing wall and divertor surfaces by electron and ion heat
conduction along open scrape-off-layer magnetic field lines. It excludes
convective particle enthalpy, absorbed radiation, and neutral-particle
energy deposition.

The defining surface integral is:

$$
P_{\mathrm{wall,cond}} = \int_{S_{\mathrm{wall}}} \left(\mathbf{q}_{e,\parallel}^{\mathrm{cond}} + \mathbf{q}_{i,\parallel}^{\mathrm{cond}}\right) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\,\mathrm{d}A
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{wall,cond}}$ is the deposited conductive power,
$S_{\mathrm{wall}}$ is the union of all plasma-facing wall and divertor
surfaces, $\mathbf{q}_{e,\parallel}^{\mathrm{cond}}$ and
$\mathbf{q}_{i,\parallel}^{\mathrm{cond}}$ are the electron and ion
conductive heat-flux vectors along open magnetic field lines,
$\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the unit normal directed from the plasma toward the
material, and $\mathrm{d}A$ is a surface-area element.

This quantity is the all-wall member of [power due to
conduction](name:power_due_to_conduction). Restricting the selected surfaces
to all divertor targets gives [power of divertor due to
conduction](name:power_of_divertor_due_to_conduction), while a single target
contribution is represented by [power at divertor target due to
conduction](name:power_at_divertor_target_due_to_conduction).

sources.leaf_definition: Power conducted by the plasma onto the wall
sources.parent_definition: Simple 0D description of plasma-wall interaction

NAMES.name: power_at_wall_due_to_convection
NAMES.short:
Power deposited on plasma-facing wall and divertor surfaces by convective
plasma particle flux, comprising thermal enthalpy and directed kinetic
energy carried by streaming ions and electrons from the scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
Convective power at plasma-facing wall and divertor surfaces quantifies the
energy transported by bulk plasma-particle flow from the scrape-off layer
into the material surfaces. It comprises thermal enthalpy and directed
kinetic-energy contributions and is the surface-integrated component of
[power due to convection](name:power_due_to_convection).

$$
P_{\mathrm{conv,wall}} = \int_{A_{\mathrm{wall}}} q_{\mathrm{conv}}(\mathbf{x})\,\mathrm{d}A
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{conv,wall}}$ is the total convective power,
$q_{\mathrm{conv}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local convective energy flux density
at surface position $\mathbf{x}$, and $A_{\mathrm{wall}}$ is the combined
plasma-facing wall and divertor surface area included in the quantity.

Only convective particle-energy transport is included; conductive and
radiative deposition are excluded. [Power at a single divertor target due to
convection](name:power_at_divertor_target_due_to_convection) isolates one
target, while [convective power summed over divertor
targets](name:power_of_divertor_due_to_convection) includes only the
divertor-target subset. The conductive counterpart is [power at the wall due
to conduction](name:power_at_wall_due_to_conduction).

sources.leaf_definition: Power convected by the plasma onto the wall
sources.parent_definition: Simple 0D description of plasma-wall interaction

NAMES.name: ratio_of_iron_density_to_electron_density
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless abundance ratio of charge-state-summed iron-ion number density
to local free-electron number density.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the local iron-to-electron abundance ratio in a plasma,
comparing the population of iron ions with unbound free electrons.

$$
R_{\mathrm{Fe}/e} = \frac{n_{\mathrm{Fe}}}{n_e}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{Fe}/e}$ is the iron-to-electron abundance ratio,
$n_{\mathrm{Fe}}$ is the total [iron-ion number density](name:iron_density),
and $n_e$ is the local [free-electron number
density](name:electron_density).

The numerator is summed over all positive iron ionization states, while the
denominator counts free electrons and excludes electrons bound in atoms,
molecules, or ions. This is a local ratio with no volume averaging, maximum
operation, or specified spatial locus.

The ratio is the iron-specific counterpart of the general
[ion-density-to-electron-density
ratio](name:ratio_of_ion_density_to_electron_density); its numerator is the
charge-state-summed iron density and its denominator is the electron-density
parent quantity.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Iron (Fe)

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_beryllium_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless beryllium abundance formed by dividing the volume-averaged
beryllium density by the volume-averaged electron density.
NAMES.long:
Dimensionless beryllium abundance formed by dividing the volume-averaged
beryllium density by the volume-averaged electron density. It represents the
abundance of ionized beryllium relative to free electrons in the confined
plasma volume.

The abundance is defined by the ratio of the two volume averages:

$$
a_{\mathrm{Be}} =
\frac{\langle n_{\mathrm{Be}} \rangle_V}{\langle n_e \rangle_V}
=
\frac{\left\langle \sum_{q=1}^{4} n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+}} \right\rangle_V}{\langle n_e \rangle_V}
$$

where $a_{\mathrm{Be}}$ is the beryllium abundance ratio, $\langle \cdot
\rangle_V$ denotes averaging over the confined plasma volume,
$n_{\mathrm{Be}}$ is the charge-state-summed beryllium ion number density,
$n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+}}$ is the number density of beryllium ions in charge
state $q$, and $n_e$ is the [electron density](name:electron_density).

The numerator is the [volume-averaged beryllium
density](name:volume_averaged_beryllium_density), summed over all ionized
beryllium charge states and excluding neutral beryllium atoms. The
denominator is the [volume-averaged electron
density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density) over the same confined
plasma volume.

This quantity is a ratio of two global volume averages, not a pointwise
impurity fraction and not the volume average of $n_{\mathrm{Be}}/n_e$. It is
not charge-weighted; a charge-weighted beryllium contribution to
quasineutrality would use terms proportional to $q n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+}}$
rather than the unweighted ion sum. The local pre-averaged counterpart of
the numerator is [beryllium density](name:beryllium_density).

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Beryllium (Be)

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_boron_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless global boron abundance ratio using separately volume-averaged
boron and electron number densities, with neutral boron and every ionic
charge state included.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the global abundance of elemental boron relative to the
electron population. It characterizes plasma composition over the full
plasma volume rather than at a local point or along a line of sight.

The defining ratio is

$$
f_B = \frac{\overline{n}_B}{\overline{n}_e}
$$

where $f_B$ is the boron-to-electron abundance ratio, $\overline{n}_B$ is
the volume-averaged elemental boron number density, and $\overline{n}_e$ is
the volume-averaged electron number density. The overbar denotes averaging
over the plasma volume.

The numerator includes neutral boron and every ionic boron charge state,
while the denominator represents the complete electron population. For the
associated plasma-composition convention, the ratio is evaluated at the time
of peak electron density.

This quantity is distinct from local [boron density](name:boron_density) and
from [line-averaged boron density](name:line_averaged_boron_density): it is
a quotient of two separately volume-averaged densities, not a volume average
of a pointwise ratio or a line average. Its numerator is the
[volume-averaged boron density](name:volume_averaged_boron_density), making
this ratio the corresponding normalized composition measure.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Boron (B)

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_carbon_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless plasma-wide carbon abundance defined as the ratio of
volume-averaged carbon number density to volume-averaged electron number
density. The carbon density is summed over all carbon charge states.
NAMES.long:
Dimensionless plasma-wide carbon abundance is the ratio of volume-averaged
carbon number density to volume-averaged electron number density. It
represents the elemental carbon abundance relative to electrons over the
same plasma volume.

The defining ratio is

$$
f_{C,V} = \frac{\langle n_C \rangle_V}{\langle n_e \rangle_V} = \frac{\left\langle \sum_{q=0}^{6} n_{\mathrm{C},q} \right\rangle_V}{\langle n_e \rangle_V}
$$

where $f_{C,V}$ is the ratio of volume-averaged carbon density to
volume-averaged electron density, $\langle n_C \rangle_V$ is the
[volume-averaged carbon density](name:volume_averaged_carbon_density),
$\langle n_e \rangle_V$ is the [volume-averaged electron
density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density), $n_C$ is the [carbon
density](name:carbon_density), $n_{\mathrm{C},q}$ is the local number
density of carbon nuclei in charge state $q$, $q$ is the carbon charge-state
index with $q=0$ for neutral carbon and $q=6$ for fully stripped carbon, and
$\langle\cdot\rangle_V$ denotes averaging over the same plasma volume for
numerator and denominator.

The population is elemental carbon in the plasma volume, with the numerator
summed over neutral carbon and all ionic charge states. The aggregation
convention is a ratio of two volume averages using the same volume
weighting; it is not the volume average of the local ratio $n_C/n_e$.

This quantity is not an ion-only carbon abundance, not a fraction of total
particle density, and not a charge-weighted impurity measure. It is the
carbon member of the same volume-averaged impurity-abundance family as the
[boron abundance
ratio](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_boron_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density),
and it differs from the [ratio of total ion density to electron
density](name:ratio_of_total_ion_density_to_electron_density), which
aggregates over all ion species rather than isolating elemental carbon.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Carbon (C)

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_oxygen_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short:
Volume-averaged oxygen ion density relative to volume-averaged electron
density for the plasma, with oxygen summed over ionized charge states and
neutral oxygen excluded.
NAMES.long:
Volume-averaged oxygen ion density relative to volume-averaged electron
density is a scalar oxygen impurity fraction for the plasma. It compares the
charge-state-summed volume average of ionized oxygen number density with the
corresponding volume average of electron number density over the same
averaging volume.

The ratio is defined by

$$
f_O = \frac{\left\langle \sum_{q=1}^{8} n_{O^{q+}} \right\rangle_V}{\langle n_e \rangle_V}
$$

where $f_O$ is this oxygen-to-electron density ratio,
$\langle\cdot\rangle_V$ denotes a volume average over the averaging volume
$V$, $q$ is the oxygen charge-state index, $n_{O^{q+}}$ is the local number
density of oxygen ions in charge state $q+$, and $n_e$ is the local electron
number density. The denominator $\langle n_e\rangle_V$ is the
[volume-averaged electron density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density).

The numerator is summed over ionized oxygen charge states $O^{1+}$ through
$O^{8+}$ and excludes neutral oxygen. This quantity is a single scalar
composition fraction formed from volume-averaged populations; it is distinct
from a local [oxygen density](name:oxygen_density), from a [line-averaged
oxygen density](name:line_averaged_oxygen_density), and from a
neutral-inclusive [volume-averaged oxygen
density](name:volume_averaged_oxygen_density) when that quantity includes
neutral oxygen.

The essential relationship is normalization: the charge-state-summed
volume-averaged oxygen ion density is divided by the [volume-averaged
electron density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density), so the result
represents oxygen ion abundance relative to the electron population rather
than an absolute density.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Oxygen (O)

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_tungsten_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless tungsten abundance ratio equal to the plasma-volume-averaged
elemental tungsten density divided by the plasma-volume-averaged electron
density.
NAMES.long:
Dimensionless tungsten abundance ratio equal to the plasma-volume-averaged
elemental tungsten density divided by the plasma-volume-averaged electron
density. It compares the charge-state-summed tungsten-ion population with
the free-electron population in the same plasma volume.

The ratio is defined from the two volume averages over the plasma volume $V$
as

$$
a_{\mathrm{W},V}
=
\frac{\langle n_{\mathrm{W}}\rangle_V}{\langle n_e\rangle_V}
=
\frac{V^{-1}\int_V \sum_{z=1}^{74} n_{\mathrm{W}^{z+}}(\mathbf{x})\, dV}{V^{-1}\int_V n_e(\mathbf{x})\, dV}
$$

where $a_{\mathrm{W},V}$ denotes this tungsten abundance ratio, $V$ denotes
the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface over which both
averages are formed, $\langle n_{\mathrm{W}}\rangle_V$ is the
[volume-averaged tungsten density](name:volume_averaged_tungsten_density),
$\langle n_e\rangle_V$ is the [volume-averaged electron
density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density),
$n_{\mathrm{W}^{z+}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local number density of tungsten
ions in charge state $z$ at position $\mathbf{x}$, $n_e(\mathbf{x})$ is the
local free-electron number density, $z=1,\ldots,74$ indexes the positive
tungsten ionization states, and $dV$ is the volume element.

The scope is the confined plasma volume: both numerator and denominator use
the same volume and the same volume-averaging operation. The tungsten
population is elemental tungsten in positive ionization states, summed over
charge state; neutral tungsten is excluded. The aggregation is the ratio of
the two volume averages, not the volume average of the local ratio
$n_{\mathrm{W}}/n_e$, and the quantity is defined only when $\langle
n_e\rangle_V$ is nonzero.

This ratio is an unweighted tungsten-nucleus abundance relative to free
electrons; it is not a charge-weighted tungsten contribution to electron
density and is not an effective-charge measure. It is the tungsten member of
the same volume-averaged composition-ratio family as the [deuterium-tritium
abundance
ratio](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_deuterium_tritium_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density)
and the [carbon abundance
ratio](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_carbon_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density),
which replace the tungsten numerator with the corresponding species volume
average while retaining the same electron-density denominator.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Tungsten (W)

NAMES.name: angular_width_of_bragg_crystal
NAMES.short:
The Bragg diffraction angle of the crystal in an X-ray crystal spectrometer
channel, fixing the central X-ray wavelength selected for diffraction
according to Bragg's law.
NAMES.long:
The Bragg angle $\theta_B$ is the angle between the incident X-ray beam and
the crystal lattice planes at which constructive interference produces
wavelength-selective Bragg diffraction. It is the primary parameter
governing the central wavelength of a measurement channel in an X-ray
crystal spectrometer.

The selected X-ray wavelength $\lambda$ is determined by Bragg's law:

$$
n\lambda = 2d\sin\theta_B
$$

where $n$ is a positive integer diffraction order and $d$ is the crystal
lattice plane spacing of the diffracting crystal. For a crystal with known
$d$-spacing, $\theta_B$ uniquely determines the central wavelength of the
spectral channel.

In X-ray crystal spectrometer systems used for fusion plasma diagnostics,
the Bragg angle is established by the geometric orientation of the crystal
relative to the plasma X-ray source and the detector. It is a key
configuration parameter for selecting specific resonance lines used in
impurity transport studies and ion temperature measurements via Doppler
line-broadening analysis. Complementary crystal geometry parameters include
the radius of curvature of the diffracting surface in the toroidal direction
and the [aperture radius of the crystal](name:radius_of_bragg_crystal),
while the physical transverse extent of the crystal along the first axis is
given by
[bragg_crystal_width](name:first_local_tangential_width_of_bragg_crystal).

sources.leaf_definition: Bragg angle of the crystal
sources.parent_definition: Characteristics of the crystal used

NAMES.name: bandwidth_of_ece_channel
NAMES.short:
Full-width frequency interval passed by the intermediate-frequency bandpass
filter of an electron-cyclotron-emission radiometer channel, setting the
emission frequencies contributing to its radiation-temperature signal.
NAMES.long:
The bandwidth is the total frequency span passed by the
intermediate-frequency bandpass filter associated with one
electron-cyclotron-emission radiometer channel. It characterizes the
channel's accepted spectral interval rather than an emission intensity or a
plasma frequency.

The full width is defined by

$$
\Delta f_{\mathrm{IF}} = f_{\mathrm{high}} - f_{\mathrm{low}}
$$

where $\Delta f_{\mathrm{IF}}$ is the intermediate-frequency bandwidth,
$f_{\mathrm{high}}$ is the upper bandpass edge frequency, and
$f_{\mathrm{low}}$ is the lower bandpass edge frequency.

This quantity applies to one ECE channel and uses the full-width convention;
it is not the center frequency, a reference carrier frequency, or a
wavelength-domain response width such as the [effective spectral width of a
spectrometer
channel](name:effective_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel). The
accepted interval determines which electron-cyclotron-emission frequencies
contribute to the [radiative temperature at an ECE
channel](name:radiative_temperature_at_ece_channel) and can therefore affect
the channel's effective radial localization.

sources.leaf_definition: Full-width of the Intermediate Frequency (IF) bandpass filter
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (frequency)

NAMES.name: bremsstrahlung_power
NAMES.short:
Total electromagnetic power emitted by free-free bremsstrahlung as electrons
accelerate in the Coulomb fields of plasma ions.
NAMES.long:
Bremsstrahlung power is the total electromagnetic power emitted by free-free
radiation from electron acceleration in the Coulomb fields of plasma ions.
It is integrated over the emitting plasma volume and the full
photon-frequency range.

$$
P_{\mathrm{brem}} = \int_V \int_0^\infty \varepsilon_{\mathrm{brem}}(\mathbf{x},\omega)\,d\omega\,d^3\mathbf{x}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{brem}}$ is the total bremsstrahlung power, $V$ is the
emitting plasma volume, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\omega$ is photon angular
frequency, and $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{brem}}$ is the spectral volumetric
bremsstrahlung emissivity. This quantity is a contribution to [total plasma
radiated power](name:total_plasma_radiated_power) and excludes discrete
[line radiation](name:power_due_to_line_radiation) and [synchrotron
radiation](name:power_due_to_synchrotron_radiation).

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Radiated power from Bremsstrahlung

NAMES.name: brightness_of_visible_camera
NAMES.short:
Visible-camera brightness is band-integrated photon radiance along a
specified viewing direction over the wavelengths admitted by a visible
passband. It gives the photon rate per projected collecting area and
accepted solid angle, with the spectral dependence integrated over that
band.
NAMES.long:
Visible-camera brightness is the photon radiance of a radiation field along
a specified viewing direction after integration over a visible wavelength
interval or passband. It is normalized to projected collecting area,
observation time, and accepted solid angle, and counts photons rather than
radiant energy.

The band-integrated photon radiance is defined by integrating the spectral
photon radiance over the visible passband:

$$
B_\mathrm{vis} = \int_{\lambda_1}^{\lambda_2} L_\lambda^{(\gamma)}(\lambda)\, d\lambda
$$

where $B_\mathrm{vis}$ is the visible-camera brightness,
$L_\lambda^{(\gamma)}(\lambda)$ is the spectral photon radiance at
wavelength $\lambda$, and $[\lambda_1,\lambda_2]$ is the wavelength interval
defining the visible passband.

The quantity is non-negative because spectral photon radiance is
non-negative over the passband. It is distinct from spectral radiance, which
retains wavelength dependence, and from [radiance at spectral
line](name:photon_radiance_at_spectral_line), which refers to an individual
spectral line or narrow line interval; it also differs from energy radiance
because photons are counted without weighting by photon energy.

sources.leaf_definition: Radiance image. First dimension : line index (horizontal axis). Second dimension: column index (vertical axis).
sources.parent_definition: Set of frames

NAMES.name: calibration_factor_of_visible_camera
NAMES.short:
Multiplicative radiometric coefficient that converts a corrected
visible-camera detector signal into absolute photon radiance integrated over
the admitted spectral band.
NAMES.long:
A visible-camera radiometric factor converts a consistently corrected
detector signal into band-integrated photon radiance. It represents the
combined response of the optical throughput, detector sensitivity, pixel
etendue, and exposure treatment rather than the radiance itself.

The defining conversion is

$$
L_{\mathrm{vis}} = C_{\mathrm{vis}} S_{\mathrm{corr}}
$$

where $L_{\mathrm{vis}}$ is the [visible-camera
brightness](name:brightness_of_visible_camera), $C_{\mathrm{vis}}$ is this
visible-camera factor, and $S_{\mathrm{corr}}$ is the corrected detector
signal. The spectral dependence is integrated over the relevant visible
passband. Unlike the resulting brightness, the factor is a calibration
coefficient and must be applied to the corrected signal; it is the
camera-specific component of the parent factor of visible camera.

sources.leaf_definition: Counts to radiance factor, for each pixel of the detector. Includes both the transmission losses in the relay optics and the quantum efficiency of the camera itself, integrated over the wavelength range
sources.parent_definition: Set of detectors

NAMES.name: cold_neutral_fraction
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless fraction of the cold recycled component of a hydrogen-isotope
neutral population relative to the total neutral atom population.
NAMES.long:
The cold neutral fraction is a dimensionless ratio bounded in $[0, 1]$
expressing the relative abundance of the cold, low-energy recycled component
of a hydrogen-isotope neutral population. It is a component of the broader
[neutral
fraction](name:ratio_of_neutral_state_density_to_total_hydrogenic_density),
distinct from the hot charge-exchange-born component.

The fraction is defined as:

$$
f_{\mathrm{cold}} = \frac{n_{\mathrm{cold}}}{n_{\mathrm{cold}} + n_{\mathrm{hot}}}
$$

where $f_{\mathrm{cold}}$ is the cold neutral fraction, $n_{\mathrm{cold}}$
is the number density of cold recycled neutral atoms, and $n_{\mathrm{hot}}$
is the number density of hot charge-exchange-born neutral atoms.

The quantity applies to a specified hydrogen isotope and uses the
two-component neutral-population model. Its denominator is the total neutral
population formed by the cold and hot components for that isotope; it is not
summed across different isotopes and does not represent the hot component
itself.

Within this model, the cold and hot fractions are complementary and sum to
unity. The [hot neutral fraction](name:hot_neutral_fraction) gives the
corresponding charge-exchange-born component, with the energy threshold
separating the two components defined by the applicable population model.

sources.leaf_definition: Fraction of cold neutrals for this isotope (n_cold_neutrals/(n_cold_neutrals+n_hot_neutrals))
sources.parent_definition: Set of isotopes

NAMES.name: deuterium_density
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short:
Deuterium density is the number density of ionized deuterium in the fuel-ion
population. It is the local density of deuterons, excluding neutral atoms,
molecules, and line- or volume-averaged deuterium densities.
NAMES.long:
Deuterium density is the number density of ionized deuterium in the fuel-ion
population. As a species-level density it is charge-state-summed over
ionized atomic charge states; for deuterium this reduces to the singly
ionized deuteron population.

The local deuterium density is defined by the charge-state sum

$$
n_D = \sum_{q>0} n_{\mathrm{D}^{q+}}
$$

where $n_D$ is the deuterium density, $q$ is the positive atomic charge
state, and $n_{\mathrm{D}^{q+}}$ is the number density of deuterium ions in
charge state $q$.

Neutral deuterium atoms, molecular deuterium, and non-deuterium species are
excluded. This quantity is local; spatial aggregations such as
[line-averaged deuterium density](name:line_averaged_deuterium_density) and
[volume-averaged deuterium density](name:volume_averaged_deuterium_density)
are distinct quantities.

NAMES.name: deuterium_deuterium_emissivity_due_to_fusion
NAMES.subject: deuterium_deuterium
NAMES.short:
Local volumetric rate of neutron production from deuterium-deuterium fusion
reactions, giving the spatial distribution of D-D neutron emission per unit
volume at each point in the plasma.
NAMES.long:
The deuterium-deuterium neutron emissivity $\varepsilon_{DD}$ is the local
number of neutrons produced per unit volume per unit time from D-D fusion
reactions. Only the neutron-emitting D-D branch contributes, so this
quantity is the local source of prompt fusion neutrons from
deuterium-deuterium reactions that produce a neutron.

For identical deuterium reactants, the branch emissivity is given by:

$$
\varepsilon_{DD} = \frac{1}{2} n_D^2 \langle \sigma v \rangle_{DD,n}
$$

where $\varepsilon_{DD}$ is the deuterium-deuterium neutron emissivity,
$n_D$ is the local deuterium reactant number density, $\sigma$ is the fusion
cross-section for the neutron-emitting D-D branch, $v$ is the relative speed
of the deuterium reactants, and $\langle \sigma v \rangle_{DD,n}$ is the
velocity average of $\sigma v$ over the local reactant distributions. The
factor $1/2$ avoids double-counting unordered pairs of identical deuterium
reactants.

The scope is the D-D reaction channel at a plasma location, aggregated over
all deuterium reactant charge states and kinetic populations that contribute
to the local neutron-emitting D-D branch unless a component-resolved
quantity is specified. It excludes the proton-emitting D-D branch,
subsequent D-T neutron production involving tritium born from D-D reactions,
and the [deuterium-tritium neutron emissivity due to
fusion](name:deuterium_tritium_emissivity_due_to_fusion). The reaction-pair
label deuterium_deuterium denotes two deuterium reactants; it is not a
charge-state-resolved fuel-state quantity.

Integrating $\varepsilon_{DD}$ over a plasma volume gives the D-D
contribution to the global neutron flux for the same reactant population,
and weighting that contribution by the branch neutron energy gives its
contribution to total neutron power. When reactant populations are resolved,
the corresponding global neutron production can be decomposed into [thermal
neutron flux](name:total_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion),
beam-thermal neutron flux, and beam-beam neutron flux contributions; those
are population decompositions of the volume-integrated source, not separate
definitions of the local D-D emissivity. Together with [deuterium-tritium
neutron emissivity due to
fusion](name:deuterium_tritium_emissivity_due_to_fusion), this quantity is a
reaction-channel-specific member of [neutron emissivity due to
fusion](name:neutron_emissivity_due_to_fusion).

sources.leaf_definition: Emissivity profile due to DD reactions
sources.parent_definition: Reconstructed emissivity parameters and data

NAMES.name: deuterium_tritium_emissivity_due_to_fusion
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short:
Local volumetric rate of neutron production from deuterium-tritium fusion
reactions, giving the spatial distribution of D-T neutron emission per unit
volume at each point in the plasma.
NAMES.long:
The deuterium-tritium neutron emissivity $\varepsilon_{DT}$ is the local
number of neutrons produced per unit volume per unit time from D-T fusion
reactions. Each D-T fusion reaction produces exactly one neutron, so this
quantity is equal to the local D-T fusion reaction-rate density.

For reacting deuterium and tritium ion populations, the emissivity is given
by:

$$
\varepsilon_{DT} = n_D \, n_T \, \langle \sigma v \rangle_{DT}
$$

where $n_D$ and $n_T$ are the local deuterium and tritium number densities
and $\langle \sigma v \rangle_{DT}$ is the D-T fusion reactivity, the
velocity-averaged fusion cross-section evaluated over the relative-velocity
distribution of the reacting ion populations; for thermal reactants it is
the thermally averaged reactivity at the local ion temperature. No symmetry
factor appears because the reactants are distinct species.

This quantity counts neutron production, not fusion energy deposition or
neutron power. It is the D-T channel of the parent emissivity_due_to_fusion
and the counterpart of
[deuterium_deuterium_emissivity_due_to_fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_emissivity_due_to_fusion),
which covers the neutron-emitting D-D branch. Its energy-weighted
counterpart is
[deuterium_tritium_power_density_due_to_fusion](name:deuterium_tritium_power_density_due_to_fusion),
and integrating the emissivity over the plasma volume and weighting by the
per-reaction neutron energy connects to the total_neutron_power.
