NAMES.name: effective_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short:
Response-equivalent wavelength interval of a spectrometer channel, defined
from the full spectral instrument function rather than a Gaussian
approximation.
NAMES.long:
Effective spectral width is the wavelength interval equivalent to the area
of the spectrometer channel's normalized instrument-function response. It
captures the integrated response of non-Gaussian line shapes and is distinct
from the Gaussian standard-deviation measure named by spectral width of a
spectrometer channel.

$$
W_{\mathrm{eff}} = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{R(\lambda)}{R_{\max}}\,d\lambda
$$

where $R(\lambda)$ is the channel response to monochromatic radiation at
wavelength $\lambda$, and $R_{\max}$ is its peak response. For a Gaussian
response with standard deviation $\sigma$, the equivalent width is
$W_{\mathrm{eff}} = \sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma$; therefore, this quantity is not
numerically identical to the Gaussian spectral width.

NAMES.name: energy_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short:
The energy of a detector pixel is the central or representative photon
energy assigned to that pixel's spectral bandpass in an X-ray crystal
spectrometer. It is distinct from the lower and upper bandpass-edge
energies.
NAMES.long:
The energy of a detector pixel is the central or representative photon
energy assigned to that pixel's spectral bandpass in an X-ray crystal
spectrometer. It is the energy counterpart of the [wavelength of detector
pixel](name:wavelength_of_detector_pixel) and identifies the pixel's
spectral-channel assignment rather than the finite width of its accepted
band.

For diffraction order $n$, the representative pixel energy is related to the
pixel Bragg angle by Bragg's law and the photon energy-wavelength relation:

$$
E_\mathrm{pix} = \frac{n h c}{2 e d \sin\theta_\mathrm{pix}}
$$

where $E_\mathrm{pix}$ is the energy of the detector pixel, $n$ is the
diffraction order, $h$ is Planck's constant, $c$ is the speed of light in
vacuum, $e$ is the elementary-charge magnitude, $d$ is the spacing of the
diffracting crystal planes, and $\theta_\mathrm{pix}$ is the Bragg angle
associated with the pixel.

This representative energy is the calibrated spectral-channel value selected
by the spectrometer energy scale; it need not equal the arithmetic midpoint
between the [lower bound energy of detector
pixel](name:lower_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel) and the [upper bound
energy of detector pixel](name:upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel), which
define the edges of the pixel's accepted photon-energy interval.

NAMES.name: etendue_of_bolometer
NAMES.short:
Geometric optical throughput of a bolometer channel, equal to the product of
its effective collecting area and accepted solid angle.
NAMES.long:
Étendue is the geometric optical throughput of a bolometer channel: the
phase-space acceptance of rays transmitted from the viewed region to the
detector. It determines how radiance is converted into collected optical
power.

For a uniform angular acceptance, the étendue is defined by

$$
G = A\Omega
$$

where $G$ is the étendue, $A$ is the effective collecting area, and $\Omega$
is the accepted solid angle. For nonuniform acceptance, $G$ denotes the
corresponding integral over the projected collecting area and accepted
directions.

The quantity describes optical throughput only; detector conversion
efficiency and electronic response are separate properties. It is the
channel-level counterpart of [line-of-sight
étendue](name:etendue_of_line_of_sight) and is closely related to the
aperture area defined by [diagnostic aperture
area](name:area_of_diagnostic_aperture).

sources.leaf_definition: Etendue (geometric extent) of the channel's optical system
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (detector or pixel of a camera)

NAMES.name: etendue_of_hard_xray_detector
NAMES.short:
Geometric optical throughput of a hard X-ray detector’s optical system,
determined by its effective collecting area and accepted solid angle.
NAMES.long:
Étendue is the geometric throughput of the optical system associated with a
hard X-ray detector. It characterizes the angular and spatial acceptance
that determines how incident radiation is coupled into the detector.

The defining relation is

$$
G = A\Omega
$$

where $G$ is the detector étendue, $A$ is the effective collecting area, and
$\Omega$ is the accepted solid angle.

This quantity applies to the detector-level optical system and uses
effective area and angular acceptance for the associated detector; it does
not specify whether those properties arise from one or multiple optical
elements. It is distinct from the detector’s linear dimensions, such as its
[height](name:height_of_hard_xray_detector) and width, which do not
determine optical throughput alone.

Étendue provides the geometric factor relating incident [hard X-ray
brightness](name:hard_xray_brightness) to radiation coupled into the
detector and is the same physical optical-throughput concept represented by
[etendue_of_spectrometer](name:etendue_of_spectrometer), with the owning
optical system changed from a spectrometer to a hard X-ray detector.

sources.leaf_definition: Etendue (geometric extent) of the channel's optical system
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (detector or pixel of a camera)

NAMES.name: etendue_of_line_of_sight
NAMES.short:
Geometric optical throughput of a charge-exchange spectroscopy line of
sight, determined by its collecting aperture and accepted solid angle.
NAMES.long:
Étendue is the geometric throughput of the optical collection system
associated with a charge-exchange spectroscopy line of sight. It specifies
the channel’s angular and collecting-area acceptance for source radiation.

The étendue $G$ is defined by

$$
G = A\Omega
$$

where $A$ is the collecting aperture area, corresponding to the [diagnostic
aperture area](name:area_of_diagnostic_aperture), and $\Omega$ is the solid
angle of the accepted rays at that aperture.

This quantity describes geometric acceptance only. It excludes detector
efficiency, optical transmission losses, and spectral response; those
factors must be treated separately when relating collected signal to
absolute photon flux.

sources.leaf_definition: Etendue (geometric extent) of the optical system for this channel
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (lines-of-sight). The line-of-sight is defined by the centre of the collimating aperture and the position of the measurements.

NAMES.name: etendue_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short:
Geometric optical throughput of a soft X-ray detector channel, set by the
collecting area and accepted solid angle of its optical system.
NAMES.long:
Etendue is the geometric throughput of the complete optical system serving a
soft X-ray detector channel. It characterizes the channel's acceptance of
radiation by combining its collecting area with the range of accepted
propagation directions.

For the channel optical system, etendue $G$ is defined by

$$
G = A\Omega
$$

where $A$ is the effective collecting area of the detector or aperture and
$\Omega$ is the accepted solid angle subtended by that area.

This quantity applies to the specified soft X-ray detector channel and
represents the geometric optical factor for that channel as a whole. It
excludes the radiation radiance, spectral response, detector conversion
efficiency, and other non-geometrical response factors.

The same geometric throughput concept is used for other diagnostic systems,
including [hard X-ray detector etendue](name:etendue_of_hard_xray_detector)
and [bolometer etendue](name:etendue_of_bolometer); those quantities differ
by the owning diagnostic object rather than by the defining relation.

sources.leaf_definition: Etendue (geometric extent) of the channel's optical system
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (detector or pixel of a camera)

NAMES.name: exposure_time_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short:
Temporal duration over which a spectrometer channel accumulates incident
photons to form one spectral measurement.
NAMES.long:
The integration duration is the elapsed time between the start and end of
the photon-accumulation interval for a spectrometer channel. It defines the
temporal window contributing to one spectral measurement and is distinct
from the channel's spectral response, including its [effective spectral
width](name:effective_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel).

It is defined by

$$
\Delta t = t_{\mathrm{end}} - t_{\mathrm{start}}
$$

where $\Delta t$ is the integration duration, and $t_{\mathrm{start}}$ and
$t_{\mathrm{end}}$ are the times at which photon accumulation begins and
ends. The accumulated signal is determined by the time integral of the
incident spectral flux over this interval.

sources.leaf_definition: Exposure time
sources.parent_definition: Quantities measured by the channel if connected to a filter spectrometer

NAMES.name: extent_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short:
Full end-to-end physical size of a soft X-ray detector along the applicable
horizontal or vertical detector-plane direction.
NAMES.long:
The detector extent is the complete end-to-end linear size of the soft X-ray
detector along one specified detector-plane direction. It characterizes the
physical detector boundary rather than a spectral or radiometric property.

For a coordinate $s$ measured along the selected detector-plane direction,
the extent $L$ is defined by

$$
L = s_{\max} - s_{\min}
$$

where $s_{\max}$ and $s_{\min}$ are the coordinates of the two opposite
physical boundaries.

The applicable direction is horizontal or vertical within the detector
plane. This quantity describes an overall detector dimension and is distinct
from pixel dimensions, collecting [area of a diagnostic
aperture](name:area_of_diagnostic_aperture), and optical throughput such as
the [étendue of a hard X-ray detector](name:etendue_of_hard_xray_detector).

sources.leaf_definition: Total camera dimension in each direction (x1, x2)
sources.parent_definition: Characteristics of the camera used

NAMES.name: first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_bragg_crystal
NAMES.short:
Signed coordinate of a Bragg-crystal outline vertex along the first local
tangential axis of the right-handed crystal-local (e1, e2, e3) frame, with
e1 the more horizontal crystal-tangential direction oriented toward
increasing toroidal angle φ in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Signed coordinate of a Bragg-crystal outline vertex along the first local
tangential axis is the scalar displacement of that vertex from the
crystal-local reference point along the first in-surface direction of the
Bragg crystal. The quantity is defined in the right-handed crystal-local
$(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1,\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2,\hat{\mathbf{e}}_3)$ frame tied to
the crystal surface.

The coordinate is the projection of the vertex displacement onto the first
local tangential unit vector:

$$
X_1 = (\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_1
$$

where $\mathbf{r}$ is the position vector of the Bragg-crystal outline
vertex, $\mathbf{r}_0$ is the position vector of the crystal-local reference
point, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$ is the first local tangential unit vector.

The crystal-local triad is fixed geometrically: $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_3$ is the
plasma-facing surface normal, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$ is the more horizontal
tangent to the crystal surface and is oriented so that its toroidal
component points in the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction of the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is
toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2 =
\hat{\mathbf{e}}_3 \times \hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$. This coordinate is distinct
from the [second local tangential
coordinate](name:second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_bragg_crystal), which
uses $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$, and from any coordinate along the surface normal.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the outline vertex is displaced from the
crystal-local reference point in the $+\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$ direction, the
more horizontal crystal-tangential direction oriented toward increasing
toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Positions along x1 axis
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the object in the (X1, X2) coordinate system, used only if geometry_type/index=1. Repeat the first point since this is a closed contour

NAMES.name: first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_reflector
NAMES.short:
Signed first local-tangential coordinate of a reflector-outline vertex in
the reflector's orthogonal local frame (X1, X2), supplying one coordinate of
its irregular polygonal boundary.
NAMES.long:
This quantity gives the position of an individual reflector-outline vertex
projected onto the first axis of the reflector-local orthogonal frame $(X_1,
X_2)$. Together with the corresponding second-axis coordinate, it specifies
the vertex locations that define the reflector's irregular polygonal
outline.

For vertex $i$, the coordinate is defined by

$$
x_{1,i} = \mathbf{r}_i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_1
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_i$ is the vertex displacement from the reflector's local
origin and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$ is the unit vector along the first local
tangential axis. The analogous coordinate for another object is defined by
the [first local-tangential coordinate of an optical
element](name:first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_optical_element).

This quantity describes reflector-outline geometry only; it is not the
reflector center, surface curvature, or an optical-path coordinate.

sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the object in the (X1, X2) coordinate system, used only if geometry_type/index=1. Repeat the first point since this is a closed contour

NAMES.name: first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short:
Signed coordinate of a soft X-ray detector outline vertex along the first
local tangential (X1) axis of the detector-local two-dimensional Cartesian
frame.
NAMES.long:
The first local tangential coordinate specifies the signed displacement of
an outline vertex along the first tangential axis (X1) of the detector-local
Cartesian frame. Together with
[second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector](name:second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector),
it defines the polygonal boundary of the soft X-ray detector's sensitive
area projected onto the object-local plane. The two coordinates $(X_1, X_2)$
form a right-handed pair intrinsic to the owning detector object; their
orientation is fixed per detector installation and is not in general aligned
with the machine cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the vertex displacement is in the direction
of the positive first local tangential axis of the detector-local frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Positions along x1 axis
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the detector/aperture in the (X1, X2) coordinate system. Repeat the first point since this is a closed contour

NAMES.name: first_local_tangential_radius_of_filter_window
NAMES.short:
Geometric radius describing the bending of an X-ray filter window along its
first local tangential direction, defined for applicable curved-surface
geometries.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the local radius describing how an X-ray filter-window
surface bends along its first local tangential direction.

For the surface normal section tangent to that direction, the curvature
radius is defined by:

$$
R = \frac{1}{|\kappa_1|}
$$

where $R$ is the first-local-tangential radius of curvature and $\kappa_1$
is the normal curvature along the first local tangent.

This quantity applies to an individual filter window when its curved-surface
geometry specifies bending along the first local tangent. It describes
surface shape, not aperture size, and is a radius rather than curvature
itself. No front/back surface distinction is implied.

This is a directional surface-curvature specialization of
[radius](name:radius). The [second-local-tangential
radius](name:second_local_tangential_radius_of_filter_window) describes
bending along the other local tangent; neither tangent is necessarily a
principal-curvature direction.

NAMES.name: first_local_tangential_width_of_bragg_crystal
NAMES.short:
Full physical extent of a rectangular Bragg crystal measured along its first
local tangential axis, the crystal-local X1 direction.
NAMES.long:
The first-local-tangential width is the full physical extent of the
diffracting Bragg crystal along its crystal-local X1 axis.

For a rectangular crystal, the width is defined by the endpoint separation:

$$
w_{X_1}=x_{1,\max}-x_{1,\min}
$$

where $w_{X_1}$ is the first-local-tangential width, and $x_{1,\max}$ and
$x_{1,\min}$ are the maximum and minimum crystal-boundary coordinates along
the first local tangential axis.

This quantity applies only to rectangular crystal geometry and represents
the complete endpoint-to-endpoint extent of the diffracting crystal. It is
not a half-width, local chord, averaged dimension, spectral width, or
aperture width; no summation over multiple crystals is implied.

The companion transverse direction is identified by the [second local
tangential coordinate of the Bragg
crystal](name:second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_bragg_crystal), whereas
the [radius of the Bragg crystal](name:radius_of_bragg_crystal) describes a
center-to-edge distance for a circular active surface rather than a full
extent along X1.

sources.leaf_definition: Full width of the object in the X1 direction, used only if geometry_type/index = 3
sources.parent_definition: Characteristics of the crystal used

NAMES.name: first_local_tangential_width_of_filter_window
NAMES.short:
First local tangential width of the filter window is its full
rectangular-aperture extent along the object-local first tangential axis.
NAMES.long:
Width of filter window

For rectangular geometry, the full width is the difference between the
greatest and least boundary coordinates along that axis:

$$
w = \xi_{1,\max} - \xi_{1,\min}
$$

where $w$ is the first local tangential width, and $\xi_{1,\max}$ and
$\xi_{1,\min}$ are the greatest and least values, respectively, of the
[first local tangential coordinate of the filter
window](name:first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_filter_window) on the
aperture boundary.

This quantity applies to one filter window only when its geometry is
rectangular. It is a full width, not a half-width or a signed boundary
coordinate, and is distinct from the [filter-window
radius](name:radius_of_filter_window), which describes the opening for
circular geometry.

Together with the [second local tangential width of the filter
window](name:second_local_tangential_width_of_filter_window), it specifies
the two orthogonal dimensions of the rectangular aperture.

NAMES.name: first_local_tangential_width_of_reflector
NAMES.short:
Full physical extent of a rectangular reflector along its object-local first
tangential axis, defining one dimension of the reflector aperture.
NAMES.long:
The first local tangential width of a reflector is the full geometric extent
of an individual rectangular reflector element along its object-local first
tangential axis. It defines one transverse dimension of the reflector
aperture.

For the two bounding edges along this axis, the width is defined as

$$
w_1 = x_{1,\max} - x_{1,\min}
$$

where $w_1$ is the first local tangential width, and $x_{1,\max}$ and
$x_{1,\min}$ are the maximum and minimum signed coordinates of the reflector
edges along the first local tangential axis.

This quantity applies to one reflector member with rectangular geometry. It
is a full width, not a half-width, radius, vertex coordinate, or aggregate
over multiple reflectors; the width is non-negative by the ordering of the
bounding coordinates.

The same full-width convention is used for an aperture's first local
tangential extent in [first local tangential width of
aperture](name:first_local_tangential_width_of_aperture), while [second
local tangential width of
aperture](name:second_local_tangential_width_of_aperture) represents the
corresponding extent along the orthogonal second local tangential axis.

sources.leaf_definition: Full width of the object in the X1 direction, used only if geometry_type/index = 3
sources.parent_definition: Set of reflectors (optional) reflecting the light coming from the plasma towards the crystal. If empty, means that the plasma light directly arrives on the crystal.

NAMES.name: first_local_tangential_width_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short:
Full physical extent of the rectangular soft X-ray detector aperture
measured between its two boundaries along the detector-local first
tangential (X1) direction.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the full end-to-end width of a soft X-ray detector's
rectangular aperture along its object-local first tangential axis, denoted
X1. It defines one dimension of the detector acceptance geometry used in
etendue calculations.

The width is defined by

$$
w_1 = x_{1,\mathrm{max}} - x_{1,\mathrm{min}}
$$

where $w_1$ is the first-local-tangential aperture width, and
$x_{1,\mathrm{max}}$ and $x_{1,\mathrm{min}}$ are the coordinates of the two
opposing aperture boundaries along X1.

The quantity applies to one soft X-ray detector aperture with rectangular
geometry and represents the complete boundary-to-boundary extent, not a
half-width, an outline coordinate, the second local tangential width, or an
aggregate over multiple detectors. The boundary coordinates used in the
defining difference are provided by the [first local tangential coordinate
of the soft X-ray
detector](name:first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector). The
same geometric convention is used for the corresponding [first local
tangential width of a hard X-ray
detector](name:first_local_tangential_width_of_hard_xray_detector), while
[extent of the soft X-ray detector](name:extent_of_soft_xray_detector)
denotes a broader detector-size quantity rather than this specifically
defined X1 aperture dimension.

sources.leaf_definition: Full width of the aperture in the X1 direction, used only if geometry_type = 3
sources.parent_definition: Detector description

NAMES.name: hard_xray_brightness
NAMES.subject: hard_xray
NAMES.short:
Band-integrated hard X-ray photon radiance received by a channel, normalized
by projected collecting area and accepted solid angle.
NAMES.long:
Hard X-ray brightness is the photon radiance received from a viewing
direction by a channel. It represents photon arrival rate with the
photon-energy dependence integrated over the selected hard X-ray band.

The band-integrated photon radiance is defined by

$$
B_{\mathrm{HX}} = \frac{dN_\gamma}{dt\,dA_{\mathrm{proj}}\,d\Omega}
$$

where $B_{\mathrm{HX}}$ is the hard X-ray brightness, $N_\gamma$ is the
number of received photons in the selected energy band, $t$ is time,
$A_{\mathrm{proj}}$ is projected collecting area, and $\Omega$ is accepted
solid angle.

This quantity applies to hard X-ray photons received by a channel and is
evaluated separately for each selected energy band. Its aggregation
convention is integration over photon energy within that band while
retaining normalization by projected area and solid angle. It is a received
radiometric quantity, not a local volumetric source term, and it counts
photons rather than their deposited or carried energy.

The local production counterpart is hard X-ray emissivity, which describes
photon generation per unit volume and solid angle before propagation to the
channel. Integrating this brightness over the collecting geometry
represented by the [etendue of a hard X-ray
detector](name:etendue_of_hard_xray_detector) gives the received photon rate
under the corresponding angular and area acceptance. Unlike [incident soft
X-ray radiance](name:incident_soft_xray_radiance), which is energy-weighted,
this quantity is photon-count radiance; photon registration probability is a
separate detector property described by [spectral efficiency of a hard X-ray
detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_hard_xray_detector).

sources.leaf_definition: Photons received by the detector per unit time, per unit solid angle and per unit area (i.e. photon flux divided by the etendue), in multiple energy bands if available from the detector
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (detector or pixel of a camera)

NAMES.name: hard_xray_emissivity
NAMES.subject: hard_xray
NAMES.short:
Local production rate of hard-X-ray bremsstrahlung photons per plasma volume
and emission solid angle, integrated over a specified photon-energy band.
NAMES.long:
Hard-X-ray emissivity is the local bremsstrahlung photon production rate per
plasma volume and emission solid angle, integrated over the selected
hard-X-ray photon-energy band. It represents emission from suprathermal
electrons at a physical location and in a specified emission direction.

The band-integrated emissivity is defined by

$$
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HXR}}(\mathbf{r},\Omega;E_1,E_2)=\int_{E_1}^{E_2}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HXR}}^{(E)}(\mathbf{r},\Omega,E)\,\mathrm{d}E
$$

where $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HXR}}$ is the band-integrated hard-X-ray photon
emissivity, $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HXR}}^{(E)}$ is the differential photon
emissivity with respect to photon energy, $\mathbf{r}$ is the emission
location, $\Omega$ is the emission direction labeled by solid angle, $E$ is
photon energy, and $E_1$ and $E_2$ are the lower and upper limits of the
selected energy band.

This quantity is local and directional: it is not integrated along a line of
sight, over a plasma volume, or over emission directions. It applies to
hard-X-ray photons produced by suprathermal-electron bremsstrahlung and
excludes the total bremsstrahlung electromagnetic power and
detector-received radiation.

In an optically thin plasma, [hard X-ray
brightness](name:hard_xray_brightness) is obtained from the corresponding
local emissivity by propagation and integration along a viewing path;
brightness is therefore a received radiance, whereas this quantity is the
local photon source density.

NAMES.name: height_of_hard_xray_detector
NAMES.short:
Height of a hard X-ray detector is the full edge-to-edge extent of its
rectangular aperture along the second local tangential axis, X2, in the
local Cartesian (X1, X2, X3) frame.
NAMES.long:
Height of hard xray detector

It applies to a rectangular detector aperture and denotes a full extent, not
a half-extent, signed coordinate, detector location, housing dimension, or
extent along the local normal. It is distinct from the extent of a separate
channel collimating aperture and from the first local tangential extent,
represented by the [first local tangential
width](name:first_local_tangential_width_of_hard_xray_detector).

For a rectangular detector aperture, this height and the [first local
tangential width](name:first_local_tangential_width_of_hard_xray_detector)
are its two orthogonal in-plane full dimensions; together they determine the
aperture opening area. That area contributes to the [hard X-ray detector
etendue](name:etendue_of_hard_xray_detector), which also depends on the
accepted solid angle.

sources.leaf_definition: Full width of the aperture in the X2 direction, used only if geometry_type = 3
sources.parent_definition: Description of a set of collimating apertures

sources.leaf_definition: Full width of the aperture in the X2 direction, used only if geometry_type = 3
sources.parent_definition: Detector description

NAMES.name: hot_neutral_fraction
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless fraction of the hot charge-exchange-born component of a
hydrogen-isotope neutral population relative to the total neutral atom
population.
NAMES.long:
The hot neutral fraction is a dimensionless ratio bounded in $[0, 1]$
expressing the relative abundance of the hot, charge-exchange-born component
of a hydrogen-isotope neutral population. It is a component of the broader
[neutral
fraction](name:ratio_of_neutral_state_density_to_total_hydrogenic_density),
distinct from the cold recycled component.

The fraction is defined as:

$$
f_{\mathrm{hot}} = \frac{n_{\mathrm{hot}}}{n_{\mathrm{cold}} + n_{\mathrm{hot}}}
$$

where $f_{\mathrm{hot}}$ is the hot neutral fraction, $n_{\mathrm{hot}}$ is
the number density of hot charge-exchange-born neutral atoms, and
$n_{\mathrm{cold}}$ is the number density of cold recycled neutral atoms.

The quantity applies to a specified hydrogen isotope and uses the
two-component neutral-population model. Its denominator is the total neutral
population formed by the cold and hot components for that isotope; it is not
summed across different isotopes and does not represent the cold component
itself.

Within this model, the hot and cold fractions are complementary and sum to
unity. The [cold neutral fraction](name:cold_neutral_fraction) gives the
corresponding recycled component, with the energy threshold separating the
two components defined by the applicable population model.

sources.leaf_definition: Fraction of hot neutrals for this isotope (n_hot_neutrals/(n_cold_neutrals+n_hot_neutrals))
sources.parent_definition: Set of isotopes

NAMES.name: hydrogenic_density
NAMES.subject: hydrogenic
NAMES.short:
Charge-state- and isotope-summed number density of hydrogenic particles in
the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Hydrogenic particle density is the local abundance of hydrogen isotopes,
including every included ionization state, expressed per unit volume.

$$
n_{\mathrm{H}} = \sum_{s \in \mathcal{H}} \sum_q n_{s,q}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{H}}$ is the total hydrogenic number density, $\mathcal{H}$
is the set of included hydrogenic isotopes, $q$ indexes their charge states,
and $n_{s,q}$ is the number density of isotope $s$ in state $q$.

The quantity includes all charge states and isotopic variants and is not
restricted to a particular isotope, ionization state, or neutral population.
The concrete catalog instance is [total hydrogenic
density](name:total_hydrogenic_density).

NAMES.name: incident_soft_xray_radiance
NAMES.short:
Incident soft X-ray power radiance gives received electromagnetic power per
projected detector area and solid angle, integrated over the selected energy
band.
NAMES.long:
Incident soft-X-ray power radiance is the energy-integrated radiant power
arriving at a receiving surface from the viewing direction, expressed per
projected area and per solid angle.

$$
L_{\rm inc} = \int_{\mathcal{E}} L_E^{\rm inc}\,dE = \frac{dP_{\rm inc}}{dA_\perp\,d\Omega}
$$

where $L_{\rm inc}$ is the incident power radiance, $L_E^{\rm inc}$ is the
incident spectral power radiance at photon energy $E$, $\mathcal{E}$ is the
selected photon-energy band or collection of bands, $P_{\rm inc}$ is
incident radiant power, $A_\perp$ is projected receiving area, and $\Omega$
is accepted solid angle.

The quantity applies to soft X-ray radiation incident on a detector channel,
with spectral dependence integrated over the selected energy band or bands.
It is an incoming radiometric quantity per area and solid angle, not a total
power integrated over the detector aperture or viewing directions, and it is
distinct from detector-registration efficiency.

Integrating this radiance over the relevant projected area and solid angle
gives the band-integrated received power represented by [power of soft X-ray
detector](name:power_of_soft_xray_detector). Unlike [hard X-ray
brightness](name:hard_xray_brightness), which is photon-number radiance,
this quantity is power radiance; [spectral efficiency of soft X-ray
detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_soft_xray_detector) instead describes
the probability that incident photons are registered.

sources.leaf_definition: Power flux received by the detector, per unit solid angle and per unit area (i.e. power divided by the etendue), in multiple energy bands if available from the detector
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (detector or pixel of a camera)

NAMES.name: inner_hard_xray_half_width_at_emissivity_peak
NAMES.subject: hard_xray
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless inward extent of the hard X-ray emissivity peak from its
maximum to the inner half-maximum point in normalized toroidal flux.
NAMES.long:
The inner half-width is the inward extent of the hard X-ray emissivity peak
produced by fast electrons, measured along the normalized toroidal flux
coordinate. It is the distance from the peak maximum toward the magnetic
axis to the point where the emissivity falls to half its peak value.

$$
w_{\mathrm{in}} = \rho_{\mathrm{peak}} - \rho_{\mathrm{half,in}}, \qquad \varepsilon_X(\rho_{\mathrm{half,in}}) = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_X(\rho_{\mathrm{peak}})
$$

where $w_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the inner half-width, $\rho$ is the normalized
toroidal flux coordinate increasing outward from the magnetic axis, and
$\varepsilon_X(\rho)$ is the hard X-ray emissivity as a function of that
coordinate. The subscript $\mathrm{peak}$ denotes the emissivity maximum,
and $\mathrm{half,in}$ denotes the inward half-maximum location.

This quantity applies only to the side of the peak toward the magnetic axis.
It is a geometric width, not an emissivity value, integrated emission, or
average, and is distinct from the corresponding outward half-width. When
both sides are defined, the full peak width is the sum of the inward and
outward half-widths.

sources.leaf_definition: Internal (towards magnetic axis) half width of the emissivity peak (in normalized toroidal flux)
sources.parent_definition: Emissivity profile per energy band (assumed common to all channels used in the profile reconstruction)

NAMES.name: lower_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short:
The lower bound energy of a detector pixel is the minimum photon energy
accepted by that pixel's spectral bandpass in an X-ray crystal spectrometer.
NAMES.long:
The lower bound energy of a detector pixel is the minimum photon energy at
the low-energy edge of the spectral interval accepted by an individual
detector pixel in an X-ray crystal spectrometer. It defines the lower
endpoint of that pixel's photon-energy acceptance range.

This quantity applies to photons assigned to one detector pixel and
represents a per-pixel spectral-channel boundary, not an integrated or
averaged energy over multiple pixels or channels. It is distinct from the
[energy of a detector pixel](name:energy_of_detector_pixel), which is the
central or representative photon energy assigned to the pixel, and from the
[upper bound energy of a detector
pixel](name:upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel), which defines the
high-energy edge. Together, the lower and upper bounds delimit the pixel's
accepted photon-energy interval.

sources.leaf_definition: Lower energy bound for the photon detection, for each pixel (horizontal, vertical)
sources.parent_definition: Measurement channel, composed of a camera, a crystal, and (optional) a set of reflectors. The light coming from the plasma passes through the (optional) set of reflectors, then the crystal and arrives at the camera

NAMES.name: lower_wavelength_of_filter
NAMES.short:
Lower wavelength of a filter is the vacuum spectral coordinate marking the
short-wavelength, high-photon-energy boundary of its transmitted passband.
NAMES.long:
Wavelength of filter

The corresponding frequency and photon-energy boundaries satisfy:

$$
\lambda_L = \frac{c}{\nu_U} = \frac{hc}{E_U}
$$

where $\lambda_L$ is the lower vacuum [wavelength] bound, $c$ is the speed
of light in vacuum, $\nu_U$ is the upper frequency bound, $h$ is Planck's
constant, and $E_U$ is the upper photon-energy bound.

This is the lower-edge specialization of [wavelength of a
filter](name:wavelength_of_filter), not its nominal passband center or
passband width. Together with the [upper wavelength of the
filter](name:upper_wavelength_of_filter), it delimits the specified
transmission interval in vacuum wavelength. It does not denote the
wavelength within the filter material or specify the detailed transmission
curve.

NAMES.name: neutron_emissivity_due_to_fusion
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short:
Local volumetric rate of neutron production from all included fusion
reactions, giving the spatial distribution of fusion neutron emission per
unit volume at each point in the plasma.
NAMES.long:
The neutron emissivity due to fusion $\varepsilon_n^{\mathrm{fus}}$ is the
local number of neutrons produced per unit volume per unit time from all
included fusion reactions. Each contributing neutron-producing branch adds
its local neutron yield, so this quantity is the reaction-channel-aggregated
fusion neutron source rather than a single-channel contribution.

For included binary fusion reaction branches, the emissivity is defined by:

$$
\varepsilon_n^{\mathrm{fus}} = \sum_{(\{a,b\},r)\in\mathcal{C}} \nu_{ab,r}^{(n)} \frac{n_a n_b}{1+\delta_{ab}} \langle \sigma v \rangle_{ab,r}
$$

where $\varepsilon_n^{\mathrm{fus}}$ is the neutron emissivity due to
fusion, $\mathcal{C}$ is the set of included unordered reacting-species
pairs and fusion reaction branches, $a$ and $b$ identify the reacting ion
species, $r$ identifies a reaction branch, $\nu_{ab,r}^{(n)}$ is the number
of neutrons produced by one reaction in that branch, $n_a$ and $n_b$ are the
local number densities of the reacting ion populations, $\delta_{ab}$ is the
Kronecker delta for identical reacting species, and $\langle \sigma v
\rangle_{ab,r}$ is the velocity-averaged fusion reactivity for that branch.

This quantity is local to each point in the plasma and is summed over the
included neutron-producing fusion branches and their reacting ion
populations. The factor $1+\delta_{ab}$ counts unordered pairs of identical
reactants once, so identical-population reactions such as
deuterium-deuterium are not double-counted. It represents neutron production
only; it excludes charged fusion products, radiation other than neutrons,
and the released fusion energy represented by
[power_density_due_to_fusion](name:power_density_due_to_fusion).

The related quantity emissivity_due_to_fusion is already restricted to
fusion neutron production; this quantity should not be interpreted as a
neutron-only component of a broader all-product emissivity. Single-channel
contributions are represented by
[deuterium_deuterium_emissivity_due_to_fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_emissivity_due_to_fusion)
and
[deuterium_tritium_emissivity_due_to_fusion](name:deuterium_tritium_emissivity_due_to_fusion);
summing the included channel contributions gives this reaction-aggregated
emissivity. Volume integration of $\varepsilon_n^{\mathrm{fus}}$ gives
neutron_rate with the same reaction-channel aggregation.

NAMES.name: opacity
NAMES.short:
Optical depth measuring cumulative attenuation of electromagnetic radiation
along a specified propagation path through a medium. It uses the wavelength,
frequency, spectral band, or broadband weighting assigned to the attenuation
coefficient.
NAMES.long:
Opacity is the optical depth accumulated by electromagnetic radiation along
a specified propagation path through a medium that removes radiation from
that path. It represents cumulative extinction by absorption and, when the
attenuation coefficient includes it, scattering out of the propagation path.

The opacity for a spectral selection $\chi$ along a path $\Gamma$ is defined
by integrating the matching local attenuation coefficient:

$$
\tau_\chi(\Gamma) = \int_\Gamma \alpha_\chi(s)\,ds
$$

where $\tau_\chi(\Gamma)$ is the opacity for path $\Gamma$ and spectral
selection $\chi$, $\alpha_\chi(s)$ is the local attenuation coefficient for
the same selection at path position $s$, and $ds$ is the differential path
element along $\Gamma$.

The spectral selection $\chi$ may be a wavelength, a frequency, a finite
spectral band, or a broadband weighting; $\tau_\chi$ and $\alpha_\chi$ must
use the same selection. This name denotes the accumulated path quantity for
the radiation component under consideration and does not by itself choose
one of those spectral conventions.

Opacity is not the local attenuation coefficient, a material-specific mass
attenuation coefficient, emitted radiance, or the [spectral absorptivity of
a filter](name:spectral_absorptivity_of_filter); it is the line-integrated
optical depth that governs attenuation along the path. For pure attenuation
with no emission into the path and no scattering into the path, incident
intensity $I_\chi^\mathrm{in}$ and transmitted intensity
$I_\chi^\mathrm{out}$ for the same spectral selection satisfy
$I_\chi^\mathrm{out}/I_\chi^\mathrm{in} = \exp[-\tau_\chi(\Gamma)]$, so
opacities of consecutive path segments add.

NAMES.name: opacity_at_ece_channel_emission_position
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless optical depth along the electron-cyclotron-emission viewing
path at a channel emission position, indicating whether the detected
emission is local and thermal.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the optical depth of the plasma evaluated at the emission
position associated with one electron-cyclotron-emission channel. It
measures the cumulative attenuation between the emitting region and the
relevant observation path.

The optical depth is defined by

$$
\tau_{\mathrm{ECE}}(s_{\mathrm{em}}) = \int_{\mathcal{P}(s_{\mathrm{em}})} \alpha_{\mathrm{ECE}}(s)\,ds
$$

where $\tau_{\mathrm{ECE}}$ is the electron-cyclotron-emission optical
depth, $s_{\mathrm{em}}$ is the channel emission position,
$\mathcal{P}(s_{\mathrm{em}})$ is the line-of-sight path used to accumulate
the optical depth at that position, $\alpha_{\mathrm{ECE}}$ is the
electron-cyclotron-emission absorption coefficient, and $s$ is distance
along that path.

The scope is one channel and its associated emission position; values are
not summed or averaged over channels or over emission positions. This
quantity is the accumulated optical depth, not the local absorption
coefficient or a channel-integrated aggregate. It is the position-specific
form of [opacity](name:opacity), with the evaluation locus made explicit.

Optical depth greater than one indicates optically thick, locally thermal
emission, whereas optical depth less than one indicates that non-local or
suprathermal contributions can be important.

sources.leaf_definition: Optical depth of the plasma at the position of the measurement. This parameter is a proxy for the local / non-local character of the ECE emission. It must be greater than 1 to guarantee that the measurement is dominated by local ECE emission (non-local otherwise)
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (frequency)

NAMES.name: outer_hard_xray_half_width_at_emissivity_peak
NAMES.subject: hard_xray
NAMES.short:
Outward extent of the hard X-ray emissivity peak from its maximum to the
outer half-maximum point toward the separatrix in normalized toroidal flux.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the outward half-width of the hard X-ray emissivity peak,
measured from the emissivity maximum toward the separatrix in normalized
toroidal flux. It characterizes the radial spread of hard X-ray emission
associated with nonthermal electrons on the outer side of the peak.

$$
h_{\mathrm{outer}} = \rho_{\mathrm{half,out}} - \rho_{\mathrm{peak}}, \qquad \epsilon_{\mathrm{HX}}(\rho_{\mathrm{half,out}}) = \frac{1}{2}\epsilon_{\mathrm{HX}}(\rho_{\mathrm{peak}})
$$

Here, $h_{\mathrm{outer}}$ is the outward half-width, $\rho_{\mathrm{peak}}$
is the normalized toroidal-flux coordinate of the hard X-ray emissivity
maximum, $\rho_{\mathrm{half,out}}$ is the outer coordinate where the
emissivity reaches half its peak value, and $\epsilon_{\mathrm{HX}}$ is the
hard X-ray emissivity as a function of normalized toroidal-flux coordinate
$\rho$.

The quantity applies only to the outer side of the emissivity peak, with
increasing $\rho$ directed toward the separatrix. It is a nonnegative extent
and is distinct from the inward half-width, which measures the corresponding
distance on the magnetic-axis side of the peak. Together, the two
directional widths characterize the asymmetric spread of the peak; the
[inner hard X-ray half-width at the emissivity
peak](name:inner_hard_xray_half_width_at_emissivity_peak) provides the
inward counterpart.

sources.leaf_definition: External (towards separatrix) half width of the emissivity peak (in normalized toroidal flux)
sources.parent_definition: Emissivity profile per energy band (assumed common to all channels used in the profile reconstruction)

NAMES.name: power_density_due_to_fusion
NAMES.short:
Local volumetric rate of energy release from all included nuclear-fusion
reaction channels, including energy carried by charged particles and
neutrons.
NAMES.long:
Fusion power density is the local energy-release rate generated by
nuclear-fusion reactions per unit volume. It may represent a specific
reaction channel or the channel-summed quantity, with unqualified fusion
power density understood as the sum over included channels.

The defining reaction-rate sum is

$$
P_{\mathrm{fus}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{r \in \mathcal{R}} \frac{n_{a,r}(\mathbf{x})\,n_{b,r}(\mathbf{x})}{1+\delta_{a_rb_r}}\,\langle\sigma v\rangle_r\,E_r
$$

where $r$ indexes fusion channels, $n_{a,r}$ and $n_{b,r}$ are reactant
number densities in m$^{-3}$, $\langle\sigma v\rangle_r$ is the
reaction-rate coefficient in m$^{3}$ s$^{-1}$, $E_r$ is the energy released
per reaction in joules, and $\delta_{a_rb_r}$ is one for identical reactants
and zero otherwise. The deuterium–deuterium and deuterium–tritium instances
are represented by [deuterium-deuterium fusion power
density](name:deuterium_deuterium_power_density_due_to_fusion) and
[deuterium-tritium fusion power
density](name:deuterium_tritium_power_density_due_to_fusion). This
energy-release quantity includes neutron and charged-particle product energy
and is distinct from fusion neutron emissivity.

NAMES.name: deuterium_deuterium_power_density_due_to_fusion
NAMES.subject: deuterium_deuterium
NAMES.short:
Local volumetric power density from deuterium-deuterium thermonuclear
reactions, including energy carried by both the neutron-producing and
proton-producing branches and characterized by their branch-weighted
per-reaction Q value.
NAMES.long:
The D-D fusion power density is the local rate at which deuterium-deuterium
thermonuclear reactions $D + D \rightarrow {}^3\mathrm{He} + n$ and $D + D
\rightarrow T + p$ release energy per unit plasma volume. It includes both
the neutron-producing branch and the proton-producing branch, so it
represents branch-summed D-D fusion energy release rather than only
neutron-branch energy.

For a thermal deuterium population, the branch-summed power density is

$$
P_{\mathrm{DD}}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{2} n_D(\mathbf{x})^2 \left[\langle\sigma v\rangle_n Q_n + \langle\sigma v\rangle_p Q_p\right]
$$

where $n_D$ is the deuterium ion number density in m$^{-3}$, $\langle\sigma
v\rangle_n$ and $\langle\sigma v\rangle_p$ are the thermonuclear rate
coefficients in m$^3$ s$^{-1}$ for the helium-3-neutron and tritium-proton
branches, $Q_n$ and $Q_p$ are the corresponding branch energies in joules,
and the factor $1/2$ avoids double counting identical deuteron pairs. The
branch Q-values are $Q_n = 3.27\,\mathrm{MeV}$ for $D + D \rightarrow
{}^3\mathrm{He} + n$ and $Q_p = 4.03\,\mathrm{MeV}$ for $D + D \rightarrow T
+ p$; equal branch probabilities give a branch-weighted $Q_{\mathrm{DD}}
\simeq 3.65\,\mathrm{MeV}$ per D-D reaction, to be converted to joules in
the equation.

The displayed expression is the thermal-thermal specialization of the
definition. For beam-thermal, beam-beam, or otherwise non-Maxwellian
deuteron populations, $P_{\mathrm{DD}}$ is still the branch-summed local
energy-release rate, with each branch reaction-rate density multiplied by
its branch energy rather than using Maxwellian rate coefficients. This
quantity is the D-D channel instance of [fusion power
density](name:power_density_due_to_fusion); it includes neutron and
charged-particle product energy and is distinct from fusion neutron
emissivity, from deposited heating of fusion products, and from [D-T fusion
power density](name:deuterium_tritium_power_density_due_to_fusion).

sources.leaf_definition: Fusion power profile due to DD reactions
sources.parent_definition: Reconstructed emissivity parameters and data

NAMES.name: deuterium_tritium_power_density_due_to_fusion
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short:
Local volumetric rate of energy release from deuterium-tritium thermonuclear
reactions, including energy carried by the alpha-particle and neutron
products and characterized by the D-T channel Q value.
NAMES.long:
The D-T fusion power density is the local rate at which deuterium-tritium
thermonuclear reactions release energy per unit plasma volume. It includes
the birth energy of both reaction products, the alpha particle and the
neutron, through the D-T channel energy release.

The defining reaction-rate expression is

$$
P_{\mathrm{DT}}(\mathbf{x}) = n_D(\mathbf{x})\,n_T(\mathbf{x})\,\langle\sigma v\rangle_{\mathrm{DT}}\,E_{\mathrm{DT}}
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is spatial position, $P_{\mathrm{DT}}$ is D-T fusion
power density, $n_D$ is deuterium reactant number density, $n_T$ is tritium
reactant number density, $\langle\sigma v\rangle_{\mathrm{DT}}$ is the
reaction-rate coefficient for deuterium-tritium fusion, and
$E_{\mathrm{DT}}$ is the total energy released per deuterium-tritium
reaction.

It is defined locally for plasma containing deuterium and tritium reactants
and has no spatial aggregation: line-integrated, flux-surface-averaged,
volume-integrated, and total fusion power quantities are distinct. It is
channel-specific, so it excludes deuterium-deuterium and other fusion
reaction channels, and it is not the local deposited heating power from
alpha particles or neutrons after they are born.

Deuterium-tritium fusion power density is the D-T channel contribution to
[fusion power density](name:power_density_due_to_fusion); a channel-summed
fusion power density adds it to other included channel contributions such as
[deuterium-deuterium fusion power
density](name:deuterium_deuterium_power_density_due_to_fusion). Because each
deuterium-tritium reaction produces one neutron, [D-T fusion
emissivity](name:deuterium_tritium_emissivity_due_to_fusion) is the
corresponding reaction-rate density, and multiplying that emissivity by
$E_{\mathrm{DT}}$ gives the D-T fusion power density.

sources.leaf_definition: Fusion power profile due to DT reactions
sources.parent_definition: Reconstructed emissivity parameters and data

NAMES.name: power_density_due_to_radiation
NAMES.short:
Local volumetric rate at which plasma energy is converted into emitted
electromagnetic radiation, with positive values denoting energy loss from
the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Radiative power density is the local rate of electromagnetic energy emission
per unit volume, summed over the radiation mechanisms included by the
physical model. It describes energy leaving the plasma as radiation rather
than energy transferred through collisional, conductive, or convective
channels.

$$
p_{\mathrm{rad}} = \frac{\partial E_{\mathrm{rad}}}{\partial V\,\partial t}
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{rad}}$ is the radiative power density, $E_{\mathrm{rad}}$
is emitted electromagnetic energy, $V$ is plasma volume, and $t$ is time. As
a radiative specialization of power_density, it may include line radiation,
continuum radiation, and other modeled emission processes; it excludes
energy that remains in the plasma or is transferred by nonradiative
channels.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when energy leaves the plasma as emitted
electromagnetic radiation.

sources.leaf_definition: Power density of radiative losses (positive sign for losses)
sources.parent_definition: Radial profiles for a set of time slices

NAMES.name: power_due_to_line_radiation
NAMES.short:
Total electromagnetic power emitted in discrete spectral lines by
bound-bound transitions of plasma atoms and ions.
NAMES.long:
Line-radiation power is the volume-integrated electromagnetic emission from
bound-bound transitions of atomic and ionic populations in the plasma. It
represents the energy carried by discrete spectral lines and is a radiative
loss from the emitting plasma.

For downward transitions, the emitted power is defined by

$$
P_{\mathrm{line}} = \int_V \sum_s \sum_{i>j} n_{s,i} A_{s,ij} h\nu_{s,ij}\,dV
$$

where $V$ is the emitting plasma volume, $n_{s,i}$ is the population density
of upper state $i$ of species $s$ in m$^{-3}$, $A_{s,ij}$ is the transition
probability in s$^{-1}$, $h$ is Planck's constant, and $\nu_{s,ij}$ is the
emitted-photon frequency in s$^{-1}$. The sums include all specified atomic
and ionic emitters and radiative transitions.

This quantity includes line emission from hydrogenic and impurity species,
but excludes continuum bremsstrahlung represented by
[bremsstrahlung_power](name:bremsstrahlung_power) and other channels such as
[power_due_to_synchrotron_radiation](name:power_due_to_synchrotron_radiation).
It contributes to
[total_plasma_radiated_power](name:total_plasma_radiated_power), while
power_due_to_impurity_radiation covers the impurity-specific component.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Radiated power from line radiation

NAMES.name: power_due_to_synchrotron_radiation
NAMES.short:
Total electromagnetic power emitted by relativistic electrons as synchrotron
radiation while their gyromotion is curved by the plasma magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
Power due to synchrotron radiation is the total electromagnetic power
emitted by relativistic electrons as synchrotron radiation while their
gyromotion is curved by the plasma magnetic field. It is a
mechanism-specific contribution to the plasma radiative power and refers to
emitted radiation, not stored electromagnetic energy.

For an emitting plasma volume $V$, the quantity is defined by the volume
integral of the local synchrotron volumetric emissivity:

$$
P_{\mathrm{syn}} = \int_V p_{\mathrm{syn}}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{syn}}$ is the power due to synchrotron radiation,
$p_{\mathrm{syn}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local synchrotron volumetric
emissivity formed from the relativistic electron phase-space distribution
and the local magnetic field, $\mathbf{x}$ denotes position, and $dV$ is a
volume element.

This quantity includes only synchrotron emission and excludes
[bremsstrahlung power](name:bremsstrahlung_power) and [power due to line
radiation](name:power_due_to_line_radiation). It denotes gross
electromagnetic power emitted by the radiating electrons and is distinct
from net synchrotron power escaping a plasma-facing or material boundary
after reabsorption or reflection.

NAMES.name: power_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short:
Band-integrated radiant power received by a soft X-ray detector channel over
its selected photon-energy band or bands.
NAMES.long:
Soft X-ray detector power is the radiant power carried by incident soft
X-ray photons and received by one detector channel after spectral selection.
It represents radiation power rather than the detector’s electrical output.

For a selected photon-energy band, the received power is defined by:

$$
P_{\mathcal{B}} = \int_{\mathcal{B}} E\,\Phi_E(E)\,dE
$$

where $P_{\mathcal{B}}$ is the received power for band $\mathcal{B}$, $E$ is
photon energy, $\Phi_E(E)$ is the photon arrival-rate density as a function
of photon energy, $\mathcal{B}$ is the selected energy interval, and $dE$ is
an infinitesimal photon-energy interval.

The quantity applies to soft X-ray radiation received by a particular
detector channel and is integrated over photon energy within its selected
bandpass. It is not summed over detector channels, viewing directions, or
distinct energy bands; when multiple bands are resolved, each band has its
own band-integrated received-power value. It excludes plasma-emitted power
before arrival at the detector and electrical power generated by detector
electronics.

The quantity is distinct from
[spectral_efficiency_of_soft_xray_detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_soft_xray_detector),
which describes the probability of registering an incident photon rather
than the received radiant power. It is also distinct from
[hard_xray_brightness](name:hard_xray_brightness), which describes photon
radiance rather than the power collected by a channel over its energy band
and collection geometry.

sources.leaf_definition: Power received on the detector, in multiple energy bands if available from the detector
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (detector or pixel of a camera)

NAMES.name: radiated_power_over_core_region
NAMES.short:
Radiated power over the core region is the electromagnetic energy emitted
per unit time, summed over all emitting plasma species and the full photon
spectrum.
NAMES.long:
Radiated power over the core region is the total rate at which plasma in
that region emits energy as electromagnetic radiation. It is integrated over
the region's emitting volume.

The defining volume integral is

$$
P = \int_{V_{\rm core}} p_{\rm rad}\,dV
$$

where $P$ is the radiated power over the core region, $V_{\rm core}$ is the
integration volume, $p_{\rm rad}$ is the local [radiated power
density](name:radiated_power_density), and $dV$ is a volume element.

The quantity sums contributions from all emitting plasma species and charge
states over the full photon spectrum and all emission directions. It
excludes radiation emitted outside the core region and nonradiative
conductive and convective energy transport.

It is the core-region contribution to [total plasma radiated
power](name:total_plasma_radiated_power), whose spatial integral covers the
entire emitting plasma volume. The [core-region power due to impurity
radiation](name:radiated_power_over_core_region_due_to_impurity_radiation)
is only the impurity-radiation component, not the full quantity.

sources.parent_definition: Bolometer diagnostic

NAMES.name: radiative_extraordinary_mode_temperature_at_ece_channel
NAMES.short:
Predicted equivalent blackbody temperature of extraordinary-mode electron
cyclotron emission evaluated at a frequency-selective ECE channel.
NAMES.long:
The extraordinary-mode radiative temperature is the blackbody-equivalent
temperature assigned to the predicted electron cyclotron emission in the
extraordinary polarization at an ECE channel. It represents radiation
intensity, not the kinetic temperature of the emitting electrons.

The defining radiance equivalence is

$$
I_{\nu,X} = B_\nu\left(T_{\mathrm{rad},X}\right)
$$

where $I_{\nu,X}$ is the predicted extraordinary-mode spectral radiance,
$\nu$ is the channel's selected emission frequency, $X$ identifies the
extraordinary polarization, $B_\nu$ is the blackbody spectral-radiance
function, and $T_{\mathrm{rad},X}$ is the corresponding radiative
temperature.

This quantity is resolved for the extraordinary polarization and evaluated
at the frequency associated with one ECE channel; it is not a sum over
channels, polarizations, or emission modes, and it excludes the
ordinary-mode contribution. The [radiative ordinary-mode temperature at an
ECE channel](name:radiative_ordinary_mode_temperature_at_ece_channel) is the
corresponding ordinary-polarization quantity, while [radiative temperature
at an ECE channel](name:radiative_temperature_at_ece_channel) denotes the
channel-level radiation temperature without this extraordinary-mode
restriction. Differences between the predicted extraordinary-mode value and
a measured channel radiation temperature can indicate mode coupling or
optical-depth effects.

sources.leaf_definition: Predicted radiation temperature of the e(X)traordinary mode
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (frequency)

NAMES.name: radiative_ordinary_mode_temperature_at_ece_channel
NAMES.short:
Predicted equivalent blackbody temperature of ordinary-mode electron
cyclotron emission at a frequency-selective ECE channel.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the equivalent blackbody temperature associated with
radiation emitted in the ordinary polarization mode of electron cyclotron
emission. It represents the theoretically predicted O-mode emission
intensity rather than the kinetic temperature of the electron population.

The radiation temperature is defined by equating the ordinary-mode spectral
radiance to that of a blackbody at the same frequency:

$$
I_{\nu}^{\mathrm{O}} = B_{\nu}\!\left(T_{\mathrm{rad}}^{\mathrm{O}}\right)
$$

where $I_{\nu}^{\mathrm{O}}$ is the predicted ordinary-mode spectral
radiance, $B_{\nu}$ is the blackbody spectral-radiance function, $\nu$ is
the channel frequency, and $T_{\mathrm{rad}}^{\mathrm{O}}$ is the
corresponding ordinary-mode radiation temperature.

The quantity applies specifically to ordinary-mode propagation at the
frequency-selective ECE channel and is not a sum or average over
polarization modes or channel frequencies. It is distinct from the
extraordinary-mode radiation temperature, represented by [radiative
extraordinary-mode temperature at an ECE
channel](name:radiative_extraordinary_mode_temperature_at_ece_channel), and
from the mode-agnostic [radiative temperature at an ECE
channel](name:radiative_temperature_at_ece_channel).

sources.leaf_definition: Predicted radiation temperature of the Ordinary mode
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (frequency)

NAMES.name: radius_of_bragg_crystal
NAMES.short:
Geometric distance from the center of a circular Bragg-crystal aperture to
the edge of its active diffracting surface.
NAMES.long:
The Bragg-crystal aperture radius is the transverse geometric extent of the
circular active diffracting surface, measured from its center to its
circumferential edge. It describes aperture size rather than the curvature
of the crystal substrate.

For a boundary point of the aperture, the radius is defined by

$$
r_{\mathrm{ap}} = \left\lVert \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{edge}} - \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{center}} \right\rVert
$$

where $r_{\mathrm{ap}}$ is the aperture radius, and
$\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{edge}}$ and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{center}}$ are position
vectors in the aperture plane, with $r_{\mathrm{ap}}$ expressed in meters.

For an ideal circular aperture, this distance is the same for every boundary
point. It is analogous to the [radius of a diagnostic
aperture](name:radius_of_diagnostic_aperture), but must not be confused with
the toroidal curvature of the Bragg crystal or its [vertical
curvature](name:vertical_curvature_of_bragg_crystal).

sources.leaf_definition: Radius of the circle, used only if geometry_type/index = 2
sources.parent_definition: Characteristics of the crystal used

NAMES.name: ratio_of_neutral_density_of_isotope_to_difference_of_total_neutral_density_and_neutral_density_of_isotope
NAMES.short:
Odds ratio of the neutral density of a selected hydrogen isotope to the
summed neutral density of all other hydrogen isotopes, distinguishing
composition odds from total isotope fraction.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the neutral-population odds ratio for one selected hydrogen
isotope relative to all other hydrogen isotopes. It characterizes isotope
composition using neutral atoms only, with the comparison population
aggregated across every other isotope.

$$
R_i = \frac{n_i}{\sum_{j \ne i} n_j}
$$

Here, $R_i$ is the isotope density ratio, $i$ identifies the selected
hydrogen isotope, $n_i$ is its neutral number density, and $n_j$ is the
neutral number density of another hydrogen isotope. The summation includes
all hydrogen isotopes other than the selected isotope.

The denominator is a total over the other neutral isotope populations, while
the numerator contains only the selected isotope. This quantity excludes
ionized populations and differs from
[total_hydrogenic_density](name:total_hydrogenic_density), which includes
the hydrogenic population across its applicable charge states and isotopes.
It is an odds ratio rather than the selected isotope's fraction of the total
neutral population; if $f_i$ denotes that corresponding neutral isotope
fraction, then $f_i = R_i/(1+R_i)$.

sources.leaf_definition: Ratio of the density of neutrals of this isotope over the summed neutral densities of all other isotopes described in the ../isotope array
sources.parent_definition: Set of isotopes

NAMES.name: reference_calibration_wavelength_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short:
Reference calibration wavelength of a spectrometer channel is the zero-pixel
intercept of its linear pixel-to-vacuum-wavelength relation.
NAMES.long:
Wavelength of spectrometer channel

The defining calibration relation is

$$
\lambda(k) = g\,k + \lambda_{\mathrm{off}}
$$

where $\lambda(k)$ is the calibrated vacuum [wavelength] assigned to pixel
index $k$, $g$ is the dispersion gain giving the wavelength change per index
increment, and $\lambda_{\mathrm{off}}$ is the reference calibration
wavelength. Pixel indexing starts at one.

The intercept is the extrapolated value at zero pixel index, not the
wavelength assigned to the first pixel; the latter is
$\lambda(1)=g+\lambda_{\mathrm{off}}$. Its calibration-intercept role is
distinct from the response-center role of the [reference wavelength of a
spectrometer channel](name:reference_wavelength_of_spectrometer_channel).

sources.leaf_definition: Offset
sources.parent_definition: Wavelength calibration data. The wavelength is obtained from the pixel index k by: wavelength =  k * gain + offset. k is starting from 1.

sources.leaf_definition: Offset
sources.parent_definition: Wavelength calibration data. The wavelength is obtained from the pixel index k by: wavelength =  k * gain + offset. k is starting from 1.

NAMES.name: reference_wavelength_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short:
Reference wavelength of a spectrometer channel is the absolute vacuum
wavelength at the center of its spectral instrument function; a bin-specific
value refers to the center of that detector bin's response.
NAMES.long:
Wavelength of spectrometer channel

The reference wavelength is the absolute vacuum wavelength at the center of
the channel's spectral instrument function. It is a response-position
wavelength, distinct from the wavelength of a spectral line or a wavelength
selected as a calibration reference.

The response-center wavelength is defined by

$$
\lambda_{\mathrm{ref}} = \operatorname{center}_{\lambda}\!\left[\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{ch}}(\lambda)\right]
$$

where $\lambda_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the reference wavelength,
$\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{ch}}(\lambda)$ is the channel's spectral instrument
function as a function of $\lambda$, $\lambda$ is [vacuum wavelength], and
$\operatorname{center}_{\lambda}$ denotes the wavelength coordinate at the
center of the response function.

The value applies to the channel response or, when specified for a vertical
detector bin, that bin's response; it is not an average across bins. The
response spread about this center is characterized separately by the [width
of a spectrometer channel](name:width_of_spectrometer_channel). The
[reference calibration wavelength of a spectrometer
channel](name:reference_calibration_wavelength_of_spectrometer_channel) is
distinct: it is the zero-pixel intercept of a linear
pixel-to-vacuum-wavelength relation.

sources.leaf_definition: Centre (in terms of absolute wavelength) of instrument function
sources.parent_definition: Instrument function for this bin (replaces the ../../instrument function in case vertical binning is used), i.e. response of the detector to a monochromatic emission passing through the spectrometer. The resulting image on the detector will be a 2-D distribution of pixel values, for each wavelength. It can be given as explicit values for each detector pixel (values node) or as a parametric function of wavelength (described by the other nodes)

sources.leaf_definition: Centre (in terms of absolute wavelength) of instrument function
sources.parent_definition: Instrument function (to be used in case vertical binning is not used), i.e. response of the detector to a monochromatic emission passing through the spectrometer. The resulting image on the detector will be a 2-D distribution of pixel values, for each wavelength. It can be given as explicit values for each detector pixel (values node) or as a parametric function of wavelength (described by the other nodes)

NAMES.name: relative_humidity_of_detector
NAMES.short:
Ratio of ambient water-vapor partial pressure to its saturation vapor
pressure at the detector, describing local moisture conditions that can
affect detector performance.
NAMES.long:
Relative humidity at the detector is the ambient water-vapor content
expressed relative to the maximum water-vapor content supported at the local
air temperature.

It is defined by

$$
RH = \frac{p_{\mathrm{H_2O}}}{p_{\mathrm{sat}}(T)}
$$

where $RH$ is relative humidity, $p_{\mathrm{H_2O}}$ is the partial pressure
of water vapor surrounding the detector, $p_{\mathrm{sat}}(T)$ is the
saturation vapor pressure of water, and $T$ is the local air temperature.
The reported fraction is bounded from 0 to 1.

This quantity describes the environmental moisture condition at the detector
and is not absolute humidity, air temperature, or a detector-response
property. It is distinct from an intrinsic detection metric such as
[spectral efficiency of a hard X-ray
detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_hard_xray_detector), which describes
photon-registration probability rather than the surrounding environment.

sources.leaf_definition: Fraction of humidity (0-1) measured at the detector level
sources.parent_definition: X-rays imaging camera (can be used for soft or hard X-rays imaging systems)

NAMES.name: second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_bragg_crystal
NAMES.short:
Signed coordinate of a Bragg-crystal outline vertex along the second local
tangential axis of the crystal-local Cartesian (X1, X2) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed position of a vertex on the Bragg-crystal
outline, resolved along the crystal-local second tangential direction. It
describes the crystal geometry in the local planar Cartesian frame $(X_1,
X_2)$ rather than in the machine cylindrical frame.

For a vertex position vector $\mathbf{r}$ and local-frame origin
$\mathbf{r}_0$, the coordinate is defined by:

$$
x_2 = (\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_2
$$

where $x_2$ is the second local tangential coordinate, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$
is the unit vector along the second local tangential axis, and
$\mathbf{r}_0$ is the origin of the crystal-local frame. Together with the
[first local tangential coordinate of the Bragg
crystal](name:first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_bragg_crystal), it
specifies the in-plane location of the outline vertex.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the vertex displacement from the
crystal-local origin has a positive projection along the second local
tangential unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$.

sources.leaf_definition: Positions along x2 axis
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the object in the (X1, X2) coordinate system, used only if geometry_type/index=1. Repeat the first point since this is a closed contour

NAMES.name: second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture
NAMES.short:
Signed coordinate of an individual diagnostic-aperture outline vertex along
the second local tangential direction, measured from the aperture-local
origin.
NAMES.long:
The second local tangential coordinate of a diagnostic-aperture outline
vertex is the signed component of the vertex's displacement from the
aperture-local origin along the second local tangential direction. It
applies to each outline vertex individually.

For an outline vertex with position vector $\mathbf{r}_v$, its coordinate is
defined by the projection:

$$
X_2 = (\mathbf{r}_v - \mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_2
$$

where $X_2$ is the second local tangential coordinate, $\mathbf{r}_v$ is the
position vector of the outline vertex, $\mathbf{r}_0$ is the position vector
of the aperture-local origin, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$ is the unit vector
along the positive second local tangential direction.

Each value describes one vertex, not an average across vertices or an
aperture width; it is a tangential displacement, not a displacement along
the aperture normal. Paired with the [first local tangential coordinate of
the diagnostic aperture] for the same vertex, it specifies that vertex's
position in the outline. Together, the paired coordinates of the outline
vertices define the aperture boundary and its
[area](name:area_of_diagnostic_aperture).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the vertex displacement from the
aperture-local origin projects along the positive second local tangential
direction.

NAMES.name: second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_filter
NAMES.short:
Second local tangential coordinate of a filter boundary point is the signed
position of that point along the filter's second in-plane basis direction in
the object-local planar frame attached to the filter.
NAMES.long:
Second local tangential coordinate of a filter boundary point is the signed
scalar coordinate obtained by projecting the point's displacement from the
filter local-frame origin onto the filter's second local tangential
direction. It is paired with the [first local tangential coordinate of a
filter](name:first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_filter) to locate points
in the filter plane.

The coordinate is defined by the projection

$$
u_{2,f} = (\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_{0,f}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{t}}_{2,f}
$$

where $u_{2,f}$ is this coordinate, $\mathbf{r}$ is the position vector of
the filter boundary point, $\mathbf{r}_{0,f}$ is the filter local-frame
origin, and $\hat{\mathbf{t}}_{2,f}$ is the second local tangential unit
vector of the filter.

The filter local frame is object-local: $\hat{\mathbf{t}}_{1,f}$ and
$\hat{\mathbf{t}}_{2,f}$ lie in the filter plane. The first local tangential
unit vector is chosen with positive projection along increasing toroidal
angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame; the
second local tangential unit vector completes the oriented in-plane basis
with the filter normal, so that $\hat{\mathbf{t}}_{1,f} \times
\hat{\mathbf{t}}_{2,f}$ points along the positive filter normal. This
quantity refers to the filter boundary itself, not to the [second local
tangential coordinate of a filter
window](name:second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_filter_window).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the displacement from the filter local-frame
origin to the point has positive projection on the second local tangential
unit vector of the filter.

sources.leaf_definition: Positions along x2 axis
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the filter in the (X1, X2) coordinate system, used only if geometry_type/index=1. Repeat the first point since this is a closed contour

NAMES.name: second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_hard_xray_detector
NAMES.short:
Signed coordinate of a hard X-ray detector outline vertex along the second
local tangential axis of the right-handed detector-local Cartesian basis
(first local tangential, second local tangential, local normal).
NAMES.long:
Second local tangential coordinate of a hard X-ray detector is the signed
scalar coordinate of a detector outline vertex along the detector-local
second tangential direction. It is defined in the right-handed object-local
Cartesian basis $(\hat{\mathbf e}_1, \hat{\mathbf e}_2, \hat{\mathbf e}_3)$,
where $\hat{\mathbf e}_1$ is the first local tangential unit vector,
$\hat{\mathbf e}_3$ is the detector-local normal unit vector, and
$\hat{\mathbf e}_2 = \hat{\mathbf e}_3 \times \hat{\mathbf e}_1$.

The coordinate $q_2$ of a vertex at position $\mathbf r$ is the signed
projection of its displacement from the detector-local origin:

$$
q_2 = (\mathbf r - \mathbf r_0) \cdot \hat{\mathbf e}_2
$$

where $\mathbf r_0$ is the detector-local origin and $\hat{\mathbf e}_2$ is
the second local tangential unit vector.

Only the component along $\hat{\mathbf e}_2$ is included. The companion
coordinate along $\hat{\mathbf e}_1$ is the first local tangential
coordinate of a hard X-ray detector; neither quantity is a radial, toroidal,
or vertical component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the vertex displacement from the
detector-local origin is toward $\hat{\mathbf e}_3 \times \hat{\mathbf
e}_1$.

sources.leaf_definition: Positions along x2 axis
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the detector/aperture in the (X1, X2) coordinate system. Repeat the first point since this is a closed contour

NAMES.name: second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_optical_element
NAMES.short:
Signed position of a fiber center or outline vertex at an optical element
along its second local tangential axis, measured relative to the
element-local origin.
NAMES.long:
The second local tangential coordinate locates an individual fiber center or
outline vertex at an optical element. It belongs to the element-local
Cartesian frame $(X_1, X_2)$, where $X_1$ and $X_2$ denote coordinates along
the first and second local tangents, respectively.

The coordinate is defined by

$$
X_2 = (\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_0)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{t}}_2
$$

where $\mathbf{r}$ is the position vector of the specified point,
$\mathbf{r}_0$ is the position vector of the element-local origin, and
$\hat{\mathbf{t}}_2$ is the unit vector along the positive second local
tangent.

Each value describes one fiber center or outline vertex, not an average over
those points. Fiber-center coordinates locate individual fibers, whereas
outline coordinates locate boundary vertices; neither denotes an element
width or a surface-normal displacement. The second tangent is object-local
and is not prescribed to be vertical.

For fiber-center positions in a fiber bundle, the [first local tangential
coordinate of the fiber bundle] supplies the complementary coordinate of the
same center in the local plane.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the displacement from the element-local
origin has a positive projection onto the designated second local tangential
axis.

NAMES.name: second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short:
Signed coordinate of a soft X-ray detector outline vertex along the second
local tangential (X2) axis of the detector-local right-handed Cartesian
frame.
NAMES.long:
The second local tangential coordinate $x_2$ locates a vertex of the soft
X-ray detector outline along the X2 axis of the detector-local frame. In
this right-handed Cartesian triad, X3 is the detector's outward
plasma-facing surface normal, X1 is the first local tangential axis directed
more horizontally toward the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$,
and X2 = X3 $\times$ X1 completes the right-handed triad. The ordered set of
$(x_1, x_2)$ vertex pairs defines the detector boundary polygon in the X1–X2
plane; $x_1$ is given by [first local tangential
coordinate](name:first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector).
Together the two tangential coordinates fully specify the detector aperture
geometry in the object-local frame, distinct from the aperture outline given
by [second local tangential coordinate of a diagnostic
aperture](name:second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture).
