NAMES.name: second_local_tangential_front_surface_radius_of_optical_element
NAMES.short:
Signed radius of curvature of an optical element's beam-entry front surface
along its second object-local tangent, for cylindrical or toroidal surface
models.
NAMES.long:
The second local tangential front-surface radius of an optical element is
the signed [radius](name:radius) of curvature in the normal section
containing the second local tangent and the front-surface normal. It
describes the beam-entry surface along an object-local direction, not an
externally defined vertical direction.

In the right-handed object-local frame $(\hat{X}_1,\hat{X}_2,\hat{z})$,
$\hat{X}_1$ and $\hat{X}_2$ are the first and second tangents at the surface
vertex, and $\hat{z}$ is the chosen front-surface normal. With planar tilt
removed at the vertex, the defining relation is:

$$
\frac{1}{R}=\left.\frac{d^2 z}{d x_2^2}\right|_{x_2=0}
$$

where $R$ is the signed second-local-tangential front-surface radius, $x_2$
is displacement along $\hat{X}_2$ from the vertex, and $z(x_2)$ is the
front-surface sag along $\hat{z}$ in this normal section, measured relative
to the vertex tangent plane. A flat section is the limiting case $1/R=0$.

This quantity applies to cylindrical or toroidal front-surface models. It is
a radius of curvature, not reciprocal curvature or the geometric [aperture
radius](name:radius_of_optical_element), and it does not describe the back
surface.

The [first-local-tangential front-surface
radius](name:first_local_tangential_front_surface_radius_of_optical_element)
describes the orthogonal normal section and need not equal this radius. The
accepted [vertical front-surface
radius](name:vertical_front_surface_radius_of_optical_element) denotes the
same object-local second-direction quantity despite its different
directional label.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the center of curvature of the front-surface
normal section lies on the $+\hat{z}$ side of the local tangent plane.

NAMES.name: spectral_efficiency_of_filter
NAMES.short:
Wavelength-resolved probability that a photon incident on a diagnostic
filter produces a registered detection event after wavelength-dependent
transmission and detection losses.
NAMES.long:
The wavelength-resolved filter efficiency is the conditional probability
that a photon arriving at the filter input with wavelength $\lambda$
produces a registered detection event. It includes the wavelength-dependent
transmission and conversion losses of the filter, optical path, detector,
and readout chain, and is distinct from material absorptivity alone.

$$
\eta_{\mathrm{filter}}(\lambda)=P(\mathrm{registered\ detection}\mid\mathrm{photon\ incident\ at\ wavelength\ }\lambda)
$$

Here, $\lambda$ is the photon wavelength and $P$ denotes a conditional
probability. The parent efficiency of filter is the
incident-spectrum-weighted average of this response, with weighting supplied
by the incident spectral flux over the relevant wavelength range.
Consequently, this quantity is dimensionless and bounded from 0 to 1.

sources.leaf_definition: Probability of detection of a photon impacting the detector as a function of its wavelength
sources.parent_definition: Filter wavelength range and detection efficiency

NAMES.name: spectral_efficiency_of_hard_xray_detector
NAMES.short:
Energy-dependent probability that a photon impacting a hard X-ray detector
is registered by its detection system.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the conditional photon-registration probability for a hard
X-ray detector at a specified photon energy. It characterizes the detector
response after a photon has impacted the detector, rather than the incident
photon flux or the geometric collection probability.

At photon energy $E$, the efficiency is defined by

$$
\epsilon(E) = \frac{N_{\mathrm{registered}}(E)}{N_{\mathrm{incident}}(E)}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{registered}}(E)$ is the number of impacting photons
registered by the detector and $N_{\mathrm{incident}}(E)$ is the number of
photons impacting it at energy $E$. The efficiency is bounded between zero
and one and is the hard-X-ray counterpart of [spectral efficiency of a soft
X-ray detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_soft_xray_detector).

sources.leaf_definition: Probability of detection of a photon impacting the detector as a function of its energy
sources.parent_definition: Set of energy bands in which photons are counted by the detector

NAMES.name: spectral_efficiency_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short:
Energy-resolved probability that a photon incident on a soft X-ray detector
produces a registered event, defining the detector’s spectral response.
NAMES.long:
The spectral detection efficiency is the probability that an incident photon
at a specified energy produces a registered detector event. It characterizes
the detector response, rather than the incident photon flux or the emitted
X-ray radiance.

The efficiency is defined by

$$
\eta(E) = \frac{N_{\mathrm{registered}}(E)}{N_{\mathrm{incident}}(E)}
$$

where $E$ is photon energy, $N_{\mathrm{incident}}(E)$ is the number of
photons incident at that energy, and $N_{\mathrm{registered}}(E)$ is the
number producing registered events. For a probability-based detector
response, $0 \leq \eta(E) \leq 1$. The energy dependence distinguishes this
quantity from the band-integrated [power of the soft X-ray
detector](name:power_of_soft_xray_detector) and makes it the soft-X-ray
counterpart of [spectral efficiency of the hard X-ray
detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_hard_xray_detector).

NAMES.name: spectral_etendue_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short:
Response-weighted optical phase-space acceptance of a spectrometer channel,
combining collecting area and accepted ray directions across its wavelength
response.
NAMES.long:
Spectral étendue is the optical phase-space acceptance of one spectrometer
channel after weighting its wavelength-dependent collecting area and
accepted ray directions by the channel response. It represents
response-weighted optical throughput rather than a wavelength interval or a
calibration coefficient.

The response-weighted étendue is defined by

$$
\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{spec}} = \int w(\lambda)\,A_{\mathrm{eff}}(\lambda)\,\Omega_{\mathrm{acc}}(\lambda)\,d\lambda
$$

where $\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{spec}}$ is the spectral étendue, $w(\lambda)$ is
the normalized wavelength-response weighting, $\lambda$ is wavelength,
$A_{\mathrm{eff}}(\lambda)$ is the effective collecting area, and
$\Omega_{\mathrm{acc}}(\lambda)$ is the accepted solid angle. The weighting
satisfies $\int w(\lambda)\,d\lambda = 1$.

The quantity applies to radiation admitted by the specified spectrometer
channel over its wavelength-response domain. It aggregates aperture
acceptance, ray-direction acceptance, and wavelength response; it does not
describe a particular plasma population or define a spatial emission region.

It specializes the geometric acceptance represented by
etendue_of_spectrometer_channel by incorporating spectral weighting. It is
distinct from
[effective_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel](name:effective_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel),
which represents a response-equivalent wavelength interval, and from
[spectral_calibration_factor_of_spectrometer_channel](name:spectral_calibration_factor_of_spectrometer_channel),
which scales an instrument response to detector count rate.

NAMES.name: spectral_signal_to_noise_ratio_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short:
Spectrometer-channel spectral signal-to-noise ratio is the scalar comparison
of spectral power integrated over a selected signal wavelength interval with
spectral power integrated over a line-free reference interval for the same
channel. It names the shared signal/reference comparison; scale-specific
child names define the numerical mapping.
NAMES.long:
Spectrometer-channel spectral signal-to-noise ratio is the scalar comparison
between selected spectral signal content and a line-free spectral reference
for one spectrometer channel. Its physical content is the comparison of
spectral power integrated over a selected signal wavelength interval with
spectral power integrated over a selected line-free reference wavelength
interval for the same channel.

The scale-specific value is determined from the integrated spectral-power
ratio:

$$
q = F\!\left(\frac{P_{\mathrm{sig}}}{P_{\mathrm{ref}}}\right)
$$

where $q$ is the spectrometer-channel spectral signal-to-noise ratio value,
$F$ is the numerical scale mapping specified by the scale-specific member,
$P_{\mathrm{sig}}$ is the spectral power integrated over the selected signal
wavelength interval, and $P_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the spectral power integrated
over the selected line-free reference wavelength interval for the same
spectrometer channel.

The scope is one spectrometer channel and one selected pair of wavelength
intervals. The aggregation convention is to integrate spectral power over
each interval before applying $F$; the numerator is the signal interval and
the denominator is the line-free reference interval. The reference interval
supplies the noise/reference comparison and is not a second signal interval.

This quantity is not an absolute spectral power, a pointwise spectral power
density, a raw detector response, or a comparison between different
spectrometer channels. As a parent quantity, it denotes the common
signal/reference spectral-power comparison shared by scale-specific
children; the [logarithmic spectral signal-to-noise ratio of a spectrometer
channel](name:spectral_signal_to_noise_ratio_logarithm_of_spectrometer_channel)
is the member that fixes $F$ to base-ten logarithmic scaling of the same
integrated-power ratio.

sources.leaf_definition: Log10 of the ratio of the powers in two bands, one with the spectral lines of interest (signal) the other without spectral lines (noise).

NAMES.name: spectral_wavelength_of_optical_element
NAMES.short:
Wavelength at an optical element specifies the vacuum spectral position at
which its transmission, absorption, or other wavelength-dependent optical
properties are evaluated.
NAMES.long:
Wavelength of optical element

The defining relation is

$$
\lambda = \frac{c}{\nu}
$$

where $\lambda$ is the vacuum wavelength, $c$ is the speed of light in
vacuum, and $\nu$ is the radiation frequency.

Each value denotes a spectral evaluation point, not a response amplitude or
wavelength interval. It does not inherently designate a passband center or
edge, and it denotes the vacuum wavelength rather than the wavelength within
the element's material. The definition is not restricted to a particular
spectral band.

The [spectral refractive index of an optical
element](name:spectral_refractive_index_of_optical_element) and, for a
filter, the [spectral absorptivity](name:spectral_absorptivity_of_filter)
are response quantities evaluated as functions of this wavelength.

NAMES.name: temperature_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short:
Thermodynamic temperature of the soft X-ray detector assembly, describing
its physical thermal state for calibration and monitoring rather than a
plasma temperature inferred from radiation.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the thermodynamic temperature of the physical soft X-ray
detector assembly and describes the thermal state of its hardware.

It applies to the detector object as a whole, with no implied plasma
population, spatial subcomponent, or charge-state aggregation. It is
distinct from the plasma electron temperature inferred from detected soft
X-ray radiation and does not represent a photon-energy or spectral-response
quantity.

The temperature is the thermal operating state relevant to calibration and
hardware-condition monitoring. It is conceptually analogous to [temperature
of neutron detector](name:temperature_of_neutron_detector), while [spectral
efficiency of soft X-ray
detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_soft_xray_detector) describes
photon-registration probability rather than detector hardware temperature.

NAMES.name: thickness_of_bragg_crystal
NAMES.short:
Physical thickness of a Bragg crystal is the normal material thickness
measured between its opposing surfaces along the local surface normal. It
excludes the X-ray ray-path length through the crystal, which depends on
incidence geometry.
NAMES.long:
Physical thickness of a Bragg crystal is the geometric separation of its
opposing crystal surfaces measured along the local surface normal. It is a
property of the crystal body, independent of the direction taken by an
incident or diffracted X-ray ray.

The local normal thickness is defined by

$$
t = \left| (\mathbf{x}_2 - \mathbf{x}_1) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} \right|
$$

where $t$ is the Bragg-crystal thickness in meters, $\mathbf{x}_1$ and
$\mathbf{x}_2$ are corresponding points on the two opposing crystal surfaces
in meters, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the unit normal to the local surface at
$\mathbf{x}_1$.

This quantity excludes the oblique material path length of an X-ray through
the crystal; for an ideal flat slab that path length also depends on the ray
angle relative to the local normal. It is distinct from
[bragg_crystal_width](name:first_local_tangential_width_of_bragg_crystal)
and height_of_bragg_crystal, which are tangential dimensions of the crystal
element.

sources.parent_definition: Characteristics of the crystal used

NAMES.name: thickness_of_optical_element
NAMES.short:
Thickness of an optical element defined by the separation between its front
and back surfaces along the element-local normal axis.
NAMES.long:
Thickness of optical element

The thickness is defined by

$$
d = \left\|\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{back}}-\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{front}}\right\|
$$

where $d$ is the thickness, and $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{front}}$ and
$\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{back}}$ are the position vectors of the front- and
back-surface intersections with the same line parallel to the element-local
normal axis.

The quantity describes one element, not a combined thickness of multiple
elements. It is distinct from the geometric path length of an obliquely
propagating ray and from optical path length, which includes
refractive-index weighting.

The [first local tangential
width](name:first_local_tangential_width_of_optical_element) and [second
local tangential
width](name:second_local_tangential_width_of_optical_element) describe the
element's complementary tangential extents rather than its front-to-back
separation.

NAMES.name: toroidal_angular_width_of_camera
NAMES.short:
Full angular span of a camera field of view in the toroidal direction of the
right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, equal to the non-negative
difference between the largest and smallest unwrapped toroidal viewing
angles.
NAMES.long:
Full angular span of a camera field of view in the toroidal direction of the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame is the non-negative difference
between the largest and smallest limiting signed toroidal viewing angles
subtended by the camera acceptance. In this frame $R$ is major radius,
$\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and
$Z$ is vertical height.

Let $\phi_{\min}$ and $\phi_{\max}$ be the minimum and maximum unwrapped
signed toroidal viewing angles of the limiting accepted rays. The toroidal
angular width is defined by:

$$
\Delta\phi_\mathrm{cam} = \phi_{\max} - \phi_{\min}
$$

where $\Delta\phi_\mathrm{cam}$ is the toroidal angular width of the camera
and the extrema are taken over the camera field-of-view boundary after
choosing a continuous branch of $\phi$.

This quantity describes only the toroidal extent of the field of view. It
excludes the central toroidal pointing angle, the detailed field-of-view
footprint or optical distortion, and the complementary [vertical angular
width](name:vertical_angular_width_of_camera).

sources.leaf_definition: Field of view in the horizontal detector plane
sources.parent_definition: Set of cameras

NAMES.name: toroidal_angular_width_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short:
Full toroidal angular width of the spectrometer-channel spatial-resolution
region in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, including effective
spatial-resolution broadening. The toroidal angle φ increases
counterclockwise when viewed from above +Z.
NAMES.long:
Full toroidal angular width of a spectrometer-channel spatial-resolution
region is the non-negative span in toroidal angle covered by the region
associated with that channel, including its effective spatial-resolution
broadening. The toroidal angle $\phi$ is the angular coordinate in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius,
$Z$ is vertical height, and $\phi$ increases counterclockwise when viewed
from the $+\hat{Z}$ side.

For a channel $c$ with spatial-resolution region $\Omega_c$, the width is

$$
\Delta\phi_c = \max_{\mathbf{x}\in\Omega_c} \tilde{\phi}(\mathbf{x}) - \min_{\mathbf{x}\in\Omega_c} \tilde{\phi}(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $\Delta\phi_c$ is the toroidal angular width, $\Omega_c$ is the
spatial-resolution region of channel $c$, and $\tilde{\phi}(\mathbf{x})$ is
a continuously unwrapped toroidal angle of point $\mathbf{x}$ over that
region.

It is an angular extent, not a center coordinate, orientation, or signed
toroidal displacement. If the region crosses a toroidal-angle branch cut,
the unwrapped angle is chosen so the expression gives the full physical span
of the region; this width may be used as a geometric factor in viewing
étendue, but it is not an étendue.

sources.leaf_definition: Toroidal angle (oriented counter-clockwise when viewing from above)
sources.parent_definition: Full width of the spatially resolved zone in the R, Z and phi directions

NAMES.name: toroidal_coordinate_of_reflector
NAMES.short:
Toroidal angular coordinate of the center of the sphere defining a
reflector’s spherical mirror surface, locating that center around the
symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the toroidal angle of the center of the sphere that defines
a reflector’s spherical mirror surface. It identifies the reflector-center
azimuth, not the mirror’s angular extent, orientation, or curvature.

The toroidal angle $[?25l\phi_c$ of the sphere center is defined from its
projection onto the horizontal plane:

$$
\phi_c = \operatorname{atan2}(y_c,x_c)
$$

where $x_c$ and $y_c$ are the center coordinates in the right-handed
Cartesian basis $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$, with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$.
Equivalently, $\phi_c$ is the angular coordinate in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. Its geometric meaning parallels [toroidal
coordinate of an optical
element](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_optical_element), but the locus here is
the reflector sphere center.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the angle is measured in the direction of
increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, counter-clockwise when viewed from above
along $+\hat{Z}$.

sources.leaf_definition: Toroidal angle (oriented counter-clockwise when viewing from above)
sources.parent_definition: Position of the center of the sphere which defines the mirror, in the case of a spherical mirror (geometry_type = 2), derived from the above geometric data

NAMES.name: toroidal_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short:
Toroidal angle of the geometric center of a soft X-ray detector in the
right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the toroidal coordinate of the geometric center of a soft
X-ray detector. The center is the detector geometry reference point,
including the center of a circular detector or the origin of its local
detector coordinate system.

The toroidal angle is defined from the detector-center Cartesian
coordinates:

$$
\phi_{\rm det} = \operatorname{atan2}(y_{\rm det}, x_{\rm det})
$$

where $x_{\rm det}$ and $y_{\rm det}$ are the Cartesian coordinate values of
the detector center in the right-handed $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis,
with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$. The corresponding vertical location is given by the
[vertical coordinate of the soft X-ray
detector](name:vertical_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the detector center lies in the direction of
increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

sources.leaf_definition: Toroidal angle (oriented counter-clockwise when viewing from above)
sources.parent_definition: If geometry_type=2, coordinates of the centre of the circle. If geometry_type=1 or 3, coordinates of the origin of the local coordinate system (X1,X2,X3) describing the plane detector/aperture. This origin is located within the detector/aperture area.

NAMES.name: total_hydrogenic_density
NAMES.subject: hydrogenic
NAMES.short:
Hydrogen-isotope abundance measure derived from included charge states and
isotopes, either averaged along a line or over a volume or used to normalize
neutral-state density.
NAMES.long:
Hydrogenic-density-derived quantities quantify the abundance of
hydrogen-isotope particles with the included isotopic species and charge
states. Depending on the derivative, the total density is averaged along a
line, averaged over a volume, or used as the reference denominator for a
neutral-state composition fraction.

The underlying [hydrogenic density](name:hydrogenic_density) is defined by

$$
n_{\mathrm{H}} = \sum_{s \in \mathcal{H}} \sum_q n_{s,q}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{H}}$ is the total hydrogenic number density, $\mathcal{H}$
is the set of included hydrogen-isotope species, $q$ is charge state, and
$n_{s,q}$ is the number density of species $s$ in state $q$.

The line-averaged total hydrogenic density and volume-averaged total
hydrogenic density retain density character under their respective averaging
operations. The [neutral-state density
ratio](name:ratio_of_neutral_state_density_to_total_hydrogenic_density) is
instead a composition fraction formed by dividing a neutral charge-state
density by $n_{\mathrm{H}}$, and is therefore not itself a density.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_neutral_state_density_to_total_hydrogenic_density
NAMES.short:
Abundance fraction of hydrogenic particles in a specified neutral internal
state, defined as the neutral internal-state density divided by the total
hydrogenic density. It is bounded from 0 to 1 when that state population is
included in the denominator.
NAMES.long:
Abundance fraction of hydrogenic particles in a specified neutral internal
state is the number-density ratio between that state and the complete
hydrogenic population. It represents the occupation of the specified neutral
internal state within the hydrogenic ensemble.

The fraction is defined by

$$
f_{n,s} = \frac{n_{n,s}}{n_{H,\mathrm{tot}}}
$$

where $n_{n,s}$ is the [neutral internal-state
density](name:neutral_internal_state_density) for state $s$ and
$n_{H,\mathrm{tot}}$ is the [total hydrogenic
density](name:total_hydrogenic_density).

The denominator is the total hydrogenic population, not only the neutral
population or only the same internal-state manifold. For a state population
that is part of the total hydrogenic population, $0 \le f_{n,s} \le 1$. This
quantity differs from the [cold neutral
fraction](name:cold_neutral_fraction), which partitions the hydrogenic
population by cold-neutral component rather than by occupation of a single
neutral internal state.

NAMES.name: total_plasma_radiated_power
NAMES.short:
Total plasma radiated power is the electromagnetic energy emitted per unit
time by all plasma species, integrated over the entire emitting volume and
full photon spectrum.
NAMES.long:
Total plasma radiated power is the rate at which the plasma emits energy as
electromagnetic radiation, integrated over the entire emitting plasma
volume.

$$
P_{\rm rad} = \int_{V_{\rm plasma}} \epsilon_{\rm rad}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $P_{\rm rad}$ is total plasma radiated power, $V_{\rm plasma}$ is the
emitting plasma volume, $\epsilon_{\rm rad}$ is the local electromagnetic
power emitted per unit volume, $\mathbf{x}$ is spatial position, and $dV$ is
a volume element. The emissivity includes all emitting species and charge
states, summed over all electromagnetic emission processes and integrated
over photon frequency and emission direction.

This quantity describes whole-plasma emission, not the radiation intercepted
by an individual detector or absorbed at a receiving surface. It excludes
conductive and convective energy losses and energy carried away by neutrons
or charged particles.

The [bremsstrahlung power](name:bremsstrahlung_power) and [power due to line
radiation](name:power_due_to_line_radiation) are mechanism-specific
contributions to this total, which also includes recombination and other
electromagnetic emission channels. The [radiated power over the core
region](name:radiated_power_over_core_region) is a regional contribution
rather than the whole-plasma aggregate.

sources.leaf_definition: Total radiated power reconstructed from bolometry data
sources.parent_definition: Bolometer diagnostic

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Total radiated power

NAMES.name: tritium_density
NAMES.subject: tritium
NAMES.short:
Local number density of tritium ions in the plasma, the foundational
fuel-ion parameter underlying chord-averaged, volume-averaged, and isotopic
ratio child quantities.
NAMES.long:
Tritium ion number density $n_T$ quantifies the local concentration of
hydrogen-3 fuel ions in the plasma. It serves as the common physical basis
for a family of derived quantities: the chord-integrated mean
[line_averaged_tritium_density](name:line_averaged_tritium_density), the
confined-volume mean
[volume_averaged_tritium_density](name:volume_averaged_tritium_density), and
dimensionless isotopic ratios such as
ratio_of_tritium_density_to_electron_density and
[ratio_of_tritium_density_to_deuterium_density](name:ratio_of_tritium_density_to_deuterium_density).

In deuterium-tritium (DT) fusion plasmas the local volumetric reaction rate
is:

$$
R_{DT} = n_T \, n_D \langle \sigma v \rangle_{DT}
$$

where $n_D$ is the deuterium ion number density and $\langle \sigma v
\rangle_{DT}$ is the Maxwellian-averaged DT fusion reactivity. The combined
DT fuel-ion purity relative to the electron population is tracked by
ratio_of_deuterium_tritium_density_to_electron_density.

Tritium density is inferred from active charge-exchange recombination
spectroscopy, neutron emission measurements in DT plasmas, or pellet
injection and fueling diagnostics.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_tritium_density_to_deuterium_density
NAMES.short:
Local ratio of tritium-ion to deuterium-ion number densities, expressing
fuel-isotope composition independently of the total fuel-ion density.
NAMES.long:
The local tritium-to-deuterium density ratio expresses the relative
abundance of the two hydrogen-isotope fuel-ion populations at the same
location. It is derived from the local [tritium
density](name:tritium_density) and [deuterium
density](name:deuterium_density).

$$
R_{T/D} = \frac{n_T}{n_D}
$$

where $R_{T/D}$ is the tritium-to-deuterium density ratio, and $n_T$ and
$n_D$ are the local number densities of tritium and deuterium ions,
respectively. The densities include the relevant isotope populations summed
over their charge states unless a charge-state-resolved quantity is
explicitly specified.

This ratio is dimensionless and does not represent the total fuel-ion
density; multiplying it by the deuterium density gives the tritium density.

NAMES.name: upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short:
The upper bound energy of a detector pixel is the maximum photon energy at
the high-energy edge of its spectral bandpass in an X-ray crystal
spectrometer.
NAMES.long:
The upper bound energy of a detector pixel is the maximum photon energy at
the high-energy edge of the spectral interval accepted by that pixel in an
X-ray crystal spectrometer. It defines the upper endpoint of the
pixel-specific photon-energy bandpass.

This quantity applies to one detector pixel and describes its individual
spectral acceptance interval; it is not an energy averaged over pixels or
over the full spectrometer. It is distinct from the representative [energy
of a detector pixel](name:energy_of_detector_pixel), which identifies the
central or calibrated spectral-channel energy, and from the [lower bound
energy of a detector pixel](name:lower_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel),
which defines the lower endpoint of the same interval.

Together, the upper and lower bounds delimit the photon-energy range
accepted by each pixel, while the representative pixel energy identifies the
spectral-channel assignment within that range.

sources.parent_definition: Measurement channel, composed of a camera, a crystal, and (optional) a set of reflectors. The light coming from the plasma passes through the (optional) set of reflectors, then the crystal and arrives at the camera

NAMES.name: upper_wavelength_of_filter
NAMES.short:
Upper wavelength of a filter specifies the long-wavelength,
low-photon-energy boundary of its transmitted passband as a vacuum spectral
coordinate.
NAMES.long:
Wavelength of filter

The upper wavelength bound corresponds to the lower frequency boundary of
the same passband:

$$
\lambda_{\mathrm{u}} = \frac{c}{\nu_{\min}}
$$

where $\lambda_{\mathrm{u}}$ is the upper wavelength bound, $c$ is the speed
of light in vacuum, and $\nu_{\min}$ is the lower frequency boundary of the
passband.

This quantity is the upper-edge specialization of [wavelength of a
filter](name:wavelength_of_filter), not its nominal band center or
bandwidth. Together with the [lower wavelength
bound](name:lower_wavelength_of_filter), it delimits the specified
transmission interval; the difference between these bounds is the wavelength
span. It denotes a vacuum spectral coordinate, not the wavelength inside the
filter material.

NAMES.name: vertical_angle_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short:
Signed elevation angle of a camera pixel’s line of sight relative to the
camera optical axis, specifying its vertical position within the field of
view.
NAMES.long:
The vertical viewing angle of a camera pixel is the signed elevation offset
of its line of sight from the camera optical axis. It specifies angular
position in the camera’s vertical image direction, rather than the full
vertical field-of-view span described by [vertical angular width of
camera](name:vertical_angular_width_of_camera).

In the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ frame, let
$\hat{\ell}$ be the pixel line-of-sight unit vector, $\hat{o}$ the
optical-axis unit vector, and $\hat{v}$ the camera image-up unit vector. The
angle is defined by

$$
\alpha_v = \operatorname{atan2}(\hat{\ell}\cdot\hat{v},\hat{\ell}\cdot\hat{o})
$$

where $\alpha_v$ is the signed vertical viewing angle and the three hatted
quantities are dimensionless unit vectors. The image-up orientation
determines the vertical angular direction.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the pixel line of sight has a positive
projection onto the camera image-up direction relative to the optical axis.

sources.leaf_definition: Beta angle of each pixel in the vertical axis
sources.parent_definition: Set of detectors

NAMES.name: vertical_angular_width_of_camera
NAMES.short:
Angular extent of a camera’s imaging coverage along the vertical Z direction
of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Vertical angular width is the total angular span covered by a camera’s
imaging region in the detector plane along the physical vertical direction.
It is a non-negative field-of-view quantity, independent of the signs of the
individual viewing angles.

The width is defined by the difference between the largest and smallest
covered vertical viewing angles:

$$
\Delta\theta_{\mathrm{vert}} = \theta_{\mathrm{vert,max}} - \theta_{\mathrm{vert,min}}
$$

where $\Delta\theta_{\mathrm{vert}}$ is the vertical angular width and
$\theta_{\mathrm{vert,max}}$ and $\theta_{\mathrm{vert,min}}$ are the upper
and lower signed vertical viewing-angle limits, expressed in radians. The
vertical direction is $+Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$
frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is
vertical height.

This full-span quantity is distinct from the signed [vertical angle of a
detector pixel](name:vertical_angle_of_detector_pixel). Its directional
counterpart is the [toroidal angular width of a
camera](name:toroidal_angular_width_of_camera).

NAMES.name: vertical_back_surface_curvature_of_optical_element
NAMES.short:
Vertical back-surface curvature of an optical element is the signed
directional radius of curvature of the rear optical surface along the second
local tangential aperture direction. Here vertical means object-local
aperture vertical, not the Z direction of the right-handed cylindrical (R,
φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Vertical back-surface curvature of an optical element is the signed
directional radius of curvature of the back optical surface in its second
local tangential aperture direction. The right-handed local optical-surface
frame is $(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1, \hat{\mathbf{e}}_2, \hat{\mathbf{n}}_b)$ with
$\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1 \times \hat{\mathbf{e}}_2 = \hat{\mathbf{n}}_b$, where
$\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$ and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$ are the first and second
surface-tangential aperture directions and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_b$ is the
positive normal of the back surface; this quantity uses
$\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$, the object-local aperture vertical direction.

The defining relation is the reciprocal of the signed normal curvature of
the back-surface normal section tangent to $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$:

$$
R_{b,2} = \frac{1}{\kappa_{n,b}(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2)}
$$

where $R_{b,2}$ is the vertical back-surface curvature of the optical
element and $\kappa_{n,b}(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2)$ is the signed normal
curvature of the back surface in the $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$ direction.

This is a local directional radius, not the scalar parent optical-element
curvature and not the direction-agnostic back-surface curvature. It equals
the first-direction radius only for locally spherical or otherwise
direction-independent curvature, and it is not a principal, sagittal, or
meridional radius unless the surface definition aligns $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$
with that direction. Together with an orthogonal directional radius it may
characterize simple aligned toroidal curvature, but it does not fully
characterize a general aspherical surface.

sources.parent_definition: Curvature of the front surface

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_camera
NAMES.short:
Vertical coordinate of the camera's geometric center, giving its signed
height relative to the origin in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z)
frame.
NAMES.long:
Vertical coordinate of the camera's geometric center specifies its signed
height relative to the coordinate origin in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Here $R$ denotes major radius, $\phi$ toroidal angle,
and $Z$ vertical position.

The coordinate is defined by the vertical projection of the center-position
vector:

$$
Z = \mathbf{x}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}}
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is the position vector from the coordinate origin to the
camera's geometric center and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is the unit vector along
the symmetry axis in the direction of increasing $Z$.

The reference point is the camera's geometric center, not an individual
pixel or a line-of-sight point. This coordinate is distinct from the
camera's vertical extent and from components of its local orientation
vectors; no averaging over pixels or cameras is implied.

Together with the camera-center major radius and toroidal angle, it
specifies the center position. The [vertical coordinate of an
aperture](name:vertical_coordinate_of_aperture) applies the same projection
to a different object's geometric center.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the camera center lies above the coordinate
origin in the direction of increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short:
Vertical coordinate at a detector pixel specifies its signed height from the
zero-height plane in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Vertical coordinate at a detector pixel is its signed height relative to the
zero-height plane in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. Here
$R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height
along the toroidal symmetry axis.

The coordinate is defined by

$$
Z = \mathbf{x}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}}
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is the detector-pixel position vector measured from the
coordinate origin and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is the unit vector parallel to the
symmetry axis toward increasing $Z$.

The quantity applies separately to each detector-pixel position, without
averaging over pixels. It is a point coordinate, not the vertical extent of
a pixel or a coordinate along a detector-local tangent direction.

The [toroidal coordinate at the detector
pixel](name:toroidal_coordinate_at_detector_pixel) supplies the angular
coordinate of the same position about the symmetry axis, whereas this
quantity supplies its vertical coordinate.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the detector pixel lies on the $+Z$ side of
the zero-height plane.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_filter_window
NAMES.short:
Vertical coordinate of the filter-window center, giving its signed height
relative to the machine midplane in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z)
frame.
NAMES.long:
In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, this quantity is the
vertical coordinate of the filter-window center, with zero at the machine
midplane. The basis $(\hat{\mathbf{R}}, \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}},
\hat{\mathbf{Z}})$ is right-handed; $R$ is major radius from the machine
symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The coordinate is the projection of the center's position vector onto the
vertical direction:

$$
Z = \mathbf{x}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}}
$$

Here $Z$ is the filter-window center's vertical coordinate, $\mathbf{x}$ is
its position vector relative to the frame origin, and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is
the unit vector parallel to the toroidal symmetry axis in the positive $Z$
direction.

This quantity specifies the location of one geometric center point of the
filter window; it is not a surface-averaged coordinate, the window's
vertical extent or orientation, or a coordinate along a filter-local axis.

Together with the [radial coordinate of the filter
window](name:radial_coordinate_of_filter_window) and [toroidal coordinate of
the filter window](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_filter_window), it specifies
the spatial location of the same center. The [vertical coordinate of an
aperture](name:vertical_coordinate_of_aperture) and [vertical coordinate of
a diagnostic aperture](name:vertical_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture)
refer to different component centers and are not substitutes for this
quantity.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the filter-window center lies above the
machine midplane, in the direction of increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short:
Vertical Z coordinate of the geometric center of a soft X-ray detector in
the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Vertical Z coordinate of the geometric center of a soft X-ray detector is
the height coordinate of that detector center in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is
toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The origin of $Z$ is the machine
midplane, so $Z=0$ lies on that midplane.

Together with the corresponding major-radius and toroidal-angle coordinates,
this quantity specifies the absolute geometric position of the detector
center. It is distinct from a detector-pixel coordinate, an aperture
position, a line-of-sight direction, and any measured soft-X-ray signal.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the detector center is above the machine
midplane in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction.

sources.parent_definition: If geometry_type=2, coordinates of the centre of the circle. If geometry_type=1 or 3, coordinates of the origin of the local coordinate system (X1,X2,X3) describing the plane detector/aperture. This origin is located within the detector/aperture area.

NAMES.name: vertical_curvature_of_bragg_crystal
NAMES.short:
Radius of curvature of the diffracting surface of a Bragg crystal along its
local vertical (X2) direction, defining one axis of its focusing geometry.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the local radius of curvature of the Bragg crystal's
diffracting surface along its local vertical, or X2, tangent direction. It
characterizes the crystal bending used for Bragg-diffraction focusing in a
doubly curved geometry.

$$
R_v = \frac{1}{|\kappa_v|}
$$

where $R_v$ is the radius of curvature in m and $\kappa_v$ is the signed
normal curvature in m$^{-1}$ along the local vertical tangent direction. A
planar surface corresponds to zero curvature and an unbounded radius.

This quantity describes the diffracting surface, not the geometric aperture
radius given by [radius of Bragg crystal](name:radius_of_bragg_crystal).
Together with the toroidal curvature of the Bragg crystal, it specifies the
directional curvature scales of a doubly curved crystal.

sources.leaf_definition: Radius of curvature in the X2 direction, to be filled only for curvature_type/index = 3 or 5
sources.parent_definition: Characteristics of the crystal used

NAMES.name: vertical_displacement_of_thomson_scattering_channel_position
NAMES.short:
Signed vertical offset applied to a Thomson-scattering channel position
relative to its static geometric location.
NAMES.long:
The vertical displacement of a Thomson-scattering channel position is the
signed incremental change in that channel’s geometric location along the
vertical direction. It represents an offset from the static channel position
rather than the absolute position itself.

The displacement is defined by

$$
\Delta Z = Z_{\mathrm{actual}} - Z_{\mathrm{static}}
$$

where $\Delta Z$ is the vertical displacement, $Z_{\mathrm{actual}}$ is the
actual vertical coordinate of the channel position, and
$Z_{\mathrm{static}}$ is its static vertical coordinate.

This quantity applies to one Thomson-scattering channel position and
includes only its vertical component. It is not averaged over channels, does
not represent a plasma-wide vertical displacement, and is distinct from the
absolute [vertical coordinate of a measurement
position](name:vertical_coordinate_of_measurement_position).

The actual vertical coordinate is obtained by adding this displacement to
the static vertical coordinate, $Z_{\mathrm{actual}} = Z_{\mathrm{static}} +
\Delta Z$.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the displacement is directed toward
increasing $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Height
sources.parent_definition: Incremental variation of the position of the measurements, due to e.g. different lasers not intersecting the line of sight at the same position. The actual position is then the static position + delta_position

NAMES.name: vertical_front_surface_radius_of_optical_element
NAMES.short:
Radius of curvature of an optical element's beam-entry front surface along
the local second tangential direction (X2, the optical-element vertical
direction) in the right-handed local optical-element frame (X1, X2, z).
NAMES.long:
Radius of curvature of an optical element's beam-entry front surface along
the local second tangential ($X_2$, optical-element vertical) direction is
the signed radius of the front-surface normal section spanned by $\hat{X}_2$
and $\hat{z}$ in the right-handed local optical-element frame
$(\hat{X}_1,\hat{X}_2,\hat{z})$. The coordinates $x_1$ and $x_2$ lie in the
local tangent plane at the surface vertex, and $z$ is the local
front-surface-normal sag coordinate. This is a radius of curvature, not a
reciprocal curvature.

At the surface vertex, after subtracting planar tilt so that $\partial
z/\partial x_2=0$ there, the signed radius is defined by the second
derivative of the sag in the $X_2$ normal section:

$$
\frac{1}{R_2} = \left.\frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial x_2^2}\right|_{x_2=0}
$$

where $z(x_2)$ is the front-surface sag along $\hat{z}$, $x_2$ is
displacement along $\hat{X}_2$, and $R_2$ is this signed radius; $z$, $x_2$,
and $R_2$ are in meters. For small sag this definition implies
$z(x_2)-z(0)\simeq x_2^2/(2R_2)$ near the vertex, and a flat section is the
limiting case $1/R_2=0$.

For spherical surface models the first- and second-local-tangential radii of
the front surface are equal. For cylindrical, toroidal, or separably curved
surface models they may differ, so this quantity is distinct from the
orthogonal first-local-tangential front-surface quantity
x_front_surface_curvature_of_optical_element and from the rear-surface
quantity
[vertical_back_surface_curvature_of_optical_element](name:vertical_back_surface_curvature_of_optical_element);
[vertical_front_surface_curvature_of_optical_element](name:second_local_tangential_front_surface_radius_of_optical_element)
uses the same second-local-tangential front-surface radius convention.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the center of curvature of the front surface
in the normal section spanned by $\hat{X}_2$ and $\hat{z}$ lies on the
$+\hat{z}$ side of the local tangent plane.

NAMES.name: viewing_efficiency_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short:
Fraction of locally emitted light collected by a spectrometer channel’s
optical system from each specified region-of-interest point, including
non-pinhole viewing geometries.
NAMES.long:
Viewing efficiency is the geometric fraction of radiation emitted locally at
a specified point that is collected by the optical system of a spectrometer
channel. It characterizes spatial light collection for non-pinhole optics,
rather than the probability that a detector registers an incident photon.

For a point at position $mathbf{r}$, the viewing efficiency is defined by

$$
\eta_{\mathrm{view}}(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{collected}}(\mathbf{r})}{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{local}}(\mathbf{r})}
$$

where $\eta_{\mathrm{view}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the viewing efficiency,
$\mathbf{r}$ is the spatial emission point,
$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{collected}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local emission
contribution collected by the optical system, and
$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{local}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the corresponding local
emitted radiation considered by the collection model.

The quantity is evaluated separately at each point defining a region of
interest and is a fraction bounded between zero and one. It represents
spatial collection and is not summed or averaged over the region-of-interest
points. It is not a wavelength-resolved efficiency and excludes
detector-registration probability or other spectral detector response.

Viewing efficiency is related to the optical phase-space acceptance
described by etendue of a spectrometer channel, but it is a pointwise
collection fraction rather than an etendue. It is distinct from [spectral
efficiency of a hard X-ray
detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_hard_xray_detector), which is an
energy-dependent photon-registration probability.

sources.leaf_definition: Values of the light collection efficiencies
sources.parent_definition: Light collection efficiencies (fraction of the local emission detected by the optical system) for a list of points defining regions of interest. To be used for non-pinhole optics.

NAMES.name: wavelength_of_bragg_crystal
NAMES.short:
Vacuum wavelength selected by Bragg diffraction from the crystal lattice
spacing and orientation, defining the central spectral passband of the
crystal.
NAMES.long:
The Bragg wavelength is the vacuum electromagnetic wavelength selected by a
crystal's lattice geometry for a specified diffraction order. It defines the
central spectral coordinate of the crystal passband and is distinct from the
pixel-specific assignment represented by [wavelength of detector
pixel](name:wavelength_of_detector_pixel).

For lattice planes with spacing $d$ and Bragg angle $\theta_B$, the selected
wavelength satisfies

$$
n\lambda_B = 2d\sin\theta_B
$$

where $\lambda_B$ is the wavelength, $n$ is the positive integer diffraction
order, $d$ is the crystal lattice-plane spacing, and $\theta_B$ is the angle
between the incident beam and the lattice planes. The angle is the crystal
diffraction geometry characterized by [angular width of Bragg
crystal](name:angular_width_of_bragg_crystal).

sources.leaf_definition: Bragg wavelength of the crystal
sources.parent_definition: Characteristics of the crystal used

NAMES.name: wavelength_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short:
Wavelength assigned to incoming photons at an X-ray crystal spectrometer
detector pixel, including Bragg dispersion and curvature-induced variation
across the detector face.
NAMES.long:
The wavelength associated with a detector pixel is the vacuum spectral
coordinate of incoming photons whose Bragg-dispersed rays reach that pixel.

The pixel-specific wavelength follows Bragg's law:

$$
\lambda_{\rm pix}=2d\sin\theta_{\rm pix}
$$

where $\lambda_{\rm pix}$ is the vacuum wavelength assigned to the incoming
photons at the pixel, $d$ is the crystal lattice-plane spacing, and
$\theta_{\rm pix}$ is the Bragg angle for rays reaching that pixel.

This quantity is a per-pixel spectral assignment for an X-ray crystal
spectrometer. It primarily varies along the dispersive detector direction
and also varies along the perpendicular detector-face direction because the
constant-wavelength surfaces have elliptical curvature. It is not a single
wavelength averaged over the detector face or over a wavelength band, and it
does not denote the crystal's wavelength independently of a pixel.

It is a detector-pixel specialization of vacuum electromagnetic wavelength.
Unlike [energy_of_detector_pixel](name:energy_of_detector_pixel), which uses
photon energy as the spectral coordinate, this quantity uses wavelength for
the same pixel-specific incoming-photon assignment.

sources.leaf_definition: Wavelength of incoming photons on each pixel of the frames, mainly varying accross the horizontal dimension of the frame. However a 2D map of the wavelength is given since it is not constant vertically due to the elliptical curvature of the photon iso-surfaces
sources.parent_definition: Measurement channel, composed of a camera, a crystal, and (optional) a set of reflectors. The light coming from the plasma passes through the (optional) set of reflectors, then the crystal and arrives at the camera

NAMES.name: wavelength_of_spectral_line
NAMES.short:
Wavelength of a spectral line in vacuum in the emitter's rest frame,
providing the unshifted reference before Doppler and motional Stark shifts.
NAMES.long:
Wavelength of spectral line

The reference wavelength satisfies:

$$
\lambda = \frac{c}{\nu_0}
$$

where $\lambda$ is the unshifted vacuum [wavelength], $c$ is the speed of
light in vacuum, and $\nu_0$ is the corresponding rest-frame transition
frequency before motional Stark shifts.

This line-specific value provides the reference for [neutral-beam Doppler
wavelength
displacements](name:difference_of_neutral_beam_doppler_wavelength_and_reference_wavelength_of_spectral_line)
and [motional Stark wavelength
displacements](name:difference_of_fast_neutral_beam_motional_stark_wavelength_and_fast_neutral_beam_reference_wavelength_of_spectral_line);
neither displacement is included in the reference wavelength itself.

Unlike the [wavelength assigned to a detector
pixel](name:wavelength_of_detector_pixel), this quantity characterizes the
transition rather than the spectral coordinate selected by the optical
response. It is not a line width or an average over different spectral
lines.

NAMES.name: wavelength_of_visible_camera
NAMES.short:
Wavelength specifying either the short-wavelength or long-wavelength edge of
a photon-detection response interval.
NAMES.long:
A response-band boundary wavelength is the spectral location of one edge of
an optical detector's photon-sensitivity interval. It identifies where the
accepted response range begins or ends, rather than describing the response
magnitude within that range.

The wavelength is related to the corresponding electromagnetic frequency by

$$
\lambda_{\mathrm{edge}} = \frac{c}{\nu_{\mathrm{edge}}}
$$

where $\lambda_{\mathrm{edge}}$ is the boundary wavelength, $c$ is the speed
of light in vacuum, and $\nu_{\mathrm{edge}}$ is the electromagnetic
frequency at that boundary.

This quantity applies to either endpoint of a photon-detection response
interval: the lower endpoint is represented by [lower-bound wavelength of a
visible camera](name:lower_bound_wavelength_of_visible_camera), and the
upper endpoint by [upper-bound wavelength of a visible
camera](name:upper_bound_wavelength_of_visible_camera). It is an endpoint
value, not a spectral average, integrated response, or response-equivalent
width.

The two boundary wavelengths delimit the admitted spectral interval; the
lower-wavelength boundary precedes the upper-wavelength boundary. This
distinguishes each boundary from [effective spectral width of a spectrometer
channel](name:effective_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel), which
characterizes the extent of a response rather than one endpoint, and from
the general wavelength quantity, which need not be associated with a
response-band boundary.

NAMES.name: lower_bound_wavelength_of_visible_camera
NAMES.short:
Short-wavelength boundary of the spectral sensitivity band accepted by a
visible-camera detector channel, defining the lower edge of its response
interval. Photons with shorter wavelengths are outside the specified
detector response interval.
NAMES.long:
Short-wavelength boundary of the spectral sensitivity band accepted by a
visible-camera detector channel is the minimum photon wavelength included in
the specified detector response interval. It defines an interval endpoint of
the spectral sensitivity band, not the value of the detector response at
that endpoint.

Together with the upper-bound wavelength, it delimits the nominal accepted
wavelength interval. Photons with wavelengths shorter than this lower bound
are outside the specified interval; photons within the interval remain
subject to the detector spectral response function. It is distinct from the
central wavelength and the wavelength bandwidth, which summarize the
interval rather than define its short-wavelength edge.

sources.leaf_definition: Lower bound of the detector wavelength range
sources.parent_definition: Set of detectors

NAMES.name: upper_bound_wavelength_of_visible_camera
NAMES.short:
Long-wavelength boundary of the spectral sensitivity band accepted by a
visible-camera detector channel for photon detection.
NAMES.long:
The upper-bound wavelength is the long-wavelength edge of the spectral
sensitivity band for a visible-camera detector channel. It identifies the
greatest wavelength included in the channel’s accepted photon-response
range.

The accepted wavelength interval is bounded by

$$
\lambda_{\mathrm{lower}} \leq \lambda \leq \lambda_{\mathrm{upper}}
$$

where $\lambda$ is photon wavelength, $\lambda_{\mathrm{lower}}$ is the
short-wavelength boundary given by [lower-bound wavelength of a visible
camera](name:lower_bound_wavelength_of_visible_camera), and
$\lambda_{\mathrm{upper}}$ is this quantity.

This is one boundary value for a visible-camera detector channel, not an
average wavelength, a band-integrated quantity, or the representative
wavelength assigned to an individual detector pixel. The paired lower and
upper boundaries delimit the channel’s spectral sensitivity band;
[wavelength of a detector pixel](name:wavelength_of_detector_pixel) instead
identifies a pixel-associated spectral coordinate.

sources.leaf_definition: Upper bound of the detector wavelength range
sources.parent_definition: Set of detectors

NAMES.name: cold_neutral_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short:
Cold neutral velocity is the line-of-sight component of the bulk flow of
low-energy neutral atoms, identified from the Doppler shift of their
emission.
NAMES.long:
Cold neutral velocity is the line-of-sight component of the bulk drift
vector of a cold neutral particle population. It represents convective
neutral motion after averaging over particle velocities and over the
contributing cold-neutral population states.

The component is defined from the parent [neutral
velocity](name:neutral_velocity) by

$$
v_{n,c,ell} = \mathbf{v}_{n,c} \cdot \hat{\ell}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{n,c}$ is the bulk velocity of the cold neutral
population, $\hat{\ell}$ is the selected line-of-sight unit vector, and
$v_{n,c,\ell}$ is the signed projected velocity. The projection is the
velocity represented by the Doppler centroid of the corresponding
cold-neutral emission component.

This quantity is distinct from [hot neutral
velocity](name:hot_neutral_velocity), which describes the energetic neutral
population, and from [neutral internal state
velocity](name:neutral_internal_state_velocity), which is resolved for a
specified internal state. It excludes thermal speed and velocity spread,
which are higher moments of the velocity distribution.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the cold-neutral bulk velocity points along
the chosen positive line-of-sight unit vector $\hat{\ell}$.

sources.leaf_definition: Projection of the cold neutral velocity along the line of sight, positive when going from first point to second point of the line of sight
sources.parent_definition: Physics quantities measured from polarized light spectroscopy

NAMES.name: hot_neutral_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short:
Hot neutral velocity is the line-of-sight component of the bulk flow of an
energetic neutral atom population, identified from the Doppler centroid
shift of its broad emission component.
NAMES.long:
Hot neutral velocity is the line-of-sight component of the bulk drift vector
of a hot neutral particle population. It represents convective neutral
motion after averaging over particle velocities and over the contributing
hot-neutral internal-state or energy subpopulations.

At position $\mathbf r$, the projected component is the first velocity
moment of the selected hot neutral distribution projected along the line of
sight:

$$
u_{\mathrm{hot},\mathrm{los}}(\mathbf r)=\hat{\ell}\cdot\frac{\sum_{a\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{hot}}}\int \mathbf v\,f_{n,a}(\mathbf r,\mathbf v)\,d^3v}{\sum_{a\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{hot}}}\int f_{n,a}(\mathbf r,\mathbf v)\,d^3v}
$$

where $\mathbf r$ is position, $\hat{\ell}$ is the line-of-sight direction
from the first point to the second point, $\mathbf v$ is particle velocity,
$f_{n,a}$ is the phase-space density of neutral subpopulation $a$, and
$\mathcal A_{\mathrm{hot}}$ is the included set of hot neutral
subpopulations.

The scope is restricted to energetic neutrals in the selected hot
population; colder neutral components are excluded unless they are part of
that selected population. The scalar is a directional projection of [neutral
velocity](name:neutral_velocity), not the magnitude of the neutral flow
vector, a particle flux, a momentum density, or a thermal spread.

It is the hot-population counterpart of [cold neutral
velocity](name:cold_neutral_velocity). It is distinct from [hot neutral
temperature](name:hot_neutral_temperature_at_plasma_boundary), which
characterizes random velocity spread rather than the centroid or
first-moment drift of the hot neutral population.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the hot-neutral bulk drift projects from the
first point to the second point along the line of sight.

sources.leaf_definition: Projection of the hot neutral velocity along the line of sight, positive when going from first point to second point of the line of sight
sources.parent_definition: Physics quantities measured from polarized light spectroscopy

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_line_of_sight
NAMES.short:
Signed normalized toroidal-flux label at the line-of-sight point closest to
the magnetic axis, positive above and negative below the axis.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the normalized toroidal flux label assigned to the point on
a line of sight that approaches the magnetic axis most closely. Its sign
records whether that closest point lies above or below the magnetic axis.

The signed closest-approach value is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{LOS}} = \operatorname{sgn}(Z_* - Z_{\mathrm{axis}})\,\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(\mathbf{x}_*),
\qquad
\mathbf{x}_* = \underset{\mathbf{x}\in\mathrm{LOS}}{\operatorname{arg\,min}}\,\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{LOS}}$ is this signed line-of-sight value,
$\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the [normalized toroidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate), $\mathbf{x}$ is a
point on the line of sight, $\mathbf{x}_*$ is the closest-approach point,
and $\mathrm{LOS}$ denotes the line of sight. The function
$\operatorname{sgn}$ supplies the sign of its argument; $Z_*$ is the
vertical coordinate of the closest-approach point and $Z_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is
the vertical coordinate of the magnetic axis. Here $R$, $\phi$, and $Z$ are
the major-radius, toroidal-angle, and vertical coordinates in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

The quantity applies to one line of sight and uses only the selected
closest-approach point; it is not a line average, line integral,
flux-surface average, or volume aggregate. Unlike normalized toroidal flux
coordinate of measurement position, it does not describe the coordinate at
an arbitrary single measurement point.

It is obtained from the parent [normalized toroidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate) by evaluating that
magnetic-surface label at the closest-approach point and appending the
above/below-axis sign. The underlying unsigned label increases outward from
the magnetic axis toward the equilibrium boundary.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the closest point on the line of sight lies
above the magnetic axis, meaning $Z_* > Z_{\mathrm{axis}}$ in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Shortest distance in rho_tor_norm between lines of sight and magnetic axis, signed with following convention : positive (resp. negative) means the point of shortest distance is above (resp. below) the magnetic axis
sources.parent_definition: Profiles proxies are given in the vertical direction of the detector. They are estimated directly from the camera, without tomographic inversion. Binning is allowed so the number of profile points may be lower than the length of z_frames. Physical quantities deduced from the measured spectra are given for each profile point. They correspond to the spectra integrated along lines of sight, defined by a first point given by the centre of the crystal and a second point (depending on the profile point) described below.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_camera
NAMES.short:
Major-radius location of a camera’s geometric center, measured from the
toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of a camera is the major-radius position of its
geometric center, measured perpendicular to the toroidal symmetry axis. It
identifies the camera center rather than any individual detector pixel,
aperture, or line-of-sight point.

The coordinate is defined from the Cartesian coordinates of the camera
center:

$$
R_{\mathrm{cam}} = \sqrt{x_{\mathrm{cam}}^2 + y_{\mathrm{cam}}^2}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{cam}}$ is the camera-center radial coordinate, and
$x_{\mathrm{cam}}$ and $y_{\mathrm{cam}}$ are the camera-center coordinates
in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis. The
corresponding cylindrical frame is the right-handed $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame,
where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical
height.

This quantity applies to the geometric center of the camera as a whole and
is not an average over pixels, viewing directions, or detector elements. It
is the camera-specific specialization of the parent [radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate). Together with the [vertical coordinate
of the camera](name:vertical_coordinate_of_camera) and [toroidal coordinate
of the camera](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_camera), it specifies the
camera-center position.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: Position of the camera centre

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_detector
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of the detector center in the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, locating the detector relative to the toroidal
symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
Radial coordinate of a detector is the major-radius coordinate of the
detector center in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. In
this frame, $R$ is major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis,
$\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above
$+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The detector-center radial coordinate is related to Cartesian coordinates of
the same point by

$$
R_d = \sqrt{x_d^2 + y_d^2}
$$

where $R_d$ is the radial coordinate of the detector center, and $x_d$ and
$y_d$ are the detector-center Cartesian coordinates in the right-handed
Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame with origin on the toroidal
symmetry axis and $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$ vertical.

The scope is the detector as a whole, and the reference point is its center.
This is a point coordinate, not an area average over the detector surface,
not an average over detector pixels, and not the coordinate of an
alternative detector-plane origin.

This quantity is a detector-specific specialization of [radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate): it applies the same major-radius
coordinate to the detector center. It is distinct from the [radial
coordinate of detector pixel](name:radial_coordinate_of_detector_pixel),
which applies to an individual pixel center, and from the [radial coordinate
of diagnostic aperture](name:radial_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture),
which applies to an aperture reference point.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: If geometry_type=2, coordinates of the centre of the circle. If geometry_type=1 or 3, coordinates of the origin of the local coordinate system (X1,X2,X3) describing the plane detector/aperture. This origin is located within the detector/aperture area.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_line_of_sight
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of the second reference point on a line of sight,
equal to its perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
Major-radius coordinate of line of sight

The coordinate is defined by

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are the horizontal coordinates of the second reference
point in the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame, with $z$ the vertical
coordinate and the $z$ axis coinciding with the toroidal symmetry axis.

The coordinate is nonnegative and vanishes on the toroidal symmetry axis. It
is distinct from a distance along the line of sight, a minor-radius distance
measured from the magnetic axis, and a magnetic flux label. Like the [radial
coordinate of a measurement
position](name:radial_coordinate_of_measurement_position), it locates a
specified point; no summation, line integration, averaging, or emission
weighting is implied.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_polarizer
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of the polarizer’s geometric reference point, namely
its circular center or local-plane origin, measured from the toroidal
symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the major-radius location of a polarizer’s geometric
reference point. This point is the center for a circular polarizer or the
origin of the local coordinate system describing a planar polarizer.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the coordinate is
defined from the point’s horizontal Cartesian coordinates by

$$
R_{\mathrm{pol}} = \sqrt{x_{\mathrm{pol}}^2+y_{\mathrm{pol}}^2}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the polarizer reference point’s major-radius
coordinate, and $x_{\mathrm{pol}}$ and $y_{\mathrm{pol}}$ are its horizontal
coordinates in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis.
Here $R$ denotes major radius, $\phi$ denotes toroidal angle, and $Z$
denotes vertical height.

The quantity applies only to the polarizer reference point and is
nonnegative; it is not the radial coordinate of an arbitrary point on the
polarizer surface and is not a flux-surface-normal projection. It is the
polarizer-specific realization of the general [radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate).

Together with the [toroidal coordinate of the
polarizer](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_polarizer), this coordinate locates
the same geometric reference point in the cylindrical frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: If geometry_type=2, coordinates of the centre of the circle. If geometry_type=1 or 3, coordinates of the origin of the local coordinate system (X1,X2,X3) describing the plane polarizer. This origin is located within the polarizer area. Note that there is some flexibility here and the data provider should choose the most convenient coordinate system for the object, respecting the definitions of (X1,X2,X3) indicated below.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of an interpolated geometry point associated with a
spectrometer channel, measured from the toroidal symmetry axis in the
right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the major-radius coordinate of an interpolated geometry
point associated with a spectrometer channel. It locates that point by its
perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

At each interpolated geometry point, the coordinate is defined from its
transverse Cartesian coordinates:

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}
$$

where $R$ is the major-radius coordinate, and $x$ and $y$ are the Cartesian
coordinates along the $\hat{x}$ and $\hat{y}$ directions. The right-handed
Cartesian basis is $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$, with $\hat{z}$ equal to the
vertical unit direction $\hat{Z}$; in the cylindrical frame, $\phi$ is
toroidal angle and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies pointwise to each interpolated geometry knot associated
with one spectrometer channel and is not summed, averaged, or integrated
over knots, channels, viewing paths, or plasma regions. It identifies a
geometry-point locus rather than a single radial location for the channel
body or a channel-wide average.

This is the spectrometer-channel-specific instance of the [radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate). It retains the parent quantity's
major-radius definition while restricting its locus to an interpolated point
in the channel geometry.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_krypton_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short:
Volume-averaged krypton density divided by volume-averaged electron density
is the plasma-volume krypton abundance ratio relative to electrons, with
krypton number density summed over all charge states.
NAMES.long:
Volume-averaged krypton density divided by volume-averaged electron density
is the plasma-volume krypton abundance ratio formed from the same averaging
volume for krypton and electrons. The krypton density is the species-level
krypton number density summed over all charge states, including neutral
through fully stripped krypton.

The ratio is defined by the quotient of the two volume averages:

$$
f_{\mathrm{Kr},V} = \frac{\langle n_{\mathrm{Kr}} \rangle_V}{\langle n_e \rangle_V} = \frac{V_p^{-1}\int_{V_p}\sum_{q=0}^{Z_{\mathrm{Kr}}} n_{\mathrm{Kr},q}(\mathbf{x})\,dV}{V_p^{-1}\int_{V_p} n_e(\mathbf{x})\,dV}
$$

where $f_{\mathrm{Kr},V}$ is this krypton abundance ratio, $\langle
n_{\mathrm{Kr}} \rangle_V$ is the [volume-averaged krypton
density](name:volume_averaged_krypton_density), $\langle n_e \rangle_V$ is
the [volume-averaged electron
density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density), $V_p$ is the averaging
plasma volume, $n_{\mathrm{Kr},q}$ is the krypton number density in charge
state $q$, $q=0$ denotes neutral krypton, $q=Z_{\mathrm{Kr}}$ denotes fully
stripped krypton, $Z_{\mathrm{Kr}}$ is the nuclear charge of krypton, $n_e$
is the electron number density, $\mathbf{x}$ is spatial position, and $dV$
is an infinitesimal volume element.

This quantity applies to the krypton and electron populations inside the
same plasma volume $V_p$. Its aggregation convention is volumetric averaging
for both numerator and denominator; because krypton density is an extensive
per-volume species amount, the species-level krypton density is
charge-state-summed before the volume average is taken.

It is not normalized by the maximum local electron density and is not a
krypton-to-electron density ratio at a single position. It is also distinct
from [line-averaged krypton density](name:line_averaged_krypton_density),
which averages krypton density along a path rather than over the plasma
volume.

The numerator is exactly [volume-averaged krypton
density](name:volume_averaged_krypton_density), and the denominator is
exactly [volume-averaged electron
density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density). Replacing the denominator
by a maximum electron density gives the related but different ratio of
volume-averaged krypton density to maximum electron density.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Krypton (Kr)

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_neon_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless elemental abundance ratio of charge-state-summed neon nuclei
to free electrons, formed from their respective mean number densities inside
the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the abundance of neon nuclei relative to free electrons,
with both species represented by number densities averaged over the plasma
volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface. Neon is summed over all
charge states, so the quantity is an elemental composition ratio rather than
a charge-state-specific abundance or a local density ratio.

The ratio of volume-averaged densities is defined by

$$
\frac{\overline{n}_{\mathrm{Ne}}}{\overline{n}_e} = \frac{\displaystyle \frac{1}{V_p}\int_{V_p} n_{\mathrm{Ne}}(\mathbf{x})\,dV}{\displaystyle \frac{1}{V_p}\int_{V_p} n_e(\mathbf{x})\,dV}
$$

where $\overline{n}_{\mathrm{Ne}}$ is the [volume-averaged neon
density](name:volume_averaged_neon_density), $\overline{n}_e$ is the
[volume-averaged electron density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density),
$n_{\mathrm{Ne}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local neon nuclear number density
summed over charge states, $n_e(\mathbf{x})$ is the local free-electron
number density, $V_p$ is the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux
surface, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, and $dV$ is the volume element.

Both operands use the same plasma volume and the same volume-averaging
convention. This quantity is the ratio of the two global means, not the
volume average of the local ratio
$n_{\mathrm{Ne}}(\mathbf{x})/n_e(\mathbf{x})$; its denominator is
specifically the parent [volume-averaged electron
density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density), while its numerator is the
corresponding [volume-averaged neon
density](name:volume_averaged_neon_density).

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Neon (Ne)

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_nitrogen_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless abundance ratio of charge-state-summed nitrogen nuclei to
electrons, with both number densities averaged over the plasma volume
bounded by the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Dimensionless abundance ratio of charge-state-summed nitrogen nuclei to
electrons, with both number densities averaged over the plasma volume
bounded by the last closed flux surface. It represents the species-level
nitrogen abundance relative to the free-electron population in the confined
plasma.

The defining ratio is:

$$
f_{\mathrm{N/e}} = \frac{\left\langle \sum_{q=0}^{7} n_{\mathrm{N}^{q+}} \right\rangle_V}{\left\langle n_e \right\rangle_V}
$$

where $f_{\mathrm{N/e}}$ is the nitrogen-to-electron abundance ratio,
$n_{\mathrm{N}^{q+}}$ is the nitrogen number density in charge state $q$,
$q=0$ denotes neutral nitrogen, $q=7$ denotes fully stripped nitrogen, $n_e$
is the [electron density](name:electron_density), and
$\langle\cdot\rangle_V$ denotes averaging over the plasma volume bounded by
the last closed flux surface.

The numerator is the charge-state-summed [nitrogen
density](name:nitrogen_density) after volume averaging, equivalently the
[volume-averaged nitrogen density](name:volume_averaged_nitrogen_density).
The denominator is the [volume-averaged electron
density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density) evaluated with the same
volume-averaging convention.

This quantity is a ratio of separate volume averages, not the volume average
of a local nitrogen-to-electron density ratio. It is species-level and
charge-state-summed, so it differs from any charge-state-resolved nitrogen
abundance that retains a single ionization state in the numerator. It
follows the same abundance-ratio convention as [ratio of volume-averaged
neon density to volume-averaged electron
density](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_neon_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density)
and [ratio of volume-averaged iron density to volume-averaged electron
density](name:ratio_of_iron_density_to_electron_density).

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Nitrogen (N)

NAMES.name: requested_voltage_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short:
Commanded detector-bias potential difference applied by the high-voltage
supply associated with one spectrometer channel.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the requested electrical potential difference that
establishes the detector-bias setpoint for one spectrometer channel.

The setpoint is defined by

$$
V_{\mathrm{set}} = V_{\mathrm{bias}} - V_{\mathrm{return}}
$$

where $V_{\mathrm{set}}$ is the requested channel bias voltage,
$V_{\mathrm{bias}}$ is the electrical potential of the high-voltage bias
terminal, and $V_{\mathrm{return}}$ is the electrical potential of the
associated supply return.

The quantity applies to one spectrometer channel and represents a commanded
setpoint rather than an aggregated value across channels. It specifies the
intended bias potential of the channel's high-voltage supply; it does not
represent the channel's actual electrical output signal, which is described
by [voltage of a spectrometer
channel](name:voltage_of_spectrometer_channel).

As a requested control quantity, it is distinct from the realized or
measured channel voltage and is analogous in semantic role to the bias
setpoint represented by [requested voltage of a neutron
detector](name:requested_voltage_of_neutron_detector).

sources.leaf_definition: Voltage set at the power supply
sources.parent_definition: Set of high voltage power supplies applied to various parts of the diagnostic

NAMES.name: total_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short:
Total neutron production rate from thermonuclear neutron-producing
deuterium-deuterium, deuterium-tritium, and tritium-tritium reaction
branches among Maxwellian bulk ions, excluding beam-target and beam-beam
fast-ion contributions.
NAMES.long:
The total neutron source rate due to thermal fusion is the number of
neutrons produced per unit time by the neutron-producing thermal
deuterium-deuterium, deuterium-tritium, and tritium-tritium reaction
branches between bulk ions with locally Maxwellian velocity distributions.
It is the channel-summed member of [neutron source rate due to thermal
fusion](name:neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion), equal to the sum of
deuterium-deuterium neutron source rate due to thermal fusion,
deuterium-tritium neutron source rate due to thermal fusion, and
[tritium-tritium neutron source rate due to thermal
