fusion](name:tritium_tritium_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion).

The channel-summed thermal neutron source rate is defined by

$$
S_{n,\mathrm{tot}}^{\mathrm{th}} = \int_V \sum_{c \in \{DD,DT,TT\}} \nu_{n,c}\,\frac{n_{a_c} n_{b_c}}{1+\delta_{a_c b_c}}\,\langle\sigma v\rangle_c(T_{a_c},T_{b_c})\,dV
$$

where $S_{n,\mathrm{tot}}^{\mathrm{th}}$ is the total source rate, $V$ is
the emitting plasma volume, $c$ labels a neutron-producing thermal fusion
branch, $\nu_{n,c}$ is the neutron multiplicity of branch $c$, $a_c$ and
$b_c$ are its reactant ion species, $n_{a_c}$ and $n_{b_c}$ are their local
bulk number densities, $\delta_{a_c b_c}$ is one for identical reactants and
zero otherwise, $\langle\sigma v\rangle_c$ is the Maxwellian-averaged
reactivity, $T_{a_c}$ and $T_{b_c}$ are the local reactant temperatures, and
$dV$ is a volume element. The denominator prevents double counting of
identical reactant pairs.

Only reactions among locally Maxwellian bulk ions are included; beam-target,
beam-beam, fusion-product, and other nonthermal fast-ion contributions are
excluded. For deuterium-deuterium fusion, only the D(d,n)$^3\mathrm{He}$
neutron branch contributes; the D(d,p)T proton branch is not counted. For
deuterium-deuterium and deuterium-tritium neutron branches $\nu_{n,c}=1$,
while for tritium-tritium fusion $\nu_{n,c}=2$.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Neutron rate from all plasma thermal reactions

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_total_runaway_electron_source_rate
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short:
Plasma-volume-averaged volumetric production rate of runaway electrons,
summed over Dreicer, avalanche, hot-tail, Compton, and tritium-decay
generation mechanisms.
NAMES.long:
Plasma-volume-averaged volumetric production rate of runaway electrons is
the spatial average, over the plasma volume, of the local total rate at
which electrons enter the runaway population. The total rate includes
generation by Dreicer, avalanche, hot-tail, Compton, and tritium-decay
mechanisms.

The volume average is defined by

$$
\left\langle S_{\mathrm{RE,total}}\right\rangle_V = \frac{1}{|\Omega_p|}\int_{\Omega_p} S_{\mathrm{RE,total}}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $\left\langle S_{\mathrm{RE,total}}\right\rangle_V$ is the
volume-averaged total runaway electron source rate,
$S_{\mathrm{RE,total}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the total runaway electron source
rate at position $\mathbf{x}$, $\Omega_p$ is the plasma-volume domain,
$|\Omega_p|$ is the volume measure of that domain, and $dV$ is the volume
element.

This quantity applies to the runaway-electron population within the plasma
volume and uses an unweighted volume average of the total local volumetric
production rate. The mechanism sum is part of the quantity definition; the
total includes component production rates such as the [Dreicer runaway
electron source rate](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer) and
the [hot-tail runaway electron source
rate](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail), but is not
restricted to either component.

It is the plasma-volume-averaged counterpart of the total runaway electron
source rate. It is a production-rate density averaged over volume, not the
absolute number of runaway electrons and not a current-density measure; in
particular it is distinct from the [volume-averaged parallel runaway
electron current
density](name:volume_averaged_parallel_runaway_electron_current_density),
which describes charge transport by the runaway population.

sources.leaf_definition: Total source of runaway electrons
sources.parent_definition: Volume average runaways parameters

NAMES.name: runaway_electron_kinetic_energy_density
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short:
Kinetic energy per unit volume carried by the runaway-electron population,
including relativistic motion and excluding rest-mass energy.
NAMES.long:
Number density of runaway electron

The local kinetic energy density is defined by:

$$
w_{\mathrm{RE}} = n_{\mathrm{RE}}\left\langle (\gamma-1)m_e c^2 \right\rangle_{\mathrm{RE}}
$$

where $w_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is the runaway-electron kinetic energy density,
$n_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is the runaway-electron number density, and
$\langle\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{RE}}$ denotes a particle-number-weighted
average over the local runaway-electron population. The Lorentz factor is
$\gamma=(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, where $v$ is electron speed, $m_e$ is the
electron rest mass, and $c$ is the speed of light.

Only the runaway-electron population is included, not the bulk
thermal-electron population. The energy includes motion both parallel and
perpendicular to the magnetic field but excludes rest-mass energy and
electromagnetic-field energy. For a magnetic-flux-surface description, the
quantity is the mean of the local energy density over each magnetic flux
surface, not a mean over the entire confined plasma volume. It is an energy
per volume, not a mean energy per electron.

Its plasma-volume integral is the total [runaway-electron kinetic
energy](name:runaway_electron_kinetic_energy), denoted $W_{\mathrm{RE}}$.
Dividing that integral by the same plasma volume gives the [volume-averaged
runaway-electron kinetic energy
density](name:volume_averaged_runaway_electron_kinetic_energy_density).

sources.leaf_definition: One scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.
sources.parent_definition: Runaways kinetic energy density, given on various grid subsets

sources.leaf_definition: Runaways kinetic mean energy density
sources.parent_definition: Radial flux surface averaged profiles for a set of time slices

NAMES.name: focal_length_of_line_of_sight
NAMES.short:
Paraxial focal length of the collector optics associated with a
charge-exchange spectroscopy line of sight, setting the distance from the
principal plane to the focal point.
NAMES.long:
The focal length is the paraxial distance from the principal plane of the
collector optical system to the focal point for collimated incident rays. It
characterizes the focusing geometry associated with a selected
charge-exchange spectroscopy line of sight.

This quantity applies to the collector optics of that line of sight and is
not the diameter of the focused image spot or the optical throughput. The
diameter of the line of sight describes the focused spot size, while the
[etendue of the line of sight](name:etendue_of_line_of_sight) describes its
accepted optical phase space; both are related to, but distinct from, focal
length.

sources.leaf_definition: Focal length of the collector lens
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (lines-of-sight). The line-of-sight is defined by the centre of the collimating aperture and the position of the measurements.

NAMES.name: radius_of_detector
NAMES.short:
Radius from the center to the circumferential edge of a detector's circular
front face, defining its geometric size for optical throughput.
NAMES.long:
The detector radius is the geometric distance from the center of a circular
detector front face to its circumferential edge.

The corresponding circular face area is defined by

$$
A_{\rm det} = \pi r_{\rm det}^{2}
$$

where $A_{\rm det}$ is the detector front-face area, $r_{\rm det}$ is the
detector radius, and $\pi$ is the mathematical constant.

This quantity applies only when the detector front face has circular
geometry. It describes the detector face itself and does not represent a
collimating aperture, a filter opening, or a width parameter for a
noncircular detector geometry.

The face area determined by this radius contributes to the geometric optical
throughput represented by [spectrometer
etendue](name:etendue_of_spectrometer); it is distinct from the radius of a
separate [spectrometer aperture](name:radius_of_aperture).

sources.leaf_definition: Radius of the circle, used only if geometry_type = 2
sources.parent_definition: Description of the front face of the micro channel plate

NAMES.name: radius_of_reflector
NAMES.short:
Geometric distance from the center of a reflector’s circular aperture to its
circumferential boundary in an X-ray crystal spectrometer.
NAMES.long:
The reflector aperture radius is the geometric distance from the center of
the circular opening to its circumferential boundary. It defines the
circular cross-section of the optical reflector through which light is
directed toward the crystal.

For a circular aperture, its area is related to the radius by

$$
A = \pi r^2
$$

where $A$ is the aperture area, $r$ is the reflector aperture radius, and
$\pi$ is the mathematical constant relating a circle’s circumference to its
diameter.

This quantity applies only to a reflector with circular aperture geometry.
It describes the aperture radius, not a curvature radius of the reflector
surface or the radius of a different optical element. The same geometric
concept is used for the circular Bragg-crystal opening represented by
[radius of Bragg crystal](name:radius_of_bragg_crystal), while [radius of
aperture](name:radius_of_aperture) describes a channel-level collimating
aperture rather than the reflector aperture.

sources.leaf_definition: Radius of the circle, used only if geometry_type/index = 2
sources.parent_definition: Set of reflectors (optional) reflecting the light coming from the plasma towards the crystal. If empty, means that the plasma light directly arrives on the crystal.

NAMES.name: surface_area_of_detector
NAMES.short:
Geometric surface area of the detector face defining the physical extent of
one diagnostic detector.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the geometric area of the specified detector surface
associated with one diagnostic channel. It characterizes the physical extent
of that detector surface as defined by its boundary and geometry.

The surface area is defined by

$$
A_{\mathrm{det}} = \int_{S_{\mathrm{det}}} dA
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{det}}$ is the detector surface area, $S_{\mathrm{det}}$ is
the specified detector surface, and $dA$ is the differential surface-area
element. The quantity applies to one detector and is not an aggregate over
multiple channels or diagnostic components. It describes geometric surface
extent, not a radiation or particle flux, detector response, or sensitivity.

The detector surface is distinct from the designated diagnostic aperture
described by [area of diagnostic
aperture](name:area_of_diagnostic_aperture), even when the two geometric
surfaces coincide. It follows the same surface-area concept as [surface area
of neutron detector](name:surface_area_of_neutron_detector), but is
associated with the specified detector rather than specifically with a
neutron-sensitive detector.

sources.leaf_definition: Surface of the detector/aperture, derived from the above geometric data
sources.parent_definition: Detector description

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_polarizer
NAMES.short:
Vertical coordinate of a polarizer is the signed Z position of the polarizer
geometric center in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Vertical coordinate of a polarizer is the $Z$ coordinate of the polarizer
geometric center in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where
$R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The coordinate is the vertical component of the position of that center:

$$
z_{\mathrm{pol}} = Z(\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{pol}})
$$

where $z_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the vertical coordinate of the polarizer and
$\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the position vector of the polarizer
geometric center.

This quantity applies to the polarizer element itself and only to its
geometric center. It is not a vertical extent, surface normal component,
orientation angle, or local tangential coordinate of the polarizer.

Together with the [radial coordinate of a
polarizer](name:radial_coordinate_of_polarizer) and [toroidal coordinate of
a polarizer](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_polarizer), it specifies the
polarizer center position in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$
frame.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the polarizer geometric center lies in the
$+\hat{Z}$ direction from the vertical origin.

sources.leaf_definition: Height
sources.parent_definition: If geometry_type=2, coordinates of the centre of the circle. If geometry_type=1 or 3, coordinates of the origin of the local coordinate system (X1,X2,X3) describing the plane detector/aperture. This origin is located within the detector/aperture area.

NAMES.name: area_of_first_wall
NAMES.short:
Total geometric area of the material surface forming the plasma-facing first
wall, including installed wall armor and bare vessel surface where
applicable.
NAMES.long:
The first-wall area is the geometric measure of the material surface exposed
toward the plasma and forming the innermost plasma-facing boundary. It
includes installed wall armor and bare vessel surface where no armor is
present, but excludes backing structures and surfaces that are not
plasma-facing.

$$
A_{\mathrm{FW}} = \int_{\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{FW}}} \mathrm{d}A
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{FW}}$ is the total first-wall area,
$\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{FW}}$ is the plasma-facing first-wall surface, and
$\mathrm{d}A$ is an elemental surface area. This surface measure is distinct
from the enclosed [volume of the first wall](name:volume_of_first_wall) and
provides the geometric basis for integrating areal loads such as energy flux
at the wall.

sources.leaf_definition: First wall surface area
sources.parent_definition: Description of the torus wall and its interaction with the plasma

NAMES.name: coolant_pressure_at_cooling_circuit_inlet
NAMES.short:
Coolant pressure at a cooling-circuit inlet is the absolute static pressure
of the coolant where it enters a hydraulically defined cooling circuit or
component. It is the coolant-specific inlet pressure boundary and excludes
gage, dynamic, and stagnation pressure.
NAMES.long:
Coolant pressure at a cooling-circuit inlet is the absolute static
thermodynamic pressure of the coolant where it enters a hydraulically
defined cooling circuit or component. It denotes the scalar upstream
boundary pressure of the coolant and excludes gage pressure, dynamic
pressure, and stagnation pressure.

For the same hydraulic flow path, the associated static pressure drop is
related to this inlet pressure by:

$$
p_{\mathrm{coolant,in}} = p_{\mathrm{coolant,out}} + \Delta p_{\mathrm{coolant}}
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{coolant,in}}$ is this inlet absolute static coolant
pressure in pascals, $p_{\mathrm{coolant,out}}$ is the corresponding outlet
absolute static coolant pressure in pascals, and $\Delta
p_{\mathrm{coolant}}$ is the total static pressure drop in pascals, defined
positive when the outlet static pressure is lower than the inlet static
pressure.

This quantity is the coolant-specific specialization of pressure at a
cooling-circuit inlet: when the working fluid is coolant, both names denote
the same inlet absolute static pressure. It is also the
cooling-circuit-inlet value of [coolant pressure](name:coolant_pressure),
and it is distinct from pressure loss, pump head, and mechanical stress in
the surrounding structure.

sources.leaf_definition: Inlet coolant pressure
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities at various time slices

NAMES.name: incident_neutron_power_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short:
Total power carried by fusion neutrons onto a single breeder blanket module
before nuclear energy is deposited in its materials.
NAMES.long:
Incident neutron power is the incoming fusion-neutron energy rate delivered
to one breeder blanket module. It represents the module-level neutron load
at the boundary before interactions convert neutron energy into deposited
heat.

The power is defined by

$$
P_{\mathrm{n,inc}} = \frac{dE_{\mathrm{n,inc}}}{dt}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{n,inc}}$ is the total incident neutron power,
$E_{\mathrm{n,inc}}$ is the cumulative energy carried by neutrons incident
on the module, and $t$ is time.

This quantity applies to a single breeder blanket module and is aggregated
over the module's complete incident neutron load. It is a total incoming
power, not a local surface power density or a power assigned to an
individual material layer. It excludes energy deposited within the module by
neutron interactions, which is represented by [nuclear heating power of a
breeder blanket
module](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_module), and it is
distinct from incident photon power represented by [incident radiated power
of a breeder blanket
module](name:incident_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module).

Incident neutron power is an input to the module energy budget and provides
the neutron-power basis for the [tritium breeding ratio of a breeder blanket
module](name:tritium_breeding_ratio_of_breeder_blanket_module). It is
therefore distinct from the broader [power of a breeder blanket
module](name:power_of_breeder_blanket_module), which encompasses multiple
incident, deposited, and transferred power components.

sources.leaf_definition: Total incident neutron power on the blanket module
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities at various time slices

NAMES.name: lower_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short:
Lower thickness of a breeder blanket module is the non-negative geometric
separation through the lower cap, measured normal to its exterior boundary
and main-body interface.
NAMES.long:
Lower thickness of a breeder blanket module is the geometric thickness of
the cap that closes the module at its lower end. The reference surfaces are
the lower exterior boundary of the cap and the interface where the lower cap
joins the main module body. It is distinct from the overall thickness of a
breeder blanket module and the corresponding [upper thickness of a breeder
blanket module](name:upper_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module).

The lower-cap thickness is the normal projection of the separation between
the reference surfaces:

$$
t_{\mathrm{lower}} = \left|\left(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ext}} - \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{int}}\right) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\right|
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{int}}$ are
corresponding points on the lower exterior boundary and cap-to-body
interface, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the local unit normal directed through the
cap, and $t_{\mathrm{lower}}$ is the lower-cap thickness. The quantity is a
non-negative geometric magnitude; it is not a signed vertical coordinate or
displacement and excludes the thicknesses of internal breeder, coolant, or
shielding layers.

sources.leaf_definition: Bottom cap poloidal thickness
sources.parent_definition: Set of modules composing the blanket

NAMES.name: net_thermal_power_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short:
Net thermal power transferred from a single breeder blanket module to its
coolant, summed over all coolant branches as an enthalpy increase.
NAMES.long:
Coolant thermal power of a single breeder blanket module is the net rate at
which heat leaves the module through its coolant circuits. It aggregates the
thermal energy carried by every coolant branch serving that module,
regardless of whether the heat originated from nuclear deposition or
absorbed incident radiation.

The defining branch balance is

$$
P_{\mathrm{cool}} = \sum_b \dot{m}_b\left(h_{b,\mathrm{out}} - h_{b,\mathrm{in}}\right)
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{cool}}$ is the coolant-transferred power, $b$ indexes
coolant branches, $\dot{m}_b$ is the mass flow rate in branch $b$, and
$h_{b,\mathrm{in}}$ and $h_{b,\mathrm{out}}$ are its inlet and outlet
specific enthalpies. The quantity is the coolant-transferred component of
thermal power of a breeder blanket module, distinct from source-specific
quantities such as [nuclear heating power of a breeder blanket
module](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_module) and [absorbed
radiated power of a breeder blanket
module](name:absorbed_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module).

sources.leaf_definition: Total thermal power that is extracted from the blanket module
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities at various time slices

NAMES.name: nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket
NAMES.short:
Total rate of heat generation in all breeder-blanket materials from neutron
and photon interactions, excluding plasma-facing surface heat loads and
external incident power.
NAMES.long:
Nuclear heating power of the breeder blanket is the total rate at which
neutron and photon interactions deposit energy as heat throughout all
included blanket materials. It is the blanket-wide nuclear component of
heating power of the breeder blanket.

The defining relation is

$$
P_{\mathrm{nuc}} = \int_{V_{\mathrm{BB}}} q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})\,dV
$$

where $q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local nuclear heating power
density in W m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{r}$ is position within the blanket, $dV$ is
differential volume in m$^3$, and $V_{\mathrm{BB}}$ is the union of the
included blanket-module and constituent-material volumes.

The integral includes energy deposited by neutron scattering, neutron
capture, and photon interactions, including secondary gamma absorption,
without double-counting overlapping material descriptions. It excludes power
carried by neutrons or photons crossing into the blanket before deposition
and separate plasma-facing surface loads. Module- and layer-restricted
integrals are represented by [nuclear heating power of the breeder blanket
module](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_module) and [nuclear
heating power of the breeder blanket
layer](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer), respectively.

sources.leaf_definition: Nuclear heating power on the blanket
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities for a set of time_slices

NAMES.name: nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer
NAMES.short:
Total rate of heat generated within one breeder-blanket material layer by
neutron and photon interactions, excluding external and surface heat loads.
NAMES.long:
Nuclear heating power of a breeder-blanket layer is the volume-integrated
rate at which neutron and photon interactions convert radiation energy into
heat within that material layer. It is the nuclear component of heating
power of a breeder-blanket layer, rather than the local volumetric quantity
[nuclear power density of a breeder-blanket
layer](name:nuclear_power_density_of_breeder_blanket_layer).

The defining relation is

$$
P_{\mathrm{nuc,layer}} = \int_{V_{\mathrm{layer}}} \dot{q}_{\mathrm{nuc}}\,\mathrm{d}V
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{nuc,layer}}$ is the layer-integrated nuclear heating
power, $\dot{q}_{\mathrm{nuc}}$ is the local nuclear energy-deposition rate
per unit volume, and $V_{\mathrm{layer}}$ is the volume of the specified
material layer.

The integral includes energy deposited by neutron interactions and
absorption of primary or secondary photons within the layer. It excludes
plasma-facing radiative heat loads, incident energy that is not deposited,
and energy deposited outside the layer; the result is non-negative.

sources.leaf_definition: Nuclear power heating this layer
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities at various time slices

NAMES.name: nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short:
Rate of nuclear energy deposited throughout one breeder blanket module by
neutron interactions and associated photon absorption, excluding incident
and externally applied heat.
NAMES.long:
Nuclear heating power of a breeder blanket module is the rate of nuclear
energy deposited within the material volume of one module by neutron
interactions and the absorption of primary or secondary photons. It is an
integrated deposition quantity, not incident radiation power or local power
density.

The module-integrated power is defined by

$$
P_{\mathrm{nuc,module}} = \int_{V_{\mathrm{module}}} q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}V
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{nuc,module}}$ is the integrated nuclear heating power,
$V_{\mathrm{module}}$ is the module material volume,
$q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local nuclear heating power density in
W m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{r}$ is position in the module in m, and $\mathrm{d}V$
is differential material volume in m$^{3}$.

The integration includes energy deposited in module materials by neutron and
photon interactions. It excludes unde posited incident radiation,
plasma-facing surface heat loads, and heat subsequently transferred to
coolant. It is distinct from the local nuclear power density of a breeder
blanket module, the layer-resolved [nuclear heating power of a breeder
blanket layer](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer), and the
blanket-wide [nuclear heating
power](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket).

sources.leaf_definition: Total neutron power (deposited + generated) in the blanket module
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities at various time slices

NAMES.name: nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_shield
NAMES.short:
Nuclear heating power deposited in the breeder blanket shield by neutron and
gamma interactions within the shield material. It excludes externally
applied, incident, or surface heat loads not produced by nuclear energy
deposition in the shield.
NAMES.long:
Nuclear heating power deposited in the breeder blanket shield is the rate at
which neutron- and gamma-induced interactions deposit energy as heat within
the shield portion of a breeder blanket. The shield is the shielding
structural region of the breeder blanket, distinct from the blanket as a
whole and from its breeding or multiplier regions.

The quantity is the volume integral of the local nuclear heat-deposition
rate over the shield region:

$$
P_{\mathrm{nuc,shield}} = \int_{V_{\mathrm{shield}}} q'''_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{nuc,shield}}$ is the nuclear heating power of the breeder
blanket shield, $V_{\mathrm{shield}}$ is the volume occupied by the shield
portion of the breeder blanket, $q'''_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the
local nuclear heat-deposition rate from neutron and gamma interactions at
spatial position $\mathbf{r}$, and $dV$ is an infinitesimal volume element.

The scope is the aggregate shield contribution, integrated over all material
volume identified as breeder-blanket shield material and summed over the
nuclear energy deposited there by neutrons and gamma radiation. It excludes
heating deposited in non-shield breeder-blanket regions, heating in adjacent
structures, and externally applied, incident, or surface heat loads that are
not generated by nuclear interactions within the shield material.

This quantity is a component of the [nuclear heating power of the breeder
blanket](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket). It is distinguished
from [nuclear heating power of a breeder blanket
module](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_module) and [nuclear
heating power of a breeder blanket
layer](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer), which restrict
the same nuclear heat-deposition concept to their respective subregions; for
any disjoint partition of the same shield region, the aggregate shield value
equals the sum over the corresponding subregion contributions.

sources.leaf_definition: Nuclear heating power on the shields
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities for a set of time_slices

NAMES.name: nuclear_heating_power_of_limiter_tile
NAMES.short:
Nuclear heating power of a limiter tile is the rate at which nuclear energy
is deposited within one limiter tile by neutron interactions and associated
primary and secondary gamma-ray absorption.
NAMES.long:
Nuclear heating power of a limiter tile is the rate at which nuclear energy
is deposited within one limiter tile by nuclear radiation transport and
interactions in the tile material. It is a scalar heating-power contribution
assigned to the material volume of that tile.

The volume-integrated relation to the local nuclear power density is

$$
P_{\mathrm{nuc},t} = \int_{V_t} q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{x}) \, dV
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{nuc},t}$ is the nuclear heating power of the limiter tile,
$V_t$ is the material volume occupied by the limiter tile,
$q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the [nuclear power density of the limiter
tile](name:nuclear_power_density_of_limiter_tile) at spatial position
$\mathbf{x}$, and $dV$ is the differential volume element.

The quantity applies to a single limiter tile and is aggregated over the
whole material volume of that tile. It includes energy deposition from
neutron interactions and absorption of primary and secondary gamma radiation
within the tile material; deposition outside the tile is outside its scope.

It is not the total nuclear energy deposited over a time interval, not a
wall-total nuclear heating power, and not a non-nuclear heat load such as
charged-particle, surface photon, ohmic, chemical, or coolant heat transfer.
It is distinct from [nuclear heating power of a breeder blanket
shield](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_shield), which refers
to nuclear heating in a different structural component.

The nuclear energy deposited in the limiter tile over a time interval is the
time integral of this power; this standard name denotes the deposition rate
itself, not that time-integrated energy.

sources.leaf_definition: Nuclear power heating this unit
sources.parent_definition: Set of limiter units. Whenever relevant, multiple units should be ordered so that they define contiguous sections, clockwise in the poloidal direction.

NAMES.name: nuclear_power_density_of_breeder_blanket_layer
NAMES.short:
Local rate of nuclear energy deposition within the material volume of one
breeder blanket layer, generated by neutron interactions and associated
photon absorption.
NAMES.long:
Nuclear power density is the local volumetric heat-generation rate within
one defined breeder blanket material layer. It includes energy deposited by
neutron interactions and by absorption of primary or secondary photons,
rather than surface heat loads or externally applied heating.

The volume integral gives the corresponding layer-integrated nuclear heating
power:

$$
P_{\mathrm{nuc,layer}} = \int_{V_{\mathrm{layer}}} q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}V
$$

where $q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local nuclear power density,
$P_{\mathrm{nuc,layer}}$ is the integrated nuclear heating power,
$\mathbf{r}$ is position, and $V_{\mathrm{layer}}$ is the material volume of
the layer. This quantity is the nuclear-deposition component of power
density of a breeder blanket layer and integrates to [nuclear heating power
of a breeder blanket
layer](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer).

sources.leaf_definition: Nuclear heating power density in the layer, evaluated at midplane
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities at various time slices

NAMES.name: nuclear_power_density_of_limiter_tile
NAMES.short:
Local volumetric rate of nuclear energy deposition in limiter-tile material
from neutron interactions and associated absorption of primary and secondary
gamma radiation.
NAMES.long:
Nuclear power density of a limiter tile is the local volumetric energy
deposition rate within the material of one limiter tile caused by neutron
interactions and associated gamma-radiation absorption. It is the nuclear
contribution to the broader power density of a limiter tile, not the total
local energy source.

$$
P_{\mathrm{nuc}} = \int_{V_{\mathrm{tile}}} q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}V
$$

where $q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the nuclear power density at
position $\mathbf{r}$, $V_{\mathrm{tile}}$ is the material volume of the
limiter tile, and $P_{\mathrm{nuc}}$ is the corresponding [nuclear power of
a limiter tile](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_limiter_tile).

The quantity includes energy deposited volumetrically by neutron scattering
and capture and by absorption of primary and secondary gamma radiation.
Surface heat loads, externally applied heating, and nonnuclear
energy-transfer mechanisms are excluded.

sources.leaf_definition: Nuclear power density heating this unit evaluated at the midplane (whenever relevant)
sources.parent_definition: Set of limiter units. Whenever relevant, multiple units should be ordered so that they define contiguous sections, clockwise in the poloidal direction.

NAMES.name: power_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short:
Power quantity associated with a single breeder blanket module, abstracting
over incident neutron surface loads, volumetric nuclear energy deposition,
plasma radiation, and total thermal output as distinct energy-budget
components.
NAMES.long:
A breeder blanket module participates in multiple distinct energy-exchange
pathways between the fusion plasma and the blanket structure. The principal
power channels resolved at the module level include the neutron surface load
characterized by
[incident_power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:incident_neutron_power_of_breeder_blanket_module),
the volumetric nuclear energy deposited inside the module through scattering
and capture reactions described by neutron_power_of_breeder_blanket_module,
and the electromagnetic photon flux from plasma bremsstrahlung and line
radiation quantified by
[radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module).

The total power delivered to the module coolant combines these channels:

$$
P_\mathrm{module} = P_n + P_\mathrm{rad,abs} + P_\mathrm{aux}
$$

where $P_n$ is the deposited neutron power, $P_\mathrm{rad,abs}$ is the
absorbed fraction of incident plasma radiation after surface reflection, and
$P_\mathrm{aux}$ covers auxiliary heating contributions; nuclear
multiplication reactions in the tritium-breeding material can amplify $P_n$
above the incident neutron surface load.

Module-level power quantities are computed from neutronics transport
simulations for nuclear deposition channels, coupled with plasma radiation
models for photon loads, and validated against calorimetric measurements of
coolant enthalpy rise, the latter captured by
[net_thermal_power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:net_thermal_power_of_breeder_blanket_module).
The blanket-wide integral summed over all modules is given by
[nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket).

NAMES.name: radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short:
Radiated power associated with a single breeder blanket module, abstracting
over plasma electromagnetic power incident on the module surface, the
reflected portion, and the absorbed portion retained as a module heat load
as distinct radiation energy-budget components.
NAMES.long:
Radiated power of a breeder blanket module quantifies the rate at which
plasma electromagnetic emission, chiefly bremsstrahlung continuum and atomic
line radiation, is assigned to the module-level radiation channel. It is the
umbrella scalar for the incident photon power crossing onto the module
surface and the absorbed photon power retained after surface reflection,
represented by
[incident_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:incident_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module)
and
[absorbed_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:absorbed_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module).

The radiated-power component for a single module is defined by integrating
the corresponding radiative surface energy flux over the module surface:

$$
P_{\mathrm{rad},c} = \int_{A_m} \Phi_{\mathrm{rad},c}\, dA,\qquad c \in \{\mathrm{inc},\mathrm{abs}\}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{rad},c}$ is the module-level radiated-power component in
watts, $A_m$ is the module plasma-facing surface, $dA$ is a surface element,
$\Phi_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{inc}}$ is the incident photon energy flux
density onto that surface, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{abs}}$ is the
retained photon energy flux density after reflection.

The incident and absorbed components are related by the surface-reflection
balance $P_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{abs}} = P_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{inc}} -
P_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{ref}}$, equivalently $P_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{abs}}
= (1-\mathcal{R})P_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{inc}}$ for an effective reflectance
$\mathcal{R}$. The parent quantity is not a sum of incident and absorbed
terms; it identifies the module radiation channel, while the component
qualifier identifies which surface-budget term is represented. Neutron
surface loads, volumetric nuclear energy deposition, auxiliary heating, and
thermal radiation emitted by the module itself are outside this
radiated-power channel; the absorbed part contributes to
thermal_power_of_breeder_blanket_module within
[power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:power_of_breeder_blanket_module).

NAMES.name: absorbed_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short:
Net photon power retained by a breeding blanket module after reflection of
incident plasma radiation at its plasma-facing surface.
NAMES.long:
The absorbed radiated power of a breeding blanket module is the net
electromagnetic photon power retained by the module after plasma radiation
interacts with its plasma-facing surface. It includes absorbed
bremsstrahlung and atomic line radiation and is the absorbed component of
the broader [radiated power of a breeder blanket
module](name:radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module).

The absorbed power is related to the [incident radiated power of a breeder
blanket module](name:incident_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module) by:

$$
P_\text{abs} = (1 - \mathcal{R}) P_\text{inc}
$$

where $P_\text{inc}$ is the incident radiative power, $\mathcal{R}$ is the
effective hemispherical surface reflectance averaged over the incident
photon spectrum, and $P_\text{abs}$ is the absorbed radiated power. This
quantity excludes photon power reflected from the surface and nuclear energy
deposited within the module.

sources.leaf_definition: Total radiated power (incident - reflected) in the blanket module
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities at various time slices

NAMES.name: incident_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short:
The incident radiated power of a breeder blanket module is the
electromagnetic photon power from plasma radiation arriving at the module
plasma-facing surface before surface reflection losses are applied. It
includes bremsstrahlung continuum and atomic line radiation.
NAMES.long:
The incident radiated power of a breeder blanket module is the
electromagnetic photon power from plasma radiation arriving at the module
plasma-facing surface before any surface reflection loss is applied. It
includes incident bremsstrahlung continuum and atomic line radiation
assigned to that module.

The incident component for a single module is defined by integrating the
incident radiative surface energy flux over the module plasma-facing
surface:

$$
P_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{inc}} = \int_{A_{\mathrm{pf},m}} \Phi_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{inc}} \, dA
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{inc}}$ is the incident radiated power of the
module, $A_{\mathrm{pf},m}$ is the module plasma-facing surface, $dA$ is a
surface element, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{inc}}$ is the incident
photon energy flux density crossing onto that surface from the plasma side.

This quantity applies to one breeder blanket module and is the
surface-integrated total over the plasma-facing face of that module, not
over non-plasma-facing structural surfaces. It counts only incoming plasma
photon radiation and excludes reflected photon power as a separate outgoing
term. Neutron surface loads, volumetric nuclear energy deposition,
charged-particle heat fluxes, auxiliary heating, and thermal radiation
emitted by the module itself are outside this radiated-power component.

The incident component is related to the [absorbed radiated
power](name:absorbed_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module) by the
surface-reflection balance $P_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{abs}} =
P_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{inc}} - P_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{ref}}$, equivalently
$P_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{abs}} =
(1-\mathcal{R})P_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{inc}}$ for effective reflectance
$\mathcal{R}$, where $P_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{abs}}$ is the absorbed
radiated power and $P_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{ref}}$ is the reflected radiated
power. The [radiated power of a breeder blanket
module](name:radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module) identifies the module
radiation channel; it is not the arithmetic sum of incident and absorbed
components.

sources.leaf_definition: Total incident radiative power on the blanket module
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities at various time slices

NAMES.name: resistance_of_vacuum_vessel
NAMES.short:
Lumped ohmic opposition to current flow through a discrete passive-conductor
element of the vacuum vessel.
NAMES.long:
Electrical resistance of a discrete passive-conductor element is the
proportionality between the voltage drop across the element and the current
through it, representing irreversible ohmic dissipation.

$$
R = \frac{\Delta V}{I}
$$

where $R$ is the resistance, $\Delta V$ is the potential difference across
the element, and $I$ is the through-current. For an approximately
homogeneous element, resistance is determined by the material resistivity
and the element geometry, as described by [resistivity of the vacuum
vessel](name:resistivity_of_vacuum_vessel) and [resistivity of wall
material](name:resistivity_of_wall_material). This lumped quantity excludes
inductive opposition and represents only the ohmic component; it is distinct
from the total resistance of a closed [passive
loop](name:resistance_of_passive_loop).

sources.leaf_definition: Resistance of the block element
sources.parent_definition: Set of block elements

NAMES.name: resistivity_of_limiter_tile
NAMES.short:
Electrical resistivity of material forming an individual limiter unit,
governing the local relation between electric field and current density
during electromagnetic response.
NAMES.long:
Electrical resistivity of a limiter unit is the material property that
determines how strongly its conducting material opposes electric current and
converts electromagnetic energy into ohmic dissipation.

The local constitutive relation is

$$
\mathbf{E} = \rho\mathbf{J}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric-field vector, $\rho$ is the electrical
resistivity, and $\mathbf{J}$ is the conventional electric-current-density
vector.

This quantity applies to the material of one limiter unit and represents a
local material property rather than a sum over limiter units or a lumped
electrical resistance of an entire structure. It excludes geometric path
effects, contact contributions, and circuit-level inductive effects. The
limiter-unit property is the component-specific counterpart of
[resistivity_of_plasma_facing_component](name:resistivity_of_plasma_facing_component)
and is distinct from the effective material property assigned to a broader
wall through
[resistivity_of_wall_material](name:resistivity_of_wall_material).

sources.leaf_definition: Resistivity of the limiter unit
sources.parent_definition: Set of limiter units. Whenever relevant, multiple units should be ordered so that they define contiguous sections, clockwise in the poloidal direction.

NAMES.name: resistivity_of_plasma_facing_component
NAMES.short:
Electrical resistivity of the material assigned to a mobile plasma-facing
component unit, relating local electric field to current density and
governing its conductive electromagnetic response.
NAMES.long:
Electrical resistivity is the material property that determines the electric
field required to sustain conduction in a mobile plasma-facing component
unit. It governs induced-current and eddy-current response within that unit.

For an isotropic material, the local constitutive relation is

$$
\mathbf{E} = \rho\,\mathbf{J}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is the local electric-field vector, $\rho$ is the
electrical resistivity, and $\mathbf{J}$ is the conventional current-density
vector.

This quantity applies to the material of one mobile plasma-facing component
unit and is not summed over multiple units or converted into a lumped
resistance. It is a local material property, distinct from the effective
resistivity of a broader passive conducting structure or [wall
material](name:resistivity_of_wall_material). When geometry is included, it
contributes to a lumped [passive-loop
resistance](name:resistance_of_passive_loop), which also depends on
current-path length and cross-sectional geometry.

sources.leaf_definition: Resistivity of the mobile unit
sources.parent_definition: Set of mobile units

NAMES.name: resistivity_of_wall_material
NAMES.short:
Electrical resistivity of wall material, relating local electric field to
current density and determining ohmic dissipation during electromagnetic
transients.
NAMES.long:
Electrical resistivity is the local bulk material property that opposes
electric current in the wall and converts electromagnetic energy into heat.
It applies to the wall material at each physical location, with values
allowed to vary between material locations.

For an isotropic local response, resistivity is defined by

$$
\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{r}) = \rho(\mathbf{r})\,\mathbf{J}(\mathbf{r})
$$

where $\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local electric-field vector,
$\mathbf{J}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local conventional current-density vector,
$\rho(\mathbf{r})$ is the local electrical resistivity, and $\mathbf{r}$
denotes physical position in the wall.

This quantity is a local bulk material property, not a wall-wide average, a
lumped current-path resistance, or an interface or contact resistance. It is
therefore distinct from the lumped [resistance of a vacuum
vessel](name:resistance_of_vacuum_vessel) and resistance of a passive
structure, which also depend on conductor geometry and current-path length.

The local irreversible heating density is $p_{\rm
ohm}=\mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E}$, where $p_{\rm ohm}$ is ohmic power density;
integrating this density over the wall material gives the [power at the wall
due to ohmic dissipation](name:power_at_wall_due_to_ohmic_dissipation).

sources.leaf_definition: One scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.
sources.parent_definition: Resistivity, given on various grid subsets

NAMES.name: thickness_of_breeder_blanket_layer
NAMES.short:
Non-negative geometric separation between the inner and outer material
interfaces of a breeder blanket layer along the specified thickness
direction.
NAMES.long:
Non-negative geometric separation between the inner and outer material
interfaces of a breeder blanket layer is the local through-thickness of that
layer along the specified thickness direction. The quantity applies to a
single material or functional layer within the blanket, not to the total
breeder blanket module build.

The layer thickness is defined by the separation of the two bounding
interfaces along the thickness coordinate:

$$
d_\ell = \left|s_{\ell,\mathrm{out}} - s_{\ell,\mathrm{in}}\right|
$$

where $d_\ell$ is the layer thickness in m, and $s_{\ell,\mathrm{in}}$ and
$s_{\ell,\mathrm{out}}$ are the signed coordinates in m of the inner and
outer layer interfaces along the specified thickness direction.

It is not the toroidal width, poloidal height, surface extent, or
volume-equivalent thickness of the layer. It is distinct from module-level
quantities such as thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module,
[lower_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:lower_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module),
and
[upper_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:upper_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module).
For a radially stacked layer, the thickness direction is the cylindrical
$\hat{R}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame,
where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical
height.

sources.leaf_definition: Thickness of this layer evaluated at the midplane
sources.parent_definition: Set of layers in the blanket module

NAMES.name: thickness_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short:
Thickness of a ferritic element is the non-negative face-to-face extent of
its rectangular poloidal cross section in the right-handed cylindrical (R,
φ, Z) frame, where R is major radius, φ is toroidal angle, and Z is vertical
height, measured along the in-plane direction normal to the element
centerline. It is distinct from width along the centerline and from toroidal
extent.
NAMES.long:
Thickness of a ferritic element is the non-negative separation between the
two opposing through-thickness faces of the rectangular poloidal cross
section of an axisymmetric ferritic element. In a plane of constant $\phi$
in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major
radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the centerline
is the geometric midline of that rectangle, and the through-thickness
direction is the in-plane direction normal to the centerline.

The thickness $d$ is the absolute face-to-face separation along the
through-thickness normal:

$$
d = \left|(\mathbf{r}_+ - \mathbf{r}_-) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{t}}\right|
$$

where $d$ is the thickness of the ferritic element, $\mathbf{r}_+$ and
$\mathbf{r}_-$ are position vectors of any points on the two opposing
through-thickness faces in the same poloidal cross section, and
$\hat{\mathbf{t}}$ is either unit normal to the centerline within that
poloidal cross section. The absolute value makes the quantity independent of
which face is chosen as the reference face.

The scope is a single rectangular cross section of a ferritic element, and
the physical population is the ferritic material belonging to that element.
Its aggregation convention is one element-level geometric extent for that
rectangle; it is not an average over multiple elements, an average around
the toroidal sweep, or a description of local surface roughness or
non-rectangular shape variation.

The [width of a ferritic element](name:width_of_ferritic_element) is the
extent parallel to the centerline of the same rectangle, whereas this
thickness is the orthogonal in-plane extent across the centerline. For the
ideal rectangular cross section, the poloidal cross-section area equals this
thickness multiplied by that width. The quantity is not a cylindrical
major-radius or vertical extent unless the local through-thickness direction
happens to align with the corresponding direction in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, and it is not the toroidal extent of the
axisymmetric element.

sources.leaf_definition: Thickness
sources.parent_definition: The element is approximated by a rectangle defined by a central segment and a thickness in the direction perpendicular to the segment

NAMES.name: thickness_of_plasma_facing_component
NAMES.short:
Through-material geometric separation between a plasma-facing component’s
exposed surface and its opposite material boundary, evaluated at the
component midplane.
NAMES.long:
The thickness is the through-material dimension of a plasma-facing component
at its midplane, separating the plasma-exposed surface from the opposite
material boundary. It is measured along the local thickness direction normal
to the exposed surface.

$$
t_{\mathrm{PFC}} = d_{\perp}\left(S_{\mathrm{plasma}}, S_{\mathrm{back}}\right)\big|_{\mathrm{midplane}}
$$

Here, $t_{\mathrm{PFC}}$ is the component thickness, $d_{\perp}$ is the
through-material normal separation, and $S_{\mathrm{plasma}}$ and
$S_{\mathrm{back}}$ are the exposed and opposite material surfaces,
respectively.

This is a geometric material dimension for the specified midplane section;
it is not a plasma-to-wall separation such as the gap at the plasma
boundary, nor a surface thermal quantity.

sources.leaf_definition: Thickness of this unit evaluated at the midplane (whenever relevant)
sources.parent_definition: Set of limiter units. Whenever relevant, multiple units should be ordered so that they define contiguous sections, clockwise in the poloidal direction.

NAMES.name: toroidal_angular_width_of_limiter_tile
NAMES.short:
Full toroidal angular span of one limiter tile between its minimum and
maximum φ coordinates in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal angular width of an individual limiter tile is the full angular
span occupied by that tile around the machine symmetry axis. It is a
non-negative geometric extent in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$
frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is
vertical height.

The width is defined from the extrema of the tile's toroidal-angle extent:

$$
\Delta\phi_{\mathrm{tile}} = \phi_{\max} - \phi_{\min}
$$

where $\Delta\phi_{\mathrm{tile}}$ is the tile's toroidal angular width, and
$\phi_{\max}$ and $\phi_{\min}$ are the maximum and minimum toroidal-angle
coordinates of the tile, evaluated on a continuous angular branch when the
extent crosses the angular periodic boundary.

This quantity applies to one individual limiter tile and represents its
complete toroidal span; it is not summed over tiles, limiter units, or
periodic repetitions. It is distinct from a toroidal-angle coordinate, a
tile-center angle, and the angular width of an entire limiter assembly.

The toroidal extent complements the boundary geometry described by the
[vertical outline of the limiter
tile](name:vertical_outline_of_limiter_tile), while the analogous camera
field-of-view quantity [toroidal angular width of a
camera](name:toroidal_angular_width_of_camera) applies to an optical viewing
extent rather than a structural tile.

sources.leaf_definition: Simplified description of toroidal angle extensions of the unit, by a list of zones defined by their centre and full width (in toroidal angle).  In each of these zones, the unit outline remains the same. Leave this node empty for an axisymmetric unit. The first dimension gives the centre and full width toroidal angle values for the unit. The second dimension represents the toroidal occurrences of the unit countour (i.e. the number of toroidal zones).
sources.parent_definition: Set of limiter units. Whenever relevant, multiple units should be ordered so that they define contiguous sections, clockwise in the poloidal direction.

NAMES.name: tritium_breeding_ratio
NAMES.short:
Tritium breeding ratio is the blanket-level ratio of tritium atoms produced
in breeder-blanket breeding regions to the incident fusion-neutron count
over the same normalization interval. Compatible module contributions share
this denominator and add to the blanket value.
NAMES.long:
Tritium breeding ratio is the blanket-level ratio of tritium atoms produced
inside the breeding regions of a breeder blanket to the incident
fusion-neutron count used to normalize the same neutronics balance. It is a
tritium production figure of merit for the blanket as a whole, distinct from
nuclear heating or power deposition.

The ratio is defined over a specified normalization interval by

$$
\mathrm{TBR} = \frac{N_{T,\mathrm{blanket}}}{N_{n,\mathrm{inc}}}
$$

where $N_{T,\mathrm{blanket}}$ is the number of tritium atoms produced in
the blanket breeding regions during that interval, and $N_{n,\mathrm{inc}}$
is the incident fusion-neutron count for the same interval.

Breeding regions are the blanket material volumes designated for
neutron-induced tritium production; tritium produced outside those volumes
is excluded unless that material is part of the breeder blanket breeding
region. The denominator is the common incident-neutron denominator, not the
number of neutrons absorbed in the blanket and not a module-specific
denominator. Compatible non-overlapping module values of
[tritium_breeding_ratio_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:tritium_breeding_ratio_of_breeder_blanket_module)
that use this same denominator are additive and sum to the blanket-level
ratio.

The quantity differs from power_of_breeder_blanket and
[power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:power_of_breeder_blanket_module),
which describe energy deposition rates rather than tritium atom yield.
Because both counts are non-negative and the denominator must be positive,
negative values are outside the physical domain; values greater than one
mean more tritium atoms are produced than the tritium atoms consumed by the
fusion reactions that generated the same incident-neutron population, which
is the breeding condition for tritium self-sufficiency.

sources.leaf_definition: Number of tritium atoms created for each fusion neutron (TBR)
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities for a set of time_slices

NAMES.name: tritium_breeding_ratio_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless tritium-production contribution from one breeder-blanket
module, normalized by the common incident fusion-neutron count used for the
blanket balance.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the contribution of one breeder-blanket module to the
blanket-level [tritium breeding ratio](name:tritium_breeding_ratio). It
counts tritium atoms produced within that module's breeding regions and uses
the common incident fusion-neutron normalization for the complete blanket.

$$
TBR_{\mathrm{module}} = \frac{N_{T,\mathrm{module}}}{N_{n,\mathrm{incident}}}
$$

where $N_{T,\mathrm{module}}$ is the number of tritium atoms produced in the
module's breeding regions and $N_{n,\mathrm{incident}}$ is the incident
fusion-neutron count used for the blanket balance.

For modules that partition the blanket breeding regions and share this
denominator, the module contributions add to the blanket tritium breeding
ratio. The quantity excludes tritium production outside the specified module
and is not a separate normalization of the module's incident neutron count.

sources.leaf_definition: Number of tritium atoms created for each fusion neutron (TBR)
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities at various time slices

NAMES.name: upper_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short:
Upper thickness of a breeder blanket module is the non-negative geometric
separation through the upper cap, measured normal to its exterior boundary
and main-body interface.
NAMES.long:
Upper thickness of a breeder blanket module is the geometric thickness of
the cap that closes the module at its upper end. The reference surfaces are
the upper exterior boundary of the cap and the interface where the upper cap
joins the main module body. It is the top-cap poloidal thickness in a
poloidal $(R,Z)$ section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$
frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is
vertical height. It is distinct from the overall thickness of a breeder
blanket module and the corresponding [lower thickness of a breeder blanket
module](name:lower_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module).

The upper-cap thickness is the normal projection of the separation between
the reference surfaces:

$$
t_{\mathrm{upper}} = \left|\left(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ext}} - \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{int}}\right) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\right|
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{int}}$ are
corresponding points on the upper exterior boundary and cap-to-body
interface, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the local unit normal directed through the
upper cap in the poloidal section, and $t_{\mathrm{upper}}$ is the upper-cap
thickness. The quantity applies to one breeder blanket module and is not
summed or averaged over modules. It is a non-negative geometric magnitude;
it is not a signed coordinate, vertical height, or displacement and excludes
the thicknesses of internal breeder, coolant, or shielding layers.

sources.leaf_definition: Top cap poloidal thickness
sources.parent_definition: Set of modules composing the blanket

NAMES.name: vertical_outline_of_limiter_tile
NAMES.short:
Signed vertical (Z) coordinate of each point on a limiter-tile boundary
contour in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical outline of a limiter tile gives the signed vertical coordinate
of each point on the tile’s geometric boundary contour. It describes the
contour geometry rather than a material property, thickness, or surface-load
quantity.

For contour point $i$, the vertical coordinate is defined by

$$
Z_i = \mathbf{r}_i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}}
$$

where $Z_i$ is the vertical coordinate of point $i$, $\mathbf{r}_i$ is its
position vector, and $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the vertical unit vector in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. Here, $R$ is major radius,
$\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies pointwise to the irregular outline of one limiter tile
in its poloidal cross section. The contour is closed by connecting its final
point to its initial point, without duplicating the initial point; no
averaging, summation, or other aggregation over contour points is implied.
Unlike the [radial outline of a limiter
tile](name:radial_outline_of_limiter_tile), this quantity gives the vertical
coordinate rather than the major-radius coordinate of the boundary.

The same geometric carrier and coordinate meaning apply to the [vertical
outline of a divertor tile](name:vertical_outline_of_divertor_tile), but
that related quantity belongs to a divertor tile rather than a limiter tile.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the contour point lies toward increasing $Z$
in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Height
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the limiting surface. Repeat the first point in case of a closed contour

NAMES.name: vertical_outline_of_plasma_facing_component
NAMES.short:
The vertical coordinate of each point on a plasma-facing component boundary
outline is the signed height in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z)
frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical outline coordinate is the signed height $Z$ of each
boundary-contour point belonging to a plasma-facing component. It describes
the component boundary in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

For outline point $i$, the coordinate is defined by

$$
Z_i = \mathbf{r}_i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}}
$$

where $Z_i$ is the vertical coordinate of point $i$, $\mathbf{r}_i$ is that
point's position vector relative to the cylindrical coordinate origin, and
$\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the unit vector in the vertical direction. The
quantity applies pointwise to one component boundary outline and is not an
average, extremum, centroid coordinate, or integrated geometric measure. A
closed outline does not repeat its first point as a closing point.

This coordinate has the same geometric meaning as the corresponding outline
coordinate for a limiter tile or divertor tile, such as [vertical outline of
limiter tile](name:vertical_outline_of_limiter_tile) and [vertical outline
of divertor tile](name:vertical_outline_of_divertor_tile), but its locus is
the plasma-facing component boundary in general.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $Z_i$ increases in the $+\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$
direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Height
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the mobile unit, for a set of time slices. Repeat the first point in case of a closed contour

NAMES.name: volume_of_first_wall
NAMES.short:
Volume enclosed by the first-wall surface, representing the interior region
inside the innermost plasma-facing boundary rather than the wall material
itself.
NAMES.long:
The first-wall volume is the total interior volume enclosed by the innermost
plasma-facing surface of the vacuum vessel. It includes the space available
to the confined plasma, edge and scrape-off-layer regions, and neutral gas,
but excludes the material volume of the wall.

For an axisymmetric first-wall contour in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the volume is defined by

$$
V_{\rm FW}=2\pi\iint_A R\,dR\,dZ
$$

where $A$ is the poloidal cross-sectional area enclosed by the first-wall
contour, $R$ is major radius in meters, and $Z$ is vertical height in
meters. For non-axisymmetric geometry, the complete three-dimensional
enclosed region, including bounded ports and recesses, defines the volume.

This enclosed volume is distinct from [volume enclosed by the plasma
boundary](name:volume_of_flux_surface), which is limited by the last closed
flux surface, and from [area of the first wall](name:area_of_first_wall),
which measures the wall's material surface rather than an enclosed region.

sources.leaf_definition: Volume available to gas or plasma enclosed by the first wall contour
sources.parent_definition: Description of the torus wall and its interaction with the plasma

NAMES.name: volumetric_force
NAMES.short:
Electromagnetic Lorentz body-force density vector acting locally on plasma,
conducting wall, or structural material, with components resolved in the
right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The volumetric force is the local electromagnetic Lorentz force density
acting on plasma and current-carrying conducting or structural material. Its
projections include the [radial volumetric
force](name:radial_volumetric_force), [toroidal volumetric
force](name:toroidal_volumetric_force), and [vertical volumetric
force](name:vertical_volumetric_force).

The electromagnetic force density is defined by

$$
\mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{vol}} = \rho_e \mathbf{E} + \mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}
$$

where $\mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{vol}}$ is the volumetric force vector, $\rho_e$
is charge density, $\mathbf{E}$ is electric field, $\mathbf{J}$ is current
density, and $\mathbf{B}$ is magnetic field. The quantity is local and is
distinct from the net force obtained by integrating it over a material
volume.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when a force component points along its
corresponding positive basis direction—increasing $R$, increasing toroidal
angle $\phi$, or increasing $Z$—in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi,
Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_volumetric_force
NAMES.short:
Radial component of the electromagnetic body-force density vector, projected
onto the direction of increasing major radius R in the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial volumetric force is the $\hat{R}$-projection of the local
electromagnetic body-force density $\mathbf{f} = \mathbf{J} \times
\mathbf{B}$ acting on plasma volumes or conducting wall and structural
elements. It characterizes the net radial push or pull arising from the
interaction of local current density with the magnetic field, driving stress
and displacement in the major-radial direction.

The defining relation is the radial projection of the Lorentz force density
in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R},
\hat{\phi}, \hat{Z})$:

$$
f_R = (\mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot \hat{R} = J_\phi B_Z - J_Z B_\phi
$$

where $\mathbf{J}$ is the current density vector, $\mathbf{B}$ is the
magnetic field, and $J_\phi$, $J_Z$, $B_\phi$, $B_Z$ are the toroidal and
vertical components respectively.

This component is computed in magnetohydrodynamic equilibrium analyzes and
disruption-load assessments to quantify radial electromagnetic stresses on
plasma-facing components, wall tiles, and blanket structures. Together with
[toroidal_volumetric_force](name:toroidal_volumetric_force) and
[vertical_volumetric_force](name:vertical_volumetric_force), it resolves the
complete local electromagnetic body-force density vector described by
[volumetric_force](name:volumetric_force).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the electromagnetic force points in the
direction of increasing major radius $R$.

sources.leaf_definition: Component along the major radius axis, one scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.
sources.parent_definition: Electromagnetic force density computed by the cross-product of j_total x b_field and given on various grid subsets

NAMES.name: toroidal_volumetric_force
NAMES.short:
Toroidal component of the electromagnetic body-force density vector acting
on plasma volumes or conducting wall and structural elements, projected onto
increasing toroidal angle φ in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal volumetric force is the $\hat{\phi}$-projection of the local
electromagnetic body-force density vector acting on plasma volumes or
conducting wall and structural elements. It characterizes the local
mechanical load per unit volume directed around the torus in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius,
$\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For the magnetic Lorentz body force, the toroidal projection is:

$$
f_\phi = \mathbf{f}\cdot\hat{\phi} = (\mathbf{J}\times\mathbf{B})\cdot\hat{\phi} = J_Z B_R - J_R B_Z
$$

where $f_\phi$ is the toroidal volumetric force, $\mathbf{f}$ is the
electromagnetic body-force density vector, $\mathbf{J}$ is current density,
$\mathbf{B}$ is magnetic field, and $J_R$, $J_Z$, $B_R$, and $B_Z$ are the
corresponding projections in the same right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi,
Z)$ frame. The magnetic-field vector entering this relation is the quantity
represented by [magnetic field](name:magnetic_field).

This quantity is one signed projection of [volumetric
force](name:volumetric_force), complementary to [radial volumetric
force](name:radial_volumetric_force) and [vertical volumetric
force](name:vertical_volumetric_force). It excludes the magnitude of the
body-force density vector and any force integrated over a finite volume.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the force density points in the direction of
increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi,
Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Toroidal component, one scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.
sources.parent_definition: Electromagnetic force density computed by the cross-product of j_total x b_field and given on various grid subsets

NAMES.name: vertical_volumetric_force
NAMES.short:
Vertical component of the electromagnetic body-force density vector acting
on plasma volumes or conducting wall and structural elements, projected onto
increasing vertical height Z in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z)
frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical volumetric force is the $\hat{Z}$-projection of the local
electromagnetic body-force density vector acting on plasma volumes or
conducting wall and structural elements. It characterizes the local
mechanical load per unit volume along the vertical coordinate in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius,
$\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical height, and $\hat{Z}$ is the
positive vertical basis direction.

The component is defined by projecting the local Lorentz force density onto
$\hat{Z}$:

$$
f_Z = (\mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $f_Z$ is the vertical volumetric force, $\mathbf{J}$ is current
density, and $\mathbf{B}$ is magnetic field.

The quantity is local to the plasma, conducting wall, or structural material
at the point where the force density is defined; no spatial or component
aggregation is implied. It is distinct from a coordinate value, a surface
traction, a pressure, the magnitude of the force-density vector, and the net
vertical force obtained by integrating over a material volume.

Together with the [radial volumetric force](name:radial_volumetric_force)
and [toroidal volumetric force](name:toroidal_volumetric_force), it forms
the component decomposition of the [volumetric force](name:volumetric_force)
in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the force component points in the direction
of increasing vertical height $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi,
Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Component along the height axis, one scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.
sources.parent_definition: Electromagnetic force density computed by the cross-product of j_total x b_field and given on various grid subsets

NAMES.name: volumetric_fraction_of_breeder_blanket_layer
NAMES.short:
Volumetric fraction of a breeder blanket layer is the share of a specified
constituent material or phase in the layer's bulk volume. It is a
dimensionless effective-medium composition parameter for homogenized
breeder-blanket layer properties.
NAMES.long:
Volumetric fraction of a breeder blanket layer is the part-to-whole volume
ratio for one specified constituent material, phase, void region, coolant
region, or gas region within a breeder blanket layer. It describes the layer
composition used for homogenized material properties over the same geometric
region.

For constituent $i$, the fraction is defined by:

$$
f_i = \frac{V_i}{V_\mathrm{layer}}
$$

where $f_i$ is the volumetric fraction, $V_i$ is the volume of constituent
$i$ in cubic meters, and $V_\mathrm{layer}$ is the total bulk volume of the
same breeder blanket layer in cubic meters over the homogenization region.

The numerator and denominator must refer to the same layer region. For an
exhaustive non-overlapping partition of that region, $0 \le f_i \le 1$ and
$\sum_i f_i = 1$; separately represented voids, coolant, or gas regions are
included as their own constituents. This quantity is distinct from mass
fraction, atomic fraction, porosity, and selected-solid packing factor, and
its layer denominator differs from the whole-blanket volume described by
volume of breeder blanket.

sources.leaf_definition: Volume fraction of each material entering the composition of this layer
sources.parent_definition: Set of layers in the blanket module

NAMES.name: y_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid
NAMES.short:
Signed y coordinate of the geometric centroid of a ferritic element in the
right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame, with z aligned to vertical Z.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the signed Cartesian y position of the geometric centroid of
one ferritic element. The coordinate is defined in the right-handed
Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis, with coordinate values
$(x,y,z)$ and $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$.

$$
y_c = \frac{1}{V_e}\int_{V_e} y\,dV
$$

where $y_c$ and $y$ are Cartesian y coordinates measured in m, $V_e$ is the
ferritic-element volume measured in m$^3$, and $dV$ is a differential volume
element. The integration covers the entire element, so this is a volume
centroid rather than a surface centroid or a selected-point coordinate. The
corresponding orthogonal centroid coordinates are [x coordinate of the
ferritic element centroid](name:x_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid)
and [z coordinate of the ferritic element
centroid](name:z_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the centroid displacement from the coordinate
origin has a positive projection onto $\hat{y}$.

sources.leaf_definition: List of Y coordinates
sources.parent_definition: List of positions of the centroids, in Cartesian coordinates

NAMES.name: argon_density
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short:
Charge-state-summed number density of argon ions, including Ar+ through
Ar18+ and excluding neutral argon; local and averaged forms share this
definition.
NAMES.long:
Argon density is the number of argon ions per unit volume, summed over all
ionization stages from singly charged Ar+ through fully stripped Ar18+.
Neutral argon is excluded.

$$
n_{\mathrm{Ar}} = \sum_{Z=1}^{18} n_{\mathrm{Ar}^{Z+}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Ar}}$ is the total argon-ion number density, $Z$ is the
integer argon charge state, and $n_{\mathrm{Ar}^{Z+}}$ is the number density
of argon ions in that charge state.

The definition applies to a local value and to averages over a specified
chord or confined plasma volume, including the [line-averaged argon
density](name:line_averaged_argon_density) and [volume-averaged argon
density](name:volume_averaged_argon_density). It is distinct from argon
count, which represents an equivalent-electron inventory rather than
particles per volume.

NAMES.name: atomic_mass
NAMES.short:
Atomic mass is the mass assigned per neutral reference atom of a specified
elemental or isotopic composition, including its bound electrons.
NAMES.long:
Atomic mass is the mass assigned to one neutral reference atom of a
specified element or isotope. It characterizes isotopic composition and
includes the bound-electron contribution of the neutral atom.

The atomic mass is related to the corresponding relative atomic mass by

$$
m = A_{\mathrm r}\,m_{\mathrm u}
$$

where $m$ is the atomic mass, $A_{\mathrm r}$ is the corresponding relative
atomic mass, and $m_{\mathrm u}$ is the atomic mass constant, defined as one
twelfth of the rest mass of a free neutral carbon-12 atom in its ground
state.

The value applies per constituent atom, not to the complete mass of a
molecule or the total mass of a particle population. For a specified
isotopic mixture, it denotes the atom-number-weighted mean of the
constituent isotope masses. It is independent of ionic charge state and
differs from the charge-dependent rest mass of an ion. It is a physical
mass, not the integer nucleon count called the mass number, a mass density,
or a mass flow rate.

The [neutral-beam atomic mass](name:neutral_beam_atomic_mass) specializes
this definition to atoms of the beam species. In contrast, [atomic
number](name:atomic_number) identifies the nuclear proton count and does not
distinguish isotopes of the same element.

NAMES.name: atomic_number
NAMES.short:
Atomic number is the nuclear proton count that identifies an element and
remains unchanged across its isotopes and ionization states.
NAMES.long:
Atomic number

The defining relation to nuclear electric charge is:

$$
Z = \frac{Q_{\mathrm{nuc}}}{e}
$$

where $Z$ is the atomic number, $Q_{\mathrm{nuc}}$ is the nuclear electric
charge, and $e$ is the positive elementary charge.

The value applies to one elemental nucleus, whether present in a neutral
atom, an ion, or a molecular constituent. It is a positive integer, not a
sum or average over nuclei or charge states. For a molecular species,
[atomic count](name:atomic_count) separately specifies how many atoms of
that element constitute one particle.

For a fully stripped ion, the ionic charge number equals $Z$; partial
ionization changes the ionic charge but not the atomic number. Thus, atomic
number differs from the [average charge number](name:average_charge_number),
which depends on the charge-state distribution. The [ion atomic
number](name:ion_atomic_number) is this same nuclear property specialized to
an ion species.
