NAMES.name: average_charge_number
NAMES.short:
Number-density-weighted mean ionic charge number over the charge-state
distribution of a specified ion population.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the mean ionic charge number of a specified ion population
distributed among multiple charge states.

$$
\overline{Z} = \frac{\sum_q q n_q}{\sum_q n_q}
$$

where $q$ is the integer charge number of charge state $q$, $n_q$ is the
number density of ions in that charge state, and the sums extend over the
included charge states.

The average applies to one specified ion population and uses number-density
weighting over its charge-state distribution. It is an average rather than a
sum, so it does not represent total charge density or the charge number of
one particular state; it is also distinct from the nuclear [atomic
number](name:atomic_number), which is independent of ionization state.

The [ion charge-state average charge
number](name:ion_charge_state_average_charge_number) is a concrete instance
of this charge-state-averaged quantity for the corresponding ion population.

NAMES.name: binormal_ion_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short:
Signed local binormal projection of the density-weighted ion velocity
contribution produced by pressure-gradient diamagnetic drift, averaged over
all ionic charge states.
NAMES.long:
The binormal ion diamagnetic-drift velocity is the signed local projection
of the ion population's velocity contribution produced by pressure-gradient
diamagnetic drift. It is a velocity component, not a momentum flux or
particle flux.

$$
v_{i,\mathrm{bin}}^{*} = \mathbf{v}_{i}^{*} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{bin}}
$$

Here, $\mathbf{v}_{i}^{*}$ is the vector ion velocity contribution from
diamagnetic drift, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{bin}}$ is the designated
positive local binormal unit vector, and $v_{i,\mathrm{bin}}^{*}$ is their
signed projection. The subscript $i$ denotes the ion population and the
superscript $*$ identifies the diamagnetic-drift contribution.

This quantity applies to the ion population with a density-weighted mean
taken over all ionic charge states. It excludes neutral particles and is not
the velocity of one specified ion charge state. The corresponding
charge-state-resolved quantity, such as [perpendicular ion charge-state
diamagnetic-drift
velocity](name:perpendicular_ion_charge_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift),
retains the individual charge-state distinction rather than applying this
aggregation.

The binormal component is one projection of the full ion diamagnetic-drift
velocity. It is distinct from the analogous [toroidal ion diamagnetic-drift
velocity](name:toroidal_ion_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), which
projects the same charge-state-averaged contribution onto the toroidal
direction, and from parallel or field-normal projections that use different
directions.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the ion diamagnetic-drift velocity points
along the designated positive local binormal direction.

NAMES.name: center_of_mass_velocity
NAMES.short:
Center-of-mass velocity is the mass-weighted barycentric velocity vector of
a multicomponent plasma, equal to total momentum density divided by total
mass density. It is the single-fluid bulk plasma velocity whose projections
define the radial, poloidal, toroidal, and field-parallel center-of-mass
velocity components.
NAMES.long:
Center-of-mass velocity is the mass-weighted barycentric velocity vector of
a multicomponent plasma. It is the velocity whose product with total mass
density equals the total plasma momentum density of the species included in
the plasma mixture.

The center-of-mass velocity $\mathbf{V}_{cm}$ is defined as total momentum
density divided by total mass density:

$$
\mathbf{V}_{cm} = \frac{\sum_s m_s n_s \mathbf{v}_s}{\sum_s m_s n_s} = \frac{\sum_s \rho_s \mathbf{v}_s}{\rho}
$$

where $s$ indexes included plasma species, $m_s$ is the particle mass of
species $s$, $n_s$ is the number density of species $s$, $\mathbf{v}_s$ is
the species fluid velocity entering the [plasma
velocity](name:plasma_velocity) aggregate, $\rho_s=m_s n_s$ is the species
contribution to mass density, and $\rho=\sum_s \rho_s$ is the total mass
density.

The weighting is by mass density, not by charge, number density alone, or an
unweighted species average. When [plasma velocity](name:plasma_velocity)
denotes the single-fluid bulk velocity of the same mixture, it is identical
to center-of-mass velocity. Projections of this vector define the
[radial](name:radial_center_of_mass_velocity),
[poloidal](name:poloidal_bulk_center_of_mass_velocity),
[toroidal](name:toroidal_center_of_mass_velocity), and
[field-parallel](name:parallel_center_of_mass_velocity) center-of-mass
velocity components.

NAMES.name: bulk_center_of_mass_velocity
NAMES.short:
Center-of-mass velocity is the mass-weighted barycentric velocity vector of
a multicomponent plasma, equal to total momentum density divided by total
mass density.
NAMES.long:
Center-of-mass velocity is the mass-weighted barycentric velocity vector of
a multicomponent plasma. It is the velocity whose product with total mass
density equals the total plasma momentum density of the species included in
the plasma mixture.

The center-of-mass velocity $\mathbf{V}_{cm}$ is defined as total momentum
density divided by total mass density:

$$
\mathbf{V}_{cm} = \frac{\sum_s m_s n_s \mathbf{v}_s}{\sum_s m_s n_s} = \frac{\sum_s \rho_s \mathbf{v}_s}{\rho}
$$

where $s$ indexes the included plasma species, $m_s$ is the particle mass of
species $s$, $n_s$ is its number density, $\mathbf{v}_s$ is its fluid
velocity, $\rho_s = m_s n_s$ is its mass-density contribution, and $\rho =
\sum_s \rho_s$ is the total mass density.

The quantity represents the full velocity vector of the included
multicomponent plasma mixture and is aggregated over those species by mass
density. It is not a single-species velocity, an unweighted species average,
a number-density-weighted average, or one selected directional projection.

The [center-of-mass velocity](name:center_of_mass_velocity) provides the
common barycentric reference from which directional components are formed.
For example, [poloidal bulk center-of-mass
velocity](name:poloidal_bulk_center_of_mass_velocity) is the projection of
this vector onto the positive poloidal tangent of its specified
flux-coordinate system.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when a resolved component of $\mathbf{V}_{cm}$
points along the positive direction of its declared basis; cylindrical
components follow increasing $R$, $\phi$, or $Z$ in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, while a poloidal component follows the
positive tangent of the specified flux coordinate $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: center_of_mass_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short:
Mass-density-weighted mean of all constituent species' diamagnetic drift
velocities, representing the diamagnetic contribution to plasma
center-of-mass motion.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the local diamagnetic contribution to the plasma
center-of-mass velocity, formed as the mass-density-weighted mean of
constituent species' diamagnetic velocity contributions. It is this
contribution alone, not the complete plasma center-of-mass velocity.

The mass-density-weighted mean is defined by:

$$
\mathbf{V}_{\mathrm{cm,dia}} = \frac{\sum_a \rho_a\,\mathbf{v}_{a,\mathrm{dia}}}{\sum_a \rho_a}
$$

where $\mathbf{V}_{\mathrm{cm,dia}}$ is the diamagnetic center-of-mass
velocity contribution, $a$ indexes the constituent species and charge-state
populations, $\rho_a$ is the mass density of population $a$, and
$\mathbf{v}_{a,\mathrm{dia}}$ is its diamagnetic velocity contribution.

The aggregation is over all constituent plasma species at the same location,
not a spatial average or a charge-weighted electric current. For an
intensive species velocity resolved by charge state, the charge-state
aggregation is a density-weighted mean over all charge states. This quantity
is the diamagnetic contribution to the [center-of-mass
velocity](name:center_of_mass_velocity); other velocity contributions are
excluded.

NAMES.name: co_passing_power_density
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface-averaged volumetric energy source rate for the co-passing orbit
population, representing energy transfer to or from particles circulating in
the co-current direction.
NAMES.long:
Co-passing power density is the flux-surface-averaged rate at which kinetic
energy is transferred to or from the co-passing orbit population per unit
physical volume. Co-passing particles are passing particles that circulate
continuously in the co-current direction.

For a flux surface labeled by poloidal magnetic flux $psi$, it is defined as

$$
p_{E,\mathrm{co}}(\psi)=\left\langle\frac{dE_{\mathrm{co}}}{dt\,dV}\right\rangle_{\psi}
$$

where $E_{\mathrm{co}}$ is the kinetic energy of the co-passing population,
$t$ is time, $V$ is physical volume, and the angle brackets denote a
flux-surface average. Positive values denote net energy gain by this
population; negative values denote net energy loss. Wave-particle
interactions, collisions, and particle sources may contribute. The related
[counter-passing power density](name:counter_passing_power_density) applies
the same energy-transfer definition to the oppositely circulating orbit
class, while power density is the unqualified parent quantity.

NAMES.name: co_passing_thermal_ion_charge_state_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface-averaged Coulomb-collisional energy transfer per unit volume
from co-passing nonthermal particles to thermal ions of one specified
species and charge state.
NAMES.long:
Co-passing thermal-ion charge-state collisional power density is the signed
rate of kinetic-energy transfer from co-passing nonthermal particles to
thermal ions of one specified species and charge state, averaged over a
magnetic flux surface. The co-passing restriction selects untrapped donor
orbits; it does not restrict the receiving thermal ions to that orbit class.

The defining relation is the flux-surface average of the receiving
population's collisional kinetic-energy moment:

$$
P_{iq,\mathrm{co}}^{\mathrm{coll}} = \left\langle \int \frac{1}{2}m_i |\mathbf{v}|^2 C_{iq,d}[f_{iq}^{\mathrm{th}},f_d^{\mathrm{co}}](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v \right\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}}
$$

Here $P_{iq,\mathrm{co}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the co-passing thermal-ion
charge-state collisional power density, $i$ identifies the receiving ion
species, $q$ identifies its ionic charge number, and $d$ identifies the
designated nonthermal donor population. The symbol $m_i$ is the
receiving-ion mass, $\mathbf{x}$ is physical position, $\mathbf{v}$ is
receiving-ion velocity, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space integration
measure. The distributions $f_{iq}^{\mathrm{th}}$ and $f_d^{\mathrm{co}}$
describe the receiving thermal ions and the co-passing donor component,
respectively. The operator $C_{iq,d}$ gives the collisional time derivative
of the receiving distribution caused by Coulomb collisions with that donor
component, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}}$ denotes
magnetic-flux-surface averaging.

This quantity includes one receiving species and charge state, with no
charge-state sum. It excludes energy transferred to thermal electrons or
fast-ion recipients and represents an energy-exchange rate, not stored
kinetic energy or volume-integrated power. Summing over all ionic charge
states of the receiving species yields [co-passing thermal-ion collisional
power density](name:co_passing_thermal_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions)
at the same averaging level.

Adding this contribution to the
[counter-passing](name:counter_passing_thermal_ion_charge_state_power_density_due_to_collisions)
and
[trapped](name:trapped_thermal_ion_charge_state_power_density_due_to_collisions)
contributions yields the flux-surface average of [thermal-ion charge-state
collisional power
density](name:thermal_ion_charge_state_power_density_due_to_collisions),
which includes all donor orbit classes.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy
into the receiving thermal ions of the specified species and charge state.

NAMES.name: coulomb_logarithm
NAMES.short:
Natural logarithm of the effective upper-to-lower impact-parameter ratio
governing cumulative small-angle Coulomb scattering between charged
particles in a plasma.
NAMES.long:
The Coulomb logarithm expresses the effective logarithmic range of impact
parameters contributing to cumulative small-angle Coulomb scattering in a
plasma.

The Coulomb logarithm $\ln\Lambda$ is defined by

$$
\ln\Lambda = \ln\left(\frac{b_{\max}}{b_{\min}}\right)
$$

where $\Lambda$ is the effective impact-parameter ratio, $b_{\max}$ is the
upper impact-parameter cutoff, $b_{\min}$ is the lower impact-parameter
cutoff, and $\ln$ denotes the natural logarithm. In a weakly coupled plasma,
screening limits the upper cutoff, while strong deflection or quantum
diffraction sets the lower cutoff; the small-angle approximation requires
well-separated cutoffs.

The unqualified quantity specifies neither a colliding species pair nor a
spatial evaluation point, and implies no species sum or spatial average. The
[Coulomb logarithm at the pedestal
top](name:coulomb_logarithm_at_pedestal_top) is this same quantity evaluated
at the pressure pedestal top.

The logarithm, rather than the impact-parameter ratio itself, enters Coulomb
collision frequencies and collisional resistivity as a multiplicative
factor.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_fast_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Counter-passing fast-electron collisional power density is the local rate of
kinetic-energy change of the counter-passing guiding-center component of the
suprathermal electron distribution caused by Coulomb collisions with other
plasma species. It is the counter-passing orbit-class contribution to the
fast-electron collisional energy balance, positive for energy gain by that
component and negative for energy loss.
NAMES.long:
Counter-passing fast-electron collisional power density is the local rate of
change of kinetic energy density of the counter-passing component of the
fast-electron distribution caused by Coulomb collisions with other plasma
species. It is the counter-passing orbit-class contribution to the
fast-electron collisional energy balance. The counter-passing component
consists of passing guiding-center states whose bounce-averaged toroidal
angular motion is opposite to the plasma-current circulation; the toroidal
angle is $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where
$R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity is the kinetic-energy moment of the Coulomb collision operator
over the counter-passing part of fast-electron phase space:

$$
P_{e,\mathrm{fast,counter}}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_s \int \chi_{\mathrm{counter}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, \frac{1}{2} m_e v^2\, C_{es}[f_{e,\mathrm{fast}}, f_s](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where the sum is over collision partners $s$, $\chi_{\mathrm{counter}}$ is
the phase-space indicator equal to one on counter-passing fast-electron
guiding-center states and zero elsewhere, $m_e$ is the electron mass,
$v=|\mathbf{v}|$ is speed, $f_{e,\mathrm{fast}}$ is normalized so that $\int
f_{e,\mathrm{fast}}\,d^3v$ gives the local fast-electron density, $f_s$ is
the distribution of species $s$, and $C_{es}$ is the Coulomb collision
operator giving the collisional time derivative of $f_{e,\mathrm{fast}}$ due
to species $s$. The counter-passing restriction is applied by
$\chi_{\mathrm{counter}}$; it does not redefine the collision partners. For
relativistic fast electrons, the kinetic-energy weight is replaced by the
appropriate relativistic kinetic energy.

The orbit-class partition is non-overlapping: co-passing, counter-passing,
and [trapped](name:trapped_fast_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions)
components sum to fast-electron collisional power density when the same
collision operator and phase-space partition are used. This quantity
excludes collisional energy exchange assigned to the thermal-electron
population.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy to
the counter-passing fast-electron component.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_fast_ion_charge_state_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface-averaged rate of Coulomb-collisional kinetic-energy transfer to
counter-passing fast particles from ions of one specified species and charge
state.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the flux-surface-averaged rate at which Coulomb collisions
with ions of one specified species and charge state change the
kinetic-energy density of counter-passing fast particles. Counter-passing
particles follow untrapped guiding-center trajectories whose parallel
transit is opposite to the reference co-passing direction.

The defining kinetic-energy moment is

$$
P_{\mathrm{counter},bq}^{\mathrm{coll}} = \left\langle \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{counter}}} \frac{1}{2}m_a v^2 C_{a,bq}[f_a,f_{bq}](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v \right\rangle
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{counter},bq}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the counter-passing
collisional power density for ion partner species $b$ and ionic charge
number $q$; $a$ identifies the fast-particle distribution species; $m_a$ is
its particle mass; $\mathbf{x}$ is position; $\mathbf{v}$ is particle
velocity; and $v=|\mathbf{v}|$ is speed. The functions $f_a$ and $f_{bq}$
are the fast-particle and ion-partner velocity distributions, respectively.
The operator $C_{a,bq}$ gives the collisional time derivative of $f_a$
caused by that ion partner, $\Omega_{\mathrm{counter}}$ selects
counter-passing phase space, $d^3v$ is the velocity-space integration
measure, and angle brackets denote a magnetic-flux-surface average.

The charge-state label identifies the ion collision partner, not a
charge-state restriction on the receiving fast particles. This is a
single-partner contribution, with no sum over partner species or charge
states. It is a collisional source or sink, not stored kinetic-energy
density or spatially integrated power.

Together with the [co-passing
contribution](name:co_passing_fast_ion_charge_state_power_density_due_to_collisions)
and the trapped contribution for the same ion partner, it reconstructs the
flux-surface average of the [all-orbit fast-particle collisional power
density for that ion charge
state](name:fast_ion_charge_state_power_density_due_to_collisions).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when collisions with the specified ion charge
state increase the kinetic-energy density of the counter-passing
fast-particle population; negative when they decrease it.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_power_density
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface-averaged volumetric energy source rate for counter-passing
particles, representing energy transfer to or from particles circulating
opposite to the plasma-current direction.
NAMES.long:
Counter-passing power density is the flux-surface-averaged rate at which
energy is transferred to or from the counter-passing orbit population per
unit physical volume. It is the orbit-class specialization of power density;
counter-passing particles are passing particles that circulate opposite to
the plasma-current direction, distinct from [co-passing power
density](name:co_passing_power_density) and [trapped power
density](name:trapped_power_density).

For the underlying local energy balance, volumetric power density is defined
by

$$
p_{\mathrm{cp}} = \frac{dE_{\mathrm{cp}}}{dt\,dV}
$$

where $E_{\mathrm{cp}}$ is the energy transferred to the counter-passing
population, $t$ is time, and $V$ is physical volume. The flux-surface
average is applied to this local rate while retaining its per-volume
meaning.

Positive values denote net energy gain by the counter-passing population;
negative values denote net energy loss. Wave-particle interactions,
collisions, and particle sources contribute when they are included in the
counter-passing energy balance.

NAMES.name: cumulative_inside_flux_surface_electron_particle_source_rate
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Electron particle source rate inside a magnetic flux surface is the net
production or removal of free electrons integrated over the enclosed plasma
volume.
NAMES.long:
Electron particle source rate inside a magnetic flux surface is the net
production or removal of free electrons integrated over the enclosed plasma
volume. It supplies the source contribution to the volume-integrated
electron particle-number balance.

The cumulative rate is defined by

$$
S_{e,\mathrm{inside}}(\psi)=\int_{V(\psi)} S_{e,\mathrm{vol}}\,\mathrm{d}V
$$

where $S_{e,\mathrm{inside}}$ is the enclosed electron particle source rate,
$S_{e,\mathrm{vol}}$ is the local net free-electron volumetric source rate,
$\psi$ labels the selected magnetic flux surface, $V(\psi)$ is the plasma
volume enclosed by that surface, and $\mathrm{d}V$ is a physical volume
element.

The integral combines local electron gains and losses throughout the
enclosed volume for the source contribution under consideration. No
thermal-population or orbit-class restriction is implied. This quantity is a
spatial integral, not a flux-surface average or a time-integrated electron
inventory; it is distinct from the electron transport flux through the
enclosing surface.

The [cumulative ion charge-state source
rate](name:cumulative_inside_flux_surface_ion_charge_state_source_rate) uses
the same enclosed-volume integration for particles in a specified ion charge
state rather than for free electrons.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when free-electron production exceeds removal
within the enclosed plasma volume.

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport
NAMES.short:
Vector conventional electric-current density attributed to turbulence-driven
anomalous transport in a plasma.
NAMES.long:
Current density due to anomalous transport is the vector conventional
electric-current density associated with turbulent, nonclassical transport
processes that produce a net charge flow. It denotes only the
anomalous-transport contribution to the plasma current, not the total
current density.

This is a phenomenological transport-current contribution; no universal
closed-form constitutive identity is part of its definition. The vector may
be resolved into
[radial_current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport](name:radial_current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport),
[toroidal_current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport),
and
[vertical_current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport](name:vertical_current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport)
in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major
radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, and into
[parallel_current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport)
along the local magnetic-field direction $\hat{b} =
\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$, where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field. It is
distinct from
[current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity](name:current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity),
which represents a perpendicular-viscous transport-current contribution.

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short:
Electric-current-density contribution driven by plasma pressure gradients,
including the perpendicular diamagnetic current and its associated
field-aligned return current.
NAMES.long:
Current density due to diamagnetic drift is the pressure-gradient-driven
contribution to [electric current density](name:current_density) in a
magnetized plasma. It includes the perpendicular diamagnetic drive and the
associated field-aligned return current, rather than denoting a projection
onto a diamagnetic direction.

In the isotropic-pressure fluid limit, its decomposition is

$$
\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{dia}}=\frac{\mathbf{B}\times\nabla p}{|\mathbf{B}|^2}+j_{\parallel,\mathrm{dia}}\hat{\mathbf{b}}
$$

where $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the diamagnetic-drift current-density
vector, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, $p$ is the total
isotropic pressure of the charged plasma populations, and $\nabla p$ is its
spatial gradient. The magnetic-field unit vector is
$\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$, and $j_{\parallel,\mathrm{dia}}$
is the [parallel current density due to diamagnetic
drift](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), defined by
$j_{\parallel,\mathrm{dia}}=\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{dia}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}}$.

The contribution is summed over charged plasma populations and is not
restricted to a particular species or to the plasma edge. It is
mechanism-resolved: projecting the total current from all mechanisms onto a
diamagnetic direction does not isolate this contribution. Independently
driven currents are excluded.

Under stationary quasineutral current closure, the associated field-aligned
return current balances the divergence of the perpendicular diamagnetic
drive. The [Pfirsch–Schlüter current density due to diamagnetic
drift](name:pfirsch_schlueter_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift)
identifies the specific return-current contribution associated with toroidal
magnetic geometry; it is not the entire current-density vector.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when a projected component represents net
positive-charge transport along its defining positive direction; the
parallel projection is positive along the local magnetic-field unit vector
$\hat{\mathbf{b}}$.

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity
NAMES.short:
Vector electric current density arising from heat-viscosity terms in the
collisional plasma fluid closure, where the divergence of the heat-viscosity
stress tensor drives net charge transport in a magnetized plasma.
NAMES.long:
The heat-viscosity current density is the electric current density vector
generated when heat-viscosity contributions in a collisional plasma fluid
model (such as the Braginskii closure) induce net species motion that
results in charge transport. In a magnetized plasma, the viscous stress
tensor $\overset{\leftrightarrow}{\pi}$ contains a heat-viscosity part
$\overset{\leftrightarrow}{\pi}_\mathrm{hv}$ that couples heat transport to
bulk plasma momentum; the divergence of this tensor enters the fluid
momentum equation for each species and drives flows carrying net electric
current.

The heat-viscosity current density vector $\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{hv}$ is
expressed as:

$$
\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{hv} = \sum_s q_s n_s \mathbf{v}_{s,\mathrm{hv}}
$$

where $q_s$ is the charge of species $s$, $n_s$ is its number density, and
$\mathbf{v}_{s,\mathrm{hv}}$ is the flow velocity component driven by
heat-viscosity forces in the species momentum balance.

This vector is decomposed into geometric projections, including the [radial
component](name:radial_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity) along
$\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The
companion quantity current_density_due_to_collisions captures the distinct
inter-species collisional friction mechanism, while
radial_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity represents the analogous
contribution from field-aligned (parallel) viscosity. Heat-viscosity current
contributions are most significant in the edge plasma where the
collisionality is high enough for fluid closures to remain valid.

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_ion_inertia
NAMES.short:
Vector current density arising from the inertial force terms of the ion
fluid in the two-fluid plasma model, principally through the polarization
drift generated by ion acceleration in the momentum equation.
NAMES.long:
The current density due to ion inertia represents the net electric current
produced by the inertial acceleration terms in the ion fluid momentum
equation. In a two-fluid plasma description, ions with finite mass
contribute to net charge transport whenever they are accelerated — through
flow convergence, curvature forces, or time-varying electric fields — giving
rise to a polarization-type current that is absent in the massless-electron
fluid.

The dominant contribution is the ion polarization drift current:

$$
\mathbf{J}_{inertia} = \frac{m_i n_i}{e B^2} \mathbf{B} \times \frac{d_i \mathbf{v}_{\perp i}}{dt}
$$

where $m_i$ is the ion mass, $n_i$ is the ion number density, $e$ is the
elementary charge, $B$ is the magnetic field magnitude, and $d_i/dt =
\partial/\partial t + \mathbf{v}_i \cdot \nabla$ is the ion convective
derivative applied to the perpendicular ion velocity $\mathbf{v}_{\perp i}$.

The divergence of this current feeds the vorticity equation and contributes
to the radial current balance, making it particularly significant in edge
and scrape-off-layer transport modeling where large ion flows develop. In
multi-fluid transport codes, the vector is evaluated on generalized geometry
grids and decomposed into cylindrical components —
[radial_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia](name:radial_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia),
[toroidal_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia),
[vertical_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia](name:vertical_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia)
— and a field-aligned component
[parallel_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia).
The analogous turbulent contribution is given by
[current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport](name:current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport).

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction
NAMES.short:
Mechanism-resolved electric current-density vector attributable to
ion–neutral frictional momentum exchange in a partially ionized plasma.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the vector contribution to electric current density
attributed to momentum exchange between plasma ions and neutral particles.
It excludes current contributions assigned to other mechanisms and does not
represent the total plasma current density.

The mechanism-resolved current density is defined from the corresponding
charged-particle velocity contributions:

$$
\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{in}} = \sum_s q_s n_s \mathbf{v}_{s,\mathrm{in}}
$$

where $q_s$ is the charge of charged species $s$ in C, $n_s$ is its number
density in m$^{-3}$, and $\mathbf{v}_{s,\mathrm{in}}$ is the velocity
contribution attributed to ion–neutral friction. Neutral particles have zero
charge and do not contribute directly to the sum.

The vector may be projected onto cylindrical, poloidal, field-aligned, or
other specified directions, including the [radial current-density
component](name:radial_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction),
[toroidal current-density
component](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction), and
[parallel current-density
component](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction).
Unlike current density due to collisions, its mechanism attribution is
restricted to ion–neutral friction.

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_non_inductive_current_drive
NAMES.short:
Vector current-density contribution produced by bootstrap and externally
driven non-inductive mechanisms, excluding current generated by an inductive
electric field.
NAMES.long:
Non-inductive current density is the vector contribution to plasma electric
current produced without inductive electric-field drive. It includes
bootstrap current and externally driven non-inductive sources, but excludes
the inductive contribution to the total plasma current.

$$
\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{NI}} = \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{bootstrap}} + \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{external,NI}}
$$

where $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{NI}}$ is the non-inductive current-density
vector, $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{bootstrap}}$ is the bootstrap-current density,
and $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{external,NI}}$ is the combined current density from
externally driven non-inductive sources. The [parallel non-inductive current
density](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_non_inductive_current_drive)
is a field-aligned, flux-surface-averaged projection of this broader
quantity.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when a resolved current-density component points
along the positive direction of its defining axis in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity
NAMES.short:
Full current-density vector arising from the divergence of the parallel
viscous stress tensor in a magnetized plasma.
NAMES.long:
Full current-density vector arising from the divergence of the parallel
viscous stress tensor in a magnetized plasma. It is the current-density
contribution associated with the parallel part of viscous momentum
transport, where parallel refers to the magnetic-field direction in the
stress tensor rather than to the direction of the resulting current.

The perpendicular force-balance drift produced by the parallel-viscous force
density is

$$
\mathbf{J}_{\Pi_\parallel} = \frac{(\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel) \times \mathbf{B}}{B^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{J}_{\Pi_\parallel}$ is this current-density vector,
$\boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel$ is the parallel viscous stress tensor, $\nabla
\cdot \boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel$ is the corresponding viscous force
density, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, and $B=|\mathbf{B}|$ is
the magnetic-field magnitude. Only the full tensor divergence enters this
relation; it is not a scalar-viscosity definition. The vector direction is
governed by the right-hand rule applied to the parallel-viscous force
density and the magnetic field, and the contribution is locally
perpendicular to $\mathbf{B}$.

This quantity excludes current density due to [perpendicular viscous
stress](name:current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity), including its
[field-aligned
projection](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity),
and the separate [heat-viscosity
contribution](name:current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity). Directional
projections include the
[radial](name:radial_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity),
[toroidal](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity), and
[vertical](name:vertical_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity)
components along $\hat{R}$, $\hat{\phi}$, and $\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is
toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above
$+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height, and the [poloidal
component](name:poloidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity) in the
plane spanned by $\hat{R}$ and $\hat{Z}$. Aggregate viscous-current
components such as
[radial_current_density_due_to_viscosity](name:radial_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity)
and toroidal_current_density_due_to_viscosity combine this contribution with
perpendicular-viscosity contributions.

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity
NAMES.short:
Vector electric current-density contribution generated by the divergence of
perpendicular viscous stress in a magnetized charged plasma.
NAMES.long:
Perpendicular-viscosity current density is the vector electric-current
contribution attributed to perpendicular viscous stress acting on charged
plasma. The word “perpendicular” identifies the viscous-stress mechanism,
not a restriction of the resulting current vector to directions
perpendicular to the magnetic field.

The current-density contribution is defined by

$$
\mathbf{J}_{\perp,\nu}=\sum_s q_s n_s\mathbf{u}_{s,\perp,\nu}
$$

where $q_s$ is the signed charge of species $s$ in coulombs, $n_s$ is its
number density in m$^{-3}$, and $\mathbf{u}_{s,\perp,\nu}$ is the
species-velocity response attributed to the divergence of perpendicular
viscous stress. The vector may be resolved into radial, toroidal, vertical,
poloidal, parallel, or diamagnetic components, including the [parallel
current-density
component](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity) and
[diamagnetic current-density
component](name:diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity).
It is distinct from the analogous [current density due to parallel
viscosity](name:current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity).

NAMES.name: current_due_to_non_inductive_current_drive
NAMES.short:
Net plasma current sustained by non-inductive mechanisms, including
bootstrap, neutral-beam, and wave-driven contributions, rather than
inductive electric-field drive.
NAMES.long:
Non-inductive plasma current is the net plasma-current contribution
sustained without inductive electric-field drive. It combines all
non-inductive mechanisms, retaining the signs of their contributions rather
than summing their magnitudes.

The aggregate current is defined by

$$
I_{\mathrm{ni}} = \sum_{k\in\mathcal{N}} I_k
$$

where $I_{\mathrm{ni}}$ is the non-inductive current, $\mathcal{N}$ is the
set of non-inductive mechanisms, $k$ identifies a mechanism, and $I_k$ is
its signed current contribution. All terms use the same projection and
integration region. The sum includes bootstrap,
[neutral-beam-driven](name:current_due_to_neutral_beam_injection), and
wave-driven current contributions.

The unqualified global value is the toroidal current integrated over the
full plasma poloidal cross-section, not the integral of the field-parallel
current density. The right-handed cylindrical frame is $(R, \phi, Z)$, where
$R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.
Projection- and region-qualified members retain those restrictions: the
[parallel cumulative current inside a flux
surface](name:parallel_cumulative_inside_flux_surface_current_due_to_non_inductive_current_drive)
uses the field-aligned projection and the enclosed integration region rather
than the global toroidal definition.

The [inductively driven Ohmic
current](name:current_due_to_ohmic_current_drive) is excluded. This
exclusion concerns the attributed current contribution; it does not require
the total plasma loop voltage to vanish or the plasma to be in steady state.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the global toroidal current flows in the
direction of increasing $\phi$, counterclockwise when viewed from above.

NAMES.name: density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.short:
Particle number density of a specified plasma population evaluated on the
flux surface assigned to an internal transport barrier, with charge-state
aggregation determined by the population.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the local number density of a selected plasma population at
the flux-surface location assigned to an internal transport barrier. It
applies to electrons, individual ion species, and compound fuel populations
treated as effective species.

The number density is defined by

$$
n = \lim_{\Delta V\to 0}\frac{\Delta N}{\Delta V}
$$

where $n$ is the number density in m$^{-3}$, $N$ is the number of counted
particles, and $V$ is volume in m$^{3}$. For an ion species, the count is
summed over its ionic charge states and excludes neutral atoms; electrons
are counted directly. The ion density at the internal transport barrier and
[electron density at the internal transport
barrier](name:electron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) are specific
population instances, while the [deuterium-tritium density at the internal
transport
barrier](name:deuterium_tritium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier)
treats the fuel mixture as one effective population. The internal transport
barrier is the designated flux-surface location where reduced cross-field
turbulent transport permits steep density gradients.

NAMES.name: beryllium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short:
Particle number density of beryllium ions evaluated on the flux surface
assigned to an internal transport barrier, summed over all beryllium ion
charge states and excluding neutral beryllium.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of beryllium ions evaluated on the flux surface
assigned to an internal transport barrier is the local density of the
beryllium-ion population at that flux-surface location. Beryllium has atomic
number $Z = 4$; unless a charge state is specified separately, this quantity
is the elemental beryllium ion density, summed over all beryllium ion charge
states and excluding neutral beryllium atoms. The internal transport barrier
is the designated flux-surface location where locally reduced cross-field
turbulent transport can sustain steep density gradients.

The charge-state aggregation is defined by

$$
n_{\mathrm{Be,ITB}} = \sum_{q=1}^{4} n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+},\mathrm{ITB}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Be,ITB}}$ is the beryllium ion number density on the
internal-transport-barrier flux surface, $n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+},\mathrm{ITB}}$
is the number density of beryllium charge state $q$ on the same flux
surface, and $q$ runs over positive beryllium ion charge states. The lower
limit excludes neutral beryllium.

This is an unweighted particle density, not the charge-weighted impurity
charge density or the electron density contributed by beryllium. It is a
species-specific instance of [density at the internal transport
barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and differs from ion
density at the internal transport barrier, which may represent a broader ion
population.

NAMES.name: boron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: boron
NAMES.short:
Number density of boron ions at the radial location of the internal
transport barrier, where suppressed cross-field turbulent transport enables
steep impurity density gradients to develop.
NAMES.long:
Boron density at the internal transport barrier is the local number density
of boron ions ($Z = 5$) on the flux surface designated as the internal
transport barrier reference location. Unless a charge state is specified
separately, this quantity represents the elemental boron ion density summed
over all ionization states (B$^{1+}$ through B$^{5+}$), excluding neutral
boron atoms.

The local particle number density is the zeroth velocity moment of the
boron-ion distribution function $f_\mathrm{B}$:

$$
n_\mathrm{B}(\rho_\text{ITB}) = \int f_\mathrm{B}(\mathbf{v},\, \rho_\text{ITB})\, d^3v
$$

where $\mathbf{v}$ is the particle velocity and $\rho_\text{ITB}$ is the
normalized minor radius identifying the ITB flux surface. The ITB is a
confined-plasma region where locally reduced cross-field transport
coefficients permit steep radial gradients in density and temperature to be
sustained; the parent concept is described in
[density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier).
For the analogous boron density at the innermost confined flux surface, see
[boron_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:boron_density_at_magnetic_axis).

sources.parent_definition: Boron (B)

NAMES.name: carbon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short:
Number density of carbon ions at the radial location of the internal
transport barrier, where suppressed cross-field turbulent transport enables
steep impurity density gradients to develop.
NAMES.long:
Carbon density at the internal transport barrier is the local number density
of carbon ions ($Z = 6$) evaluated at the flux surface designated as the
internal transport barrier reference location. Unless a charge state is
specified separately, this quantity is summed over all carbon ionization
states from $\mathrm{C}^{1+}$ through $\mathrm{C}^{6+}$, providing the total
elemental impurity concentration at the barrier, consistent with the parent
[density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier).

The total carbon number density at the ITB is defined as:

$$
n_{\mathrm{C,ITB}} = \left. \sum_{k=1}^{6} n_{\mathrm{C}^{k+}} \right|_{r = r_\mathrm{ITB}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{C}^{k+}}$ is the number density of carbon ions in charge
state $k$ and $r_\mathrm{ITB}$ is the radial coordinate of the barrier
reference surface.

Carbon enters fusion plasmas through erosion of carbon-based plasma-facing
components such as graphite limiters and divertor tiles. At an ITB, where
cross-field turbulent transport is locally suppressed, neoclassical impurity
transport can drive steep radial carbon density gradients — local
accumulation or depletion depending on the sign of the radial electric field
and density-gradient scale lengths. This quantity is inferred from
charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or soft X-ray continuum emission
combined with atomic-physics modeling.

Carbon density evaluated at other plasma locations includes
[carbon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:carbon_density_at_magnetic_axis),
[carbon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:carbon_density_at_plasma_boundary),
and
[carbon_density_at_divertor_target](name:carbon_density_at_divertor_target);
the total ion number density at the same barrier position is given by
[total_ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:total_ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier).

NAMES.name: density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short:
Local particle concentration of a specified plasma population at the
magnetic axis, with ion charge states aggregated and compound fuel mixtures
treated as defined populations.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density at the magnetic axis is the local number of
particles of a specified plasma population per physical volume at the
innermost location of nested closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces. The
quantity is population-specific and does not denote an unrestricted sum over
all plasma species.

It is defined locally by:

$$
n_P(\mathbf{x}_{\rm axis}) = \lim_{\Delta V \to 0} \frac{N_P(\Delta V;\mathbf{x}_{\rm axis})}{\Delta V}
$$

where $n_P$ is the particle number density of population $P$,
$\mathbf{x}_{\rm axis}$ is the location of the magnetic axis, $N_P(\Delta
V;\mathbf{x}_{\rm axis})$ is the number of particles from population $P$
within a physical volume $\Delta V$ centered at that location, and $\Delta
V$ is the shrinking volume used to define the local limit.

The value is evaluated at the magnetic axis, rather than over a flux
surface, plasma region, or volume, so it is not an average. For an ion
species, the population count is summed over all positive ionic charge
states and excludes neutral atoms; for electrons, it counts electrons
directly. When the population is deuterium–tritium, the mixture is treated
as one effective fuel population and includes the ionic charge states of
both isotopes. These conventions distinguish particle number density from
mass density, charge density, and the density of a single resolved charge
state.

Species-specific instances include [argon density at the magnetic
axis](name:argon_density_at_magnetic_axis), [electron density at the
magnetic axis](name:electron_density_at_magnetic_axis), and
[deuterium–tritium density at the magnetic
axis](name:deuterium_tritium_density_at_magnetic_axis). The same
population-specific density concept at another geometric locus is
represented by [density at the plasma
boundary](name:density_at_plasma_boundary) and [density at the internal
transport barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier); those
quantities differ in their evaluation location.

NAMES.name: argon_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short:
Particle number density of argon ions evaluated at the magnetic axis is the
local argon-ion count per physical volume at that location, summed over all
argon ionic charge states.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of argon ions evaluated at the magnetic axis is the
local argon-ion count per physical volume at that location, summed over all
argon ionic charge states. It represents argon ions specifically, rather
than electrons, neutrals, or another plasma population.

The defining relation is

$$
n_{\mathrm{Ar},\mathrm{axis}} = \left.\frac{dN_{\mathrm{Ar}}}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Ar},\mathrm{axis}}$ is the argon-ion number density at the
magnetic axis, $N_{\mathrm{Ar}}$ is the number of argon ions summed over all
ionic charge states, and $V$ is physical volume.

The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested
closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the gradient of the poloidal
magnetic flux vanishes. It applies to the complete ionic argon population at
that location and is charge-state summed; neutral argon is excluded. It is
neither a flux-surface or volume integral nor a density for another species.

This is the argon-specific realization of [density at the magnetic
axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis), with the population fixed to argon
ions and the aggregation fixed to a sum over ionic charge states. The
corresponding species specialization for oxygen is [oxygen density at the
magnetic axis](name:oxygen_density_at_magnetic_axis), which uses the same
magnetic-axis locus but a different ion population.

sources.parent_definition: Argon (Ar)

NAMES.name: beryllium_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short:
Particle number density of the beryllium ion population evaluated at the
magnetic axis is the local beryllium-ion count per physical volume there,
summed over all beryllium ionization states.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of the beryllium ion population evaluated at the
magnetic axis is the local beryllium-ion count per physical volume at that
location, summed over all beryllium ionization states. It represents
beryllium ions specifically, rather than neutral beryllium, electrons, or
other ion species.

The defining relation is

$$
n_{\mathrm{Be},\mathrm{axis}} = \sum_Z n_{\mathrm{Be}^{Z+},\mathrm{axis}} = \left.\frac{dN_{\mathrm{Be}}}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Be},\mathrm{axis}}$ is the total beryllium-ion number
density at the magnetic axis, $n_{\mathrm{Be}^{Z+},\mathrm{axis}}$ is the
number density of beryllium ions in charge state $Z$, $Z$ is the ionic
charge-state number, $N_{\mathrm{Be}}$ is the number of beryllium ions
included in the sum, and $V$ is physical volume.

The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested
closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the poloidal-flux gradient
vanishes. It applies to the complete beryllium-ion population at that
location and is summed over all beryllium ionic charge states. It excludes
neutral beryllium and is neither a flux-surface or volume integral nor the
density of another species.

This is the beryllium-specific realization of the population-independent
[density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis). Like [boron
density at the magnetic axis](name:boron_density_at_magnetic_axis), it is
species-resolved while retaining charge-state aggregation; it differs from
[beryllium density at the plasma
boundary](name:beryllium_density_at_plasma_boundary) only in its evaluation
locus.

sources.parent_definition: Beryllium (Be)

NAMES.name: boron_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: boron
NAMES.short:
Particle number density of the boron ion population evaluated at the
magnetic axis is the local boron-ion count per physical volume, summed over
all boron ionic charge states.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of the boron ion population evaluated at the
magnetic axis is the local boron-ion count per physical volume at that
location. It represents boron ions specifically, rather than electrons,
neutrals, or another plasma population, and is summed over all boron ionic
charge states.

The defining relation is

$$
n_{\mathrm{B,axis}} = \left.\frac{dN_{\mathrm{B}}}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{B,axis}}$ is the boron ion number density at the magnetic
axis, $N_{\mathrm{B}}$ is the number of boron ions summed over all ionic
charge states, and $V$ is physical volume.

The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested
closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the poloidal-flux gradient
vanishes. It applies to the complete ionized boron population at that
location and excludes neutral boron; it is neither a flux-surface or volume
integral nor a density for another species.

This is the boron-specific realization of the population-independent
[density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis). It has the
same locus and aggregation convention as [beryllium density at the magnetic
axis](name:beryllium_density_at_magnetic_axis), but represents boron ions
rather than beryllium ions. It differs from [boron density at the internal
transport barrier](name:boron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier), which
is evaluated at a different plasma location.

NAMES.name: carbon_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short:
Particle number density of the carbon-ion population evaluated at the
magnetic axis is the local carbon-ion count per physical volume, summed over
all carbon ion charge states.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of the carbon-ion population evaluated at the
magnetic axis is the local carbon-ion count per physical volume at that
location, summed over all carbon ion charge states. It represents carbon
ions specifically, rather than electrons, other ion species, or neutral
carbon.

The defining relation is

$$
n_{\mathrm{C,axis}} = \left.\frac{dN_{\mathrm{C}}}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{C,axis}}$ is the carbon-ion number density at the magnetic
axis, the subscript $\mathrm{C}$ denotes the carbon-ion population,
$N_{\mathrm{C}}$ is the number of carbon ions, $V$ is physical volume, and
the subscript axis denotes evaluation at the magnetic axis.

The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested
closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the poloidal-flux gradient
vanishes. It applies to the complete carbon-ion population at that location
and is summed over all carbon ion charge states; it is neither a
flux-surface or volume integral nor a neutral-carbon density.

This is the carbon-specific realization of the population-independent
[density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis). It differs
from [oxygen density at the magnetic
axis](name:oxygen_density_at_magnetic_axis) only in the counted ion species,
and from [carbon density at the internal transport
barrier](name:carbon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) in the
evaluation locus.

NAMES.name: deuterium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short:
Number density of deuterium ions at the radial location of the internal
transport barrier, where suppressed turbulent cross-field transport enables
steep fuel-species density gradients to develop.
NAMES.long:
Deuterium density at the internal transport barrier is the local number
density of deuterium ions on the flux surface assigned as the barrier
reference location. Deuterium ($^2$H, mass number $A = 2$) is the heavier
hydrogen isotope used as primary fuel in magnetic-confinement fusion and is
fully ionized to D$^+$ in the hot plasma core, requiring no summation over
charge states.

An internal transport barrier is a radially localized region of reduced
cross-field turbulent transport within the confined plasma, enabling steep
radial gradients in particle density and temperature to be sustained. The
deuterium density at the barrier is the point value of the local number
density $n_D(\rho)$ evaluated at the normalized minor radius
$\rho_\mathrm{ITB}$ of the barrier:

$$
n_D^\mathrm{ITB} = n_D(\rho_\mathrm{ITB})
$$

where $\rho_\mathrm{ITB}$ is identified by the location of the maximum
logarithmic gradient in the density or temperature profile.

This quantity is inferred from main-ion charge-exchange recombination
spectroscopy, or derived from transport analysis constrained by Thomson
scattering and interferometry, with the steep gradients at the ITB making
precise radial localization critical. It is the deuterium-isotope
counterpart to
[hydrogen_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:hydrogen_density_at_internal_transport_barrier);
together they represent the two lightest hydrogenic fuel species. The full
family of species-specific barrier densities is described by
[density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier),
and
[electron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:electron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier)
provides the quasi-neutral electron counterpart.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Deuterium (D)

NAMES.name: deuterium_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short:
Particle number density of the deuterium ion population evaluated at the
magnetic axis is the local deuterium-ion count per physical volume there,
summed over all deuterium ionic charge states.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of the deuterium ion population evaluated at the
magnetic axis is the local deuterium-ion count per physical volume at that
location, summed over all deuterium ionic charge states. It represents
deuterium ions specifically, rather than neutral deuterium, electrons, or
another ion species.

The defining relation is

$$
n_{D,\mathrm{axis}} = \left.\frac{dN_D}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $n_{D,\mathrm{axis}}$ is the deuterium ion number density at the
magnetic axis, $N_D$ is the number of deuterium ions summed over all ionic
charge states, and $V$ is physical volume.

The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested
closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the poloidal-flux gradient
vanishes. It applies to the complete deuterium ion population at that
location and is charge-state-summed; it is neither a flux-surface or volume
integral nor a neutral, electron, or other-ion density.

This is the deuterium-specific realization of the population-independent
[density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis). It must be
distinguished from [hydrogen density at the magnetic
axis](name:hydrogen_density_at_magnetic_axis), which counts hydrogen ions
rather than deuterium ions.

sources.parent_definition: Deuterium (D)

NAMES.name: deuterium_tritium_density
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short:
Deuterium-tritium density is the local ion number density of the
deuterium-tritium fuel-ion pseudo-species, treating deuterium and tritium as
one effective species.
NAMES.long:
Deuterium-tritium density is the local ion number density of the
deuterium-tritium fuel-ion pseudo-species, treating deuterium and tritium
ions as one effective species. It is a species-level per-volume particle
count summed over all ion charge states.

The defining relation is the sum of the component fuel-ion number densities:

$$
n_{DT} = n_D + n_T
$$

where $n_{DT}$ is the deuterium-tritium density, $n_D$ is the [deuterium
density](name:deuterium_density), and $n_T$ is the [tritium
density](name:tritium_density). Each component density is
charge-state-summed over the corresponding ion charge states; the
dimensionless tritium fraction, where used, is $f_T = n_T/n_{DT}$.

This quantity includes only deuterium and tritium fuel ions represented by
the effective deuterium-tritium species. Neutral deuterium or tritium atoms,
neutral molecules such as D$_2$, T$_2$, and DT, reaction products, and
impurity ions are excluded. As a number density, its value domain is $n_{DT}
\ge 0$.

NAMES.name: deuterium_tritium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short:
Particle number density of the combined deuterium-tritium fuel-ion
pseudo-species evaluated on the flux surface assigned to an internal
transport barrier, where locally reduced cross-field turbulent transport can
sustain steep fuel-density gradients; deuterium and tritium ions are treated
as one effective population.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of the combined deuterium-tritium fuel-ion
pseudo-species at the internal transport barrier is the local number density
of deuterium and tritium fuel ions treated as one effective population on
the flux surface selected as the barrier reference location. The internal
transport barrier is a confined-plasma flux-surface location where locally
reduced cross-field turbulent transport permits steep fuel-density gradients
across neighboring flux surfaces.

The combined density is defined as the sum of the isotope ion densities at
the barrier flux surface:

$$
n_{\mathrm{DT,ITB}} = n_{\mathrm{D,ITB}} + n_{\mathrm{T,ITB}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{DT,ITB}}$ is the deuterium-tritium pseudo-species density
at the internal transport barrier, and $n_{\mathrm{D,ITB}}$ and
$n_{\mathrm{T,ITB}}$ are the deuterium and tritium ion densities at the same
barrier flux surface. This species-level number density is summed over all
charge states of deuterium and tritium ions and excludes neutral deuterium
and tritium atoms.

The deuterium-tritium pseudo-species denotes a fuel-state quantity, not a
fusion reaction rate or reaction-product population. If represented by mean
mass number $A = 2.5$, it corresponds to an equal deuterium-tritium
number-density mixture; for unequal isotope mixtures the density remains the
isotope sum, while the effective mass number is composition-weighted. It is
distinct from the isotope-resolved [deuterium density at the internal
transport barrier](name:deuterium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and
[tritium density at the internal transport
barrier](name:tritium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier), and from
spatially aggregated deuterium-tritium quantities such as [volume-averaged
deuterium-tritium density](name:volume_averaged_deuterium_tritium_density).

NAMES.name: deuterium_tritium_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short:
Particle number density of the deuterium-tritium fuel-ion pseudo-species
evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local effective fuel-ion count per
physical volume at that location.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of the deuterium-tritium fuel-ion pseudo-species
evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local effective fuel-ion count per
physical volume at that location. It represents the deuterium–tritium
mixture as one effective ion population rather than as separate deuterium
and tritium species.

The defining relation is

$$
n_{\mathrm{DT,axis}} = \left.\frac{dN_{\mathrm{DT}}}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{DT,axis}}$ is the deuterium-tritium pseudo-species number
density at the magnetic axis, $N_{\mathrm{DT}}$ is the number of effective
deuterium-tritium pseudo-ions, and $V$ is physical volume.

The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested
closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the poloidal-flux gradient
vanishes. The aggregation convention treats the deuterium-tritium mixture as
one effective ion population; this quantity is not separately resolved by
isotope and is neither a flux-surface, line, nor volume average or integral.

This is the deuterium-tritium specialization of the population-independent
[density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis). It differs
from [deuterium-tritium density](name:deuterium_tritium_density) by
explicitly fixing the evaluation locus at the magnetic axis rather than
leaving the locus unspecified.

NAMES.name: diamagnetic_energy
NAMES.short:
Diamagnetic energy is three-halves of the plasma-volume integral of total
pressure perpendicular to the local magnetic field, including thermal and
fast-particle contributions.
NAMES.long:
Diamagnetic energy is a global plasma stored-energy measure defined by the
total pressure perpendicular to the local magnetic field. It includes both
thermal and fast-particle contributions.

The defining relation is:

$$
W_{\mathrm{dia}} = \frac{3}{2}\int_{V_{\mathrm{p}}} p_\perp\,dV
$$

where $W_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the diamagnetic energy, $V_{\mathrm{p}}$ is the
plasma volume, $p_\perp$ is the total perpendicular pressure, and $dV$ is
the physical volume element. Perpendicular pressure is the mean of the two
pressure-tensor components perpendicular to the local magnetic field, summed
over electron and ion species, charge states, and thermal and fast-particle
populations.

This quantity is a volume-integrated pressure measure, not magnetic-field
energy or a thermal-only energy. The population described by [fast-particle
energy](name:fast_particle_energy) contributes through its perpendicular
pressure rather than necessarily through its full kinetic energy. For
nonrelativistic isotropic populations, diamagnetic energy equals their total
random kinetic energy; this equality does not hold generally for anisotropic
populations. Comparison with MHD stored energy requires consistent pressure
and population conventions.

The [time derivative of diamagnetic
energy](name:time_derivative_of_diamagnetic_energy) is the rate of change of
this stored-energy measure, rather than an additional energy contribution.

NAMES.name: diamagnetic_momentum_convection_velocity
NAMES.short:
Effective velocity coefficient for diamagnetic, advective, non-diffusive
transport of selected momentum populations, components, and transport
directions.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the effective coefficient describing the diamagnetic
contribution to advective, non-diffusive transport of momentum for a
selected population, momentum component, and transport direction. It is a
transport-closure quantity, not the population’s actual bulk flow velocity.

For the selected momentum component and transport direction, the diamagnetic
convective momentum flux is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{P,\mathrm{dia}} = V_{\mathrm{dia}} P
$$

where $\Gamma_{P,\mathrm{dia}}$ is the diamagnetic contribution to
convective momentum flux, $V_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is this convection velocity,
and $P$ is the corresponding momentum density.

This quantity isolates the diamagnetic contribution from the total momentum
convection velocity. A charge-state-resolved realization is the [ion
charge-state diamagnetic momentum convection
velocity](name:ion_charge_state_diamagnetic_momentum_convection_velocity),
while [diamagnetic momentum
diffusivity](name:diamagnetic_momentum_diffusivity) describes the distinct
diffusive contribution.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the associated diamagnetic momentum flux is
in the chosen positive transport direction for positive transported momentum
density.

NAMES.name: difference_of_total_plasma_heating_power_and_time_derivative_of_plasma_stored_energy
NAMES.short:
Instantaneous plasma power available for confinement losses after correcting
total coupled heating for the rate of change of stored plasma energy.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the instantaneous global power-balance residual available
to account for energy leaving the plasma confinement system. It corrects the
total plasma heating power for transient changes in the plasma’s stored
energy.

It is defined by

$$
P_{\mathrm{loss}} = P_{\mathrm{heat,total}} - \frac{dW_{\mathrm{plasma}}}{dt}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{loss}}$ is the power-balance residual represented by this
quantity, $P_{\mathrm{heat,total}}$ is the total plasma heating power,
$W_{\mathrm{plasma}}$ is the total stored energy of the plasma, and $t$ is
time.

The quantity is global and aggregated over all heating contributions
included in total plasma heating power and over the complete stored
plasma-energy reservoir. It is not the heating input itself, a single-source
heating contribution, or a regional radiation measurement; [radiated power
over the core region](name:radiated_power_over_core_region) is a specific
loss channel rather than this balance residual. A positive value means
heating exceeds the instantaneous increase in stored energy, while a
negative value means stored energy is increasing faster than the heating
input.

This residual is the loss-power term in the conventional energy-confinement
relation $\tau_E = W_{\mathrm{plasma}}/P_{\mathrm{loss}}$, where $\tau_E$ is
the energy confinement time; transient storage changes are therefore
excluded from the inferred loss power rather than counted as losses.

NAMES.name: effective_charge_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.short:
Effective charge at the internal transport barrier is the local effective
ion charge of the plasma mixture evaluated at the internal transport
barrier, expressed as the electron-density-normalized second charge moment
over all ion populations.
NAMES.long:
Effective charge at the internal transport barrier is the local effective
ion charge of the plasma mixture evaluated at the internal transport
barrier. It characterizes the charge-state composition of the ion population
at that locus through the second moment of ion charge number normalized by
electron density.

Using the local ion populations, it is defined by:

$$
Z_{\mathrm{eff,itb}} = \frac{\sum_s n_s Z_s^2}{n_e}
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{eff,itb}}$ is the effective charge at the internal
transport barrier, $s$ labels each ion population present at that locus,
$n_s$ is the number density of ion population $s$, $Z_s$ is its ion charge
number, and $n_e$ is the electron number density at the same locus.

This quantity is local to the internal transport barrier and represents the
plasma ion mixture there. The summation includes all ion species and charge
states present at the locus; it is not a value at the pedestal top, limiter,
or divertor target, and it is not an average over the confined plasma
volume.

Under quasineutrality, $n_e = \sum_s n_s Z_s$, so higher-charge ion
populations contribute in proportion to $Z_s^2$ in the numerator. This local
quantity is distinct from [volume-averaged effective
charge](name:volume_averaged_effective_charge), which characterizes
effective charge after aggregation over the plasma volume.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Effective charge

NAMES.name: effective_charge_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short:
Effective charge at the magnetic axis is the local charge-squared-weighted
ion charge sum divided by the electron density, evaluated at the magnetic
axis. It equals 1 for a plasma containing only singly charged
hydrogen-isotope ions and increases with impurity charge content.
NAMES.long:
Effective charge at the magnetic axis is the local charge-squared-weighted
ion charge sum divided by the electron density, evaluated at the magnetic
axis. It is the on-axis value of [effective charge](name:effective_charge).
It equals unity for a plasma containing only singly charged hydrogen-isotope
ions, and higher-charge impurity ions contribute disproportionately because
the charge number is squared.

For a local ion mixture, the on-axis effective charge is defined by:

$$
Z_{\mathrm{eff,axis}} = \frac{\sum_s n_s(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{axis}}) Z_s^2}{n_e(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{axis}})}
$$

where $s$ indexes ion species or ionization states present at the
magnetic-axis location, $n_s$ is the corresponding ion number density in
$\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $Z_s$ is the positive ion charge number, $n_e$ is the
electron number density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and
$\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{axis}}$ denotes the magnetic-axis location.

The sum includes charged ions and excludes neutral atoms, neutral molecules,
and electrons. For a locally quasineutral plasma, $n_e = \sum_s n_s Z_s$, so
the same quantity may be interpreted as the ion-density-weighted ratio
$\langle Z^2 \rangle / \langle Z \rangle$. This locus-specific value is
distinct from effective charge at the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: electric_field
NAMES.short:
Local vector electric field equal to the force per unit charge on a positive
stationary test charge, including electrostatic, inductive, and
electromagnetic-wave contributions.
NAMES.long:
The electric field $\mathbf{E}$ is the local force per unit positive charge
on a stationary test charge. It is the complete vector quantity from which
projections such as the [vertical electric
field](name:vertical_electric_field) and field-parallel electric field are
formed.

In terms of electromagnetic potentials, the field is defined by

$$
\mathbf{E} = -\nabla\Phi - \frac{\partial\mathbf{A}}{\partial t}
$$

where $\Phi$ is the electrostatic potential, $\mathbf{A}$ is the magnetic
vector potential, and $t$ is time. The first term is electrostatic and the
second is inductive; their sum also describes wave fields, including the
[wave electric field](name:wave_electric_field). The electrostatic
contribution is related to the [electrostatic
potential](name:electrostatic_potential). Cylindrical projections use the
right-handed $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is
increasing toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when a resolved cylindrical component points
toward increasing $R$, $\phi$, or $Z$, or when a field-parallel component
points along the local magnetic field.

NAMES.name: electron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Particle number density of electrons evaluated on the flux surface assigned
to an internal transport barrier, where reduced cross-field turbulent
transport can sustain steep electron-density gradients.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of electrons evaluated on the flux surface assigned
to an internal transport barrier is the local density of the electron
population at that flux-surface location. Electrons are counted directly as
mobile negative charge carriers; no ion charge-state aggregation is
involved.

The number density is defined by

$$
n_e = \lim_{\Delta V\to 0}\frac{\Delta N_e}{\Delta V}
$$

where $n_e$ is the electron number density in m$^{-3}$, $\Delta N_e$ is the
dimensionless number of electrons in the volume element, and $\Delta V$ is
the volume element in m$^{3}$.

This is the electron-specific member of [density at the internal transport
barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier). It is distinct from
ion density at the internal transport barrier, which counts ions rather than
electrons; in a quasineutral plasma the electron density is related to ion
charge densities at the same flux surface by charge balance. The internal
transport barrier is the designated flux-surface location where reduced
cross-field turbulent transport permits steep density gradients.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Electron density

NAMES.name: electron_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Particle number density of the electron population evaluated at the magnetic
axis is the local electron count per physical volume at that location.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of the electron population evaluated at the magnetic
axis is the local electron count per physical volume at that location. It
represents electrons specifically, rather than ions, neutrals, or another
plasma population.

The defining relation is

$$
n_{e,\mathrm{axis}} = \left.\frac{dN_e}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $n_{e,\mathrm{axis}}$ is the electron number density at the magnetic
axis, $N_e$ is the number of electrons, and $V$ is physical volume.

The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested
closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the poloidal-flux gradient
vanishes. It applies to the complete electron population at that location
and is neither a flux-surface or volume integral nor an ion or neutral
density.

This is the electron-specific realization of the population-independent
[density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis). It must be
distinguished from [total ion density at the magnetic
axis](name:total_ion_density_at_magnetic_axis), which counts ions, and from
[electron temperature at the magnetic
axis](name:electron_temperature_at_magnetic_axis), which characterizes
electron energy rather than particle count.

NAMES.name: electron_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Electron particle transport coefficient relating diffusive flux to the
opposing number-density gradient without specifying a spatial direction.
NAMES.long:
The electron diffusion coefficient characterizes electron particle diffusion
through a local Fickian relation between diffusive particle flux and the
electron number-density gradient. It does not select a spatial direction or
a particular transport mechanism.

For a scalar Fickian closure, the defining relation is:

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_e^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_e\nabla n_e
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_e^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive electron
particle flux density, $D_e$ is the electron diffusion coefficient, $n_e$ is
the electron number density, and $\nabla$ denotes the spatial gradient. The
minus sign expresses down-gradient transport for positive diffusivity.

This is an electron-specific [particle
diffusivity](name:particle_diffusivity), not an electron energy or momentum
transport coefficient. It excludes convective contributions to the electron
particle flux and is not a sum of directional diffusion coefficients.

The [poloidal electron diffusion
coefficient](name:poloidal_electron_diffusion_coefficient) is the
poloidal-poloidal diagonal specialization within an anisotropic
particle-diffusion tensor. The scalar closure above applies when a single
coefficient represents the flux-gradient response; the general quantity does
not require equal diffusion in all directions or encode off-diagonal tensor
couplings.

NAMES.name: electron_emissivity
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Local electromagnetic radiation power emitted by the electron population per
unit volume, without specifying a particular radiation mechanism.
NAMES.long:
Electron emissivity is the local electromagnetic radiation power emitted by
the electron population per unit volume. It represents an emission source
attributable to electrons, not the net energy change of the electron
population.

At position $\mathbf{x}$, the emissivity is defined by

$$
\varepsilon_e(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{dP_e^{\mathrm{rad}}}{dV}
$$

where $\varepsilon_e$ is electron emissivity, $P_e^{\mathrm{rad}}$ is the
radiation power emitted by electrons, $V$ is volume, and $\mathbf{x}$ is
position.

A particular radiation mechanism may be selected by the surrounding physical
context, but no mechanism is implied by this name. The quantity excludes
absorbed power and differs from [power density due to
radiation](name:power_density_due_to_radiation), which is not
electron-specific, and from electron power density, which denotes net energy
transfer in the electron energy balance.
