NAMES.name: electron_energy_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Effective transport velocity that multiplies electron thermal-energy density
to give the convective electron energy flux, appearing as the convective
velocity in the energy flux term; distinct from gradient-driven diffusion
and mean electron flow.
NAMES.long:
Electron energy convection velocity is the effective vector coefficient
relating the convective electron thermal-energy flux to the local electron
thermal-energy density. It is the electron-specific specialization of
[energy convection velocity](name:energy_convection_velocity) and appears as
the convective velocity in the energy-flux term.

The convective electron thermal-energy flux density is the product of the
local electron thermal-energy density and this velocity:

$$
\mathbf{Q}_{e,\mathrm{conv}} = \mathcal{W}_e\,\mathbf{v}_{e,W}
$$

where $\mathbf{Q}_{e,\mathrm{conv}}$ is the convective electron
thermal-energy flux density, $\mathcal{W}_e$ is the local electron
thermal-energy density, and $\mathbf{v}_{e,W}$ is the electron energy
convection velocity. The subscripts identify the electron population and the
energy-convection channel.

This quantity applies to electron thermal-energy transport in core and edge
plasma, without restricting it to a spatial direction or aggregating it with
ion or neutral energy transport. It specifies only the convective
contribution to [electron energy flux](name:electron_energy_flux), excluding
gradient-driven diffusion; it is not the total electron energy flux or the
bulk electron particle-flow velocity.

The [radial](name:radial_electron_energy_convection_velocity),
[poloidal](name:poloidal_electron_energy_convection_velocity), and
[parallel](name:parallel_electron_energy_convection_velocity) electron
energy convection velocities are directional projections of this vector. The
radial projection is the $\hat R$ component in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and
$Z$ is vertical height; the parallel projection is along the local magnetic
field. This energy-transport coefficient need not equal the [electron
particle velocity due to
convection](name:electron_particle_velocity_due_to_convection), which
describes particle rather than energy transport.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when a projected velocity points along its
positive direction; the radial component is positive toward increasing major
radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, and the
parallel component is positive along the local magnetic field.

NAMES.name: electron_energy_flux
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Electron energy flux is the signed rate of electron kinetic-energy transport
through an oriented surface per unit physical area.
NAMES.long:
Electron energy flux represents net kinetic-energy transport by electrons
across an oriented surface. It includes the total electron energy-transport
contribution rather than only its diffusive or convective part.

The defining relation is:

$$
\Gamma_{e,W} = \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{e,W}\cdot\hat{\mathbf n} = \frac{d\dot W_e}{dA}
$$

where $\Gamma_{e,W}$ is the signed electron energy flux through the surface,
$\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{e,W}$ is the electron kinetic-energy flux vector,
$\hat{\mathbf n}$ is the selected unit surface normal, $\dot W_e$ is the
signed rate of electron kinetic-energy transfer across the surface, and $A$
is its physical area.

The quantity applies to the electron population without selecting a
particular transport mechanism or plasma region. It excludes energy carried
by ions, neutrals, or electromagnetic fields and is distinct from electron
particle-number flux. No radial, poloidal, or magnetic-field-aligned
direction is implicit.

The convective contribution is the electron energy density multiplied by the
normal projection of the [energy convection
velocity](name:energy_convection_velocity); diffusive transport contributes
separately to the total. The [parallel electron energy
flux](name:parallel_electron_energy_flux) is the specialization obtained by
choosing the surface normal along the magnetic field.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the net electron kinetic-energy transport is
in the direction of the selected surface normal.

NAMES.name: electron_particle_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Effective advective velocity vector whose product with electron number
density gives the convective electron particle flux, excluding
density-gradient-driven diffusion.
NAMES.long:
Electron particle convection velocity is the effective vector coefficient of
the density-proportional advective electron particle flux. It describes
directed electron transport after density-gradient-driven diffusion has been
separated.

The convective electron particle flux is defined by

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_e^{\mathrm{conv}} = n_e\mathbf{v}_e^{\mathrm{conv}}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_e^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the electron particle flux
due to convection, $n_e$ is the electron number density, and
$\mathbf{v}_e^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is this electron particle convection
velocity.

The quantity applies to the electron particle channel without selecting a
directional projection. It is an effective coefficient for the electron
population, not a sum over particle species or an energy- or
momentum-transport coefficient. The [ion particle convection
velocity](name:ion_particle_convection_velocity) is the corresponding
coefficient for the ion particle channel, not a contribution to this
electron coefficient.

The quantity excludes density-gradient-driven diffusive transport and need
not equal the bulk electron flow velocity. The [parallel electron particle
convection velocity](name:parallel_electron_particle_convection_velocity)
and [poloidal electron particle convection
velocity](name:poloidal_electron_particle_convection_velocity) are
projections of this vector along the magnetic field and in the poloidal
direction, respectively, in edge-plasma particle transport.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the projected electron convective particle
flux points along the positive direction of the corresponding component; the
direction follows electron particle transport, not conventional electric
current.

sources.leaf_definition: One scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.

NAMES.name: electron_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Electron particle flux is the net number of electrons crossing an oriented
surface per unit actual surface area and time, with opposite crossing
directions counted with opposite signs.
NAMES.long:
Electron particle flux is the signed net number flow of free electrons
through an oriented surface per unit actual surface area and time. It is the
surface-normal projection of electron number transport, without selecting a
fixed geometric or magnetic-field direction.

The local flux is defined by the normal velocity moment of the electron
distribution:

$$
\Gamma_e = \int (\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}) f_e(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $\Gamma_e$ is the electron particle flux, $\mathbf{v}$ is electron
velocity relative to the surface, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the chosen surface
unit normal, $f_e$ is the local electron velocity distribution normalized so
that its velocity integral equals the electron number density, and $d^3v$ is
the velocity-space volume element.

This quantity enters the electron number balance and does not select a
particular electron subpopulation, transport mechanism, or plasma region.
Diffusive and convective contributions add to the net particle transport. It
is a local per-area flux, not an area-integrated particle rate or a one-way
incident or emitted flux.

The [radial](name:radial_electron_particle_flux),
[poloidal](name:poloidal_electron_particle_flux), and [parallel electron
particle fluxes](name:parallel_electron_particle_flux) specialize this
definition by choosing the corresponding direction for the surface normal.
Unlike [electron energy flux](name:electron_energy_flux), this quantity
counts electrons rather than weighting their crossings by kinetic energy.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the net electron flow follows the chosen
surface normal; the negative electric charge of electrons does not reverse
this particle-flux sign.

NAMES.name: electron_pressure
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Electron kinetic pressure is one-third of the trace of the velocity-space
stress, covering thermal, suprathermal, and combined populations.
NAMES.long:
Electron kinetic pressure is the isotropic scalar measure of momentum flux
generated by random electron motion about the population mean velocity. It
may describe a suprathermal component, a thermal component, or their
combined electron population.

The defining pressure is

$$
p_e = \frac{m_e}{3}\int \lvert \mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_e\rvert^2 f_e(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $p_e$ is the electron kinetic pressure, $m_e$ is the electron mass,
$\mathbf{v}$ is an individual electron velocity, $\mathbf{u}_e$ is the mean
velocity of the represented electron population, $f_e(\mathbf{v})$ is its
velocity distribution, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element.

At parent scope, the quantity applies to a selected thermal or suprathermal
electron population or to their full aggregate. Aggregation is over the
represented electrons in velocity space, not over ion or neutral species;
the full aggregate combines disjoint thermal and suprathermal contributions.

This quantity is the trace-based scalar reduction of the electron kinetic
stress and does not specify a directional pressure-tensor component. An
anisotropic electron stress is therefore represented here only through its
trace, while ion pressure, neutral pressure, and individual tensor
components are excluded.

The [fast-electron pressure contribution](name:fast_electron_pressure) is
the suprathermal component within this common kinetic-pressure concept. The
[total electron pressure](name:total_electron_pressure) is the aggregate
over the designated thermal and suprathermal electron populations and equals
their sum when those components are disjoint.

NAMES.name: electron_temperature_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Kinetic temperature of the electron population evaluated on the flux surface
assigned to an internal transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
Kinetic temperature at an internal transport barrier is the
energy-equivalent measure of random motion for the electron population on
the barrier’s assigned flux surface. It is the electron-specific member of
the temperature family.

For an isotropic electron population, the defining relation is:

$$
T_e = \frac{2}{3}\langle E_e\rangle
$$

where $T_e$ is the electron kinetic temperature and $\langle E_e\rangle$ is
the mean random kinetic energy per electron. The quantity applies only to
electrons and is distinct from the ion-population average temperature at an
internal transport barrier. It is a local value on the assigned core flux
surface, not an integral across the barrier; the population-unspecified
parent is temperature at an internal transport barrier.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Electron temperature

NAMES.name: electron_velocity
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Local bulk-flow velocity of the electron fluid, defined by the
density-weighted first moment of its velocity distribution and distinct from
random thermal motion.
NAMES.long:
Electron fluid velocity is the local bulk translational velocity of the
electron population, describing collective advective motion rather than the
random thermal motion of individual electrons.

At position $\mathbf{x}$, the velocity is defined by the first moment of the
electron distribution:

$$
\mathbf{u}_e(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{n_e(\mathbf{x})}\int \mathbf{v}\,f_e(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v,\qquad n_e(\mathbf{x})=\int f_e(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $\mathbf{u}_e$ is the electron fluid velocity in m s$^{-1}$,
$\mathbf{x}$ is position in m, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity in m
s$^{-1}$, $f_e$ is the electron velocity distribution, and $n_e$ is electron
number density in m$^{-3}$.

This is the complete vector before directional projection. Its projections
include [radial electron velocity](name:radial_electron_velocity), [toroidal
electron velocity](name:toroidal_electron_velocity), [vertical electron
velocity](name:vertical_electron_velocity), [poloidal electron
velocity](name:poloidal_electron_velocity), and [parallel electron
velocity](name:parallel_electron_velocity). It is distinct from the bulk
velocities of ions and neutrals, such as [ion velocity](name:ion_velocity)
and [neutral velocity](name:neutral_velocity).

NAMES.name: electron_volumetric_source_rate
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Electron volumetric source rate is the signed local rate of free-electron
production or removal per physical volume, entering the source term in the
electron density continuity equation.
NAMES.long:
Electron volumetric source rate is the signed local rate of free-electron
production or removal per physical volume. It contributes to the source term
in the electron particle-number continuity equation.

The local particle balance is

$$
\frac{\partial n_e}{\partial t}+\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_e=S_{e,\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_k S_{e,k}
$$

where $n_e$ is free-electron number density, $t$ is time,
$\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_e$ is electron particle flux density, $\nabla\cdot$
denotes spatial divergence, $S_{e,\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total volumetric
electron source rate, $S_{e,k}$ is the $k$th additive electron source
contribution, and $k$ indexes those contributions. The documented quantity
may be an individual contribution or the total source; the total is the
algebraic sum of its contributions.

This quantity applies locally to the free-electron population, without a
thermal-population or orbit-class restriction, and is neither
volume-integrated nor inherently flux-surface-averaged. An individual
decomposed contribution need not include every production or loss process; a
contribution may be independent of electron density, but density
independence is not intrinsic to the quantity. Spatial transport represented
by the flux-divergence term is distinct from the source, so the source rate
alone is not generally the time derivative of electron density. It describes
particle-number change, not energy transfer as described by [electron power
density](name:electron_power_density).

Integrating the total source over the plasma volume gives the [total
electron source rate](name:total_electron_source_rate); integrating it over
the volume enclosed by a magnetic flux surface gives the [cumulative inside
flux-surface electron particle source
rate](name:cumulative_inside_flux_surface_electron_particle_source_rate).
Integrating an individual contribution gives its contribution to those
volume-integrated rates. The corresponding ion quantity is the [ion-state
source rate](name:ion_state_source_rate), which applies to an ion charge
state rather than free electrons.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the source adds free electrons to the
electron population.

NAMES.name: energy_confinement_time
NAMES.short:
Characteristic timescale for loss of confined plasma thermal energy, defined
as stored thermal energy divided by the net power leaving that energy
reservoir.
NAMES.long:
Energy confinement time is the characteristic timescale on which the
confined plasma loses its stored thermal energy through net outward energy
transport and other thermal-energy loss channels. The stored energy is the
volume-integrated quantity defined by [thermal plasma
energy](name:thermal_plasma_energy), not a particle confinement time or the
duration of plasma confinement.

$$
\tau_E = \frac{W_{\mathrm{th}}}{P_{\mathrm{loss}}}
$$

where $\tau_E$ is the energy confinement time, $W_{\mathrm{th}}$ is the
stored thermal energy in J, and $P_{\mathrm{loss}}$ is the net power loss
from that thermal-energy reservoir in W. In a stationary power balance,
$P_{\mathrm{loss}}$ equals the net heating power deposited in the plasma. It
is distinct from plasma confinement time, which denotes the elapsed duration
of confinement rather than an energy-loss timescale.

NAMES.name: fast_electron_pressure
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Kinetic pressure associated with the fast electron population, retaining
directional momentum transport rather than imposing an isotropic thermal
approximation.
NAMES.long:
Fast electron pressure is the kinetic pressure-tensor contribution of the
suprathermal electron population, representing random electron momentum
transport carried by fast electrons.

For the fast-electron distribution function, its defining relation is

$$
\mathbf{P}_{e,f}=m_e\int (\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_{e,f})(\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_{e,f})f_{e,f}(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $\mathbf{P}_{e,f}$ is the fast-electron pressure tensor, $m_e$ is
electron mass, $\mathbf{v}$ is electron velocity, $\mathbf{u}_{e,f}$ is the
mean velocity of the fast-electron population, $f_{e,f}(\mathbf{v})$ is its
velocity distribution function, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume
element.

The scope is the aggregate suprathermal electron population, including its
directional pressure response and excluding the bulk thermal-electron
contribution. It is not restricted to a single magnetic-field direction or
to an isotropic stress representation.

The directional projections of this quantity are represented by [parallel
fast electron pressure](name:parallel_fast_electron_pressure) and
[perpendicular fast electron
pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_electron_pressure). Within the broader
[electron pressure](name:electron_pressure) concept, it supplies the
fast-population contribution; [total electron
pressure](name:total_electron_pressure) combines fast and thermal electron
contributions in the complete electron population.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the relevant pressure-tensor projection is
compressive rather than tensile.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_charge_state_power_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short:
Volume-integrated Coulomb-collisional power transferred to the fast
(non-Maxwellian) ion population of a specified species and charge state.
NAMES.long:
Volume-integrated Coulomb-collisional power transferred to the fast
(non-Maxwellian) ion population of a specified species and charge state,
obtained by integrating the local Coulomb-collisional energy-exchange rate
density over the plasma volume:

$$
P_{\rm coll,fast}^{s,z} = \int Q_{\rm coll,fast}^{s,z}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $Q_{\rm coll,fast}^{s,z}$ is the local Coulomb-collisional power
density for fast ions of species $s$ in charge state $z$, and $V$ is the
plasma volume. Fast ions are those whose velocity distribution departs
significantly from a Maxwellian, such as neutral-beam-injected or
fusion-born ions undergoing thermalization.

This quantity is the fast-population component of
[total_ion_charge_state_power_due_to_collisions](name:total_ion_charge_state_power_due_to_collisions);
summing it with
[thermal_ion_charge_state_power_due_to_collisions](name:thermal_ion_charge_state_power_due_to_collisions)
recovers the total collisional power for that charge state. Aggregating over
all charge states yields
[fast_ion_power_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_power_due_to_collisions).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when net energy is transferred into the fast ion
charge state by Coulomb collisions.

sources.leaf_definition: Collisional power to the fast particle population
sources.parent_definition: Collisional exchange with the various states of the ion species (ionization, energy, excitation, ...)

NAMES.name: fast_ion_charge_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short:
Collisional torque density is the local angular-momentum transfer rate per
plasma volume delivered to a specified fast ion charge state through Coulomb
collisions.
NAMES.long:
Collisional torque density is the local angular-momentum source associated
with Coulomb momentum transfer to a specified fast ion charge state. Orbit
classes and directional components select particular contributions without
changing this common physical meaning.

For a selected angular-momentum direction, the torque density is defined by

$$
\tau_{\mathrm{coll},a} = (\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{coll}}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_a
$$

where $\tau_{\mathrm{coll},a}$ is the torque density about direction $a$,
$\mathbf{r}$ is the position vector relative to the rotation axis,
$\mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the collisional force density transferred to
the specified fast ion charge state, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_a$ is the
corresponding unit vector. For toroidal angular momentum in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, this relation reduces to $R f_\phi$.

This quantity is the fast-ion, charge-state-resolved realization of ion
charge-state torque density due to collisions; [co-passing fast ion
charge-state torque density due to
collisions](name:co_passing_fast_ion_charge_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions)
and [toroidal fast ion charge-state torque density due to
collisions](name:toroidal_fast_ion_charge_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions)
are orbit-resolved or component-resolved instances.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the selected angular-momentum transfer is in
the positive orientation of its stated axis; for toroidal angular momentum,
positive is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: co_passing_fast_ion_charge_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short:
Torque density vector giving the angular-momentum source per unit volume
deposited by Coulomb collisions on co-passing fast ions in a specified
charge state.
NAMES.long:
The collisional torque density vector for co-passing fast ions in charge
state $q$ quantifies the angular-momentum source per unit volume arising
from Coulomb collisions of those ions with background plasma particles.
Co-passing fast ions are suprathermal ions whose guiding-center orbits
circulate continuously around the torus in the same direction as the plasma
current.

The quantity is the first angular-momentum moment of the Coulomb collision
operator restricted to the co-passing phase-space domain
$\Omega_\mathrm{co}$:

$$
\boldsymbol{\tau}_{q,\mathrm{co}} = m_i \int_{\Omega_\mathrm{co}} (\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v})\, C[f_q]\, d^3v
$$

where $m_i$ is the fast-ion mass, $\mathbf{r}$ is the position vector,
$\mathbf{v}$ is the particle velocity, $C[f_q]$ is the Coulomb collision
operator acting on the fast-ion distribution function $f_q$ for ions in
charge state $q$, and $\Omega_\mathrm{co}$ is the co-passing region of phase
space.

This quantity is the co-passing orbit-class contribution to the
charge-state-resolved fast-ion collisional torque density
[fast_ion_charge_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_charge_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions),
excluding trapped and counter-passing populations. Its toroidal projection
is
[toroidal_co_passing_fast_ion_charge_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_co_passing_fast_ion_charge_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions).
The orbit-integrated counterpart without charge-state resolution is
co_passing_fast_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the toroidal angular-momentum source acts in
the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_fast_ion_charge_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short:
Collisional torque-density vector transferred to counter-passing fast ions
in a specified charge state by Coulomb collisions with background plasma
particles.
NAMES.long:
The collisional torque-density vector for counter-passing fast ions in
charge state $q$ quantifies the angular-momentum source per unit volume
arising from Coulomb collisions with background plasma particles.

$$
\boldsymbol{\tau}_{q,\mathrm{coll}}^{\mathrm{cp}} = \left.\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\ell}_{q}^{\mathrm{cp}}}{\partial t}\right|_{\mathrm{coll}}
$$

Here $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{q,\mathrm{coll}}^{\mathrm{cp}}$ is the
torque-density vector, $\boldsymbol{\ell}_{q}^{\mathrm{cp}}$ is the
angular-momentum density of the counter-passing fast-ion population in
charge state $q$, and the subscript indicates the collisional contribution.

The quantity includes only transfer to the specified counter-passing
fast-ion charge-state population; it excludes co-passing and thermal-ion
populations and noncollisional transfer. It is the counter-passing component
of the broader
[fast_ion_charge_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_charge_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions),
while
[co_passing_fast_ion_charge_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:co_passing_fast_ion_charge_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions)
represents the corresponding co-passing branch.

The vector components are expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,
\phi, Z)$ frame.
NAMES.sign:
Positive components point along the corresponding positive
$R$, $\phi$, or $Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$
basis.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_critical_energy
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short:
Threshold energy at which Coulomb drag on a fast ion from thermal electrons
equals that from thermal ions, determining the partition of fast-ion power
between electron and ion heating channels.
NAMES.long:
The fast-ion critical energy $E_c$ separates two collisional energy-loss
regimes for suprathermal ions decelerating in a thermal plasma. Above $E_c$,
fast ions lose energy predominantly to thermal electrons via Coulomb drag;
below $E_c$, energy is deposited preferentially in the bulk thermal ion
population, directly controlling the electron-to-ion power balance in
transport modeling.

The critical energy follows from equating the electron and ion frictional
forces on the decelerating fast ion:

$$
E_c = T_e \left(\frac{3\sqrt{\pi}}{4}\right)^{2/3} \left(\frac{m_f}{m_e}\right)^{1/3} \left(\sum_i \frac{n_i Z_i^2}{n_e} \frac{m_f}{m_i}\right)^{2/3}
$$

where $T_e$ is the electron temperature, $m_f$ and $m_e$ are the fast-ion
and electron masses, $n_i$, $Z_i$, and $m_i$ are the density, charge number,
and mass of background ion species $i$, and $n_e$ is the electron density.

The critical energy varies radially through its dependence on local $T_e$
and plasma composition and is computed from kinetic plasma data rather than
measured directly. For NBI-injected deuterons at $T_e \approx 3$–$8$ keV,
$E_c$ falls in the range 30–150 keV; for fusion alpha particles, it reaches
several hundred keV at reactor-relevant temperatures.

This quantity is the ion-specific form of fast_particle_critical_energy,
which spans both electron and ion fast-particle populations. The equivalent
name with the thermalization mechanism made explicit is
critical_fast_particle_energy_due_to_thermalization. The thermal-plasma
heating power that accumulates as fast ions slow through $E_c$ is quantified
by
[thermal_particle_heating_power_due_to_thermalization_of_fast_particles](name:thermal_particle_power_due_to_thermalization).

NAMES.name: fast_ion_power_due_to_charge_exchange
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short:
Volume-integrated kinetic-energy loss rate from the confined fast-ion
population due to charge exchange.
NAMES.long:
Volume-integrated kinetic-energy loss rate from the confined fast-ion
population due to charge exchange is the rate at which electron-transfer
reactions with neutral particles remove kinetic energy from confined fast
ions. The removed energy is not Coulomb energy transfer to plasma particles;
it is a loss from the confined fast-ion energy content.

The volume integral is taken over the corresponding local loss-rate density:

$$
P_{\mathrm{CX},f} = \int_V p_{\mathrm{CX},f}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{CX},f}$ is the fast-ion power due to charge exchange,
$p_{\mathrm{CX},f}(\mathbf{x})$ is the fast-ion power density due to charge
exchange, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, and $V$ is the region over which the
confined fast-ion population is defined. Locally, $p_{\mathrm{CX},f}$ is the
charge-exchange event-rate density weighted by the kinetic energy removed
from the confined fast-ion population per event, summed over all included
fast-ion species and charge states.

This quantity excludes Coulomb collisional energy transfer, ionization
losses not involving charge exchange, prompt orbit loss, power that was
never absorbed into the fast-ion population, and charge-exchange loss
assigned solely to thermal ions. It is the fast-ion component of ion power
due to charge exchange and contributes to the broader power due to charge
exchange; in a fast-ion energy balance written with positive gains, this
loss magnitude enters as a sink.

sources.leaf_definition: Power loss due to Charge Exchange loss of fast ions
sources.parent_definition: Global quantities (integrated over plasma volume for moments of the distribution, collisional exchange and source terms), for various time slices

NAMES.name: fast_neutral_internal_state_number_density
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short:
Fast neutral internal-state number density is the local abundance per
physical volume of nonthermal neutral particles of one species in one
specified internal state.
NAMES.long:
Fast neutral internal-state number density is the local abundance per
physical volume of suprathermal neutral particles of one selected species in
one specified internal state. It counts particles rather than weighting them
by charge, mass, or energy.

The density is the zeroth velocity-space moment of the fast population:

$$
n_{s,a}^{0,\mathrm{fast}} = \int f_{s,a}^{0,\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $n_{s,a}^{0,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the fast neutral number density, $s$
labels the neutral species, and $a$ labels its internal state. The
superscript $0$ denotes electrical neutrality, and $\mathrm{fast}$
identifies the nonthermal population. The function
$f_{s,a}^{0,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the local velocity distribution of that
population, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and $d^3v$ is the
velocity-space volume element; the integral covers all velocity space.

No summation over species or internal states is implied. Thermal neutrals,
neutral particles in other internal states, and charged particles are
excluded. No spatial averaging or restriction to the scrape-off layer is
implied.

For the same species and internal state, [neutral internal-state
density](name:neutral_internal_state_density) is the sum of this fast
contribution and [thermal neutral internal-state
density](name:thermal_neutral_internal_state_density). Summing this
contribution over all internal states gives the [fast neutral
density](name:fast_neutral_density) of the selected species. Combining the
fast and thermal populations across those states gives its [total neutral
number density](name:total_neutral_number_density).

NAMES.name: fast_neutral_pressure
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short:
Gyrotropic kinetic pressure of the suprathermal (fast) neutral particle
population, decomposing into components parallel and perpendicular to the
local magnetic field direction, summed over all internal quantum states of
the neutral species.
NAMES.long:
The fast neutral pressure characterizes the second-order velocity moment of
the suprathermal neutral distribution function projected onto the two
principal axes defined by the local magnetic field. Unlike magnetized ions,
fast neutrals are insensitive to the magnetic force directly, yet they
retain an anisotropic pressure signature inherited from their birth
mechanism — charge exchange between fast ions and cold neutrals, or direct
neutral beam injection — producing unequal stress along and across the
magnetic field direction.

The gyrotropic pressure tensor for the fast neutral population is:

$$
\mathbf{P}_{\rm fn} = P_{\perp,\rm fn}\,\mathbf{I} + (P_{\parallel,\rm fn} - P_{\perp,\rm fn})\,\hat{b}\hat{b}
$$

where $P_{\parallel,\rm fn}$ is the [parallel fast neutral
pressure](name:parallel_fast_neutral_pressure) along the magnetic field unit
vector $\hat{b}$, $P_{\perp,\rm fn}$ is the [perpendicular fast neutral
pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_neutral_pressure) across $\hat{b}$, and
$\mathbf{I}$ is the unit tensor. The equivalent isotropic scalar pressure is
$p_{\rm fn} = (P_{\parallel,\rm fn} + 2P_{\perp,\rm fn})/3$. State-resolved
analogs are captured in
[parallel_fast_neutral_state_pressure](name:parallel_fast_neutral_internal_state_pressure)
and
[perpendicular_fast_neutral_state_pressure](name:perpendicular_suprathermal_neutral_internal_state_pressure).
This quantity is distinct from the thermal neutral_pressure measured by
vacuum gages, which represents the isotropic equilibrium cold-gas limit.

In high-power neutral beam injection scenarios the fast neutral pressure can
reach a few percent of the total plasma pressure in the core; it is inferred
from neutral particle analyzer energy spectra combined with
distribution-function modeling or Monte Carlo fast-particle transport codes.

NAMES.name: fast_particle_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.short:
Local net rate at which Coulomb collisions change the kinetic-energy density
of a fast-particle population, including all guiding-center orbit classes.
NAMES.long:
Fast-particle collisional power density is the local rate at which Coulomb
collisions change the kinetic-energy density of a designated nonthermal
particle population. It is a signed collisional source or sink, not the
stored kinetic-energy density or the power transferred to the bulk thermal
population.

The defining relation is the kinetic-energy moment of the Coulomb collision
operator:

$$
P_{\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{a\in\mathrm{fast}} \sum_b \int \mathcal{E}_a(\mathbf{v})\, C_{ab}[f_a,f_b](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the fast-particle collisional
power density at position $\mathbf{x}$, $a$ labels species included in the
designated fast population, $b$ labels the charged collision partners
included in the exchange, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and
$\mathcal{E}_a$ is the kinetic energy of a particle of species $a$. The
functions $f_a$ and $f_b$ are the corresponding phase-space number
distributions, and $C_{ab}$ gives the collisional time derivative of $f_a$
caused by interactions with $b$. The integral covers the full velocity
space, with $d^3v$ denoting its volume element.

The quantity includes all guiding-center orbit classes and does not select a
particular fast-particle species or collision partner. An electron-partner
contribution describes energy exchange from electrons to the fast
population; it does not imply that the receiving fast particles are
electrons. This is a local quantity, not a flux-surface average or a
volume-integrated power.

The [co-passing
contribution](name:co_passing_fast_particle_power_density_due_to_collisions)
and [counter-passing
contribution](name:counter_passing_fast_particle_power_density_due_to_collisions),
together with the trapped-orbit contribution, sum to this orbit-unrestricted
quantity when those classes partition the fast-particle phase space.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when Coulomb collisions increase the
kinetic-energy density of the designated fast-particle population.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_fast_particle_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.short:
Local Coulomb-collisional power density changing the kinetic-energy density
of fast particles on counter-passing guiding-center orbits.
NAMES.long:
Counter-passing fast-particle collisional power density is the local rate at
which Coulomb collisions change the kinetic-energy density of fast particles
on counter-passing guiding-center orbits. Counter-passing orbits are passing
trajectories whose parallel transit is opposite to the reference co-passing
direction; this quantity is the collisional source or sink for that orbit
class, not its stored kinetic-energy density.

For fast species $a$, the counter-passing contribution is the kinetic-energy
moment of the Coulomb collision operator restricted to counter-passing phase
space:

$$
P_{\mathrm{counter}}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{a\in\mathrm{fast}} \sum_b \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{counter}}} \frac{1}{2} m_a v^2 C_{ab}[f_a,f_b](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{counter}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the counter-passing
fast-particle collisional power density at position $\mathbf{x}$, $m_a$ is
the mass of fast species $a$, $v=|\mathbf{v}|$ is speed, $C_{ab}$ is the
Coulomb collision operator giving the collisional time derivative of the
fast-species distribution $f_a$ due to charged partner species $b$, and
$\Omega_{\mathrm{counter}}$ is the counter-passing region of velocity or
guiding-center phase space.

Together with [co-passing fast-particle collisional power
density](name:co_passing_fast_particle_power_density_due_to_collisions) and
trapped fast-particle collisional power density, it forms the orbit-class
decomposition of [fast-particle collisional power
density](name:fast_particle_power_density_due_to_collisions):
$P_{\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{coll}} = P_{\mathrm{co}}^{\mathrm{coll}} +
P_{\mathrm{counter}}^{\mathrm{coll}} +
P_{\mathrm{trapped}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$. The partner sum includes only the
charged collision partners represented in the collisional model; a
partner-resolved quantity would use the corresponding single partner
contribution.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when Coulomb collisions increase the
kinetic-energy density of the counter-passing fast-particle population.

NAMES.name: fast_particle_power_due_to_collisions
NAMES.short:
Fast-particle power due to collisions is the volume-integrated Coulomb
collisional power transferred from the fast, non-Maxwellian particle
population to the bulk electron population.
NAMES.long:
Fast-particle power due to collisions is the net rate at which Coulomb
collisions transfer kinetic energy from the fast, non-Maxwellian particle
population to the bulk electron population. It is the plasma-volume integral
of the local collisional energy-transfer density for this donor-recipient
population pair.

The volume-integrated transfer is defined by

$$
P_{\mathrm{fast}\to e}^{\mathrm{coll}} = \int_{V_{\mathrm{plasma}}} p_{\mathrm{fast}\to e}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{fast}\to e}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the fast-particle power
due to collisions, $p_{\mathrm{fast}\to e}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x})$ is
the local Coulomb collisional energy-transfer density from the fast-particle
population to the bulk electron population, $\mathbf{x}$ is position,
$V_{\mathrm{plasma}}$ is the plasma volume, and $dV$ is the differential
volume element.

The quantity applies to all fast particles belonging to the non-Maxwellian
population in the plasma, including all orbit classes and any unresolved
subdivisions such as source, energy, pitch, species, or charge-state groups.
Its aggregation convention is a sum over all included fast-particle
subpopulations and over the plasma volume.

It excludes collisional power transferred from fast particles to bulk ion
populations, collisional exchange internal to the bulk thermal populations,
non-collisional heating, field or wave power, launched or generator power,
and power retained in or lost with fast particles rather than deposited in
bulk electrons.

This quantity is the fast-particle donor component of [thermal electron
power due to collisions](name:thermal_electron_power_due_to_collisions) when
that electron power is decomposed by source population. Summing analogous
recipient-species components gives the total Coulomb collisional energy loss
of the fast-particle population.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when net Coulomb collisional energy transfer is
from the fast-particle population to the bulk electron population.

NAMES.name: flux_limiter_coefficient
NAMES.short:
Flux limiter coefficient is a multiplicative factor, or vector of factors,
that scales a collisionless free-streaming bound on a flux density while
preserving the direction or sign of each resolved flux component.
NAMES.long:
Flux limiter coefficient is a multiplicative factor, or vector of factors,
that scales a collisionless free-streaming upper bound on a flux density in
a transport closure. It limits the magnitude permitted by that bound while
preserving the direction or sign assigned to each resolved flux component by
the underlying closure.

For a resolved flux-density component indexed by $i$, a direction-preserving
limited flux can be expressed as:

$$
F_i = \operatorname{sgn}\!\left(F_i^{\mathrm{cl}}\right)\min\!\left(\left|F_i^{\mathrm{cl}}\right|, L_i F_i^{\mathrm{fs}}\right)
$$

where $F_i$ is the limited flux-density component, $F_i^{\mathrm{cl}}$ is
the unconstrained closure value, $F_i^{\mathrm{fs}}$ is the corresponding
collisionless free-streaming bound, and $L_i$ is the flux limiter
coefficient for that component. The limiting range is typically $0 \le L_i
\le 1$, with smaller values imposing a stricter cap.

This parent quantity does not specify the transported quantity, resolved
component, or spatial region. It covers both generic region-scoped flux
limiting, such as the edge-region flux limiter coefficient, and
quantity-specific limiting, such as the [momentum-flux limiter
coefficient](name:momentum_flux_limiter_coefficient); child names identify
any additional component or region semantics.

NAMES.name: energy_flux_limiter_coefficient
NAMES.short:
Energy flux limiter coefficient is a multiplicative factor that scales the
collisionless free-streaming upper bound on population-resolved energy flux
density while preserving its direction.
NAMES.long:
Energy flux limiter coefficient is a multiplicative factor that scales a
collisionless free-streaming upper bound on population-resolved energy flux
density in a transport closure. It limits the permitted magnitude while
preserving the direction or sign assigned by the underlying closure.

For a resolved energy-flux channel, the limited flux is defined by:

$$
F_E = \operatorname{sgn}\!\left(F_E^{\mathrm{cl}}\right)\min\!\left(\left|F_E^{\mathrm{cl}}\right|, L_E F_E^{\mathrm{fs}}\right)
$$

where $F_E$ is the limited energy flux density, the subscript $E$ identifies
the energy channel, $F_E^{\mathrm{cl}}$ is the unconstrained closure value,
$F_E^{\mathrm{fs}}$ is the corresponding positive collisionless
free-streaming bound, $L_E$ is the energy flux limiter coefficient, and
$\operatorname{sgn}$ is the sign function. The limiter convention uses $0
\leq L_E \leq 1$, with smaller values imposing a stricter cap.

This parent covers energy-flux limiting for either an ion population or a
neutral population resolved by internal state. For ions, the energy flux is
aggregated by summing contributions over all ion charge states; for
neutrals, the coefficient applies to the specified internal state rather
than to an unspecified sum over states. No particular spatial region or
directional component is imposed by this parent.

The coefficient is not the energy flux density, its collisionless bound, or
the unconstrained closure value; it specifies only the multiplicative
limiting factor. It does not describe momentum-flux limiting, which is
represented by the distinct [momentum flux limiter
coefficient](name:momentum_flux_limiter_coefficient).

This quantity is the energy-flux specialization of the general [flux limiter
coefficient](name:flux_limiter_coefficient). Its concrete instances include
the charge-state-summed [ion energy flux limiter
coefficient](name:ion_energy_flux_limiter_coefficient) and the
internal-state-resolved [neutral-state energy flux limiter
coefficient](name:neutral_state_energy_flux_limiter_coefficient).

NAMES.name: greenwald_density
NAMES.short:
Greenwald density is the empirical electron number-density limit associated
with a confined plasma, set by the magnitude of plasma current and the
effective minor radius. It is the density reference used by Greenwald
fractions, not the fraction itself.
NAMES.long:
Greenwald density is the empirical electron number-density limit associated
with a confined toroidal plasma. It is a global density reference for
proximity-to-limit quantities, not a measured local or averaged electron
density.

The Greenwald density is defined by scaling the magnitude of the plasma
current by the plasma cross-sectional area represented through the effective
minor radius:

$$
n_G = C_G \frac{\left|I_p\right|}{\pi a_\mathrm{eff}^2}
$$

where $n_G$ is the Greenwald density, $C_G$ is the Greenwald proportionality
constant, $I_p$ is the [plasma current](name:plasma_current), and
$a_\mathrm{eff}$ is the effective minor radius of the confined plasma
cross-section.

This quantity denotes the empirical limit density itself. It does not denote
a local electron density, a line-averaged electron density, a
volume-averaged electron density, or any normalized Greenwald fraction.

For Greenwald-fraction quantities, this density is the common denominator:
the [ratio of line-averaged electron density to Greenwald
density](name:ratio_of_line_averaged_electron_density_to_greenwald_density)
divides a specified line-averaged electron-density measure by $n_G$.

NAMES.name: gyrocenter_frequency
NAMES.subject: gyrocenter
NAMES.short:
Angular velocity vector of a charged-particle gyrocenter orbit in a
magnetized plasma, with toroidal and poloidal components giving the rates of
gyrocenter advance in their respective angular coordinates.
NAMES.long:
The gyrocenter frequency vector characterizes how rapidly a charged
particle's guiding center advances angularly in the confining magnetic
geometry, after averaging over the fast cyclotron gyration to isolate the
slower drift and bounce or transit dynamics relevant to transport and
stability.

The vector decomposes into two principal angular components. The [toroidal
gyrocenter frequency](name:toroidal_gyrocenter_frequency) $\dot{\phi}_{gc} =
d\phi_{gc}/dt$ is the rate of change of the gyrocenter toroidal angle $\phi$
in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major
radius and $Z$ is the vertical height. The [poloidal gyrocenter
frequency](name:poloidal_gyrocenter_frequency) $\dot{\theta}_{gc} =
d\theta_{gc}/dt$ is the rate of advance in poloidal angle $\theta$ as
measured in flux coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$, where $\rho$ is a
radial flux-surface label. The two components have qualitatively different
characters: passing particles circulate continuously in the poloidal
direction, while trapped particles bounce and primarily precess toroidally.

These frequencies are computed in gyrokinetic codes from the guiding-center
orbit equations derived from the gyrocenter Hamiltonian, and may be averaged
over the particle distribution function to yield population-representative
angular velocities. They enter directly into the calculation of resonance
conditions for wave-particle interactions and neoclassical transport
coefficients.
NAMES.sign:
Positive toroidal component when the gyrocenter advances in
the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$; positive poloidal
component when the gyrocenter advances in the direction of increasing
poloidal angle $\theta$.

NAMES.name: helium_3_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: helium_3
NAMES.short:
Particle number density of helium-3 ions evaluated on the flux surface
assigned to an internal transport barrier, summed over all helium-3 ion
charge states and excluding neutral helium-3.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of helium-3 ions evaluated on the flux surface
assigned to an internal transport barrier is the local density of the
helium-3-ion population at that flux-surface location. Helium-3
(${}^3\mathrm{He}$, mass number $A = 3$, atomic number $Z = 2$) has a
nucleus with two protons and one neutron; at species level this quantity
includes singly ionized ${}^3\mathrm{He}^{+}$ and fully ionized
${}^3\mathrm{He}^{2+}$ and excludes neutral ${}^3\mathrm{He}$ atoms.

The charge-state-summed particle number density is defined by

$$
n_{{}^3\mathrm{He},\mathrm{ITB}} = \left.\lim_{\Delta V\to 0}\frac{\Delta N_{{}^3\mathrm{He}^{+}} + \Delta N_{{}^3\mathrm{He}^{2+}}}{\Delta V}\right|_{\mathrm{ITB}}
$$

where $n_{{}^3\mathrm{He},\mathrm{ITB}}$ is the helium-3 ion number density
at the internal-transport-barrier reference flux surface, $\Delta
N_{{}^3\mathrm{He}^{+}}$ and $\Delta N_{{}^3\mathrm{He}^{2+}}$ are the
counted singly ionized and fully ionized helium-3 ions in the volume element
$\Delta V$, and the vertical bar denotes evaluation at that assigned flux
surface.

This is a particle number density, not a charge-weighted density; both
ionization stages contribute one counted ion per particle. It is the
internal-transport-barrier evaluation of [helium-3
density](name:helium_3_density) and the helium-3-specific member of [density
at the internal transport
barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier), distinct from broader
ion aggregates such as ion density at the internal transport barrier and
from isotope counterparts such as [helium-4 density at the internal
transport barrier](name:helium_4_density_at_internal_transport_barrier). The
internal transport barrier is the designated flux-surface location where
reduced cross-field turbulent transport permits steep density gradients.

NAMES.name: helium_3_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: helium_3
NAMES.short:
Particle number density of the helium-3 ion population evaluated at the
magnetic axis is the local helium-3 ion count per physical volume at that
location. It is summed over all helium-3 ionic charge states.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of the helium-3 ion population evaluated at the
magnetic axis is the local helium-3 ion count per physical volume at that
location. It represents helium-3 ions specifically, rather than neutral
helium-3, electrons, or another plasma population.

The defining relation is

$$
n_{3,\mathrm{axis}} = \left.\frac{dN_3}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $n_{3,\mathrm{axis}}$ is the helium-3 ion number density at the
magnetic axis, $N_3$ is the number of helium-3 ions, and $V$ is physical
volume.

The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested
closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the poloidal-flux gradient
vanishes. It applies to the complete helium-3 ion population at that
location and is summed over all helium-3 ionic charge states; it is neither
a flux-surface or volume integral nor a neutral-helium or other-species
density.

This is the helium-3-specific realization of the population-independent
[density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis). The
unlocalized [helium-3 density](name:helium_3_density) describes the same
charge-state-summed helium-3 ion population without this specified
magnetic-axis locus, while [helium-4 density at the magnetic
axis](name:helium_4_density_at_magnetic_axis) represents the corresponding
density for a different helium isotope.

NAMES.name: helium_4_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: helium_4
NAMES.short:
Particle number density of helium-4 ions at the internal transport barrier,
the flux-surface location where locally reduced cross-field turbulent
transport permits steep radial helium-4 density gradients to form.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of helium-4 ions at the internal transport barrier
is the local, isotope-resolved helium-ion density on the flux surface
selected as the barrier reference location. Helium-4 ($^4\mathrm{He}$, mass
number $A = 4$) is the stable alpha-particle product of deuterium-tritium
fusion and may also be present from helium fueling or wall recycling. The
internal transport barrier is a confined-plasma flux-surface region where
locally reduced cross-field transport permits steep radial gradients to
form.

The local density is the charge-state-summed zeroth velocity moment
evaluated at the ITB reference radius:

$$
n_{{}^4\mathrm{He},\mathrm{ITB}} = \sum_{q>0} \int f_{{}^4\mathrm{He}^{q+}}(\mathbf{v}, \rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm,ITB}})\, d^3v
$$

where $q$ indexes positive ion charge states, $f_{{}^4\mathrm{He}^{q+}}$ is
the phase-space distribution function of helium-4 ions with charge state
$q+$, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, the integral is over velocity
space, and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm,ITB}}$ is the normalized toroidal-flux
radius of the ITB reference flux surface.

Unless a charge state is specified separately, this species-level density is
summed over all helium-4 ion charge states and excludes neutral helium-4
atoms; in hot core plasma the ionic population is commonly dominated by
fully stripped $\mathrm{He}^{2+}$. This is the helium-4 member of
[density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier)
and a species-specific instance of
ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier; it is distinct from
[helium_3_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:helium_3_density_at_internal_transport_barrier)
by isotope mass and from
[electron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:electron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier)
by particle species.

sources.parent_definition: Helium isotope with 4 nucleons (4He)

NAMES.name: helium_4_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: helium_4
NAMES.short:
Particle number density of the helium-4 ion population evaluated at the
magnetic axis is the local helium-4 ion count per physical volume at that
location, summed over all helium-4 ionic charge states.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of the helium-4 ion population evaluated at the
magnetic axis is the local helium-4 ion count per physical volume at that
location, summed over all helium-4 ionic charge states. It represents
helium-4 ions specifically, rather than neutral helium, electrons, other
isotopes, or another plasma population.

The defining relation is

$$
n_{{}^{4}\mathrm{He},\mathrm{axis}} = \left.\frac{dN_{{}^{4}\mathrm{He},\mathrm{ion}}}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $n_{{}^{4}\mathrm{He},\mathrm{axis}}$ is the helium-4 ion number
density at the magnetic axis, $N_{{}^{4}\mathrm{He},\mathrm{ion}}$ is the
number of helium-4 ions summed over all ionic charge states, and $V$ is
physical volume. The superscript $4$ identifies the helium isotope with four
nucleons.

The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested
closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the poloidal-flux gradient
vanishes. It applies to the complete helium-4 ion population at that
location and is summed over all helium-4 ionic charge states; it is neither
a flux-surface or volume integral nor a density of neutral helium or another
isotope.

This is the helium-4-specific realization of the population-independent
[density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis), whose
population is left unspecified at the parent level. It is distinguished from
[helium-3 density at the magnetic
axis](name:helium_3_density_at_magnetic_axis), which counts helium-3 ions
rather than helium-4 ions.

NAMES.name: helium_confinement_time
NAMES.subject: helium
NAMES.short:
Characteristic e-folding time for the loss of confined thermalized helium-4
ash ions when their outward loss rate is proportional to the confined
inventory.
NAMES.long:
The global particle confinement time of thermalized helium-4 ash is the
characteristic retention timescale for fully ionized helium-4 ions in the
confined plasma. It describes particle loss from the total confined
inventory, rather than the confinement of thermal energy or the survival of
the plasma as a whole.

For source-free decay, the confinement time is defined by

$$
\frac{dN_{\mathrm{He}}}{dt}=-\frac{N_{\mathrm{He}}}{\tau_{\mathrm{p,He}}}, \qquad \tau_{\mathrm{p,He}}=\frac{N_{\mathrm{He}}}{\Gamma_{\mathrm{He,loss}}}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{He}}$ is the total confined helium-4 ion inventory, $t$ is
time, and $\Gamma_{\mathrm{He,loss}}$ is the corresponding outward
particle-loss rate. The definition assumes loss proportional to inventory
and excludes helium sources during the decay interval. It is distinct from
[energy confinement time](name:energy_confinement_time) and plasma
confinement time.

NAMES.name: hydrogen_density
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short:
Local number density of hydrogen (protium) ions in the plasma, giving the
count of H+ particles per unit volume at a specified spatial position.
NAMES.long:
The hydrogen density quantifies the local concentration of protium ions
($^1$H$^+$, the lightest hydrogen isotope with mass number $A = 1$) at a
point in the plasma. It is distinct from the neutral atomic hydrogen density
and from the number densities of heavier hydrogenic isotopes such as
deuterium ($^2$H) and tritium ($^3$H).

The number density $n_H$ at position $\mathbf{r}$ is defined as

$$
n_H(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{dN_H}{dV}
$$

where $N_H$ is the number of hydrogen ions within the infinitesimal volume
element $dV$ centered at $\mathbf{r}$.

Spatially averaged forms provide experimentally accessible measures of the
same quantity:
[line_averaged_hydrogen_density](name:line_averaged_hydrogen_density) gives
the path-length-normalized ion count along a spectroscopic or
interferometric chord, while
[volume_averaged_hydrogen_density](name:volume_averaged_hydrogen_density)
integrates the ion content over the full plasma volume. The isotopic
composition of the hydrogenic fuel is tracked by
[ratio_of_hydrogen_density_to_total_hydrogenic_density](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_hydrogen_density_to_volume_averaged_total_hydrogenic_density),
which expresses $n_H$ relative to the combined protium, deuterium, and
tritium ion density. The aggregate over all three hydrogen isotopes is given
by hydrogenic_density, and the full multi-species ion sum by
[total_ion_density](name:total_ion_number_density).

NAMES.name: hydrogen_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short:
Particle number density of hydrogen ions evaluated on the flux surface
assigned to an internal transport barrier, summed over all protium ion
charge states and excluding neutral hydrogen. Hydrogen denotes protium, mass
number 1; the barrier is where locally reduced cross-field turbulent
transport can sustain steep fuel-density gradients.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of hydrogen ions evaluated on the flux surface
assigned to an internal transport barrier is the local density of the
hydrogen-ion population at that flux-surface location. Here hydrogen denotes
protium, $^1\mathrm{H}$, with mass number $A = 1$, distinct from deuterium
and tritium fuel isotopes.

The species-level hydrogen density is the charge-state sum

$$
n_\mathrm{H} = \sum_{q=1}^{Z_\mathrm{H}} n_{\mathrm{H}^{q+}}
$$

where $n_\mathrm{H}$ is the hydrogen-ion number density,
$n_{\mathrm{H}^{q+}}$ is the density of protium ions with charge state $q$,
and $Z_\mathrm{H}=1$ is the hydrogen atomic number. The neutral population
$q=0$ is excluded.

This quantity is the hydrogen isotope instance of [density at the internal
transport barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and an
ion-species contribution to ion density at the internal transport barrier,
without charge weighting. It is distinct from [deuterium density at the
internal transport
barrier](name:deuterium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and from the
combined [deuterium-tritium density at the internal transport
barrier](name:deuterium_tritium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier). The
internal transport barrier is the designated flux-surface location where
locally reduced cross-field turbulent transport permits steep fuel-density
gradients.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Hydrogen (H)

NAMES.name: hydrogen_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short:
Particle number density of the hydrogen ion population evaluated at the
magnetic axis is the local hydrogen-ion count per physical volume at that
location, summed over all hydrogen ionic charge states.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of the hydrogen ion population evaluated at the
magnetic axis is the local hydrogen-ion count per physical volume at that
location, summed over all hydrogen ionic charge states. It represents
hydrogen ions specifically, rather than electrons, neutral hydrogen, or
another plasma population.

The defining relation is

$$
n_{\mathrm{H},\mathrm{axis}} = \left.\frac{dN_{\mathrm{H}}}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{H},\mathrm{axis}}$ is the hydrogen-ion number density at
the magnetic axis, $N_{\mathrm{H}}$ is the number of hydrogen ions summed
over all ionic charge states, and $V$ is physical volume.

The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested
closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the poloidal-flux gradient
vanishes. It applies to the complete hydrogen-ion population at that
location and is neither a flux-surface or volume integral nor an electron or
neutral density.

This is the hydrogen-specific realization of the population-independent
[density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis). It differs
from [deuterium density at the magnetic
axis](name:deuterium_density_at_magnetic_axis), which counts deuterium ions,
and from [hydrogenic density](name:hydrogenic_density), which aggregates
hydrogen-isotope populations rather than isolating hydrogen.

NAMES.name: implicit_electron_energy_source_rate
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Implicit electron energy source rate is the signed coefficient whose product
with the energy equation's primary quantity gives the implicitly treated
electron energy source or sink.
NAMES.long:
Implicit electron energy source rate is the multiplicative coefficient of
the implicitly treated part of a decomposed electron energy source term. It
specifies a source or sink contribution proportional to the primary quantity
of the electron energy transport equation.

The source decomposition is:

$$
F_{e,W} = F_{e,W}^{\mathrm{exp}} + S_{e,W}^{\mathrm{imp}} u_e
$$

where $F_{e,W}$ is the complete source term in the chosen electron energy
equation, $F_{e,W}^{\mathrm{exp}}$ is its additive explicit contribution,
$S_{e,W}^{\mathrm{imp}}$ is the implicit electron energy source rate, and
$u_e$ is the equation's primary quantity. The subscripts $e$ and $W$
identify the electron population and energy channel. In a temperature-based
formulation, $u_e$ is electron temperature; all source terms must correspond
to that same formulation.

This coefficient applies to the electron energy channel and is neither the
additive explicit source nor the complete source term. It has the same
decomposition role as the [implicit ion energy source
rate](name:implicit_ion_energy_source_rate), but applies to electrons rather
than ions. Unlike the [implicit electron particle source
rate](name:implicit_electron_particle_source_rate), which multiplies
electron number density in particle balance, it multiplies the primary
quantity of the energy equation.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when multiplication by a positive primary quantity
gives an energy gain for electrons; negative when it gives an energy loss.

NAMES.name: implicit_electron_particle_source_rate
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Implicit electron particle source rate is the coefficient multiplying
electron number density to give the implicitly treated contribution to
free-electron production or removal.
NAMES.long:
Implicit electron particle source rate is the signed coefficient of the
density-proportional contribution to a decomposed electron particle source.
Its designation identifies the contribution assigned to implicit treatment
in the electron density transport equation, not a separate physical
production mechanism.

The source decomposition is defined by

$$
S_e = S_e^{\mathrm{exp}} + S_e^{\mathrm{imp}} n_e
$$

where $S_e$ is the [electron volumetric source
rate](name:electron_volumetric_source_rate) being decomposed,
$S_e^{\mathrm{exp}}$ is its additive explicit contribution,
$S_e^{\mathrm{imp}}$ is the implicit electron particle source coefficient
defined here, and $n_e$ is the free-electron number density.

This coefficient applies to the electron population and the particular
source contribution being decomposed; it does not imply aggregation over all
source mechanisms. It excludes the additive explicit contribution. The
coefficient itself is neither a volumetric source nor a volume-integrated
production rate: its product with electron number density supplies the
implicit volumetric contribution. The analogous [implicit ion particle
source rate](name:implicit_ion_particle_source_rate) multiplies ion density
instead.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the implicit contribution produces free
electrons, and negative when it removes them.

NAMES.name: implicit_ion_energy_source_rate
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short:
Implicit ion energy source rate is the coefficient multiplying ion
temperature in the stiff contribution to a decomposed ion energy source or
sink.
NAMES.long:
The implicit ion energy source rate specifies the temperature-proportional,
stiff part of a decomposed ion energy source term. It is a coefficient, not
the complete source term or a heating power density.

In the temperature-based form of the ion energy equation, the source
decomposition is:

$$
S_{i,W} = S_{i,W}^{\mathrm{explicit}} + S_{i,W}^{\mathrm{implicit}} T_i
$$

where $S_{i,W}$ is the ion energy source expressed as a temperature-change
rate, $S_{i,W}^{\mathrm{explicit}}$ is its additive explicit contribution,
$S_{i,W}^{\mathrm{implicit}}$ is the implicit coefficient defined here, and
$T_i$ is the temperature of the represented ion population. The subscripts
$i$ and $W$ identify ions and the energy channel, respectively.

The population scope follows the corresponding ion energy equation; this
general coefficient does not itself prescribe aggregation over species or
resolution by charge state. The [total implicit ion energy source
rate](name:total_implicit_ion_energy_source_rate) specializes this
definition to the combined ion energy channel, whereas the [implicit
ion-state energy source rate](name:implicit_ion_state_energy_source_rate)
resolves a specified ion state. A total-ion coefficient is not defined
merely by summing species coefficients.

The implicit and explicit contributions together reproduce the source term.
Their decomposition distinguishes proportional and additive contributions,
not separate physical heating mechanisms.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the implicit contribution supplies energy to
the represented ion population.

NAMES.name: ion_atomic_mass
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short:
Ion atomic mass is the neutral-atom reference mass of a selected elemental
or isotopic constituent of an ion species, independent of ionic charge
state.
NAMES.long:
Ion atomic mass is the reference mass assigned to one atom of a selected
constituent element or isotope in an ion species. It specifies atomic
composition using the corresponding neutral atom, including its bound
electrons, rather than the charge-dependent rest mass of the ion.

The atomic mass is related to the corresponding relative atomic mass by

$$
m_i = A_{\mathrm r,i}\,m_{\mathrm u}
$$

where $m_i$ is the neutral-atom reference mass of the selected constituent
of ion species labeled $i$, $A_{\mathrm r,i}$ is that constituent's relative
atomic mass, and $m_{\mathrm u}$ is the atomic mass constant, defined as one
twelfth of the rest mass of a free neutral carbon-12 atom in its ground
state.

The value applies per atom of the selected constituent, not to the total ion
population. For a molecular ion, it describes one constituent atom rather
than the complete molecule. It is a physical mass, not the integer nucleon
count called the mass number, a mass density, or a mass flow rate. No
restriction to thermal or fast ions is implied.

This quantity specializes [atomic mass](name:atomic_mass) to a constituent
of an ion species. It uses the same neutral-atom reference convention as
[neutral-beam atomic mass](name:neutral_beam_atomic_mass), but does not
restrict the constituent to an injected beam species.

NAMES.name: ion_average_temperature
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short:
Temperature of the combined ion population, given by the
number-density-weighted mean over all ion species and states, including all
ionic charge states.
NAMES.long:
Temperature of the combined ion population is the number-density-weighted
mean of the temperatures of all ion species and ion states. It characterizes
random ion kinetic energy rather than directed-flow energy.

The population average is defined by

$$
T_i = \frac{\sum_s\sum_a n_{s,a}T_{s,a}}{\sum_s\sum_a n_{s,a}}
$$

where $T_i$ is the combined ion temperature, $s$ labels ion species, $a$
labels the states of each species, $n_{s,a}$ is the number density of that
species and state, and $T_{s,a}$ is its temperature. The sums include all
ion species and all ion states, including all ionic charge states; the total
ion number density in the denominator must be nonzero.

The averaging combines ion populations at the same spatial evaluation
location, not temperatures across a spatial region. It is a density-weighted
mean, not a sum of temperatures or an equal-weight mean over species.
Electrons and neutral particles are excluded; unlike [plasma
temperature](name:plasma_temperature), it does not combine ion and electron
thermal contributions.

When the included population consists of thermal ions, this mean corresponds
to the [total ion temperature](name:total_ion_temperature), which likewise
combines species and charge-state contributions through number-density
weighting.

NAMES.name: ion_average_temperature_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short:
Kinetic temperature of the charged-ion population at an internal transport
barrier, defined as the arithmetic mean of charged-ion species temperatures,
excluding electrons and neutral species.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the arithmetic mean of the kinetic temperatures of all
charged ion species on the flux surface assigned to an internal transport
barrier. It retains the locus and population scope of average temperature at
an internal transport barrier.

$$
T_{i,\mathrm{avg}} = \frac{1}{N_i}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{C}} T_{i,s}
$$

where $\mathcal{C}$ is the set of included charged ion species, $N_i$ is the
number of species in that set, and $T_{i,s}$ is the kinetic temperature of
species $s$. For each species, $T_{i,s}$ is the density-weighted mean over
its charge-state temperatures, using $T_{i,s}=\sum_Z n_{s,Z}T_{s,Z}/\sum_Z
n_{s,Z}$, where $n_{s,Z}$ is the number density of charge state $Z$ and
$T_{s,Z}$ is its [ion charge-state
temperature](name:ion_charge_state_temperature). Charge-state weighting is
therefore applied within each species, but distinct ion species are averaged
equally; electrons and neutral species are excluded.

NAMES.name: ion_average_temperature_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short:
Density-weighted effective temperature of the combined thermal ion
population at the magnetic axis, with all ion species and charge states
contributing according to their number densities. The magnetic axis is the
geometric center of the nested closed magnetic flux surfaces, where the
poloidal magnetic flux is stationary.
NAMES.long:
Density-weighted effective temperature of the combined thermal ion
population at the magnetic axis is the local ion temperature obtained by
weighting each thermal ion species and charge state by its local number
density. The magnetic axis is the geometric center of the nested closed
magnetic flux surfaces, equivalently the locus where the poloidal magnetic
flux is stationary.

For resolved ion populations, the effective temperature is defined by the
density-weighted average at the magnetic axis:

$$
T_{i,\mathrm{avg}}^{\mathrm{axis}} = \frac{\sum_s \sum_\zeta n_{s,\zeta}^{\mathrm{axis}} T_{s,\zeta}^{\mathrm{axis}}}{\sum_s \sum_\zeta n_{s,\zeta}^{\mathrm{axis}}}
$$

where $s$ labels ion species, $\zeta$ labels charge state,
$n_{s,\zeta}^{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the local number density of that species
and charge state at the magnetic axis, and $T_{s,\zeta}^{\mathrm{axis}}$ is
its local temperature at the magnetic axis. The sums include the same
thermal ion populations in the numerator and denominator.

This is a local on-axis quantity, not a volume average and not the
temperature of a single species unless the included ion population is
effectively single-component or all included components have the same
temperature. It is the magnetic-axis counterpart of [total ion
temperature](name:total_ion_temperature) and is distinct from
[volume-averaged total ion
temperature](name:volume_averaged_total_ion_temperature). It excludes
electrons, neutral particles, and nonthermal energetic-ion components that
are not part of the thermal ion population, and it does not imply the
maximum ion temperature in the plasma.

NAMES.name: ion_charge_state_average_charge_number
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short:
Concentration-weighted mean ionic charge number within a specified
charge-state bundle of one ion species, expressing the bundle's mean
ionization state.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the mean ionic charge number of a specified charge-state
bundle of one ion species. It is the bundle-restricted instance of [average
charge number](name:average_charge_number).

The concentration-weighted mean is defined by

$$
\overline{Z}_{\mathcal{B}} = \frac{\sum_{q\in\mathcal{B}} q\,n_q}{\sum_{q\in\mathcal{B}} n_q}
$$

where $\overline{Z}_{\mathcal{B}}$ is the bundle's mean charge number,
$\mathcal{B}$ is the set of charge states included in the bundle, $q$ is the
integer ionic charge number, and $n_q$ is the number density of ions in
charge state $q$. The denominator is the total number density within the
bundle and must be nonzero.

The mean includes all charge states represented by the specified bundle, but
not states outside it or other ion species. It is a normalized,
number-density-weighted mean, not a sum of charge numbers. For a bundle
containing one charge state, it equals that state's charge number. It
differs from the [mean squared charge
number](name:square_of_ion_charge_state_charge_number), which averages
squared charge numbers rather than charge numbers.

The [volume-averaged ion charge-state average charge
number](name:volume_averaged_ion_charge_state_average_charge_number) is the
plasma-volume mean of this local bundle quantity. Spatial averaging is an
additional operation and is not part of the charge-state averaging defined
here.

NAMES.name: ion_charge_state_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short:
Effective advective velocity vector governing particle transport of a
specified ion charge state, with projections for distinct plasma transport
directions.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the effective advective velocity vector assigned to the
particle population of a specified ion charge state. It describes the
velocity that multiplies the charge-state number density to produce the
convective part of particle transport, including the applicable thermal and
nonthermal populations.

The convective particle flux is defined by

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{s,\mathrm{conv}} = n_s \mathbf{v}_s
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{s,\mathrm{conv}}$ is the convective particle
flux, $n_s$ is the number density of the specified ion charge state, and
$\mathbf{v}_s$ is this convection-velocity vector. The total particle flux
may additionally contain a diffusive contribution, which is excluded here.

The vector may be resolved into directional quantities, including the
[poloidal ion charge-state convection
velocity](name:poloidal_ion_charge_state_convection_velocity) and [parallel
ion charge-state convection
velocity](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_convection_velocity). It is
distinct from [ion momentum convection
velocity](name:ion_momentum_convection_velocity), which describes advective
transport of aggregate ion momentum.
NAMES.sign:
Positive for the radial transport component when directed
outward toward the last closed flux surface; negative when directed inward
toward the magnetic axis.

NAMES.name: ion_charge_state_diamagnetic_momentum_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short:
Effective velocity coefficient governing advective, non-diffusive transport
of the diamagnetic momentum component carried by ions of one specified
species and charge state.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the effective vector coefficient for advective,
non-diffusive transport of the diamagnetic component of
[momentum](name:momentum) carried by a specified ion species in a specified
charge state. It specializes [diamagnetic momentum convection
velocity](name:diamagnetic_momentum_convection_velocity) by resolving the
ion population and charge state.

The advective closure for the selected momentum component is:

$$
\boldsymbol{\Pi}_{s,\mathrm{dia}}^{\mathrm{conv}} = p_{s,\mathrm{dia}}\,\mathbf{V}_{s,\mathrm{dia}}^{\mathrm{conv}}
$$

where $s$ identifies the ion species and charge state,
$\boldsymbol{\Pi}_{s,\mathrm{dia}}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the vector flux of
its diamagnetic momentum component, $p_{s,\mathrm{dia}}$ is the
corresponding momentum density, and
$\mathbf{V}_{s,\mathrm{dia}}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is this effective convection
velocity. The superscript denotes the advective contribution.

The coefficient applies to one charge state; it is neither summed nor
averaged over charge states. The [ion diamagnetic momentum convection
velocity](name:ion_diamagnetic_momentum_convection_velocity) instead
concerns aggregate ion momentum. The [ion charge-state momentum convection
velocity](name:ion_charge_state_momentum_convection_velocity) is the
corresponding quantity without restriction to the diamagnetic momentum
component. No particular transport-direction projection or plasma region is
specified here.

This transport-closure coefficient is distinct from the ions' actual bulk
velocity and pressure-gradient diamagnetic drift velocity. The defined flux
excludes diffusive momentum transport and residual stress; external momentum
sources are separate terms in the momentum balance.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when a projection of the effective transport
velocity directs advection along the chosen positive transport direction;
the sign of the corresponding momentum flux also depends on the signed
momentum density.

NAMES.name: ion_charge_state_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short:
Effective Fickian coefficient for particle transport by ions in a specified
charge state, relating diffusive flux to that charge state’s density
gradient without selecting a spatial direction.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the effective Fickian particle diffusion coefficient for
ions in a specified charge state. It describes transport of that
charge-state population without summing over ion charge states or selecting
a spatial projection.

The diffusive particle flux is defined by

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{i,q}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{i,q}\nabla n_{i,q}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{i,q}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive particle
flux of ion charge state $q$, $D_{i,q}$ is this diffusion coefficient, and
$n_{i,q}$ is the number density of that charge state.

The [radial ion charge-state diffusion
coefficient](name:radial_ion_charge_state_diffusion_coefficient) and
[poloidal ion charge-state diffusion
coefficient](name:poloidal_ion_charge_state_diffusion_coefficient) are
directional forms of this quantity. The charge-state-specific scope
distinguishes it from the [electron diffusion
coefficient](name:electron_diffusion_coefficient), which describes electron
particle transport.

sources.leaf_definition: One scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.
