NAMES.name: radial_neutral_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short:
Fickian diffusivity governing aggregate neutral-particle transport along the
cylindrical radial direction, relating radial flux to the neutral
number-density gradient.
NAMES.long:
The radial neutral diffusion coefficient is the Fickian diffusivity for the
aggregate neutral population, with neutral internal states combined into one
particle population. It is the radial component of the directional quantity
defined by
[neutral_diffusion_coefficient](name:neutral_diffusion_coefficient).

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the radial neutral
particle flux is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{n,R} = -D_{n,R}\frac{\partial n_n}{\partial R}
$$

where $\Gamma_{n,R}$ is the neutral particle flux in the cylindrical
$\hat{R}$ direction, $D_{n,R}$ is the radial neutral diffusion coefficient,
$n_n$ is the aggregate neutral number density, and $R$ is the major-radius
coordinate. The coefficient applies to particle transport, not to the
separate diffusion of neutral momentum or thermal energy. For passive
Fickian diffusion, $D_{n,R}$ is non-negative.

sources.leaf_definition: One scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.
sources.parent_definition: Particle effective diffusivity (in the radial direction), on various grid subsets

NAMES.name: radial_neutral_internal_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short:
Fick's-law radial neutral internal-state energy diffusion coefficient
multiplying the R-direction temperature gradient, in the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, of neutral particles in a specified internal
state in diffusive thermal-energy transport. It is internal-state-resolved
and represents only the Fickian radial contribution.
NAMES.long:
Fick's-law radial neutral internal-state energy diffusion coefficient is the
scalar radial diffusivity for energy transport by neutral particles in a
specified internal state, and is the radial component form of the [neutral
internal-state energy diffusion
coefficient](name:neutral_internal_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient). Here
radial denotes projection along $\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle,
and $Z$ is vertical height. It is resolved for one internal state, not
summed or averaged over internal states.

The radial Fickian contribution is defined by

$$
q^{\mathrm{diff}}_{E,n,s,R} = - n_{n,s} D_{E,n,s,R} \frac{\partial T_{n,s}}{\partial R}
$$

where $q^{\mathrm{diff}}_{E,n,s,R}$ is the radial component of the diffusive
thermal-energy flux carried by neutral particles in internal state $s$,
$n_{n,s}$ is their number density, $D_{E,n,s,R}$ is this coefficient, and
$T_{n,s}$ is their temperature.

The coefficient includes only the Fickian term driven by $\partial
T_{n,s}/\partial R$ and excludes convective energy transport, sources,
sinks, and effective coefficients that absorb non-diffusive contributions.
It specializes the internal-state energy diffusion coefficient to neutral
particles and is the internal-state-resolved counterpart of the [neutral
energy diffusion coefficient](name:neutral_energy_diffusion_coefficient); it
is distinct from the [poloidal neutral internal-state energy diffusion
coefficient](name:poloidal_neutral_internal_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when a negative radial temperature derivative
produces a diffusive thermal-energy flux in the $+\hat{R}$ direction of the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: One scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.
sources.parent_definition: Energy effective diffusivity (in the radial direction), on various grid subsets

NAMES.name: radial_neutral_internal_state_momentum_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short:
Effective transport velocity relating the convective flux of major-radius
momentum to its density for one neutral species in a specified internal
quantum or energy state.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the effective convection coefficient for transport of the
major-radius component of [momentum](name:momentum) carried by one neutral
species in a specified internal quantum or energy state. Major-radius
momentum is the projection onto the direction of increasing $R$ in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius,
$\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The density-proportional convective contribution to the momentum flux is
defined by:

$$
\Pi^{\mathrm{conv}}_{0a,R;n} = V^{\mathrm{conv}}_{0a,R}\,g_{0a,R}
$$

where $\Pi^{\mathrm{conv}}_{0a,R;n}$ is the convective flux of major-radius
momentum through a surface with chosen unit normal $\hat{n}$,
$V^{\mathrm{conv}}_{0a,R}$ is this convection coefficient, and $g_{0a,R}$ is
the corresponding momentum density. The subscript $0$ denotes neutral
particles, $a$ identifies their internal state, and $n$ labels the
surface-normal flux direction. The momentum density is $g_{0a,R}=m_0
n_{0a}u_{0a,R}$, where $m_0$ is the neutral-particle mass, $n_{0a}$ is the
state-resolved number density, and $u_{0a,R}$ is the major-radius component
of the state-resolved mean translational velocity.

The major-radius label identifies the transported momentum component, not
the direction through which it is transported. The surface normal need not
coincide with the major-radius direction or a magnetic-flux-surface normal.
The coefficient excludes diffusive momentum transport and momentum source
terms. Unlike the [bulk neutral internal-state
velocity](name:bulk_neutral_internal_state_velocity), it is a
transport-closure coefficient and need not equal the particle-flow velocity.

This quantity applies to one neutral species and one internal state, without
summation over species or internal states. State-resolved convective fluxes
sum to the species-level convective flux associated with the [radial
neutral-species momentum convection
velocity](name:radial_neutral_species_momentum_convection_velocity); the
coefficients themselves are not summed.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the convective flux of major-radius momentum
along the chosen surface normal has the same sign as the corresponding
momentum density.

NAMES.name: radial_neutral_internal_state_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short:
Signed major-radius projection of the mean translational velocity of neutral
particles in one specified internal quantum or energy state.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the major-radius component of the [neutral internal-state
velocity](name:neutral_internal_state_velocity) of one neutral species in
one specified quantum or energy state. It represents directed bulk motion
after averaging over particle velocities within that state.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the component is defined
by:

$$
u_{0,a,R}=\hat{R}\cdot\mathbf u_{0,a}=\frac{\int (\mathbf v\cdot\hat{R})f_{0,a}(\mathbf r,\mathbf v)\,d^3v}{\int f_{0,a}(\mathbf r,\mathbf v)\,d^3v}
$$

where $u_{0,a,R}$ is the major-radius velocity component, $\mathbf u_{0,a}$
is the state-resolved bulk velocity vector, $0$ identifies neutral
particles, and $a$ identifies the specified internal state. The function
$f_{0,a}$ is the phase-space number density of the selected neutral species
in that state, $\mathbf r$ is position, $\mathbf v$ is particle velocity,
and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element. The coordinate $R$ is
distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is
vertical height, and $\hat{R}$ is the unit vector toward increasing major
radius.

The average retains internal-state resolution and does not combine different
states or neutral species. It is a signed vector projection, not the flow
speed, thermal velocity spread, or particle flux. The major-radius direction
need not coincide with the magnetic-flux-surface normal.

The corresponding [radial neutral velocity](name:radial_neutral_velocity)
combines internal-state contributions through a number-density-weighted
mean; this quantity retains the contribution of the specified state.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the state-resolved neutral bulk motion has a
component away from the toroidal symmetry axis, toward increasing major
radius.

NAMES.name: radial_neutral_particle_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short:
Signed radial component of the effective convection velocity multiplying
neutral-particle density in the advective part of edge-plasma transport.
NAMES.long:
Radial neutral-particle convection velocity is the effective coefficient of
the density-proportional advective flux of neutral particles in edge-plasma
transport. It represents directed drift, pinch, or outward convection after
density-gradient-driven diffusive transport has been separated.

The radial convective particle flux is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{n,r}^{\mathrm{conv}} = n_n v_{n,r}
$$

where $\Gamma_{n,r}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the radial particle flux due to
convection, $n_n$ is the neutral-particle number density, and $v_{n,r}$ is
this radial convection velocity.

The quantity applies to the neutral-particle channel in the edge plasma and
is the radial component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$
frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is
vertical height. It is an effective coefficient for the named
neutral-particle population, not a sum of energy or momentum transport
coefficients.

The quantity excludes density-gradient-driven diffusive transport and is
distinct from the full
[neutral_particle_convection_velocity](name:neutral_particle_convection_velocity),
which has no directional projection. The
[parallel_neutral_particle_convection_velocity](name:parallel_neutral_particle_convection_velocity)
represents the corresponding projection along the magnetic field rather than
along increasing major radius.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the neutral-particle convective velocity
points toward increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_neutral_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short:
Radial neutral particle flux is the signed net number flow per unit area and
time toward increasing major radius for one neutral atomic or molecular
species, summed over its internal states. It is the cylindrical major-radius
component, not the flux-surface-normal component.
NAMES.long:
Radial neutral particle flux is the signed component of neutral
particle-number transport in the direction of increasing major radius. It
gives the net number flow per area and time for one neutral atomic or
molecular species, with that species’ internal states combined.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, its defining
projection and internal-state aggregation are:

$$
\Gamma_{0,R} = \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_0 \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}} = \sum_a \Gamma_{0,a,R}
$$

where $\Gamma_{0,R}$ is the radial neutral particle flux,
$\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_0$ is the [neutral particle
flux](name:neutral_particle_flux) for one species summed over its internal
states, $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the unit vector toward increasing major
radius, $a$ indexes the internal states of that species, and
$\Gamma_{0,a,R}$ is its [radial neutral internal-state particle
flux](name:radial_neutral_internal_state_particle_flux). Here, $R$ is major
radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle,
and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies to one neutral species, includes all its internal
states, and does not sum over distinct neutral species or include charged
particles. It is a flux density, not a surface-integrated particle rate. A
flux-surface-averaged transport value is the average of this radial
component over the surface; the major-radius direction is not generally
normal to a magnetic flux surface, so this average is not the
flux-surface-normal component.

This is the major-radius projection of [neutral particle
flux](name:neutral_particle_flux), and summing the state-resolved radial
contributions gives the species-level quantity. [Poloidal neutral particle
flux](name:poloidal_neutral_particle_flux) and [parallel neutral particle
flux](name:parallel_neutral_particle_flux) are distinct directional
projections of neutral particle transport. The flux-surface-averaged form
represents radial neutral transport in the neutral particle balance.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the net neutral particle flux has a component
toward increasing major radius $R$, away from the toroidal symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: radial_neutral_state_momentum_flux_limiter_coefficient
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short:
Coefficient scaling the free-streaming cap on the flux of cylindrical radial
momentum carried by one neutral species in a specified internal state in
edge-plasma transport.
NAMES.long:
This coefficient scales the collisionless free-streaming upper bound on the
gradient-driven flux of radial [momentum](name:momentum) carried by a
specified neutral species in one internal state. It specializes the
[momentum flux limiter coefficient](name:momentum_flux_limiter_coefficient)
for that population and momentum component in edge-plasma transport
closures.

The limiting flux magnitude is defined by:

$$
\Pi_{s,R}^{\max} = f_{s,R}\Pi_{s,R}^{\mathrm{fs}}
$$

where $s$ identifies the selected neutral species and internal state,
$f_{s,R}$ is this nonnegative limiter coefficient, $\Pi_{s,R}^{\mathrm{fs}}$
is the nonnegative free-streaming reference magnitude for the flux of that
state's radial momentum across an oriented surface, and $\Pi_{s,R}^{\max}$
is the corresponding upper bound on the limited flux magnitude.

The radial component is directed along increasing major radius $R$ in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is distance from
the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical
height. Radial identifies the transported momentum component, not the
direction of transport across the surface, and does not mean
flux-surface-normal.

The coefficient applies separately to the selected neutral species and
internal state; it is neither summed nor averaged over states or species and
excludes ionic populations. The limiter restricts the controlled flux
magnitude without reversing its direction; it is distinct from momentum
diffusivity and does not specify a particular interpolation between
diffusive and free-streaming limits. The [parallel neutral momentum flux
limiter
coefficient](name:parallel_neutral_momentum_flux_limiter_coefficient)
instead limits transport of magnetic-field-parallel neutral momentum.

NAMES.name: radial_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short:
Signed major-radius component of the effective pressure-gradient transport
velocity assigned to one neutral species in a specified internal state,
distinct from direct magnetic drift of neutral particles.
NAMES.long:
The radial neutral-state diamagnetic-drift velocity is the signed
major-radius projection of an effective pressure-gradient transport velocity
assigned to one neutral species in a specified internal state in the edge
plasma. It represents a fluid-transport contribution rather than direct
magnetic drift of individual neutral particles.

For neutral species $a$ in internal state $k$, the defining projection is:

$$
v_{\mathrm{dia},ak,R}=\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{dia},ak}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{R}}
$$

where $v_{\mathrm{dia},ak,R}$ is the radial velocity contribution,
$\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{dia},ak}$ is the effective diamagnetic transport
velocity assigned to that species and state, and $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the
unit vector toward increasing major radius. The right-handed cylindrical
frame is $(R,\phi,Z)$, where $R$ is distance from the toroidal symmetry
axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

Only the specified neutral species and internal state are included; no
summation or averaging over species or states is implied. This contribution
is distinct from the state's total flow velocity. Because neutral particles
have zero net electric charge, the charged-particle diamagnetic-drift
formula does not apply directly. Radial denotes the geometric major-radius
projection, not a flux-surface-normal or magnetic-field-perpendicular
projection.

This quantity specializes [neutral-state velocity due to diamagnetic
drift](name:neutral_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) to the
cylindrical radial direction. The [vertical neutral-state velocity due to
diamagnetic
drift](name:vertical_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift)
instead projects the same effective transport velocity onto the vertical
direction.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the effective diamagnetic transport velocity
of the specified neutral state has a component toward increasing major
radius $R$, away from the toroidal symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: radial_neutral_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short:
Major-radius component of a neutral species' mean flow in the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, with number-density-weighted averaging over
contributing internal states.
NAMES.long:
The radial neutral velocity is the major-radius projection of the bulk flow
of a selected neutral species. It describes directed motion after averaging
over particle velocities. The direction is defined in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is distance from the toroidal
symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

At a given position, the component is defined by

$$
u_{0R}=\hat{R}\cdot\mathbf{u}_0=\frac{\sum_a n_{0,a}\,\hat{R}\cdot\mathbf{u}_{0,a}}{\sum_a n_{0,a}}
$$

where $u_{0R}$ is the radial neutral velocity, $\hat{R}$ is the unit vector
toward increasing major radius, and $\mathbf{u}_0$ is the [neutral
velocity](name:neutral_velocity) vector. The index $a$ labels the
contributing neutral internal states, $n_{0,a}$ is their individual number
density, and $\mathbf{u}_{0,a}$ is their individual mean particle velocity.

The quantity applies to one neutral species and excludes charged particles.
When multiple internal states contribute, their velocities are combined as a
number-density-weighted mean, not summed; [bulk neutral internal-state
velocity](name:bulk_neutral_internal_state_velocity) instead retains a
single state's flow. The mean requires nonzero total neutral density.

This is a signed directional component, not the flow magnitude, a particle
flux, or an effective momentum-convection coefficient. The major-radius
direction is not generally normal to a magnetic flux surface. The [vertical
neutral velocity](name:vertical_neutral_velocity) is the vertical projection
of the same mean-flow vector.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the neutral bulk flow has a component toward
increasing major radius, away from the toroidal symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: radial_particle_convection_velocity
NAMES.short:
Signed major-radius component of the effective velocity multiplying neutral
energy density in the convective energy flux of the edge plasma.
NAMES.long:
Radial neutral-energy convection velocity is the effective coefficient of
the energy-density-proportional advective flux carried by neutral particles
in edge-plasma transport. It represents directed energy transport after the
diffusive contribution has been separated.

The radial convective neutral-energy flux is defined by

$$
F_{E,n,R}^{\mathrm{conv}} = U_n v_{E,n,R}
$$

where $F_{E,n,R}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the radial neutral-energy flux due to
convection, $U_n$ is the energy density of the specified neutral population,
and $v_{E,n,R}$ is this radial convection velocity.

The quantity applies to the neutral-energy channel, not the total-ion-energy
channel or a sum over charged-particle energy channels. Its direction is the
major-radius direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame,
where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical
height. This direction is not generally normal to a magnetic flux surface.

The quantity excludes diffusive energy transport and need not equal the bulk
neutral flow velocity. It is distinct from the [neutral particle convection
velocity](name:neutral_particle_convection_velocity), which multiplies
neutral number density to define a convective particle flux; the
energy-channel and particle-channel coefficients need not coincide.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the neutral-energy convection velocity points
toward increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,
\phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: rate_due_to_beam_beam_fusion
NAMES.short:
Global volume-integrated rate of fusion events or reaction-product
generation attributable to fusion between two nonthermal fuel-ion
populations supplied by neutral beams.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the global rate of beam-beam fusion events or of production
of a specified reaction product caused by collisions between two nonthermal
fuel-ion populations originating from beam injection. It is a
reaction-source quantity, not a local source density or directional flux.

The global rate is the volume integral of the local beam-beam fusion source
rate:

$$
\dot{N}_X = \int_V S_X^{\mathrm{BB}}(\mathbf{r})\,d^3\mathbf{r}
$$

where $\dot{N}_X$ is the global rate for counted entity $X$, $X$ denotes
either a fusion event or a specified reaction product, $V$ is the plasma
volume over which beam-beam reactions occur, $S_X^{\mathrm{BB}}(\mathbf{r})$
is the corresponding local source rate density, and $\mathbf{r}$ is
position.

The quantity aggregates the volume-integrated contribution from all
represented beam-beam fuel-ion reaction channels and, when a product is
specified, applies the corresponding product yield. Both reacting fuel-ion
populations are nonthermal beam-origin populations; the generic quantity
does not select a particular isotope pair, charge state, reaction product,
or product channel. It excludes beam-thermal and thermal-thermal fusion
contributions, as well as local source densities and surface or directional
fluxes.

The [neutron rate due to beam-beam
fusion](name:neutron_rate_due_to_beam_beam_fusion) is a product-specific
specialization that counts neutrons while retaining the same global volume
integration and beam-beam channel aggregation. The [source rate due to
beam-beam fusion](name:source_rate_due_to_beam_beam_fusion) represents the
corresponding product-resolved source-rate family, whereas [rate due to
beam-thermal fusion](name:rate_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion) uses one
beam-origin and one thermal reacting population and is therefore a distinct
fusion mechanism.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_line_averaged_electron_density_to_greenwald_density
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless Greenwald fraction comparing the electron number density
averaged along a plasma chord with the empirical density limit set by plasma
current and effective minor radius.
NAMES.long:
The Greenwald fraction measures the proximity of a confined plasma's
line-averaged electron density to its empirical Greenwald density limit.

It is defined by:

$$
f_G = \frac{\bar{n}_e}{n_G}
$$

where $f_G$ is the Greenwald fraction, $\bar{n}_e$ is the [line-averaged
electron density](name:line_averaged_electron_density), and $n_G$ is the
[Greenwald density](name:greenwald_density) determined from the
plasma-current magnitude and effective minor radius.

The numerator represents the electron population averaged along a plasma
chord; the denominator is the empirical density reference for the confined
plasma. This quantity is a global normalized ratio, not a local electron
density, a density limit itself, or an average over charge states or spatial
regions.

The fraction is the direct normalization of line-averaged electron density
by Greenwald density: values near unity indicate proximity to the empirical
reference limit, while values above or below unity indicate a line-averaged
density respectively above or below that reference.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Greenwald fraction =line_average/n_e/value divided by (global_quantities/ip/value *1e6 * pi * minor_radius^2)

NAMES.name: runaway_electron_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short:
Effective runaway-electron convection velocity is the vector velocity
assigned to advective, non-diffusive transport of the runaway-electron
population. It denotes the full vector quantity; component or projection
quantities are specializations.
NAMES.long:
Effective runaway-electron convection velocity is the vector velocity
assigned to the advective part of runaway-electron transport. It represents
non-diffusive motion of the runaway-electron population in a transport
representation, independent of any particular component or projection.

The convective contribution to the runaway-electron particle flux density is
defined by:

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{RE}}^{\mathrm{conv}} = n_{\mathrm{RE}}\,\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{RE}}^{\mathrm{conv}}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{RE}}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the convective
runaway-electron particle flux density, $n_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is the
runaway-electron number density, and
$\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{RE}}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the runaway-electron
convection velocity.

This quantity excludes diffusive transport terms, source terms, and the
total runaway-electron particle flux density. Component or projection
quantities, such as the [perpendicular runaway-electron convection
velocity](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_convection_velocity), are
specializations of this vector and do not redefine the parent quantity.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when a resolved component of
$\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{RE}}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ points in the positive sense of
that component's stated direction.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_runaway_electron_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short:
Signed cross-field component of the effective runaway-electron convection
velocity, projected along the outward normal to nested magnetic flux
surfaces.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the directed transport velocity of runaway electrons across
magnetic flux surfaces, isolated from the field-aligned component of the
[runaway-electron convection
velocity](name:runaway_electron_convection_velocity).

The perpendicular component is defined by

$$
v_{\perp}^{\rm RE} = \mathbf{v}_{\rm RE} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\psi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{\rm RE}$ is the effective runaway-electron
convection-velocity vector and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\psi}$ is the outward unit
normal to nested magnetic flux surfaces. This convective quantity describes
directed cross-field transport and excludes diffusive spreading, which is
characterized by the [perpendicular runaway-electron
diffusivity](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_diffusivity). It
contributes to the [perpendicular runaway-electron particle
flux](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_particle_flux) together with the
runaway-electron density.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when runaway-electron convection is directed
outward from the magnetic axis toward increasing flux label.

sources.leaf_definition: Effective convection
sources.parent_definition: Effective perpendicular transport to the magnetic field for runaways

NAMES.name: runaway_electron_density
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short:
Number density of runaway electrons, the suprathermal electron population
for which electric-field acceleration can overcome collisional drag.
NAMES.long:
Number density of runaway electron

The local density is the zeroth momentum-space moment of the
runaway-electron distribution:

$$
n_{e,\mathrm{RE}} = \int f_{e,\mathrm{RE}}(\mathbf{p})\,\mathrm{d}^3p
$$

where $n_{e,\mathrm{RE}}$ is the runaway-electron number density,
$\mathbf{p}$ is electron momentum, and $f_{e,\mathrm{RE}}$ is the
runaway-electron momentum distribution at the same spatial position and
time. The integral covers all momenta represented in that population.

Thermal electrons and suprathermal electrons outside the runaway population
are excluded. No orbit-class restriction or spatial averaging is implicit.
Unlike [runaway-electron current
density](name:runaway_electron_current_density), this quantity counts
particles without weighting them by charge and velocity.

The [volume-averaged runaway-electron
density](name:volume_averaged_runaway_electron_density) is the integral of
this local density over the confined plasma volume divided by that volume.
The [volume-integrated runaway-electron
density](name:volume_integrated_runaway_electron_density) is the integral
itself and represents the total runaway-electron count rather than a number
density.

sources.leaf_definition: One scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.
sources.parent_definition: Runaway electrons density, given on various grid subsets

sources.leaf_definition: Runaway electrons density
sources.parent_definition: Radial flux surface averaged profiles for a set of time slices

NAMES.name: runaway_electron_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short:
Directional transport coefficient describing the diffusive spatial spreading
of runaway-electron density through the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Runaway-electron diffusivity is the effective coefficient governing spatial
spreading of the runaway-electron population by diffusive transport. Its
directional instances include [perpendicular runaway electron
diffusivity](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_diffusivity), which
describes cross-field spreading.

For a resolved transport direction $i$, the diffusive particle flux is
related to the runaway-electron density gradient by

$$
\Gamma_{\mathrm{re,diff},i} = -D_{\mathrm{re},i}\,\frac{\partial n_{\mathrm{re}}}{\partial x_i}
$$

where $\Gamma_{\mathrm{re,diff},i}$ is the diffusive runaway-electron
particle flux, $D_{\mathrm{re},i}$ is the diffusivity for direction $i$,
$n_{\mathrm{re}}$ is the runaway-electron number density, and $x_i$ is the
corresponding spatial coordinate. The quantity describes the diffusive
contribution only and is distinct from the effective convection velocity
represented by [perpendicular runaway electron convection
velocity](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_convection_velocity).

NAMES.name: perpendicular_runaway_electron_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short:
Perpendicular runaway-electron diffusivity is the effective scalar diffusion
coefficient governing runaway-electron spreading perpendicular to the
magnetic field and across magnetic flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
Perpendicular runaway-electron diffusivity is the effective scalar
coefficient for Fickian diffusion of runaway electrons perpendicular to the
magnetic field. In flux-surface transport descriptions, it represents the
cross-surface diffusive transport component along the flux-surface normal,
positive toward increasing flux label.

The diffusive contribution to the perpendicular runaway-electron particle
flux is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{\mathrm{RE},\perp}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{\mathrm{RE},\perp}\,\frac{\partial n_{\mathrm{RE}}}{\partial \ell_\perp}
$$

where $D_{\mathrm{RE},\perp}$ is the perpendicular runaway-electron
diffusivity, $\Gamma_{\mathrm{RE},\perp}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive
part of the [perpendicular runaway-electron particle
flux](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_particle_flux), $n_{\mathrm{RE}}$
is the [runaway-electron density](name:runaway_electron_density), and
$\ell_\perp$ is distance along the local flux-surface-normal direction
perpendicular to the magnetic field. The minus sign states that a positive
diffusivity gives diffusive flux from larger toward smaller runaway-electron
density.

This quantity applies only to the runaway-electron population and only to
its perpendicular diffusive particle transport. It is not a parallel
transport coefficient, not a convective velocity, and not the full
[runaway-electron diffusivity](name:runaway_electron_diffusivity) when that
broader quantity includes additional directional components.

The [perpendicular runaway-electron convection
velocity](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_convection_velocity) gives the
advective contribution to the same perpendicular particle balance, whereas
$D_{\mathrm{RE},\perp}$ multiplies the density gradient. The sum of
diffusive and convective contributions forms the modeled [perpendicular
runaway-electron particle
flux](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_particle_flux).

sources.leaf_definition: Effective diffusivity
sources.parent_definition: Effective perpendicular transport to the magnetic field for runaways

NAMES.name: runaway_electron_kinetic_energy
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short:
Relativistic kinetic energy summed over the entire runaway-electron
population, giving the total energy carried by runaway electrons.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the total kinetic energy carried by all electrons
classified as runaway, integrated over the complete population and its
occupied plasma volume. It excludes electron rest-mass energy and energy
carried by non-runaway populations.

The total energy is defined from the runaway-electron distribution function
by

$$
E_{\mathrm{RE}} = \int_V \int \left[\gamma(\mathbf{p})-1\right]m_e c^2 f_{\mathrm{RE}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{p})\,d^3p\,d^3x
$$

where $E_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is the total kinetic energy in J, $V$ is the plasma
volume, $\mathbf{x}$ is position in m, $\mathbf{p}$ is electron momentum in
kg m s$^{-1}$, $m_e$ is the electron rest mass, $c$ is the speed of light,
$f_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is the runaway-electron phase-space number distribution,
and $\gamma(\mathbf{p})=\sqrt{1+p^2/(m_e^2c^2)}$ is the Lorentz factor. The
corresponding local density is [runaway electron energy
density](name:runaway_electron_kinetic_energy_density), while volume
averaging gives [volume-averaged runaway electron kinetic energy
density](name:volume_averaged_runaway_electron_kinetic_energy_density).

sources.leaf_definition: Total runaway kinetic energy
sources.parent_definition: Global quantities

NAMES.name: runaway_electron_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short:
Directed number flow of runaway electrons across an oriented surface per
unit area and time, including convective, diffusive, drift, and turbulent
transport.
NAMES.long:
Runaway-electron particle flux quantifies the directed transport of runaway
electrons across an oriented reference surface. It is the
runaway-electron-specific realization of particle_flux, with the electron
population restricted to the runaway regime.

For a fluid description, the particle flux vector is:

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{RE}} = n_{\mathrm{RE}}\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{RE}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is the runaway-electron number density and
$\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is their mean velocity. The scalar flux through
an oriented surface is $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{RE}}\cdot\hat{n}$,
where $\hat{n}$ is the chosen unit surface normal; kinetically, the vector
is the first velocity moment of the runaway-electron distribution.

This parent quantity is not restricted to a particular direction or
projection. The [perpendicular runaway-electron particle
flux](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_particle_flux) is its cross-field
specialization obtained by projecting the vector onto the outward magnetic
flux-surface normal.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when runaway electrons flow in the direction of
the outward surface normal, away from the enclosed plasma volume.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_runaway_electron_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short:
Cross-field number flux of runaway electrons through magnetic flux surfaces,
obtained by projecting their particle-flux vector onto the outward
flux-surface normal.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the cross-field component of runaway-electron particle
transport through magnetic flux surfaces. It describes the directed rate at
which the suprathermal runaway-electron population crosses those surfaces,
rather than transport along magnetic field lines.

The component is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{\mathrm{RE},\perp}=\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{RE}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}_{\mathrm{FS}}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is the [runaway electron particle
flux](name:runaway_electron_particle_flux) vector and $\hat{\mathbf
n}_{\mathrm{FS}}$ is the unit normal to the magnetic flux surface, directed
toward increasing flux label. The subscript $\perp$ denotes the cross-field
projection.

This is a signed normal component, not the magnitude of the full
particle-flux vector and not a field-aligned flux. It is distinct from
cross-field transport coefficients such as [perpendicular runaway electron
diffusivity](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_diffusivity) and from
[perpendicular runaway electron convection
velocity](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_convection_velocity).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when runaway-electron particle transport is
directed toward increasing flux label, outward from the magnetic axis.

sources.leaf_definition: Flux
sources.parent_definition: Effective perpendicular transport to the magnetic field for runaways

NAMES.name: runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_compton_scattering
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short:
Compton runaway-electron source rate is the volumetric rate at which
high-energy gamma-ray scattering transfers thermal electrons into the
runaway population.
NAMES.long:
The Compton runaway-electron source rate describes the production of runaway
electrons through energy transfer from high-energy gamma-ray photons to
initially thermal electrons. Only scattering events that place an electron
in the runaway regime contribute, rather than all events that produce
energetic electrons.

The source contribution to the runaway-electron density evolution is defined
by

$$
S_{\mathrm C}=\left.\frac{\partial n_{\mathrm{RE}}}{\partial t}\right|_{\mathrm{Compton\ source}}
$$

where $S_{\mathrm C}$ is the Compton source rate, $n_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is the
runaway-electron number density, and $t$ is time. The restriction denotes
the density change attributable solely to Compton production.

This term counts transfer into the runaway population, not creation of
additional electrons. It excludes other production mechanisms, particle
transport, and runaway-electron losses, and therefore is not the full
density time derivative. It contributes to the [total runaway-electron
source rate](name:total_runaway_electron_source_rate), which sums all active
production mechanisms.

No spatial averaging is imposed by this definition. The [volume-averaged
Compton runaway-electron source
rate](name:volume_averaged_runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_compton_scattering)
is the plasma-volume average of this quantity, not its volume integral.

sources.leaf_definition: One scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.
sources.parent_definition: Compton source of runaway electrons, given on various grid subsets

sources.leaf_definition: Compton source of runaway electrons
sources.parent_definition: Radial flux surface averaged profiles for a set of time slices

NAMES.name: runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short:
Runaway-electron source rate due to Dreicer generation is the volumetric
rate at which parallel electric acceleration drives electrons from the
thermal distribution's suprathermal tail into runaway motion.
NAMES.long:
Runaway-electron source rate due to Dreicer generation is the volumetric
production rate of electrons entering the runaway population through Dreicer
acceleration. The electric-field component parallel to the magnetic field
drives suprathermal electrons across the critical velocity-space boundary
beyond which electric acceleration overcomes collisional friction.

The kinetic definition is the velocity-space flux across that critical
boundary into the runaway population:

$$
S_{\mathrm{D}} = \int_{\Sigma_c} \boldsymbol{\Gamma}^{\mathrm{D}}_v \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_v \, dA_v
$$

where $S_{\mathrm{D}}$ is the runaway-electron source rate due to Dreicer
generation, $\Sigma_c$ is the critical boundary separating the collisional
and runaway regions of velocity space, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}^{\mathrm{D}}_v$
is the electron velocity-space flux associated with parallel electric
acceleration and collisional friction, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_v$ is the unit
normal pointing into the runaway region, and $dA_v$ is a surface element of
that boundary.

This quantity counts primary production from the thermal distribution's
tail. It excludes avalanche multiplication, [hot-tail
production](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail), and other
non-Dreicer sources. It is a source contribution to the runaway-electron
density balance, not the full density time derivative, which also includes
other sources, losses, and transport.

Spatial averaging preserves this population and mechanism scope: the
[volume-averaged Dreicer source
rate](name:volume_averaged_runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer) is
the volume-weighted plasma mean of this production term, not a
volume-integrated generation rate. The [fast-electron Dreicer source rate]
instead counts entry into the defined fast-electron population; the two
coincide only when that population is defined to coincide with the runaway
population.

NAMES.name: runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short:
Hot-tail runaway-electron source rate is the production of runaway electrons
per unit volume and time from a suprathermal tail surviving rapid cooling of
the bulk electrons.
NAMES.long:
Hot-tail runaway-electron source rate quantifies production of runaway
electrons from the high-energy electron tail that survives rapid cooling of
the bulk population. These tail electrons relax collisionally more slowly
than the bulk cools, allowing some to enter the regime where electric-field
acceleration overcomes collisional drag.

The hot-tail contribution to runaway-electron density evolution is defined
by

$$
S_{\mathrm{ht}} = \left.\frac{\partial n_{\mathrm{RE}}}{\partial t}\right|_{\mathrm{hot\text{-}tail}}
$$

where $S_{\mathrm{ht}}$ is the volumetric hot-tail production rate,
$n_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is the [runaway-electron number
density](name:runaway_electron_density), and $t$ is time. The restriction on
the derivative selects only production through the hot-tail mechanism.

This source counts electrons entering the runaway population, not all
suprathermal electrons. It excludes generation through other mechanisms,
transport, and losses, so it is not the full time derivative of
runaway-electron density. It contributes to the [total runaway-electron
source rate](name:total_runaway_electron_source_rate), which sums all active
generation mechanisms.

The [volume-averaged hot-tail runaway-electron source
rate](name:volume_averaged_runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail) is
this same volumetric source integrated over the plasma volume and divided by
that volume.

NAMES.name: safety_factor
NAMES.short:
Safety factor is the signed number of toroidal turns made by a magnetic
field line per complete poloidal circuit on a toroidal magnetic flux
surface.
NAMES.long:
Safety factor is the signed toroidal-to-poloidal winding ratio of magnetic
field lines on a toroidal magnetic flux surface. It characterizes magnetic
geometry without selecting a particular surface or plasma region.

In axisymmetry, or using straight-field-line flux coordinates
$(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, the defining relation is

$$
q = \frac{1}{2\pi}\oint \frac{\mathbf{B}\cdot\nabla\phi}{\mathbf{B}\cdot\nabla\theta}\,d\theta
$$

where $q$ is the safety factor, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field, $\nabla$
is the spatial gradient operator, $\rho$ labels magnetic flux surfaces,
$\theta$ is the poloidal angle, and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle. The
integral follows a magnetic field line through one complete poloidal
circuit. The toroidal angle belongs to the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height;
$\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above.

The quantity describes winding on an individual magnetic surface, not a
volume average or a sum over surfaces. It applies to closed magnetic
surfaces in both core and edge regions. On open scrape-off-layer field
lines, a complete poloidal circuit need not exist, so any extension of this
definition requires an additional convention.

The [magnetic-axis safety factor](name:safety_factor_at_magnetic_axis) and
[plasma-boundary safety factor](name:safety_factor_at_plasma_boundary) are
limiting values approached from neighboring closed surfaces; a separatrix
limit need not be finite. The [minimum safety
factor](name:minimum_safety_factor) instead selects the signed value on the
closed surface where the safety-factor magnitude is smallest, rather than
evaluating it at a prescribed locus.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the toroidal angle advance of a magnetic
field line is in the direction of increasing $\phi$ as the poloidal angle
$\theta$ increases.

NAMES.name: safety_factor_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.short:
Signed field-line winding ratio evaluated on the magnetic flux surface
designated as the internal transport barrier, giving toroidal turns per
poloidal circuit.
NAMES.long:
The safety factor at the internal transport barrier is the signed helical
winding of magnetic field lines on the flux surface designated as the
barrier. It counts toroidal turns per poloidal circuit at that specific
locus.

The defining flux-increment relation is:

$$
q_{\mathrm{ITB}} = \left.\frac{d\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}}{d\Phi_{\mathrm{pol}}}\right|_{\mathrm{ITB}}
$$

where $q_{\mathrm{ITB}}$ is the safety factor evaluated on the
internal-transport-barrier flux surface, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is toroidal
magnetic flux, $\Phi_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is poloidal magnetic flux, and the
subscript $\mathrm{ITB}$ denotes evaluation on that designated surface.

This quantity applies only to the flux surface associated with the internal
transport barrier. It is a single flux-surface value, with no averaging or
aggregation over neighboring surfaces, plasma volume, or other regions
implied.

It is distinct from safety-factor values evaluated at other loci, such as
the safety factor at the pedestal top, and it does not represent a general
radial profile or a value at the magnetic axis or plasma boundary.

The [safety factor](name:safety_factor) is the corresponding
locus-independent flux-surface quantity; this name specializes it by fixing
the evaluation surface. The [rotational
transform](name:rotational_transform) uses the reciprocal field-line winding
convention, counting poloidal turns per toroidal circuit.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the toroidal and poloidal flux increments
have the same sign, taking $\phi$ as the toroidal angle in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius, $Z$ the vertical
height, and the positive poloidal circuit defined by increasing
$\Phi_{\mathrm{pol}}$.

NAMES.name: source_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short:
Area-normalized vector source term due to diamagnetic drift is the
pressure-gradient-driven contribution to a transport momentum balance. It
represents directional transfer of linear momentum associated with
diamagnetic drift, not the total source from all mechanisms.
NAMES.long:
Area-normalized vector source term due to diamagnetic drift is the part of a
transport momentum-balance source vector produced by diamagnetic drift in a
magnetized plasma. The diamagnetic-drift contribution is the
pressure-gradient-driven part of the directional transfer of linear
momentum, separated from other transport mechanisms.

When represented from a local source density over a balance region, the
area-normalized source is defined by

$$
\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{dia}} = \frac{1}{A}\int_V \mathbf{s}_{\mathrm{dia}}\,dV
$$

where $\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the area-normalized vector source term
due to diamagnetic drift, $\mathbf{s}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the local vector
source density due to diamagnetic drift, $V$ is the balance region, $dV$ is
the volume element, $A$ is the surface area used for the normalization, and
the subscript $\mathrm{dia}$ denotes the diamagnetic-drift contribution.

The scope is restricted to the diamagnetic-drift part of the source, meaning
the contribution associated with pressure gradients in the charged plasma
population and balance region specified by the more specific quantity. At
this parent level no species, charge state, momentum projection, or vector
component is selected; the aggregation convention is integration over the
balance region followed by normalization by the associated surface area.

This quantity does not denote the total source from all mechanisms, a volume
average, or a scalar particle, heat, or energy source. It also excludes
source terms from other drift, collisional, neutral, wave, or externally
applied mechanisms except insofar as they are part of the diamagnetic-drift
contribution itself.

The [momentum source due to diamagnetic
drift](name:momentum_source_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) is the momentum-source
specialization of this parent: it keeps the same diamagnetic-drift mechanism
and area normalization while specifying the balanced transferred quantity as
projected linear momentum.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when a component of $\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{dia}}$
transfers linear momentum in the positive direction of the basis vector onto
which that component is projected.

NAMES.name: momentum_source_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short:
Diamagnetic-drift contribution to an area-normalized momentum-balance
source, representing pressure-gradient-driven transport of a specified
projected linear momentum.
NAMES.long:
Diamagnetic-drift contribution to an area-normalized momentum-balance source
is the part of the source for a specified projected linear momentum caused
by pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic transport in a magnetized plasma. It
represents the net effect of the diamagnetic projected-momentum stress on
the momentum balance after normalization by the area through which the
balance is written.

An area-normalized source is defined from the corresponding volumetric
projected-momentum source density over a balance volume:

$$
S_{\mathrm{mom,dia}} = \frac{1}{A}\int_V q_{\mathrm{mom,dia}}\,dV,\qquad q_{\mathrm{mom,dia}}=-\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\Pi}_{\mathrm{dia}}
$$

where $S_{\mathrm{mom,dia}}$ is the area-normalized diamagnetic-drift
momentum source, $A$ is the normalizing area, $V$ is the balance volume,
$q_{\mathrm{mom,dia}}$ is the volumetric projected-momentum source density
with dimensions of force per volume, and $\boldsymbol{\Pi}_{\mathrm{dia}}$
is the diamagnetic projected-momentum flux tensor with dimensions of force
per area. The division by $A$ makes this quantity area-normalized rather
than a volumetric force density; the minus sign follows the conservation-law
convention that an outward divergence of momentum flux is a sink.

This quantity is the momentum-specific member of
source_due_to_diamagnetic_drift. It differs from
[momentum_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:momentum_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift),
which is the flux or stress before taking its divergence and area
normalization, and it is not the effective transport coefficient
[diamagnetic_momentum_diffusivity](name:diamagnetic_momentum_diffusivity).
The scalar projection is a projected linear-momentum component; an
angular-momentum moment arm or torque normalization is not implied.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the diamagnetic-drift term increases the
projected linear momentum in the positive direction of the momentum
projection used in the balance.

NAMES.name: ion_momentum_source_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short:
Diamagnetic-drift contribution to the local ion momentum-balance source,
summed over ion charge states and resolved for the represented momentum
projection.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the diamagnetic-drift contribution to an area-normalized
local source in the ion linear-momentum balance. It represents
pressure-gradient-driven transport of the represented momentum projection
and combines the contributions from all ion charge states, excluding neutral
momentum.

$$
S_{i,\ell}^{\mathrm{dia}} = \sum_Z S_{i,Z,\ell}^{\mathrm{dia}}
$$

where $S_{i,\ell}^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the aggregate ion momentum source,
$S_{i,Z,\ell}^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is its contribution for ionic charge state
$Z$, and $\ell$ denotes the represented linear-momentum projection. This is
the ion-specific contribution to the generic [momentum source due to
diamagnetic drift](name:momentum_source_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), distinct
from the associated [ion momentum flux due to diamagnetic
drift](name:ion_momentum_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when diamagnetic-drift momentum transfer acts in
the positive direction of the represented momentum projection.

NAMES.name: source_rate_due_to_beam_beam_fusion
NAMES.short:
Source rate due to beam-beam fusion is the volume-integrated production rate
of specified fusion reaction products generated by reactions between
energetic ions from beam populations in the plasma. Multiple elements may
represent different products or reaction channels; it is not a
spatial-vector component quantity.
NAMES.long:
Source rate due to beam-beam fusion is the volume-integrated rate at which
specified fusion reaction products are produced in the plasma by fusion
reactions between energetic ions belonging to beam populations. The quantity
is product- or channel-resolved as applicable; its vector character denotes
a collection of scalar production rates for selected products or reaction
channels, not components of a geometrical vector.

For a specified product or reaction channel $p$, the corresponding beam-beam
source rate is defined by the volume integral of its local production-rate
density:

$$
\Gamma_p^{\mathrm{bb}} = \int_V s_p^{\mathrm{bb}}(\mathbf{r})\,dV
$$

where $\Gamma_p^{\mathrm{bb}}$ is the source rate due to beam-beam fusion
for product or channel $p$, $s_p^{\mathrm{bb}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local
volumetric production-rate density of that product or channel due only to
beam-beam fusion at spatial point $\mathbf{r}$, and $V$ is the plasma volume
over which the source is integrated.

The scope is restricted to fusion reactions in which both reacting ions are
energetic ions from beam populations. It excludes fusion involving thermal
ion populations, beam-thermal fusion, total fusion source rates from all
reactant populations, injected beam particle rates, launched or absorbed
beam power, particle flux through a surface, and loss rates of the reaction
products.

The [neutron source rate due to beam-beam
fusion](name:neutron_source_rate_due_to_beam_beam_fusion) is the
specialization for neutron production. If several reaction channels
contribute to the same specified product and are represented separately, the
product total is the sum of the corresponding channel-resolved elements.

NAMES.name: neutron_source_rate_due_to_beam_beam_fusion
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short:
Neutron source rate due to beam-beam fusion is the volume-integrated rate at
which neutrons are produced by fusion reactions between energetic ions from
beam populations in the plasma. It is generic with respect to the
neutron-producing reaction channel.
NAMES.long:
Neutron source rate due to beam-beam fusion is the plasma-volume-integrated
production rate of neutrons from fusion reactions in which both reacting
ions belong to energetic beam populations. The quantity fixes the fusion
product to neutrons while leaving the neutron-producing reaction channel to
be specified by more specific child names.

It is defined from the local volumetric neutron production rate density by

$$
R_n^{\mathrm{bb}} = \int_{V_p} s_n^{\mathrm{bb}}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $R_n^{\mathrm{bb}}$ is the neutron source rate due to beam-beam
fusion, $s_n^{\mathrm{bb}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local volumetric neutron
production rate density from beam-beam fusion at position $\mathbf{x}$,
$V_p$ is the plasma volume, and $dV$ is an element of that volume.

The scope is restricted to neutron-producing fusion reactions between pairs
of energetic beam ions in the plasma. The aggregation convention is
integration over the plasma volume; this parent does not by itself impose a
sum over different isotope reaction channels.

This quantity excludes neutron production from beam-thermal and
thermal-thermal fusion reactions, and excludes source rates of charged
fusion products or photons. It is a neutron count-rate quantity, not the
fusion power, absorbed power, or particle energy carried by the products.

A channel-specific child such as [deuterium-deuterium neutron source rate
due to beam-beam
fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_neutron_source_rate_due_to_beam_beam_fusion)
fixes the reacting isotope pair while preserving the same neutron-product
and beam-beam-reaction meaning. The broader [source rate due to beam-beam
fusion](name:source_rate_due_to_beam_beam_fusion), when used, allows the
produced fusion species to vary; this name is its neutron-product
specialization.

NAMES.name: deuterium_deuterium_neutron_source_rate_due_to_beam_beam_fusion
NAMES.subject: deuterium_deuterium
NAMES.short:
Volume-integrated neutron production rate from beam-beam fusion between
deuterons originating from fast beam populations in the plasma.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the total neutron production rate associated with the
neutron-producing deuterium–deuterium beam–beam fusion branch. It represents
reactions between deuterons belonging to beam populations, rather than
reactions involving the thermal deuteron population.

The rate is defined as the volume integral of the local beam–beam
neutron-production rate:

$$
S_{DD,bb} = \int_{V_{\rm plasma}} \varepsilon_{DD,bb}(\mathbf{x})\,d^3\mathbf{x}
$$

where $S_{DD,bb}$ is the integrated neutron production rate,
$\varepsilon_{DD,bb}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local neutron-production rate from
beam–beam deuterium–deuterium fusion, $V_{\rm plasma}$ is the plasma volume
included in the aggregation, and $\mathbf{x}$ is the spatial position. The
subscripts $DD$ and $bb$ identify the deuterium–deuterium reaction and
beam–beam fusion branch, respectively.

The scope is restricted to the neutron-producing deuterium–deuterium branch
and to reactions between beam-origin deuterons. It is a single
volume-integrated total over the plasma and excludes thermal
deuterium–deuterium fusion, beam–thermal fusion, other fusion reaction
channels, and the local volumetric emissivity represented by
[deuterium-deuterium emissivity due to
fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_emissivity_due_to_fusion).

This branch-resolved rate contributes to neutron flux, which aggregates
neutron production over the applicable fusion reaction channels. It is
distinct from deuterium-deuterium neutron source rate due to thermal fusion,
whose corresponding contribution arises from the thermonuclear
deuterium–deuterium branch.

NAMES.name: source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion
NAMES.short:
Source rate due to thermal fusion is the volume-integrated production rate
of a specified fusion-reaction product or source term generated by
thermonuclear reactions among thermal bulk ions. More specific names define
the emitted product or channel aggregation; the thermal qualifier excludes
fast-ion fusion contributions.
NAMES.long:
Source rate due to thermal fusion is the volume-integrated production rate
of a specified fusion-reaction product or source term generated by
thermonuclear reactions among thermal, approximately Maxwellian ion
populations in the plasma. It is a parent concept for source rates whose
child names identify the produced particle or source component.

The source rate is defined by integrating the corresponding local
source-rate density over the plasma volume:

$$
S_{\mathrm{tf}} = \int_{V_{\mathrm{p}}} s_{\mathrm{tf}}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $S_{\mathrm{tf}}$ is the source rate due to thermal fusion,
$s_{\mathrm{tf}}$ is the local source-rate density due to thermal fusion for
the same specified product or source term, and $V_{\mathrm{p}}$ is the
plasma volume.

This parent does not by itself specify the reaction-product species,
fusion-reaction channel, or channel aggregation. For example, the [neutron
source rate due to thermal
fusion](name:neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion) specializes this
concept to neutron production. The thermal-fusion qualifier restricts the
contributing reactions to thermal bulk-ion fusion and excludes beam-target,
beam-beam, and other fast-ion fusion contributions.

NAMES.name: neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short:
Global neutron production rate from thermonuclear reactions among Maxwellian
bulk ions, applicable to individual neutron-producing reaction channels or
their aggregate total, excluding fast-ion fusion contributions.
NAMES.long:
The neutron source rate due to thermal fusion is the global rate at which
neutrons are generated by thermonuclear reactions between plasma ion species
whose velocity distributions are Maxwellian. It encompasses both per-channel
rates for a single neutron-producing reaction (DD, DT, or TT) and the
aggregate sum over all channels, and is an instance of the general
[source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion](name:source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion)
restricted to the neutron product.

For each neutron-producing reaction channel $c$ between reactant species $a$
and $b$, the channel source rate is:

$$
S_{n,c}^{\rm th} = \frac{1}{1 + \delta_{ab}} \int n_a \, n_b \, \langle \sigma v \rangle_c \, dV
$$

where $n_a$ and $n_b$ are the number densities of the two reactant species,
$\langle \sigma v \rangle_c$ is the Maxwell-averaged reaction-rate
coefficient for channel $c$, $\delta_{ab} = 1$ when the two reactants are
identical (as in DD and TT channels) and 0 otherwise, and the integral
extends over the confined plasma volume. The aggregate quantity sums
contributions from all neutron-producing channels.

This quantity excludes neutrons from beam-target fusion (see
flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion), beam-beam fusion, fusion-product
reactivation, and radio-frequency-tail ion populations. Per-channel
instances include
deuterium_deuterium_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion and
tritium_tritium_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion; the
channel-summed total is
[total_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion](name:total_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion).

NAMES.name: square_of_ion_charge_state_charge_number
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short:
Concentration-weighted mean of squared ionic charge numbers within one
charge-state bundle of one ion species, distinct from the square of its mean
charge number.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the concentration-weighted second moment of the ionic
charge-number distribution in one charge-state bundle of one ion species. It
averages squared charge numbers within the bundle rather than squaring their
mean.

The bundle's mean squared charge number is defined by

$$
\langle Z^2\rangle_{\mathcal B} = \sum_{Z\in\mathcal B} Z^2 x_Z
$$

where $\mathcal B$ is the specified bundle of charge states, $Z$ is the
ionic charge number, $x_Z$ is the relative number concentration of charge
state $Z$ within the bundle, and $\langle Z^2\rangle_{\mathcal B}$ is the
resulting second moment. The concentrations satisfy $\sum_{Z\in\mathcal
B}x_Z=1$.

Only charge states belonging to the specified bundle contribute; other
bundles and other ion species are excluded. For an unbundled, single charge
state, the result is $Z_{\min}^2$, where $Z_{\min}$ is the bundle's minimum
charge number. Charge-state averaging is distinct from spatial averaging: a
plasma-volume-averaged form additionally averages this moment with
physical-volume weighting over the plasma radius.

This is the second-moment specialization of [ion charge-state charge
number](name:ion_charge_state_charge_number). It exceeds the square of the
[bundle's mean charge number](name:ion_charge_state_average_charge_number)
by the charge-number variance, with equality for a single populated charge
state. The related [species-level mean squared charge
number](name:square_of_ion_charge_number) instead includes all charge states
of the ion species.

NAMES.name: suprathermal_neutral_internal_state_pressure
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short:
Kinetic pressure contributed by suprathermal neutral particles occupying a
specified internal quantum or excitation state, including anisotropic
velocity-space contributions from the nonthermal population.
NAMES.long:
Suprathermal neutral internal-state pressure is the state-resolved
anisotropic kinetic pressure of suprathermal neutral atoms or molecules
occupying a specified internal quantum or excitation state. It is a partial
pressure for the selected internal state and suprathermal population, not a
sum over all internal states and not the thermal neutral contribution.

For state $a$, the pressure tensor of the suprathermal population is the
central second velocity-space moment:

$$
\mathbf{P}^{\mathrm{sup}}_a = m_a \int (\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{sup}}_a) \otimes (\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{sup}}_a) f^{\mathrm{sup}}_a(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $m_a$ is the particle mass, $f^{\mathrm{sup}}_a(\mathbf{v})$ is the
velocity distribution of suprathermal neutrals in state $a$,
$\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{sup}}_a$ is the mean velocity of that selected
population, and $\otimes$ denotes the dyadic product. The central moment
excludes dynamic pressure from directed bulk flow.

Directional or gyrotropic components are projections or averages of this
tensor; for example, [perpendicular suprathermal neutral internal-state
pressure](name:perpendicular_suprathermal_neutral_internal_state_pressure)
is the component transverse to the local magnetic field. [Thermal neutral
internal-state pressure](name:thermal_neutral_internal_state_pressure) is
the corresponding thermal contribution, while [total neutral internal-state
pressure](name:total_neutral_internal_state_pressure) combines thermal and
suprathermal contributions for the same internal state.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_suprathermal_neutral_internal_state_pressure
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short:
Pressure of suprathermal neutrals of one species in one internal state is
their mean normal kinetic stress in the two directions perpendicular to the
local magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
Pressure of suprathermal neutrals in a specified internal quantum or
excitation state is the mean of the two normal kinetic stresses
perpendicular to the local magnetic field. It describes the transverse
stress of that nonthermal population without requiring equality with its
field-parallel stress.

The perpendicular pressure is defined by the transverse projection of the
pressure tensor:

$$
p_{\perp,0,a}^{\mathrm{fast}} = \frac{1}{2}\left[\operatorname{tr}\mathsf{P}_{0,a}^{\mathrm{fast}} - \hat{b}\cdot\mathsf{P}_{0,a}^{\mathrm{fast}}\cdot\hat{b}\right]
$$

where $p_{\perp,0,a}^{\mathrm{fast}}$ is the perpendicular pressure,
$\mathsf{P}_{0,a}^{\mathrm{fast}}$ is the kinetic pressure tensor of the
selected suprathermal neutral population, the subscript $0$ denotes the
selected neutral species, $a$ labels its internal state, and
$\operatorname{tr}$ denotes the tensor trace. The superscript
$\mathrm{fast}$ denotes the suprathermal population. The unit vector
$\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ follows the nonzero local magnetic field
$\mathbf{B}$.

This is a partial pressure for one neutral species and one internal state,
not a sum over species or internal states. It excludes thermal-neutral and
charged-particle contributions. The internal-state label selects the
particles contributing translational kinetic stress; their internal
excitation energy is not itself a pressure contribution.

This quantity is the field-perpendicular component of the [suprathermal
neutral internal-state
pressure](name:suprathermal_neutral_internal_state_pressure), rather than
its isotropic trace pressure. Together with the [parallel fast-neutral
internal-state
pressure](name:parallel_fast_neutral_internal_state_pressure), it specifies
the gyrotropic part of the selected population's pressure tensor.

NAMES.name: temperature_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short:
Energy-equivalent temperature scale at the magnetic axis, representing
either particle thermal energy or radiation brightness.
NAMES.long:
Temperature at the magnetic axis is an energy-equivalent measure of a
thermal state or radiation field evaluated at the magnetic axis. It provides
a shared parent concept for kinetic temperatures and brightness
temperatures, which need not represent the same underlying physical state.

For a temperature parameter expressed as an energy-equivalent quantity, the
defining conversion is:

$$
\Theta = k_{\mathrm B} T
$$

where $\Theta$ is the energy-equivalent temperature, $T$ is the underlying
thermodynamic or brightness-temperature parameter, and $k_{\mathrm B}$ is
Boltzmann's constant. This conversion does not imply that a radiation
brightness temperature equals the local kinetic temperature.

The quantity is evaluated at the magnetic axis, the innermost location of
nested closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces. The parent name specifies no
particle species, charge-state aggregation, radiation band, or
population-weighting convention; it is therefore neither a charge-state sum
nor an all-plasma aggregate by itself.

The [electron temperature at the magnetic
axis](name:electron_temperature_at_magnetic_axis) is the kinetic-temperature
specialization for electrons. The [radiative temperature at the magnetic
axis](name:radiative_temperature_at_magnetic_axis) is the
brightness-temperature specialization for electron-cyclotron radiation and
is not necessarily the local kinetic electron temperature. Unlike [plasma
temperature](name:plasma_temperature), this parent does not require an
effective fluid or magnetohydrodynamic aggregation.

NAMES.name: electron_temperature_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Temperature of electrons at the magnetic axis measures their local mean
random kinetic energy per particle, excluding coherent electron flow.
NAMES.long:
Temperature of electron at magnetic axis

The nonrelativistic defining relation is

$$
T_{e,\mathrm{axis}} = \frac{2}{3}\left\langle E_{e,\mathrm{random}}\right\rangle_{\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $T_{e,\mathrm{axis}}$ is the electron temperature at the magnetic
axis, $E_{e,\mathrm{random}}$ is the electron kinetic energy relative to the
local mean electron flow, and the angle brackets denote a
particle-number-weighted average over the local electron population. The
subscript $\mathrm{axis}$ denotes evaluation at the magnetic axis.

This quantity is a local value, not a volume average or a maximum over the
plasma. It specializes [temperature at the magnetic
axis](name:temperature_at_magnetic_axis) to the electron kinetic
temperature, unlike [radiative temperature at the magnetic
axis](name:radiative_temperature_at_magnetic_axis), which represents
radiation brightness.

It forms the numerator of the [ratio of on-axis to volume-averaged electron
temperature](name:ratio_of_electron_temperature_at_magnetic_axis_to_volume_averaged_electron_temperature).
That ratio expresses central temperature peaking relative to the
electron-temperature volume average inside the last closed magnetic flux
surface.

The closed magnetic-field line about which nested toroidal magnetic flux
surfaces are arranged. Where $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{p}}(R_{\mathrm{axis}},
Z_{\mathrm{axis}}) = 0$, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{p}}$ is poloidal magnetic
field; $R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the O-point inside the
nested closed flux surfaces.

NAMES.name: thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Signed local rate of Coulomb-collisional energy transfer from nonthermal
particles to bulk thermal electrons, including all nonthermal guiding-center
orbit classes.
NAMES.long:
Thermal-electron collisional power density is the signed local rate of
kinetic-energy transfer from nonthermal particles to the bulk thermal
electron population. It includes all guiding-center orbit classes of the
nonthermal population and represents an energy source or sink, not stored
energy density.

The transfer rate is the kinetic-energy moment of the thermal-electron
collision operator:

$$
P_e^{\mathrm{th}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_a \int \frac{1}{2}m_e |\mathbf{v}|^2 C_{ea}[f_e^{\mathrm{th}},f_a](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $P_e^{\mathrm{th}}$ is the thermal-electron collisional power density,
$\mathbf{x}$ is spatial position, $m_e$ is electron mass, $\mathbf{v}$ is
electron velocity, $f_e^{\mathrm{th}}$ is the thermal-electron velocity
distribution, and $f_a$ is the nonthermal velocity distribution of species
$a$. The Coulomb collision operator $C_{ea}$ gives the change in the
thermal-electron distribution caused by collisions with nonthermal species
$a$. The integral covers electron velocity space, and the sum includes all
contributing nonthermal species; multiple nonthermal distributions belonging
to the same species are superposed.

This quantity specializes [electron collisional power
density](name:electron_power_density_due_to_collisions) by selecting bulk
thermal electrons as the target population. It excludes energy gained by
nonthermal electron targets and all noncollisional energy-transfer
mechanisms. No flux-surface averaging or volume integration is implicit; a
flux-surface-averaged member denotes the corresponding average of this local
exchange rate.

The
[co-passing](name:co_passing_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions),
[counter-passing](name:counter_passing_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions),
and [trapped
contributions](name:trapped_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions)
partition the nonthermal donor population, not the thermal-electron target.
These contributions sum to the orbit-unrestricted quantity when evaluated
locally at the same position or subjected to the same spatial average.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer net kinetic
energy to the bulk thermal electron population.

NAMES.name: co_passing_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Volumetric rate of Coulomb-collisional energy transfer from co-passing fast
particles to bulk thermal electrons, averaged over a magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Co-passing thermal-electron collisional power density is the signed rate of
kinetic-energy transfer from co-passing fast particles to bulk thermal
electrons, averaged over a magnetic flux surface. The orbit restriction
applies to the donating fast-particle distribution, not to the receiving
thermal electrons.

It is defined by the thermal-electron kinetic-energy moment of the
corresponding Coulomb collision operator:

$$
P_{\mathrm{e,co}}^{\mathrm{coll}} = \left\langle \sum_a \int \frac{1}{2}m_{\mathrm e}|\mathbf v|^2 C_{\mathrm ea}[f_{\mathrm e}^{\mathrm{th}},f_a^{\mathrm{co}}] \, d^3v \right\rangle_{\psi}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{e,co}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is this collisional power density,
$m_{\mathrm e}$ is the electron mass, $\mathbf v$ is electron velocity, and
$d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element. The index $a$ runs over the
fast species represented by the donating distribution; $f_{\mathrm
e}^{\mathrm{th}}$ is the bulk thermal-electron velocity distribution, and
$f_a^{\mathrm{co}}$ is the fast-species distribution restricted to
co-passing guiding-center orbits. The operator $C_{\mathrm ea}$ gives the
collisional rate of change of the thermal-electron distribution caused by
that fast-species contribution. Angle brackets denote the
volume-shell-weighted flux-surface average, and $\psi$ labels the averaging
surface.

This quantity is an energy source or sink, not stored thermal-electron
energy. It excludes energy transferred to ions or suprathermal electrons and
excludes the counter-passing and trapped parts of the donating distribution.

With the same flux-surface averaging applied to every term, this
contribution, the [counter-passing
contribution](name:counter_passing_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions),
and the [trapped
contribution](name:trapped_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions)
sum to the orbit-unrestricted [thermal-electron collisional power
density](name:thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer net kinetic
energy from co-passing fast particles to bulk thermal electrons.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface-averaged rate of Coulomb-collisional energy transfer per unit
volume from counter-passing nonthermal particles to bulk thermal electrons.
NAMES.long:
Counter-passing thermal-electron collisional power density is the signed
volumetric rate of kinetic-energy transfer from counter-passing nonthermal
particles to bulk thermal electrons, averaged over a magnetic flux surface.
Counter-passing particles follow untrapped guiding-center trajectories whose
transit is opposite to the reference co-passing direction.

The transfer is defined by the thermal-electron kinetic-energy moment of the
Coulomb collision operator:

$$
P_{e,\mathrm{counter}}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\psi) = \left\langle \sum_a \int \frac{1}{2}m_e v^2 C_{ea}[f_e^{\mathrm{th}},f_{a,\mathrm{counter}}] \, d^3v \right\rangle_\psi
$$

where $P_{e,\mathrm{counter}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the flux-surface-averaged
power density transferred to thermal electrons, $\psi$ labels the magnetic
flux surface, $a$ indexes the represented nonthermal donor species, $m_e$ is
the electron mass, $\mathbf{v}$ is electron velocity, and $v=|\mathbf{v}|$
is electron speed. The distribution $f_e^{\mathrm{th}}$ describes bulk
thermal electrons, $f_{a,\mathrm{counter}}$ is the counter-passing part of
the nonthermal distribution of species $a$, and $C_{ea}$ gives the
collisional time derivative of the thermal-electron distribution caused by
that donor population. The integral covers all electron velocities; the
angle brackets denote the physical-volume-weighted average over an
infinitesimal shell between neighboring flux surfaces.

The orbit restriction applies to the nonthermal donors, not to the receiving
thermal electrons. The donor contributions are summed over the represented
nonthermal species. Energy transferred to ions or fast electrons,
contributions from co-passing or trapped donors, and noncollisional heating
are excluded. This quantity describes energy gained by thermal electrons
rather than energy gained by the counter-passing donors; the corresponding
donor energy exchange has the opposite sign.

After applying the same flux-surface average to each contribution, adding
the [co-passing thermal-electron
contribution](name:co_passing_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions)
and the [trapped thermal-electron
contribution](name:trapped_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions)
recovers the flux-surface average of [thermal-electron collisional power
density](name:thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions), which
includes all represented donor orbit classes.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when Coulomb collisions with counter-passing
nonthermal particles transfer net kinetic energy to bulk thermal electrons.
